From this parley between Philip and Nathanael, we may observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That many people are kept from the ways of religion by the unreasonable prejudices they have conceived against religion, upon the account of some foreign circumstances which do not at all touch the merits of the case. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The best way to remove the prejudices they have entertained against religion is to prove themselves, and make trial of it. Let us not answer this matter before we hear it. <div eID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> 2. What passed between Nathanael and our Lord Jesus. He came and <hi type="italic">saw,</hi> not in vain. <div eID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> (1.) Our Lord Jesus bore a very honourable testimony to Nathanael's integrity: <hi type="italic">Jesus saw him</hi> coming, and met him with favourable encouragement; he said of him to those about him, Nathanael himself being within hearing, <hi type="italic">Behold an Israelite indeed.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26691" type="x-p"/> [1.] That he <hi type="italic">commended</hi> him; not to flatter him, or puff him up with a good conceit of himself, but perhaps because he knew him to be a <hi type="italic">modest</hi> man, if not a <hi type="italic">melancholy</hi> man, one that had hard and mean thoughts of himself, was ready to doubt his own sincerity; and Christ by this testimony put the matter out of doubt. Nathanael had, more than any of the candidates, objected against Christ; but Christ hereby showed that he excused it, and was not extreme to mark what he had said amiss, because he knew his heart was upright. He did not retort upon him, <hi type="italic">Can any good thing come out of Cana</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.21.2">ch. xxi. 2</reference>), an obscure town in Galilee? But kindly gives him this character, to encourage us to hope for acceptance with Christ, notwithstanding our weakness, and to teach us to speak honourably of those who without cause have spoken slightly of us, and to give them their due praise. <div eID="gen26691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he commended him for his <hi type="italic">integrity. First, Behold an Israelite indeed.</hi> It is Christ's prerogative to know what men are <hi type="italic">indeed;</hi> we can but <hi type="italic">hope the best.</hi> The whole nation were Israelites in name, but <hi type="italic">all are not Israel that are of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.6">Rom. ix. 6</reference>); here, however, was <hi type="italic">an Israelite indeed.</hi> 1. A sincere follower of the good example of Israel, whose character it was that he was a <hi type="italic">plain man,</hi> in opposition to Esau's character of a <hi type="italic">cunning man.</hi> He was a genuine son of <hi type="italic">honest Jacob,</hi> not only of his <hi type="italic">seed,</hi> but of his <hi type="italic">spirit.</hi> 2. A sincere professor of the faith of Israel; he was true to the religion he professed, and lived up to it: he was really as good as he seemed, and his practice was <hi type="italic">of a piece</hi> with his profession. He is the Jew that is one <hi type="italic">inwardly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>), so is he <hi type="italic">the Christian. Secondly,</hi> He is one in whom is <hi type="italic">no guile</hi>—that is the character of an Israelite indeed, a Christian indeed: <hi type="italic">no guile</hi> towards men; a man without trick or design; a man that one may trust; <hi type="italic">no guile</hi> towards God, that is, sincere in his repentance for sin; sincere in his covenanting with God; in whose spirit is <hi type="italic">no guile,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">Ps. xxxii. 2</reference>. He does not say without <hi type="italic">guilt,</hi> but without <hi type="italic">guile.</hi> Though in many things he is foolish and forgetful, yet in nothing false, nor <hi type="italic">wickedly departing from God:</hi> there is no allowed approved guilt in him; not painted, though he have his spots: "<hi type="italic">Behold</hi> this Israelite <hi type="italic">indeed.</hi>" 1. "Take notice of him, that you may learn his way, and do like him." 2. "Admire him; <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and <hi type="italic">wonder.</hi>" The hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees had so leavened the Jewish church and nation, and their religion was so degenerated into formality or state-policy, that an Israelite indeed was a <hi type="italic">man wondered at,</hi> a miracle of divine grace, like Job, <reference osisRef="John.1.8">ch. i. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> (2.) Nathanael is much surprised at this, upon which Christ gives him a further proof of his omnisciency, and a kind memorial of his former devotion. <div eID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> [1.] Here is Nathanael's modesty, in that he was soon put out of countenance at the kind notice Christ was pleased to take of him: "<hi type="italic">Whence knowest thou me,</hi> me that am unworthy of thy cognizance? <hi type="italic">who am I, O Lord God?</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>. This was an evidence of his sincerity, that he did not catch at the praise he met with, but declined it. Christ knows us better than we know ourselves; we know not what is in a man's heart by looking in his face, but all things are naked and open before Christ, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>. Doth Christ know us? Let us covet to know him. <div eID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> [2.] Here is Christ's further <hi type="italic">manifestation</hi> of himself to him: <hi type="italic">Before Philip called thee, I saw thee. First,</hi> He gives him to understand that he <hi type="italic">knew him,</hi> and so manifests his divinity. It is God's prerogative infallibly to know all persons and all things; by this Christ proved himself to be God upon many occasions. It was prophesied concerning the Messiah that he should be of <hi type="italic">quick understanding in the fear of the Lord,</hi> that is, in judging the sincerity and degree of the fear of God in others, and that he should not <hi type="italic">judge after the sight of his eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2-Isa.11.3">Isa. xi. 2, 3</reference>. Here he answers that prediction. See <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That before Philip called him he saw him under the fig-tree; this manifests a particular kindness for him. 1. His eye was towards him before Philip called him, which was the first time that ever Nathanael was acquainted with Christ. Christ has knowledge of us before we have any knowledge of him; see <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. 2. His eye was upon him when he as <hi type="italic">under the fig-tree;</hi> this was a private token which nobody understood but Nathanael: "When thou wast retired <hi type="italic">under the fig-tree</hi> in thy garden, and thoughtest that no eye saw thee, I have then my eye upon thee, and saw that which was very acceptable." It is most probable that Nathanael under the fig-tree was employed, as Isaac in the field, in meditation, and prayer, and communion with God. Perhaps then and there it was that he solemnly joined himself to the Lord in an inviolable covenant. Christ saw in secret, and by this public notice of it did in part reward him openly. <hi type="italic">Sitting under the</hi> fig-tree denotes quietness and composedness of spirit, which much befriend communion with God. See <reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">Mic. iv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.10">Zech. iii. 10</reference>. Nathanael here in was an Israelite indeed, that, like Israel, he <hi type="italic">wrestled with God alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen. xxxii. 24</reference>), prayed not like the hypocrites, in the corners of the streets, but under the fig-tree. <div eID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> (3.) Nathanael hereby obtained a full assurance of faith in Jesus Christ, expressed in that noble acknowledgment (<reference osisRef="John.1.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the king of Israel;</hi> that is, in short, thou art the true Messiah. Observe here, [1.] How <hi type="italic">firmly</hi> he believed <hi type="italic">with the heart.</hi> Though he had lately laboured under some prejudices concerning Christ, they had now all vanished. Note, The grace of God, in working faith, casts down imaginations. Now he asks no more, <hi type="italic">Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?</hi> For he believes Jesus of Nazareth to be the chief good, and embraces him accordingly. [2.] How <hi type="italic">freely</hi> he confessed <hi type="italic">with the mouth.</hi> His confession is made in form of an adoration, directed to our Lord Jesus himself, which is a proper way of confessing our faith. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He confesses Christ's prophetical office, in calling him <hi type="italic">Rabbi,</hi> a title which the Jews commonly gave to their teachers. Christ is the great rabbi, at whose feet we must all be <hi type="italic">brought up. Secondly,</hi> He confesses his divine nature and mission, in calling him the Son of God (that Son of God spoken of <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>); though he had but a human <hi type="italic">form</hi> and <hi type="italic">aspect,</hi> yet having a divine knowledge, the knowledge of the heart, and of things distant and secret, Nathanael thence concludes him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God. Thirdly,</hi> He confesses, "<hi type="italic">Thou art the king of Israel;</hi> that king of Israel whom we have been long waiting for." If he be the Son of God, he is king of the Israel of God. Nathanael hereby proves himself an Israelite indeed that he so readily owns and submits to the king of Israel. <div eID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ hereupon raises the hopes and expectations of Nathanael to something further and greater than all this, <reference osisRef="John.1.50-John.1.51">v. 50, 51</reference>. Christ is very tender of young converts, and will encourage good beginnings, though weak, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.20">Matt. xii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> [1.] He here signifies his acceptance, and (it should seem) his admiration, of the ready faith of Nathanael: <hi type="italic">Because I said, I saw thee under the fig-tree, believest thou?</hi> He wonders that such a small indication of Christ's divine knowledge should have such an effect; it was a sign that Nathanael's heart was prepared beforehand, else the work had not been done so suddenly. Note, It is much for the honour of Christ and his grace, when the heart is surrendered to him at the first summons. <div eID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> [2.] He promises him much greater helps for the confirmation and increase of his faith than he had had for the first production of it. <div eID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In general: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt see greater things than these,</hi> stronger proofs of my being the Messiah;" the miracles of Christ, and his resurrection. Note, 1. To him that hath, and maketh good use of what he hath, more shall be given. 2. Those who truly believe the gospel will find its evidences grow upon them, and will see more and more cause to believe it. 3. Whatever discoveries Christ is pleased to make of himself to his people while they are here in this world, he hath still greater things than these to make known to them; a glory yet further <hi type="italic">to be revealed.</hi> <div eID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In particular: "Not thou only, but you, all you my disciples, whose faith this is intended for the confirmation of, you <hi type="italic">shall see heaven opened;</hi>" this is more than telling Nathanael of his being under the fig-tree. This is introduced with a solemn preface, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily I say unto you,</hi> which commands both a <hi type="italic">fixed attention</hi> to what is said as very weighty, and a <hi type="italic">full assent</hi> to it as undoubtedly true: "I say it, whose word you may rely upon, <hi type="italic">amen, amen.</hi>" None used this word at the beginning of a sentence but Christ, though the Jews often used it at the close of a prayer, and sometimes doubled it. It is a solemn asseveration. Christ is called the <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev. iii. 14</reference>), and so some take it here, <hi type="italic">I the Amen, the Amen, say unto you.</hi> I the faithful witness. Note, The assurances we have of the glory to be revealed are built upon the word of Christ. Now see what it is that Christ assures them of: <hi type="italic">Hereafter,</hi> or <hi type="italic">within awhile,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ere long,</hi> or henceforth, ye shall see heaven opened. <div eID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> It is a mean title that Christ here takes to himself: <hi type="italic">The Son of man;</hi> a title frequently applied to him in the gospel, but always by himself. Nathanael had called him the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">king of Israel:</hi> he calls himself <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) To express his <hi type="italic">humility</hi> in the midst of the honours done him. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) To teach his <hi type="italic">humanity,</hi> which is to be believed as well as his divinity. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) To intimate his present state of humiliation, that Nathanael might not expect this king of Israel to appear in external pomp. <div eID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26703" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Yet they are great things which he here foretels: <hi type="italic">You shall see heaven opened,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Some understand it literally, as pointing at some particular event. Either, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] There was some vision of Christ's glory, in which this was exactly fulfilled, which Nathanael was an eye-witness of, as Peter, and James, and John were of his transfiguration. There were many things which Christ did, and those in the presence of his disciples, which were not written (<reference osisRef="John.20.30">ch. xx. 30</reference>), and why not this? Or, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] It was fulfilled in the many ministrations of the angels to our Lord Jesus, especially that at his ascension, when heaven was opened to receive him, and the angels <hi type="italic">ascended</hi> and <hi type="italic">descended,</hi> to attend him and to do him honour, and this in the sight of the disciples. Christ's ascension was the great proof of his mission, and much confirmed the faith of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.6.62">ch. vi. 62</reference>. Or, [<hi type="italic">c.</hi>] It may refer to Christ's second coming, to judge the world, when the heavens shall be <hi type="italic">open,</hi> and every eye shall see him, and the angels of God shall ascend and descend about him, as attendants on him, every one employed; and a busy day it will be. See <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2 Thess. i. 10</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Others take it figuratively, as speaking of a state or series of things to commence <hi type="italic">from henceforth;</hi> and so we may understand it, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Of Christ's <hi type="italic">miracles.</hi> Nathanael believed, because Christ, as the prophets of old, could tell him things secret; but what is this? Christ is now beginning a dispensation of miracles, much more great and strange than this, as if heaven were opened; and such a power shall be exerted by the Son of man as if the angels, which excel in strength, were continually attending his orders. Immediately after this, Christ began to work miracles, <reference osisRef="John.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>. Or, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Of his <hi type="italic">mediation,</hi> and that blessed intercourse which he hath settled between heaven and earth, which his disciples should be degrees be let into the mystery of. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By Christ, as Mediator, they shall see <hi type="italic">heaven opened,</hi> that we may <hi type="italic">enter into the holiest</hi> by his blood (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.20">Heb. x. 19, 20</reference>); heaven opened, that by faith we may <hi type="italic">look in,</hi> and at length may <hi type="italic">go in;</hi> may now behold the glory of the Lord, and hereafter enter into the joy of our Lord. And, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They shall <hi type="italic">see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man.</hi> Through Christ we have communion with and benefit by the holy angels, and things in heaven and things on earth are <hi type="italic">reconciled</hi> and <hi type="italic">gathered together.</hi> Christ is to us as Jacob's ladder (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.12">Gen. xxviii. 12</reference>), by whom angels continually ascend and descend for the good of the saints.  <chapter eID="John.1"/> <div eID="gen26703" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen26706" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26705" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Water Turned into Wine.</title> <div sID="gen26707" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there: <hi type="super">2</hi> And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage. <hi type="super">3</hi> And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine. <hi type="super">4</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come. <hi type="super">5</hi> His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> 6 And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece. <hi type="super">7</hi> Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom, <hi type="super">10</hi> And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: <hi type="italic">but</hi> thou hast kept the good wine until now. <hi type="super">11</hi> This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him. <div eID="gen26707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26708" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of Christ's miraculous conversion of water into wine at a marriage in Cana of Galilee. There were some few so well disposed as to believe in Christ, and to follow him, when he <hi type="italic">did no miracle;</hi> yet it was not likely that many should be wrought upon till he had something wherewith to answer those that asked, <hi type="italic">What sign showest thou?</hi> He could have wrought miracles before, could have made them the common actions of his life and the common entertainments of his friends; but, miracles being designed for the sacred and solemn seals of his doctrine, he began not to work any till he began to preach his doctrine. Now observe, <div eID="gen26708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26709" type="x-p"/> I. The occasion of this miracle. Maimonides observes it to be to the honour of Moses that all the signs he did in the wilderness he did <hi type="italic">upon necessity;</hi> we needed food, he brought us manna, and so did Christ. Observe, <div eID="gen26709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26710" type="x-p"/> 1. The time: the <hi type="italic">third day</hi> after he came into Galilee. The evangelist keeps a journal of occurrences, for no day passed without something extraordinary done or said. Our Master filled up his time better than his servants do, and never lay down at night complaining, as the Roman emperor did, that he had <hi type="italic">lost a day.</hi> <div eID="gen26710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26711" type="x-p"/> 2. The place: it was at Cana in Galilee, in the tribe of Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.28">Josh. xix. 28</reference>), of which, before, it was said that <hi type="italic">he shall yield royal dainties,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.20">Gen. xlix. 20.</reference> Christ began to work miracles in an obscure corner of the country, remote from Jerusalem, which was the public scene of action, to show that he <hi type="italic">sought not honour from men</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.41">ch. v. 41</reference>), but would put honour <hi type="italic">upon the lowly.</hi> His doctrine and miracles would not be so much opposed by the plain and honest Galileans as they would be by the proud and prejudiced rabbies, politicians, and grandees, at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen26711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26712" type="x-p"/> 3. The occasion itself was a <hi type="italic">marriage;</hi> probably one or both of the parties were akin to our Lord Jesus. The <hi type="italic">mother of Jesus</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">there,</hi> and not to be <hi type="italic">called,</hi> as Jesus and his disciples were, which intimates that she was there as one at home. Observe the honour which Christ hereby put upon the ordinance of marriage, that he graced the solemnity of it, not only with his presence, but with his first miracle; because it was instituted and blessed in innocency, because by it he would still <hi type="italic">seek a godly seed,</hi> because it resembles the mystical union between him and his church, and because he foresaw that in the papal kingdom, while the marriage ceremony would be unduly <hi type="italic">dignified</hi> and advanced into a <hi type="italic">sacrament,</hi> the <hi type="italic">married state</hi> would be unduly <hi type="italic">vilified,</hi> as inconsistent with any sacred function. There was a <hi type="italic">marriage</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">gamos</hi></hi>, a <hi type="italic">marriage-feast,</hi> to grace the solemnity. Marriages were usually celebrated with festivals (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.22">Gen. xxix. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.14.10">Judg. xiv. 10</reference>), in token of joy and friendly respect, and for the confirming of love. <div eID="gen26712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26713" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ and his mother and disciples were principal guests at this entertainment. <hi type="italic">The mother of Jesus</hi> (that was her most honourable title) <hi type="italic">was there;</hi> no mention being made of Joseph, we conclude him dead before this. Jesus was <hi type="italic">called,</hi> and he came, accepted the invitation, and feasted with them, to teach us to be <hi type="italic">respectful</hi> to our relations, and <hi type="italic">sociable</hi> with them, though they be mean. Christ was to come in a way different from that of John Baptist, who came <hi type="italic">neither eating nor drinking,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.18-Matt.11.19">Matt. xi. 18, 19</reference>. It is the wisdom of the prudent to study how to <hi type="italic">improve</hi> conversation rather than how to <hi type="italic">decline</hi> it. <div eID="gen26713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26714" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">There was a marriage, and Jesus was called.</hi> Note, [1.] It is very desirable, when there is a <hi type="italic">marriage,</hi> to have Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">present</hi> at it; to have his spiritual gracious presence, to have the marriage owned and blessed by him: the <hi type="italic">marriage</hi> is then <hi type="italic">honourable</hi> indeed; and they that <hi type="italic">marry in</hi> the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.39">1 Cor. vii. 39</reference>) do not marry <hi type="italic">without him.</hi> [2.] They that would have Christ with them at their marriage must invite him by prayer; that is the messenger that must be sent to heaven for him; and he will come: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt call, and I will answer.</hi> And he will turn the water into wine. <div eID="gen26714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26715" type="x-p"/> (2.) The disciples also were invited, those five whom he had called ( <reference osisRef="John.1.35-John.1.51">ch. 1</reference>), for as yet he had no more; they were his family, and were invited with him. They had thrown themselves upon his care, and they soon found that, though he had no wealth, he had good friends. Note, [1.] Those that <hi type="italic">follow</hi> Christ shall <hi type="italic">feast</hi> with him, they shall <hi type="italic">fare</hi> as he <hi type="italic">fares,</hi> so he has <hi type="italic">bespoken</hi> for them (<reference osisRef="John.12.26">ch. xii. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where I am, there shall my servant be also.</hi> [2.] Love to Christ is testified by a love to those that are his, for his sake; <hi type="italic">our goodness extendeth not to him,</hi> but <hi type="italic">to the saints.</hi> Calvin observes how <hi type="italic">generous</hi> the maker of the feast was, though he seems to have been but of small substance, to invite four or five strangers more than he thought of, because they were followers of Christ, which shows, saith he, that there is more of freedom, and liberality, and true friendship, in the conversation of some meaner persons than among many of higher rank. <div eID="gen26715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26716" type="x-p"/> II. The miracle itself. In which observe, <div eID="gen26716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26717" type="x-p"/> 1. They <hi type="italic">wanted wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) There was <hi type="italic">want</hi> at a <hi type="italic">feast;</hi> though much was provided, yet all was spent. While we are in this world we sometimes find ourselves <hi type="italic">in straits,</hi> even then when we think ourselves in the <hi type="italic">fulness of our sufficiency.</hi> If always <hi type="italic">spending,</hi> perhaps all is spent ere we are aware. (2.) There was want at a <hi type="italic">marriage feast.</hi> Note, They who, being <hi type="italic">married,</hi> are come to <hi type="italic">care for the things of the world</hi> must expect <hi type="italic">trouble in the flesh,</hi> and count upon disappointment. (3.) It should seem, Christ and his disciples were the occasion of this want, because there was more company than was expected when the provision was made; but they who straiten themselves for Christ shall not lose by him. <div eID="gen26717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26718" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">mother of Jesus</hi> solicited him to assist her friends in this strait. We are told (<reference osisRef="John.2.3-John.2.5">v. 3-5</reference>) what passed between Christ and his mother upon this occasion. <div eID="gen26718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26719" type="x-p"/> (1.) She acquaints him with the difficulty they were in (<reference osisRef="John.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">She saith unto him, They have no wine.</hi> Some think that she did not expect from him any miraculous supply (he having as yet wrought no miracle), but that she would have him make some <hi type="italic">decent</hi> excuse to the company, and make the best of it, to save the bridegroom's reputation, and keep him in countenance; or (as Calvin suggests) would have him make up the want of wine with some holy profitable discourse. But, most probably, she looked for a miracle; for she knew he was now appearing as the great prophet, like unto Moses, who so often seasonably supplied the wants of Israel; and, though this was his first public miracle, perhaps he had sometimes relieved her and her husband in their low estate. The bridegroom might have sent out for more wine, but she was for going to the fountain-head. Note, [1.] We ought to be concerned for the wants and straits of our friends, and not <hi type="italic">seek our own things</hi> only. [2.] In our own and our friends' straits it is our wisdom and duty to apply ourselves to Christ by prayer. [3.] In our addresses to Christ, we must not prescribe to him, but humbly spread our case before him, and then <hi type="italic">refer ourselves</hi> to him to do as he pleases. <div eID="gen26719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26720" type="x-p"/> (2.) He gave her a reprimand for it, for he saw more amiss in it than we do, else he had not treated it thus.—Here is, <div eID="gen26720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26721" type="x-p"/> [1.] The rebuke itself: <hi type="italic">Woman, what have I to do with thee?</hi> As many as Christ loves, he rebukes and chastens. He calls her <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> not <hi type="italic">mother.</hi> When we begin to be assuming, we should be reminded what we are, <hi type="italic">men</hi> and <hi type="italic">women,</hi> frail, foolish, and corrupt. The question, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ti emoi kai soi</hi></hi>, might be read, <hi type="italic">What is that to me and thee?</hi> What is it to us if they do want? But it is always as we render it, <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> as <reference osisRef="Judg.11.12">Judges xi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">2 Sam. xvi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.3">Ezra iv. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">Matt. viii. 29</reference>. It therefore bespeaks a resentment, yet not at all inconsistent with the reverence and subjection which he paid to his mother, according to the fifth commandment (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.51">Luke ii. 51</reference>); for there was a time when it was Levi's praise that he <hi type="italic">said to his father, I have not known him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. Now this was intended to be, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A check to his mother for interposing in a matter which was the act of his Godhead, which had no dependence on her, and which she was not the mother of. Though, as man, he was David's Son and hers; yet, as God, he was David's Lord and hers, and he would have her know it. The greatest advancements must not make us forget ourselves and our place, nor the familiarity to which the covenant of grace admits us breed contempt, irreverence, or any kind or degree of presumption. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was an instruction to others of his relations (many of whom were present here) that they must never expect him to have any regard to his kindred according to the flesh, in his working miracles, or that therein he should gratify them, who in this matter were no more to him than other people. In the things of God we must not <hi type="italic">know faces. Thirdly,</hi> It is a standing testimony against that idolatry which he foresaw his church would in after-ages sink into, in giving undue honours to the virgin Mary, a crime which the Roman catholics, as they call themselves, are notoriously guilty of, when they call her the <hi type="italic">queen of heaven,</hi> the <hi type="italic">salvation of the world,</hi> their <hi type="italic">mediatrix,</hi> their <hi type="italic">life</hi> and <hi type="italic">hope;</hi> not only depending upon her merit and intercession, but beseeching her to <hi type="italic">command her Son</hi> to do them good: <hi type="italic">Monstra te esse matrem—Show that thou art his mother. Jussu matris impera salvatori—Lay thy maternal commands on the Saviour.</hi> Does he not here expressly say, when a miracle was to be wrought, even in the days of his humiliation, and his mother did but tacitly hint an intercession, <hi type="italic">Woman, what have I to do with thee?</hi> This was plainly designed either to <hi type="italic">prevent</hi> or <hi type="italic">aggravate</hi> such gross idolatry, such horrid blasphemy. The Son of God is appointed our Advocate with the Father; but the mother of our Lord was never designed to be our advocate with the Son. <div eID="gen26721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26722" type="x-p"/> [2.] The reason of this rebuke: <hi type="italic">Mine hour is not yet come.</hi> For every thing Christ did, and that was done to him, he had <hi type="italic">his hour,</hi> the <hi type="italic">fixed</hi> time and the <hi type="italic">fittest</hi> time, which was punctually observed. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "Mine hour for <hi type="italic">working miracles</hi> is not yet come." Yet afterwards he wrought this, before the hour, because he foresaw it would confirm the faith of his infant disciples (<reference osisRef="John.2.11">v. 11</reference>), which was the end of all his miracles: so that this was an earnest of the many miracles he would work when his <hi type="italic">hour was come. Secondly,</hi> "Mine hour of working miracles <hi type="italic">openly</hi> is <hi type="italic">not yet come;</hi> therefore do not talk of it thus <hi type="italic">publicly." Thirdly,</hi> "It <hi type="italic">not the hour</hi> of my exemption from thy authority <hi type="italic">yet come,</hi> now that I have begun to act as a prophet?" So Gregory Nyssen. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> "Mine hour for working <hi type="italic">this miracle</hi> is not yet come." His mother moved him to help them <hi type="italic">when the wine began to fail</hi> (so it may be read, <reference osisRef="John.2.3">v. 3</reference>), but his hour was not yet come till it was quite spent, and there was a <hi type="italic">total want;</hi> not only to prevent any suspicion of mixing some of the wine that was left with the water, but to teach us that man's extremity is God's opportunity to appear for the help and relief of his people. Then <hi type="italic">his hour is come</hi> when we are reduced to the utmost strait, and know not what to do. This encouraged those that waited for him to believe that though his hour was not <hi type="italic">yet come</hi> it would come. Note, The delays of mercy are not to be construed the denials of prayer. <hi type="italic">At the end it shall speak.</hi> <div eID="gen26722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26723" type="x-p"/> (3.) Notwithstanding this, she encouraged herself with expectations that he would help her friends in this strait, for she bade the servants <hi type="italic">observe his orders,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.5">v. 5</reference>. [1.] She took the reproof very submissively, and did not reply to it. It is best not to deserve reproof from Christ, but next best to be meek and quiet under it, and to count it a kindness, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>. [2.] She kept her hope in Christ's mercy, that he would yet grant her desire. When we come to God in Christ for any mercy, two things discourage us:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> Sense of <hi type="italic">our own follies</hi> and infirmities "Surely such imperfect prayers as ours cannot speed." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Sense of <hi type="italic">our Lord's frowns and rebukes.</hi> Afflictions are continued, deliverances delayed, and God seems angry at our prayers. This was the case of the mother of our Lord here, and yet she encourages herself with hope that he will at length give in an answer of peace, to teach us to wrestle with God by faith and fervency in prayer, even when he seems in his providence to walk contrary to us. We must <hi type="italic">against hope believe in hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.18">Rom. iv. 18</reference>. [3.] She directed the servants to have an eye <hi type="italic">to him</hi> immediately, and not to make their applications to her, as it is probable <hi type="italic">they had done.</hi> She quits all pretensions to an <hi type="italic">influence</hi> upon him, or <hi type="italic">intercession</hi> with him; let their souls <hi type="italic">wait only</hi> on him, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.5">Ps. lxii. 5</reference>. [4.] She directed them punctually to observe his orders, without disputing, or asking questions. Being conscious to herself of a fault in <hi type="italic">prescribing</hi> to him, she cautions the servants to take heed of the same fault, and to attend both his time and his way for supply: "<hi type="italic">Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it,</hi> though you may think it ever so improper. If he saith, Give the guests water, when they call for wine, do it. If he saith, Pour out from the bottoms of the vessels that are spent, do it. He can make a few drops of wine multiply to so many draughts." Note, Those that expect Christ's <hi type="italic">favours</hi> must with an implicit obedience observe his <hi type="italic">orders.</hi> The way of duty is the way to mercy; and Christ's methods must not be objected against. <div eID="gen26723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26724" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ did at length miraculously supply them; for he is often better than his word, but never worse. <div eID="gen26724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26725" type="x-p"/> [1.] The miracle itself was <hi type="italic">turning water into wine;</hi> the substance of water acquiring a new form, and having all the accidents and qualities of wine. Such a <hi type="italic">transformation</hi> is a <hi type="italic">miracle;</hi> but the popish <hi type="italic">transubstantiation,</hi> the substance changed, the accidents remaining the same, is a monster. By this Christ showed himself to be the God of nature, who maketh the earth to bring forth wine, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14-Ps.104.15">Ps. civ. 14, 15</reference>. The extracting of the blood of the grape every year from the moisture of the earth is no less a work of power, though, being according to the common law of nature, it is not such a work of wonder, as this. The beginning of Moses's miracles was turning water into blood (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.9">Exod. iv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.7.20">vii. 20</reference>), the beginning of Christ's miracles was turning water into wine; which intimates the difference between the law of Moses and the gospel of Christ. The curse of the law turns water into blood, common comforts into bitterness and terror; the blessing of the gospel turns water into wine. Christ hereby showed that his errand into the world was to heighten and improve creature-comforts to all believers, and make them comforts indeed. Shiloh is said to <hi type="italic">wash his garments in wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen. xlix. 11</reference>), the water for washing being <hi type="italic">turned into wine.</hi> And the gospel call is, <hi type="italic">Come ye to the waters, and buy wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa. lv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen26725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26726" type="x-p"/> [2.] The circumstances of it magnified it and freed it from all suspicion of cheat or collusion; for, <div eID="gen26726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was done in water-pots (<reference osisRef="John.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">There were set there six water-pots of stone.</hi> Observe, 1. For what use these water-pots were intended: for the legal purifications from ceremonial pollutions enjoined by the law of God, and many more by the tradition of the elders. The <hi type="italic">Jews eat not, except they wash often</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.3">Mark vii. 3</reference>), and they used much water in their washing, for which reason here were six large water-pots provided. It was a saying among them, <hi type="italic">Qui mult&#226; utitur aqu&#226; in lavando, multas consequetur in hoc mundo divitias—He who uses much water in washing will gain much wealth in this world.</hi> 2. To what use Christ put them, quite different from what they were intended for; to be the receptacles of the miraculous wine. Thus Christ came to bring in the grace of the gospel, which is as <hi type="italic">wine,</hi> that cheereth God and man (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.13">Judg. ix. 13</reference>), instead of the shadows of the law, which were as water, <hi type="italic">weak and beggarly elements.</hi> These were <hi type="italic">water-pots,</hi> that had never been used to have wine in them; and of <hi type="italic">stone,</hi> which is not apt to retain the scent of former liquors, if ever they had had wine in them. They contained <hi type="italic">two or three firkins apiece;</hi> two or three <hi type="italic">measures, baths,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ephahs;</hi> the quantity is uncertain, but very considerable. We may be sure that it was not intended to be all drank at this feast, but for a further kindness to the new-married couple, as the multiplied oil was to the poor widow, out of which she might <hi type="italic">pay her debt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">live of the rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.7">2 Kings iv. 7</reference>. Christ gives like himself, gives abundantly, according to his riches in glory. It is the penman's language to say, <hi type="italic">They contained two or three firkins,</hi> for the Holy Spirit could have ascertained just how much; thus (as <reference osisRef="John.6.19">ch. vi. 19</reference>) teaching us to speak cautiously, and not confidently, of those things of which we have not good assurance. <div eID="gen26727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26728" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The water-pots were filled <hi type="italic">up to the brim</hi> by the servants at Christ's word, <reference osisRef="John.2.7">v. 7</reference>. As Moses, the servant of the Lord, when God bade him, went to the rock, to draw water; so these servants, when Christ bade them, went to the water, to fetch wine. Note, Since no difficulties can be opposed to the arm of God's power, no improbabilities are to be objected against the word of his command. <div eID="gen26728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The miracle was wrought suddenly, and in such a manner as greatly magnified it. <div eID="gen26729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26730" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> As soon as they had filled the water-pots, presently he said, <hi type="italic">Draw out now</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.8">v. 8</reference>), and it was done, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Without any ceremony, in the eye of the spectators. One would have thought, as Naaman, he should have come out, and <hi type="italic">stood,</hi> and <hi type="italic">called on the name of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.11">2 Kings v. 11</reference>. No, he sits still in his place, says not a word, but <hi type="italic">wills</hi> the thing, and so works it. Note, Christ does great things and marvellous <hi type="italic">without noise,</hi> works manifest changes in a hidden way. Sometimes Christ, in working miracles, used words and signs, but it was <hi type="italic">for their sakes that stood by,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.42">ch. xi. 42</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Without any hesitation or uncertainty in his own breast. He did not say, <hi type="italic">Draw out now,</hi> and let me <hi type="italic">taste it,</hi> questioning whether the thing were done as he willed it or no; but with the greatest assurance imaginable, though it was his <hi type="italic">first miracle,</hi> he recommends it to the master of the feast <hi type="italic">first.</hi> As he knew what he <hi type="italic">would</hi> do, so he knew what he <hi type="italic">could</hi> do, and made no essay in his work; but all was good, very good, even in the beginning. <div eID="gen26730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Our Lord Jesus directed the servants, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) To <hi type="italic">draw it out;</hi> not to let it alone in the vessel, to be admired, but to <hi type="italic">draw it out,</hi> to be drank. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Christ's works are all <hi type="italic">for use;</hi> he gives no man a talent to be <hi type="italic">buried,</hi> but to be <hi type="italic">traded with.</hi> Has he turned thy water into wine, given thee knowledge and grace? It is to <hi type="italic">profit withal;</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">draw out now.</hi> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Those that would know Christ must make trial of him, must attend upon him in the use of ordinary means, and then may expect extraordinary influence. That which is <hi type="italic">laid up</hi> for all that <hi type="italic">fear God</hi> is <hi type="italic">wrought for those that trust in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Ps. xxxi. 19</reference>), that by the exercise of faith <hi type="italic">draw out</hi> what is <hi type="italic">laid up.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) To present it to <hi type="italic">the governor of the feast.</hi> Some think that this <hi type="italic">governor of the feast</hi> was only the chief guest, that sat at the upper end of the table; but, if so, surely our Lord Jesus should have had that place, for he was, upon all accounts, the principal guest; but it seems another had the uppermost room, probably one that <hi type="italic">loved</hi> it (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.6">Matt. xxiii. 6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">chose</hi> it, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.7">Luke xiv. 7</reference>. And Christ, according to his own rule, <hi type="italic">sat down in the lowest room;</hi> but, though he was not treated as the Master of the feast, he kindly approved himself a friend to the feast, and, if not its founder, yet its best benefactor. Others think that this <hi type="italic">governor</hi> was the inspector and monitor of the feast: the same with Plutarch's <hi type="italic">symposiarcha,</hi> whose office it was to see that each had enough, and none did exceed, and that there were no indecencies or disorders. Note, Feasts have need of governors, because too many, when they are at feasts, have not the government of themselves. Some think that this <hi type="italic">governor</hi> was the <hi type="italic">chaplain,</hi> some priest or Levite that craved a blessing and gave thanks, and Christ would have the cup brought to him, that he might bless it, and bless God for it; for the extraordinary tokens of Christ's presence and power were not to supersede, or jostle out, the ordinary rules and methods of piety and devotion. <div eID="gen26731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26732" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The wine which was thus miraculously provided was of the best and richest kind, which was acknowledged by the governor of the feast; and that it was really so, and not his fancy, is certain, because he knew not whence it was, <reference osisRef="John.2.9-John.2.10">v. 9, 10.</reference> 1. It was certain that this was <hi type="italic">wine.</hi> The governor knew this when he drank it, though he knew not <hi type="italic">whence it was;</hi> the servants knew whence it was, but had not yet tasted it. If the taster had seen the drawing of it, or the drawers had had the tasting of it, something might have been imputed to fancy; but now no room is left for suspicion. 2. That it was the best wine. Note, Christ's works commend themselves even to those that know not their author. The products of miracles were always the best in their kind. This wine had a <hi type="italic">stronger body,</hi> and <hi type="italic">better flavour,</hi> than ordinary. This the governor of the feast takes notice of to the bridegroom, with an air of pleasantness, as <hi type="italic">uncommon.</hi> (1.) The common method was otherwise. Good wine is brought out to the best advantage at the beginning of a feast, when the guests have their heads clear and their appetites fresh, and can relish it, and will commend it; but <hi type="italic">when they have well drank,</hi> when their heads are confused, and their appetites palled, good wine is but thrown away upon them, worse will serve then. See the vanity of all the pleasures of sense; they soon surfeit, but never satisfy; the longer they are enjoyed, the less pleasant they grow. (2.) This bridegroom obliged his friends with a reserve of the best wine for the grace-cup: <hi type="italic">Thou hast kept the good wine until now;</hi> not knowing to whom they were indebted for this good wine, he returns the thanks of the table to the bridegroom. <hi type="italic">She did not know that I gave her corn and wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Hos. ii. 8</reference>. Now, [1.] Christ, in providing thus plentifully for the guests, though he hereby allows a sober cheerful use of wine, especially in times of rejoicing (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>), yet he does not invalidate his own caution, nor invade it, in the least, which is, that our hearts be not <hi type="italic">at any time,</hi> no not at a marriage feast, <hi type="italic">overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.34">Luke xxi. 34</reference>. When Christ provided so much <hi type="italic">good wine</hi> for them that had <hi type="italic">well drunk,</hi> he intended to try their sobriety, and to teach them <hi type="italic">how to abound,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">how to want.</hi> Temperance <hi type="italic">per force</hi> is a thankless virtue; but if divine providence gives us abundance of the delights of sense, and divine grace enables us to use them moderately, this is self-denial that is praiseworthy. He also intended that some should be left for the confirmation of the truth of the miracle to the faith of others. And we have reason to think that the guests at this table were so well <hi type="italic">taught,</hi> or at least were now so well awed by the presence of Christ, that none of them abused this wine to excess. Theses two considerations, drawn from this story, may be sufficient at any time to fortify us against temptations to intemperance: <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That our meat and drink are the <hi type="italic">gifts of God's bounty</hi> to us, and we owe our liberty to use them, and our comfort in the use of them, to the mediation of Christ; it is therefore ungrateful and impious to abuse them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That, wherever we are, Christ has his eye upon us; we should <hi type="italic">eat bread before God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.12">Exod. xviii. 12</reference>), and then we should not <hi type="italic">feed ourselves without fear.</hi> [2.] He has given us a specimen of the method he takes in dealing with those that deal with him, which is, to reserve the <hi type="italic">best</hi> for the <hi type="italic">last,</hi> and therefore they must <hi type="italic">deal upon trust.</hi> The recompence of their services and sufferings is reserved for the other world; it is a glory <hi type="italic">to be revealed.</hi> The pleasures of sin give their colour in the cup, but <hi type="italic">at the last bite;</hi> but the pleasures of religion will be <hi type="italic">pleasures for evermore.</hi> <div eID="gen26732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26733" type="x-p"/> III. In the conclusion of this story (<reference osisRef="John.2.11">v. 11</reference>) we are told, 1. That this was <hi type="italic">the beginning of miracles</hi> which Jesus did. Many miracles had been wrought <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> him at his birth and baptism, and he himself was the greatest miracle of all; but this was the first that was wrought <hi type="italic">by</hi> him. He could have wrought miracles when he disputed with the doctors, but his hour was not come. He had power, but there was a <hi type="italic">time of the hiding of his power.</hi> 2. That herein he <hi type="italic">manifested his glory;</hi> hereby he proved himself to be the Son of God, and his glory to be that of the only-begotten of the Father. He also discovered the nature and end of his office; the power of a God, and the grace of a Saviour, appearing in all his miracles, and particularly in this, manifested the glory of the long-expected Messiah. 3. That <hi type="italic">his disciples believed on him.</hi> Those whom he had called (<reference osisRef="John.1.35-John.1.51">ch. i.</reference>), who had seen no miracle, and yet followed him, now saw this, shared in it, and had their faith strengthened by it. Note, (1.) Even the faith that is true is at first but weak. The strongest men were once babes, so were the strongest Christians. (2.) The manifesting of the glory of Christ is the great confirmation of the faith of Christians.

<div eID="gen26733" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Temple-Merchandise Punished; Christ's Death and Resurrection Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen26734" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> After this he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the Jews' passover was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem, <hi type="super">14</hi> And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting: <hi type="super">15</hi> And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables; 16 And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house a house of merchandise. <hi type="super">17</hi> And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then answered the Jews and said unto him, What sign showest thou unto us, seeing that thou doest these things? <hi type="super">19</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then said the Jews, Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days? <hi type="super">21</hi> But he spake of the temple of his body. <hi type="super">22</hi> When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said. <div eID="gen26734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26735" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen26735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26736" type="x-p"/> I. The short visit Christ made to Capernaum, <reference osisRef="John.2.12">v. 12</reference>. It was a large and populous city, about a day's journey from Cana; it is called <hi type="italic">his own city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.1">Matt. ix. 1</reference>), because he made it his head-quarters in Galilee, and what little rest he had was there. It was a place of concourse, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> Christ chose it, that the fame of his doctrine and miracles might thence spread the further. Observe, <div eID="gen26736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26737" type="x-p"/> 1. The company that attended him thither: <hi type="italic">his mother, his brethren, and his disciples.</hi> Wherever Christ went, (1.) He <hi type="italic">would not</hi> go alone, but would take those with him who had put themselves under his guidance, that he might instruct them, and that they might attest his miracles. (2.) He <hi type="italic">could not</hi> go alone, but they would follow him, because they liked the sweetness either of his doctrine or of his wine, <reference osisRef="John.6.26">ch. vi. 26</reference>. His mother, though he had lately given her to understand that in the works of his ministry he should pay no more respect to her than to any other person, yet followed him; not to intercede with him, but to learn of him. His <hi type="italic">brethren</hi> also and relations, who were at the marriage and were wrought upon by the miracle there, and <hi type="italic">his disciples,</hi> who attended him wherever he went. It should seem, people were more affected with Christ's miracles at first than they were afterwards, when custom made them seem less strange. <div eID="gen26737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26738" type="x-p"/> 2. His continuance there, which was at this time <hi type="italic">not many days,</hi> designing now only to <hi type="italic">begin</hi> the acquaintance he would afterwards <hi type="italic">improve</hi> there. Christ was still upon the remove, would not confine his usefulness to <hi type="italic">one</hi> place, because <hi type="italic">many</hi> needed him. And he would teach his followers to look upon themselves but as <hi type="italic">sojourners</hi> in this world, and his ministers to follow their opportunities, and go where their work led them. We do not now find Christ in the synagogues, but he privately instructed his friends, and thus entered upon his work <hi type="italic">by degrees.</hi> It is good for young ministers to accustom themselves to pious and edifying discourse in private, that they may with the better preparation, and greater awe, approach their public work. He did not stay long at Capernaum, because the passover was at hand, and he must attend it at Jerusalem; for every thing is beautiful in its season. The less good must give way to the greater, and all the dwellings of Jacob must give place to the gates of Zion. <div eID="gen26738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26739" type="x-p"/> II. The passover he kept at Jerusalem; it is the <hi type="italic">first</hi> after his baptism, and the evangelist takes notice of all the passovers he kept henceforward, which were four in all, the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> that at which he suffered (three years after this), and half a year was now past since his baptism. Christ, being <hi type="italic">made under the law,</hi> observed the passover at Jerusalem; see <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Exod. xxiii. 17</reference>. Thus he taught us by his example a strict observance of divine institutions, and a diligent attendance on religious assemblies. He went up to Jerusalem when <hi type="italic">the passover was at hand,</hi> that he might be there <hi type="italic">with the first.</hi> It is called <hi type="italic">the Jews' passover,</hi> because it was peculiar to them (Christ is <hi type="italic">our</hi> Passover); now shortly God will no longer own it for his. Christ kept the passover at Jerusalem yearly, ever since he was twelve years old, in obedience to the law; but now that he has entered upon his public ministry we may expect something more from him than before; and two things we are here told he did there:— <div eID="gen26739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26740" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">purged the temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.14-John.2.17">v. 14-17</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen26740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26741" type="x-p"/> (1.) The first place we find him in at Jerusalem was the <hi type="italic">temple,</hi> and, it should seem, he did not make any public appearance till he came thither; for his presence and preaching there were that glory of the latter house which was to <hi type="italic">exceed the glory of the former,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag. ii. 9</reference>. It was foretold (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal. iii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will send my messenger,</hi> John Baptist; he never preached in the temple, but <hi type="italic">the Lord, whom ye seek,</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">suddenly come to his temple,</hi> suddenly after the appearing of John Baptist; so that this was the time, and the temple the place, when, and where, the Messiah was to be expected. <div eID="gen26741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26742" type="x-p"/> (2.) The first work we find him at in the temple was the <hi type="italic">purging</hi> of it; for so it was foretold there (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.2-Mal.3.3">Mal. iii. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall sit as a refiner and purify the sons of Levi.</hi> Now was come the <hi type="italic">time of reformation.</hi> Christ came to be the great reformer; and, according to the method of the reforming kings of Judah, he first <hi type="italic">purged out</hi> what was amiss (and that used to be passover-work too, as in Hezekiah's time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.14-2Chr.30.15">2 Chron. xxx. 14, 15</reference>, and Josiah's, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">2 Kings xxiii. 4</reference>, &c.), and then taught them to do well. First <hi type="italic">purge out the old leaven,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">keep the feast.</hi> Christ's design in coming into the world was to reform the world; and he expects that all who come to him should reform their hearts and lives, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen. xxxv. 2</reference>. And this he has taught us by purging the temple. See here, <div eID="gen26742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26743" type="x-p"/> [1.] What were the corruptions that were to be purged out. He found a market in one of the courts of the temple, that which was called the <hi type="italic">court of the Gentiles,</hi> within the <hi type="italic">mountain of that house.</hi> There, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They sold <hi type="italic">oxen, and sheep, and doves,</hi> for sacrifice; we will suppose, not for common use, but for the convenience of those who came out of the country, and could not bring their sacrifices <hi type="italic">in kind</hi> along with them; see <reference osisRef="Deut.14.24-Deut.14.26">Deut. xiv. 24-26</reference>. This <hi type="italic">market</hi> perhaps had been kept by the pool of Bethesda (<reference osisRef="John.5.2">ch. v. 2</reference>), but was admitted into the temple by the chief priests, for filthy lucre; for, no doubt, the rents for standing there, and fees for searching the beasts sold there, and certifying that they were <hi type="italic">without blemish,</hi> would be a considerable revenue to them. Great corruptions in the church owe their rise to the love of money, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1 Tim. vi. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">10.</reference> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They <hi type="italic">changed money,</hi> for the convenience of those that were to pay a half-shekel <hi type="italic">in specie</hi> every year, by way of poll, for the service of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.12">Exod. xxx. 12</reference>), and no doubt they got by it. <div eID="gen26743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26744" type="x-p"/> [2.] What course our Lord took to purge out those corruptions. He had seen these in the temple formerly, when he was in a private station; but never went about to drive them out till now, when he had taken upon him the public character of a prophet. He did not complain to the chief priests, for he knew they countenanced those corruptions. But he himself, <div eID="gen26744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First, Drove out the sheep and oxen,</hi> and those that <hi type="italic">sold them,</hi> out of the temple. He never used <hi type="italic">force</hi> to drive any <hi type="italic">into</hi> the temple, but only to drive those out that profaned it. He did not seize the sheep and oxen for himself, did not <hi type="italic">distrain</hi> and impound them, though he found them <hi type="italic">damage faissant-actual trespassers</hi> upon his Father's ground; he only drove them out, and their owners with them. He made a scourge of <hi type="italic">small cords,</hi> which probably they had led their sheep and oxen with, and thrown them away upon the ground, whence Christ gathered them. Sinners prepare the scourges with which they themselves will be driven out from the temple of the Lord. He did not make a scourge to chastise the offenders (his punishments are of another nature), but only to drive out the cattle; he aimed no further than at reformation. See <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3-Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.8">2 Cor. x. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen26745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26746" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He <hi type="italic">poured out the changers' money,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to kerma</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the small money</hi>—the <hi type="italic">Nummorum Famulus.</hi> In <hi type="italic">pouring out</hi> the money, he showed his contempt of it; he threw it to the ground, to the earth as it <hi type="italic">was.</hi> In <hi type="italic">overthrowing</hi> the tables, he showed his displeasure against those that make religion a matter of worldly gain. Money-changers in the temple are the scandal of it. Note, In reformation, it is good to make thorough work; he <hi type="italic">drove them all out;</hi> and not only threw out the money, but, in overturning the tables, threw out the trade too. <div eID="gen26746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly, He said to them that sold doves</hi> (sacrifices for the poor), <hi type="italic">Take these things hence.</hi> The doves, though they took up less room, and were a less nuisance than the oxen and sheep, yet must not be allowed there. The sparrows and swallows were welcome, that were left to God's providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Ps. lxxxiv. 3</reference>), but not the doves, that were appropriated to man's profit. God's temple must not be made a pigeon-house. But see Christ's prudence in his zeal. When he drove out the sheep and oxen, the owners might follow them; when he poured out the money, they might gather it up again; but, if he had turned the doves flying, perhaps they could not have been retrieved; therefore to them that sold doves he said, <hi type="italic">Take these things hence.</hi> Note, Discretion must always guide and govern our zeal, that we do nothing unbecoming ourselves, or mischievous to others. <div eID="gen26747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He gave them a good reason for what he did: <hi type="italic">Make not my Father's house a house of merchandise.</hi> Reason for conviction should accompany force for correction. <div eID="gen26748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Here is a reason why they should not profane the temple, because it was the <hi type="italic">house of God,</hi> and not to be made a house of merchandise. Merchandise is a good thing in the exchange, but not in the temple. This was, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) to <hi type="italic">alienate</hi> that which was dedicated to the honour of God; it was <hi type="italic">sacrilege;</hi> it was robbing God. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It was to debase that which was solemn and awful, and to make it mean. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) It was to disturb and distract those services in which men ought to be most solemn, serious, and intent. It was particularly an affront to the <hi type="italic">sons of the stranger</hi> in their worship to be forced to herd themselves with the sheep and oxen, and to be distracted in their worship by the noise of a market, for this market was kept in the court of the Gentiles. (<hi type="italic">d.</hi>) It was to make the business of religion subservient to a secular interest; for the holiness of the place must advance the market, and promote the sale of their commodities. Those make God's house a house of merchandise, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Whose minds are filled with cares about worldly business when they are attending on religious exercises, as those, <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amos viii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 31</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Who perform divine offices for filthy lucre, and sell the gifts of the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.18">Acts viii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen26749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26750" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Here is a reason why he was concerned to purge it, because it <hi type="italic">was his Father's house.</hi> And, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Therefore he had authority to purge it, for he was faithful, as a Son <hi type="italic">over his own house.</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5-Heb.3.6">Heb. iii. 5, 6</reference>. In calling God his Father, he intimates that he was the Messiah, of whom it was said, <hi type="italic">He shall build a house for my name, and I will be his Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.13-2Sam.7.14">2 Sam. vii. 13, 14</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Therefore he had a zeal for the purging of it: "It is <hi type="italic">my Father's house,</hi> and therefore I cannot bear to see it profaned, and <hi type="italic">him</hi> dishonoured." Note, If God be our Father in heaven, and it be therefore our desire that his name may be sanctified, it cannot but be our grief to see it polluted. Christ's purging the temple thus may justly be reckoned among his <hi type="italic">wonderful works. Inter omnia signa quæ fecit Dominus, hoc mihi videtur esse mirabilius—Of all Christ's wonderful works this appears to me the most wonderful.</hi>—Hieron. Considering, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] That he did it without the <hi type="italic">assistance</hi> of any of his <hi type="italic">friends;</hi> probably it had been no hard matter to have raised the <hi type="italic">mob,</hi> who had a great veneration for the temple, against these profaners of it; but Christ never countenanced any thing that was tumultuous or disorderly. There was one to <hi type="italic">uphold,</hi> but his own arm did it. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] That he did it without the <hi type="italic">resistance</hi> of any of his <hi type="italic">enemies,</hi> either the market-people themselves, or the chief priests that gave them their licences, and had the <hi type="italic">posse templi—temple force,</hi> at their command. But the corruption was too plain to be justified; sinners' own consciences are reformers' best friends; yet that was not all, there was a divine power put forth herein, a power over the spirits of men; and in this non-resistance of theirs that scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.2-Mal.3.3">Mal. iii. 2, 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who shall stand when he appeareth?</hi> <div eID="gen26750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> Here is the remark which his disciples made upon it (<reference osisRef="John.2.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">They remembered that it was written, The Zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.</hi> They were somewhat surprised at first to see him to whom they were directed as the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God</hi> in such a heat, and him whom they believed to be the <hi type="italic">King of Israel</hi> take so little state upon him as to do this himself; but one scripture came to their thoughts, which taught them to reconcile this action both with the meekness of the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God</hi> and with the majesty of the <hi type="italic">King of Israel;</hi> for David, speaking of the Messiah, takes notice of his <hi type="italic">zeal for God's house,</hi> as so great that it even <hi type="italic">ate him up,</hi> it made him forget himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Ps. lxix. 9</reference>. Observe, 1. The disciples came to understand the meaning of what Christ did, by remembering the scriptures: <hi type="italic">They remembered</hi> now <hi type="italic">that it was written.</hi> Note, The word of God and the works of God do mutually explain and illustrate each other. Dark scriptures are expounded by their accomplishment in providence, and difficult providences are made easy by comparing them with the scriptures. See of what great use it is to the disciples of Christ to be <hi type="italic">ready</hi> and <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> in the scriptures, and to have their memories well stored with scripture truths, by which they will be <hi type="italic">furnished for every good work,</hi> 2. The scripture they remembered was very apposite: <hi type="italic">The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.</hi> David was in this a type of Christ that he was <hi type="italic">zealous for God's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.2-Ps.132.3">Ps. cxxxii. 2, 3</reference>. What he did for it was <hi type="italic">with all his might;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">1 Chron. xxix. 2</reference>. The latter part of that verse (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Ps. lxix. 9</reference>) is applied to Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>), as the former part of it here. All the graces that were to be found among the Old-Testament saints were eminently in Christ, and particularly this of zeal for the house of God, and in them, as they were patterns to us, so they were types of him. Observe, (1.) Jesus Christ was zealously affected to the house of God, his church: he loved it, and was always jealous for its honour and welfare. (2.) This zeal did even <hi type="italic">eat him up;</hi> it made him <hi type="italic">humble</hi> himself, and <hi type="italic">spend</hi> himself, and <hi type="italic">expose</hi> himself. <hi type="italic">My zeal has consumed me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.139">Ps. cxix. 139</reference>. Zeal for the house of God forbids us to consult our own credit, ease, and safety, when they come in competition with our duty and Christ's service, and sometimes carries on our souls in our duty so far and so fast that our bodies cannot keep pace with them, and makes us as deaf as our Master was to those who suggested, <hi type="italic">Spare thyself.</hi> The grievances here redressed might seem but small, and such as should have been connived at; but such was Christ's zeal that he could not bear even <hi type="italic">those</hi> that <hi type="italic">sold and bought in the temple. Si ibi ebrios inveniret quid faceret Dominus!</hi> (saith St. Austin.) <hi type="italic">If he had found drunkards in the temple, how much more would he have been displeased!</hi> <div eID="gen26751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26752" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ, having thus purged the temple, gave a sign to those who demanded it to prove his authority for so doing. Observe here, <div eID="gen26752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26753" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their demand of a sign: <hi type="italic">Then answered the Jews,</hi> that is the multitude of the people, with their leaders. Being Jews, they should rather have stood by him, and assisted him to vindicate the honour of their temple; but, instead of this, they objected against it. Note, Those who apply themselves in good earnest to the work of reformation must expect to meet with opposition. When they could object nothing against the thing itself, they questioned his authority to do it: "<hi type="italic">What sign showest thou unto us,</hi> to prove thyself authorized and commissioned to do these things?" It was indeed a good work to purge the temple; but what had he to do to undertake it, who was in no office there? They looked upon it as an act of jurisdiction, and that he must prove himself <hi type="italic">a prophet, yea, more than a prophet.</hi> But was not the thing itself sign enough? His ability to drive so many from their posts, without opposition, was a proof of his authority; he that was armed with such a divine power was surely armed with a divine commission. <hi type="italic">What ailed these</hi> buyers and sellers, <hi type="italic">that they fled, that they were driven back?</hi> Surely it was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.5">Ps. cxiv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">7</reference>), no less a presence. <div eID="gen26753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26754" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ's answer to this demand, <reference osisRef="John.2.19">v. 19</reference>. He did not immediately work a miracle to convince them, but gave them a sign in something <hi type="italic">to come,</hi> the truth of which must appear by the event, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.18.21-Deut.18.22">Deut. xviii. 21, 22</reference>. <div eID="gen26754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26755" type="x-p"/> Now, [1.] The sign that he gives them is his own <hi type="italic">death</hi> and <hi type="italic">resurrection.</hi> He refers them to that which would be, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His <hi type="italic">last</hi> sign. If they would not be convinced by what they saw and heard, let them <hi type="italic">wait. Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">great sign</hi> to prove him to be the Messiah; for concerning him it was foretold that he should be bruised (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">Isa. liii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>), and yet that he should not see corruption, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Ps. xvi. 10.</reference> These things were fulfilled in the blessed Jesus, and therefore <hi type="italic">truly he was the Son of God,</hi> and had authority in the temple, his Father's house. <div eID="gen26755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26756" type="x-p"/> [2.] He foretels his death and resurrection, not in plain terms, as he often did to his disciples, but in figurative expressions; as afterwards, when he gave this for a sign, he called it the <hi type="italic">sign of the prophet Jonas,</hi> so here, <hi type="italic">Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.</hi> Thus he spoke in parables to those who were willingly ignorant, that <hi type="italic">they might not perceive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.13-Matt.13.14">Matt. xiii. 13, 14</reference>. Those that will not see shall not see. Nay, this figurative speech used here proved such a <hi type="italic">stumbling-block</hi> to them that it was produced in evidence against him at his trial to prove him a blasphemer. <reference osisRef="Matt.26.60-Matt.26.61">Matt. xxvi. 60, 61</reference>. Had they humbly asked him the meaning of what he said, he would have told them, and it had been a savour of life unto life to them, but they were resolved to cavil, and it proved a savour of death unto death. They that would not be convinced were hardened, and the manner of expressing this prediction occasioned the accomplishment of the prediction itself. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He foretels his death by the Jews' malice, in these words, <hi type="italic">Destroy you this temple;</hi> that is, "You will destroy it, I know you will. I will permit you to destroy it." Note, Christ, even at the beginning of his ministry, had a clear foresight of all his sufferings at the end of it, and yet went on cheerfully in it. It is good, at <hi type="italic">setting out,</hi> to expect the <hi type="italic">worst.
