Secondly,</hi> He foretels his resurrection by his own power: In <hi type="italic">three days I will raise it up.</hi> There were others that <hi type="italic">were raised,</hi> but Christ raised himself, resumed his own life. <div eID="gen26756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26757" type="x-p"/> [3.] He chose to express this by <hi type="italic">destroying</hi> and <hi type="italic">re-edifying</hi> the temple, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because he was now to justify himself in purging the temple, which they had profaned; as if he had said, "You that defile one temple will destroy another; and I will prove my authority to <hi type="italic">purge</hi> what you have <hi type="italic">defiled</hi> by <hi type="italic">raising</hi> what you will <hi type="italic">destroy.</hi>" The profaning of the temple is the <hi type="italic">destroying</hi> of it, and its reformation its <hi type="italic">resurrection. Secondly,</hi> Because the death of Christ was indeed the destruction of the Jewish temple, the procuring cause of it; and his resurrection was the raising up of another temple, the gospel church, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">Zech. vi. 12</reference>. The ruins of their place and <hi type="italic">nation</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.48">ch. xi. 48</reference>) were the riches of the world. See <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Amos ix. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Acts xv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen26757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26758" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their cavil at this answer: "<hi type="italic">Forty and six years was this temple in building,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.20">v. 20.</reference> Temple work was always slow work, and canst thou make such quick work of it?" Now here, [1.] They show <hi type="italic">some knowledge;</hi> they could tell how long the temple was in building. Dr. Lightfoot computes that it was just forty-six years from the founding of Zerubbabel's temple, in the second year of Cyrus, to the complete settlement of the temple service, in the 32nd year of Artaxerxes; and the same from Herod's beginning to build this temple, in the 18th year of his reign, to this very time, when the Jews said that this as just forty-six years: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">okodomethe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">hath this temple been built.</hi> [2.] They show <hi type="italic">more ignorance, First,</hi> Of the <hi type="italic">meaning of Christ's words.</hi> Note, Men often run into gross mistakes by understanding that literally which the scripture speaks figuratively. What abundance of mischief has been done by interpreting, <hi type="italic">This is my body,</hi> after a corporal and carnal manner! <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of <hi type="italic">the almighty power of Christ,</hi> as if he could do no more than another man. Had they known that this was he who <hi type="italic">built all things</hi> in six days they would not have made it such an absurdity that he should build a temple in three days. <div eID="gen26758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26759" type="x-p"/> (4.) A vindication of Christ's answer from their cavil. The difficulty is soon solved by explaining the terms: <hi type="italic">He spoke of the temple of his body,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.21">v. 21</reference>. Though Christ had discovered a great respect for the temple, in <hi type="italic">purging</hi> it, yet he will have us know that the holiness of it, which he was so jealous for, was but <hi type="italic">typical,</hi> and leads us to the consideration of another temple of which that was but a shadow, the substance being Christ, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9">Heb. ix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.17">Col. ii. 17</reference>. Some think that when he said, Destroy <hi type="italic">this</hi> temple, he pointed to his own body, or laid his hand upon it; however, it is certain that he <hi type="italic">spoke of the temple of his body.</hi> Note, The body of Christ is the true temple, of which that at Jerusalem was a type. [1.] Like the temple, it was built by immediate divine direction: "<hi type="italic">A body hast thou prepared me,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.19">1 Chron. xxviii. 19</reference>. [2.] Like the temple, it was a <hi type="italic">holy house;</hi> it is called <hi type="italic">that holy thing.</hi> [3.] It was, like the temple, the habitation of God's glory; there the eternal Word dwelt, the true shechinah. He is <hi type="italic">Emmanuel—God with us.</hi> [4.] The temple was the place and <hi type="italic">medium</hi> of intercourse between God and Israel: there God revealed himself to them; there they presented themselves and their services to him. Thus by Christ God speaks to us, and we speak to him. Worshippers looked <hi type="italic">towards</hi> that house, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.30">1 Kings viii. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.35">35</reference>. So we must worship God with an eye to Christ. <div eID="gen26759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26760" type="x-p"/> (5.) A reflection which the disciples made upon this, long after, inserted here, to illustrate the story (<reference osisRef="John.2.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he was risen from the dead,</hi> some years after, <hi type="italic">his disciples remembered that he had said this.</hi> We found them, <reference osisRef="John.2.17">v. 17</reference>, remembering what had been <hi type="italic">written before of him,</hi> and here we find them remembering what they had <hi type="italic">heard from him.</hi> Note, The memories of Christ's disciples should be like the treasure of the good house-holder, furnished with things both <hi type="italic">new</hi> and <hi type="italic">old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">Matt. xiii. 52</reference>. Now observe, <div eID="gen26760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26761" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">When they remembered</hi> that saying: <hi type="italic">When he was risen from the dead.</hi> It seems, they did not at this time fully understand Christ's meaning, for they were as yet but babes in knowledge; but they laid up the saying in their hearts, and afterwards it became both intelligible and useful. Note, It is good to <hi type="italic">hear for the time to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.23">Isa. xlii. 23</reference>. The juniors in years and profession should treasure up those truths of which at present they do not well understand either the meaning or the use, for they will be serviceable to them hereafter, when they come to greater proficiency. It was said of the scholars of Pythagoras that his precepts seemed to freeze in them till they were forty years old, and then they began to thaw; so this saying of Christ revived in the memories of his disciples <hi type="italic">when he was risen from the dead;</hi> and why the? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because <hi type="italic">then</hi> the Spirit was poured out to bring things to their remembrance which Christ had said to them, and to make them both <hi type="italic">easy</hi> and <hi type="italic">ready</hi> to them, <reference osisRef="John.14.26">ch. xiv. 26</reference>. That very day that Christ rose form the dead he <hi type="italic">opened their understandings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.45">Luke xxiv. 45</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because then this saying of Christ was fulfilled. When the temple of his body had been <hi type="italic">destroyed</hi> and was <hi type="italic">raised again,</hi> and that upon the <hi type="italic">third day,</hi> then they remembered this among other words which Christ had said to this purport. Note, It contributes much to the understanding of the scripture to observe the fulfilling of the scripture. The event will expound the prophecy. <div eID="gen26761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26762" type="x-p"/> [2.] What use they made of it: <hi type="italic">They believed the scripture, and the word that Jesus had said;</hi> their belief of these was confirmed and received fresh support and vigour. They were slow of heart to believe (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.25">Luke xxiv. 25</reference>), but they were <hi type="italic">sure.</hi> The <hi type="italic">scripture</hi> and the <hi type="italic">word of Christ</hi> are here put together, not because they concur and exactly agree together, but because they mutually illustrate and strengthen each other. When the disciples saw both what they had read in the Old Testament, and what they had heard from Christ's own mouth, fulfilled in his death and resurrection, they were the more confirmed in their belief of both.

<div eID="gen26762" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Success of Christ's Ministry.</title> <div sID="gen26763" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast <hi type="italic">day,</hi> many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did. <hi type="super">24</hi> But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man. <div eID="gen26763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26764" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the success, the poor success, of Christ's preaching and miracles at Jerusalem, while he kept the passover there. Observe, <div eID="gen26764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> I. That our Lord Jesus, when he was at Jerusalem at the passover, did preach and work miracles. People's <hi type="italic">believing on him</hi> implied that he preached; and it is expressly said, <hi type="italic">They saw the miracles he did.</hi> He was now in Jerusalem, the holy city, whence the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> was to go <hi type="italic">froth.</hi> His residence was mostly in Galilee, and therefore when he was <hi type="italic">in Jerusalem</hi> he was very busy. The time was holy time, <hi type="italic">the feast-day,</hi> time appointed for the service of God; at the passover the <hi type="italic">Levites taught the good knowledge of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.30.22">2 Chron. xxx. 22</reference>), and Christ took that opportunity of preaching, when the concourse of people was great, and thus he would own and honour the divine institution of the passover. <div eID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26766" type="x-p"/> II. That hereby many were brought to <hi type="italic">believe in his name,</hi> to acknowledge him a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God,</hi> as Nicodemus did (<reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>), a great prophet; and, probably, some of those who <hi type="italic">looked for redemption in Jerusalem</hi> believed him to be the Messiah promised, so ready were they to welcome the first appearance of that <hi type="italic">bright and morning star.</hi> <div eID="gen26766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26767" type="x-p"/> III. That yet <hi type="italic">Jesus did not commit himself unto them</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk episteuen heauton autois</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He did not trust himself with them.</hi> It is the same word that is used for <hi type="italic">believing</hi> in him. So that to believe in Christ is to <hi type="italic">commit ourselves</hi> to him and to his guidance. Christ did not see cause to repose any confidence in these new converts at Jerusalem, where he had many enemies that sought to destroy him, either, 1. Because they were <hi type="italic">false,</hi> at least some of them, and would betray him if they had an opportunity, or were strongly tempted to do so. He had more disciples that he could trust among the Galileans than among the dwellers at Jerusalem. In dangerous times and places, it is wisdom to take heed in whom you confide; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">memneso apistein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">learn to distrust.</hi> Or, 2. Because they were <hi type="italic">weak,</hi> and I would hope that this was the worst of it; not that they were <hi type="italic">treacherous</hi> and designed him a mischief, but, (1.) They were <hi type="italic">timorous,</hi> and wanted zeal and courage, and might perhaps be frightened to do a wrong thing. In times of difficulty and danger, cowards are not fit to be trusted. Or, (2.) They were <hi type="italic">tumultuous,</hi> and wanted discretion and management. These in Jerusalem perhaps had their expectations of the <hi type="italic">temporal</hi> reign of the Messiah more raised than others, and, in that expectation, would be ready to give some bold strokes at the government if Christ would have <hi type="italic">committed himself to them</hi> and put himself at the head of them; but he would not, for his kingdom is not of this world. We should be shy of turbulent unquiet people, as our Master here was, though they profess to <hi type="italic">believe in Christ,</hi> as these did. <div eID="gen26767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26768" type="x-p"/> IV. That the reason why he did not <hi type="italic">commit himself</hi> to them was because he <hi type="italic">knew</hi> them (<reference osisRef="John.2.25">v. 25</reference>), knew the wickedness of some and the weakness of others. The evangelist takes this occasion to assert Christ's omniscience. 1. He <hi type="italic">knew all men,</hi> not only their names and faces, as it is possible for us to know many, but their nature, dispositions, affections, designs, as we do not know <hi type="italic">any man,</hi> scarcely <hi type="italic">ourselves.</hi> He knows <hi type="italic">all men,</hi> for his powerful hand made them all, his piercing eye sees them all, sees into them. He knows his <hi type="italic">subtle enemies,</hi> and all their secret projects; his <hi type="italic">false friends,</hi> and their true characters; what they really are, whatever they pretend to be. He knows them that are truly his, knows their integrity, and knows their infirmity too. He <hi type="italic">knows their frame.</hi> 2. He <hi type="italic">needed not that any should testify of man.</hi> His knowledge was not by information from others, but by his own infallible intuition. It is the infelicity of earthly princes that they must see with other men's eyes, and hear with other men's ears, and take things as they are represented to them; but Christ goes purely upon his own knowledge. Angels are his messengers, but not his spies, for <hi type="italic">his own eyes run to and fro through the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>. This may comfort us in reference to Satan's accusations, that Christ will not take men's characters from him. 3. He <hi type="italic">knew what was in man;</hi> in particular persons, in the nature and race of man. We know what is done <hi type="italic">by men;</hi> Christ knows what is <hi type="italic">in them, tries the heart and the reins.</hi> This is the prerogative of that essential eternal Word, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>. We invade his prerogative if we presume to judge men's hearts. How fit is Christ to be the <hi type="italic">Saviour of men,</hi> very fit to be the physician, who has such a perfect knowledge of the patient's state and case, temper and distemper; knows what is in him! How fit also to be the <hi type="italic">Judge of all!</hi> For the judgment of him who knows <hi type="italic">all men,</hi> all <hi type="italic">in</hi> men, must needs be <hi type="italic">according to truth.</hi> <div eID="gen26768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26769" type="x-p"/> Now this is all the success of Christ's preaching and miracles at Jerusalem, in this journey. The Lord comes to his temple, and none come to him but a parcel of weak simple people, that he can neither have <hi type="italic">credit</hi> from nor put <hi type="italic">confidence</hi> in; yet he shall at length <hi type="italic">see of the travail of his soul.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.2"/> <div eID="gen26769" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen26772" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26771" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Interview with Nicodemus.</title> <div sID="gen26773" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews: <hi type="super">2</hi> The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him. <hi type="super">3</hi> Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. <hi type="super">4</hi> Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born? <hi type="super">5</hi> Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and <hi type="italic">of</hi> the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. 6 That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. <hi type="super">7</hi> Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again. <hi type="super">8</hi> The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit. <hi type="super">9</hi> Nicodemus answered and said unto him, How can these things be? <hi type="super">10</hi> Jesus answered and said unto him, Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things? 11 Verily, verily, I say unto thee, We speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen; and ye receive not our witness. <hi type="super">12</hi> If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you <hi type="italic">of</hi> heavenly things? <hi type="super">13</hi> And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the Son of man which is in heaven. <hi type="super">14</hi> And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: <hi type="super">15</hi> That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. <hi type="super">16</hi> For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. <hi type="super">17</hi> For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved. <hi type="super">18</hi> He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. 19 And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. <hi type="super">20</hi> For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. <hi type="super">21</hi> But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God. <div eID="gen26773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26774" type="x-p"/> We found, in the close of the foregoing chapter, that few were brought to Christ at Jerusalem; yet here was <hi type="italic">one,</hi> a considerable one. It is worth while to go a great way for the salvation though but of <hi type="italic">one soul.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26775" type="x-p"/> I. Who this Nicodemus was. Not many mighty and noble are called; yet some are, and here was one. <hi type="italic">Not many</hi> of the <hi type="italic">rulers, or of the Pharisees;</hi> yet. 1. This was a <hi type="italic">man of the Pharisees,</hi> bred to learning, a scholar. Let it not be said that all Christ's followers are <hi type="italic">unlearned and ignorant men.</hi> The principles of the Pharisees, and the peculiarities of their sect, were directly contrary to the spirit of Christianity; yet there were some in whom even those high thoughts were cast down and brought into obedience to Christ. The grace of Christ is able to subdue the greatest opposition. 2. He was a <hi type="italic">ruler of the Jews,</hi> a member of the great sanhedrim, a senator, a privy-counsellor, a man of authority in Jerusalem. Bad as things were, there were some rulers <hi type="italic">well inclined,</hi> who yet could do little good because the stream was so strong against them; they were over-ruled by the majority, and yoked with those that were corrupt, so that the good which they wished to do they could not do; yet Nicodemus continued in his place, and did what he <hi type="italic">could,</hi> when he could not do what he <hi type="italic">would.</hi> <div eID="gen26775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26776" type="x-p"/> II. His solemn address to our Lord Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="John.3.2">v. 2</reference>. See here, <div eID="gen26776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> 1. When he came: <hi type="italic">He came to Jesus by night.</hi> Observe, (1.) He made a private and particular address to Christ, and did not think it enough to hear his public discourses. He resolved to talk with him by himself, where he might be free with him. Personal converse with skilful faithful ministers about the affairs of our souls would be of great use to us, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>. (2.) He made this address <hi type="italic">by night,</hi> which may be considered, [1.] As an act of <hi type="italic">prudence</hi> and <hi type="italic">discretion.</hi> Christ was engaged all day in <hi type="italic">public</hi> work, and he would not interrupt him then, nor expect his attendance then, but observed <hi type="italic">Christ's hour,</hi> and waited on him when he was <hi type="italic">at leisure.</hi> Note, Private advantages to ourselves and our own families must give way to those that are public. The greater good must be preferred before the less. Christ had many enemies, and therefore Nicodemus came to him <hi type="italic">incognito,</hi> lest being known to the chief priests they should be the more enraged against Christ. [2.] As an act of <hi type="italic">zeal</hi> and <hi type="italic">forwardness.</hi> Nicodemus was a man of business, and could not spare time all day to make Christ a visit, and therefore he would rather take time from the diversions of the <hi type="italic">evening,</hi> or the rest of the <hi type="italic">night,</hi> than not converse with Christ. When others were sleeping, he was getting knowledge, as David by meditation, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.6">Ps. lxiii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.148">and cxix. 148</reference>. Probably it was the very next night after he saw Christ's miracles, and he would not neglect the first opportunity of pursuing his convictions. He knew not how soon Christ might leave the town, nor what might happen betwixt that and another feast, and therefore would lose no time. In the night his converse with Christ would be more free, and less liable to disturbance. These were <hi type="italic">Noctes Christianæ—Christian nights,</hi> much more instructive than the <hi type="italic">Noctes Atticæ—Attic nights.</hi> Or, [3.] As an act of <hi type="italic">fear</hi> and <hi type="italic">cowardice.</hi> He was afraid, or ashamed, to be <hi type="italic">seen</hi> with Christ, and therefore came <hi type="italic">in the night.</hi> When religion is out <hi type="italic">of fashion,</hi> there are many Nicodemites, especially among the rulers, who have a better affection to Christ and his religion than they would be known to have. But observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Though he came by night, Christ bade him welcome, accepted his integrity, and pardoned his infirmity; he considered his <hi type="italic">temper,</hi> which perhaps was <hi type="italic">timorous,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">temptation</hi> he was in from his place and office; and hereby taught his ministers to become all things to all men, and to encourage good beginnings, though weak. <hi type="italic">Paul preached privately to those of reputation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.2.2">Gal. ii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Though now he came <hi type="italic">by night,</hi> yet afterwards, when there was occasion, he owned Christ <hi type="italic">publicly,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.50">ch. vii. 50</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.39">xix. 39</reference>. The grace which is at first but a grain of mustard-seed may grow to be a great tree. <div eID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26778" type="x-p"/> 2. What he said. He did not come to talk with Christ about politics and state-affairs (though he was a ruler), but about the concerns of his own soul and its salvation, and, without circumlocution, comes immediately to the business; he calls Christ <hi type="italic">Rabbi,</hi> which signifies a <hi type="italic">great man;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Isa.19.20">Isa. xix. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall send them a Saviour, and a great one;</hi> a <hi type="italic">Saviour and a rabbi,</hi> so the word is. There are hopes of those who have a respect for Christ, and think and speak honourably of him. He tells Christ how far <hi type="italic">he had attained:</hi> We <hi type="italic">know that thou art a teacher.</hi> Observe, (1.) His <hi type="italic">assertion</hi> concerning Christ: <hi type="italic">Thou art a teacher come from God;</hi> not educated nor ordained by men, as other teachers, but supported with divine inspiration and divine authority. He that was to be the sovereign Ruler came first to be a <hi type="italic">teacher;</hi> for he would rule with reason, not with rigour, by the power of truth, not of the sword. The world lay in ignorance and mistake; the Jewish teachers were corrupt, and caused them to err: <hi type="italic">It is time for the Lord to work.</hi> He came a <hi type="italic">teacher from God,</hi> from God as the <hi type="italic">Father of mercies,</hi> in pity to a dark deceived world; from God as the <hi type="italic">Father of lights</hi> and <hi type="italic">fountain of truth,</hi> all the light and truth upon which we may venture our souls. (2.) His <hi type="italic">assurance</hi> of it: <hi type="italic">We know,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">I,</hi> but <hi type="italic">others;</hi> so he took it for granted, the thing being so plain and self-evident. Perhaps he knew that there were divers of the Pharisees and rulers with whom he conversed that were under the same convictions, but had not the grace to own it. Or, we may suppose that he speaks in the plural number (<hi type="italic">We know</hi>) because he brought with him one or more of his friends and pupils, to receive instructions from Christ, knowing them to be of common concern. "Master," saith he, "we come with a desire to be taught, to be thy scholars, for we are fully satisfied thou art a divine teacher." (3.) The ground of this assurance: <hi type="italic">No man can do those miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.</hi> Here, [1.] We are assured of the truth of Christ's miracles, and that they were not counterfeit. Here was Nicodemus, a judicious, sensible, inquisitive man, one that had all the <hi type="italic">reason</hi> and <hi type="italic">opportunity</hi> imaginable to examine them, so fully satisfied that they were real miracles that he was wrought upon by them to go contrary to his interest, and to the stream of those of his own rank, who were prejudiced against Christ. [2.] We are directed what inference to draw from Christ's miracles: Therefore we are to receive him as a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God.</hi> His miracles were his credentials. The course of nature could not be altered but by the power of the God of nature, who, we are sure, is the God of truth and goodness, and would never set his seal to a lie or a cheat. <div eID="gen26778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26779" type="x-p"/> III. The discourse between Christ and Nicodemus hereupon, or, rather, the sermon Christ preached to him; the contents of it, and that perhaps an abstract of Christ's public preaching; see <reference osisRef="John.3.11-John.3.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Four things our Saviour here discourses of:— <div eID="gen26779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26780" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning the <hi type="italic">necessity and nature of regeneration</hi> or the <hi type="italic">new birth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.3-John.3.8">v. 3-8</reference>. Now we must consider this, <div eID="gen26780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26781" type="x-p"/> (1.) As <hi type="italic">pertinently answered</hi> to Nicodemus's address. Jesus <hi type="italic">answered,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.3">v. 3</reference>. This answer was wither, [1.] A <hi type="italic">rebuke</hi> of what he saw <hi type="italic">defective</hi> in the address of Nicodemus. It was not enough for him to admire Christ's miracles, and acknowledge his mission, but he must be <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> It is plain that he expected the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> the kingdom of the Messiah now shortly to appear. He is betimes aware of the dawning of that day; and, according to the common notion of the Jews, he expects it to appear in external pomp and power. He doubts not but this Jesus, who works these miracles, is either the Messiah or his prophet, and therefore makes his court to him, compliments him, and so hopes to secure a share to himself of the advantages of that kingdom. But Christ tells him that he can have no benefit by that <hi type="italic">change of the state,</hi> unless there be a <hi type="italic">change of the spirit,</hi> of the principles and dispositions, equivalent to a new birth. Nicodemus came <hi type="italic">by night:</hi> "But this will not do," saith Christ. His religion must be owned before men; so Dr. Hammond. Or, [2.] A <hi type="italic">reply</hi> to what he saw <hi type="italic">designed</hi> in his address. When Nicodemus owned Christ a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God,</hi> one entrusted with an extraordinary revelation from heaven, he plainly intimated a desire to know what this revelation was and a readiness to receive it; and Christ declares it. <div eID="gen26781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26782" type="x-p"/> (2.) As <hi type="italic">positively</hi> and <hi type="italic">vehemently</hi> asserted by our Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto thee. I the Amen, the Amen, say it;</hi> so it may be read: "I the faithful and true witness." The matter is settled irreversibly that <hi type="italic">except a man be born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.</hi> "I say it to <hi type="italic">thee,</hi> though a Pharisee, though a master in Israel." Observe, <div eID="gen26782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26783" type="x-p"/> [1.] What it is that is required: to be <hi type="italic">born again;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We must <hi type="italic">live a new life.</hi> Birth is the beginning of life; to be <hi type="italic">born again</hi> is to begin anew, as those that have hitherto lived either much amiss or to little purpose. We must not think to patch up the old building, but begin from the foundation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We must <hi type="italic">have a new nature,</hi> new principles, new affections, new aims. We must be born <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anothen</hi></hi>, which signifies both <hi type="italic">denuo—again,</hi> and <hi type="italic">desuper—from above.</hi> 1. We must be born <hi type="italic">anew;</hi> so the word is taken, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>, and <hi type="italic">ab initio—from the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Luke i. 3</reference>. By our <hi type="italic">first birth</hi> we are corrupt, shapen in sin and iniquity; we must therefore undergo a second birth; our souls must be <hi type="italic">fashioned</hi> and <hi type="italic">enlivened</hi> anew. 2. We must be born <hi type="italic">from above,</hi> so the word is used by the evangelist, <reference osisRef="John.3.31">ch. iii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.11">xix. 11</reference>, and I take this to be especially intended here, not excluding the other; for to be born <hi type="italic">from above</hi> supposes being <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> But this new birth has its rise <hi type="italic">from</hi> heaven (<reference osisRef="John.1.13">ch. i. 13</reference>) and its tendency <hi type="italic">to</hi> heaven: it is to be born to a <hi type="italic">divine</hi> and <hi type="italic">heavenly</hi> life, a life of communion with God and the upper world, and, in order to this, it is to partake of a <hi type="italic">divine nature</hi> and bear the <hi type="italic">image of the heavenly.</hi> <div eID="gen26783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26784" type="x-p"/> [2.] The indispensable necessity of this: "Except <hi type="italic">a man</hi> (Any one that partakes of the human nature, and consequently of its corruptions) <hi type="italic">be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God,</hi> the kingdom of the Messiah begun in <hi type="italic">grace</hi> and perfected in <hi type="italic">glory.</hi>" Except we be <hi type="italic">born from above,</hi> we cannot <hi type="italic">see</hi> this. That is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We cannot <hi type="italic">understand</hi> the <hi type="italic">nature</hi> of it. Such is the nature of things pertaining to the kingdom of God (in which Nicodemus desired to be instructed) that the soul must be re-modelled and moulded, the natural man must become a spiritual man, before he is capable of receiving and understanding them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We cannot <hi type="italic">receive the comfort</hi> of it, cannot expect any benefit by Christ and his gospel, nor have any part or lot in the matter. Note, Regeneration is absolutely necessary to our happiness here and hereafter. Considering what we are by nature, how corrupt and sinful,—what <hi type="italic">God</hi> is, in whom alone we can be happy,—and <hi type="italic">what heaven</hi> is, to which the perfection of our happiness is reserved,—it will appear, in the nature of the thing, that we must be <hi type="italic">born again,</hi> because it is impossible that we should be <hi type="italic">happy</hi> if we be not <hi type="italic">holy;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11-1Cor.6.12">1 Cor. vi. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen26784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26785" type="x-p"/> This great truth of the necessity of regeneration being thus solemnly laid down, <div eID="gen26785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> It is objected against by Nicodemus (<reference osisRef="John.3.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">How can a man be born when he is old,</hi> old as I am: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">geron on</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">being an old man? Can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?</hi> Herein appears, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) His weakness in knowledge; what Christ spoke spiritually he seems to have understood after a corporal and carnal manner, as if there were no other way of regenerating and new-moulding an immortal soul than by new-framing the body, and bringing that back to the <hi type="italic">rock out of which it was hewn,</hi> as if there was such a connection between the soul and the body that there could be no fashioning the <hi type="italic">heart anew</hi> but by forming the <hi type="italic">bones anew.</hi> Nicodemus, as others of the Jews, valued himself, no doubt, very much on his <hi type="italic">first birth</hi> and its dignities and privileges,—the <hi type="italic">place</hi> of it, the Holy Land, perhaps the holy city,—his <hi type="italic">parentage,</hi> such as that which Paul could have gloried in, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Phil. iii. 5</reference>. And therefore it is a great surprise to him to hear of being <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> Could he be better bred and born than bred and born an Israelite, or by any other birth stand fairer for a place in the kingdom of the Messiah? Indeed they looked upon a proselyted Gentile to be as one <hi type="italic">born again</hi> or <hi type="italic">born anew,</hi> but could not imagine how a Jew, a Pharisee, could ever <hi type="italic">better himself</hi> by being <hi type="italic">born again;</hi> he therefore thinks, if he must be <hi type="italic">born again,</hi> it must be of <hi type="italic">her</hi> that <hi type="italic">bore him first.</hi> They that are proud of their <hi type="italic">first birth</hi> are hardly brought to a <hi type="italic">new birth.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) His willingness to be taught. He does not turn his back upon Christ because of his hard saying, but ingenuously acknowledges his ignorance, which implies a desire to be better informed; and so I take this, rather than that he had such gross notions of the new birth Christ spoke of: "Lord, make me to understand this, for it is a riddle to me; I am such a fool as to know no other way for a man to be born than of his mother." When we meet with that in the things of God which is <hi type="italic">dark,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hard to be understood,</hi> we must with humility and industry continue our attendance upon the means of knowledge, till God <hi type="italic">shall reveal even that unto us.</hi> <div eID="gen26786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26787" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> It is opened and further explained by our Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="John.3.5-John.3.8">v. 5-8</reference>. From the objection he takes occasion, <div eID="gen26787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26788" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) To repeat and confirm what he had said (<reference osisRef="John.3.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto thee,</hi> the very same that I said before." Note, The word of God is not yea and nay, but yea and amen; what he hath said he will abide by, whoever saith against it; nor will he retract any of his sayings for the ignorance and mistakes of men. Though Nicodemus understood not the mystery of regeneration, yet Christ asserts the necessity of it as positively as before. Note, It is folly to think of evading the obligation of evangelical precepts, by pleading that they are unintelligible, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.3-Rom.3.4">Rom. iii. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen26788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26789" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) To expound and clear what he had said concerning regeneration; for the explication of which he further shows, <div eID="gen26789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26790" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The <hi type="italic">author</hi> of this blessed change, and who it is that works it. To be born again is to be <hi type="italic">born of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.5-John.3.8">v. 5-8</reference>. The change is not wrought by any wisdom or power of our own, but by the power and influence of the blessed Spirit of grace. It is the <hi type="italic">sanctification of the Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1 Pet. i. 2</reference>) and <hi type="italic">renewing of the Holy Ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit. iii. 5</reference>. The word he works by is his inspiration, and the heart to be wrought on he has access to. <div eID="gen26790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26791" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The <hi type="italic">nature</hi> of this change, and what that is which is wrought; it is <hi type="italic">spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Those that are regenerated are made <hi type="italic">spiritual,</hi> and refined from the dross and dregs of sensuality. The dictates and interests of the rational and immortal soul have retrieved the dominion they ought to have over the flesh. The Pharisees placed their religion in external purity and external performances; and it would be a mighty change indeed with them, no less than a new birth, to become <hi type="italic">spiritual.</hi> <div eID="gen26791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26792" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">c.</hi>] The <hi type="italic">necessity</hi> of this change. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ here shows that it is necessary in the <hi type="italic">nature of the thing,</hi> for we are not fit to enter into the kingdom of God till we are born again: <hi type="italic">That which is born of the flesh if flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Here is our malady, with the causes of it, which are such that it is plain there is no remedy but we must be <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> 1. We are here told <hi type="italic">what we are:</hi> We are <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">corporeal</hi> but <hi type="italic">corrupt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. The soul is still a spiritual substance, but so wedded to the flesh, so captivated by the will of the flesh, so in love with the delights of the flesh, so employed in making provision for the flesh, that it is mostly called <hi type="italic">flesh;</hi> it is carnal. And what communion can there be between God, who is a <hi type="italic">spirit,</hi> and a soul in this condition? 2. How we <hi type="italic">came to be so;</hi> by being <hi type="italic">born of the flesh.</hi> It is a corruption that is bred <hi type="italic">in the bone</hi> with us, and therefore we cannot have a new nature, but we must be <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> The corrupt nature, which is <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> takes rise from our <hi type="italic">first birth;</hi> and therefore the new nature, which is <hi type="italic">spirit,</hi> must take rise from a second birth. Nicodemus spoke of entering again into his mother's womb, and being born; but, if he could do so, to what purpose? If he were born of his mother a hundred times, that would not mend the matter, for still that <hi type="italic">which is born of the flesh if flesh;</hi> a clean thing cannot be brought out of an unclean. He must seek for another original, must be born of the Spirit, or he cannot become spiritual. The case is, in short, this: though man is made to consist of body and soul, yet his spiritual part had then so much the dominion over his corporeal part that he was denominated a <hi type="italic">living soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen. ii. 7</reference>), but by indulging the appetite of the flesh, in eating forbidden fruit, he prostituted the just dominion of the soul to the tyranny of sensual lust, and became no longer a <hi type="italic">living soul,</hi> but flesh: <hi type="italic">Dust thou art.</hi> The living soul became dead and inactive; thus in <hi type="italic">the day</hi> he sinned he <hi type="italic">surely died,</hi> and so he became <hi type="italic">earthly.</hi> In this degenerate state, he begat a son <hi type="italic">in his own likeness;</hi> he transmitted the human nature, which had been entirely deposited in his hands, thus corrupted and depraved; and in the same plight it is still propagated. Corruption and sin are woven into our nature; we are <hi type="italic">shapen in iniquity,</hi> which makes it necessary that the nature be changed. It is not enough to put on a new coat or a new face, but we must put on the <hi type="italic">new man,</hi> we must be new creatures. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ makes it further necessary, by his own word: <hi type="italic">Marvel not that I said unto thee, You must be born again,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.7">v. 7</reference>. 1. Christ hath said it, and as he himself never did, nor ever will, unsay it, so all the world cannot gainsay it, that we <hi type="italic">must be born</hi> again. He who is the great <hi type="italic">Lawgiver,</hi> whose will is a law,—he who is the great Mediator of the new covenant, and has full power to settle the terms of our reconciliation to God and happiness in him,—he who is the great Physician of souls, knows their case, and what is necessary to their cure,—he hath said, <hi type="italic">You must be born again.</hi> "I said unto <hi type="italic">thee</hi> that which all are concerned in, You must, you all, one as well as another, <hi type="italic">you must be born again:</hi> not only the common people, but the rulers, the <hi type="italic">masters in Israel.</hi>" 2. We are not to <hi type="italic">marvel</hi> at it; for when we consider the holiness of the God with whom we have to do, the great design of our redemption, the depravity of our nature, and the constitution of the happiness set before us, we shall not think it strange that so much stress is laid upon this as the one thing needful, that <hi type="italic">we must be born again.</hi> <div eID="gen26792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26793" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">d.</hi>] This change is illustrated by two comparisons. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The regenerating work of the Spirit is compared to <hi type="italic">water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.5">v. 5</reference>. To be born again is to be <hi type="italic">born of water</hi> and of the Spirit, that is, of the Spirit working like water, as (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Matt. iii. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">with the Holy Ghost and with fire</hi> means with the Holy Ghost <hi type="italic">as</hi> with fire. 1. That which is primarily intended here is to show that the Spirit, in sanctifying a soul, (1.) <hi type="italic">Cleanses</hi> and purifies it as water, takes away its filth, by which it was unfit for the kingdom of God. It is the <hi type="italic">washing of regeneration,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit. iii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">You are washed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">Ezek. xxxvi. 25</reference>. (2.) Cools and refreshes it, as water does the hunted hart and the weary traveller. The Spirit is compared to water, <reference osisRef="John.7.38-John.7.39">ch. vii. 38, 39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa. xliv. 3</reference>. In the first creation, the fruits of heaven were <hi type="italic">born of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.20">Gen. i. 20</reference>), in allusion to which, perhaps, they that are born from above are said to be born of water. 2. It is probable that Christ had an eye to the ordinance of baptism, which John had used and he himself had begun to use, "You must be born again of the Spirit," which regeneration by the Spirit should be signified by washing with water, as the visible sign of that spiritual grace: not that all they, and they only, that are baptized, are saved; but without that new birth which is wrought by the Spirit, and signified by baptism, none shall be looked upon as the <hi type="italic">protected privileged</hi> subjects of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven.</hi> The Jews cannot partake of the benefits of the Messiah's kingdom, they have so long looked for, unless they quit all expectations of being justified by the works of the law, and submit to the <hi type="italic">baptism of repentance,</hi> the great gospel duty, <hi type="italic">for the remission of sins,</hi> the great gospel privilege. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is compared to <hi type="italic">wind: The wind bloweth where it listeth, so is every one that is born of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.8">v. 8</reference>. The same word (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pneuma</hi></hi>) signifies both the wind and the Spirit. The Spirit came upon the apostles in a <hi type="italic">rushing mighty wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Acts ii. 2</reference>), his <hi type="italic">strong</hi> influences on the hearts of sinners are compared to the <hi type="italic">breathing of the wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.9">Ezek. xxxvii. 9</reference>), and his <hi type="italic">sweet</hi> influences on the souls of saints to the north and south wind, <reference osisRef="Song.4.16">Cant. iv. 16</reference>. This comparison is here used to show, 1. That the Spirit, in regeneration, works <hi type="italic">arbitrarily,</hi> and as a free agent. The <hi type="italic">wind bloweth where it listeth</hi> for us, and does not attend our order, nor is subject to our command. God <hi type="italic">directs</hi> it; it <hi type="italic">fulfils his word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.148.8">Ps. cxlviii. 8</reference>. The Spirit dispenses his influences where, and when, on whom, and in what measure and degree, he pleases, <hi type="italic">dividing to every man severally as he will,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1 Cor. xii. 11</reference>. 2. That he works <hi type="italic">powerfully,</hi> and with evident effects: <hi type="italic">Thou hearest the sound thereof;</hi> though its causes are hidden, its effects are manifest. When the soul is brought to mourn for sin, to groan under the burden of corruption, to breathe after Christ, to cry <hi type="italic">Abba—Father,</hi> then we <hi type="italic">hear the sound of the Spirit,</hi> we find he is at work, as <reference osisRef="Acts.9.11">Acts ix. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold he prayeth.</hi> 3. That he works <hi type="italic">mysteriously,</hi> and in secret hidden ways: <hi type="italic">Thou canst not tell whence it comes, nor whither it goes.</hi> How it gathers and how it spends its strength is a riddle to us; so the manner and methods of the Spirit's working are a mystery. <hi type="italic">Which way went the Spirit?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">1 Kings xxii. 24</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Eccl. xi. 5</reference>, and compare it with <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Ps. cxxxix. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen26793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26794" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a discourse concerning the <hi type="italic">certainty and sublimity of gospel truths,</hi> which Christ takes occasion for from the weakness of Nicodemus. Here is, <div eID="gen26794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26795" type="x-p"/> (1.) The objection which Nicodemus still made (<reference osisRef="John.3.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">How can these things be?</hi> Christ's explication of the doctrine of the necessity of regeneration, it should seem, made it never the clearer to him. The corruption of nature which makes it <hi type="italic">necessary,</hi> and the way of the Spirit which makes it <hi type="italic">practicable,</hi> are as much mysteries to him as the thing itself; though he had in general owned Christ a divine teacher, yet he was unwilling to receive his teachings when they did not agree with the notions he had imbibed. Thus many profess to admit the doctrine of Christ in general, and yet will neither believe the truths of Christianity nor submit to the laws of it further than <hi type="italic">they please.</hi> Christ shall be their teacher, provided they may choose their lesson. Now here, [1.] Nicodemus owns himself ignorant of Christ's meaning, after all: "<hi type="italic">How can these things be?</hi> They are things I do not understand, my capacity will not reach them." Thus the <hi type="italic">things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to the natural man.</hi> He is not only estranged from them, and therefore they are dark to him, but prejudiced against them, and therefore they are foolishness to him. [2.] Because this doctrine was <hi type="italic">unintelligible</hi> to him (so he was pleased to make it), he questions the truth of it; as if, because it was a <hi type="italic">paradox</hi> to him, it was a <hi type="italic">chimera</hi> in itself. Many have such an opinion of their own capacity as to think that that cannot be <hi type="italic">proved</hi> which they cannot <hi type="italic">believe;</hi> by <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> they <hi type="italic">knew not</hi> Christ. <div eID="gen26795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26796" type="x-p"/> (2.) The reproof which Christ gave him for his dulness and ignorance: "<hi type="italic">Art thou a master in Israel,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Didaskalos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a teacher,</hi> a tutor, one who sits in Moses's chair, and yet not only unacquainted with the doctrine of regeneration, but incapable of understanding it?" This word is a reproof, [1.] To those who undertake to teach others and yet are ignorant and unskilful in the word of righteousness themselves. [2.] To those that spend their time in learning and teaching notions and ceremonies in religion, niceties and criticisms in the scripture, and neglect that which is practical and tends to reform the heart and life. Two words in the reproof are very emphatic:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> The place where his lot was cast: in <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> where there was such great plenty of the means of knowledge, where divine revelation was. He might have learned this out of the Old Testament. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The things he was thus ignorant in: <hi type="italic">these</hi> things, these <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> things, there <hi type="italic">great</hi> things, these <hi type="italic">divine</hi> things; had he never read <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5 Ps.50.10 Ezek.18.31 Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.26">Ps. l. 5, 10; Ezek. xviii. 31; xxxvi. 25, 26</reference>? <div eID="gen26796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26797" type="x-p"/> (3.) Christ's discourse, hereupon, of the certainty and sublimity of gospel truths (<reference osisRef="John.3.11-John.3.13">v. 11-13</reference>), to show the folly of those who make strange of these things, and to recommend them to our search. Observe here, <div eID="gen26797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the truths Christ taught were very <hi type="italic">certain</hi> and what we may venture upon (<reference osisRef="John.3.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">We speak that we do know. We;</hi> whom does he mean besides himself? Some understand it of those that bore witness to him and with him on earth, the prophets and John Baptist; they <hi type="italic">spoke</hi> what they <hi type="italic">knew,</hi> and had seen, and were themselves abundantly satisfied in: divine revelation carries its own proof along with it. Others of those that bore witness from heaven, the Father and the Holy Ghost; the Father was with him, the Spirit of the Lord was upon him; therefore he speaks in the plural number, as <reference osisRef="John.14.23">ch. xiv. 23</reference>: <hi type="italic">We will come unto him.</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the truths of Christ are of undoubted certainty. We have all the reason in the world to be assured that the sayings of Christ are <hi type="italic">faithful sayings,</hi> and such as we may venture our souls upon; for he is not only a <hi type="italic">credible</hi> witness, who would not go about to deceive us, but a <hi type="italic">competent</hi> witness, who could not himself be deceived: <hi type="italic">We testify that we have seen.</hi> He spoke not upon hear-say, but upon the clearest evidence, and therefore with the greatest assurance. What he spoke of God, of the invisible world, of heaven and hell, of the divine will concerning us, and the counsels of peace, was what he <hi type="italic">knew,</hi> and <hi type="italic">had seen,</hi> for he was <hi type="italic">by him as one brought up with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. Whatever Christ spoke, he spoke <hi type="italic">of his own knowledge. Secondly,</hi> That the unbelief of sinners is greatly aggravated by the infallible certainty of the truths of Christ. The things are thus sure, thus clear; and yet <hi type="italic">you receive not our witness.</hi> Multitudes to be <hi type="italic">unbelievers</hi> of that which yet (so cogent are the motives of credibility) they cannot <hi type="italic">disbelieve!</hi> <div eID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26799" type="x-p"/> [2.] The truths Christ taught, though communicated in language and expressions borrowed from common and earthly things, yet in their own nature were most sublime and heavenly; this is intimated, <reference osisRef="John.3.12">v. 12</reference>: "<hi type="italic">If I have told them earthly things,</hi> that is, have told them the great things of God in similitudes taken from earthly things, to make them the more easy and intelligible, as that of the <hi type="italic">new birth</hi> and the <hi type="italic">wind,—</hi> if I have thus accommodated myself to your capacities, and lisped to you in your own language, and cannot make you to understand my doctrine,—<hi type="italic">what would you do</hi> if I should accommodate myself to the nature of the things, and speak with the tongue of angels, that language which mortals cannot utter? If such <hi type="italic">familiar expressions</hi> be stumbling-blocks, what would <hi type="italic">abstract ideas</hi> be, and spiritual things painted <hi type="italic">proper?</hi>" Now we may learn hence, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To admire the height and depth of the doctrine of Christ; it is a great mystery of godliness. The things of the gospel are <hi type="italic">heavenly</hi> things, out of the road of the enquiries of human reason, and much more out of the reach of its discoveries. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To acknowledge with thankfulness the condescension of Christ, that he is pleased to suit the manner of the gospel revelation to our capacities, <hi type="italic">to speak to us as to children.</hi> He considers our <hi type="italic">frame,</hi> that we are <hi type="italic">of</hi> the earth, and our <hi type="italic">place,</hi> that we are <hi type="italic">on</hi> the earth, and therefore speaks to us earthly things, and makes things sensible the vehicle of things spiritual, to make them the more easy and familiar to us. Thus he has done both in parables and in sacraments. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> To lament the corruption of our nature, and our great unaptness to receive and entertain the truths of Christ. Earthly things are despised because they are <hi type="italic">vulgar,</hi> and heavenly things because they are <hi type="italic">abstruse;</hi> and so, whatever method is taken, still some fault or other is found with it (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.17">Matt. xi. 17</reference>), but Wisdom is, and will be, <hi type="italic">justified of her children,</hi> notwithstanding. <div eID="gen26799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26800" type="x-p"/> [3.] Our Lord Jesus, and he alone, was fit to reveal to us a doctrine thus certain, thus sublime: <hi type="italic">No man hath ascended up into heaven but he,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.13">v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen26800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26801" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> None but Christ was able to reveal to us the will of God for our salvation. Nicodemus addressed Christ as a prophet; but he must know that he is greater than all the Old-Testament prophets, for none of them <hi type="italic">had ascended into heaven.</hi> They wrote by divine inspiration, and not of their own knowledge; see <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>. Moses ascended into the mount, but not into heaven. No man hath attained to the certain knowledge of God and heavenly things as Christ has; see <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. It is not for us to send to heaven for instructions; we must wait to receive what instructions Heaven will send to us; see <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Prov. xxx. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.12">Deut. xxx. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen26801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26802" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Jesus Christ is able, and fit, and every way qualified, to reveal the will of God to us; for it is <hi type="italic">he that came down from heaven</hi> and <hi type="italic">is in heaven.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="John.3.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">How shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things?</hi> Now here, 1. He gives them an instance of those <hi type="italic">heavenly things</hi> which he could tell them of, when he tells them of one that <hi type="italic">came down from heaven,</hi> and yet is the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> and yet is <hi type="italic">in heaven.</hi> If the regeneration of the <hi type="italic">soul of man</hi> is such a mystery, what then is the incarnation of the <hi type="italic">Son of God?</hi> These are divine and heavenly things indeed. We have here an intimation of Christ's two distinct natures in one person: his divine nature, in which he <hi type="italic">came down from heaven;</hi> his human nature, in which he is the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> and that union of those two, in that while he is the Son of man yet he is <hi type="italic">in heaven.</hi> 2. He gives them a proof of his ability to speak to them <hi type="italic">heavenly things,</hi> and to lead them into the arcana of the kingdom of heaven, by telling them, (1.) That <hi type="italic">he came down from heaven.</hi> The intercourse settled between God and man began <hi type="italic">above;</hi> the first motion towards it did not arise from this earth, but <hi type="italic">came down from heaven.</hi> We love him, and send to him, because he first loved us, and sent to us. Now this intimates, [1.] Christ's divine nature. He that came down from heaven is certainly more than a mere man; he is the <hi type="italic">Lord from heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.47">1 Cor. xv. 47</reference>. [2.] His intimate acquaintance with the divine counsels; for, coming from the court of heaven, he had been from eternity conversant with them. [3.] The <hi type="italic">manifestation of God.</hi> Under the Old Testament God's favours to his people are expressed by his <hi type="italic">hearing from heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.14">2 Chron. vii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">looking from heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.14">Ps. lxxx. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">speaking from heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.13">Neh. ix. 13</reference>), sending from heaven, <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Ps. lvii. 3</reference>. But the New Testament shows us God <hi type="italic">coming down</hi> from heaven, to teach and save us. That he thus <hi type="italic">descended</hi> is an admirable <hi type="italic">mystery,</hi> for the Godhead cannot change places, nor did he bring his body from heaven; but that he thus <hi type="italic">condescended</hi> for our redemption is a more admirable <hi type="italic">mercy;</hi> herein he commended his love. (2.) That <hi type="italic">he is the Son of man, that</hi> Son of man spoken of by Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">vii. 13</reference>), by which the Jews always understand to be meant the Messiah. Christ, in calling himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> shows that he is the <hi type="italic">second Adam,</hi> for the first Adam was the <hi type="italic">father of man.</hi> And of all the Old-Testament titles of the Messiah he chose to make use of <hi type="italic">this,</hi> because it was most expressive of his <hi type="italic">humility,</hi> and most agreeable to his present state of <hi type="italic">humiliation.</hi> (3.) That he <hi type="italic">is in heaven.</hi> Now at this time, when he is talking with Nicodemus on earth, yet, as God, he is <hi type="italic">in heaven.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> as such, was not in heaven till his ascension; but he that was the Son of man was now, by his divine nature, every where present, and particularly in heaven. Thus the Lord of glory, as such, could not be crucified, nor could God, as such, shed his blood; yet that person who was the Lord of glory was crucified (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>), and God purchased the church with <hi type="italic">his own blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>. So close is the union of the two natures in one person that there is a communication of properties. He doth not say <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hos esti</hi></hi>. <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> is the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho on to ourano</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he that is,</hi> and heaven is the habitation of <hi type="italic">his holiness.</hi> <div eID="gen26802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26803" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ here discourses of the <hi type="italic">great design of his own coming into the world, and the happiness of those that believe in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.14-John.3.18">v. 14-18</reference>. Here we have the very marrow and quintessence of the whole gospel, that <hi type="italic">faithful saying</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1 Tim. i. 15</reference>), that Jesus Christ came to seek and to save the children of men from death, and recover them to life. Now sinners are <hi type="italic">dead men</hi> upon a twofold account:— (1.) As one that is mortally wounded, or sick of an incurable disease, is said to be a <hi type="italic">dead man,</hi> for he is dying; and so Christ came to save us, by <hi type="italic">healing</hi> us, as the brazen serpent healed the Israelites, <reference osisRef="John.3.14-John.3.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. (2.) As one that is justly condemned to die for an unpardonable crime is a <hi type="italic">dead man,</hi> he is <hi type="italic">dead in law;</hi> and, in reference to this part of our danger, Christ came to save as a prince or judge, publishing an act of indemnity, or general pardon, under certain provisos; this saving here is opposed to condemning, <reference osisRef="John.3.16-John.3.18">v. 16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen26803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26804" type="x-p"/> [1.] Jesus Christ came to save us by <hi type="italic">healing</hi> us, as the children of Israel that were stung with fiery serpents were cured and <hi type="italic">lived</hi> by looking up to the brazen serpent; we have the story of it, <reference osisRef="Num.21.6-Num.21.9">Num. xxi. 6-9</reference>. It was the <hi type="italic">last</hi> miracle that passed through the hand of Moses before his death. Now in this type of Christ we may observe, <div eID="gen26804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26805" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">deadly</hi> and <hi type="italic">destructive</hi> nature of <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> which is implied here. The guilt of sin is like the <hi type="italic">pain</hi> of the biting of a fiery serpent; the power of corruption is like the <hi type="italic">venom</hi> diffused thereby. The devil is the old serpent, subtle at first (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.1">Gen. iii. 1</reference>), but ever since <hi type="italic">fiery,</hi> and his temptations <hi type="italic">fiery darts,</hi> his assaults terrifying, his victories destroying. Ask awakened consciences, ask damned sinners, and they will tell you, how charming soever the allurements of sin are, <hi type="italic">at the last it bites like a serpent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.30-Prov.23.32">Prov. xxiii. 30-32</reference>. God's wrath against us for sin is as those fiery serpents which God sent among the people, to punish them for their murmurings. The curses of the law are as fiery serpents, so are all the tokens of divine wrath. <div eID="gen26805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26806" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The powerful remedy provided against this fatal malady. The case of poor sinners is deplorable; but is it desperate? Thanks be to God, it is not; there is balm in Gilead. The <hi type="italic">Son of man is lifted up,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">serpent of brass</hi> was by Moses, which cured the stung Israelites. 1. It was a <hi type="italic">serpent of brass</hi> that cured them. Brass is <hi type="italic">bright;</hi> we read of Christ's feet <hi type="italic">shining like brass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.15">Rev. i. 15</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">durable;</hi> Christ is the same. It was made in the shape of a <hi type="italic">fiery serpent,</hi> and yet had no poison, no sting, fitly representing Christ, who was <hi type="italic">made sin for us</hi> and yet knew no sin; was <hi type="italic">made in the likeness of sinful flesh</hi> and yet not sinful; as harmless as a serpent of brass. The serpent was a cursed creature; Christ was made a <hi type="italic">curse.</hi> That which cured them reminded them of their plague; so in Christ sin is set before us most fiery and formidable. 2. It was lifted up upon a pole, and so <hi type="italic">must</hi> the Son of man be lifted up; thus it <hi type="italic">behoved him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.26">Luke xxiv. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.46">46</reference>. No remedy now. Christ is lifted up, (1.) In his <hi type="italic">crucifixion.</hi> He was lifted up upon the cross. His death is called his being <hi type="italic">lifted up,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.32-John.12.33">ch. xii. 32, 33</reference>. He was lifted up as a spectacle, as a mark, lifted up between heaven and earth, as if he had been unworthy of either and abandoned by both. (2.) In his <hi type="italic">exaltation.</hi> He was lifted up to the Father's right hand, to give repentance and remission; he was lifted up to the cross, to be further lifted up to the crown. (3.) In the <hi type="italic">publishing</hi> and <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> of his everlasting gospel, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Rev. xiv. 6</reference>. The serpent was lifted up that all the thousands of Israel might see it. Christ in the gospel is exhibited to us, evidently set forth; Christ is <hi type="italic">lifted up</hi> as an <hi type="italic">ensign,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa. xi. 10</reference>. 3. It was lifted up by Moses. Christ was made under the law of Moses, and Moses testified of him. 4. Being thus lifted up, it was appointed for the cure of those that were bitten by fiery serpents. He that sent the plague provided the remedy. None could redeem and save us but he whose justice had condemned us. It was God himself that <hi type="italic">found the ransom,</hi> and the efficacy of it depends upon his appointment. The <hi type="italic">fiery serpents</hi> were sent to punish them for their <hi type="italic">tempting Christ</hi> (so the apostle saith, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.9">1 Cor. x. 9</reference>), and yet they were healed by virtue derived from him. He whom we have offended is <hi type="italic">our peace.</hi> <div eID="gen26806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26807" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The way of <hi type="italic">applying</hi> this remedy, and that is by <hi type="italic">believing,</hi> which plainly alludes to the Israelites' <hi type="italic">looking up</hi> to the brazen serpent, in order to their being healed by it. If any stung Israelite was either so little sensible of his pain and peril, or had so little confidence in the word of Moses as not to look up to the brazen serpent, justly did he die of his wound; but every one that <hi type="italic">looked up to it</hi> did well, <reference osisRef="Num.21.9">Num. xxi. 9</reference>. If any so far slight either their disease by sin or the method of cure by Christ as not to embrace Christ upon his own terms, their blood is upon their own head. He hath said, <hi type="italic">Look, and be saved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Isa. xlv. 22</reference>), look and live. We must take a complacency in and give consent to the methods which Infinite Wisdom has taken is saving a guilty world, by the mediation of Jesus Christ, as the great sacrifice and intercessor. <div eID="gen26807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26808" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The great encouragements given us by faith to look up to him. 1. It was for this end that he was <hi type="italic">lifted up,</hi> that his followers might be saved; and he will pursue his end. 2. The offer that is made of salvation by him is general, that <hi type="italic">whosoever believes</hi> in him, without exception, might have benefit by him. 3. The salvation offered is complete. (1.) They <hi type="italic">shall not perish,</hi> shall not die of their wounds; though they may be pained and ill frightened, iniquity shall not be their ruin. But that is not all. (2.) They shall <hi type="italic">have eternal life.</hi> They shall not only not die of their wounds in the wilderness, but they shall reach Canaan (which they were then just ready to enter into); they shall enjoy the promised rest. <div eID="gen26808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26809" type="x-p"/> [2.] Jesus Christ came to save us by <hi type="italic">pardoning us,</hi> that we might not die by the sentence of the law, <reference osisRef="John.3.16-John.3.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Here is <hi type="italic">gospel</hi> indeed, good <hi type="italic">news,</hi> the best that ever came from heaven to earth. Here is <hi type="italic">much,</hi> here is <hi type="italic">all</hi> in a little, the word of reconciliation in miniature. <div eID="gen26809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26810" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Here is God's <hi type="italic">love</hi> in <hi type="italic">giving his Son for the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">v. 16</reference>), where we have three things:— 1. The great <hi type="italic">gospel mystery</hi> revealed: <hi type="italic">God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.</hi> The love of God the Father is the original of our regeneration by the Spirit and our reconciliation by the lifting up of the Son. Note, (1.) Jesus Christ is the <hi type="italic">only-begotten Son of God.</hi> This magnifies his love in giving him for us, in giving him to us; now know we that he loves us, when he has given his <hi type="italic">only-begotten Son for us,</hi> which expresses not only his dignity in himself, but his dearness to his Father; he was <hi type="italic">always his delight.</hi> (2.) In order to the redemption and salvation of man, it pleased God to <hi type="italic">give his only-begotten Son.</hi> He not only sent him into the world with full and ample power to negotiate a peace between heaven and earth, but he <hi type="italic">gave him,</hi> that is, he gave him up to suffer and die for us, as the great propitiation or expiatory sacrifice. It comes in here as a reason why he <hi type="italic">must be lifted up;</hi> for so it was determined and designed by the Father, who gave him for this purpose, and <hi type="italic">prepared him a body</hi> in order to it. His enemies could not have <hi type="italic">taken him</hi> if his Father had not <hi type="italic">given</hi> him. Though he was not yet crucified, yet in the determinate counsel of God he was <hi type="italic">given</hi> up, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. Nay, further, God has <hi type="italic">given him,</hi> that is, he has made an offer of him, to all, and given him to all true believers, to all the intents and purposes of the new covenant. He has given him to be our <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> a <hi type="italic">witness to the people,</hi> the high priest of our profession, to be our peace, to be head of the church and head over all things to the church, to be to us all we need. (3.) Herein God has commended his <hi type="italic">love to the world:</hi> God so <hi type="italic">loved the world,</hi> so really, so richly. Now his creatures shall see that he loves them, and wishes them well. He so loved the world of fallen man as he did not love that of fallen angels; see <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">Rom. v. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.10">1 John iv. 10</reference>. Behold, and wonder, that the <hi type="italic">great God</hi> should love such a <hi type="italic">worthless</hi> world! That the <hi type="italic">holy God</hi> should love such a <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> world with a love of good will, when he could not look upon it with any complacency. This was a <hi type="italic">time of love indeed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8">8</reference>. The Jews vainly conceited that the Messiah should be sent only in love to <hi type="italic">their nation,</hi> and to advance them upon the ruins of their neighbours; but Christ tells them that he came in love to the <hi type="italic">whole world,</hi> Gentiles as well as Jews, <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1 John ii. 2</reference>. Though many of the world of mankind perish, yet God's giving his only-begotten Son was an instance of his love to the whole world, because through him there is a <hi type="italic">general offer</hi> of life and salvation made to all. It is love to the revolted rebellious province to issue out a proclamation of pardon and indemnity to all that will come in, plead it upon their knees, and return to their allegiance. So <hi type="italic">far God loved the</hi> apostate lapsed <hi type="italic">world</hi> that he sent his Son with this fair proposal, that <hi type="italic">whosoever believes in him,</hi> one or other, <hi type="italic">shall not perish. Salvation</hi> has been <hi type="italic">of the Jews,</hi> but now Christ is <hi type="italic">known as salvation to the ends of the earth,</hi> a <hi type="italic">common salvation.</hi> 2. Here is the great <hi type="italic">gospel duty,</hi> and that is to <hi type="italic">believe in Jesus Christ</hi> (Whom God has thus given, given <hi type="italic">for us,</hi> given <hi type="italic">to us</hi>), to accept the gift, and answer the intention of the giver. We must yield an unfeigned assent and consent to the record God hath given in his word concerning his Son. God having given him to us to be our prophet, priest, and king, we must give up ourselves to be ruled, and taught, and saved by him. 3. Here is the great gospel benefit: <hi type="italic">That whosoever believes in Christ shall not perish.</hi> This he had said before, and here repeats it. It is the unspeakable happiness of all true believers, for which they are eternally indebted to Christ, (1.) That they are saved from the miseries of hell, delivered from <hi type="italic">going down to the pit;</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall not perish.</hi> God has taken away their sin, they shall not die; a pardon is purchased, and so the attainder is reversed. (2.) They are entitled to the joys of heaven: they shall <hi type="italic">have everlasting life.</hi> The convicted traitor is not only pardoned, but preferred, and made a favourite, and treated as one whom the King of kings <hi type="italic">delights to honour. Out of prison he comes to reign,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.14">Eccl. iv. 14</reference>.
