If believers, then children; and, if <hi type="italic">children, then heirs.</hi> <div eID="gen26810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26811" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Here is God's design in sending hi Son into the world: it was <hi type="italic">that the world through him might be saved.</hi> He came into the world with salvation in <hi type="italic">his eye,</hi> with salvation <hi type="italic">in his hand.</hi> Therefore the aforementioned offer of live and salvation is sincere, and shall be made good to all that by faith accept it (<reference osisRef="John.3.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">God sent his Son into the world,</hi> this guilty, rebellious, apostate world; sent him as his agent or ambassador, not as sometimes he had sent angels into the world as visitants, but as resident. Ever since man sinned, he has dreaded the approach and appearance of any special messenger from heaven, as being conscious of guilt and looking for judgment: <hi type="italic">We shall surely die, for we have seen God.</hi> If therefore the Son of God himself come, we are concerned to enquire on what errand he comes: <hi type="italic">Is it peace?</hi> Or, as they asked Samuel trembling, <hi type="italic">Comest thou peaceably?</hi> And this scripture returns the answer, <hi type="italic">Peaceably.</hi> 1. He did not come to <hi type="italic">condemn the world.</hi> We had reason enough to expect that he should, for it is a guilty world; it is <hi type="italic">convicted,</hi> and what cause can be shown why judgment should not be given, and execution awarded, according to law? That <hi type="italic">one blood</hi> of which all <hi type="italic">nations</hi> of men are made (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Acts xvii. 26</reference>) is not only <hi type="italic">tainted</hi> with an hereditary <hi type="italic">disease,</hi> like Gehazi's leprosy, but it is <hi type="italic">tainted</hi> with an hereditary <hi type="italic">guilt,</hi> like that of the Amalekites, with whom God had war <hi type="italic">from generation to generation;</hi> and justly may such a world as this be <hi type="italic">condemned;</hi> and if God would have sent to condemn it he had angels at command, to pour out the vials of his wrath, a cherub with a flaming sword ready to do execution. <hi type="italic">If the Lord had been pleased to kill us,</hi> he would not have sent his Son amongst us. He came with full powers indeed to <hi type="italic">execute judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">ch. v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>), but did not begin with a judgment of condemnation, did not proceed upon the outlawry, nor take advantage against us for the breach of the <hi type="italic">covenant of innocency,</hi> but put us upon a new trial before a <hi type="italic">throne of grace.</hi> 2. He came <hi type="italic">that the world through him might be saved,</hi> that a door of salvation might be opened to the world, and whoever would might enter in by it. God was in Christ <hi type="italic">reconciling the world to himself,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">saving</hi> it. An act of indemnity is passed and published, through Christ a remedial law made, and the world of mankind dealt with, not according to the rigours of the first covenant, but according to the riches of the second; <hi type="italic">that the world</hi> through him might be saved, for it could never be saved but <hi type="italic">through him; there is not salvation in any other.</hi> This is good news to a convinced conscience, healing to broken bones and bleeding wounds, that Christ, our judge, came not to <hi type="italic">condemn,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">save.</hi> <div eID="gen26811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26812" type="x-p"/> [3.] From all this is inferred the happiness of true believers: <hi type="italic">He that believeth on him is not condemned,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.18">v. 18</reference>. Though he has been a sinner, a great sinner, and <hi type="italic">stands convicted</hi> (<hi type="italic">habes confilentem reum—by his own confession</hi>), yet, upon his believing, process is stayed, judgment is arrested, and he is <hi type="italic">not condemned.</hi> This denotes more than a reprieve; he <hi type="italic">is not condemned,</hi> that is, he is acquitted; he <hi type="italic">stand upon his deliverance</hi> (as we say), and if he be not condemned he is discharged; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou krinetai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he is not judged,</hi> not dealt with in strict justice, according to the desert of his sins. He is <hi type="italic">accused,</hi> and he cannot plead <hi type="italic">not guilty</hi> to the indictment, but he can plead <hi type="italic">in bar,</hi> can plead a <hi type="italic">noli prosequi</hi> upon the indictment, as blessed Paul does, <hi type="italic">Who is he that condemns? It is Christ that died.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">afflicted,</hi> chastened of God, persecuted by the world; but he is not <hi type="italic">condemned.</hi> The cross perhaps lies heavy upon him, but he is saved from the curse: condemned <hi type="italic">by the world,</hi> it may be, but not <hi type="italic">condemned with the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom. viii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1 Cor. xi. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen26812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26813" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ, in the close, discourses concerning the <hi type="italic">deplorable condition of those that persist in unbelief and wilful ignorance,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.18-John.3.21">v. 18-21</reference>. <div eID="gen26813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26814" type="x-p"/> (1.) Read here the doom of those that will not <hi type="italic">believe in Christ:</hi> they <hi type="italic">are condemned already.</hi> Observe, [1.] How great the <hi type="italic">sin</hi> of unbelievers is; it is aggravated from the dignity of the person they slight; they <hi type="italic">believe not in the name of the only-begotten Son of God,</hi> who is infinitely <hi type="italic">true,</hi> and deserves to be believed, <hi type="italic">infinitely good,</hi> and deserves to be embraced. God sent one to save us that was <hi type="italic">dearest</hi> to himself; and shall not he be <hi type="italic">dearest to us?</hi> Shall we not believe on his name who has a name above every name? [2.] How great the <hi type="italic">misery</hi> of unbelievers is: they are <hi type="italic">condemned already;</hi> which bespeaks, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A <hi type="italic">certain</hi> condemnation. They are as sure to be condemned in the judgment of the great day as if they were condemned already. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A <hi type="italic">present</hi> condemnation. The curse has already taken hold of them; the wrath of God now fastens upon them. They are condemned already, for their own hearts condemn them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> A condemnation <hi type="italic">grounded upon their former guilt:</hi> He is condemned <hi type="italic">already,</hi> for he lies open to the law for all his sins; the obligation of the law is in full force, power, and virtue, against him, because he is not by faith interested in the gospel defeasance; <hi type="italic">he is condemned already, because he has not believed.</hi> Unbelief may truly be called <hi type="italic">the great damning sin,</hi> because it leaves us under the guilt of all our other sins; it is a sin against the <hi type="italic">remedy,</hi> against our <hi type="italic">appeal.</hi> <div eID="gen26814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26815" type="x-p"/> (2.) Read also the doom of those that would not so much as <hi type="italic">know him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.19">v. 19</reference>. Many <hi type="italic">inquisitive</hi> people had knowledge of Christ and his doctrine and miracles, but they were prejudiced against him, and would not believe in him, while the generality were sottishly careless and stupid, and would not <hi type="italic">know</hi> him. And <hi type="italic">this is the condemnation,</hi> the sin that ruined them, <hi type="italic">that light is come into the world, and they loved darkness rather.</hi> Now here observe, [1.] That the gospel is light, and, when the gospel came, <hi type="italic">light came into the world,</hi> Light is <hi type="italic">self-evidencing,</hi> so is the gospel; it proves its own divine origin. Light is <hi type="italic">discovering,</hi> and <hi type="italic">truly the light is sweet,</hi> and rejoices the heart. It is a light shining in a dark place, and a dark place indeed the world would be without it. It is <hi type="italic">come into all the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col. i. 6</reference>), and not confined to one corner of it, as the Old-Testament light was. [2.] It is the unspeakable folly of the most of men that they loved darkness rather than light, rather than <hi type="italic">this</hi> light. The Jews loved the dark shadows of their law, and the instructions of their <hi type="italic">blind guides,</hi> rather than the doctrine of Christ. The Gentiles loved their superstitious services of <hi type="italic">an unknown God,</hi> whom they <hi type="italic">ignorantly worshipped,</hi> rather than the <hi type="italic">reasonable service</hi> which the gospel enjoins. Sinners that were wedded to their lusts loved their ignorance and mistakes, which supported them in their sins, rather than the truths of Christ, which would have parted them from their sins. Man's apostasy began in an affectation of forbidden knowledge, but is kept up by an affectation of forbidden ignorance. Wretched man is in love with his sickness, in love with his slavery, and will not be made <hi type="italic">free,</hi> will not be <hi type="italic">made whole.</hi> [3.] The true reason why men love darkness rather than light is <hi type="italic">because their deeds are evil.</hi> They love darkness because they think it is an excuse for their evil deeds, and they hate the light because it robs them of the good opinion they had of themselves, by showing them their sinfulness and misery. Their case is sad, and, because they are resolved that they will not <hi type="italic">mend</hi> it, they are resolved that they will not <hi type="italic">see it.</hi> [4.] Wilful ignorance is so far from excusing sin that it will be found, at the great day, to aggravate the condemnation: <hi type="italic">This is the condemnation,</hi> this is what ruins souls, that they shut their eyes against the light, and will not so much as admit a parley with Christ and his gospel; they set God so much at defiance that they desire not the knowledge of his ways, <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job xxi. 14</reference>. We must account in the judgment, not only for the knowledge we <hi type="italic">had,</hi> and <hi type="italic">used not,</hi> but for the knowledge we <hi type="italic">might have had,</hi> and <hi type="italic">would not;</hi> not only for the knowledge we <hi type="italic">sinned against,</hi> but for the knowledge we <hi type="italic">sinned away.</hi> For the further illustration of this he shows (<reference osisRef="John.3.20-John.3.21">v. 20, 21</reference>) that according as men's hearts and lives are good or bad, so they stand affected to the light Christ has brought into the world. <div eID="gen26815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is not strange if those that do evil, and resolve to persist in it, hate the light of Christ's gospel; for it is a common observation that <hi type="italic">every one that doeth evil hateth the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.20">v. 20</reference>. Evil-doers seek concealment, out of a sense of shame and fear of punishment; see <reference osisRef="Job.24.13">Job xxiv. 13</reference>, &c. Sinful works are <hi type="italic">works of darkness;</hi> sin from the first affected concealment, <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job xxxi. 33</reference>. The <hi type="italic">light shakes</hi> the wicked, <reference osisRef="Job.38.12-Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 12, 13</reference>. Thus the gospel is a terror to the wicked world: <hi type="italic">They come not to this light,</hi> but keep as far off it as they can, <hi type="italic">lest their deeds should be reproved.</hi> Note, 1. The light of the gospel is sent into the world to <hi type="italic">reprove the evil deeds</hi> of sinners; to make them manifest (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.13">Eph. v. 13</reference>), to <hi type="italic">show</hi> people <hi type="italic">their transgressions,</hi> to show that to be sin which was not thought to be so, and to show them the evil of their transgressions, <hi type="italic">that sin by the</hi> new <hi type="italic">commandment</hi> might appear <hi type="italic">exceeding sinful.</hi> The gospel has its convictions, to make way for its consolations. 2. It is for this reason that evil-doers <hi type="italic">hate the light</hi> of the gospel. There were those who <hi type="italic">had done evil</hi> and were sorry for it, who bade this light welcome, as the <hi type="italic">publicans and harlots.</hi> But he that <hi type="italic">does evil,</hi> that does it and resolves to go on in it, <hi type="italic">hateth the light,</hi> cannot bear to be told of his faults. All that opposition which the gospel of Christ has met with in the world comes from the <hi type="italic">wicked heart,</hi> influenced by the <hi type="italic">wicked one.</hi> Christ is hated because sin is loved. 3. They who do not <hi type="italic">come to the light</hi> thereby evidence a secret <hi type="italic">hatred</hi> of the light. If they had not an antipathy to <hi type="italic">saving knowledge,</hi> they would not sit down so contentedly in <hi type="italic">damning ignorance.</hi> <div eID="gen26816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> On the other hand, upright hearts, that approve themselves to God in their integrity, bid this light welcome (<reference osisRef="John.3.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that doeth truth cometh to the light.</hi> It seems, then, that though the gospel had many enemies it had some friends. It is a common observation that <hi type="italic">truth seeks no corners.</hi> Those who mean and act honestly dread not a scrutiny, but desire it rather. Now this is applicable to the gospel light; as it <hi type="italic">convinces</hi> and <hi type="italic">terrifies</hi> evil-doers, so it <hi type="italic">confirms</hi> and <hi type="italic">comforts</hi> those that walk in their integrity. Observe here, 1. The character of a <hi type="italic">good man.</hi> (1.) He is one that <hi type="italic">doeth truth;</hi> that is, he acts truly and sincerely in all he does. Though sometimes he comes short of <hi type="italic">doing good,</hi> the good he would do, yet he <hi type="italic">doeth truth,</hi> he aims honestly; he has his infirmities, but holds fast his integrity; as Gaius, that <hi type="italic">did faithfully</hi> (<reference osisRef="3John.1.5">3 John 5</reference>), as Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>), as Nathanael (<reference osisRef="John.1.47">ch. i. 47</reference>), as Asa, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">1 Kings xv. 14</reference>. (2.) He is one that <hi type="italic">cometh to the light.</hi> He is ready to receive and entertain divine revelation as far as it appears to him to be so, what uneasiness soever it may create him. He that <hi type="italic">doeth truth</hi> is willing to know the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> by himself, and to <hi type="italic">have his deeds made manifest.</hi> A good man is much employed in trying himself, and is desirous that God would try him, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">Ps. xxvi. 2</reference>. He is solicitous to <hi type="italic">know</hi> what the will of God is, and resolves to <hi type="italic">do</hi> it, though ever so contrary to his own will and interest. 2. Here is the character of a <hi type="italic">good work:</hi> it is <hi type="italic">wrought in God,</hi> in union with him by a covenanting faith, and in communion with him by devout affections. Our works are <hi type="italic">then</hi> good, and will bear the test, when the will of God is the rule of them and the glory of God the end of them; when they are done in his strength, and for his sake, to him, and not to men; and if, by the light of the gospel, it be manifest to us that our works are thus wrought, <hi type="italic">then shall we have rejoicing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Gal. vi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>.

<div eID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Testimony to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> After these things came Jesus and his disciples into the land of Judæa; and there he tarried with them, and baptized. <hi type="super">23</hi> And John also was baptizing in Ænon near to Salim, because there was much water there: and they came, and were baptized. <hi type="super">24</hi> For John was not yet cast into prison. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then there arose a question between <hi type="italic">some</hi> of John's disciples and the Jews about purifying. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they came unto John, and said unto him, Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> come to him. <hi type="super">27</hi> John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven. <hi type="super">28</hi> Ye yourselves bear me witness, that I said, I am not the Christ, but that I am sent before him. <hi type="super">29</hi> He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled. <hi type="super">30</hi> He must increase, but I <hi type="italic">must</hi> decrease. <hi type="super">31</hi> He that cometh from above is above all: he that is of the earth is earthly, and speaketh of the earth: he that cometh from heaven is above all. 32 And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony. <hi type="super">33</hi> He that hath received his testimony hath set to his seal that God is true. <hi type="super">34</hi> For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God: for God giveth not the Spirit by measure <hi type="italic">unto him.</hi> <hi type="super">35</hi> The Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into his hand. <hi type="super">36</hi> He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him. <div eID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's removal into the land of Judea (<reference osisRef="John.3.22">v. 22</reference>), and there he tarried with his disciples. Observe, 1. Our Lord Jesus, after he entered upon his public work, travelled much, and removed often, as the patriarchs in their sojournings. As it was a good part of his humiliation that he had no certain dwelling-place, but was, as Paul, <hi type="italic">in journeyings often,</hi> so it was an instance of his unwearied industry, in the work for which he came into the world, that he went about in prosecution of it; many a weary step he took to do good to souls. The <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> took a large circuit to diffuse his light and heat, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 6</reference>. 2. He was not wont to stay long at Jerusalem. Though he went frequently thither, yet he soon returned into the country; as here. <hi type="italic">After these things,</hi> after he had had this discourse with Nicodemus, he came into the land of Judea; not so much for <hi type="italic">greater privacy</hi> (though mean and obscure places best suited the humble Jesus in his humble state) as for <hi type="italic">greater usefulness.</hi> His preaching and miracles, perhaps, made <hi type="italic">most noise</hi> at Jerusalem, the fountain-head of news, but did <hi type="italic">least good</hi> there, where the most considerable men of the Jewish church had so much the ascendant. 3. When he came into the land of Judea his <hi type="italic">disciples came with him;</hi> for these were <hi type="italic">they that continued with him in his temptations.</hi> Many that flocked to him at Jerusalem could not follow his motions into the country, they had no business there; but his disciples attended him. If the ark remove, it is better to <hi type="italic">remove and go after it</hi> (as those did, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.3">Josh. iii. 3</reference>) than sit still without it, though it be in Jerusalem itself. 4. There he <hi type="italic">tarried with them,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dietribe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He conversed</hi> with them, <hi type="italic">discoursed</hi> with them. He did not retire into the country for his ease and pleasure, but for more free conversation with his disciples and followers. See <reference osisRef="Song.7.11-Song.7.12">Cant. vii. 11, 12</reference>. Note, Those that are ready to <hi type="italic">go with Christ</hi> shall find him as ready to <hi type="italic">stay with them.</hi> It is supposed that he now staid five or six months in this country. 5. There <hi type="italic">he baptized;</hi> he admitted disciples, such as believed in him, and had more honesty and courage than those had at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="John.2.42">ch. ii. 24</reference>. John began to baptize in the land of Judea (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Matt. iii. 1</reference>), therefore Christ began there, for John had said, <hi type="italic">There comes one after me.</hi> He himself <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> not, with his own hand, but his disciples by his orders and directions, as appears, <reference osisRef="John.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>. But his disciples' baptizing was his baptizing. Holy ordinances are Christ's, though administered by weak men. <div eID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26821" type="x-p"/> II. John's continuance in his work, as long as his opportunities lasted, <reference osisRef="John.3.23-John.3.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. Here we are told, <div eID="gen26821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26822" type="x-p"/> 1. That <hi type="italic">John was baptizing.</hi> Christ's baptism was, for substance, the same with John's, for John bore witness to Christ, and therefore they did not at all clash or interfere with one another. But, (1.) Christ began the work of preaching and baptizing before <hi type="italic">John laid it down,</hi> that he might be ready to receive John's disciples when he should be taken off, and so the wheels might be kept going. It is a comfort to useful men, when they are going off the stage, to see those rising up who are likely to fill up their place. (2.) John continued the work of preaching and baptizing though Christ had <hi type="italic">taken it up;</hi> for he would still, according to the <hi type="italic">measure given to him,</hi> advance the interests of God's kingdom. There was still work for John to do, for Christ was not yet <hi type="italic">generally known,</hi> nor were the minds of people <hi type="italic">thoroughly prepared</hi> for him by repentance. From heaven John had received his <hi type="italic">command,</hi> and he would go on in his work till he thence received his <hi type="italic">countermand,</hi> and would have his dismission from the same hand that gave him his commission. He does not <hi type="italic">come in</hi> to Christ, lest what had formerly passed should look like a combination between them; but <hi type="italic">he goes on</hi> with his work, till Providence lays him aside. The greater gifts of some do not <hi type="italic">render</hi> the labours of others, that come short of them, <hi type="italic">needless</hi> and <hi type="italic">useless;</hi> there is work enough for all hands. They are sullen that will sit down and do nothing when they see themselves out-shone. Though we have but one talent, we must account for that: and, when we see ourselves <hi type="italic">going off,</hi> must yet <hi type="italic">go on</hi> to the last. <div eID="gen26822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26823" type="x-p"/> 2. That he baptized in Enon near Salim, places we find nowhere else mentioned, and therefore the learned are altogether at a loss where to find them. Wherever it was, it seems that John removed from <hi type="italic">place to place;</hi> he did not think that there was any virtue in Jordan, because Jesus was baptized there, which should engage him to stay there, but as he saw cause he removed to other waters. Ministers must follow their opportunities. He chose a place where there was much water, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hydata polla</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">many waters,</hi> that is, many <hi type="italic">streams</hi> of water; so that wherever he met with any that were willing to submit to his baptism water was at hand to baptize them with, <hi type="italic">shallow</hi> perhaps, as is usual where there are <hi type="italic">many</hi> brooks, but such as would serve his purpose. And in that country plenty of water was a valuable thing. <div eID="gen26823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26824" type="x-p"/> 3. That thither people <hi type="italic">came to him</hi> and <hi type="italic">were baptized.</hi> Though they did not come in such vast crowds as they did when he first appeared, yet now he was not without encouragement, but there were still those that attended and owned him. Some refer this both to John and to Jesus: <hi type="italic">They came and were baptized;</hi> that is, some came to John, and were baptized by him, some to Jesus, and were baptized by him, and, as their baptism was one, so were their hearts. <div eID="gen26824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> 4. It is noted (<reference osisRef="John.3.24">v. 24</reference>) that <hi type="italic">John was not yet cast into prison,</hi> to clear the order of the story, and to show that these passages are to come in before <reference osisRef="Matt.6.12">Matt. vi. 12</reference>. John never desisted from his work as long as he had his liberty; nay, he seems to have been the more industrious, because he foresaw his time was short; he was not <hi type="italic">yet cast into prison,</hi> but he expected it ere long, <reference osisRef="John.9.4">ch. ix. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> III. A contest between <hi type="italic">John's disciples and the Jews about purifying,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.25">v. 25</reference>. See how the gospel of Christ came not to <hi type="italic">send peace upon earth,</hi> but <hi type="italic">division.</hi> Observe, 1. Who were the disputants: <hi type="italic">some of John's disciples, and the Jews</hi> who had not submitted to his baptism of repentance. Penitents and impenitents divide this sinful world. In this contest, it should seem, John's disciples were the <hi type="italic">aggressors,</hi> and gave the <hi type="italic">challenge;</hi> and it is a sign that they were novices, who had more zeal than discretion. The truths of God have often suffered by the rashness of those that have undertaken to defend them before they were able to do it. 2. What was the matter in dispute: <hi type="italic">about purifying,</hi> about <hi type="italic">religious washing.</hi> (1.) We may suppose that John's disciples cried up his baptism, his purifying, as <hi type="italic">instar omnium—superior to all others,</hi> and gave the preference to that as perfecting and superseding all the purifications of the Jews, and they were in the right; but <hi type="italic">young</hi> converts are too apt to boast of their attainments, whereas he that finds the <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> should <hi type="italic">hide it</hi> till he is sure that he has it, and not talk of it too much at first. (2.) No doubt the Jews with as much assurance applauded the <hi type="italic">purifyings</hi> that were in use among them, both those that were instituted by the law of Moses and those that were imposed by the tradition of the elders; for the former they had a divine warrant, and for the latter the usage of the church. Now it is very likely that the Jews in this dispute, when they could not <hi type="italic">deny</hi> the excellent nature and design of John's baptism, raised an objection against it from Christ's baptism, which gave occasion for the complaint that follows here (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>): "Here is John baptizing in one place." say they, "and Jesus at the same time baptizing in another place; and therefore John's baptism, which his disciples so much applaud, is either," [1.] "<hi type="italic">Dangerous,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">ill consequence</hi> to the peace of the church and state, for you see it opens a door to endless parties. Now that John has begun, we shall have every little teacher set up for a baptist presently. Or," [2.] "At the best it is <hi type="italic">defective</hi> and <hi type="italic">imperfect.</hi> If John's baptism, which you cry up thus, have any good in it, yonder the baptism of Jesus goes beyond it, so that for your parts you are shaded already by a greater light, and your baptism is soon gone out of request." Thus objections are made against the gospel from the advancement and improvement of gospel light, as if childhood and manhood were contrary to each other, and the superstructure were against the foundation. There was no reason to object Christ's baptism against John's, for they consisted very well together. <div eID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> IV. A complaint which John's disciples made to their master concerning Christ and his baptizing, <reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>. They, being <hi type="italic">nonplussed</hi> by the fore-mentioned objection, and probably <hi type="italic">ruffled</hi> and put into a heat by it, come to their master, and tell him, "<hi type="italic">Rabbi, he that was with thee,</hi> and was baptized of thee, is now set up for himself; he <hi type="italic">baptizeth, and all men come to him;</hi> and wilt thou suffer it?" Their itch for disputing occasioned this. It is common for men, when they find themselves run aground in the heat of disputation, to fall foul upon those that do them no harm. If these disciples of John had not undertaken to dispute about <hi type="italic">purifying,</hi> before they understood the <hi type="italic">doctrine of baptism,</hi> they might have answered the objection without being put into a passion. In their complaint, they speak respectfully to their own master, <hi type="italic">Rabbit;</hi> but speak very slightly of our Saviour, though they do not name him. 1. They suggest that Christ's setting up a baptism of his own was a piece of presumption, very unaccountable; as if John, having first set up this rite of baptizing, must have the monopoly of it, and, as it were, a patent for the invention: "<hi type="italic">He that was with thee beyond Jordan,</hi> as a disciple of thine, <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and wonder, <hi type="italic">the same,</hi> the very same, <hi type="italic">baptizes,</hi> and takes thy work out of thy hand." Thus the voluntary condescensions of the Lord Jesus, as that of his being baptized by John, are often unjustly and very unkindly turned to his reproach. 2. They suggest that it was a piece of ingratitude to John. He <hi type="italic">to whom thou barest witness</hi> baptizes; as if Jesus owed all his reputation to the honourable character John gave of him, and yet had very unworthily improved it to the prejudice of John. But Christ needed not John's testimony, <reference osisRef="John.5.36">ch. v. 36</reference>. He reflected more honour upon John than he received from him, yet thus it is incident to us to think that others are more indebted to us than really they are. And besides, Christ's baptism was not in the least an <hi type="italic">impeachment,</hi> but indeed the greatest <hi type="italic">improvement,</hi> of John's baptism, which was but to lead the way to Christ's. John was <hi type="italic">just</hi> to Christ, in bearing witness to him; and Christ's answering his testimony did rather enrich than impoverish John's ministry. 3. They conclude that it would be a total eclipse to John's baptism: "<hi type="italic">All men come to him;</hi> they that used to follow with us now flock after him, it is therefore time for us to look about us." It was not indeed strange that <hi type="italic">all men came to him.</hi> As far as Christ is <hi type="italic">manifested</hi> he will be <hi type="italic">magnified;</hi> but why should John's disciples grieve at this? Note, Aiming at the monopoly of honour and respect has been in all ages the bane of the church, and the shame of its members and ministers; as also a vying of interests, and a jealousy of rivalship and competition. We mistake if we think that the excelling gifts and graces, and labours and usefulness, of one, are a diminution and disparagement to another that has obtained mercy to be faithful; for the Spirit is a free agent, <hi type="italic">dispensing to every one severally as he will.</hi> Paul rejoiced in the usefulness even of those that <hi type="italic">opposed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.18">Phil. i. 18</reference>. We must leave it to God to choose, employ, and honour his own instruments as he pleaseth, and not covet to be <hi type="italic">placed alone.</hi> <div eID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> V. Here is John's answer to this complaint which his disciples made, <reference osisRef="John.3.27">v. 27</reference>, &c. His disciples expected that he would have resented this matter as they did; but Christ's <hi type="italic">manifestation to Israel</hi> was no <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> to John, but what he looked for; it was not <hi type="italic">disturbance</hi> to him, but what he wished for. He therefore checked the complaint, as Moses, <hi type="italic">Enviest thou for my sake?</hi> and took this occasion to confirm the testimonies he had formerly borne to Christ as superior to him, cheerfully consigning and turning over to him all the interest he had in Israel. In this discourse here, the first minister of the gospel (for so John was) is an excellent pattern to all ministers to <hi type="italic">humble</hi> themselves and to <hi type="italic">exalt</hi> the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> 1. John here <hi type="italic">abases himself in comparison with Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.27-John.3.30">v. 27-30</reference>. The more others magnify us, the more we must humble ourselves, and fortify ourselves against the temptation of flattery and applause, and the jealousy of our friends for our honour, by remembering our place, and what we are, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.5">1 Cor. iii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">John acquiesces</hi> in the divine disposal, and satisfies himself with that (<reference osisRef="John.3.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven,</hi> whence <hi type="italic">every good gift</hi> comes (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">James i. 17</reference>), a general truth very applicable in this case. Different employments are according to the direction of divine Providence, different endowments according to the distribution of the divine grace. <hi type="italic">No man can take</hi> any true <hi type="italic">honour</hi> to himself, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4">Heb. v. 4</reference>. We have as necessary and constant a dependence upon the grace of God in all the motions and actions of the spiritual life as we have upon the providence of God in all the motions and actions of the natural life: now this comes in here as a reason, [1.] Why we should not <hi type="italic">envy</hi> those that have a larger share of gifts than we have, or move in a larger sphere of usefulness. John reminds his disciples that Jesus would not have thus excelled him <hi type="italic">except he had received it from heaven,</hi> for, as <hi type="italic">man</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mediator,</hi> he <hi type="italic">received gifts;</hi> and, if God gave him <hi type="italic">the Spirit without measure</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">v. 34</reference>), shall they grudge at it? The same reason will hold as to others. If God is <hi type="italic">pleased</hi> to give to others more ability and success than to us, shall we be displeased at it, and reflect upon him as unjust, unwise, and partial? See <reference osisRef="Matt.20.15">Matt. xx. 15</reference>. [2.] Why we should not be <hi type="italic">discontented,</hi> though we be inferior to others in gifts and usefulness, and be eclipsed by their excellencies. John was ready to own that it was the gift, the free gift, of heaven, that made him a preacher, a prophet, a baptist: it was God that gave him the interest he had in the love and esteem of the people; and, if now his interest decline, God's will be done! He that <hi type="italic">gives</hi> may <hi type="italic">take.</hi> What we <hi type="italic">receive</hi> from heaven we must take as it is <hi type="italic">given.</hi> Now John never received a commission for a standing <hi type="italic">perpetual</hi> office, but only for a <hi type="italic">temporary</hi> one, which must soon expire; and therefore, when he has fulfilled his ministry, he can contentedly see it go out of date. Some give quite another sense of these words: John had taken pains with his disciples, to teach them the reference which his baptism had to Christ, who should come after him, and yet be preferred before him, and do that for them which he could not do; and yet, after all, they dote upon John, and grudge this preference of Christ above him: Well saith John, I see <hi type="italic">a man can receive</hi> (that is, perceive) <hi type="italic">nothing, except it be given him from heaven.</hi> The labour of ministers if all lost labour, unless the grace of God make it effectual. Men do not understand that which is made most <hi type="italic">plain,</hi> nor believe that which is made most <hi type="italic">evident,</hi> unless it be given them from heaven to understand and believe it. <div eID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26831" type="x-p"/> (2.) John appeals to the testimony he had formerly given concerning Christ (<reference osisRef="John.3.28">v. 28</reference>): You can bear me witness that I said, again and again, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ, but I am sent before him.</hi> See how steady and constant John was in his testimony to Christ, and not as a <hi type="italic">reed shaken with the wind;</hi> neither the frowns of the chief priests, nor the flatteries of his own disciples, could make him change his note. Now this serves here, [1.] As a <hi type="italic">conviction</hi> to his disciples of the unreasonableness of their complaint. They had spoken of the witness which their master bore to Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>): "Now," saith John, "do you not remember what the testimony was that I did bear? Call that to mind, and you will see your own cavil answered. Did I not say, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ?</hi> Why then do you set me up as a rival with him that is? Did I not say, <hi type="italic">I am sent before him?</hi> Why then does it seem strange to you that I should stand by and give way to him?" [2.] It is a <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> to himself that he had never <hi type="italic">given</hi> his disciples <hi type="italic">any occasion</hi> thus to set him up in competition with Christ; but, on the contrary, had particularly <hi type="italic">cautioned</hi> them against this mistake, though he might have made a hand of it for himself. It is a satisfaction to faithful ministers when they have done what they could in their places to prevent any extravagances that their people ran into. John had not only not encouraged them to hope that he was the Messiah, but had plainly told them the contrary, which was now a satisfaction to him. It is a common excuse for those who have undue honour paid them, <hi type="italic">Si populus vult decipi, decipiatur—If the people will be deceived, let them;</hi> but that is an ill maxim for those to go by whose business it is to <hi type="italic">undeceive</hi> people. <hi type="italic">The lip of truth shall be established.</hi> <div eID="gen26831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26832" type="x-p"/> (3.) John professes the great satisfaction he had in the advancement of Christ and his interest. He was so far from <hi type="italic">regretting</hi> it, as his disciples did, that he <hi type="italic">rejoiced</hi> in it. This he expresses (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">v. 29</reference>) by an elegant similitude. [1.] He compares our Saviour to the <hi type="italic">bridegroom: "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom.</hi> Do <hi type="italic">all men come to him?</hi> It is well, whither else should they go? Has he got the throne in men's affections? Who else should have it? It is his right; to whom should the bride be brought but to the bridegroom?" Christ was prophesied of in the Old Testament as a bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">Ps. xlv</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Word was made flesh,</hi> that the disparity of nature might not be a <hi type="italic">bar to the match.</hi> Provision is made for the purifying of the church, that the defilement of sin might be no bar. Christ espouses his church to himself; he <hi type="italic">has</hi> the bride, for he has her love, he has her promise; <hi type="italic">the church is subject to Christ.</hi> As far as particular souls are devoted to him in faith and love, so far the bridegroom has the bride. [2.] He compares himself to the <hi type="italic">friend of the bridegroom,</hi> who attends upon him, to do him honour and service, assists him in prosecuting the match, speaks a good word for him, uses his interest on his behalf, rejoices when the match goes on, and most of all when the point is gained, and he <hi type="italic">has the bride.</hi> All that John had done in preaching and baptizing was to introduce him; and, now that he was come, he had what he wished for: <hi type="italic">The friend of the bridegroom stands, and hears him;</hi> stands expecting him, and waiting for him; <hi type="italic">rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice,</hi> because he is come to the marriage after he had been long expected. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Faithful ministers are friends of the bridegroom, to recommend him to the affections and choice of the children of men; to bring letters and messages from him, for he courts by proxy; and herein they must be faithful to him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The friends of the bridegroom must <hi type="italic">stand, and hear the bridegroom's voice;</hi> must receive instructions from him, and attend his orders; must desire to have proofs of Christ speaking in them, and with them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.3">2 Cor. xiii. 3</reference>); that is the <hi type="italic">bridegroom's voice. Thirdly,</hi> The espousing of souls to Jesus Christ, in faith and love, is the fulfilling of the joy of every good minister. If the day of Christ's espousals be the day of the gladness of his heart (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>), it cannot but be of their too who love him and wish well to his honour and kingdom. Surely they have <hi type="italic">no greater joy.</hi> <div eID="gen26832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26833" type="x-p"/> (4.) He owns it highly fit and necessary that the reputation and interest of Christ should be advanced, and his own diminished (<reference osisRef="John.3.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">He must increase, but I must decrease.</hi> If they grieve at the growing greatness of the Lord Jesus, they will have more and more occasion to grieve, as those have that indulge themselves in envy and emulation. John speaks of Christ's increase and his own decrease, not only as <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> and <hi type="italic">unavoidable,</hi> which could not be <hi type="italic">helped</hi> and therefore must be <hi type="italic">borne,</hi> but as highly <hi type="italic">just</hi> and <hi type="italic">agreeable,</hi> and affording him entire satisfaction. [1.] He was <hi type="italic">well pleased</hi> to see the kingdom of Christ getting ground: "<hi type="italic">He must increase.</hi> You think he has gained a great deal, but it is nothing to what he will gain." Note, The kingdom of Christ is, and will be, a growing kingdom, like the light of the morning, like the grain of mustard-seed. [2.] He was not at all <hi type="italic">displeased</hi> that the effect of this was the diminishing of his own interest: <hi type="italic">I must decrease.</hi> Created excellencies are under this law, they <hi type="italic">must decrease. I have seen an end of all perfection.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The shining forth of the glory of Christ eclipses the lustre of all other glory. The glory that stands in <hi type="italic">competition</hi> with Christ, that of the world and the flesh, decreases and loses ground in the soul as the knowledge and love of Christ increase and get ground; but it is here spoken of that which is <hi type="italic">subservient</hi> to him. As the light of the morning increases, that of the morning star decreases. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> If our diminution or abasement may but in the least contribute to the advancement of Christ's name, we must cheerfully submit to it, and be content to be <hi type="italic">any thing,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">nothing,</hi> so that Christ may be <hi type="italic">all.</hi> <div eID="gen26833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26834" type="x-p"/> 2. John Baptist here <hi type="italic">advances</hi> Christ, and instructs his disciples concerning him, that, instead of grieving that so many come to him, they might come to him themselves. <div eID="gen26834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26835" type="x-p"/> (1.) He instructs them concerning the <hi type="italic">dignity of Christ's person</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that cometh from above,</hi> that <hi type="italic">cometh from heaven, is above all.</hi> Here, [1.] He supposes his divine origin, that he came <hi type="italic">from above,</hi> from <hi type="italic">heaven,</hi> which bespeaks not only his divine extraction, but his divine nature. He had a being before his conception, a heavenly being. None but he that came from heaven was fit to show us the will of heaven, or the way to heaven. When God would save man, he <hi type="italic">sent from above.</hi> [2.] Hence he infers his sovereign authority: he is <hi type="italic">above all,</hi> above all things and all persons, <hi type="italic">God over all, blessed for evermore.</hi> It is daring presumption to dispute precedency with him. When we come to speak of the honours of the Lord Jesus, we find they transcend all conception and expression, and we can say but this, <hi type="italic">He is above all.</hi> It was said of John Baptist, <hi type="italic">There is not a greater among them that are born of women.</hi> But the descent of Christ from heaven put such a dignity upon him as he was not divested of by his being made flesh; still he was <hi type="italic">above all.</hi> This he further illustrates by the meanness of those who stood in competition with him: <hi type="italic">He that is of the earth, is earthly,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho on ek tes ges, ek tes ges esti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He that is of the earth is of the earth;</hi> he that has his origin of the earth has his food out of the earth, has his converse with earthly things, and his concern is for them. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Man has his rise out of the earth; not only Adam at first, but we also still are <hi type="italic">formed out of the clay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job xxxiii. 6</reference>. Look to the rock whence we were hewn. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Man's constitution is therefore <hi type="italic">earthly;</hi> not only his body frail and mortal, but his soul corrupt and carnal, and its bent and bias strong towards earthly things. The prophets and apostles were of the same mould with other men; they were but <hi type="italic">earthen vessels,</hi> though they had a rich treasure lodged in them; and shall these be set up as rivals with Christ? <hi type="italic">Let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth;</hi> but let them not cope with him that <hi type="italic">came from heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen26835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26836" type="x-p"/> (2.) Concerning the <hi type="italic">excellency and certainty of his doctrine.</hi> His disciples were displeased that Christ's preaching was admired, and attended upon, more than his; but he tells them that there was reason enough for it. For, <div eID="gen26836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26837" type="x-p"/> [1.] He, for his part, <hi type="italic">spoke of the earth,</hi> and so do all those that are <hi type="italic">of the earth.</hi> The prophets were men and spoke like men; <hi type="italic">of themselves</hi> they could not speak but <hi type="italic">of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2 Cor. iii. 5</reference>. The preaching of the prophets and of John was but low and flat compared with Christ's preaching; as heaven is high above the earth, so were his thoughts above theirs. By them God spoke <hi type="italic">on earth,</hi> but in Christ he speaketh <hi type="italic">from heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen26837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> [2.] But he that cometh from heaven is not only in his person, but in his doctrine, above all the prophets that ever lived on earth; none teacheth like him. The doctrine of Christ is here recommended to us, <div eID="gen26838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26839" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As infallibly <hi type="italic">sure</hi> and <hi type="italic">certain,</hi> and to be entertained accordingly (<reference osisRef="John.3.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">What he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth.</hi> See here, 1. Christ's divine knowledge; he testified nothing but <hi type="italic">what he had seen and heard,</hi> what he was perfectly apprized of and thoroughly acquainted with. What he discovered of the divine nature and of the invisible world was what he had <hi type="italic">seen;</hi> what he revealed of the mind of God was what he had <hi type="italic">heard</hi> immediately from him, and not at second hand. The prophets testified what was made known to them in creams and visions by the mediation of angels, but not what they had seen and heard. John was the crier's <hi type="italic">voice,</hi> that said, "<hi type="italic">Make room for the witness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep silence</hi> while the charge is given," but then leaves it to the witness to give in his testimony himself, and the judge to give the charge himself. The gospel of Christ is not a doubtful opinion, like an hypothesis or new notion in philosophy, which every one is at liberty to believe or not; but it is a revelation of the mind of God, which is of <hi type="italic">eternal truth</hi> in itself, and of <hi type="italic">infinite concern</hi> to us. 2. His divine grace and goodness: that which he had <hi type="italic">seen</hi> and <hi type="italic">heard</hi> he was pleased to make known to us, because he knew it nearly concerned us. What Paul had seen and heard in the third heavens he could not testify (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2 Cor. xii. 4</reference>), but Christ knew how to utter what he had <hi type="italic">seen</hi> and <hi type="italic">heard.</hi> Christ's preaching is here called his <hi type="italic">testifying,</hi> to denote, (1.) The <hi type="italic">convincing evidence</hi> of it; it was not <hi type="italic">reported</hi> as news by hearsay, but it was <hi type="italic">testified</hi> as evidence given in court, with great caution and assurance. (2.) The affectionate earnestness of the delivery of it: it was testified with concern and importunity, as <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Acts xviii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen26839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26840" type="x-p"/> From the <hi type="italic">certainty</hi> of Christ's doctrine, John takes occasion, [1.] To lament the infidelity of the most of men: though he testifies what is infallibly true, yet <hi type="italic">no man re</hi>ceiveth his testimony, that is, very few, next to none, none in comparison with those that refuse it. They receive it not, they will not hear it, they do not heed it, or give credit to it. This he speaks of not only as a matter of <hi type="italic">wonder,</hi> that such a testimony should not be received (Who hath believed our report? How stupid and foolish are the greatest part of mankind, what enemies to themselves!) but as matter of <hi type="italic">grief;</hi> John's disciples grieved that <hi type="italic">all men came to Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.26">v. 26</reference>); they thought his followers too many. But John grieves that <hi type="italic">no man came to him;</hi> he thought them too few. Note, The unbelief of sinners is the grief of saints. It was for this that St. Paul had <hi type="italic">great heaviness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.2">Rom. ix. 2</reference>. [2.] He takes occasion to commend the faith of the chosen remnant (<reference osisRef="John.3.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hath received his testimony</hi> (and some such there were, though very few) hath <hi type="italic">set to his seal that God is true.</hi> God is true, though we do not <hi type="italic">set our seal to it;</hi> let God be true, and every man a liar; his truth needs not our faith to support it, but by faith we do ourselves the honour and justice to subscribe to his truth, and hereby God reckons himself honoured. God's promises are all <hi type="italic">yea and amen;</hi> by faith we put our <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to them, as <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Rev. xxii. 20</reference>. Observe, He that receives the testimony of Christ subscribes not only to the truth of Christ, but to the truth of <hi type="italic">God,</hi> for his name is the <hi type="italic">Word of God;</hi> the commandments of God and the testimony of Christ are put together, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.17">Rev. xii. 17</reference>. By believing in Christ we set to our seal, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That God is true to all the promises which he has made <hi type="italic">concerning Christ,</hi> that which he spoke by the mouth of <hi type="italic">all his holy prophets;</hi> what he <hi type="italic">swore to our fathers</hi> is all accomplished, and not one iota or tittle of it fallen to the ground, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.70 Acts.13.32-Acts.13.33">Luke i. 70, &c. Acts xiii. 32, 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he is true to all the promises he has made <hi type="italic">in Christ;</hi> we venture our souls upon God's veracity, being satisfied that he is <hi type="italic">true;</hi> we are willing to deal with him <hi type="italic">upon trust,</hi> and to quit all in this world for a happiness in reversion and out of sight. By this we greatly honour God's faithfulness. Whom we <hi type="italic">give credit</hi> to we <hi type="italic">give honour</hi> to. <div eID="gen26840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is recommended to us as a <hi type="italic">divine</hi> doctrine; not his own, but <hi type="italic">his that sent</hi> him (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">For he whom God hath sent speaketh the word of God,</hi> which he was sent to speak, and enabled to speak; <hi type="italic">for God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him.</hi> The prophets were as messengers that brought letters from heaven; but Christ came under the character of an <hi type="italic">ambassador,</hi> and treats with us as such; for, 1. He spoke the <hi type="italic">words of God,</hi> and nothing he said savoured of human infirmity; both substance and language were divine. He proved himself <hi type="italic">sent of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>), and therefore his words are to be received as the words of God. By this rule we may try the spirits: those that speak <hi type="italic">as the oracles of God,</hi> and prophesy <hi type="italic">according to the proportion of faith,</hi> are to be received as <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> 2. He spoke as no other prophet did; for <hi type="italic">God giveth not the Spirit by measure to him.</hi> None can speak the <hi type="italic">words of God</hi> without the <hi type="italic">Spirit of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10-1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 10, 11</reference>. The Old-Testament prophets had the Spirit, and in different degrees, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.9-2Kgs.2.10">2 Kings ii. 9, 10</reference>. But, whereas God gave them the Spirit by <hi type="italic">measure</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1 Cor. xii. 4</reference>), he gave him to Christ <hi type="italic">without measure;</hi> all fulness dwelt in him, the fulness of the Godhead, an immeasurable fulness. The Spirit was not in Christ as in a vessel, but as in a fountain, as in a bottomless ocean. "The prophets that had the Spirit in a limited manner, only with respect to some particular revelation, sometimes spoke of <hi type="italic">themselves;</hi> but he that had the Spirit always residing in him, without stint, always spoke <hi type="italic">the words of God.</hi>" So Dr. Whitby. <div eID="gen26841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26842" type="x-p"/> (3.) Concerning <hi type="italic">the power and authority he is invested with,</hi> which gives him the pre-eminence above all others, and a more excellent name than they. <div eID="gen26842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26843" type="x-p"/> [1.] He is the <hi type="italic">beloved Son of the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Father loveth the Son.</hi> The prophets were faithful as servants, but Christ as a Son; they were employed as servants, but Christ <hi type="italic">beloved</hi> as a son, always <hi type="italic">his delight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. The Father was well pleased in him; not only he <hi type="italic">did</hi> love him, but he <hi type="italic">doth</hi> love him; he continued his love to him even in his estate of humiliation, loved him never the less for his poverty and sufferings. <div eID="gen26843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26844" type="x-p"/> [2.] He is <hi type="italic">Lord of all.</hi> The Father, as an evidence of his love for him, <hi type="italic">hath given all things into his hand.</hi> Love is generous. The Father took such a complacency and had such a confidence in him that he constituted him the great <hi type="italic">feoffee in trust</hi> for mankind. Having given <hi type="italic">him the Spirit without measure,</hi> he gave him <hi type="italic">all things;</hi> for he was hereby qualified to be master and manager of all. Note, It is the honour of Christ, and the unspeakable comfort of all Christians, that the Father hath <hi type="italic">given all things</hi> into the hands of the Mediator. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> All <hi type="italic">power;</hi> so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Matt. xxviii. 18</reference>. All the works of creation being put under his feet, all the affairs of redemption are put into his hand; he is Lord of all. Angels are his servants; devils are his captives. He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh,</hi> the <hi type="italic">heathen</hi> given <hi type="italic">him for his inheritance.</hi> The kingdom of providence is committed to his administration. He has power to settle the terms of the covenant of peace as the great <hi type="italic">plenipotentiary,</hi> to govern his church as the great <hi type="italic">lawgiver,</hi> to dispense divine favours as the great <hi type="italic">almoner,</hi> and to call all to account as the great <hi type="italic">Judge.</hi> Both the golden sceptre and the iron rod are given into his hand. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> All <hi type="italic">grace</hi> is given into his hand as the channel of conveyance; <hi type="italic">all things,</hi> all those good things which God intended to give to the children of men; <hi type="italic">eternal life,</hi> and all its preliminaries. We are unworthy that the Father should give those things <hi type="italic">into our hands,</hi> for we have made ourselves the <hi type="italic">children of his wrath;</hi> he hath therefore appointed the <hi type="italic">Son of his love</hi> to be trustee for us, and the things he intended for us he gives <hi type="italic">into his hands,</hi> who is worthy, and has merited both honours for himself and favours for us. They are given <hi type="italic">into his hands,</hi> by him to be given into ours. This is a great encouragement to faith, that the riches of the new covenant are deposited in so sure, so kind, so good a hand, the hand of him that purchased them for us, and us for himself, who is able to keep all that which both God and believers have agreed to <hi type="italic">commit to him.</hi> <div eID="gen26844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26845" type="x-p"/> [3.] He is the object of that faith which is made the great condition of eternal happiness, and herein he has the pre-eminence above all others: <hi type="italic">He that believeth on the Son, hath life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.36">v. 36</reference>. We have here the application of what he had said concerning Christ and his doctrine; and it is the <hi type="italic">conclusion of the whole matter.</hi> If God has put this honour upon the Son, we must by faith give honour to him. As God offers and conveys good things to us by the <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> of Jesus Christ, whose word is the vehicle of divine favours, so we receive and partake of those favours by <hi type="italic">believing</hi> the testimony, and entertaining that word as <hi type="italic">true</hi> and <hi type="italic">good;</hi> this way of <hi type="italic">receiving</hi> fitly answers that way of <hi type="italic">giving.</hi> We have here the sum of that gospel which is to be preached to every creature, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen26845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The blessed state of all true Christians: <hi type="italic">He that believes on the Son hath everlasting life.</hi> Note, 1. It is the character of every true Christian that he believes on <hi type="italic">the Son of God;</hi> not only <hi type="italic">believes him,</hi> that what he saith is true, but believes <hi type="italic">on him,</hi> consents to him, and confides in him. The benefit of true Christianity is no less than <hi type="italic">everlasting life;</hi> this is what Christ came to purchase for us and confer upon us; it can be no less than the happiness of an immortal soul <hi type="italic">in</hi> an immortal God. 2. True believers, even now, <hi type="italic">have</hi> everlasting life; not only they shall have it hereafter, but they have it now. For, (1.) They <hi type="italic">have</hi> very good security for it. The deed by which it passeth is sealed and delivered to them, and so they <hi type="italic">have</hi> it; it is put into the hands of their guardian for them, and so they have it, though the use be not yet transferred into possession. They have the Son of God, and in him <hi type="italic">they have life;</hi> and the Spirit of God, the earnest of this life. (2.) They have the comfortable <hi type="italic">foretastes</hi> of it, in present communion with God and the tokens of his love. Grace is glory begun.  <chapter eID="John.3"/> <div eID="gen26846" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen26849" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26848" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Journey into Galilee.</title> <div sID="gen26850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When therefore the Lord knew how the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John, 2 (Though Jesus himself baptized not, but his disciples,) 3 He left Judæa, and departed again into Galilee. <div eID="gen26850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26851" type="x-p"/> We read of Christ's coming into Judea (<reference osisRef="John.3.22">ch. iii. 22</reference>), after he had kept the feast at Jerusalem; and now he left Judea four months before harvest, as is said here (<reference osisRef="John.4.35">v. 35</reference>); so that it is computed that he staid in Judea about six months, to build upon the foundation John had laid there. We have no particular account of his sermons and miracles there, only in general, <reference osisRef="John.4.1">v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen26851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26852" type="x-p"/> I. That he <hi type="italic">made disciples;</hi> he prevailed with many to embrace his doctrine, and to follow him as a teacher come from God. His ministry was successful, notwithstanding the opposition it met with (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2-Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 2, 3</reference>); <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mathetas poiei</hi></hi>—it signifies the same with <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">matheteuo</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to disciples.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Gen. xii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">The souls which they had gotten,</hi> which they had <hi type="italic">made</hi> (so the word is), which they had <hi type="italic">made proselytes.</hi> Note, It is Christ's prerogative to <hi type="italic">make disciples,</hi> first to bring them to his foot, and then to form and fashion them to his will. <hi type="italic">Fit, non nascitur, Christianus—The Christian is made such, not born such.</hi> Tertullian. <div eID="gen26852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26853" type="x-p"/> II. That he <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> those whom he <hi type="italic">made disciples,</hi> admitted them by <hi type="italic">washing them with water;</hi> not himself, but by the ministry of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.4.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. Because he would put a difference between his baptism and that of John, who baptized all himself; for he baptized as a servant, Christ as a master. 2. He would apply himself more to preaching work, which was the more excellent, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">1 Cor. i. 17</reference>. 3. He would put honour upon his disciples, by empowering and employing them to do it; and so train them up to further services. 4. If he had baptized some himself, they would have been apt to value themselves upon that, and despise others, which he would prevent, as Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13-1Cor.1.14">1 Cor. i. 13, 14</reference>. 5. He would reserve himself for the honour of baptizing with the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.5">Acts i. 5</reference>. 6. He would teach us that the efficacy of the sacraments depends not on any virtue in the hand that administers them, as also that what is done by his ministers, according to his direction, he owns as done by himself. <div eID="gen26853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26854" type="x-p"/> III. That he made and baptized <hi type="italic">more disciples than John;</hi> not only more than John did at this time, but more than he had done at any time. Christ's converse was more winning than John's. His miracles were convincing, and the cures he wrought <hi type="italic">gratis</hi> very inviting. <div eID="gen26854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26855" type="x-p"/> IV. That the Pharisees were informed of this; they heard what multitudes he baptized, for they had, from his first appearing, a jealous eye upon him, and wanted not spies to give them notice concerning him. Observe, 1. When the Pharisees thought they had got rid of John (for he was by this time imprisoned), and were pleasing themselves with that, Jesus appears, who was a greater vexation to them than ever John had been. The witnesses will rise again. 2. That which grieved them was that Christ made so many disciples. The success of the gospel exasperates its enemies, and it is a good sign that it is getting ground when the powers of darkness are enraged against it. <div eID="gen26855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26856" type="x-p"/> V. That our Lord Jesus knew very well what informations were given in against him to the Pharisees. It is probable the informers were willing to have their names concealed, and the Pharisees loth to have their designs known; but none can dig so keep as to <hi type="italic">hide their counsels from the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa. xxix. 15</reference>), and Christ is here called <hi type="italic">the Lord.</hi> He knew what was told the Pharisees, and how much, it is likely, it exceeded the truth; for it is not likely that Jesus had yet baptized <hi type="italic">more than John;</hi> but so the thing was represented, to make him appear the more formidable; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.12">2 Kings vi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen26856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26857" type="x-p"/> VI. That hereupon our Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">left Judea</hi> and <hi type="italic">departed again</hi> to go to Galilee. <div eID="gen26857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26858" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">left Judea,</hi> because he was likely to be persecuted there even to the death; such was the rage of the Pharisees against him, and such their impious policy to devour the man-child in his infancy. To escape their designs, Christ quitted the country, and went where what he did would be less provoking than just under their eye. For, (1.) His hour was not yet come (<reference osisRef="John.7.30">ch. vii. 30</reference>), the time fixed in the counsels of God, and the Old-Testament prophecies, for Messiah's being cut off. He had not finished his testimony, and therefore would not surrender or expose himself. (2.) The disciples he had gathered in Judea were not able to bear hardships, and therefore he would not expose them. (3.) Hereby he gave an example to his own rule: <hi type="italic">When they persecute you in one city, flee to another.</hi> We are not called to suffer, while we may avoid it without sin; and therefore, though we may not, for our own preservation, change our religion, yet we may change our place. Christ secured himself, not by a miracle, but in a way <hi type="italic">common to men,</hi> for the direction and encouragement of his suffering people. <div eID="gen26858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26859" type="x-p"/> 2. He departed into Galilee, because he had work to do there, and many friends and fewer enemies. He went to Galilee now, (1.) Because John's ministry had now <hi type="italic">made way</hi> for him there; for Galilee, which was under Herod's jurisdiction, was the last scene of John's baptism. (2.) Because John's imprisonment had now <hi type="italic">made room</hi> for him there. That light being now put under a bushel, the minds of people would not be divided between him and Christ. Thus both the liberties and restraints of good ministers are for the furtherance of the gospel, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. But to what purpose does he go into Galilee for safety? Herod, the persecutor of John, will never be the protector of Jesus. Chemnitius here notes, <hi type="italic">Pii in h&#225;c vit&#180; quos fugiant habent; ad quos vero fugiant ut in tuto sint non habent, nisi ad te, Deus, qui solus regugium nostrum es</hi>—<hi type="italic">The pious have those, in this life, to whom they can fly; but they have none to fly to, who can afford them refuge, except thee, O God.</hi>

<div eID="gen26859" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ at the Well of Samaria.</title> <div sID="gen26860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And he must needs go through Samaria. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then cometh he to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with <hi type="italic">his</hi> journey, sat thus on the well: <hi type="italic">and</hi> it was about the sixth hour. <hi type="super">7</hi> There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink. <hi type="super">8</hi> (For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.) <hi type="super">9</hi> Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. <hi type="super">10</hi> Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water. <hi type="super">11</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water? <hi type="super">12</hi> Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle? <hi type="super">13</hi> Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: <hi type="super">14</hi> But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life. <hi type="super">15</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw. <hi type="super">16</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Go, call thy husband, and come hither. 17 The woman answered and said, I have no husband. Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband: <hi type="super">18</hi> For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly. <hi type="super">19</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet. <hi type="super">20</hi> Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. <hi type="super">21</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father. <hi type="super">22</hi> Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews. <hi type="super">23</hi> But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. <hi type="super">24</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship <hi type="italic">him</hi> in spirit and in truth. <hi type="super">25</hi> The woman saith unto him, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things. <hi type="super">26</hi> Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am <hi type="italic">he.</hi> <div eID="gen26860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26861" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the good Christ did in Samaria, when he <hi type="italic">passed through</hi> that country in his way to Galilee. The Samaritans, both in <hi type="italic">blood</hi> and <hi type="italic">religion,</hi> were <hi type="italic">mongrel Jews,</hi> the posterity of those colonies which the king of Assyria planted there after the captivity of the ten tribes, with whom the poor of the land that were left behind, and many other Jews afterwards, incorporated themselves. They worshipped the God of Israel only, to whom they erected a temple on mount Gerizim, in competition with that at Jerusalem. There was great enmity between them and the Jews; the Samaritans would not admit Christ, when they saw he was going to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.53">Luke ix. 53</reference>); the Jews thought they could not give him a worse name than to say, <hi type="italic">He is a Samaritan.</hi> When the Jews were in prosperity, the Samaritans claimed kindred to them (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezra iv. 2</reference>), but, when the Jews were in distress, they were Medes and Persians; see Joseph. <hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 11. 340-341; 12. 257. Now observe, <div eID="gen26861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26862" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's coming into Samaria. He charged his disciples not to <hi type="italic">enter into any city of the Samaritans</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">Matt. x. 5</reference>), that is, not to preach the gospel, or work miracles; nor did he here preach publicly, or work any miracle, his eye being to <hi type="italic">the lost sheep of the house of Israel.</hi> What kindness he here did them was <hi type="italic">accidental;</hi> it was only a <hi type="italic">crumb</hi> of the children's bread that casually <hi type="italic">fell from the master's table.</hi> <div eID="gen26862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26863" type="x-p"/> 1. His <hi type="italic">road</hi> from Judea to Galilee lay through the <hi type="italic">country</hi> of Samaria (<reference osisRef="John.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He must needs go through Samaria.</hi> There was no other way, unless he would have fetched a compass on the other side <hi type="italic">Jordan,</hi> a great way about. The wicked and profane are at present so intermixed with God's Israel that, unless we will go <hi type="italic">out of the world,</hi> we cannot avoid <hi type="italic">going through</hi> the company of such, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">1 Cor. v. 10</reference>. We have therefore need of the armour or righteousness on the right hand and on the left, that we may neither give <hi type="italic">provocation</hi> to them nor contract <hi type="italic">pollution</hi> by them. We should not go into places of temptation but when we <hi type="italic">needs must;</hi> and then we should not reside in them, but <hi type="italic">hasten through</hi> them. Some think that Christ <hi type="italic">must needs</hi> go through Samaria because of the good work he had to do there; a poor woman to be converted, a lost sheep to be sought and saved. This was work his heart was upon, the <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he <hi type="italic">must needs</hi> go this way. It was happy for Samaria that it lay <hi type="italic">in Christ's way,</hi> which gave him an opportunity of calling on them. <hi type="italic">When I passed by thee, I said unto thee, Live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen26863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26864" type="x-p"/> 2. His baiting place happened to be at a <hi type="italic">city of Samaria.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen26864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26865" type="x-p"/> (1.) The place described.
