Concerning this he saith, [1.] That it was such <hi type="italic">meat</hi> as the disciples <hi type="italic">knew not of.</hi> They did not imagine that he had any design or prospect of planting his gospel among the Samaritans; this was a piece of usefulness they never thought of. Note, Christ by his gospel and Spirit does more good to the souls of men than his own disciples <hi type="italic">know of</hi> or <hi type="italic">expect.</hi> This may be said of good Christians too, who live by faith, that they have meat to eat which others know not of, joy with which a stranger does not intermeddle. Now this word made them ask, <hi type="italic">Has any man brought him aught to eat?</hi> so apt were even his own disciples to understand him after a corporal and carnal manner when he used similitudes. [2.] That the reason why his work was his meat and drink was because it was his Father's work, his Father's will: <hi type="italic">My meat is to do the will of him that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.34">v. 34</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The salvation of sinners is the <hi type="italic">will of God,</hi> and the instruction of them in order thereunto is <hi type="italic">his work.</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1 Tim. ii. 4</reference>. There is a chosen remnant whose salvation is in a particular manner his will. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ was <hi type="italic">sent into the world</hi> on this errand, to bring people to God, to know him and to be happy in him. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He made this work his business and delight. When his body needed food, his mind was so taken up with this that he forgot both hunger and thirst, both meat and drink. Nothing could be more grateful to him than doing good; when he was invited <hi type="italic">to meat</hi> he went, that he might <hi type="italic">do good,</hi> for that was his meat always. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He was not only ready upon all occasions to go to his work, but he was <hi type="italic">earnest</hi> and in care to go <hi type="italic">through</hi> it, and to <hi type="italic">finish his work</hi> in all the parts of it. He resolved never to quit it, nor lay it down, till he could say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> Many have zeal to carry them <hi type="italic">out</hi> at first, but not zeal to carry them <hi type="italic">on</hi> to the last; but our Lord Jesus was intent upon <hi type="italic">finishing his work.</hi> Our Master has herein left us an example, that we may learn to do the will of God as he did; 1. With diligence and close application, as those that make a business of it. 2. With delight and pleasure in it, as in our element. 3. With constancy and perseverance; not only minding to <hi type="italic">do,</hi> but aiming to <hi type="italic">finish,</hi> our work. <div eID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> 2. See here how Christ, having expressed his delight in <hi type="italic">his</hi> work, excites his disciples to diligence in <hi type="italic">their</hi> work; they were workers <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> and therefore should be workers <hi type="italic">like him,</hi> and make their work their <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> as he did. The work they had to do was to <hi type="italic">preach the gospel,</hi> and to set up the kingdom of the Messiah. Now this work he here compares to <hi type="italic">harvest work,</hi> the gathering in of the fruits of the earth; and this similitude he prosecutes throughout the discourse, <reference osisRef="John.4.35-John.4.38">v. 35-38</reference>. Note, gospel time is harvest time, and gospel work harvest work. The harvest is before <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> and expected; so was the gospel. Harvest time is <hi type="italic">busy</hi> time; all hands must be then at work: every one must work for <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> that he may reap of the graces and comforts of the gospel: ministers must work <hi type="italic">for God,</hi> to gather in souls to him. Harvest time is <hi type="italic">opportunity,</hi> a short and limited time, which will not last always; and harvest work is work that must be done <hi type="italic">then</hi> or not at all; so the time of the enjoyment of the gospel is a particular season, which must be improved for its proper purposes; for, once past, it cannot be recalled. The disciples were to gather in a harvest of souls for Christ. Now he here suggests three things to them to quicken them to diligence:— <div eID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> (1.) That it was <hi type="italic">necessary work,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">occasion</hi> for it very urgent and pressing (<reference osisRef="John.4.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">You say, It is four months to harvest;</hi> but I say, <hi type="italic">The fields are already white.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> [1.] A saying of Christ's disciples concerning the <hi type="italic">corn-harvest;</hi> there <hi type="italic">are yet four months, and then comes harvest,</hi> which may be taken either <hi type="italic">generally</hi>—"You say, for the encouragement of the sower at seed-time, that it will be but four months to the harvest." With us it is but about four months between the barley-sowing and the barley-harvest, probably it was so with them as to other grain; or, "Particularly, now at this time you reckon it will be four months to next harvest, according to the ordinary course of providence." The Jews' harvest began at the Passover, about Easter, much earlier in the year than ours, by which it appears that this journey of Christ from Judea to Galilee was in the winter, about the end of November, for he travelled <hi type="italic">all weathers</hi> to do good. God has not only promised us a harvest every year, but has appointed the <hi type="italic">weeks of harvest;</hi> so that we know <hi type="italic">when</hi> to expect it, and take our measures accordingly. <div eID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> [2.] A saying of Christ's concerning the <hi type="italic">gospel harvest;</hi> his heart was as much upon the fruits of his gospel as the hearts of others were upon the fruits of the earth; and to this he would lead the thoughts of his disciples: <hi type="italic">Look, the fields are already white unto the harvest. First,</hi> Here in <hi type="italic">this</hi> place, where they <hi type="italic">now</hi> were, there was harvest work for <hi type="italic">him</hi> to do. They would have him to <hi type="italic">eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.31">v. 31</reference>. "Eat!" saith he, "I have other work to do, that is more needful; <hi type="italic">look</hi> what crowds of Samaritans are coming out of the town over the fields that are ready to receive the gospel;" probably there were many now in view. People's forwardness to hear the word is a great excitement to ministers' diligence and liveliness in preaching it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In <hi type="italic">other places,</hi> all the country over, there was harvest work enough for them all to do. "<hi type="italic">Consider the regions,</hi> think of the state of the country, and you will find there are multitudes as ready to receive the gospel as a field of corn that is fully ripe is ready to be reaped." The fields were now made <hi type="italic">white to the harvest,</hi> 1. By the <hi type="italic">decree of God</hi> revealed in the prophecies of the Old Testament. Now was the time when the gathering of the people should be to Christ ( <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>), when great accessions should be made to the church and the bounds of it should be enlarged, and therefore it was time for them to be busy. It is a great encouragement to us to engage in any work for God, if we understand by the signs of the times that this is the proper season for that work, for then it will prosper. 2. By the <hi type="italic">disposition of men.</hi> John Baptist had <hi type="italic">made ready a people prepared for the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>. Since he began to preach the kingdom of God <hi type="italic">every man pressed into it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>. This, therefore, was a time for the preachers of the gospel to apply themselves to their work with the utmost vigour, to <hi type="italic">thrust in their sickle,</hi> when the harvest was ripe, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> to work now, pity that such a season should be let slip. If the corn that is <hi type="italic">ripe</hi> be not reaped, it will <hi type="italic">shed</hi> and be lost, and the fowls will pick it up. If souls that are under convictions, and have some good inclinations, be not helped now, their hopeful beginnings will come to nothing, and they will be a prey to pretenders. It was also <hi type="italic">easy</hi> to work now; when the people's hearts are <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> the work will be done <hi type="italic">suddenly,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.36">2 Chron. xxix. 36</reference>. It cannot but quicken ministers to take <hi type="italic">pains</hi> in preaching the word when they observe that people <hi type="italic">take pleasure</hi> in hearing it. <div eID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> (2.) That it was <hi type="italic">profitable</hi> and <hi type="italic">advantageous</hi> work, which they themselves would be gainers by (<reference osisRef="John.4.36">v. 36</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He that reapeth receiveth wages,</hi> and so shall you." Christ has undertaken to pay those well whom he employs in his work; for he will never do as Jehoiakim did, <hi type="italic">who used his neighbour's service without wages</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jer. xxii. 13</reference>), or those who <hi type="italic">by fraud kept back the hire of those</hi> particularly <hi type="italic">who reaped their corn-fields,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. Christ's reapers, though they cry <hi type="italic">to him</hi> day and night, shall never have cause to cry <hi type="italic">against him,</hi> nor to say they served a hard Master. He that reapeth, not only <hi type="italic">shall</hi> but <hi type="italic">does</hi> receive wages. There is a present reward in the service of Christ, and his work is <hi type="italic">its own wages.</hi> [1.] Christ's reapers have <hi type="italic">fruit: He gathereth fruit unto life eternal;</hi> that is, he shall both save himself and those that hear him, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. If the faithful reaper save his own soul, that is fruit abounding to his account, it is fruit gathered to <hi type="italic">life eternal;</hi> and if, over and above this, he be instrumental to save the souls of others too, there is <hi type="italic">fruit gathered.</hi> Souls gathered to Christ are fruit, good fruit, the fruit that Christ seeks for (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.13">Rom. i. 13</reference>); it is gathered for Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.8.11-Song.8.12">Cant. viii. 11, 12</reference>); it is gathered to <hi type="italic">life eternal.</hi> This is the comfort of faithful ministers, that their work has a tendency to the eternal salvation of precious souls. [2.] They have <hi type="italic">joy: That he that sows and they that reap may rejoice together.</hi> The minister who is the happy instrument of beginning a good work is <hi type="italic">he that sows,</hi> as John Baptist; he that is employed to carry it on and perfect it is <hi type="italic">he that reaps:</hi> and both shall rejoice together. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Though God is to have all the glory of the success of the gospel, yet faithful ministers may themselves take the comfort of it. The reapers share in the <hi type="italic">joy of harvest,</hi> though the profits belong to the master, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1 Thess. ii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those ministers who are variously gifted and employed should be so far from envying one another that they should rather mutually rejoice in each other's success and usefulness. Though all Christ's ministers are not alike <hi type="italic">serviceable,</hi> nor alike <hi type="italic">successful,</hi> yet, if they have obtained mercy of the Lord to be <hi type="italic">faithful,</hi> they shall all enter <hi type="italic">together into the joy of their Lord</hi> at last. <div eID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> (3.) That it was <hi type="italic">easy work,</hi> and work that was half done to their hands by those that were gone before them: <hi type="italic">One soweth, and another reapeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.37-John.4.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. This sometimes denotes a grievous judgment upon him that sows, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.15">Mic. vi. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deut. xxviii. 30</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt sow, and another shall reap;</hi> as <reference osisRef="Deut.6.11">Deut. vi. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not.</hi> So here. Moses, and the prophets, and John Baptist, had <hi type="italic">paved</hi> the way to the gospel, had sown the good seed which the New-Testament ministers did in effect but gather the fruit of. <hi type="italic">I send you to reap that whereon you bestowed,</hi> in comparison, no <hi type="italic">labour.</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3-Isa.40.5">Isa. xl. 3-5</reference>. [1.] This intimates <hi type="italic">two things</hi> concerning the Old-Testament ministry:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it was very much <hi type="italic">short</hi> of the New-Testament ministry. Moses and the <hi type="italic">prophets</hi> sowed, but they could not be said to <hi type="italic">reap,</hi> so little did they see of the fruit of their labours. Their writings have done much more good since they left us than ever their preaching did. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it was very <hi type="italic">serviceable</hi> to the New-Testament ministry, and made way for it. The writings of the prophets, which were read in the synagogues every sabbath day, raised people's expectations of the Messiah, and so prepared them to bid him welcome. Had it not been for the seed sown by the prophets, this Samaritan woman could not have said, <hi type="italic">We know that Messias cometh.</hi> The writings of the Old Testament are in some respects more useful to us than they could be to those to whom they were first written, because better understood by the accomplishment of them. See <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1 Pet. i. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb. iv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25-Rom.16.26">Rom. xvi. 25, 26</reference>. [2.] This also intimates <hi type="italic">two things</hi> concerning the ministry of the <hi type="italic">apostles of Christ. First,</hi> That it was a <hi type="italic">fruitful</hi> ministry: they were reapers that gathered in a great harvest of souls to Jesus Christ, and did more in seven years towards the setting up of the kingdom of God among men than the prophets of the Old Testament had done in twice so many ages. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it was much <hi type="italic">facilitated,</hi> especially among the Jews, to whom they were first sent, by the writings of the prophets. The prophets <hi type="italic">sowed in tears,</hi> crying out, <hi type="italic">We have laboured in vain;</hi> the apostles <hi type="italic">reaped in joy,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who always causeth us to triumph.</hi> Note, From the labours of ministers that are dead and gone much good fruit may be reaped by the people that <hi type="italic">survive</hi> them and the ministers that <hi type="italic">succeed</hi> them. John Baptist, and those that assisted him, had <hi type="italic">laboured,</hi> and the disciples of Christ entered into their labours, built upon their foundation, and reaped the fruit of what they sowed. See what reason we have to bless God for those that are <hi type="italic">gone before us,</hi> for their preaching and their writing, for what they <hi type="italic">did</hi> and <hi type="italic">suffered</hi> in their day, for we are <hi type="italic">entered into their labours;</hi> their studies and services have made our work the easier. And when the ancient and modern labourers, those that came into the vineyard at the third hour and those that came in at the eleventh, meet in the day of account, they will be so far from envying one another the honour of their respective services that both <hi type="italic">they that sowed</hi> and they that <hi type="italic">reaped</hi> shall rejoice together; and the great Lord of thee harvest shall have the glory of all. <div eID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> IV. The <hi type="italic">good effect</hi> which this visit Christ made to the Samaritans (<hi type="italic">en passant</hi>) had upon them, and the fruit which was now presently gathered among them, <reference osisRef="John.4.39-John.4.42">v. 39-42</reference>. See what impressions were made on them, <div eID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> 1. By the <hi type="italic">woman's testimony</hi> concerning <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> though a single testimony, and of one of no good report, and the testimony no more than this, <hi type="italic">He told me all that ever I did,</hi> yet it had a good influence upon many. One would have thought that his telling the woman of her secret sins would have made them afraid of coming to him, lest he should tell them also of their faults; but they will venture that rather than not be acquainted with one who they had reason to think was a prophet. And <hi type="italic">two things</hi> they were brought to:— <div eID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> (1.) To <hi type="italic">credit</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">word</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman.</hi> So far they <hi type="italic">believed on him</hi> that they took him for a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> and were desirous to know the mind of God from him; this is favourably interpreted as believing on him. Now observe, [1.] Who they were that believed: <hi type="italic">Many of the Samaritans,</hi> who were not of the house of Israel. Their faith was not only an <hi type="italic">aggravation</hi> of the <hi type="italic">unbelief</hi> of the Jews, from whom better might have been expected, but an <hi type="italic">earnest</hi> of the <hi type="italic">faith</hi> of the Gentiles, who would welcome that which the Jews rejected. [2.] Upon what inducement they believed: <hi type="italic">For the saying of the woman.</hi> See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How God is sometimes pleased to use very weak and unlikely instruments for the beginning and carrying on of a good work. A little maid directed a great prince to Elisha, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.2">2 Kings v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How great a matter a little fire kindles. Our Saviour, by instructing one poor woman, spread instruction to a whole town. Let not ministers be either <hi type="italic">careless</hi> in their preaching, or <hi type="italic">discouraged</hi> in it, because their hearers are <hi type="italic">few</hi> and <hi type="italic">mean;</hi> for, by doing good to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> good may be conveyed to <hi type="italic">more,</hi> and those that are more considerable. If they <hi type="italic">teach every man his neighbour,</hi> and <hi type="italic">every man his brother,</hi> a great number may learn at <hi type="italic">second hand.</hi> Philip preached the gospel to a single gentleman in his chariot upon the road, and he not only received it himself, but carried it into his country, and propagated it there. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> See how good it is to speak <hi type="italic">experimentally</hi> of Christ and the things of God. This woman could say little of Christ, but what she did say she spoke feelingly: <hi type="italic">He told me all that ever I did.</hi> Those are most likely to do good that can tell what God has done <hi type="italic">for their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were brought to <hi type="italic">court his stay</hi> among them (<reference osisRef="John.4.40">v. 40</reference>): When they were come to him <hi type="italic">they besought him that he would tarry with them.</hi> Upon the woman's report, they believed him to be a prophet, and <hi type="italic">came to him;</hi> and, when they <hi type="italic">saw</hi> him, the meanness of his appearance and the manifest poverty of his outward condition did not lessen their esteem of him and expectations from him, but still they respected him as a prophet. Note, There is hope of those who are got over the vulgar prejudices that men have against <hi type="italic">true worth</hi> in a <hi type="italic">low estate.</hi> Blessed are they that are not offended in Christ at the <hi type="italic">first sight.</hi> So far were they from being offended in him that they begged he would tarry with them; [1.] That they might <hi type="italic">testify their respect</hi> to him, and treat him with the honour and kindness due to his character. God's prophets and ministers are welcome guests to all those who sincerely embrace the gospel; as to Lydia, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.15">Acts xvi. 15</reference>. [2.] That they might receive instruction from him. Those that are taught of God are truly desirous to learn more, and to be better acquainted with Christ. Many would have flocked to one that would tell them <hi type="italic">their fortune,</hi> but these flocked to one that would tell them <hi type="italic">their faults,</hi> tell them of their sin and duty. The historian seems to lay an emphasis upon their being Samaritans; as <reference osisRef="Luke.10.33">Luke x. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.17.16">xvii. 16</reference>. The Samaritans had not that reputation for religion which the Jews had; yet the Jews, who saw Christ's miracles, drove him from them: while the Samaritans, who saw not his miracles, nor shared in his favours, invited him to them. The <hi type="italic">proof</hi> of the gospel's success is not always according to the <hi type="italic">probability,</hi> nor what is <hi type="italic">experienced</hi> according to what is <hi type="italic">expected</hi> either way. The Samaritans were taught by the custom of their country to be shy of conversation with the Jews. There were Samaritans that refused to let Christ go through their town (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.53">Luke ix. 53</reference>), but these begged him to tarry with them. Note, It adds much to the praise of our love to Christ and his word if it conquers the prejudices of education and custom, and sets light by the censures of men. Now we are told that Christ granted their request. <div eID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He <hi type="italic">abode there.</hi> Though it was a city of the Samaritans nearly adjoining to their temple, yet, when he was <hi type="italic">invited,</hi> he <hi type="italic">tarried</hi> there; though he was upon a journey, and had further to go, yet, when he had an opportunity of doing good, he <hi type="italic">abode there.</hi> That is no real <hi type="italic">hindrance</hi> which will <hi type="italic">further</hi> our account. Yet he abode there but <hi type="italic">two days,</hi> because he had other places to visit and other work to do, and those <hi type="italic">two</hi> days were as many as came to the share of this city, out of the few days of our Saviour's sojourning upon earth. <div eID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We are told what impressions were made upon them by Christ's own word, and his personal converse with them (<reference osisRef="John.4.41-John.4.42">v. 41, 42</reference>); what he <hi type="italic">said</hi> and <hi type="italic">did</hi> there is not related, whether he healed their sick or no; but it is intimated, in the effect, that he said and did that which convinced them that he was the Christ; and the labours of a minister are best told by the good fruit of them. Their hearing of <hi type="italic">him</hi> had a good effect, but <hi type="italic">now their eyes saw him;</hi> and the effect was, 1. That their number grew (<reference osisRef="John.4.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many more believed:</hi> many that would not be persuaded to go out of the town to him were yet wrought upon, when he came among them, to believe in him. Note, It is comfortable to see the number of believers; and sometimes the zeal and forwardness of some may be a means to provoke many, and to stir them up to a holy emulation, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>. 2. That their faith grew. Those who had been wrought upon by the report of the woman now saw cause to say, <hi type="italic">Now we believe, not because of thy saying,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.42">v. 42</reference>. Here are three things in which their <hi type="italic">faith grew:</hi>—(1.) In the matter of it, or that which they did believe. Upon the testimony of the woman, they believed him to be <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> or some extraordinary messenger from heaven; but now that they have conversed with him they believe that he is <hi type="italic">the Christ,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Anointed One,</hi> the very same that was promised to the fathers and expected by them, and that, being the <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> he is the <hi type="italic">Saviour of the world;</hi> for the work to which he was anointed was to <hi type="italic">save his people from their sins.</hi> They believed him to be the Saviour not only of the Jews, but <hi type="italic">of the world,</hi> which they hoped would take them in, though Samaritans, for it was promised that he should be <hi type="italic">Salvation to the ends of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">Isa. xlix. 6</reference>. (2.) In the <hi type="italic">certainty</hi> of it; their faith now grew up to a full assurance: <hi type="italic">We know</hi> that this is indeed the <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alethos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">truly;</hi> not a pretended Christ, but a real one; not a <hi type="italic">typical</hi> Saviour, as many under the Old Testament, but <hi type="italic">truly</hi> one. Such an assurance as this of divine truths is what we should labour after; not only, We think it probable, and are willing to suppose that <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> may be the <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> but, We know that he is <hi type="italic">indeed the Christ.</hi> (3.) In the <hi type="italic">ground</hi> of it, which was a kind of spiritual sensation and experience: <hi type="italic">Now we believe, not because of thy saying, for we have heard him ourselves.</hi> They had before <hi type="italic">believed for her saying,</hi> and it was well, it was a good step; but now they find <hi type="italic">further</hi> and much <hi type="italic">firmer</hi> footing for their faith: "<hi type="italic">Now we believe</hi> because we have <hi type="italic">heard him ourselves,</hi> and have heard such excellent and divine truths, accompanied with such commanding power and evidence, that we are abundantly satisfied and assured that <hi type="italic">this is the Christ.</hi>" This is like what the queen of Sheba said of Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.6-1Kgs.10.7">1 Kings x. 6, 7</reference>): The <hi type="italic">one half was not told me.</hi> The Samaritans, who believed for the woman's saying, now gained further light; for <hi type="italic">to him that hath shall be given;</hi> he that is faithful in a little shall be trusted with more. In this instance we may see how <hi type="italic">faith comes by hearing.</hi> [1.] Faith comes <hi type="italic">to the birth</hi> by hearing the <hi type="italic">report of men.</hi> These Samaritans, for the sake of the woman's saying, believed so far as to <hi type="italic">come and see,</hi> to come and make trial. Thus the instructions of parents and preachers, and the testimony of the church and our experienced neighbours, <hi type="italic">recommend</hi> the doctrine of Christ <hi type="italic">to our acquaintance,</hi> and incline us to entertain it as highly probable. But, [2.] Faith <hi type="italic">comes to its growth,</hi> strength, and maturity, by hearing the testimony of Christ himself; and this goes further, and recommends his doctrine <hi type="italic">to our acceptance,</hi> and obliges us to believe it as undoubtedly certain. We were induced to look into the scriptures <hi type="italic">by the saying</hi> of those who told us that in them they had found eternal life; but when we ourselves have found it in them too, have experienced the enlightening, convincing, regenerating, sanctifying, comforting, power of the word, now we believe, <hi type="italic">not for their saying,</hi> but because we have searched them ourselves: and our faith <hi type="italic">stands not in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.5">1 Cor. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.9-1John.5.10">1 John v. 9, 10</reference>.

<div eID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Nobleman's Son Restored.</title> <div sID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> Now after two days he departed thence, and went into Galilee. <hi type="super">44</hi> For Jesus himself testified, that a prophet hath no honour in his own country. <hi type="super">45</hi> Then when he was come into Galilee, the Galilæans received him, having seen all the things that he did at Jerusalem at the feast: for they also went unto the feast. <hi type="super">46</hi> So Jesus came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made the water wine. And there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum. <hi type="super">47</hi> When he heard that Jesus was come out of Judæa into Galilee, he went unto him, and besought him that he would come down, and heal his son: for he was at the point of death. <hi type="super">48</hi> Then said Jesus unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe. <hi type="super">49</hi> The nobleman saith unto him, Sir, come down ere my child die. <hi type="super">50</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way. <hi type="super">51</hi> And as he was now going down, his servants met him, and told <hi type="italic">him,</hi> saying, Thy son liveth. <hi type="super">52</hi> Then enquired he of them the hour when he began to amend. And they said unto him, Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. <hi type="super">53</hi> So the father knew that <hi type="italic">it was</hi> at the same hour, in the which Jesus said unto him, Thy son liveth: and himself believed, and his whole house. <hi type="super">54</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> again the second miracle <hi type="italic">that</hi> Jesus did, when he was come out of Judæa into Galilee. <div eID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's <hi type="italic">coming</hi> into Galilee, <reference osisRef="John.4.43">v. 43</reference>. Though he was as welcome among the Samaritans as he could be any where, and had better success, yet <hi type="italic">after two days</hi> he left them, not so much because they were Samaritans, and he would not confirm those in their prejudices against him who said, <hi type="italic">He is a Samaritan</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.48">ch. viii. 48</reference>), but because <hi type="italic">he must preach to other cities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.4.43">Luke iv. 43</reference>. <hi type="italic">He went into Galilee,</hi> for there he spent much of his time. Now see here, <div eID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> 1. Whither Christ went; into Galilee, into the country of Galilee, but not to Nazareth, which was strictly <hi type="italic">his own</hi> country. He went among the villages, but declined going to Nazareth, the head city, for a reason here given, which <hi type="italic">Jesus himself testified,</hi> who knew the temper of his countrymen, the hearts of all men, and the experiences of all prophets, and it is this, That <hi type="italic">a prophet has no honour in his own country.</hi> Note, (1.) Prophets ought to have honour, because God has put honour upon them and we do or may receive benefit by them. (2.) The honour due to the Lord's prophets has very often been denied them, and contempt put upon them. (3.) This <hi type="italic">due</hi> honour is more frequently denied them <hi type="italic">in their own country;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Luke.4.24">Luke iv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.57">Matt. xiii. 57</reference>. Not that it is universally true (no rule but has some exceptions), but it holds for the most part. Joseph, when he began to be a prophet, was most hated by his brethren; David was disdained by his brother (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.28">1 Sam. xvii. 28</reference>); Jeremiah was maligned by the men of Anathoth (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">Jer. xi. 21</reference>), Paul by his countrymen the Jews; and Christ's near kinsmen spoke most slightly of him, <reference osisRef="John.7.5">ch. vii. 5</reference>. Men's pride and envy make them scorn to be instructed by those who once were their school-fellows and play-fellows. Desire of novelty, and of that which is far-fetched and dear-bought, and seems to drop out of the sky to them, makes them despise those persons and things which they have been long used to and know the rise of. (4.) It is a great discouragement to a minister to go among a people who have no value for him or his labours. Christ would not go to Nazareth, because he knew how little respect he should have there. (5.) It is just with God to deny his gospel to those that despise the ministers of it. They that mock the messengers forfeit the benefit of the message. <reference osisRef="Matt.21.35">Matt. xxi. 35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.41">41</reference>. <div eID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> 2. What entertainment he met with among the Galileans in the country (<reference osisRef="John.4.45">v. 45</reference>): They <hi type="italic">received him,</hi> bade him welcome, and cheerfully attended on his doctrine. Christ and his gospel are not sent in vain; if they have not honour with <hi type="italic">some,</hi> they shall have with <hi type="italic">others.</hi> Now the reason given why these Galileans were so ready to receive Christ is because they had seen <hi type="italic">the miracles he did at Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.45">v. 45</reference>. Observe, (1.) They went up to Jerusalem at the feast, the feast of the passover. The Galileans lay very remote from Jerusalem, and their way thither lay through the country of the Samaritans, which was troublesome for a Jew to pass through, worse than Baca's valley of old; yet, in obedience to God's command, they <hi type="italic">went up to the feast,</hi> and there they became acquainted with Christ. Note, They that are diligent and constant in attending on public ordinances some time or other meet with more spiritual benefit than they expect. (2.) At Jerusalem they <hi type="italic">saw</hi> Christ's miracles, which recommended him and his doctrine very much to their faith and affections. The miracles were wrought for the benefit of those at Jerusalem; yet the Galileans who were accidentally there got more advantage by them than they did for whom they were chiefly designed. Thus the word preached to a <hi type="italic">mixed multitude</hi> may perhaps edify <hi type="italic">occasional</hi> hearers more than the constant auditory. <div eID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> 3. What city he went to. When he would go to a city, he chose to go to Cana of Galilee, <hi type="italic">where he had made the water wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.46">v. 46</reference>); thither he went, to see if there were any good fruits of that miracle remaining; and, if there were, to confirm their faith, and water what he had planted. The evangelist mentions this miracle here to teach us to keep in remembrance what we <hi type="italic">have seen</hi> of the works of Christ. <div eID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> II. His <hi type="italic">curing</hi> the <hi type="italic">nobleman's son</hi> that was sick of a fever. This story is not recorded by any other of the evangelists; it comes in <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Matt. iv. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Who the <hi type="italic">petitioner</hi> was, and who the <hi type="italic">patient:</hi> the petitioner was a <hi type="italic">nobleman;</hi> the patient was his son: <hi type="italic">There was a certain nobleman. Regulus</hi> (so the Latin), a <hi type="italic">little king;</hi> so called, either for the largeness of his estate, or the extent of his power, or the royalties that belonged to his manor. Some understand it as denoting his <hi type="italic">preferment</hi>—he was a courtier in some office about the king; others as denoting his <hi type="italic">party</hi>—he was an Herodian, a royalist, a prerogative-man, one that espoused the interests of the Herods, father and son; perhaps it was Chuza, Herod's steward (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Luke viii. 3</reference>), or Manæn, Herod's foster-brother, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1">Acts xiii. 1</reference>. There were saints in Cæsar's household. The father a nobleman, and yet the son sick; for dignities and titles of honour will be no security to persons and families from the assaults of sickness and death. It was fifteen miles from Capernaum where this nobleman lived to Cana, where Christ now was; yet this affliction in his family sent him so far to Christ. <div eID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> 2. How the petitioner made <hi type="italic">his application</hi> to the physician. Having heard that <hi type="italic">Jesus was come out of</hi> Judea to Galilee, and finding that he did not come towards Capernaum, but turned off towards the other side of the country, he <hi type="italic">went to him</hi> himself, and <hi type="italic">besought him to come and heal his son,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.47">v. 47</reference>. See here, (1.) His <hi type="italic">tender affection</hi> to his son, that when he was sick he would spare no pains to get help for him. (2.) His <hi type="italic">great respect</hi> to our Lord Jesus, that he would come himself to wait upon him, when he might have sent a servant; and that he <hi type="italic">besought him,</hi> when, as a man in authority, some would think he might have ordered his attendance. The greatest men, when they come to God, must become beggars, and sue <hi type="italic">sub forma pauperis—as paupers.</hi> As to the errand he came upon, we may observe a mixture in <hi type="italic">his faith.</hi> [1.] There was <hi type="italic">sincerity</hi> in it; he did believe that Christ could heal his son, though his disease was dangerous. It is probable he had physicians to him, who had given him over; but he believed that Christ could cure him when the case seemed deplorable. [2.] Yet there was <hi type="italic">infirmity</hi> in his faith; he believed that Christ could heal his son, but, as it should seem, he thought he could not heal him at a distance, and therefore he besought him that he would <hi type="italic">come down</hi> and heal him, expecting, as Naaman did, that he would come and <hi type="italic">strike his hand</hi> over the patient, as if he could not cure him but by a <hi type="italic">physical contact.</hi> Thus we are apt to <hi type="italic">limit the Holy One of Israel,</hi> and to stint him to our forms. The centurion, a Gentile, a soldier, was so strong in faith as to say, <hi type="italic">Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.8">Matt. viii. 8</reference>. This nobleman, a Jew, must have Christ to come down, though it was a good day's journey, and despairs of a cure unless he come down, as if he must teach Christ how to work. We are encouraged to <hi type="italic">pray,</hi> but we are not allowed to prescribe: Lord, heal me; but, whether with a word or a touch, <hi type="italic">thy will be done.</hi> <div eID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> 3. The gentle rebuke he met with in this address (<reference osisRef="John.4.48">v. 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jesus said to him,</hi> "I see how it is; <hi type="italic">except you see signs and wonders, you will not believe,</hi> as the Samaritans did, though they saw no signs and wonders, and therefore I must work miracles among you." Though he was a <hi type="italic">nobleman,</hi> and now in <hi type="italic">grief</hi> about his son, and had shown great respect to Christ in coming so far to him, yet Christ gives him a reproof. Men's dignity in the world shall not exempt them from the rebukes of the word or providence; for Christ reproves not <hi type="italic">after the hearing of his ears,</hi> but <hi type="italic">with equity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3-Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 3, 4</reference>. Observe, Christ first shows him his sin and weakness, to prepare him for mercy, and then grants his request. Those whom Christ intends to honour with his <hi type="italic">favours</hi> he first <hi type="italic">humbles</hi> with his <hi type="italic">frowns.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Comforter</hi> shall first <hi type="italic">convince.</hi> Herod longed to see some miracle (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Luke xxiii. 8</reference>), and this courtier was of the same mind, and the generality of the people too. Now that which is blamed is, (1.) That, whereas they had heard by credible and incontestable report of the miracles he had wrought in other places, they would not believe except they saw them with their own eyes, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.23">Luke iv. 23</reference>. They must be <hi type="italic">honoured,</hi> and they must be <hi type="italic">humoured,</hi> or they will not be <hi type="italic">convinced.</hi> Their country must be graced, and their curiosity gratified, with signs and wonders, or else, though the doctrine of Christ be sufficiently proved by miracles wrought elsewhere, they <hi type="italic">will not believe.</hi> Like Thomas, they will yield to no method of conviction but what they shall prescribe. (2.) That, whereas they had seen divers miracles, the evidence of which they could not gainsay, but which sufficiently proved Christ to be a teacher come from God, and should now have applied themselves to him for instruction in his doctrine, which by its native excellency would have <hi type="italic">gently led them on,</hi> in believing, to a spiritual perfection, instead of this they would go no further in believing than they were <hi type="italic">driven</hi> by signs and wonders. The <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> power of the word did not <hi type="italic">affect them,</hi> did not <hi type="italic">attract</hi> them, but only the <hi type="italic">sensible</hi> power of miracles, which were <hi type="italic">for those</hi> who believe not, while <hi type="italic">prophesying</hi> was for <hi type="italic">those that believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1 Cor. xiv. 22</reference>. Those that admire <hi type="italic">miracles</hi> only, and <hi type="italic">despise prophesying,</hi> rank themselves with unbelievers. <div eID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> 4. His continued importunity in his address (<reference osisRef="John.4.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sir, come down ere my child die.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kyrie</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> so it should be rendered. In this reply of his we have, (1.) Something that was commendable: he took the reproof patiently; he spoke to Christ respectfully. Though he was one of those that wore soft clothing, yet he could bear reproof. It is none of the privileges of peerage to be above the reproofs of the word of Christ; but it is a sign of a good temper and disposition in men, especially in great men, when they can be told of their faults and not be angry. And, as he did not take the reproof for an affront, so he did not take it for a denial, but still prosecuted his request, and continued to wrestle till he prevailed. Nay, he might argue thus: "If Christ heal <hi type="italic">my soul,</hi> surely he will heal <hi type="italic">my son;</hi> if he cure <hi type="italic">my</hi> unbelief, he will cure <hi type="italic">his</hi> fever." This is the method Christ takes, first to work <hi type="italic">upon</hi> us, and then to work <hi type="italic">for</hi> us; and there is hope if we find him entering upon this method. (2.) Something that was blameworthy, that was his infirmity; for, [1.] He seems to take no notice of the reproof Christ gave him, says nothing to it, by way either of confession or of excuse, for he is so wholly taken up with concern about his child that he can mind nothing else. Note, The sorrow of the world is a great prejudice to our profiting by the word of Christ. Inordinate care and grief are thorns that choke the good seed; see <reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">Exod. vi. 9</reference>. [2.] He still discovered the weakness of his faith in the power of Christ. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He must have Christ to come down, thinking that else he could do the child no kindness. It is hard to persuade ourselves that distance of time and place are no obstructions to the knowledge and power of our Lord Jesus; yet so it is: he sees afar off, for his word, the word of his power, <hi type="italic">runs very swiftly. Secondly,</hi> He believes that Christ could heal a <hi type="italic">sick</hi> child, but not that he could raise a <hi type="italic">dead</hi> child, and therefore, "O <hi type="italic">come down, ere my child die,</hi>" as if then it would be too late; whereas Christ has the same power over death that he has over bodily diseases. He forgot that Elijah and Elisha had raised dead children; and is Christ's power inferior to theirs? Observe what haste he is in: <hi type="italic">Come down, ere my child die;</hi> as if there were danger of Christ's slipping his time. <hi type="italic">He that believeth does not make haste,</hi> but refers himself to Christ. "Lord, what and when and how thou pleasest." <div eID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26955" type="x-p"/> 5. The answer of peace which Christ gave to his request at last (<reference osisRef="John.4.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go thy way, thy son liveth.</hi> Christ here gives us an instance, (1.) Of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> that he not only could heal, but could heal with so much ease, without the trouble of a visit. Here is nothing <hi type="italic">said,</hi> nothing <hi type="italic">done,</hi> nothing <hi type="italic">ordered</hi> to be done, and yet the cure wrought: <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth.</hi> The healing beams of the Sun of righteousness dispense benign influences from one end of heaven to another, and <hi type="italic">there is nothing hid from the heat thereof.</hi> Though Christ is now in heaven, and his church on earth, he can <hi type="italic">send from above.</hi> This nobleman would have Christ <hi type="italic">come down and heal his son;</hi> Christ will heal his son, and not <hi type="italic">come down.</hi> And thus the cure is the sooner wrought, the nobleman's mistake rectified, and his faith confirmed; so that the thing was better done in Christ's way. When he denies what we ask, he gives what is much more to our advantage; we ask for ease, he gives patience. Observe, His power was exerted by his word. In saying, <hi type="italic">Thy son lives,</hi> he showed that he has <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and power to <hi type="italic">quicken whom he will.</hi> Christ's saying, <hi type="italic">Thy soul lives,</hi> makes it alive. (2.) Of his <hi type="italic">pity;</hi> he observed the nobleman to be <hi type="italic">in pain</hi> about his son, and his natural affection discovered itself in that word, <hi type="italic">Ere my child,</hi> my dear child, die; and therefore Christ dropped the reproof, and gave him assurance of the recovery of his child; for he knows how a father <hi type="italic">pities his children.</hi> <div eID="gen26955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26956" type="x-p"/> 6. The nobleman's belief of the word of Christ: He <hi type="italic">believed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">went away.</hi> Though Christ did not gratify him so far as to go down with him, he is satisfied with the method Christ took, and reckons he has gained his point. How quickly, how easily, is that which is lacking in our faith perfected by the word and power of Christ. Now he <hi type="italic">sees no sign or wonder,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">believes</hi> the wonder done. (1.) Christ said, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth,</hi> and the man <hi type="italic">believed</hi> him; not only believed the omniscience of Christ, that he <hi type="italic">knew</hi> the child had recovered, but the omnipotence of Christ, that the cure was <hi type="italic">effected</hi> by his word. He left him <hi type="italic">dying;</hi> yet, when Christ said, <hi type="italic">He lives,</hi> like the father of the faithful, <hi type="italic">against hope he believed in hope,</hi> and <hi type="italic">staggered not through unbelief.</hi> (2.) Christ said, <hi type="italic">Go thy way;</hi> and, as an evidence of the sincerity of his faith, he <hi type="italic">went his way,</hi> and gave neither Christ nor himself any further disturbance. He did not press Christ to come down, did not say, "If he do recover, yet a visit will be acceptable;" no, he seems no further solicitous, but, like Hannah, he goes his way, and his countenance is <hi type="italic">no more sad.</hi> As one entirely satisfied, he made no great haste home; did not hurry home that night, but returned leisurely, as one that was perfectly easy in his own mind. <div eID="gen26956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> 7. The further confirmation of his faith, by comparing notes with his servants at his return. (1.) His servants met him with the agreeable news of the child's recovery, <reference osisRef="John.4.51">v. 51</reference>. Probably they met him not far from his own house, and, knowing what their master's cares were, they were willing as soon as they could to make him easy. David's servants were loth to tell him when the child was dead. Christ said, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth;</hi> and now the servants say the same. Good news will meet those that hope in God's word. (2.) He enquired what hour the child began to recover (<reference osisRef="John.4.52">v. 52</reference>); not as if he doubted the influence of Christ's word upon the child's recovery, but he was desirous to have his faith confirmed, that he might be able to satisfy any to whom he should mention the miracle; for it was a material circumstance. Note, [1.] It is good to furnish ourselves with all the corroborating proofs and evidences that may be, to strengthen our faith in the word of Christ, that it may grow up to <hi type="italic">a full assurance. Show me a token for good.</hi> [2.] The diligent comparison of the works of Christ with his word will be of great use to us for the confirming of our faith. This was the course the nobleman took: <hi type="italic">He enquired of the servants the hour when he began to amend;</hi> and they told him, <hi type="italic">Yesterday at the seventh hour</hi> (at one o'clock in the afternoon, or, as some think this evangelist reckons, at seven o'clock at night) the <hi type="italic">fever left him;</hi> not only he began to amend, but he was perfectly well on a sudden; so <hi type="italic">the father knew that it was at the same hour</hi> when Jesus said to him, <hi type="italic">Thy son liveth.</hi> As the word of God, well-studied, will help us to understand his providences, so the providence of God, well observed, will help us to understand his word; for God is every day <hi type="italic">fulfilling the scripture.</hi> Two things would help to confirm his faith:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the child's recovery was <hi type="italic">sudden</hi> and not <hi type="italic">gradual.</hi> They name the precise time to an hour: <hi type="italic">Yesterday,</hi> not <hi type="italic">about,</hi> but <hi type="italic">at</hi> the seventh hour, <hi type="italic">the fever left him;</hi> not it <hi type="italic">abated,</hi> or began to <hi type="italic">decrease,</hi> but it <hi type="italic">left him</hi> in an instant. The word of Christ did not work like physic, which must have time to operate, and produce the effect, and perhaps <hi type="italic">cures by expectation</hi> only; no, with Christ it was <hi type="italic">dictum factum—he spoke and it was done;</hi> not, He spoke and it was <hi type="italic">set a doing. Secondly,</hi> That it was just at the same time that Christ spoke to him: <hi type="italic">at that very hour.</hi> The synchronisms and coincidents of events add very much to the beauty and harmony of Providence. Observe the <hi type="italic">time,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">thing</hi> itself will be more illustrious, for every thing is beautiful <hi type="italic">in its time;</hi> at the very time when it is <hi type="italic">promised,</hi> as Israel's deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exod. xii. 41</reference>); at the very time when it is <hi type="italic">prayed for,</hi> as Peter's deliverance, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Acts xii. 12</reference>. In men's works, distance of place is the delay of time and the retarding of business; but it is not so in the works of Christ. The pardon, and peace, and comfort, and spiritual healing, which he speaks in heaven, are, if he pleases, at the same time effected and wrought in the souls of believers; and, when these two come to be <hi type="italic">compared</hi> in the great day, Christ will be <hi type="italic">glorified in his saints, and admired in all them that believe.</hi> <div eID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> 8. The <hi type="italic">happy effect and issue of this.</hi> The bringing of the cure to the family brought salvation to it. (1.) The nobleman <hi type="italic">himself believed.</hi> He had before <hi type="italic">believed</hi> the word of Christ, with reference to this particular occasion; but now he <hi type="italic">believed in Christ</hi> as the Messiah promised, and became one of his disciples. Thus the <hi type="italic">particular</hi> experience of the power and efficacy of <hi type="italic">one</hi> word of Christ may be a happy means to introduce and settle the whole authority of Christ's dominion in the soul. Christ has many ways of gaining the heart, and by the grant of a <hi type="italic">temporal</hi> mercy may make way for <hi type="italic">better</hi> things. (2.) His <hi type="italic">whole house</hi> believed likewise. [1.] Because of the <hi type="italic">interest</hi> they all had in the miracle, which preserved the <hi type="italic">blossom</hi> and <hi type="italic">hopes</hi> of the family; this affected them all, and endeared Christ to them, and recommended him to their best thoughts. [2.] Because of the <hi type="italic">influence</hi> the master of the family had upon them <hi type="italic">all.</hi> A master of a family cannot give faith to those under his charge, nor <hi type="italic">force</hi> them to believe, but he may be instrumental to remove <hi type="italic">external prejudices,</hi> which obstruct the operation of the evidence, and then the work is more than half done. <hi type="italic">Abraham</hi> was famous for this (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>), and Joshua, <reference osisRef="John.24.15">ch. xxiv. 15</reference>. This was a <hi type="italic">nobleman,</hi> and probably he had a <hi type="italic">great household;</hi> but, when he comes into Christ's school, he brings them all along with him. What a blessed change was here in this house, occasioned by the sickness of the child! This should reconcile us to afflictions; we know not what good may follow from them. Probably, the conversion of this <hi type="italic">nobleman</hi> and his family at Capernaum might induce Christ to come afterwards, and settle at Capernaum, as his head-quarters in Galilee. When great men receive the gospel, they may be instrumental to bring it to the places where they live. <div eID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26959" type="x-p"/> 9. Here is the evangelist's remark upon this cure (<reference osisRef="John.4.54">v. 54</reference>); <hi type="italic">This is the second miracle,</hi> referring to <reference osisRef="John.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>, where the turning of water into wine is said to be the first; that was soon after his first return out of Judea, this soon after his second. In Judea he had wrought many miracles, <reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.45">iv. 45</reference>. They had the first offer; but, being driven thence, he wrought miracles in Galilee. Somewhere or other Christ will find a welcome. People may, if they please, shut the sun out of <hi type="italic">their own houses,</hi> but they cannot shut it <hi type="italic">out of the world.</hi> This is noted to be the <hi type="italic">second</hi> miracle, 1. To remind us of the first, wrought in the same place some months before. <hi type="italic">Fresh</hi> mercies should revive the remembrance of former mercies, as former mercies should encourage our hopes of further mercies. Christ keeps account of his favours, whether we do or no. 2. To let us know that <hi type="italic">this</hi> cure was <hi type="italic">before</hi> those many cures which the other evangelists mention to be wrought in Galilee, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Matt. iv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.1.34">Mark i. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.40">Luke iv. 40</reference>. Probably, the patient being a person of quality, the cure was the more talked of and sent him crowds of patients; when this nobleman applied himself to Christ, multitudes followed. What abundance of good may great men do, if they be good men!  <chapter eID="John.4"/> <div eID="gen26959" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen26962" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26961" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cure at the Pool of Bethesda.</title> <div sID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After this there was a feast of the Jews; and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep <hi type="italic">market</hi> a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches. <hi type="super">3</hi> In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water. <hi type="super">4</hi> For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had. <hi type="super">5</hi> And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years. <hi type="super">6</hi> When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time <hi type="italic">in that case,</hi> he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? <hi type="super">7</hi> The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me. <hi type="super">8</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. <hi type="super">9</hi> And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath. <hi type="super">10</hi> The Jews therefore said unto him that was cured, It is the sabbath day: it is not lawful for thee to carry <hi type="italic">thy</hi> bed. <hi type="super">11</hi> He answered them, He that made me whole, the same said unto me, Take up thy bed, and walk. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then asked they him, What man is that which said unto thee, Take up thy bed, and walk? <hi type="super">13</hi> And he that was healed wist not who it was: for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in <hi type="italic">that</hi> place. <hi type="super">14</hi> Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole. <hi type="super">16</hi> And therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus, and sought to slay him, because he had done these things on the sabbath day. <div eID="gen26963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> This miraculous cure is not recorded by any other of the evangelists, who confine themselves mostly to the miracles wrought in Galilee, but John relates those wrought at Jerusalem. Concerning this observe, <div eID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The time when</hi> this cure was wrought: it was at a <hi type="italic">feast of the Jews,</hi> that is, the passover, for that was the most celebrated feast. Christ, though residing in Galilee, yet <hi type="italic">went up to Jerusalem</hi> at the feast, <reference osisRef="John.5.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Because it was an <hi type="italic">ordinance of God,</hi> which, as a <hi type="italic">subject,</hi> he would observe, being made under the law; though as a <hi type="italic">Son</hi> he might have pleaded an exemption. Thus he would teach us to attend religious assemblies. <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">Heb. x. 25</reference>. 2. Because it was an <hi type="italic">opportunity of good;</hi> for, (1.) there were great numbers gathered together there at that time; it was a general rendezvous, at least of all serious thinking people, from all parts of the country, besides proselytes from other nations: and Wisdom must <hi type="italic">cry in the places of concourse,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>. (2.) It was to be hoped that they were in a <hi type="italic">good frame,</hi> for they came together to <hi type="italic">worship God</hi> and to spend their time in religious exercises. Now a mind <hi type="italic">inclined to devotion,</hi> and sequestering itself to the exercises of piety, <hi type="italic">lies very open</hi> to the further discoveries of divine light and love, and to it Christ will be acceptable. <div eID="gen26965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">place where</hi> this cure was wrought: at the <hi type="italic">pool of Bethesda,</hi> which had a miraculous healing virtue in it, and is here particularly described, <reference osisRef="John.5.2-John.5.4">v. 2-4</reference>. <div eID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> 1. Where it was situated: <hi type="italic">At Jerusalem, by the sheep-market;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi te probatike</hi></hi>. It might as well be rendered the <hi type="italic">sheep-cote,</hi> where the sheep were kept, or the <hi type="italic">sheep-gate,</hi> which we read of, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh. iii. 1</reference>, through which the sheep were <hi type="italic">brought,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">sheep-market,</hi> where they were <hi type="italic">sold.</hi> Some think it was near the temple, and, if so, it yielded a melancholy but profitable spectacle to those that went up to the temple to pray. <div eID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> 2. How it was called: It was a <hi type="italic">pool</hi> (a pond or bath), <hi type="italic">which is called in Hebrew, Bethesda—the house of mercy;</hi> for therein appeared much of the <hi type="italic">mercy of God</hi> to the sick and diseased. In a world of so much misery as this is, it is well that there are some <hi type="italic">Bethesdas—houses of mercy</hi> (remedies against those maladies), that the scene is not all melancholy. An <hi type="italic">alms-house,</hi> so Dr. Hammond. Dr. Lightfoot's conjecture is that this was the <hi type="italic">upper pool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Isa. vii. 3</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">old pool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa. xxii. 11</reference>; that it had been used for <hi type="italic">washing</hi> from ceremonial pollutions, for convenience of which the porches were built to dress and undress in, but it was lately become medicinal. <div eID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> 3. How it was fitted up: It had <hi type="italic">five porches, cloisters, piazzas,</hi> or <hi type="italic">roofed walks,</hi> in which the sick lay. Thus the charity of men concurred with the mercy of God for the relief of the distressed. Nature has provided <hi type="italic">remedies,</hi> but men must provide <hi type="italic">hospitals.</hi> <div eID="gen26969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> 4. How it was frequented with sick and cripples (<reference osisRef="John.5.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">In these lay a great multitude of impotent folks.</hi> How many are the afflictions of the afflicted in this world! How full of complaints are all places, and what multitudes of impotent folks! It may do us good to visit the hospitals sometimes, that we may take occasion, from the calamities of others, to thank God for our comforts. The evangelist specifies three sorts of diseased people that lay here, <hi type="italic">blind, halt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">withered</hi> or <hi type="italic">sinew—shrunk,</hi> either in one particular part, as the man with the <hi type="italic">withered hand,</hi> or all over paralytic. These are mentioned because, being least able to help themselves into the water, they lay longest waiting in the <hi type="italic">porches.</hi> Those that were sick of these bodily diseases took the pains to come <hi type="italic">far</hi> and had the patience to wait <hi type="italic">long</hi> for a cure; any of us would have done the same, and we ought to do so: but O that men were as wise for their souls, and as solicitous to get their spiritual diseases healed! We are all by nature <hi type="italic">impotent folks</hi> in spiritual things, <hi type="italic">blind, halt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">withered;</hi> but effectual provision is made for our cure if we will but observe orders. <div eID="gen26970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> 5. What virtue it had for the cure of these impotent folks (<reference osisRef="John.5.4">v. 4</reference>). <hi type="italic">An angel went down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">troubled the water;</hi> and <hi type="italic">whoso first stepped in was made whole.</hi> That this strange virtue in the pool was <hi type="italic">natural,</hi> or <hi type="italic">artificial</hi> rather, and was the effect of the washing of the sacrifices, which impregnated the water with I know not what healing virtue even for <hi type="italic">blind</hi> people, and that the angel was a <hi type="italic">messenger,</hi> a common person, sent down to stir the water, is altogether groundless; there was a room in the temple on purpose to wash the sacrifices in. Expositors generally agree that the virtue this pool had was supernatural. It is true the Jewish writers, who are not sparing in recounting the praises of Jerusalem, do none of them make the least mention of this <hi type="italic">healing pool,</hi> of which silence in this matter perhaps this is the reason, that it was taken for a presage of the near approach of the Messiah, and therefore those who denied him to be come industriously concealed such an indication of his coming; so that this is all the account we have of it. Observe, <div eID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">preparation</hi> of the medicine by an angel, who <hi type="italic">went down into the pool,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stirred the water.</hi> Angels are God's servants, and friends to mankind; and perhaps are more active in the removing of diseases (as evil angels in the inflicting of them) than we are aware of. Raphael, the apocryphal name of an angel, signifies <hi type="italic">medicina Dei—God's physic,</hi> or <hi type="italic">physician</hi> rather. See what mean offices the holy angels condescend to, for the good of men. If we would do the will of God as the angels do it, we must think nothing below us but sin. The <hi type="italic">troubling of the water</hi> was the signal given of the descent of the angel, as the <hi type="italic">going upon the tops of the mulberry trees</hi> was to David, and then they must <hi type="italic">bestir themselves.</hi> The waters of the sanctuary are then <hi type="italic">healing</hi> when they are put in <hi type="italic">motion.</hi> Ministers must <hi type="italic">stir up the gift</hi> that is in them. When they are cold and dull in their ministrations, the waters <hi type="italic">settle,</hi> and are not apt to <hi type="italic">heal.</hi> The angel descended, to <hi type="italic">stir the water,</hi> not daily, perhaps not frequently, but <hi type="italic">at a certain season;</hi> some think, at the three solemn feasts, to grace those solemnities; or, <hi type="italic">now and then,</hi> as Infinite Wisdom saw fit. God is a free agent in dispensing his favours. <div eID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">operation</hi> of the medicine: <hi type="italic">Whoever first stepped in was made whole.</hi> here is, [1.] miraculous extent of the virtue as to the <hi type="italic">diseases</hi> cured; what disease soever it was, this water cured it. Natural and artificial baths are as <hi type="italic">hurtful</hi> in some cases as they are useful in others, but this was a remedy for every malady, even for those that came from contrary causes. The power of miracles <hi type="italic">succeeds</hi> where the power of nature <hi type="italic">succumbs.</hi> [2.] A miraculous limitation of the virtue as to the <hi type="italic">persons</hi> cured: He that first stepped in had the benefit; that is, he or they that stepped in immediately were cured, not those that lingered and came in afterwards. This teaches us to observe and improve our opportunities, and to <hi type="italic">look about us,</hi> that we slip not a season which may never return. The angel <hi type="italic">stirred</hi> the waters, but left the diseased to themselves to <hi type="italic">get in.</hi> God has put virtue into the scriptures and ordinances, for he would have healed us; but, if we do not make a due improvement of them, it is our own fault, we <hi type="italic">would not be healed.</hi> <div eID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> Now this is all the account we have of this <hi type="italic">standing</hi> miracle; it is uncertain when it began and when it ceased. Some conjecture it began when Eliashib the high priest began the building of the wall about Jerusalem, and sanctified it with prayer; and that God testified his acceptance by putting this virtue into the adjoining pool. Some think it began now lately at Christ's birth; nay, others at his baptism. Dr. Lightfoot, finding in <hi type="italic">Josephus, Antiq.</hi> 15. 121-122, mention of a great earthquake in the seventh year of Herod, thirty years before Christ's birth, supposed, since there used to be earthquakes at the descent of angels, that then the angel first descended to stir this water. Some think it ceased with this miracle, others at Christ's death; however, it is certain it had a gracious signification. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> it was a <hi type="italic">token</hi> of God's good will to that people, and an indication that, though they had been long without prophets and miracles, yet God had not <hi type="italic">cast them off;</hi> though they were now an oppressed despised people, and many were ready to say, <hi type="italic">Where are all the wonders that our fathers told us of?</hi> God did hereby let them know that he had still a kindness for the <hi type="italic">city of their solemnities.</hi> We may hence take occasion to acknowledge with thankfulness God's power and goodness in the mineral waters, that contribute so much to the health of mankind; for God <hi type="italic">made the fountains of water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was a type of the Messiah, who is the <hi type="italic">fountain opened;</hi> and was intended to raise people's expectations of him who is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> that arises <hi type="italic">with healing under his wings.</hi> These waters had formerly been used for purifying, now for healing, to signify both the <hi type="italic">cleansing</hi> and <hi type="italic">curing</hi> virtue of the blood of Christ, that incomparable bath, which <hi type="italic">heals all our diseases.</hi> The waters of Siloam, which filled this pool, signified the kingdom of David, and of Christ the Son of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa. viii. 6</reference>); fitly therefore have they now this <hi type="italic">sovereign</hi> virtue put into them. The laver of regeneration is to us as Bethesda's pool, healing our spiritual diseases; not at certain seasons, but at all times. <hi type="italic">Whoever will, let him come.</hi> <div eID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> III. The patient on whom this cure was wrought (<reference osisRef="John.5.5">v. 5</reference>): one that <hi type="italic">had been infirm thirty-eight years.</hi> 1. His <hi type="italic">disease</hi> was <hi type="italic">grievous:</hi> He had an <hi type="italic">infirmity,</hi> a weakness; he had lost the use of his limbs, at least on one side, as is usual in palsies. It is sad to have the body so disabled that, instead of being the soul's instrument, it is become, even in the affairs of this life, its burden. What reason have we to thank God for bodily strength, to use it for him, and to pity those who are <hi type="italic">his prisoners!</hi> 2. The duration of it was <hi type="italic">tedious: Thirty-eight years.</hi> He was lame longer than most live. Many are so long disabled for the offices of life that, as the psalmist complains, they seem to be <hi type="italic">made in vain;</hi> for suffering, not for service; born to be always dying. Shall we complain of one wearisome night, or one fit of illness, who perhaps for many years have scarcely known what it has been to be a day sick, when many others, better than we, have scarcely known what it has been to be a day well? Mr. Baxter's note on this passage is very affecting: "How great a mercy was it to live thirty-eight years under God's wholesome discipline! O my God," saith he, "I thank thee for the like discipline of fifty-eight years; how safe a life is this, in comparison of full prosperity and pleasure!" <div eID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> IV. The cure and the circumstances of it briefly related, <reference osisRef="John.5.6-John.5.9">v. 6-9</reference>. <div eID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Jesus saw him lie.</hi> Observe, When Christ came up to Jerusalem he visited not the palaces, but the hospitals, which is an instance of his humility, and condescension, and tender compassion, and an <hi type="italic">indication</hi> of his great design in coming into the world, which was to seek and save the sick and wounded. There was a great multitude of poor cripples here at Bethesda, but Christ fastened his eye upon this one, and singled him out from the rest, because he was <hi type="italic">senior</hi> of the house, and in a more deplorable condition than any of the rest; and Christ delights to help the helpless, and hath mercy <hi type="italic">on whom he will have mercy.</hi> Perhaps his companions in tribulation insulted over him, because he had often been disappointed of a cure; therefore Christ took him for his patient: it is his honour to side with the weakest, and bear up those whom he sees <hi type="italic">run down.</hi> <div eID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> 2. He knew and considered <hi type="italic">how long he had lain</hi> in this condition. Those that have been long in affliction may comfort themselves with this, that God keeps account <hi type="italic">how long,</hi> and knows our frame. <div eID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> 3. He asked him, <hi type="italic">Wilt thou be made whole?</hi> A strange question to be asked one that had been so long ill. Some indeed would not be made whole, because their sores serve them to beg by and serve them for an excuse for idleness; but this poor man was as unable to <hi type="italic">go a begging</hi> as to <hi type="italic">work,</hi> yet Christ put it to him, (1.) To <hi type="italic">express</hi> his own pity and concern for him. Christ is tenderly inquisitive concerning the desires of those that are in affliction, and is willing to know <hi type="italic">what is their petition:</hi> "What shall I do for you?" (2.) To try him whether he would be beholden for a cure to him against whom the great people were so prejudiced and sought to prejudice others. (3.) To teach him to value the mercy, and to excite in him desires after it. In spiritual cases, people are not willing to be cured of their sins, are loth to part with them. If this point therefore were but gained, if people were willing to be <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> the work were half done, for Christ is willing to heal, if we be but willing to be healed, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.3">Matt. viii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> 4. The poor impotent man takes this opportunity to renew his complaint, and to set forth the misery of his case, which makes his cure the more illustrious: <hi type="italic">Sir, I have no man to put me into the pool,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.7">v. 7</reference>. He seems to take Christ's question as an imputation of carelessness and neglect: "If thou hadst had a mind to be healed, thou wouldest have looked better to thy hits, and have got into the healing waters long before now." "No, Master," saith the poor man, "It is not for want of a <hi type="italic">good will,</hi> but of a <hi type="italic">good friend,</hi> that I am unhealed.
