I have done what I could to help myself, but in vain, for no one else will help me." (1.) He does not think of any other way of being cured than by these waters, and desires no other friendship than to be helped into <hi type="italic">them;</hi> therefore, when Christ cured him, his imagination or expectation could not contribute to it, for he thought of no such thing. (2.) He complains for want of friends to help him in: "<hi type="italic">I have no man,</hi> no friend to do me that kindness." One would think that some of those who had been themselves healed should have lent him a hand; but it is common for the poor to be destitute of friends; <hi type="italic">no man careth for their soul.</hi> To the sick and impotent it is as true a piece of charity to work for them as to relieve them; and thus the poor are capable of being charitable to one another, and ought to be so, though we seldom find that they are so; I speak it to their shame. (3.) He bewails his infelicity, that very often when <hi type="italic">he</hi> was coming <hi type="italic">another stepped in before him.</hi> But a step between him and a cure, and yet he continues impotent. None had the charity to say, "Your case is worse than mine, do you go in now, and I will stay till the next time;" for there is no getting over the old maxim, <hi type="italic">Every one for himself.</hi> Having been so often disappointed, he begins to despair, and now is Christ's time to come to his relief; he delights to help in desperate cases. Observe, How mildly this man speaks of the unkindness of those about him, without any peevish reflections. As we should be thankful for the least kindness, so we should be patient under the greatest contempts; and, let our resentments be ever so <hi type="italic">just,</hi> yet our expressions should ever be <hi type="italic">calm.</hi> And observe further, to his praise, that, though he had waited so long in vain, yet still he continued lying by the pool side, hoping that some time or other help would come, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> 5. Our Lord Jesus hereupon cures him with a word speaking, though he neither asked it nor thought of it. Here is, <div eID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> (1.) The word he said: <hi type="italic">Rise, take up thy bed,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.8">v. 8</reference>. [1.] He is bidden to <hi type="italic">rise and walk;</hi> a strange command to be given to an <hi type="italic">impotent</hi> man, that had been long disabled; but this divine word was to be the vehicle of a divine power; it was a command to the disease to <hi type="italic">be gone,</hi> to nature to <hi type="italic">be strong,</hi> but it is expressed as a command to him to <hi type="italic">bestir himself.</hi> He must <hi type="italic">rise and walk,</hi> that is, attempt to do it, and in the <hi type="italic">essay</hi> he should receive strength to do it. The conversion of a sinner is the cure of a chronic disease; this is ordinarily done by the word, a word of command: Arise, and walk; <hi type="italic">turn, and live; make ye a new heart;</hi> which no more supposes a power in us to do it, without the grace of God, <hi type="italic">distinguishing</hi> grace, than this supposed such a power in the impotent man. But, if he had not attempted to help himself, he had not been cured, and he must have <hi type="italic">borne the blame;</hi> yet it does not therefore follow that, when he did rise and walk, it was by his own strength; no, it was by the power of Christ, and he must have all the glory. Observe, Christ did not bid him rise and go into the waters, but <hi type="italic">rise and walk.</hi> Christ did that for us which the law could not do, and set that aside. [2.] He is bidden to <hi type="italic">take up his bed. First,</hi> To make it to appear that it was a <hi type="italic">perfect cure,</hi> and purely miraculous; for he did not recover strength by degrees, but from the extremity of weakness and impotency he suddenly stepped into the highest degree of bodily strength; so that he was able to carry as great a load as any porter that had been as long <hi type="italic">used</hi> to it as he had been <hi type="italic">disused.</hi> He, who this minute was not able to turn himself in his bed, the next minute was able to carry his bed. The man sick of the palsy (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.6">Matt. ix. 6</reference>) was bidden to <hi type="italic">go to his house,</hi> but probably this man had no house to go to, the hospital was his home; therefore he is bidden to <hi type="italic">rise and walk. Secondly,</hi> It was to <hi type="italic">proclaim</hi> the cure, and make it public; for, being the sabbath day, whoever carried a burden through the streets made himself very remarkable, and every one would enquire what was the meaning of it; thereby notice of the miracle would spread, to the honour of God. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christ would thus witness against the tradition of the elders, which had stretched the law of the sabbath beyond its intention; and would likewise show that he was <hi type="italic">Lord of the sabbath,</hi> and had power to make what alterations he pleased about it, and to over-rule the law. Joshua, and the host of Israel, marched about Jericho on the sabbath day, when God commanded them, so did this man carry his bed, in obedience to a command. The case may be such that it may become a work of <hi type="italic">necessity,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> to carry a bed on the sabbath day; but here it was more, it was a work of <hi type="italic">piety,</hi> being designed purely for the glory of God. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He would hereby try the faith and obedience of his patient. By carrying his bed publicly, he exposed himself to the censure of the ecclesiastical court, and was liable, at least, to be <hi type="italic">scourged in the synagogue.</hi> Now, will he run the hazard of this, in obedience to Christ? Yes, he will. Those that have been <hi type="italic">healed by Christ's word</hi> should be <hi type="italic">ruled by his word,</hi> whatever it cost them. <div eID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> (2.) The efficacy of this word (<reference osisRef="John.5.9">v. 9</reference>): a divine power went alone with it, and immediately he was <hi type="italic">made whole, took up his bed, and walked.</hi> [1.] He felt the power of Christ's word healing him: <hi type="italic">Immediately he was made whole.</hi> What a joyful surprise was this to the poor cripple, to find himself all of a sudden so easy, so strong, so able to help himself! What a new world was he in, in an instant! Nothing is too hard for Christ to do. [2.] He obeyed the power of Christ's word commanding him. He <hi type="italic">took up his bed and walked,</hi> and did not care who blamed him or threatened him for it. The proof of our spiritual cure is our rising and walking. Hath Christ healed our spiritual diseases? Let us go whithersoever he sends us, and <hi type="italic">take up</hi> whatever he is pleased to lay upon us, and <hi type="italic">walk before him.</hi> <div eID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> V. What became of the poor man after he was cured. We are here told, <div eID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> 1. What passed between him and the Jews who saw him carry his bed on the sabbath day; for on that day this cure was wrought, and it was the sabbath that fell within the passover week, and therefore a <hi type="italic">high day,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.19.31">ch. xix. 31</reference>. Christ's work was such that he needed not make any difference between sabbath days and other days, for he was always about his Father's business; but he wrought many remarkable cures on that day, perhaps to encourage his church to expect those spiritual favours from him, in their observance of the Christian sabbath, which were typified by his miraculous cures. Now here, <div eID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> (1.) The Jews quarrelled with the man for carrying his bed on the sabbath day, telling him that <hi type="italic">it was not lawful,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.10">v. 10</reference>. It does not appear whether they were magistrates, who had power to <hi type="italic">punish</hi> him, or common people, who could only <hi type="italic">inform</hi> against him; but thus far was commendable, that, while they knew not by <hi type="italic">what authority</hi> he did it, they were jealous for the honour of the sabbath, and could not unconcernedly see it <hi type="italic">profaned;</hi> like Nehemiah. <reference osisRef="Neh.13.17">Neh. xiii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> (2.) The man justified himself in what he did by a warrant that would bear him out, <reference osisRef="John.5.11">v. 11</reference>. "I do not do it in contempt of the law and the sabbath, but in obedience to one who, by <hi type="italic">making me whole,</hi> has given me an undeniable proof that he is greater than either. He that could work such a miracle as to <hi type="italic">make me whole</hi> no doubt might give me such a command as to carry <hi type="italic">my bed;</hi> he that could overrule the powers of nature no doubt might overrule a positive law, especially in an instance not of the essence of the law. He that was so kind as to make me whole would not be so unkind as to bid me do what is sinful." Christ, by curing another paralytic, proved his power to <hi type="italic">forgive sin,</hi> here to <hi type="italic">give law;</hi> if his pardons are valid, his edicts are so, and his miracles prove both. <div eID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> (3.) The Jews enquired further who it was that gave him this warrant (<reference osisRef="John.5.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">What man is that?</hi> Observe, How industriously they <hi type="italic">overlooked</hi> that which might be a ground of their <hi type="italic">faith in Christ.</hi> They enquire not, no, not for curiosity, "Who is it that <hi type="italic">made thee whole?</hi>" While they industriously caught at that which might be a ground of reflection upon Christ (<hi type="italic">What man is</hi> it who said unto thee, <hi type="italic">Take up thy bed?</hi>) they would fain <hi type="italic">subpoena</hi> the patient to be witness against his physician, and to be his betrayer. In their question, observe, [1.] They resolve to look upon Christ as a <hi type="italic">mere man: What man is that?</hi> For, though he gave ever such convincing proofs of it, they were resolved that they would never own him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> [2.] They resolve to look upon him as a bad <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and take it for granted that he who bade this man carry his bed, whatever divine commission he might <hi type="italic">produce,</hi> was certainly a delinquent, and as such they resolve to prosecute him. <hi type="italic">What man is that</hi> who durst give such orders? <div eID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> (4.) The poor man was unable to give them any account of him: <hi type="italic">He wist not who he was,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.13">v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ was <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> to him when he healed him. Probably he had heard of the name of Jesus, but had never seen him, and therefore could not tell that this was he. Note, Christ does many a good turn for those that know him not, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4-Isa.45.5">Isa. xlv. 4, 5</reference>. He enlightens, strengthens, quickens, comforts us, and we <hi type="italic">wist not who he is;</hi> nor are aware how much we receive daily by his mediation. This man, being unacquainted with Christ, could not actually believe in him for a cure; but Christ knew the dispositions of his soul, and suited his favours to them, as to the blind man in a like case, <reference osisRef="John.9.36">ch. ix. 36</reference>. Our covenant and communion with God take rise, not so much from our knowledge of him, as from his knowledge of us. We <hi type="italic">know God,</hi> or, rather, are <hi type="italic">known of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> [2.] For the present he <hi type="italic">kept himself unknown;</hi> for as soon as he had wrought the cure he <hi type="italic">conveyed himself away,</hi> he <hi type="italic">made himself unknown</hi> (so some read it), <hi type="italic">a multitude being in that place.</hi> This is mentioned to show, either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How Christ conveyed himself away—by retiring into the crowd, so as not to be distinguished from a common person. He that was the chief of ten thousand often made himself one of the throng. It is sometimes the lot of those who have by their services signalized themselves to be levelled with the multitude, and overlooked. Or <hi type="italic">Secondly, Why</hi> he conveyed himself away, because there was <hi type="italic">a multitude</hi> there, and he industriously avoided both the <hi type="italic">applause</hi> of those who would admire the miracle and <hi type="italic">cry that up,</hi> and the censure of those who would censure him as a sabbath-breaker, and <hi type="italic">run him down.</hi> Those that are active for God in their generation must expect to pass through <hi type="italic">evil report</hi> and <hi type="italic">good report;</hi> and it is wisdom as much as may be to keep out of the hearing of both; lest by the one we be <hi type="italic">exalted,</hi> and by the other <hi type="italic">depressed,</hi> above measure. Christ left the miracle to commend itself, and the man on whom it was wrought to justify it. <div eID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> 2. What passed between him and our Lord Jesus at their next interview, <reference osisRef="John.5.14">v. 14</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen26992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> (1.) Where Christ found him: <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> the place of public worship. In our attendance on public worship we may expect to meet with Christ, and improve our acquaintance with him. Observe, [1.] Christ <hi type="italic">went to the temple.</hi> Though he had many enemies, yet he appeared in public, because there he bore his testimony to divine institutions, and had opportunity of doing good. [2.] The man that was cured <hi type="italic">went to the temple.</hi> There Christ found him the same day, as it should seem, that he was healed; thither he straightway went, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because he had, <hi type="italic">by his infirmity,</hi> been so long <hi type="italic">detained</hi> thence. Perhaps he had not been there for thirty-eight years, and therefore, as soon as ever the embargo is taken off, his first visit shall be to the temple, as Hezekiah intimates his shall be (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">Isa. xxxviii. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord? Secondly,</hi> Because he had <hi type="italic">by his recovery</hi> a good errand thither; he went up to the temple to return thanks to God for his recovery. When God has at any time restored us our health we ought to attend him with solemn praises (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.18-Ps.116.19">Ps. cxvi. 18, 19</reference>), and the sooner the better, while the sense of the mercy is fresh. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Because he had, by <hi type="italic">carrying his bed,</hi> seemed to put a contempt on the sabbath, he would thus show that he had an honour for it, and made conscience of sabbath-sanctification, in that on which the chief stress of it is laid, which is the <hi type="italic">public worship</hi> of God. Works of necessity and mercy are allowed; but when they are over we must <hi type="italic">go to the temple.</hi> <div eID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he said to him. When Christ has cured us, he has not done with us; he now applies himself to the healing of his soul, and this <hi type="italic">by the word</hi> too. [1.] He gives him a <hi type="italic">memento</hi> of his cure: <hi type="italic">Behold thou art made whole.</hi> He found himself made whole, yet Christ calls his attention to it. <hi type="italic">Behold, consider</hi> it seriously, how sudden, how strange, how cheap, how easy, the cure was: <hi type="italic">admire it;</hi> behold, and wonder: <hi type="italic">Remember it;</hi> let the impressions of it abide, and never be lost, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Isa. xxxviii. 9</reference>. [2.] He gives him a caution against sin, in consideration hereof, <hi type="italic">Being made whole, sin no more.</hi> This implies that his disease was the punishment of sin; whether of some remarkably flagrant sin, or only of sin in general, we cannot tell, but we know that sin is the procuring cause of sickness, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.17-Ps.107.18">Ps. cvii. 17, 18</reference>. Some observe that Christ did not make mention of sin to any of his patients, except to this <hi type="italic">impotent</hi> man, and another who was in like manner diseased, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.5">Mark ii. 5</reference>. While those chronical diseases lasted, they prevented the outward acts of many sins, and therefore watchfulness was the more necessary when the disability was removed. Christ intimates that those who are <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> who are eased of the present sensible punishment of sin, are in danger of <hi type="italic">returning</hi> to sin when the terror and restraint are over, unless divine grace dry up the fountain. When the trouble which only dammed up the current is over, the waters will return to their old course; and therefore there is great need of watchfulness, lest after healing mercy we return again to folly. The <hi type="italic">misery</hi> we were <hi type="italic">made whole from</hi> warns us to sin no more, having felt the smart of sin; the <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> we were <hi type="italic">made whole by</hi> is an engagement upon us not to offend him who healed us. This is the voice of every providence, <hi type="italic">Go and sin no more.</hi> This man began his new life very hopefully <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> yet Christ saw it necessary to give him this caution; for it is common for people, when they are sick, to <hi type="italic">promise much,</hi> when newly recovered to <hi type="italic">perform something,</hi> but after awhile to <hi type="italic">forget all.</hi> [3.] He gives him warning of his danger, in case he should return to his former sinful course: <hi type="italic">Lest a worse thing come to thee.</hi> Christ, who knows all men's hearts, knew that he was one of those that must be <hi type="italic">frightened</hi> from sin. Thirty-eight years' lameness, one would think, was a thing bad enough; yet there is something <hi type="italic">worse</hi> that will come to him if he relapse into sin after God has <hi type="italic">given him such a deliverance</hi> as this, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.13-Ezra.9.14">Ezra ix. 13, 14</reference>. The hospital where he lay was a melancholy place, but hell is much more so: the doom of apostates is a worse thing than thirty-eight years' lameness. <div eID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> VI. Now, after this interview between Christ and his patient, observe in the <reference osisRef="John.5.15-John.5.16">two following verses</reference>, 1. The notice which the poor simple man gave to the Jews concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="John.5.15">v. 15</reference>. He told them it was Jesus that had <hi type="italic">made him whole.</hi> We have reason to think that he intended this for the honour of Christ and the benefit of the Jews, little thinking that he who had so much power and goodness could have <hi type="italic">any</hi> enemies; but those who wish well to Christ's kingdom must have the <hi type="italic">wisdom of the serpent,</hi> lest they do more hurt than good with their zeal, and must not cast pearls before swine. 2. The rage and enmity of the Jews against him: <hi type="italic">Therefore did the</hi> rulers of the Jews <hi type="italic">persecute Jesus.</hi> See, (1.) How absurd and unreasonable their enmity to Christ was. <hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because he had made a poor sick man well, and so eased the public charge, upon which, it is likely, he had subsisted; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they persecuted him, because he did good in Israel. (2.) How bloody and cruel it was: <hi type="italic">They sought to slay him;</hi> nothing less than his blood, his life, would satisfy them. (3.) How it was varnished over with a colour of zeal for the honour of the sabbath; for this was the pretended crime, <hi type="italic">Because he had done these things on the sabbath day,</hi> as if that circumstance were enough to vitiate the best and most divine actions, and to render <hi type="italic">him</hi> obnoxious whose deeds were otherwise most meritorious. Thus hypocrites often cover their real enmity against the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of godliness with a pretended zeal for the <hi type="italic">form</hi> of it.

<div eID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Jews; All Judgment Committed to Christ; The Christian Charter.</title> <div sID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work. <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise. <hi type="super">20</hi> For the Father loveth the Son, and showeth him all things that himself doeth: and he will show him greater works than these, that ye may marvel. <hi type="super">21</hi> For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth <hi type="italic">them;</hi> even so the Son quickeneth whom he will. <hi type="super">22</hi> For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son: <hi type="super">23</hi> That all <hi type="italic">men</hi> should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him. <hi type="super">24</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life. <hi type="super">25</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. <hi type="super">26</hi> For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself; <hi type="super">27</hi> And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man. <hi type="super">28</hi> Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, <hi type="super">29</hi> And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation. <hi type="super">30</hi> I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me. <div eID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26997" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's discourse upon occasion of his being accused as a sabbath-breaker, and it seems to be his vindication of himself before the sanhedrim, when he was arraigned before them: whether on the same day, or two or three days after, does not appear; probably the same day. Observe, <div eID="gen26997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26998" type="x-p"/> I. The doctrine laid down, by which he justified what he did on the sabbath day (<reference osisRef="John.5.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">He answered them.</hi> This supposes that he had something laid to his charge: or what they suggested one to another, when they sought to slay him (<reference osisRef="John.5.16">v. 16</reference>), he <hi type="italic">knew,</hi> and gave this reply to, <hi type="italic">My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.</hi> At other times, in answer to the like charge, he had pleaded the example of David's eating the show-bread, of the priests' slaying the sacrifices, and of the people's watering their cattle on the sabbath day; but here he goes higher and alleges the example of his Father and his divine authority; waiving all other pleas, he insists upon that which was <hi type="italic">instar omnium—equivalent to the whole,</hi> and abides by it, which he had mentioned, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.8">Matt. xii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day;</hi> but he here enlarges on it. 1. He pleads that he was the Son of God, <hi type="italic">plainly intimated in his calling God his Father;</hi> and, if so, his holiness was <hi type="italic">unquestionable</hi> and his sovereignty <hi type="italic">incontestable;</hi> and he might make what alterations he pleased of the divine law. <hi type="italic">Surely they will reverence the Son,</hi> the heir of all things. 2. That he was a worker together with God. (1.) <hi type="italic">My Father worketh hitherto.</hi> The example of God's resting on the seventh day from all his work is, in the fourth commandment, made the ground of our observing it as a <hi type="italic">sabbath</hi> or <hi type="italic">day of rest.</hi> Now God rested only from such work as he had done the six days before; otherwise he <hi type="italic">worketh hitherto,</hi> he is every day working, sabbath days and week-days, upholding and governing all the creatures, and concurring by his common providence to all the motions and operations of nature, <hi type="italic">to his own glory;</hi> therefore, when we are appointed to rest on the sabbath day, yet we are not restrained from doing that which has a direct tendency <hi type="italic">to the glory of God,</hi> as the man's carrying his bed had. (2.) <hi type="italic">I work;</hi> not only therefore I <hi type="italic">may</hi> work, <hi type="italic">like him,</hi> in doing good on sabbath days as well as other days, but I also <hi type="italic">work with him.</hi> As God created all things by Christ, so he supports and governs all by him, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. This sets what he does above all exception; he that is so great a worker must needs be an uncontrollable governor; he that does all is Lord of all, and therefore <hi type="italic">Lord of the sabbath,</hi> which particular branch of his authority he would now assert, because he was shortly to show it further, in the change of the day from the seventh to the first. <div eID="gen26998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> II. The offence that was taken at his doctrine (<reference osisRef="John.5.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Jews sought the more to kill him.</hi> His defence was made his offence, as if by justifying himself he had made bad worse. Note, Those that will not be enlightened by the word of Christ will be enraged and exasperated by it, and nothing more vexes the enemies of Christ than his asserting his authority; see <reference osisRef="Ps.2.3-Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 3-5</reference>. They sought to kill him, <div eID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he had broken the sabbath; for, let him say what he would in his own justification, they are resolved, right or wrong, to <hi type="italic">find him guilty</hi> of sabbath breaking. When malice and envy sit upon the bench, reason and justice may even be silent at the bar, for whatever they can say will undoubtedly be over-ruled. <div eID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> 2. Not only so, but he had said also <hi type="italic">that God was his Father.</hi> Now they pretend a jealousy for <hi type="italic">God's honour,</hi> as before for the sabbath day, and charge Christ with it as a heinous crime that he made himself equal with God; and a heinous crime it had been if he had not really been so. It was the sin of Lucifer, <hi type="italic">I will be like the Most High.</hi> Now, (1.) This was justly inferred from what he said, that he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and that God was <hi type="italic">his Father,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">patera idion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">his own Father;</hi> his, so as he was no one's else. He had said that he worked with his Father, by the same authority and power, and hereby he made himself equal with God. <hi type="italic">Ecce intelligunt Judæi, quod non intelligunt Ariani—Behold, the Jews understand what the Arians do not.</hi> (2.) Yet it was unjustly imputed to him as an offence that he equalled himself with God, for he was and is God, equal with the Father (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.6">Phil. ii. 6</reference>); and therefore Christ, in answer to this charge, does not except against the innuendo as strained or forced, makes out his claim and proves that he is equal with God in power and glory. <div eID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's discourse upon this occasion, which continues without interruption to the end of the chapter. In <reference osisRef="John.5.19-John.5.47">these verses</reference> he explains, and afterwards confirms, his commission, as Mediator and plenipotentiary in the treaty between God and man. And, as the honours he is hereby <hi type="italic">entitled to</hi> are such as it is not fit for any creature to receive, so the work he is hereby entrusted with is such as it is not possible for any creature to go through with, and therefore he is God, equal with the Father. <div eID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">In general.</hi> He is one with the Father in all he does as Mediator, and there was a perfectly good understanding between them in the whole matter. It is ushered in with a solemn preface (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> I the Amen, the Amen, say it. This intimates that the things declared are, (1.) Very awful and great, and such as should command the most serious attention. (2.) Very sure, and such as should command an unfeigned assent. (3.) That they are matters purely of divine revelation; things which Christ has told us, and which we could not otherwise have come to the knowledge of. Two things he saith in general concerning the Son's oneness with the Father in working:— <div eID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Son <hi type="italic">conforms to the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Son can do nothing of himself but what he sees the Father do;</hi> for <hi type="italic">these things does the Son.</hi> The Lord Jesus, as Mediator, is <hi type="italic">First, Obedient to his Father's will;</hi> so entirely obedient that he <hi type="italic">can do nothing of himself,</hi> in the same sense as it is said, <hi type="italic">God cannot</hi> lie, <hi type="italic">cannot deny</hi> himself, which expresses the perfection of his truth, not any imperfection in his strength; so here, Christ was so entirely devoted to his Father's will that it was impossible for him in any thing to act separately. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">observant of his Father's counsel;</hi> he can, he will, do nothing <hi type="italic">but what he sees the Father do.</hi> No man can <hi type="italic">find out the work of God,</hi> but the only-begotten Son, who lay in his bosom, sees what he does, is intimately acquainted with his purposes, and has the plan of them ever before him. What he did as Mediator, throughout his whole undertaking, was the exact transcript or counterpart of what the Father did; that is, what he designed, when he formed the plan of our redemption in his eternal counsels, and settled those measures in every thing which never could be <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> nor ever needed to be <hi type="italic">altered.</hi> It was the copy of that <hi type="italic">great original;</hi> it was Christ's faithfulness, as it was Moses's, that he did all <hi type="italic">according to the pattern shown him in the mount.</hi> This is expressed in the present tense, what he <hi type="italic">sees the Father do,</hi> for the same reason that, when he was here upon earth, it was said, He <hi type="italic">is</hi> in heaven (<reference osisRef="John.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the bosom of the Father (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>); as he was even then by his divine nature present in heaven, so the things done in heaven were <hi type="italic">present</hi> to his knowledge. What the Father did in his counsels, the Son had ever in his view, and still he had his eye upon it, as David in spirit spoke of him, <hi type="italic">I have set the Lord always before me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Ps. xvi. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Yet he is <hi type="italic">equal</hi> with the Father in <hi type="italic">working;</hi> for <hi type="italic">what things soever</hi> the Father does <hi type="italic">these also does the Son likewise;</hi> he did the <hi type="italic">same</hi> things, not <hi type="italic">such</hi> things, but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tauta</hi></hi>, the <hi type="italic">same</hi> things; and he did them in the <hi type="italic">same manner,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">homoios</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">likewise,</hi> with the same authority, and liberty, and wisdom, the same energy and efficacy. Does the Father enact, repeal, and alter, positive laws? Does he over-rule the course of nature, know men's hearts? So does the Son. The power of the Mediator is a divine power. <div eID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the Father <hi type="italic">communicates</hi> to the Son, <reference osisRef="John.5.20">v. 20</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The inducement to it: <hi type="italic">The Father loveth the Son;</hi> he declared, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> He had not only a good will to the undertaking, but an infinite complacency in the undertaker. Christ was now hated of men, one whom the nation abhorred (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Isa. xlix. 7</reference>); but he comforted himself with this, that his Father loved him. <div eID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The instances of it. He shows it, 1. In what he <hi type="italic">does</hi> communicate to him: <hi type="italic">He shows him all things that himself doth.</hi> The Father's measures in making and ruling the world are shown to the Son, that he may take the same measures in framing and governing the church, which work was to be a duplicate of the work of creation and providence, and it is therefore called <hi type="italic">the world to come.</hi> He shows him all things <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ha autos poiei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">which he does,</hi> that is, which the <hi type="italic">Son</hi> does, so it might be construed; all that the Son does is by direction from the Father; he <hi type="italic">shows</hi> him. 2. In what he <hi type="italic">will</hi> communicate; he will <hi type="italic">show him,</hi> that is, will appoint and direct him to do <hi type="italic">greater works than these.</hi> (1.) Works of greater <hi type="italic">power</hi> than the <hi type="italic">curing of the impotent man;</hi> for he should raise the dead, and should himself rise from the dead. By the power of nature, with the use of means, a disease may possibly in time be cured; but nature can never, by the use of any means, in any time raise the dead. (2.) Works of greater <hi type="italic">authority</hi> than warranting the man to <hi type="italic">carry his bed on the sabbath day.</hi> They thought this a daring attempt; but what was this to his abrogating the whole ceremonial law, and instituting new ordinances, which he would shortly do, "<hi type="italic">that you may marvel!</hi>" Now they looked upon his works with contempt and indignation, but he will shortly do that which they will look upon with amazement, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.16">Luke vii. 16</reference>. Many are brought to marvel at Christ's works, whereby he has the honour of them, who are not brought to believe, by which they would have the benefit of them. <div eID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">In particular.</hi> He proves his equality with the Father, by specifying some of those works which he does that are the peculiar works of God. This is enlarged upon, <reference osisRef="John.5.21-John.5.30">v. 21-30</reference>. He does, and shall do, that which is the peculiar work of God's sovereign dominion and jurisdiction—<hi type="italic">judging</hi> and <hi type="italic">executing judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22-John.5.24">v. 22-24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. These two are interwoven, as being nearly connected; and what is said once is repeated and inculcated; put both together, and they will prove that Christ said not amiss when he made himself <hi type="italic">equal with God.</hi> <div eID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> (1.) Observe what is here said concerning the Mediator's power to <hi type="italic">raise the dead</hi> and <hi type="italic">give life.</hi> See [1.] His <hi type="italic">authority</hi> to do it (<reference osisRef="John.5.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Father raiseth up the dead,</hi> so <hi type="italic">the Son quickeneth whom he will. First,</hi> It is God's prerogative to raise the dead, and give life, even his who first <hi type="italic">breathed</hi> into man the <hi type="italic">breath of life,</hi> and so made him a <hi type="italic">living soul;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deut. xxxii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.6">1 Sam. ii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.20">Ps. lxviii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Rom. iv. 17</reference>. This God had done by the prophets Elijah and Elisha, and it was a confirmation of their mission. A <hi type="italic">resurrection from the dead</hi> never lay in the common road of nature, nor ever fell within the thought of those that studied only the compass of nature's power, one of whose received axioms was point blank against it: <hi type="italic">A privatione ad habitum non datur regressus—Existence, when once extinguished, cannot be rekindled.</hi> It was therefore ridiculed at Athens as an <hi type="italic">absurd</hi> thing, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.32">Acts xvii. 32</reference>. It is purely the work of a divine power, and the knowledge of it purely by divine revelation. This the Jews would own. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The Mediator is invested with this prerogative: <hi type="italic">He quickens whom he will;</hi> raises to life whom he pleases, and when he pleases. He does not enliven things by natural necessity, as the sun does, whose beams revive of course; but he acts as a free agent, has the dispensing of his power in his own hand, and is never either <hi type="italic">con</hi>strained, or <hi type="italic">re</hi>strained, in the use of it. As he has the power, so he has the wisdom and sovereignty, of a God; has the <hi type="italic">key of the grave and of death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Rev. i. 18</reference>), not as a servant, to open and shut as he is bidden, for he has it as the <hi type="italic">key of David,</hi> which he is master of, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Rev. iii. 7</reference>. An absolute prince is described by this (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">Dan. v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom he would he slew or kept alive;</hi> it is true of Christ without hyperbole. <div eID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> [2.] His <hi type="italic">ability</hi> to do it. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he has power to quicken whom he will as the Father does, because <hi type="italic">he has life in himself, as the Father has,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.26">v. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is certain that the Father <hi type="italic">has life in himself.</hi> Not only he is a <hi type="italic">self-existent</hi> Being, who does not derive from, or depend upon, any other (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>), but he is a sovereign giver of life; he has the disposal of life in himself; and of all good (for so <hi type="italic">life</hi> sometimes signifies); it is all derived from him, and dependent on him. He is to his creatures the fountain of life, and all good; author of their being and well-being; the living God, and the God of all living. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is as certain that he has <hi type="italic">given to the Son to have life in himself.</hi> As the Father is the original of all natural life and good, being the great Creator, so the Son, as Redeemer, is the original of all spiritual life and good; is that to the church which the Father is to the world; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1 Cor. viii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col. i. 19</reference>. The kingdom of grace, and all the life in that kingdom, are as fully and absolutely in the hand of the Redeemer as the kingdom of providence is in the hand of the Creator; and as God, who gives being to all things, has his being of himself, so Christ, who gives life, raised himself to life by his own power, <reference osisRef="John.10.18">ch. x. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> [3.] His <hi type="italic">acting</hi> according to this authority and ability. Having <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and being authorized to <hi type="italic">quicken whom he will,</hi> by virtue hereof there are, accordingly, two resurrections performed by his powerful word, both which are here spoken of:— <div eID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A resurrection that <hi type="italic">now is</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.29">v. 29</reference>), a resurrection from the death of sin to the life of righteousness, by the power of Christ's grace. <hi type="italic">The hour is coming, and now is.</hi> It is a resurrection begun already, and further to be carried on, <hi type="italic">when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God.</hi> This is plainly distinguished from that in <reference osisRef="John.5.28">v. 28</reference>, which speaks of the resurrection at the end of time. This says nothing, as that does, of the dead in their graces, and of all of them, and their coming forth. Now, 1. Some think this was fulfilled in those whom he miraculously raised to life, Jairus's daughter, the widow's son, and Lazarus; and it is observable that all whom Christ raised were <hi type="italic">spoken to,</hi> as, <hi type="italic">Damsel, arise; Young man, arise; Lazarus, come forth;</hi> whereas those raised under the Old Testament were raised, not by a word, but other applications, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.21">1 Kings xvii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.34">2 Kings iv. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.21">xiii. 21</reference>. Some understand it of those saints that rose with Christ; but we do not read of the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God</hi> calling them. But, 2. I rather understand it of the power of the doctrine of Christ, for the recovering and quickening of those that were <hi type="italic">dead in trespasses and sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Eph. ii. 1</reference>. The <hi type="italic">hour</hi> was <hi type="italic">coming</hi> when dead souls should be made alive by the <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> of the gospel, and a spirit of life from God accompanying it: nay, it <hi type="italic">then was,</hi> while Christ was upon earth. It may refer especially to the <hi type="italic">calling of the Gentiles,</hi> which is said to be as life from the dead, and, some think, was prefigured by Ezekiel's vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1">ch. xxxvii. 1</reference>), and foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy dead men shall live.</hi> But it is to be applied to all the wonderful success of the gospel, among both Jews and Gentiles; an hour which still <hi type="italic">is,</hi> and is still <hi type="italic">coming,</hi> till all the elect be effectually called. Note, (1.) Sinners are spiritually <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> destitute of spiritual life, sense, strength, and motion, dead to God, miserable, but neither sensible of their misery nor able to help themselves out of it. (2.) The conversion of a soul to God is its resurrection from death to life; then it begins to live when it begins to <hi type="italic">live to God,</hi> to breathe after him, and move towards him. (3.) It is by the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God</hi> that souls are raised to spiritual life; it is wrought by his power, and that power conveyed and communicated by his word: <hi type="italic">The dead shall hear,</hi> shall be made to hear, to understand, receive, and believe, the <hi type="italic">voice of the Son of God,</hi> to hear it as his voice; then the Spirit by it gives life, otherwise the <hi type="italic">letter kills.</hi> (4.) The voice of Christ must be heard by us, that we may live by it. They that hear, and attend to what they hear, shall live. <hi type="italic">Hear and your soul shall live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A resurrection yet <hi type="italic">to come;</hi> this is spoken of, <reference osisRef="John.5.28-John.5.29">v. 28, 29</reference>, introduced with, "<hi type="italic">Marvel not at this,</hi> which I have said of the <hi type="italic">first</hi> resurrection, do not reject it as incredible and absurd, for at the end of time you shall all see a more sensible and amazing proof of the power and authority of the Son of man." As <hi type="italic">his own</hi> resurrection was reserved to be the final and concluding proof of his personal commission, so the resurrection of <hi type="italic">all men</hi> is reserved to be a like proof of his commission to be executed by his spirit. Now observe here, <div eID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> When this resurrection shall be: <hi type="italic">The hour is coming;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">fixed</hi> to an hour, so very punctual is this great appointment. The judgment is not adjourned <hi type="italic">sine die—to some time not yet pitched upon;</hi> no, <hi type="italic">he hath appointed a day. The hour is coming.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) It is <hi type="italic">not yet</hi> come, it is not the hour spoken of at <reference osisRef="John.5.25">v. 25</reference>, that is coming, and <hi type="italic">now is.</hi> Those erred dangerously who said that the <hi type="italic">resurrection was past already,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2 Tim. ii. 18</reference>, But, (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It <hi type="italic">will certainly</hi> come, it is coming on, nearer every day than other; it is at the door. How far off it is we know not; but we know that it is infallibly designed and unalterably determined. <div eID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Who shall be raised: <hi type="italic">All that are in the graves,</hi> all that have died from the beginning of time, and all that shall die to the end of time. It was said (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Many</hi> shall arise; Christ here tells us that those <hi type="italic">many</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">all; all</hi> must appear before the Judge, and therefore <hi type="italic">all</hi> must be raised; every person, and the whole of every person; every soul shall return to its body, and every <hi type="italic">bone to its bone.</hi> The grave is the prison of dead bodies, where they are <hi type="italic">detained;</hi> their furnace, where they are <hi type="italic">consumed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.24.19">Job xxiv. 19</reference>); yet, in prospect of their resurrection, we may call it their <hi type="italic">bed,</hi> where they sleep to be <hi type="italic">awaked</hi> again; their treasury, where they are laid up to be used again. Even those that are not <hi type="italic">put into graves</hi> shall arise; but, because most are put into graves, Christ uses this expression, <hi type="italic">all that are in the graves.</hi> The Jews used the word <hi type="italic">sheol</hi> for the <hi type="italic">grave,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">the state of the dead;</hi> all that are in that state <hi type="italic">shall hear.</hi> <div eID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> How they shall be raised. Two things are here told us:—(<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The efficient of this resurrection: <hi type="italic">They shall hear his voice;</hi> that is, he shall cause them to hear it, as Lazarus was made to hear that word, <hi type="italic">Come forth;</hi> a divine power shall go along with the voice, to put life into them, and enable them to obey it. When Christ rose, there was no voice heard, not a word spoken, because he rose by his own power; but at the resurrection of the children of men we find three voices spoken of, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1 Thess. iv. 16</reference>. The Lord shall descend with a <hi type="italic">shout,</hi> the shout of a king, with <hi type="italic">the voice of the archangel;</hi> either Christ himself, the prince of the angels, or the commander-in-chief, under him, of the heavenly hosts; and with <hi type="italic">the trumpet of God:</hi> the soldier's trumpet sounding the alarm of war, the judge's trumpet publishing the summons to the court. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The effect of it: <hi type="italic">They shall come forth</hi> out of their graves, as prisoners out of their prison-house; they shall <hi type="italic">arise out</hi> of the dust, and shake themselves from it; see <reference osisRef="Isa.52.1-Isa.52.2">Isa. lii. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">11</reference>. But this is not all; they shall <hi type="italic">appear</hi> before Christ's tribunal, shall <hi type="italic">come forth</hi> as those that are to be tried, <hi type="italic">come forth</hi> to the bar, publicly to receive their doom. <div eID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> To what they shall be raised; to a different state of happiness or misery, according to their different character; to a state of retribution, according to what they did in the state of probation. <div eID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) <hi type="italic">They that have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life;</hi> they shall live again, to live for ever. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Whatever name men are called by, or whatever plausible profession they make, it will be well in the great day with those only that have <hi type="italic">done good,</hi> have done that which is pleasing to God and profitable to others. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The resurrection of the body will be a resurrection of life to all those, and those only, that have been sincere and constant in <hi type="italic">doing good.</hi> They shall not only be publicly <hi type="italic">acquitted,</hi> as a pardoned criminal, we say, has <hi type="italic">his life,</hi> but they shall be <hi type="italic">admitted</hi> into the presence of God, and that is life, it is better than life; they shall be <hi type="italic">attended</hi> with comforts in perfection. To live is to be <hi type="italic">happy,</hi> and they shall be <hi type="italic">advanced</hi> above the fear of death; that is <hi type="italic">life</hi> indeed in which <hi type="italic">mortality</hi> is for ever <hi type="italic">swallowed</hi> up. <div eID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) <hi type="italic">They that have done evil to the resurrection of damnation;</hi> they shall live again, to be for ever dying. The Pharisees thought that the resurrection pertained only to the just, but Christ here rectifies that mistake. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] <hi type="italic">Evil doers,</hi> whatever they pretend, will be treated in the day of judgment as <hi type="italic">evil men.</hi> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The resurrection will be to evil doers, who did not by repentance undo what they had done amiss, a <hi type="italic">resurrection</hi> of damnation. They shall come forth to be publicly convicted of rebellion against God, and publicly <hi type="italic">condemned</hi> to everlasting punishment; to be <hi type="italic">sentenced</hi> to it, and immediately <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to it without reprieve. Such will the resurrection be. <div eID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> (2.) Observe what is here said concerning the Mediator's <hi type="italic">authority to execute judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.22-John.5.24">v. 22-24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. As he has an almighty power, so he has a sovereign jurisdiction; and who so fit to preside in the great affairs of the other life as he who is the Father and fountain of life? Here is, <div eID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ's commission or delegation to the office of a judge, which is twice spoken of here (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath committed all judgment to the Son;</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="John.5.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">he hath given him authority.</hi> <div eID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">Father judges no man;</hi> not that the Father hath resigned the government, but he is pleased to govern by Jesus Christ; so that man is not under the terror of dealing with God immediately, but has the comfort of access to him by a Mediator. Having made us, he <hi type="italic">may</hi> do what he <hi type="italic">pleases</hi> with us, as the potter with the clay; yet he does not take advantage of this, but draws us <hi type="italic">with the cords of a man.</hi> 2. He does not determine our everlasting condition by the <hi type="italic">covenant of innocency,</hi> nor take the advantage he has against us for the violation of that covenant. The Mediator having undertaken to make a <hi type="italic">vicarious</hi> satisfaction, the matter is referred to him, and God is willing to enter upon a new treaty; <hi type="italic">not under the law</hi> of the Creator, <hi type="italic">but the grace</hi> of the Redeemer. <div eID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, He has committed all judgment to the Son,</hi> has constituted him <hi type="italic">Lord of all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.36">Acts x. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.9">Rom. xiv. 9</reference>), as Joseph in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.40">Gen. xli. 40</reference>. This was prophesied of, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1 Isa.11.3-Isa.11.4 Jer.23.5 Mic.5.1-Mic.5.4">Ps. lxxii. 1; Isa. xii. 3, 4; Jer. xxiii. 5; Mic. v. 1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">Ps. lxvii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">xcvi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">xcviii. 9</reference>. All judgment is committed to our Lord Jesus; for 1. He is <hi type="italic">entrusted</hi> with the administration of the <hi type="italic">providential kingdom,</hi> is <hi type="italic">head over all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>), head of every man, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>. All things consist by him, <reference osisRef="Col.1.17">Col. i. 17</reference>. 2. He is empowered to make laws immediately to bind conscience. <hi type="italic">I say unto you</hi> is now the form in which the statues of the kingdom of heaven run. <hi type="italic">Be it enacted</hi> by the Lord Jesus, and by <hi type="italic">his</hi> authority. All the acts now in force are touched with his sceptre. 3. He is authorized to appoint and settle the terms of the new covenant, and to draw up the articles of peace between God and man; it is God in Christ that reconciles the world, and to him he has given power to confer eternal life. The book of life is the Lamb's book; by his award we must stand or fall. 4. He is commissioned to carry on and complete the war with the powers of darkness; to cast out and <hi type="italic">give judgment against the prince of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.31">ch. xii. 31</reference>. He is commissioned not only to <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">make war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Rev. xix. 11</reference>. All that will fight <hi type="italic">for God against Satan</hi> must enlist themselves under <hi type="italic">his</hi> banner. 5. He is constituted sole manager of the judgment of the great day. The ancients generally understood these words of that <hi type="italic">crowning act</hi> of his judicial power. The final and universal judgment is committed to the Son of man; the tribunal is <hi type="italic">his,</hi> it is the judgment-seat of Christ; the retinue is his, <hi type="italic">his</hi> mighty angels; he will try the causes, and pass the sentence. <reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He has <hi type="italic">given him authority to execute judgment also,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.27">v. 27</reference>. Observe, 1. What the authority is which our Redeemer is invested with: <hi type="italic">An authority to execute judgment;</hi> he has not only a legislative and judicial power, but an <hi type="italic">executive</hi> power too. The phrase here is used particularly for the judgment of condemnation, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poiesai krisin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to execute judgment</hi> upon all; the same with his <hi type="italic">taking vengeance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. The ruin of impenitent sinners comes from the hand of Christ; he that <hi type="italic">executes judgment</hi> upon them is the same that would have <hi type="italic">wrought salvation</hi> for them, which makes the sentence unexceptionable; and there is no relief against the sentence of the Redeemer; salvation itself cannot save those whom the Saviour <hi type="italic">condemns,</hi> which makes the ruin <hi type="italic">remediless.</hi> 2. Whence he has that authority: the Father <hi type="italic">gave it to him.</hi> Christ's authority as Mediator is delegated and derived; he acts as the Father's Viceregent, as the Lord's Anointed, the Lord's Christ. Now all this redounds very much to the honour of Christ, acquitting him from the guilt of blasphemy, in making himself <hi type="italic">equal with God;</hi> and very much to the comfort of all believers, who may with the greatest assurance venture their all in such hands. <div eID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> [2.] Here are the reasons (reasons of state) for which this commission was given him. He has all judgment committed to him for two reasons:— <div eID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because he is the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> which denotes these three things:—1. His humiliation and gracious condescension. Man is a worm, the son of man a worm; yet this was the nature, this the character, which the Redeemer assumed, in pursuance of the counsels of love; to this low estate he stooped, and submitted to all the mortifications attending it, because it was <hi type="italic">his Father's will;</hi> in recompence therefore of this wonderful obedience, God did thus dignify him. Because he condescended to be the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> his Father made him <hi type="italic">Lord of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.8-Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 8, 9</reference>. 2. His affinity and alliance to us. The Father has committed the government of the children of men to him, because, being the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> he is of the same nature with those whom he is <hi type="italic">set over,</hi> and therefore the more unexceptionable, and the more acceptable, as a Judge. <hi type="italic">Their governor shall proceed from the midst of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. Of this that law was typical; <hi type="italic">One of thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.17.15">Deut. xvii. 15</reference>. 3. His being the Messiah promised. In that famous vision of his kingdom and glory, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14">Dan. vii. 13, 14</reference>, he is called the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6">Ps. viii. 4-6</reference>. Thou has made the Son of man have <hi type="italic">dominion over the works of thy hands.</hi> He is the Messiah, and therefore is invested with all this power. The Jews usually called the Christ the <hi type="italic">Son of David;</hi> but Christ usually called himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> which was the more humble title, and bespeaks him a prince and Saviour, not the Jewish nation only, but to the whole race of mankind. <div eID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, That all men should honour the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.23">v. 23</reference>. The honouring of Jesus Christ is here spoken of as God's great design (the Son intended to glorify the Father, and therefore the Father intended to glorify the Son, <reference osisRef="John.12.32">ch. xii. 32</reference>); and as man's great duty, in compliance with that design. If God will have the Son honoured, it is the duty of all to whom he is made known to honour him. Observe here, 1. The <hi type="italic">respect</hi> that is to be paid to our Lord Jesus: We must <hi type="italic">honour the Son,</hi> must look upon him as one that is to be <hi type="italic">honoured,</hi> both on account of his transcendent excellences and perfections in himself, and of the relations he stands in to us, and must study to give him honour accordingly; must <hi type="italic">confess that he is Lord,</hi> and worship him; must honour him who was dishonoured for us. 2. The degree of it: <hi type="italic">Even as they honour the Father.</hi> This <hi type="italic">supposes</hi> it to be our duty to <hi type="italic">honour the Father;</hi> for revealed religion is founded on natural religion, and <hi type="italic">directs</hi> us to <hi type="italic">honour the Son,</hi> to honour him with <hi type="italic">divine</hi> honour; we must honour the Redeemer with the same honour with which we honour the Creator. So far was it from blasphemy for him to make himself <hi type="italic">equal with God</hi> that it is the highest injury that can be for us to make him otherwise. The truths and laws of the Christian religion, so far as they are revealed, are as sacred and honourable as those of natural religion, and to be equally had in estimation; for we lie under the same obligations to Christ, the Author of our being; and have as necessary a dependence upon the Redeemer's grace as upon the Creator's providence, which is a sufficient ground for this law—<hi type="italic">to honour the Son as we honour the Father.</hi> To enforce this law, it is added, <hi type="italic">He that honours not the Son honours not the Father</hi> who has sent him. Some pretend a reverence for the Creator, and speak <hi type="italic">honourably</hi> of him, who make light of the Redeemer, and speak <hi type="italic">contemptibly</hi> of him; but let such know that the honours and interests of the Father and Son are so inseparably twisted and interwoven that the Father never reckons himself <hi type="italic">honoured</hi> by any that <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> the Son. Note, (1.) Indignities done to the Lord Jesus reflect upon God himself, and will so be construed and reckoned for in the court of heaven. The Son having so far espoused the Father's honour as to take <hi type="italic">to himself</hi> the <hi type="italic">reproaches cast on him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>), the Father does no less espouse the Son's honour, and counts himself struck at through him. (2.) The reason of this is because the Son is sent and commissioned by the Father; it is the <hi type="italic">Father who hath sent him.</hi> Affronts to an ambassador are justly resented by the prince that sends him. And by this rule those who truly <hi type="italic">honour the Son honour the Father also;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Phil.2.11">Phil. ii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> [3.] Here is the rule by which the Son goes in executing this commission, so those words seem to come in (<reference osisRef="John.5.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that heareth and believeth</hi> hath <hi type="italic">everlasting life.</hi> Here we have the substance of the whole gospel; the preface commands <hi type="italic">attention</hi> to a thing most weighty, and <hi type="italic">assent</hi> to a thing most certain: "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you, I,</hi> to whom you hear <hi type="italic">all judgment is committed,</hi> I, in whose lips is a divine sentence; take from <hi type="italic">me</hi> the Christian's <hi type="italic">character</hi> and <hi type="italic">charter.</hi>" <div eID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">character</hi> of a Christian: <hi type="italic">He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me.</hi> To be a Christian indeed is, 1. To <hi type="italic">hear the word of Christ.</hi> It is not enough to be within hearing of it, but we must <hi type="italic">attend on</hi> it, as scholars on the instructions of their teachers; and <hi type="italic">attend to</hi> it, as servants to the commands of their masters; we must hear and obey it, must abide by the gospel of Christ as the fixed rule of our faith and practice. 2. To <hi type="italic">believe on him that sent him;</hi> for Christ's design is to <hi type="italic">bring us to God;</hi> and, as he is the first original of all grace, so is he the last object of all faith. Christ is our <hi type="italic">way;</hi> God is our rest. We must believe on God as <hi type="italic">having sent</hi> Jesus Christ, and recommended himself to our faith and love, by manifesting his glory in <hi type="italic">the face of Jesus Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>), as <hi type="italic">his</hi> Father and <hi type="italic">our Father.</hi> <div eID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">charter</hi> of a Christian, in which all that are Christians indeed are interested. See what we get by Christ. 1. A charter of pardon: <hi type="italic">He shall not come into condemnation.</hi> The grace of the gospel is a full discharge from the curse of the law. A believer shall not only not <hi type="italic">lie under</hi> condemnation eternally, but shall not <hi type="italic">come into condemnation</hi> now, not come into the danger of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom. viii. 1</reference>), not <hi type="italic">come into judgment,</hi> not be so much as arraigned. 2. A charter of privileges: He is <hi type="italic">passed out of death to life,</hi> is invested in a present happiness in spiritual life and entitled to a future happiness in eternal life. The tenour of the first covenant was, <hi type="italic">Do this and live;</hi> the man that doeth them shall live in them. Now this proves Christ equal with the Father that he has power to propose the <hi type="italic">same</hi> benefit to the <hi type="italic">hearers of his word</hi> that had been proposed to the <hi type="italic">keepers of the old law,</hi> that is, life: <hi type="italic">Hear and live, believe and live,</hi> is what we may venture our souls upon, when we are disabled to <hi type="italic">do and live;</hi> see <reference osisRef="John.17.2">ch. xvii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> [4.] Here is the righteousness of his proceedings pursuant to this commission, <reference osisRef="John.5.30">v. 30</reference>. All judgment being committed to him, we cannot but ask <hi type="italic">how he manages it.</hi> And here he answers, <hi type="italic">My judgment is just.</hi> All Christ's acts of government, both <hi type="italic">legislative</hi> and <hi type="italic">judicial,</hi> are exactly agreeable to the rules of equity; see <reference osisRef="Prov.8.8">Prov. viii. 8</reference>. There can lie no exceptions against any of the determinations of the Redeemer; and therefore, as there shall be no repeal of any of his statutes, so there shall be no appeal from any of his sentences. His judgments are certainly just, for they are directed, <div eID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By the Father's <hi type="italic">wisdom: I can of my ownself</hi> do nothing, nothing without the Father, but <hi type="italic">as I hear I judge,</hi> as he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">v. 19</reference>), The Son <hi type="italic">can do nothing but what he sees the Father do;</hi> so here, nothing but what he hears the Father <hi type="italic">say: As I hear,</hi> 1. From the secret eternal counsels of the Father, <hi type="italic">so I judge.</hi> Would we know what we may depend upon in our dealing with God? <hi type="italic">Hear the word</hi> of Christ. We need not dive into the divine counsels, those <hi type="italic">secret things</hi> which belong not to us, but attend to the revealed dictates of Christ's government and judgment, which will furnish us with an unerring guide; for what Christ has adjudged is an exact copy or counterpart of what the Father has decreed. 2. From the published records of the Old Testament. Christ, in all the execution of his undertaking, had an eye to the scripture, and made it his business to conform to this, and <hi type="italic">fulfil</hi> it: <hi type="italic">As it was written in the volume of the book.</hi> Thus he taught us to do <hi type="italic">nothing of ourselves,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">as we hear</hi> from the word of God, <hi type="italic">so to judge</hi> of things, and act accordingly. <div eID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By the Father's <hi type="italic">will: My judgment is just,</hi> and cannot be otherwise, <hi type="italic">because I seek not my own will,</hi> but <hi type="italic">his who sent me.</hi> Not as if the will of Christ were contrary to the will of the Father, as the flesh is contrary to the spirit in us; but, 1. Christ had, as man, the natural and innocent affections of the human nature, <hi type="italic">sense of pain</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleasure,</hi> an inclination to life, an aversion to death: yet he <hi type="italic">pleased not himself,</hi> did not confer with these, nor consult these, when he was to go on his undertaking, but acquiesced entirely in the will of his Father. 2. What he did as Mediator was not the result of any <hi type="italic">peculiar</hi> or <hi type="italic">particular</hi> purpose and design of his own; what he did <hi type="italic">seek</hi> to do was not for his own mind's sake, but he was therein guided by his Father's will, and the purpose which he had <hi type="italic">purposed to himself.</hi> This our Saviour did upon all occasions <hi type="italic">refer himself to</hi> and govern himself by.

<div eID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Proves His Divine Mission; Infidelity of the Jews Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. <hi type="super">32</hi> There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true. 33 Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth. 34 But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved. <hi type="super">35</hi> He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light. <hi type="super">36</hi> But I have greater witness than <hi type="italic">that</hi> of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me. <hi type="super">37</hi> And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape. <hi type="super">38</hi> And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not. <hi type="super">39</hi> Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. <hi type="super">40</hi> And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life. <hi type="super">41</hi> I receive not honour from men. 42 But I know you, that ye have not the love of God in you. 43 I am come in my Father's name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive. <hi type="super">44</hi> How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> from God only? <hi type="super">45</hi> Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father: there is <hi type="italic">one</hi> that accuseth you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Moses, in whom ye trust. <hi type="super">46</hi> For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me. <hi type="super">47</hi> But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words? <div eID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> In these verses our Lord Jesus proves and confirms the commission he had produced, and makes it out that he was sent of God to be the Messiah. <div eID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> I. He <hi type="italic">sets aside</hi> his own testimony of himself (<reference osisRef="John.5.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I bear witness of myself,</hi> though it is infallibly true (<reference osisRef="John.8.14">ch. viii. 14</reference>), yet, according to the common rule of judgment among men, you will not admit it as <hi type="italic">legal proof,</hi> nor allow it to be <hi type="italic">given in evidence.</hi>" Now, 1. This reflects reproach upon the sons of men, and their veracity and integrity. Surely we may say deliberately, what David said in haste, <hi type="italic">All men are liars,</hi> else it would never have been such a received maxim that a man's testimony of himself is suspicious, and not to be relied on; it is a sign that self-love is stronger than the love of truth. And yet, 2. It reflects honour on the Son of God, and bespeaks his wonderful condescension, that, though he is the <hi type="italic">faithful witness,</hi> the truth itself, who may challenge to be credited <hi type="italic">upon his honour,</hi> and his own single testimony, yet he is pleased to <hi type="italic">waive his privilege,</hi> and, for the confirmation of our faith, refers himself to his <hi type="italic">vouchers,</hi> that we may have full satisfaction. <div eID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> II. He produces other witnesses that bear testimony to him that he was sent of God. <div eID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> 1. The Father himself bore testimony to him (<reference osisRef="John.5.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is another that beareth witness.</hi> I take this to be meant of God the Father, for Christ mentions <hi type="italic">his</hi> testimony with his own (<reference osisRef="John.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">I bear witness of myself, and the Father beareth witness of me.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> (1.) The seal which the Father put to his commission: He <hi type="italic">beareth witness of me,</hi> not only has done so by a voice from heaven, but still does so by the tokens of his presence with me. See who they are to whom God will bear witness. [1.] Those whom he <hi type="italic">sends</hi> and <hi type="italic">employs;</hi> where he gives commissions he give credentials. [2.] Those who <hi type="italic">bear witness</hi> to him; so Christ did. God will own and honour those that own and honour him. [3.] Those who decline <hi type="italic">bearing witness of themselves;</hi> so Christ did. God will take care that those who humble and abase themselves, and seek not their own glory, shall not <hi type="italic">lose by it.</hi> <div eID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> (2.) The satisfaction Christ had in this testimony: "<hi type="italic">I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true.</hi> I am very well assured that I have a divine mission, and do not in the least hesitate concerning it; thus he had the <hi type="italic">witness in himself.</hi>" The devil tempted him to question his being the Son of God, but he never yielded. <div eID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> 2. John Baptist witnessed to Christ, <reference osisRef="John.5.33">v. 33</reference>, &c. John came to <hi type="italic">bear witness of the light</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.7">ch. i. 7</reference>); his business was to prepare his way, and direct people to him: <hi type="italic">Behold the Lamb of God.</hi> <div eID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> (1.) Now the testimony of John was, [1.] A <hi type="italic">solemn</hi> and public testimony: "You sent an embassy of priests and Levites to John, which gave him an opportunity of publishing what he had to say; it was not a popular, but a judicial testimony."
