[2.] It was a <hi type="italic">true</hi> testimony: <hi type="italic">He bore witness to the truth,</hi> as a witness ought to do, the <hi type="italic">whole truth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nothing but the truth.</hi> Christ does not say, <hi type="italic">He bore witness to me</hi> (though every one knew he did), but, like an honest man, <hi type="italic">He bore witness to the truth.</hi> Now John was confessedly such a holy, good man, so mortified to the world, and so conversant with divine things, that it could not be imagined he should be guilty of such a forgery and imposture as to say what he did concerning Christ if it had not been so, and if he had not been sure of it. <div eID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27043" type="x-p"/> (2.) Two things are added concerning John's testimony:— <div eID="gen27043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27044" type="x-p"/> [1.] That it was a testimony <hi type="italic">ex abundanti</hi>—<hi type="italic">more than he needed to vouch</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">I receive not testimony from man.</hi> Though Christ saw fit to quote John's testimony, it was with a protestation that it shall not be deemed or construed so as to prejudice the prerogative of his self-sufficiency. Christ needs no letters or commendation, no testimonials or certificates, but what his own worth and excellency bring with him; why then did Christ here urge the testimony of John? Why, <hi type="italic">these things I say, that you may be saved.</hi> This he aimed at in all this discourse, to save not his own life, but the souls of others; he produced John's testimony because, being one <hi type="italic">of themselves,</hi> it was to be hoped that they would hearken to it. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ desires and designs the salvation even of his enemies and persecutors. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The word of Christ is the ordinary means of salvation. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christ in his word considers our infirmities and condescends to our capacities, consulting not so much what it befits so great a prince to say as what we can bear, and what will be most likely to do us good. <div eID="gen27044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27045" type="x-p"/> [2.] That it was a testimony <hi type="italic">ad hominem</hi>—<hi type="italic">to the man,</hi> because John Baptist was one whom <hi type="italic">they</hi> had a respect for (<reference osisRef="John.5.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was a light</hi> among you. <div eID="gen27045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The character of John Baptist: <hi type="italic">He was a burning and a shining light.</hi> Christ often spoke honourably of John; he was now in prison under a cloud, yet Christ gives him his <hi type="italic">due praise,</hi> which we must be ready to do to all that faithfully serve God. 1. He was a <hi type="italic">light,</hi> not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">phos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">lux, light</hi> (so Christ was <hi type="italic">the</hi> light), but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">lyknos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">lucerna, a luminary,</hi> a derived subordinate light. His office was to enlighten a dark world with notices of the Messiah's approach, to whom he was as the <hi type="italic">morning star.</hi> 2. He was a <hi type="italic">burning</hi> light, which denotes <hi type="italic">sincerity;</hi> painted fire may be made to shine, but that which burns is true fire. It denotes also his <hi type="italic">activity,</hi> zeal, and fervency, burning in love to God and the souls of men; fire is always working on itself or something else, so is a good minister. 3. He was a <hi type="italic">shining</hi> light, which denotes either his <hi type="italic">exemplary conversation,</hi> in which our light should shine (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Matt. v. 16</reference>), or an <hi type="italic">eminent</hi> diffusive influence. He was illustrious in the sight of others; though he affected obscurity and retirement, and was <hi type="italic">in the deserts,</hi> yet such were his doctrine, his baptism, his life, that he became very <hi type="italic">remarkable,</hi> and attracted the eyes of the nation. <div eID="gen27046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27047" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The affections of the people to him: <hi type="italic">you were willing for a season to rejoice in his light.</hi> 1. It was a <hi type="italic">transport</hi> that they were <hi type="italic">in,</hi> upon the appearing of John: "<hi type="italic">You were willing</hi>— <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ethelesate</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">you delighted to rejoice in his light;</hi> you were very proud that you had such a man among you, who was the honour of your country; you were willing <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">agalliasthenai</hi></hi>—willing to <hi type="italic">dance,</hi> and make a noise about this light, as boys about a bonfire." 2. It was but <hi type="italic">transient,</hi> and soon over: "You were fond of him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pros horan</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for an hour,</hi> for <hi type="italic">a season,</hi> as little children are fond of a new thing, you were pleased with John awhile, but soon grew weary of him and his ministry, and said that <hi type="italic">he had a devil,</hi> and now you have him in prison." Note, Many, that seem to be affected and pleased with the gospel at first, afterwards despise and reject it; it is common for forward and noisy professors to cool and fall off. These here rejoiced in John's light, but never walked in it, and therefore did not keep to it; they were like the stony ground. While Herod was a friend to John Baptist, the people caressed him; but when he fell under Herod's frowns he lost their favours: "<hi type="italic">You were willing</hi> to countenance John, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pros horan</hi></hi> that is, for <hi type="italic">temporal ends</hi>" (so some take it); "you were glad of him, in hopes to make a tool of him, by his interest and under the shelter of his name to have shaken off the Roman yoke, and recovered the civil liberty and honour of your country." Now, (1.) Christ mentions their respect to John, to <hi type="italic">condemn</hi> them for their present opposition to himself, to whom John bore witness. If they had continued their veneration for John, as they ought to have done, they would have embraced Christ. (2.) He mentions the passing away of their respect, to justify God in depriving them, as he had now done, of John's ministry, and putting that light under a bushel. <div eID="gen27047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27048" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's own works witnessed to him (<reference osisRef="John.5.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have a testimony greater than that of John;</hi> for <hi type="italic">if we believe the witness of men</hi> sent of God, as John was, the <hi type="italic">witness of God</hi> immediately, and not by the ministry of men, <hi type="italic">is greater,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.9">1 John v. 9</reference>. Observe, Though the witness of John was a less <hi type="italic">cogent</hi> and less <hi type="italic">considerable</hi> witness, yet our Lord was pleased to make use of it. We must be glad of all the supports that offer themselves for the confirmation of our faith, though they may not amount to a demonstration, and we must not <hi type="italic">invalidate</hi> any, under pretence that there are others more <hi type="italic">conclusive;</hi> we have occasion for them all. Now this greater testimony was that of the <hi type="italic">works</hi> which <hi type="italic">his Father had given him to finish.</hi> That is, (1.) In general the whole course of his life and ministry—his revealing God and his will to us, setting up his kingdom among men, reforming the world, destroying Satan's kingdom, restoring fallen man to his primitive purity and felicity, and shedding abroad in men's hearts the love of God and of one another—all that work of which he said when he died, <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> it was all, from first to last, <hi type="italic">opus Deo dignum—a work worthy of God;</hi> all he said and did was <hi type="italic">holy</hi> and <hi type="italic">heavenly,</hi> and a divine purity, power, and grace shone in it, proving abundantly that he was <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> (2.) In particular. The miracles he wrought for the proof of his divine mission witnessed of him. Now it is here said, [1.] That these works were <hi type="italic">given him by the Father,</hi> that is, he was both <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> and <hi type="italic">empowered</hi> to work them; for, as Mediator, he <hi type="italic">derived</hi> both commission and strength from his Father. [2.] They were given to him to <hi type="italic">finish;</hi> he must do all those works of wonder which the counsel and foreknowledge of God had before determined to be done; and his finishing them proves a divine power; for as <hi type="italic">for God his work is perfect.</hi> [3.] These works did <hi type="italic">bear witness of him,</hi> did prove that he was sent of God, and that what he said concerning himself was true; see <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">Heb. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.22">Acts ii. 22</reference>. That the Father had sent him as <hi type="italic">a Father,</hi> not as a master sends his servant on an errand, but as a father sends his son to take possession for himself; if God had not sent him, he would not have <hi type="italic">seconded</hi> him, would not have <hi type="italic">sealed</hi> him, as he did by the works he gave him to do; for the world's Creator will never be its deceiver. <div eID="gen27048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27049" type="x-p"/> 4. He produces, more fully than before, his Father's testimony concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.5.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Father that sent me hath borne witness of me.</hi> The prince is not accustomed to follow his ambassador himself, to confirm his commission <hi type="italic">viva voce—by speaking;</hi> but God was pleased to bear witness of his Son himself by a voice from heaven at his baptism (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>): This is my ambassador, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> The Jews reckoned <hi type="italic">Bath-kol;—the daughter of a voice,</hi> a voice from heaven, one of the ways by which God made known his mind; and in that way he had owned Christ publicly and solemnly, and repeated it, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Matt. xvii. 5</reference>. Note, (1.) Those whom God <hi type="italic">sends</hi> he will <hi type="italic">bear witness</hi> of; where he gives a commission, he will not fail to seal it; he that never <hi type="italic">left himself without witness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>) will never leave any of his servants so, who go upon his errand. (2.) Where God demands belief, he will not fail to give sufficient <hi type="italic">evidence,</hi> as he has done concerning Christ. That which was to be witnessed concerning Christ was chiefly this, that the God we had offended was willing to accept of him as a Mediator. Now concerning this he has <hi type="italic">himself</hi> given us full satisfaction (and he was fittest to do it), declaring himself well-pleased in him; if we be so, the work is done. Now, it might be suggested, if God himself thus bore witness of Christ, how came it to pass that he was not universally received by the Jewish nation and their rulers? To this Christ here answers that it was not to be thought strange, nor could their infidelity weaken his credibility, for two reasons:—[1.] Because they were not acquainted with such extraordinary revelations of God and his will: <hi type="italic">You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape,</hi> or <hi type="italic">appearance.</hi> They showed themselves to be as ignorant of God, though they professed relation to him, as we are of a man we never either saw or heard. "But why do I talk to you of God's bearing witness of me? He is one you know nothing of, nor have any acquaintance or communion with." Note, Ignorance of God is the true reason of men's rejecting the record he has given concerning his Son. A right understanding of <hi type="italic">natural religion</hi> would discover to us such admirable congruities in the <hi type="italic">Christian</hi> religion as would greatly dispose our minds to the entertainment of it. Some give this sense of it: "The Father bore witness of me by a <hi type="italic">voice,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">descent of a dove,</hi> which is such an extraordinary thing that you never saw or heard the like; and yet for my sake there was such a voice and appearance; yea, and you might have <hi type="italic">heard that voice,</hi> you might have <hi type="italic">seen that appearance,</hi> as others did, if you had closely attended the ministry of John, but by slighting it you missed of that testimony." [2.] Because they were not affected, no, not with the ordinary ways by which God had revealed himself to them: <hi type="italic">You have not his word abiding in you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.38">v. 38</reference>. They had the scriptures of the Old Testament; might they not by them be disposed to receive Christ? Yes, if they had had their due influence upon them. But, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The word of God was not in them; it was <hi type="italic">among them,</hi> in their country, in their hands, but not <hi type="italic">in them,</hi> in their hearts; not ruling in their souls, but only shining in their eyes and sounding in their ears. What did it avail them that they had the oracles of God <hi type="italic">committed</hi> to them (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">Rom. iii. 2</reference>), when they had not these oracles <hi type="italic">commanding</hi> in them? If they had, they would readily have embraced Christ. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It did not <hi type="italic">abide.</hi> Many have the word of God coming into them, and making some impressions for awhile, but it does not <hi type="italic">abide</hi> with them; it is not constantly in them, as a man at home, but only now and then, as a <hi type="italic">wayfaring man.</hi> If the word <hi type="italic">abide in</hi> us, if we converse with it by frequent meditation, consult with it upon every occasion, and conform to it in our conversation, we shall then readily receive the witness of the Father concerning Christ; see <reference osisRef="John.7.17">ch. vii. 17</reference>. But how did it appear that they <hi type="italic">had not the word of God abiding in them?</hi> It appeared by this, <hi type="italic">Whom he hath sent, him ye believe not.</hi> There was so much said in the Old Testament concerning Christ, to direct people when and where to look for him, and so to facilitate the discovery of him, that, if they had duly considered these things, they could not have avoided the conviction of Christ's being sent of God; so that their not believing in Christ was a certain sign that the word of God did not abide in them. Note, The in-dwelling of the word, and Spirit, and grace of God in us, is best tried by its effects, particularly by our <hi type="italic">receiving what he sends,</hi> the commands, the messengers, the providences he sends, especially Christ whom he hath sent. <div eID="gen27049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27050" type="x-p"/> 5. The last witness he calls is the Old Testament, which witnessed of him, and to it he appeals (<reference osisRef="John.5.39">v. 39</reference>, &c.): <hi type="italic">Search the scriptures,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ereunate</hi></hi>. <div eID="gen27050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27051" type="x-p"/> (1.) This may be read, either, [1.] "<hi type="italic">You search the scriptures,</hi> and you do well to do so; you read them daily in your synagogues, you have rabbies, and doctors, and scribes, that make it their business to study them, and criticize upon them." The Jews boasted of the flourishing of scripture-learning in the days of Hillel, who died about twelve years after Christ's birth, and reckoned some of those who were then members of the sanhedrim the <hi type="italic">beauties of their wisdom</hi> and the <hi type="italic">glories of their law;</hi> and Christ owns that they did indeed search the scriptures, but it was in search of their <hi type="italic">own glory: "You search the scriptures,</hi> and therefore, if you were not <hi type="italic">wilfully blind,</hi> you would <hi type="italic">believe in me.</hi>" Note, It is possible for men to be very studious in the letter of the scripture, and yet to be strangers to the power and influence of it. Or, [2.] As we read it: <hi type="italic">Search the scriptures;</hi> and so, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was spoken to <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the nature of an <hi type="italic">appeal:</hi> "You profess to receive and believe the scripture; here I will <hi type="italic">join issue</hi> with you, let this be the judge, provided you will not <hi type="italic">rest in the letter" (hærere in cortice</hi>), "but will <hi type="italic">search</hi> into it." Note, when appeals are made to the scriptures, they must be searched. Search the whole book of scripture <hi type="italic">throughout,</hi> compare one passage with another, and explain one by another. We must likewise search particular passages <hi type="italic">to the bottom,</hi> and see not what they <hi type="italic">seem</hi> to say <hi type="italic">prima facie—at the first appearance,</hi> but what they say <hi type="italic">indeed. Secondly,</hi> It is spoken to <hi type="italic">us</hi> in the nature of an <hi type="italic">advice,</hi> or a command to all Christians to search the scriptures. Note, All those who would <hi type="italic">find Christ</hi> must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures;</hi> not only read them, and hear them, but search them, which denotes, 1. <hi type="italic">Diligence</hi> in seeking, labour, and study, and close application of mind. 2. <hi type="italic">Desire</hi> and <hi type="italic">design</hi> of finding. We must aim at some spiritual benefit and advantage in reading and studying the scripture, and often ask, "What am I now searching for?" We must search as for <hi type="italic">hidden treasures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Prov. ii. 4</reference>), as those that <hi type="italic">sink</hi> for gold or silver, or that <hi type="italic">dive</hi> for pearl, <reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.11">Job xxviii. 1-11</reference>. This ennobled the Bereans, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Acts xvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen27051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27052" type="x-p"/> (2.) Now there are two things which we are here directed to have in our eye, in our searching the scripture: <hi type="italic">heaven</hi> our end, and <hi type="italic">Christ</hi> our way. [1.] We must search the scriptures for <hi type="italic">heaven</hi> as our <hi type="italic">great end: For in them you think you have eternal life.</hi> The scripture assures us of an eternal state set before us, and offers to us an eternal life in that state: it contains the <hi type="italic">chart</hi> that <hi type="italic">describes</hi> it, the <hi type="italic">charter</hi> that <hi type="italic">conveys</hi> it, the <hi type="italic">direction</hi> in the way that leads to it, and the <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> upon which the hope of it is built; and this is worth searching for where we are sure to find it. But to the Jews Christ saith only, <hi type="italic">You think</hi> you have <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> in the scriptures, because, though they did retain the belief and hope of eternal life, and grounded their expectations of it upon the scriptures, yet herein they missed it, that they looked for it by the bare reading and studying of the scripture. It was a common but corrupt saying among them, <hi type="italic">He that has the words of the law has eternal life;</hi> they thought they were sure of heaven if they could say by <hi type="italic">heart,</hi> or rather by <hi type="italic">rote,</hi> such and such passages of scripture as they were directed to by the tradition of the elders; as they thought all the <hi type="italic">vulgar</hi> cursed because they did not thus know the law (<reference osisRef="John.7.49">ch. vii. 49</reference>), so they concluded all the <hi type="italic">learned</hi> undoubtedly <hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> [2.] We must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures</hi> for <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> as the new and living <hi type="italic">way</hi> that leads to this <hi type="italic">end.</hi> These are <hi type="italic">they,</hi> the great and principal witnesses, <hi type="italic">that testify of me.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The scriptures, even those of the Old Testament, <hi type="italic">testify</hi> of Christ, and by them God <hi type="italic">bears witness</hi> to him. The Spirit of Christ in the prophets testified beforehand of him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>), the purposes and promises of God concerning him, and the previous notices of him. The Jews knew very well that the Old Testament testified of the Messiah, and were critical in their remarks upon the passages that looked that way; and yet were careless, and wretchedly overseen, in the application of them. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Therefore</hi> we must <hi type="italic">search the scriptures,</hi> and may hope to find eternal life in that search, because they testify of Christ; for this is <hi type="italic">life eternal, to know him;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1 John v. 11</reference>. Christ is the treasure hid in the field of the scriptures, the water in those wells, the milk in those breasts. <div eID="gen27052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27053" type="x-p"/> (3.) To this testimony he annexes a reproof of their infidelity and wickedness in four instances; particularly, <div eID="gen27053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27054" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their <hi type="italic">neglect of him</hi> and his doctrine: "<hi type="italic">You will not come tome, that you might have life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.40">v. 40</reference>. You search the scriptures, you believe the prophets, who you cannot but see testify of me; and yet you will not <hi type="italic">come to me,</hi> to whom they direct you." Their estrangement from Christ was the fault not so much of their <hi type="italic">understandings</hi> as of their <hi type="italic">wills.</hi> This is expressed as a complaint; Christ offered life, and it was not accepted. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There is <hi type="italic">life</hi> to be had with Jesus Christ for poor souls; we may have life, the life of <hi type="italic">pardon</hi> and <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> and <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> and <hi type="italic">glory:</hi> life is the perfection of our being, and inclusive of all happiness; and Christ is our life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that would have this life must <hi type="italic">come</hi> to Jesus Christ for it; we may have it for the coming for. It <hi type="italic">supposes</hi> an assent of the understanding to the doctrine of Christ and the record given concerning him; it <hi type="italic">lies in</hi> the consent of the will to his government and grace, and it <hi type="italic">produces</hi> an answerable compliance in the affections and actions. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The only reason why sinners die is because they <hi type="italic">will not come</hi> to Christ for life and happiness; it is not because they <hi type="italic">cannot,</hi> but because they <hi type="italic">will not.</hi> They will neither <hi type="italic">accept</hi> the life offered, because <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> and <hi type="italic">divine,</hi> nor will they <hi type="italic">agree</hi> to the terms on which it is offered, nor <hi type="italic">apply</hi> themselves to the use of the appointed means: they will not be cured, for they will not observe the methods of cure. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The wilfulness and obstinacy of sinners in rejecting the tenders of grace are a great grief to the Lord Jesus, and what he complains of. Those words (<reference osisRef="John.5.41">v. 41</reference>), <hi type="italic">I receive not honour from men,</hi> come in a parenthesis, to obviate an objection against him, as if he sought his own glory, and made himself the head of a party, in obliging all to come to <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and applaud him. Note, 1. He did not <hi type="italic">covet</hi> nor <hi type="italic">court</hi> the applause of men, did not in the least affect that worldly pomp and splendour in which the carnal Jews expected their Messiah to appear. He charged those whom he cured not to make him known, and withdrew from those that would have made him king. 2. He <hi type="italic">had not</hi> the applause of men. Instead of <hi type="italic">receiving honour</hi> from men, he received a great deal of <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> and disgrace from men, for he made himself of no reputation. 3. He <hi type="italic">needed</hi> not the applause of men; it was no addition to his glory whom all the angels of God worship, nor was he any otherwise pleased with it than as it was according to his Father's will, and for the happiness of those who, in giving honour <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> received much greater honour <hi type="italic">from him.</hi> <div eID="gen27054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> [2.] Their <hi type="italic">want of the love of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.42">v. 42</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I know you</hi> very well, <hi type="italic">that you have not the love of God in you.</hi> Why should I wonder that you do not come to me, when you want even the first principle of <hi type="italic">natural religion,</hi> which is the <hi type="italic">love of God?</hi>" Note, The reason why people <hi type="italic">slight Christ</hi> is because they do not <hi type="italic">love God;</hi> for, if we did indeed love God, we should love him who is his express image, and hasten to him by whom only we may be restored to the favour of God. He charged them (<reference osisRef="John.5.37">v. 37</reference>) with <hi type="italic">ignorance</hi> of God, and here with want of love to him; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> men have not the love of God because they desire not the knowledge of him. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The crime charged upon them: <hi type="italic">You have not the love of God in you.</hi> They pretended a great love to God, and thought they proved it by their zeal for the law, the temple, and the sabbath; and yet they were really without the love of God. Note, There are many who make a great profession of religion who yet show they want the love of God by their neglect of Christ and their contempt of his commandments; they hate his holiness and undervalue his goodness. Observe, It is the love of God <hi type="italic">in</hi> us, that love seated <hi type="italic">in the heart,</hi> a living active principle there, that God will <hi type="italic">accept;</hi> the love <hi type="italic">shed abroad</hi> there, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Rom. v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The proof of this charge, by the personal knowledge of Christ, who <hi type="italic">searches the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>) and knows what is <hi type="italic">in man: I know you.</hi> Christ sees through all our disguises, and can say to each of us, <hi type="italic">I know thee.</hi> 1. Christ knows men better than <hi type="italic">their neighbours know them.</hi> The people thought that the scribes and Pharisees were very devout and good men, but Christ knew that they had not the love of God in them. 2. Christ knows men better than <hi type="italic">they know themselves.</hi> These Jews had a very good opinion of themselves, but Christ knew how corrupt their inside was, notwithstanding the speciousness of their outside; we may deceive ourselves, but we cannot deceive him. 3. Christ knows men who do not, and will not, know him; he looks <hi type="italic">on</hi> those who industriously look <hi type="italic">off</hi> from him, and calls by their own name, their true name, those who have not known him. <div eID="gen27055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> [3.] Another crime charged upon them is their readiness to entertain false Christs and false prophets, while they obstinately opposed him who was the true Messias (<reference osisRef="John.5.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am come in my Father's name, and you receive me not. If another shall come in his own name, him you will receive. Be astonished, O heavens, at this</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.12-Jer.2.13">Jer. ii. 12, 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">for my people have committed two evils,</hi> great evils indeed. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They have <hi type="italic">forsaken the fountain of living waters,</hi> for they would not receive Christ, who came in his Father's name, had his commission from his Father, and did all for his glory. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They have <hi type="italic">hewn out broken cisterns,</hi> they hearken to every one that will set up in his own name. They forsake their own mercies, which is bad enough; and it is for <hi type="italic">lying vanities,</hi> which is worse. Observe here, 1. Those are false prophets who come in their own name, who run without being sent, and set up for themselves only. 2. It is just with God to suffer those to be deceived with false prophets who receive not the truth in the love of it. <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.11">2 Thess. ii. 10, 11</reference>. The errors of antichrist are the just punishment of those who obey not the doctrine of Christ. They that shut their eyes against the true light are by the judgment of God given up to wander endlessly after <hi type="italic">false lights,</hi> and to be led aside after every <hi type="italic">ignis fatuus.</hi> 3. It is the gross folly of many that, while they <hi type="italic">nauseate</hi> ancient truths, they are <hi type="italic">fond</hi> of upstart errors; they loathe manna, and at the same time <hi type="italic">feed upon ashes.</hi> After the Jews had rejected Christ and his gospel, they were continually haunted with spectres, with <hi type="italic">false Christs</hi> and <hi type="italic">false prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Matt. xxiv. 24</reference>), and their proneness to follow such occasioned those distractions and seditions that hastened their ruin. <div eID="gen27056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> [4.] They are here charged with pride and vain-glory, and unbelief, the effect of them, <reference osisRef="John.5.44">v. 44</reference>. Having sharply reproved their unbelief, like a wise physician, he here searches into the cause, lays the axe to the root. They <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> slighted and undervalued Christ because they <hi type="italic">admired</hi> and <hi type="italic">overvalued</hi> themselves. Here is, <div eID="gen27057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their ambition of worldly honour. Christ despised it, <reference osisRef="John.5.41">v. 41</reference>. They set their hearts upon it: <hi type="italic">You receive honour one of another;</hi> that is, "You look for a Messiah in outward pomp, and promise yourselves worldly honour by him." <hi type="italic">You receive honour:</hi>—1. "You desire to receive it, and aim at this in all you do." 2. "You give honour to others, and applaud them, only that they may return it, and may applaud you." <hi type="italic">Petimus dabimusque vicissim—We ask and we bestow.</hi> It is the proud man's art to throw honour upon others only that it may rebound upon himself. 3. "You are very careful to keep all the honours to yourselves, and confine them to your own party, as if you had the monopoly of that which is honourable." 4. "What respect is shown to you you <hi type="italic">receive</hi> yourselves, and do not transmit to God, as Herod." Idolizing men and their sentiments, and affecting to be idolized by them and their applauses, are pieces of idolatry as directly contrary to Christianity as any other. <div eID="gen27058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their neglect of spiritual honour, called here <hi type="italic">the honour that comes from God only;</hi> this they sought not, nor minded. Note, 1. True honour is that which <hi type="italic">comes from God only,</hi> that is real and lasting honour; those are honourable indeed whom he takes into covenant and communion with himself. 2. <hi type="italic">This honour have all the saints.</hi> All that believe in Christ, through him receive the honour that comes from God. He is not partial, but will give glory wherever he gives grace. 3. This honour that comes from God we must <hi type="italic">seek,</hi> must aim at it, and act for it, and take up with nothing short of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>); we must account it <hi type="italic">our reward,</hi> as the Pharisees accounted the praise of men. 4. Those that will not come to Christ, and those that are ambitious of worldly honour, make it appear that they seek not the honour that comes from God, and it is their folly and ruin. <div eID="gen27059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The influence this had upon their infidelity. <hi type="italic">How can you believe</hi> who are thus affected? Observe here, 1. The difficulty of believing arises from ourselves and our own corruption; we make our work hard to ourselves, and then complain it is impracticable. 2. The ambition and affectation of worldly honour are a great hindrance to faith in Christ. How can they believe who make the praise and applause of men their idol? When the profession and practice of serious godliness are unfashionable, are <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi>—when Christ and his followers are men wondered at, and to be a Christian is to be like a <hi type="italic">speckled bird</hi> (and this is the common case),—how can they believe the summit of whose ambition is to <hi type="italic">make a fair show in the flesh?</hi> <div eID="gen27060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> 6. The last witness here called is Moses, <reference osisRef="John.5.45">v. 45</reference>, &c. The Jews had a great veneration for Moses, and valued themselves upon their being the <hi type="italic">disciples</hi> of Moses, and pretended to adhere to Moses, in their opposition to Christ; but Christ here shows them, <div eID="gen27061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> (1.) That Moses was a witness against the unbelieving Jews, <hi type="italic">and accused them to the Father: There is one that accuses you, even Moses.</hi> This may be understood either, [1.] As showing the difference between the law and the gospel. Moses, that is, the law, <hi type="italic">accuses you,</hi> for by the law is the knowledge of sin; it <hi type="italic">condemns</hi> you, it is to those that trust to it a ministration of death and condemnation. But it is not the design of Christ's gospel to <hi type="italic">accuse</hi> us: <hi type="italic">Think not that I will accuse you.</hi> Christ did not come into the world as a <hi type="italic">Momus,</hi> to find fault and pick quarrels with every body, or as a <hi type="italic">spy</hi> upon the actions of men, or a <hi type="italic">promoter,</hi> to fish for crimes; no, he came to be an advocate, not an accuser; to reconcile God and man, and not to set them more at variance. What fools were they then that adhered to Moses against Christ, and <hi type="italic">desired to be under the law!</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.21">Gal. iv. 21</reference>. Or, [2.] As showing the manifest unreasonableness of their infidelity: "Think not that I will appeal from your bar to God's and challenge you to answer there for what you do against me, as injured innocency usually does; no, I do not need; you are already accused, and cast, in the court of heaven; Moses himself says enough to convict you of, and condemn you for, your unbelief." Let them not mistake <hi type="italic">concerning Christ;</hi> though he was a prophet, he did not improve his interest in heaven against those that persecuted him, did not, as Elias, <hi type="italic">make intercession against Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.2">Rom. vi. 2</reference>), nor as Jeremiah desire to <hi type="italic">see God's vengeance on them.</hi> Nor let them mistake concerning Moses, as if he would stand by them in rejecting Christ; no, <hi type="italic">There is one that accuses you, even Moses in whom you trust.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> External privileges and advantages are commonly the vain confidence of those who reject Christ and his grace. The Jews <hi type="italic">trusted</hi> in Moses, and thought their having his laws and ordinances would save them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that confide in their privileges, and do not improve them, will find not only that their confidence is disappointed, but that those very privileges will be witnesses against them. <div eID="gen27062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27063" type="x-p"/> (2.) That Moses was a witness for Christ and to his doctrine (<reference osisRef="John.5.46-John.5.47">v. 46, 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">He wrote of me.</hi> Moses did particularly prophesy of Christ, as the Seed of the woman, the Seed of Abraham, the Shiloh, the great Prophet; the ceremonies of the law of Moses were <hi type="italic">figures of him that was to come.</hi> The Jews made Moses the patron of their opposition to Christ; but Christ here shows them their error, that Moses was so far from writing against Christ that he wrote <hi type="italic">for him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">of him.</hi> But, [1.] Christ here charges it on the Jews that they <hi type="italic">did not believe Moses.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="John.5.45">v. 45</reference>) that they <hi type="italic">trusted</hi> in Moses, and yet here he undertakes to make out that they did not believe Moses; they trusted to his name, but they did not receive his doctrine in its true sense and meaning; they did not rightly understand, nor give credit to, what there was in the writings of Moses concerning the Messiah. [2.] He proves this charge from their disbelief of him: <hi type="italic">Had you believed Moses, you would have believed me.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The surest trial of faith is by the effects it produces. Many say that they believe whose actions give their words the lie; for had they believed the scriptures they would have done otherwise than they did. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those who rightly believe one part of scripture will receive every part. The prophecies of the old Testament were so fully accomplished in Christ that those who rejected Christ did in effect deny those prophecies, and set them aside. [3.] From their disbelief of Moses he infers that it was not strange that they rejected him: <hi type="italic">If you believe not his writings, how shall you believe my words?</hi> How can it be thought that you should? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "If you do not believe sacred <hi type="italic">writings,</hi> those oracles which are in black and white, which is the most certain way of conveyance, <hi type="italic">how shall you believe my words,</hi> words being usually less regarded?" <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "If you do not believe Moses, for whom you have such a profound veneration, how is it likely that you should believe me, whom you look upon with so much contempt?" See <reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Exod. vi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> "If you believe not what Moses spoke and wrote of me, which is a strong and cogent testimony for me, how shall you believe me and my mission?" If we admit not the premises, how shall we admit the conclusion? The truth of the Christian religion, it being a matter purely of divine revelation, depends upon the divine authority of the scripture; if therefore we believe not the divine inspiration of those writings, how shall be receive the doctrine of Christ?  <chapter eID="John.5"/> <div eID="gen27063" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27066" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27065" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Five Thousand Fed.</title> <div sID="gen27067" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things Jesus went over the sea of Galilee, which is <hi type="italic">the sea</hi> of Tiberias. <hi type="super">2</hi> And a great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles which he did on them that were diseased. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Jesus went up into a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the passover, a feast of the Jews, was nigh. <hi type="super">5</hi> When Jesus then lifted up <hi type="italic">his</hi> eyes, and saw a great company come unto him, he saith unto Philip, Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat? <hi type="super">6</hi> And this he said to prove him: for he himself knew what he would do. <hi type="super">7</hi> Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little. <hi type="super">8</hi> One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, saith unto him, <hi type="super">9</hi> There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many? <hi type="super">10</hi> And Jesus said, Make the men sit down. Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would. <hi type="super">12</hi> When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore they gathered <hi type="italic">them</hi> together, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then those men, when they had seen the miracle that Jesus did, said, This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world. <div eID="gen27067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27068" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's feeding five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, which miracle is in <hi type="italic">this</hi> respect remarkable, that it is the only passage of the actions of <hi type="italic">Christ's life</hi> that is recorded by all the four evangelists. John, who does not usually relate what had been recorded by those who wrote before him, yet relates this, because of the reference the following discourse has to it. Observe, <div eID="gen27068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27069" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">place</hi> and <hi type="italic">time</hi> where and when this miracle was wrought, which are noted for the greater evidence of the truth of the story; it is not said that it was done once upon a time, nobody knows where, but the circumstances are specified, that the fact might be enquired into. <div eID="gen27069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27070" type="x-p"/> 1. The country that Christ was in (<reference osisRef="John.6.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He went over the sea of Galilee,</hi> called elsewhere <hi type="italic">the lake of Gennesareth,</hi> here <hi type="italic">the sea of Tiberias,</hi> from a city adjoining, which Herod had lately enlarged and beautified, and called so in honour of Tiberius the emperor, and probably had made his metropolis. Christ did not go directly over cross this inland sea, but made a <hi type="italic">coasting</hi> voyage to another place on the same side. It is not tempting God to choose to go <hi type="italic">by water,</hi> when there is convenience for it, even to those places whither we might go <hi type="italic">by land;</hi> for Christ never <hi type="italic">tempted the Lord his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.4.7">Matt. iv. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen27070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27071" type="x-p"/> 2. The company that he was attended with: <hi type="italic">A great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus, while he went about <hi type="italic">doing good,</hi> lived continually in <hi type="italic">a crowd,</hi> which gave him more trouble than honour. Good and useful men must not complain of a <hi type="italic">hurry</hi> of business, when they are serving God and their generation; it will be time enough to <hi type="italic">enjoy ourselves</hi> when we come to that world where we shall <hi type="italic">enjoy God.</hi> (2.) Christ's miracles drew many <hi type="italic">after him</hi> that were not effectually drawn <hi type="italic">to him.</hi> They had their curiosity gratified by the strangeness of them, who had not their consciences convinced by the power of them. <div eID="gen27071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27072" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's posting himself advantageously to entertain them (<reference osisRef="John.6.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">He went up into a mountain,</hi> and there he <hi type="italic">sat with his disciples,</hi> that he might the more conveniently be seen and heard by the multitude that crowded after him; this was a <hi type="italic">natural</hi> pulpit, and not, like Ezra's, made <hi type="italic">for the purpose.</hi> Christ was now driven to be a <hi type="italic">field preacher;</hi> but his word was never the worse, nor the less acceptable, for that, to those who knew how to value it, who followed him still, not only when he <hi type="italic">went out</hi> to a desert place, but when he <hi type="italic">went up</hi> to a mountain, though <hi type="italic">up-hill</hi> be <hi type="italic">against heart.</hi> He <hi type="italic">sat</hi> there, as teachers do <hi type="italic">in cathedra—in the chair of instruction.</hi> He did not sit at ease, not sit in state, yet he sat as one having authority, sat ready to receive addresses that were made to him; whoever would might come, and find him there. He sat <hi type="italic">with his disciples;</hi> he condescended to take them to <hi type="italic">sit with him,</hi> to put a reputation upon them before the people, and give them an earnest of the glory in which they should shortly sit with him. We are said to <hi type="italic">sit with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Eph. ii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen27072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27073" type="x-p"/> 4. The time when it was. The first words, <hi type="italic">After those things,</hi> do not signify that this immediately followed what was related in the foregoing chapter, for it was a considerable time after, and they signify no more than in process of time; but we are told (<reference osisRef="John.6.4">v. 4</reference>) that it was <hi type="italic">when the passover was nigh,</hi> which is here noted, (1.) Because, perhaps, that had brought in all the apostles from their respective expeditions, whither they were sent as itinerant preachers, that they might attend their Master to Jerusalem, to keep the feast. (2.) Because it was a custom with the Jews religiously to observe the approach of the passover <hi type="italic">thirty days</hi> before, with some sort of solemnity; so long before they had it in their eye, repaired the roads, mended bridges, if there was occasion, and discoursed of the passover and the institution of it. (3.) Because, perhaps, the approach of the passover, when every one knew Christ would go up to Jerusalem, and be absent for some time, made the multitude flock the more after him and attend the more diligently on him. Note, The prospect of losing our opportunities should quicken us to improve them with double diligence; and, when solemn ordinances are approaching, it is good to prepare for them by conversing with the word of Christ. <div eID="gen27073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27074" type="x-p"/> II. The miracle itself. And here observe, <div eID="gen27074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27075" type="x-p"/> 1. The notice Christ took of the crowd that attended him (<reference osisRef="John.6.5">v. 5</reference>): He <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">saw a great company come to him,</hi> poor, mean, ordinary people, no doubt, for such make up the multitudes, especially in such remote corners of the country; yet Christ showed himself pleased with their attendance, and concerned for their welfare, to teach us to <hi type="italic">condescend to those of low estate,</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">set</hi> those <hi type="italic">with the dogs of our flock</hi> whom Christ hath set with the lambs of his. The souls of the poor are as precious to Christ, and should be so to us, as those of the rich. <div eID="gen27075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27076" type="x-p"/> 2. The enquiry he made concerning the way of providing for them. He directed himself to Philip, who had been his disciple from the first, and had seen all his miracles, and particularly that of his turning water into wine, and therefore it might be expected that he should have said, "Lord, if thou wilt, it is easy to thee to feed them all." Those that, like Israel, have been witnesses of Christ's works, and have shared in the benefit of them, are inexcusable if they say, <hi type="italic">Can he furnish a table in the wilderness?</hi> Philip was of Bethsaida, in the neighbourhood of which town Christ now was, and therefore he was most likely to help them to provision at the best hand; and probably much of the company was known to him, and he was concerned for them. Now Christ asked, <hi type="italic">Whence shall we buy bread, that these</hi> may eat? (1.) He takes it for granted that they must all <hi type="italic">eat with him.</hi> One would think that when he had taught and healed them he had done his part; and that now they should rather have been contriving how to treat him and his disciples, for some of the people were probably <hi type="italic">rich,</hi> and we are sure that Christ and his disciples were <hi type="italic">poor;</hi> yet he is solicitous to entertain them. Those that will accept Christ's spiritual gifts, instead of <hi type="italic">paying</hi> for them, shall be <hi type="italic">paid</hi> for their acceptance of them. Christ, having fed their souls with the bread of life, feeds their bodies also with <hi type="italic">food convenient,</hi> to show that the Lord is for the body, and to encourage us to pray for our daily bread, and to set us an example of compassion to the poor, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">James ii. 15, 16</reference>. (2.) His enquiry is, <hi type="italic">Whence shall we buy bread?</hi> One would think, considering his poverty, that he should rather have asked, <hi type="italic">Where shall we have money to buy for them?</hi> But he will rather lay out all he has than they shall want. He will buy to give, and we must <hi type="italic">labour,</hi> that we may give, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen27076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27077" type="x-p"/> 3. The design of this enquiry; it was only to try the faith of Philip, <hi type="italic">for he himself knew what he would do,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus is never at a loss in his counsels; but, how difficult soever the case is, he knows what he has to do and what course he will take, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.18">Acts xv. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">He knows the thoughts he has towards his people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>) and is never at uncertainty; when we know not, he <hi type="italic">himself knows what he will do.</hi> (2.) When Christ is pleased to <hi type="italic">puzzle</hi> his people, it is only with a design to <hi type="italic">prove</hi> them. The question put Philip to a nonplus, yet Christ proposed it, to try whether he would say, "Lord, if thou wilt exert thy power for them, we need not buy bread." <div eID="gen27077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27078" type="x-p"/> 4. Philip's answer to this question: "<hi type="italic">Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.7">v. 7</reference>. Master, it is to no purpose to talk of buying bread for them, for neither will the country afford so much bread, nor can we afford to lay out so much money; ask Judas, who carries the bag." Two hundred pence of <hi type="italic">their</hi> money amount to about six pounds of <hi type="italic">ours,</hi> and, if they lay out all that at once, it will exhaust their fund, and break them, and they must starve themselves. Grotius computes that <hi type="italic">two hundred pennyworth of bread</hi> would scarcely reach to <hi type="italic">two thousand,</hi> but Philip would go as near hand as he could, would have <hi type="italic">every one to take a little;</hi> and nature, we say, is content with a little. See the weakness of Philip's faith, that in this strait, as if the Master of the family had been an <hi type="italic">ordinary person,</hi> he looked for supply only in an <hi type="italic">ordinary way.</hi> Christ might now have said to him, as he did afterwards, Have I <hi type="italic">been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip?</hi> Or, as God to Moses in a like case, <hi type="italic">Is the Lord's hand waxen short?</hi> We are apt thus to distrust God's power when visible and ordinary means fail, that is, to trust him no further than we can see him. <div eID="gen27078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27079" type="x-p"/> 5. The information which Christ received from another of his disciples concerning the provision they had. It was Andrew, here said to be <hi type="italic">Simon Peter's brother;</hi> though he was senior to Peter in discipleship, and instrumental to bring Peter to Christ, yet Peter afterwards so far outshone him that he is described by his relation to Peter: he acquainted Christ with what they had at hand; and in this we may see, <div eID="gen27079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27080" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">strength</hi> of his <hi type="italic">love</hi> to those for whom he saw his Master concerned, in that he was willing to bring out all they had, though he knew not but they might want themselves, and any one would have said, <hi type="italic">Charity begins at home.</hi> He did not go about to conceal it, under pretence of being a better husband of their provision than the master was, but honestly gives in an account of all they had. There is a lad here, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paidarion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a little lad,</hi> probably one that used to follow this company, as settlers do the camp, with provisions to sell, and the disciples had bespoken what he had for themselves; and it was <hi type="italic">five barley-loaves,</hi> and two small fishes. Here, [1.] The provision was <hi type="italic">coarse</hi> and <hi type="italic">ordinary;</hi> they were <hi type="italic">barley loaves.</hi> Canaan was a <hi type="italic">land of wheat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.8">Deut. viii. 8</reference>); its inhabitants were commonly fed with the finest wheat (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.16">Ps. lxxxi. 16</reference>), the kidneys of wheat (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deut. xxxii. 14</reference>); yet Christ and his disciples were glad of <hi type="italic">barley-bread.</hi> It does not follow hence that we should tie ourselves to such coarse fare, and place religion in it (when God brings that which is finer to our hands, let us receive it, and be thankful); but it does follow that therefore we must not be <hi type="italic">desirous of dainties</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Ps. xxiii. 3</reference>); nor murmur if we be reduced to coarse fare, but be content and thankful, and well reconciled to it; barley-bread is what Christ <hi type="italic">had,</hi> and better than we <hi type="italic">deserve.</hi> Nor let us despise the mean provision of the poor, nor look upon it with contempt, remembering how Christ was provided for. [2.] It was but <hi type="italic">short</hi> and <hi type="italic">scanty;</hi> there were but <hi type="italic">five loaves,</hi> and those so small that one little lad carried them all; and we find (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42-2Kgs.4.43">2 Kings iv. 42, 43</reference>) that <hi type="italic">twenty barley-loaves,</hi> with some other provision to help out, would not dine a hundred men without a miracle. There were but two fishes, and those <hi type="italic">small</hi> ones (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dyo opsaria</hi></hi>), so small that one of them was but a morsel, <hi type="italic">pisciculi assati.</hi> I take the fish to have been <hi type="italic">pickled,</hi> or <hi type="italic">soused,</hi> for they had not fire to dress them with. The provision of <hi type="italic">bread</hi> was <hi type="italic">little,</hi> but that of <hi type="italic">fish</hi> was <hi type="italic">less</hi> in proportion to it, so that many a bit of dry bread they must eat before they could make a meal of this provision; but they were content with it. <hi type="italic">Bread</hi> is meat for our hunger; but of those that murmured for flesh it is said, <hi type="italic">They asked meat for their lust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.18">Ps. lxxviii. 18</reference>. Well, Andrew was willing that the people should have this, as far as it would go. Note, A distrustful fear of wanting ourselves should not hinder us from needful charity to others. <div eID="gen27080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27081" type="x-p"/> (2.) See here the <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> of his <hi type="italic">faith</hi> in that word, "<hi type="italic">But what are they among so many?</hi> To offer this to such a multitude is but to mock them." Philip and he had not that actual consideration of the power of Christ (of which they had had such large experience) which they should have had. Who fed the camp of Israel in the wilderness? He that could make <hi type="italic">one man chase a thousand</hi> could make one loaf feed a thousand. <div eID="gen27081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27082" type="x-p"/> 6. The directions Christ gave the disciples to seat the guests (<reference osisRef="John.6.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Make the men sit down,</hi> though you have nothing to set before them, and trust me for that." This was like <hi type="italic">sending providence</hi> to <hi type="italic">market,</hi> and going to buy without money: Christ would thus try their obedience. Observe, (1.) The furniture of the dining-room: <hi type="italic">there was much grass in that place,</hi> though a desert place; see how bountiful nature is, it <hi type="italic">makes grass to grow upon the mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.8">Ps. cxlvii. 8</reference>. This grass was uneaten; God gives not only enough, but more then enough. Here was this plenty of grass where Christ was preaching; the gospel brings other blessings along with it: <hi type="italic">Then shall the earth yield her increase,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Ps. lxvii. 6</reference>. This plenty of grass made the place the more commodious for those that must sit on the ground, and served them for cushions, or <hi type="italic">beds</hi> (as they called what they sat on at meat, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.6">Esth. i. 6</reference>), and, considering what Christ says of the grass of the field (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.29-Matt.6.30">Matt. vi. 29, 30</reference>), these beds excelled those of Ahasuerus: nature's pomp is the most glorious. (2.) The number of the guests: <hi type="italic">About five thousand:</hi> a great entertainment, representing that of the gospel, which is a <hi type="italic">feast for all nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>), a feast for all <hi type="italic">comers.</hi> <div eID="gen27082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27083" type="x-p"/> 7. The distribution of the provision, <reference osisRef="John.6.11">v. 11</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27084" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was done with thanksgiving: <hi type="italic">He gave thanks.</hi> Note, [1.] We ought to give thanks to God for our food, for it is a mercy to have it, and we have it from the hand of God, and must <hi type="italic">receive it with thanksgiving,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4-1Tim.4.5">1 Tim. iv. 4, 5</reference>. And this is the sweetness of our creature-comforts, that they will furnish us with <hi type="italic">matter,</hi> and give us occasion, for that excellent duty of thanksgiving. [2.] Though our provision be coarse and scanty, though we have neither plenty nor dainty, yet we must give thanks to God for what we have. <div eID="gen27084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27085" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was distributed from the hand of Christ by the hands of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.6.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, [1.] All our comforts come to us <hi type="italic">originally</hi> from the hand of Christ; whoever <hi type="italic">brings</hi> them, it is he that <hi type="italic">sends</hi> them, he distributes to those who distribute to us. [2.] In distributing the bread of life to those that follow him, he is pleased to make use of the ministration of his disciples; they are the servitors at Christ's table, or rather rulers in his household, to give to <hi type="italic">every one his portion of meat in due season.</hi> <div eID="gen27085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27086" type="x-p"/> (3.) It was done to universal satisfaction. They did not every one take a little, but all had <hi type="italic">as much as they would;</hi> not a short allowance, but a full meal; and considering how long they had fasted, with what an appetite they sat down, how agreeable this miraculous food may be supposed to have been, above common food, it was not a little that served them when they ate as much as they would and on free cost. Those whom Christ feeds with the bread of life he does not stint, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.10">Ps. lxxxi. 10</reference>. There were but <hi type="italic">two small fishes,</hi> and yet they had <hi type="italic">of them</hi> too <hi type="italic">as much as they would.</hi> He did not reserve them for the better sort of the guests, and put off the poor with dry bread, but treated them all alike, for they were all alike welcome. Those who call feeding upon fish <hi type="italic">fasting</hi> reproach the entertainment Christ here made, which was a <hi type="italic">full feast.</hi> <div eID="gen27086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27087" type="x-p"/> 8. The care that was taken of the broken meat. (1.) The orders Christ gave concerning it (<reference osisRef="John.6.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">When they were filled,</hi> and every man had within him a sensible witness to the truth of the miracle, Christ <hi type="italic">said to the disciples,</hi> the servants he employed, <hi type="italic">Gather up the fragments.</hi> Note, We must always take care that we make no waste of any of God's good creatures; for the grant we have of them, though large and full, is with this proviso, <hi type="italic">wilful waste only excepted.</hi> It is just with God to bring us to the want of that which we make waste of. The Jews were very careful not to lose any bread, nor let it fall to the ground, to be trodden upon. <hi type="italic">Qui panem contemnit in gravem incidit paupertatem—He who despises bread falls into the depths of poverty,</hi> was a saying among them. Though Christ could command supplies whenever he pleased, yet he would have the fragments gathered up. When we are filled we must remember that others want, and we may want. Those that would have wherewith to be <hi type="italic">charitable</hi> must be <hi type="italic">provident.</hi> Had this broken meat been left upon the grass, the beasts and fowls would have gathered it up; but that which is fit to be meat for men is wasted and lost if it be thrown to the brute-creatures. Christ did not order the broken meat to be gathered up till all were filled; we must not begin to hoard and lay up till all is laid out that ought to be, for that is withholding more than is meet. Mr. Baxter notes here, "How much less should we lose God's word, or helps, or our time, or such greater mercies!" (2.) The observance of these orders (<reference osisRef="John.6.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They filled twelve baskets with the fragments,</hi> which was an evidence not only of the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> of the miracle, that they were fed, not with fancy, but with real food (witness those remains), but of the <hi type="italic">greatness</hi> of it; they were not only filled, but there was all this over and above. See how large the divine bounty is; it not only <hi type="italic">fills</hi> the cup, but makes it <hi type="italic">run over;</hi> bread enough, and to spare, in our Father's house. The fragments filled twelve baskets, one for each disciple; they were thus repaid with interest for their willingness to part with what they had for public service; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.10">2 Chron. xxxi. 10</reference>. The Jews lay it as a law upon themselves, when they have eaten a meal, to be sure to leave a piece of bread upon the table, upon which the blessing after meat may rest; for it is a curse upon the wicked man (<reference osisRef="Job.20.21">Job xx. 21</reference>) that <hi type="italic">there shall none of his meat be left.</hi> <div eID="gen27087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27088" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the influence which this miracle had upon the people who tasted of the benefit of it (<reference osisRef="John.6.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They said, This is of a truth that prophet.</hi> Note, 1. Even the vulgar Jews with great assurance expected the Messiah to come into the world, and to be a <hi type="italic">great prophet,</hi> They speak here with assurance of his coming. The Pharisees despised them as <hi type="italic">not knowing the law;</hi> but, it should seem, they knew more of him that is the <hi type="italic">end of the law</hi> than the Pharisees did. 2. The miracles which Christ wrought did clearly demonstrate that he was the Messiah promised, a teacher come from God, the great prophet, and could not but convince the amazed spectators that this was he that should come. There were many who were convinced he was that prophet that should come into the world who yet did not cordially receive his doctrine, for they did not continue in it. Such a wretched incoherence and inconsistency there is between the faculties of the corrupt unsanctified soul, that it is possible for men to acknowledge that Christ is that prophet, and yet to turn a deaf ear to him.

<div eID="gen27088" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Walks on the Water.</title> <div sID="gen27089" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when even was <hi type="italic">now</hi> come, his disciples went down unto the sea, <hi type="super">17</hi> And entered into a ship, and went over the sea toward Capernaum. And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the sea arose by reason of a great wind that blew. <hi type="super">19</hi> So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid. <hi type="super">20</hi> But he saith unto them, It is I; be not afraid. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went. <div eID="gen27089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27090" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Christ's retirement from the multitude. <div eID="gen27090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27091" type="x-p"/> 1. Observe what induced him to retire; because he perceived that those who acknowledged him to be that prophet that should come into the world would come, and <hi type="italic">take him by force, to make him a king,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.15">v. 15</reference>. Now here we have an instance, <div eID="gen27091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27092" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of the irregular zeal of some of Christ's followers; nothing would serve but they would make him <hi type="italic">a king.</hi> Now, [1.] This was <hi type="italic">an act of zeal</hi> for the honour of Christ, and against the contempt which the ruling part of the Jewish church put upon him. They were concerned to see so great a benefactor to the world so little esteemed in it; and therefore, since royal titles are counted the most illustrious, they would make him a king, knowing that the Messiah was to be a king; and if a prophet, like Moses, then a sovereign prince and lawgiver, like him; and, if they cannot set him up <hi type="italic">upon the holy hill of Zion,</hi> a <hi type="italic">mountain</hi> in Galilee shall serve for the present. Those whom Christ has feasted with the royal dainties of heaven should, in return for his favour, make him <hi type="italic">their</hi> king, and set him upon the throne in their souls: let him that has <hi type="italic">fed</hi> us <hi type="italic">rule us.</hi> But, [2.] It was an <hi type="italic">irregular</hi> zeal; for <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was grounded upon a mistake concerning the nature of Christ's kingdom, as if it were to be <hi type="italic">of this world,</hi> and he must appear with outward pomp, a crown on his head, and an army at his foot; such a king as this they would make him, which was as great a disparagement to his glory as it would be to lacquer gold or paint a ruby. Right notions of Christ's kingdom would keep us to right methods for advancing it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was excited by the love of the flesh; they would make <hi type="italic">him</hi> their king who could feed them so plentifully without their toil, and save them from the curse of <hi type="italic">eating their bread in the sweat of their face. Thirdly,</hi> It was intended to carry on a <hi type="italic">secular</hi> design; they hoped this might be a fair opportunity of shaking off the Roman yoke, of which they were weary. If they had one to head them who could victual an army cheaper than another could provide for a family, they were sure of the sinews of the war, and could not fail of success, and the recovery of their ancient liberties. Thus is religion often prostituted to a secular interest, and Christ is served only to <hi type="italic">serve a turn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Rom. xvi. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Vix quæritur</hi> Jesus <hi type="italic">propter</hi> Jesum, <hi type="italic">sed propter aliud—Jesus is usually sought after for something else, not for his own sake.</hi>—Augustine. Nay, <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It was a tumultuous, seditious attempt, and a disturbance of the public peace; it would make the country a seat of war, and expose it to the resentments of the Roman power. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> It was contrary to the mind of our Lord Jesus himself; for they would take him <hi type="italic">by force,</hi> whether he would or no. Note, Those who force honours upon Christ which he has not required at their hands displease him, and do him the greatest dishonour. Those that say <hi type="italic">I am of Christ,</hi> in opposition to those that are of Apollos and Cephas (so making Christ the head of a party), take him by force, to make him a king, contrary to his own mind. <div eID="gen27092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27093" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is an instance of the humility and self-denial of the Lord Jesus, that, when they would have made him a king, he <hi type="italic">departed;</hi> so far was he from countenancing the design that he effectually quashed it. Herein he has left a testimony, [1.] Against ambition and affectation of worldly honour, to which he was perfectly mortified, and has taught us to be so. Had they come to take him by force and make him a prisoner, he could not have been more industrious to abscond than he was when they would make him a king. Let us not then covet to be the <hi type="italic">idols of the crowd,</hi> nor be <hi type="italic">desirous of vainglory.</hi> [2.] Against faction and sedition, treason and rebellion, and whatever tends to disturb the peace of kings and provinces. By this it appears that he was no enemy to Cæsar, nor would have his followers be so, but the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land;</hi> that he would have his ministers decline every thing that looks <hi type="italic">like</hi> sedition, or looks <hi type="italic">towards</hi> it, and improve their interest only for their work's sake. <div eID="gen27093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27094" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe <hi type="italic">whither</hi> he retired: <hi type="italic">He departed again into a mountain,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis to oros</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">into the</hi> mountain, the mountain where he had preached (<reference osisRef="John.6.3">v. 3</reference>), whence he came down into the plain, to feed the people, and then returned to it alone, to be private. Christ, though so useful in the places of concourse, yet chose sometimes to be alone, to teach us to sequester ourselves from the world now and then, for the more free converse with God and our own souls; and <hi type="italic">never less alone,</hi> says the serious Christian, <hi type="italic">than when alone.</hi> Public services must not jostle out private devotions. <div eID="gen27094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27095" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the disciples' distress at sea. <hi type="italic">They that go down to the sea in ships, these see the works of the Lord, for he raiseth the stormy wind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.23-Ps.17.24">Ps. xvii. 23, 24</reference>. Apply this to these disciples. <div eID="gen27095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27096" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is their <hi type="italic">going down to the sea</hi> in a ship (<reference osisRef="John.6.16-John.6.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">When even was come,</hi> and they had done their day's work, it was time to look homeward, and therefore they went aboard, and set sail for Capernaum. This they did by particular direction from their Master, with design (as it should seem) to get them out of the way of the temptation of countenancing those that would have made him a king. <div eID="gen27096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27097" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the <hi type="italic">stormy wind</hi> arising and <hi type="italic">fulfilling the word of God.</hi> They were Christ's disciples, and were now in the way of their duty, and Christ was now in the mount praying for them; and yet they were in this distress. The perils and afflictions of this present time may very well consist with our interest in Christ and his intercession. They had lately been feasted at Christ's table; but after the sun-shine of comfort expect a storm. (1.) <hi type="italic">It was now dark;</hi> this made the storm the more dangerous and uncomfortable. Sometimes the people of God are in trouble, and cannot see their way out; in the dark concerning the cause of their trouble, concerning the design and tendency of it, and what the issue will be. (2.) Jesus <hi type="italic">was not come to them.</hi> When they were in that storm (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.23">Matt. viii. 23</reference>, &c.) <hi type="italic">Jesus was with them;</hi> but now their beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone. The absence of Christ is the great aggravation of the troubles of Christians. (3.) The <hi type="italic">sea arose by reason of a great wind.</hi> It was calm and fair when they put to sea (they were not so presumptuous as to launch out in a storm), but it arose when they were <hi type="italic">at sea.</hi> In times of tranquillity we must prepare for trouble, for it may arise when we little think of it. Let it comfort good people, when they happen to be in storms at sea, that the disciples of Christ were so; and let the promises of a gracious God balance the threats of an angry sea. Though in a storm, and <hi type="italic">in the dark,</hi> they are no worse off than Christ's disciples were. Clouds and darkness sometimes surround the children of the light, and of the day. <div eID="gen27097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27098" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is Christ's seasonable approach to them when they were in this peril, <reference osisRef="John.6.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">They had rowed</hi> (being forced by the contrary winds to betake themselves to their oars) <hi type="italic">about twenty-five or thirty furlongs.</hi> The Holy Spirit that indicted this could have ascertained the number of furlongs precisely, but this, being only circumstantial, is left to be expressed according to the conjecture of the penman. And, when they were got off a good way at sea, they <hi type="italic">see Jesus walking on the sea.</hi> See here, (1.) The power Christ has over the laws and customs of nature, to control and dispense with them at his pleasure. It is natural for heavy bodies to sink in water, but Christ walked <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the water as upon dry land, which was more than Moses's dividing the water and walking <hi type="italic">through</hi> the water. (2.) The concern Christ has for his disciples in distress: <hi type="italic">He drew nigh to the ship;</hi> for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he walked upon the water, as he <hi type="italic">rides upon the heavens, for the help of his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">Deut. xxxiii. 26</reference>. He will not leave them comfortless when they seem to be <hi type="italic">tossed with tempests</hi> and <hi type="italic">not comforted.</hi> When they are banished (as John) into remote places, or shut up (as Paul and Silas) in close places, he will find access to them, and will be nigh them. (3.) The relief Christ gives to his disciples in their fears. They <hi type="italic">were afraid,</hi> more afraid of an apparition (for so they supposed him to be) than of the winds and waves. It is more terrible to wrestle with the rulers of the darkness of this world than with a tempestuous sea. When they thought a demon haunted them, and perhaps was instrumental to raise the storm, they were more terrified than they had been while they saw nothing in it but what was natural. Note, [1.] Our real distresses are often much increased by our imaginary ones, the creatures of our own fancy. [2.] Even the approaches of comfort and deliverance are often so misconstrued as to become the occasions of fear and perplexity.
