We are often not only <hi type="italic">worse frightened than hurt,</hi> but <hi type="italic">then</hi> most <hi type="italic">frightened</hi> when we are ready to be <hi type="italic">helped.</hi> But, when they were in this fright, how affectionately did Christ silence their fears with that compassionate word (<reference osisRef="John.6.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">It is I, be not afraid!</hi> Nothing is more powerful to convince sinners than that word, <hi type="italic">I am Jesus whom thou persecutest;</hi> nothing more powerful to comfort saints than this, "<hi type="italic">I am Jesus whom thou lovest;</hi> it is I that love thee, and seek thy good; be not afraid of me, nor of the storm." When trouble is nigh Christ is nigh. <div eID="gen27098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27099" type="x-p"/> 4. Here is their speedy arrival at the port they were bound for, <reference osisRef="John.6.17">v. 17</reference>. (1.) They <hi type="italic">welcomed</hi> Christ into the ship; they <hi type="italic">willingly received him.</hi> Note, Christ's absenting himself for a time is but so much the more to <hi type="italic">endear himself,</hi> at his return, to his disciples, who value his presence above any thing; see <reference osisRef="Song.3.4">Cant. iii. 4</reference>. (2.) Christ brought them safely to the shore: <hi type="italic">Immediately the ship was at the land whither they went.</hi> Note, [1.] The ship of the church, in which the disciples of Christ have <hi type="italic">embarked</hi> themselves and their all, may be much shattered and distressed, yet it shall come safe to the harbour at last; <hi type="italic">tossed</hi> at sea, but not <hi type="italic">lost;</hi> cast down, but not destroyed; the bush burning, but not consumed. [2.] The power and presence of the church's King shall expedite and facilitate her deliverance, and conquer the difficulties which have baffled the skill and industry of all her other friends. The disciples had rowed hard, but could not make their point till they had got Christ in the ship, and then the work was <hi type="italic">done suddenly.</hi> If we have received Christ Jesus the Lord, have received him willingly, though the night be dark and the wind high, yet we may comfort ourselves with this, that we shall be at shore shortly, and are nearer to it than we think we are. Many a doubting soul is fetched to heaven by a pleasing surprise, or ever it is aware.

<div eID="gen27099" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Multitude.</title> <div sID="gen27100" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but <hi type="italic">that</hi> his disciples were gone away alone; <hi type="super">23</hi> (Howbeit there came other boats from Tiberias nigh unto the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks:) <hi type="super">24</hi> When the people therefore saw that Jesus was not there, neither his disciples, they also took shipping, and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus. <hi type="super">25</hi> And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said unto him, Rabbi, when camest thou hither? 26 Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled. <hi type="super">27</hi> Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed. <div eID="gen27100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27101" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen27101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27102" type="x-p"/> I. The careful enquiry which the people made after Christ, <reference osisRef="John.6.23-John.6.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. They saw the disciples go to sea; they saw Christ retire to the mountain, probably with an intimation that he desired to be private for some time; but, their hearts being set upon <hi type="italic">making him a king,</hi> they way-laid his return, and <hi type="italic">the day following,</hi> the hot fit of their zeal still continuing, <div eID="gen27102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27103" type="x-p"/> 1. They were <hi type="italic">much at a loss</hi> for him. He was gone, and they knew not what was become of him. They saw there was <hi type="italic">no boat there</hi> but that in which the disciples went off, Providence so ordering it for the confirming of the miracle of his walking on the sea, for there was no boat for him to go in. They observed also that <hi type="italic">Jesus did not go with his disciples,</hi> but that they went off alone, and left him among <hi type="italic">them</hi> on <hi type="italic">their</hi> side of the water. Note, Those that would find Christ must diligently observe all his motions, and learn to understand the tokens of his presence and absence, that they may steer accordingly. <div eID="gen27103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27104" type="x-p"/> 2. They were very <hi type="italic">industrious in seeking</hi> him. They searched the places thereabouts, and when <hi type="italic">they saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples</hi> (neither he nor any one that could give tidings of him), they resolved to search elsewhere. Note, Those that would find Christ must accomplish a diligent search, must seek till they find, must go from sea to sea, to seek the word of God, rather than live without it; and those whom Christ has feasted with the bread of life should have their souls carried out in earnest desires towards him. Much would have more, in communion with Christ. Now, (1.) They resolved to go to Capernaum in quest of him. There were his head-quarters, where he usually resided. Thither his disciples were gone; and they knew he would not be long absent from <hi type="italic">them.</hi> Those that would find Christ must go forth by the footsteps of the flock. (2.) Providence favoured them with an opportunity of going thither by sea, which was the speediest way; for there <hi type="italic">came other boats from Tiberias,</hi> which lay further off upon the same shore, <hi type="italic">nigh,</hi> though not so nigh to the place where they did <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> in which they might soon make a trip to Capernaum, and probably the boats were bound for that port. Note, Those that in sincerity seek Christ, and seek opportunities of converse with him, are commonly owned and assisted by Providence in those pursuits. The evangelist, having occasion to mention their eating the <hi type="italic">multiplied</hi> bread, adds, <hi type="italic">After that the Lord had given thanks,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.11">v. 11</reference>. So much were the disciples affected with their Master's giving thanks that they could never forget the impressions made upon them by it, but took a pleasure in remembering the gracious words that then proceeded out of his mouth. This was the grace and beauty of that meal, and made it remarkable; their hearts burned within them. <div eID="gen27104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27105" type="x-p"/> 3. They laid hold of the opportunity that offered itself, and <hi type="italic">they also took shipping, and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus.</hi> They did not defer, in hopes to see him again <hi type="italic">on this side the water;</hi> but their convictions being strong, and their desires warm, they followed him presently. Good motions are often crushed, and come to nothing, for want of being <hi type="italic">prosecuted</hi> in <hi type="italic">time.</hi> They came to Capernaum, and, for aught that appears, these unsound hypocritical followers of Christ had a <hi type="italic">calm</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleasant</hi> passage, while his sincere disciples had a <hi type="italic">rough</hi> and <hi type="italic">stormy</hi> one. It is not strange if it fare worst with the best men in this evil world. They <hi type="italic">came, seeking Jesus.</hi> Note, Those that would find Christ, and find comfort in him, must be willing to take pains, and, as here, to <hi type="italic">compass</hi> sea and land to seek and serve him who came from heaven to earth to seek and save us. <div eID="gen27105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27106" type="x-p"/> II. The success of this enquiry: <hi type="italic">They found him on the other side of the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, Christ will be found of those that seek him, first or last; and it is worth while to cross a sea, nay, to go <hi type="italic">from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth,</hi> to seek Christ, if we may but find him at last. These people appeared afterwards to be unsound, and not actuated by any good principle, and yet were thus zealous. Note, Hypocrites may be very forward in their attendance on God's ordinances. If men have <hi type="italic">no more</hi> to show for their love to Christ than their running after sermons and prayers, and their pangs of affection to good preaching, they have reason to suspect themselves no better than this <hi type="italic">eager crowd.</hi> But though these people were no better principled, and Christ knew it, yet he was willing to be found of them, and admitted them into fellowship with him. If we could know the hearts of hypocrites, yet, while their profession is plausible, we must not exclude them from our communion, much less when we do not know their hearts. <div eID="gen27106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27107" type="x-p"/> III. The question they put to him when they found him: <hi type="italic">Rabbi, when camest thou hither?</hi> It should seem by <reference osisRef="John.6.59">v. 59</reference> that they found him <hi type="italic">in the synagogue.</hi> They knew this was the likeliest place to seek Christ in, for it was <hi type="italic">his custom</hi> to attend public assemblies for religious worship, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16">Luke iv. 16</reference>. Note, Christ must be sought, and will be found, in the congregations of his people and in the administration of his ordinances; public worship is what Christ chooses to own and grace with his presence and the manifestations of himself. There they found him, and all they had to say to him was, <hi type="italic">Rabbi, when camest thou hither?</hi> They saw he would not be made a king, and therefore say no more of this, but call him Rabbi, their teacher. Their enquiry refers not only to the <hi type="italic">time,</hi> but to the <hi type="italic">manner,</hi> of his conveying himself thither; not only <hi type="italic">When,</hi> but, "<hi type="italic">How,</hi> camest thou thither?" for there was no boat for him to come in. They were curious in asking concerning Christ's motions, but not solicitous to observe their own. <div eID="gen27107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27108" type="x-p"/> IV. The answer Christ gave them, not direct to their question (what was it to them <hi type="italic">when</hi> and <hi type="italic">how</hi> he came thither?) but such an answer as their case required. <div eID="gen27108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27109" type="x-p"/> 1. He discovers the <hi type="italic">corrupt principle</hi> they <hi type="italic">acted from</hi> in following him (<reference osisRef="John.6.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you,</hi> I that search the heart, and know what is in man, I the Amen, the faithful witness, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14-Rev.3.15">Rev. iii. 14, 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">You seek me;</hi> that is well, but it is not from a good principle." Christ knows not only <hi type="italic">what</hi> we do, but <hi type="italic">why</hi> we do it. These followed Christ, (1.) Not for his doctrine's sake: <hi type="italic">Not because you saw the miracles.</hi> The miracles were the great confirmation of his doctrine; Nicodemus sought for him for the sake of them (<reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>), and argued from the power of his works to the truth of his word; but these were so stupid and mindless that they never considered this. But, (2.) It was for their own bellies' sake: <hi type="italic">Because you did eat of the loaves, and were filled;</hi> not because he taught them, but because he fed them. He had given them, [1.] A <hi type="italic">full</hi> meal's meat: <hi type="italic">They did eat, and were filled;</hi> and some of them perhaps were so poor that they had not known of a long time before now what it was to have enough, to eat and leave. [2.] A <hi type="italic">dainty</hi> meal's meat; it is probable that, as the miraculous wine was the best wine, so was the miraculous food more than usually pleasant. [3.] A <hi type="italic">cheap</hi> meal's meat, that cost them nothing; no reckoning was brought in. Note, Many follow Christ for <hi type="italic">loaves,</hi> and not for <hi type="italic">love.</hi> Thus those do who aim at secular advantage in their profession of religion, and follow it because by this craft they get their preferments. <hi type="italic">Quantis profuit nobis hæc fabula de Christo—This fable respecting Christ, what a gainful concern we have made of it!</hi> said one of the popes. These people <hi type="italic">complimented</hi> Christ with Rabbi, and showed him great respect, yet he told them thus faithfully of their hypocrisy; his ministers must hence learn not to flatter those that flatter them, nor to be <hi type="italic">bribed</hi> by fair words to cry <hi type="italic">peace</hi> to all that cry <hi type="italic">rabbi</hi> to them, but to give faithful reproofs where there is cause for them. <div eID="gen27109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27110" type="x-p"/> 2. He directs them to better principles (<reference osisRef="John.6.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Labour for that meat which endures to everlasting life.</hi> With the woman of Samaria he had discoursed of spiritual things under the similitude of <hi type="italic">water;</hi> here he speaks of them under the similitude of <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> taking occasion from the loaves they had eaten. His design is, <div eID="gen27110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27111" type="x-p"/> (1.) To moderate our worldly pursuits: <hi type="italic">Labour not for the meat that perishes.</hi> This does not forbid honest labour for food convenient, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">2 Thess. iii. 12</reference>. But we must not make the things of this world our chief care and concern. Note, [1.] The things of the world are <hi type="italic">meat that perishes.</hi> Worldly wealth, honour, and pleasure, are <hi type="italic">meat;</hi> they <hi type="italic">feed the fancy</hi> (and many times this is all) and <hi type="italic">fill the belly.</hi> These are things which mean <hi type="italic">hunger</hi> after as <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> and glut themselves with, and which a carnal heart, as long as they last, may make a shift to live upon; but they <hi type="italic">perish,</hi> are of a perishing nature, wither of themselves, and are exposed to a thousand accidents; those that have the largest share of them are not sure to have them while they live, but are sure to leave them and lose them when they die. [2.] It is therefore folly for us inordinately to labour after them. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We must not labour in religion, nor work the works thereof, <hi type="italic">for this perishing meat,</hi> with an eye to this; we must not make our religion subservient to a worldly interest, nor aim at <hi type="italic">secular advantages</hi> in <hi type="italic">sacred exercises. Secondly,</hi> We must not at all <hi type="italic">labour</hi> for this meat; that is, we must not make these perishing things our <hi type="italic">chief good,</hi> nor make our care and pains about them our <hi type="italic">chief business;</hi> not seek those things <hi type="italic">first</hi> and <hi type="italic">most,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.4-Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27112" type="x-p"/> (2.) To quicken and excite our gracious pursuits: "Bestow your pains to better purpose, and <hi type="italic">labour for that meat</hi> which belongs to the soul," of which he shows, <div eID="gen27112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27113" type="x-p"/> [1.] That it is <hi type="italic">unspeakably desirable:</hi> It is meat which <hi type="italic">endures to everlasting life;</hi> it is a happiness which will last as long as we must, which not only itself endures eternally, but will nourish us up to everlasting life. The blessings of the new covenant are our preparative for eternal life, our preservative to it, and the pledge and earnest of it. <div eID="gen27113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27114" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is <hi type="italic">undoubtedly attainable.</hi> Shall all the treasures of the world be ransacked, and all the fruits of the earth gathered together, to furnish us with provisions that will last to eternity? No, <hi type="italic">The sea saith, It is not in me,</hi> among all the treasures hidden in the sand. <hi type="italic">It cannot be gotten for gold;</hi> but it is that <hi type="italic">which the Son of man shall give;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hen dosei</hi></hi>, either which <hi type="italic">meat,</hi> or which <hi type="italic">life,</hi> the Son of man shall give. Observe here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Who gives this meat: the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> the great householder and master of the stores, who is entrusted with the administration of the kingdom of God among men, and the dispensation of the gifts, graces, and comforts of that kingdom, and has power to give eternal life, with all the means of it and preparatives for it. We are told to <hi type="italic">labour for it,</hi> as if it were to be got by our own industry, and sold upon that valuable consideration, as the heathen said, <hi type="italic">Dii laboribus omnia vendunt—The gods sell all advantages to the industrious.</hi> But when we have laboured ever so much for it, we have not merited it as our <hi type="italic">hire,</hi> but the Son of man <hi type="italic">gives it.</hi> And what more free than gift? It is an encouragement that he who has the giving of it is the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> for then we may hope the <hi type="italic">sons of men</hi> that seek it, and labour for it, shall not fail to have it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What authority he has to give it; for <hi type="italic">him has God the Father sealed,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">touton gar ho Pater esphragisen, ho Theos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for him the Father has sealed</hi> (proved and evidenced) <hi type="italic">to be God;</hi> so some read it; he has declared him to be the Son of God with power. He has <hi type="italic">sealed him,</hi> that is, has given him full authority to deal between God and man, as God's <hi type="italic">ambassador</hi> to man and man's <hi type="italic">intercessor</hi> with God, and has proved his commission by miracles. Having given him <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> he has given us <hi type="italic">assurance</hi> of it; having entrusted him with <hi type="italic">unlimited powers,</hi> he has satisfied us with <hi type="italic">undoubted proofs</hi> of them; so that as he might go on with confidence in his undertaking for us, so may we in our resignations to him. <hi type="italic">God the Father</hi> scaled him with the Spirit that rested on him, by the voice from heaven, by the testimony he bore to him in signs and wonders. Divine revelation is perfected in him, in him the <hi type="italic">vision</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophecy</hi> is <hi type="italic">sealed up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>), to him all believers <hi type="italic">seal</hi> that he is true (<reference osisRef="John.3.33">ch. iii. 33</reference>), and in him they are all <hi type="italic">sealed,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.22">2 Cor. i. 22</reference>.

<div eID="gen27114" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ the True Bread from Heaven; Christ Welcomes All that Come to Him; Necessity of Feeding upon Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27115" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Then said they unto him, What shall we do, that we might work the works of God? <hi type="super">29</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent. <hi type="super">30</hi> They said therefore unto him, What sign showest thou then, that we may see, and believe thee? what dost thou work? <hi type="super">31</hi> Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat. <hi type="super">32</hi> Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven. <hi type="super">33</hi> For the bread of God is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread. <hi type="super">35</hi> And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst. <hi type="super">36</hi> But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not. <hi type="super">37</hi> All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. <hi type="super">38</hi> For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me. <hi type="super">39</hi> And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day. <hi type="super">40</hi> And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day. <hi type="super">41</hi> The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven. <hi type="super">42</hi> And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven? <hi type="super">43</hi> Jesus therefore answered and said unto them, Murmur not among yourselves. <hi type="super">44</hi> No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. <hi type="super">45</hi> It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me. 46 Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father. <hi type="super">47</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life. <hi type="super">48</hi> I am that bread of life. <hi type="super">49</hi> Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. <hi type="super">50</hi> This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. 51 I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. 52 The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us <hi type="italic">his</hi> flesh to eat? <hi type="super">53</hi> Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you. <hi type="super">54</hi> Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day. <hi type="super">55</hi> For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. <hi type="super">56</hi> He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him. <hi type="super">57</hi> As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me. 58 This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever. <hi type="super">59</hi> These things said he in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum. <div eID="gen27115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27116" type="x-p"/> Whether this conference was with the Capernaites, in whose synagogue Christ now was, or with those who came from the other side of the sea, is not certain nor material; however, it is an instance of Christ's condescension that he gave them leave to ask him questions, and did not resent the interruption as an affront, no, not from his common hearers, though not his immediate followers. Those that would be apt to teach must be swift to hear, and study to answer. It is the wisdom of teachers, when they are asked even impertinent unprofitable questions, thence to take occasion to answer in that which is profitable, that the question may be rejected, but not the request. Now, <div eID="gen27116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27117" type="x-p"/> I. Christ having told them that <hi type="italic">they</hi> must <hi type="italic">work for the meat</hi> he spoke of, must <hi type="italic">labour</hi> for it, they enquire what work they must do, and he answers them, <reference osisRef="John.6.28-John.6.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. 1. Their <hi type="italic">enquiry</hi> was <hi type="italic">pertinent</hi> enough (<reference osisRef="John.6.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?</hi> Some understand it as a pert question: "What works of God can we do more and better than those we do in obedience to the law of Moses?" But I rather take it as a humble serious question, showing them to be, at least for the present, in a good mind, and willing to know and do their duty; and I imagine that those who asked this question, How and What (<reference osisRef="John.6.30">v. 30</reference>), and made the request (<reference osisRef="John.6.34">v. 34</reference>), were not the same persons with those that murmured (<reference osisRef="John.6.41-John.6.42">v. 41, 42</reference>), and strove (<reference osisRef="John.6.52">v. 52</reference>), for those are expressly called <hi type="italic">the Jews,</hi> who came out of Judea (for those were strictly called Jews) to cavil, whereas these were of Galilee, and came to be taught. This question here intimates that they were convinced that those who would obtain this everlasting meat, (1.) Must aim to do something great. Those who <hi type="italic">look high</hi> in their expectations, and hope to enjoy the <hi type="italic">glory of God,</hi> must <hi type="italic">aim high</hi> in those endeavours, and study to <hi type="italic">do the works of God,</hi> works which he requires and will accept, <hi type="italic">works of God,</hi> distinguished from the works of worldly men in their worldly pursuits. It is not enough to speak the words of God, but we must do the works of God. (2.) Must be willing to do any thing: <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> Lord, I am ready to do whatever thou shalt appoint, though ever so displeasing to flesh and blood, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">Acts ix. 6</reference>. 2. Christ's answer was plain enough (<reference osisRef="John.6.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the work of God that ye believe.</hi> Note, (1.) The work of faith is the work of God. They enquire after the <hi type="italic">works</hi> of God (in the plural number), being careful about <hi type="italic">many things;</hi> but Christ directs them to one work, which includes all, the one thing needful: that <hi type="italic">you believe,</hi> which supersedes all the works of the ceremonial law; the work which is necessary to the acceptance of all the other works, and which produces them, for without faith you cannot please God. It is <hi type="italic">God's work,</hi> for it is of his <hi type="italic">working in us,</hi> it subjects the soul to his working on us, and quickens the soul in working <hi type="italic">for him,</hi> (2.) That faith is the work of God which closes with Christ, and relies upon him. It is to <hi type="italic">believe on him</hi> as one whom God <hi type="italic">hath sent,</hi> as God's commissioner in the great affair of peace between God and man, and as such to <hi type="italic">rest</hi> upon him, and <hi type="italic">resign ourselves</hi> to him. See <reference osisRef="John.14.1">ch. xiv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen27117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27118" type="x-p"/> II. Christ having told them that the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> would <hi type="italic">give them this meat,</hi> they enquire concerning him, and he answers their enquiry. <div eID="gen27118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27119" type="x-p"/> 1. Their enquiry is after <hi type="italic">a sign</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">What sign showest thou?</hi> Thus far they were right, that, since he required them to give him <hi type="italic">credit,</hi> he should produce his <hi type="italic">credentials,</hi> and make it out by miracle that he was <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> Moses having confirmed his mission by <hi type="italic">signs,</hi> it was requisite that Christ, who came to set aside the ceremonial law, should in like manner confirm his: "<hi type="italic">What dost thou work?</hi> What doest thou drive at? What lasting characters of a divine power does thou design to leave upon thy doctrine?" But <hi type="italic">herein</hi> they missed it, <div eID="gen27119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27120" type="x-p"/> (1.) That they overlooked the many miracles which they had seen wrought by him, and which amounted to an abundant proof of his divine mission. Is this a time of day to ask, "What sign showest thou?" especially at Capernaum, the <hi type="italic">staple</hi> of miracles, where he had done so <hi type="italic">many mighty works, signs</hi> so significant of his office and undertaking? Were not these very persons but the other day miraculously fed by him? None so blind as they that will not see; for they may be so blind as to question whether it be day or no, when the sun shines in their faces. <div eID="gen27120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27121" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they preferred the miraculous feeding of Israel in the wilderness before all the miracles Christ wrought (<reference osisRef="John.6.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our fathers did eat manna in the desert;</hi> and, to strengthen the objection, they quote a scripture for it: <hi type="italic">He gave them bread from heaven</hi> (taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.78.24">Ps. lxxviii. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">he gave them of the corn of heaven.</hi> What a good use might be made of this story to which they here refer! It was a memorable instance of God's power and goodness, often mentioned to the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Neh.19.20-Neh.19.21">Neh. xix. 20, 21</reference>), yet see how these people perverted it, and made an ill use of it. [1.] Christ reproved them for their fondness of the miraculous bread, and bade them not set their hearts upon <hi type="italic">meat which perisheth;</hi> "Why," say they, "<hi type="italic">meat for the belly</hi> was the great good thing that God gave to our fathers in the desert; and why should not we then labour for that meat? If God made much of them, why should not we be for those that will make much of us?" [2.] Christ had fed five thousand men with five loaves, and had given them that as one sign to prove him <hi type="italic">sent of God;</hi> but, under colour of <hi type="italic">magnifying</hi> the miracles of Moses, they tacitly <hi type="italic">undervalue</hi> this miracle of Christ, and <hi type="italic">evade</hi> the evidence of it. "Christ fed his thousands; but Moses his hundreds of thousands; Christ fed them but once, and then reproved those who followed him in hope to be still fed, and put them off with a discourse of spiritual food; but Moses fed his followers forty years, and miracles were not their rarities, but their daily bread: Christ fed them with bread out of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> barley-bread, and fishes out of <hi type="italic">the sea;</hi> but Moses fed Israel with bread <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> angel's food." Thus big did these Jews talk of the <hi type="italic">manna</hi> which <hi type="italic">their fathers did eat;</hi> but their fathers had slighted it as much as they did now the barley-loaves, and called <hi type="italic">light bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.21.5">Num. xxi. 5</reference>. Thus apt are we to slight and overlook the appearances of God's power and grace in our own times, while we pretend to admire the wonders of which <hi type="italic">our fathers told us.</hi> Suppose <hi type="italic">this</hi> miracle of Christ was outdone by that of Moses, yet there were other instances in which Christ's miracles outshone his; and, besides, all true miracles prove a divine doctrine, though not equally illustrious in the circumstances, which were ever <hi type="italic">diversified</hi> according as the occasion did require. As much as the manna excelled the barley-loaves, so much, and much more, did the doctrine of Christ excel the law of Moses, and his heavenly institutions the carnal ordinances of that dispensation. <div eID="gen27121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27122" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is Christ's reply to this enquiry, wherein, <div eID="gen27122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27123" type="x-p"/> (1.) He <hi type="italic">rectifies</hi> their <hi type="italic">mistake</hi> concerning the <hi type="italic">typical</hi> manna. It was true that their fathers did eat <hi type="italic">manna</hi> in the desert. But, [1.] It was not Moses that gave it to them, nor were they obliged to him for it; he was but the instrument, and therefore they must look beyond him to God. We do not find that Moses did so much as pray to God for the <hi type="italic">manna;</hi> and he spoke unadvisedly when he said, <hi type="italic">Must we fetch water out of the rock?</hi> Moses gave them not either <hi type="italic">that</hi> bread or <hi type="italic">that water.</hi> [2.] It was not given them, as they imagined, <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> from the highest heavens, but only from <hi type="italic">the clouds,</hi> and therefore not so much superior to that which had its rise from the earth as they thought. Because the scripture saith, <hi type="italic">He gave them bread from heaven,</hi> it does not follow that it was <hi type="italic">heavenly bread,</hi> or was intended to be the nourishment of souls. Misunderstanding scripture language occasions many mistakes in the things of God. <div eID="gen27123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27124" type="x-p"/> (2.) He <hi type="italic">informs</hi> them concerning the <hi type="italic">true</hi> manna, of which that was a type: <hi type="italic">But my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven;</hi> that which is truly and properly the <hi type="italic">bread from heaven,</hi> of which the manna was but a shadow and figure, is <hi type="italic">now given,</hi> not to <hi type="italic">your fathers,</hi> who are dead and gone, but <hi type="italic">to you</hi> of this present age, for whom the <hi type="italic">better things were reserved:</hi> he is <hi type="italic">now giving</hi> you that <hi type="italic">bread from heaven,</hi> which is <hi type="italic">truly</hi> so called. As much as the throne of God's glory is above the clouds of the air, so much does the <hi type="italic">spiritual bread</hi> of the everlasting gospel excel the <hi type="italic">manna.</hi> In calling God <hi type="italic">his Father,</hi> he proclaims himself greater than Moses; for Moses was faithful but as a servant, Christ as a <hi type="italic">Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.5-Heb.3.6">Heb. iii. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen27124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27125" type="x-p"/> III. Christ, having replied to their enquiries, takes further occasion from their objection concerning the <hi type="italic">manna</hi> to discourse of <hi type="italic">himself</hi> under the similitude of <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">believing</hi> under the similitude of <hi type="italic">eating and drinking;</hi> to which, together with his putting both together in the <hi type="italic">eating</hi> of <hi type="italic">his flesh</hi> and <hi type="italic">drinking</hi> of his <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> and with the remarks made upon it by the hearers, the rest of this conference may be reduced. <div eID="gen27125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27126" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ having spoken of <hi type="italic">himself</hi> as the great <hi type="italic">gift of God,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">true bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">v. 32</reference>), largely <hi type="italic">explains</hi> and <hi type="italic">confirms</hi> this, that we may rightly know him. <div eID="gen27126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27127" type="x-p"/> (1.) He here shows that he is the <hi type="italic">true bread;</hi> this he repeats again and again, <reference osisRef="John.6.33">v. 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.35">35</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.48-John.6.51">48-51</reference>. Observe, [1.] That Christ is <hi type="italic">bread</hi> is that to the soul which bread is to the body, nourishes and supports the spiritual life (is the staff of it) as bread does the bodily life; <hi type="italic">it is the staff of life.</hi> The doctrines of the gospel concerning Christ—that he is the mediator between God and man, that he is our peace, our righteousness, our Redeemer; <hi type="italic">by these things do men live.</hi> Our bodies could better live without food than our souls without Christ. <hi type="italic">Bread-corn</hi> is <hi type="italic">bruised</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">Isa. xxviii. 28</reference>), so was Christ; he was born at Bethlehem, the <hi type="italic">house of bread,</hi> and typified by the <hi type="italic">show-bread.</hi> [2.] That he is the <hi type="italic">bread of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.33">v. 33</reference>), divine bread; it is he that is <hi type="italic">of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.46">v. 46</reference>), bread which my Father gives (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">v. 32</reference>), which he has made to be the food of our souls; the bread of God's family, his <hi type="italic">children's bread.</hi> The Levitical sacrifices are called the <hi type="italic">bread of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.21-Lev.21.22">Lev. xxi. 21, 22</reference>), and Christ is the great sacrifice; Christ, in his word and ordinances, the <hi type="italic">feast</hi> upon the sacrifice. [3.] That he is the <hi type="italic">bread of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.35-John.6.48">v. 35, and again, v. 48</reference>), <hi type="italic">that</hi> bread of life, alluding to the tree of life in the midst of the garden of Eden, which was to Adam the seal of that part of the covenant, <hi type="italic">Do this and live,</hi> of which he might <hi type="italic">eat and live.</hi> Christ is the bread of life, for he is the fruit of the <hi type="italic">tree of life. First,</hi> He is the <hi type="italic">living bread</hi> (so he explains himself, <reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am the living bread.</hi> Bread is itself a dead thing, and nourishes not but by the help of the faculties of a living body; but Christ is himself <hi type="italic">living bread,</hi> and nourishes by his own power. Manna was a dead thing; if kept but one night, it putrefied and bred worms; but Christ is ever living, everlasting bread, that never moulds, nor waxes old. The doctrine of Christ crucified is now as strengthening and comforting to a believer as ever it was, and his mediation still of as much value and efficacy as ever. <hi type="italic">Secondly, He gives life unto the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.33">v. 33</reference>), spiritual and eternal life; the life of the soul in union and communion with God here, and in the vision and fruition of him hereafter; a life that includes in it all happiness. The <hi type="italic">manna</hi> did only reserve and support life, did not preserve and perpetuate life, much less restore it; but Christ <hi type="italic">gives</hi> life to those that were dead in sin. The manna was ordained only for the life of the Israelites, but Christ is given for the <hi type="italic">life of the world;</hi> none are excluded from the benefit of this bread, but such as exclude themselves. Christ came to <hi type="italic">put life</hi> into the minds of men, principles productive of acceptable performances. [4.] That he is the <hi type="italic">bread which came down from heaven;</hi> this is often repeated here, <reference osisRef="John.6.33">v. 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.50">50</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.51">51,</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.58">58</reference>. This denotes, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The divinity of Christ's person. As God, he had a being in heaven, whence he came to take our nature upon him: <hi type="italic">I came down from heaven,</hi> whence we may infer his <hi type="italic">antiquity,</hi> he was in the beginning with God; his <hi type="italic">ability,</hi> for heaven is the firmament of power; and his <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> he came with a divine commission. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The divine original of all that good which flows to us through him. He <hi type="italic">comes,</hi> not only <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">katabas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that came down</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>), but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">katabainoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that comes down;</hi> he is descending, denoting a constant communication of light, life, and love, from God to believers through Christ, as the <hi type="italic">manna</hi> descended daily; see <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Eph. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Omnia desuper—All things from above.</hi> [5.] That he is <hi type="italic">that bread</hi> of which the <hi type="italic">manna</hi> was a type and figure (<reference osisRef="John.6.58">v. 58</reference>), <hi type="italic">that</hi> bread, the true bread, <reference osisRef="John.6.32">v. 32</reference>. As the rock that they drank of was Christ, so was the manna they ate of <hi type="italic">spiritual bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3-1Cor.10.4">1 Cor. x. 3, 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Manna</hi> was given to Israel; so Christ to the spiritual Israel. There was <hi type="italic">manna</hi> enough for them all; so in Christ a fulness of grace for all believers; he that <hi type="italic">gathers much</hi> of this <hi type="italic">manna</hi> will have none to spare when he comes to use it; and he that gathers little, when his grace comes to be perfected in glory, shall find that <hi type="italic">he has no lack. Manna</hi> was to be gathered in the morning; and those that would find Christ must <hi type="italic">seek him early.</hi> Manna was sweet, and, as the author of the <hi type="italic">Wisdom of Solomon</hi> tells us (<reference osisRef="Wis.16.20">Wisd. xvi. 20</reference>), was agreeable to every palate; and to those that believe Christ is <hi type="italic">precious.</hi> Israel lived upon <hi type="italic">manna</hi> till they came to Canaan; and Christ is our life. There was a memorial of the <hi type="italic">manna</hi> preserved in the ark; so of Christ in the Lord's supper, as the food of souls. <div eID="gen27127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27128" type="x-p"/> (2.) He here shows what his undertaking was, and what his errand into the world. Laying aside the metaphor, he speaks plainly, and speaks no proverb, giving us an account of his business among men, <reference osisRef="John.6.38-John.6.40">v. 38-40</reference>. <div eID="gen27128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27129" type="x-p"/> [1.] He assures us, in general, that he came from heaven upon his Father's business (<reference osisRef="John.6.38">v. 38</reference>), not <hi type="italic">do his own will, but the will of him that sent him.</hi> He <hi type="italic">came from heaven,</hi> which bespeaks him an intelligent active being, who voluntarily descended to this lower world, a long journey, and a great step downward, considering the glories of the world he came from and the calamities of the world he came to; we may well ask with wonder, "What moved him to such an expedition?" Here he tells that he came to do, not <hi type="italic">his own will,</hi> but the will of his Father; not that he had any will that stood in competition with the will of his Father, but those to whom he spoke suspected he might. "No," saith he, "my own will is not the spring I act from, nor the rule I go by, but I am come to <hi type="italic">do the will of him that sent me.</hi>" That is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ did not come into the world as a <hi type="italic">private</hi> person, that acts for himself only, but under a <hi type="italic">public character,</hi> to act for others as an ambassador, or plenipotentiary, authorized by a public commission; he came into the world as God's great agent and the world's great physician. It was not any private business that brought him hither, but he came to settle affairs between parties no less considerable than the great Creator and the whole creation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ, when he was in the world, did not carry on any <hi type="italic">private</hi> design, nor had any <hi type="italic">separate interest</hi> at all, distinct from theirs for whom he acted. The scope of his whole life was to glorify God and do good to men. He therefore never consulted his own ease, safety, or quiet; but, when he was to lay down his life, though he had a human nature which startled at it, he set aside the consideration of that, and resolved his will as man into the will of God: <hi type="italic">Not as I will, but as thou wilt.</hi> <div eID="gen27129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27130" type="x-p"/> [2.] He acquaints us, in particular, with that will of the Father which he came to do; he here <hi type="italic">declares the decree,</hi> the instructions he was to pursue. <div eID="gen27130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27131" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">private instructions</hi> given to Christ, that he should be sure to save all the chosen remnant; and this is the <hi type="italic">covenant of redemption</hi> between the Father and the Son (<reference osisRef="John.6.38">v. 38</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This is the Father's will, who hath sent me;</hi> this is the charge I am entrusted with, that <hi type="italic">of all whom he hath given me I should lose none.</hi>" Note, 1. There is a certain number of the children of men <hi type="italic">given</hi> by the Father to Jesus Christ, to be his care, and so to be to him for a name and a praise; given him for <hi type="italic">an inheritance,</hi> for a possession. Let him do all that for them which their case requires; teach them, and heal them, pay their debt, and plead their cause, prepare them for, and preserve them to, eternal life, and then let him make his best of them. The Father might dispose of them as he pleased: as creatures, their lives and beings were <hi type="italic">derived from</hi> him; as sinners, their lives and beings were <hi type="italic">forfeited to him.</hi> He might have sold them for the satisfaction of his justice, and delivered them <hi type="italic">to the tormentors;</hi> but he pitched upon them to be the monuments of his mercy, and delivered them to the Saviour. Those whom God chose to be the objects of his special love he lodged as a trust in the hands of Christ. 2. Jesus Christ has undertaken that he will <hi type="italic">lose none</hi> of those that were thus <hi type="italic">given him</hi> of the Father. The <hi type="italic">many sons</hi> whom he was to <hi type="italic">bring to glory</hi> shall all be forth-coming, and none of them missing, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.14">Matt. xviii. 14</reference>. None of them shall be lost, for want of a sufficient grace to sanctify them. <hi type="italic">If I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.43.9">Gen. xliii. 9</reference>. 3. Christ's undertaking for those that are given him extends to the resurrection of their bodies. <hi type="italic">I will raise it up again at the last day,</hi> which supposes all that goes before, but this is to crown and complete the undertaking. The body is a part of the man, and therefore a part of Christ's purchase and charge; it pertains to the promises, and therefore it shall not be <hi type="italic">lost.</hi> The undertaking is not only that he shall <hi type="italic">lose none,</hi> no <hi type="italic">person,</hi> but that he shall <hi type="italic">lose nothing,</hi> no part of the person, and therefore not the body. Christ's undertaking will never be accomplished till the resurrection, when the souls and bodies of the saints shall be re-united and gathered to Christ, that he may present them to the Father: <hi type="italic">Behold I, and the children that thou has given me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>. 4. The spring and original of all this is the <hi type="italic">sovereign will of God,</hi> the counsels of his will, according to which he works all this. This was the commandment he gave to his Son, when he sent him into the world, and to which the Son always had an eye. <div eID="gen27131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27132" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">public instructions</hi> which were to be given to the children of men, in what way, and upon what terms, they might obtain salvation by Christ; and this is the <hi type="italic">covenant of grace</hi> between God and man. Who the particular persons were that were given to Christ is a <hi type="italic">secret: The Lord knows them that are his,</hi> we do not, nor is it fit we should; but, though their names are concealed, their characters are published. An offer is made of life and happiness upon gospel terms, that by it those that were given to Christ might be brought to him, and others left inexcusable (<reference osisRef="John.6.40">v. 40</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This is the will,</hi> the revealed will, <hi type="italic">of him that sent me,</hi> the method agreed upon, upon which to proceed with the children of men, that <hi type="italic">every one,</hi> Jew or Gentile, that <hi type="italic">sees the Son, and believes on him,</hi> may have <hi type="italic">everlasting life,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I will raise him up.</hi>" This is <hi type="italic">gospel</hi> indeed, good news. Is it now reviving to hear this? 1. That <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> may be had, if it be not our own fault; that whereas, upon the sin of the first Adam, the <hi type="italic">way of the tree of life</hi> was blocked up, by the grace of the second Adam it is laid upon again. The crown of glory is set before us as the prize of our high calling, which we may run for and obtain. 2. Every one may have it. This gospel is to be preached, this offer made, to all, and none can say, "It belongs not to me," <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Rev. xxii. 17</reference>. 3. This everlasting life is sure to all those who believe in Christ, and to them only. He that <hi type="italic">sees the Son,</hi> and <hi type="italic">believes on him,</hi> shall be saved. Some understand this <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> as a <hi type="italic">limitation</hi> of this condition of salvation to those only that have the revelation of Christ and his grace made to them. Every one that has the opportunity of being acquainted with Christ, and improves this so well as to <hi type="italic">believe</hi> in him, shall have everlasting life, so that none shall be condemned for unbelief (however they maybe for other sins) but those who have had the gospel preached to them, who, like these Jews here (<reference osisRef="John.6.36">v. 36</reference>), have <hi type="italic">seen,</hi> and yet have <hi type="italic">not</hi> believed; have known Christ, and yet not trusted in him. But I rather understand <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> here to mean the same thing with <hi type="italic">believing,</hi> for it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">theoron</hi></hi>, which signifies not so much the sight of the eye (as <reference osisRef="John.6.36">v. 36</reference>, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">heorakate me</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">ye have seen me</hi>) as the <hi type="italic">contemplation of the mind.</hi> Every one that <hi type="italic">sees the Son,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">believes on him,</hi> sees him with an eye of faith, by which we come to be duly acquainted and affected with the doctrine of the gospel concerning him. It is to look upon him, as the stung Israelites upon the brazen serpent. It is not a <hi type="italic">blind</hi> faith that Christ requires, that we should be willing to have our <hi type="italic">eyes put out,</hi> and then follow him, but that we should <hi type="italic">see him,</hi> and see what ground we go upon in our faith. It is <hi type="italic">then</hi> right when it is not taken up upon <hi type="italic">hearsay</hi> (believing as the church believes), but is the result of a due consideration of, and insight into, the motives of credibility: <hi type="italic">Now mine eye sees thee. We have heard him ourselves.</hi> 4. Those who believe in Jesus Christ, in order to their having everlasting life, shall be raised up by his power at the last day. He had it in charge as his Father's will (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">v. 39</reference>), and here he solemnly makes it his own undertaking: I <hi type="italic">will raise him up,</hi> which signifies not only the return of the body to life, but the putting of the <hi type="italic">whole man</hi> into a full possession of the eternal life promised. <div eID="gen27132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27133" type="x-p"/> 2. Now Christ discoursing thus concerning himself, as the <hi type="italic">bread of life</hi> that came down from heaven, let us see what remarks his hearers made upon it. <div eID="gen27133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27134" type="x-p"/> (1.) When they heard of such a thing as the <hi type="italic">bread of God,</hi> which <hi type="italic">gives life,</hi> they heartily prayed for it (<reference osisRef="John.6.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lord, evermore give us this bread.</hi> I cannot think that this is spoken scoffingly, and in a way of derision, as most interpreters understand it: "Give us such bread as this, if thou canst; let us be fed with it, not for one meal, as with the five loaves, but <hi type="italic">evermore;</hi>" as if this were no better a prayer than that of the impenitent thief: <hi type="italic">If thou be the Christ, save thyself and us.</hi> But I take this request to be made, though ignorantly, yet honestly, and to be well meant; for they call him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> and desire a share in what he <hi type="italic">gives,</hi> whatever he means by it. General and confused notions of divine things produce in carnal hearts some kind of desires towards them, and wishes of them; like Balaam's wish, to die the <hi type="italic">death of the righteous.</hi> Those who have an indistinct knowledge of the things of God, who see men as trees walking, make, as I may call them, <hi type="italic">inarticulate</hi> prayers for spiritual blessings. They think the favour of God a <hi type="italic">good thing,</hi> and heaven a <hi type="italic">fine place,</hi> and cannot but wish them their own, while they have no value nor desire at all for that holiness which is necessary both to the one and to the other. Let this be the desire of our souls; have we tasted that the Lord is gracious, been feasted with the word of God, and Christ in the word? Let us say, "<hi type="italic">Lord, evermore give us this bread;</hi> let the bread of life be our daily bread, the heavenly manna our continual feast, and let us never know the want of it." <div eID="gen27134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27135" type="x-p"/> (2.) But, when they understood that by this <hi type="italic">bread of life</hi> Jesus meant <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> then they <hi type="italic">despised</hi> it. Whether they were the same persons that had prayed for it (<reference osisRef="John.6.34">v. 34</reference>), or some others of the company, does not appear; it seems to be some others, for they are called <hi type="italic">Jews.</hi> Now it is said (<reference osisRef="John.6.41">v. 41</reference>), <hi type="italic">They murmured at him.</hi> This comes in immediately after that solemn declaration which Christ had made of God's will and his own undertaking concerning man's salvation (<reference osisRef="John.6.39-John.6.40">v. 39, 40</reference>), which certainly were some of the most weighty and gracious words that ever proceeded out of the mouth of our Lord Jesus, the most faithful, and best worthy of all acceptation. One would think that, like Israel in Egypt, when they heard that God had thus <hi type="italic">visited</hi> them, they should have <hi type="italic">bowed their heads and worshipped;</hi> but on the contrary, instead of closing with the offer made them, they <hi type="italic">murmured,</hi> quarrelled with what Christ said, and, though they did not openly oppose and contradict it, yet they privately whispered among themselves in contempt of it, and instilled into one another's minds prejudices against it. Many that will not professedly contradict the doctrine of Christ (their cavils are so weak and groundless that they are either ashamed to own them or afraid to have them silenced), yet say in their hearts that they <hi type="italic">do not like it.</hi> Now, [1.] That which offended them was Christ's asserting his origin to be <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.41-John.6.42">v. 41, 42</reference>. How is it that he saith, <hi type="italic">I came down from heaven?</hi> They had heard of angels coming down <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> but never of a man, overlooking the proofs he had given them of his being more than a man. [2.] That which they thought justified them herein was that they knew his extraction on earth: <hi type="italic">Is not this Jesus the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?</hi> They took it amiss that he should say that he came down from heaven, when he was <hi type="italic">one of them.</hi> They speak slightly of his blessed name, <hi type="italic">Jesus: Is not this Jesus.</hi> They take it for granted that Joseph was really his father, though he was only <hi type="italic">reputed</hi> to be so. Note, Mistakes concerning the person of Christ, as if he were a mere man, conceived and born by ordinary generation, occasion the offence that is taken at his doctrine and offices. Those who set him on a level with the other sons of men, whose father and mother we know, no wonder if they derogate from the honour of his satisfaction and the mysteries of his undertaking, and, like the Jews here, murmur at his promise to <hi type="italic">raise us up at the last day.</hi> <div eID="gen27135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27136" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ, having spoken of faith as the great <hi type="italic">work of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.29">v. 29</reference>), discourses largely concerning this work, instructing and encouraging us in it. <div eID="gen27136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27137" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows what it is to <hi type="italic">believe in Christ.</hi> [1.] To believe in Christ is to <hi type="italic">come to Christ.</hi> He that <hi type="italic">comes to</hi> me is the same with him that <hi type="italic">believes in me</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.35">v. 35</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="John.6.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that comes unto me;</hi> so <reference osisRef="John.6.44-John.6.45">v. 44, 45</reference>. Repentance towards God is <hi type="italic">coming to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jer. iii. 22</reference>) as our chief good and highest end; and so faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ is coming to him as our prince and Saviour, and our way to the Father. It denotes the out-goings of our affection towards him, for these are the motions of the soul, and actions agreeable; it is to <hi type="italic">come off</hi> from all those things that stand in opposition to him or competition with him, and to <hi type="italic">come up</hi> to those terms upon which life and salvation are offered to us through him. When he was here on earth it was more that barely coming where he was; so it is now more than coming to his word and ordinances. [2.] It is to <hi type="italic">feed upon Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>): <hi type="italic">If any man eat of this bread.</hi> The former denotes applying ourselves to Christ; this denotes applying Christ to ourselves, with appetite and delight, that we may receive life, and strength, and comfort from him. To feed on him as the Israelites on the manna, having quitted the <hi type="italic">fleshpots</hi> of Egypt, and not depending on the <hi type="italic">labour of their hands</hi> (to eat of that), but living purely on the bread given them from heaven. <div eID="gen27137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27138" type="x-p"/> (2.) He shows what is to be got by believing in Christ. What will he give us if we <hi type="italic">come to him?</hi> What shall we be the better of we <hi type="italic">feed upon him? Want</hi> and <hi type="italic">death</hi> are the chief things we dread; may we but be assured of the comforts of our being, and the continuance of it in the midst of these comforts, we have enough; now these two are here secured to true believers. <div eID="gen27138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27139" type="x-p"/> [1.] They shall never want, <hi type="italic">never hunger, never thirst,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.35">v. 35</reference>. Desires they have, earnest desires, but these so suitably, so seasonably, so abundantly satisfied, that they cannot be called hunger and thirst, which are uneasy and painful. Those that did eat manna, and drink of the rock, hungered and thirsted afterwards. Manna surfeited them; water out of the rock failed them. But there is such an <hi type="italic">over-flowing fulness</hi> in Christ as can never be <hi type="italic">exhausted,</hi> and there are such <hi type="italic">ever-flowing communications</hi> from him as can never be interrupted. <div eID="gen27139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27140" type="x-p"/> [2.] They shall <hi type="italic">never die,</hi> not die eternally; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He that believes on Christ <hi type="italic">has everlasting life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.47">v. 47</reference>); he has the assurance of it, the grant of it, the earnest of it; he has it in the promise and first-fruits. Union with Christ and communion with God in Christ are <hi type="italic">everlasting life</hi> begun. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Whereas they that did <hi type="italic">eat manna</hi> died, Christ is such bread as a man may eat of and never die, <reference osisRef="John.6.49-John.6.50">v. 49, 50</reference>. Observe here, 1. The insufficiency of the typical manna: <hi type="italic">Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.</hi> There may be much good use made of the death of our fathers; their graves speak to us, and their monuments are our memorials, particularly of this, that the greatest <hi type="italic">plenty</hi> of the most <hi type="italic">dainty</hi> food will neither prolong the thread of life nor avert the stroke of death. Those that did eat manna, angel's food, died like other men. There could be nothing amiss in their diet, to shorten their days, nor could their deaths be hastened by the toils and fatigues of life (for they neither sowed nor reaped), and <hi type="italic">yet they died.</hi> (1.) Many of them died by the immediate strokes of God's vengeance for their unbelief and murmurings; for, <hi type="italic">though they did eat that spiritual meat,</hi> yet with many of them God <hi type="italic">was not well-pleased, but they were overthrown in the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3-1Cor.10.5">1 Cor. x. 3-5</reference>. Their eating manna was no security to <hi type="italic">them</hi> from the <hi type="italic">wrath of God,</hi> as believing in Christ is to <hi type="italic">us.</hi> (2.) The rest of them died in a course of nature, and their carcases fell, under a divine sentence, in that wilderness where they did <hi type="italic">eat manna.</hi> In that very age when miracles were <hi type="italic">daily bread</hi> was the life of man reduced to the stint it now stands at, as appears, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Ps. xc. 10</reference>. Let them not then boast so much of <hi type="italic">manna.</hi> 2. The all-sufficiency of the true <hi type="italic">manna,</hi> of which the other was a type: <hi type="italic">This is the bread that cometh down from heaven,</hi> that truly divine and heavenly food, <hi type="italic">that a man may eat thereof and not die;</hi> that is, not fall under the wrath of God, which is killing to the soul; <hi type="italic">not die</hi> the second death; no, nor the first death finally and irrecoverably. <hi type="italic">Not die,</hi> that is, not perish, not come short of the heavenly Canaan, as the Israelites did of the earthly, for want of <hi type="italic">faith,</hi> though they had <hi type="italic">manna.</hi> This is further explained by that promise in the next words: <hi type="italic">If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>. This is the meaning of this <hi type="italic">never dying:</hi> though he go down <hi type="italic">to death,</hi> he shall pass through it to that world where there shall be <hi type="italic">no more death.</hi> To <hi type="italic">live for ever</hi> is not to <hi type="italic">be</hi> for ever (the damned in hell shall <hi type="italic">be</hi> for ever, the soul of man was made for an endless state), but to be <hi type="italic">happy</hi> for ever. And because the body must needs die, and be as water spilt upon the ground, Christ here undertakes for the gathering of that up too (as before, <reference osisRef="John.6.44">v. 44</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will raise him up at the last day</hi>); and even that shall live for ever. <div eID="gen27140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27141" type="x-p"/> (3.) He shows what encouragements we have to believe in Christ. Christ here speaks of some who <hi type="italic">had seen him and yet believed not,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.36">v. 36</reference>. They saw his person and miracles, and heard him preach, and yet were not wrought upon to believe in him. Faith is not always the effect of sight; the soldiers were eye-witnesses of his resurrection, and yet, instead of <hi type="italic">believing</hi> in him, they <hi type="italic">belied</hi> him; so that it is a difficult thing to bring people to believe in Christ: and, by the operation of the Spirit of grace, those that <hi type="italic">have not seen have yet believed.</hi> Two things we are here assured of, to encourage our faith:— <div eID="gen27141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27142" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Son will bid all those welcome that come to him (<reference osisRef="John.6.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.</hi> How welcome should this word be to our souls which bids us welcome to Christ! <hi type="italic">Him</hi> that cometh; it is in the singular number, denoting favour, not only to the body of believers in general, but to every particular soul that applies itself to Christ. Here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The duty required is a pure gospel duty: to <hi type="italic">come to Christ,</hi> that we may come to God by him. His beauty and love, those great attractives, must <hi type="italic">draw</hi> us to him; sense of need and fear of danger must <hi type="italic">drive</hi> us to him; any thing to bring us to Christ. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The promise is a pure gospel promise: <hi type="italic">I will in no wise cast out</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou me ekbago exo</hi></hi>. There are two negatives: <hi type="italic">I will not, no, I will not.</hi> 1. Much favour is expressed here. We have reason to fear that he should <hi type="italic">cast us out.</hi> Considering our meanness, our vileness, our unworthiness to come, our weakness in coming, we may justly expect that he should frown upon us, and shut his doors against us; but he obviates these fears with this assurance, he <hi type="italic">will not</hi> do it; will not disdain us though we are mean, will not reject us though we are sinful. Do poor scholars come to him to be taught? Though they be dull and slow, he will not <hi type="italic">cast them out.</hi> Do poor <hi type="italic">patients</hi> come to him to be <hi type="italic">cured,</hi> poor <hi type="italic">clients</hi> come to him to be <hi type="italic">advised?</hi> Though their case be bad, and though they come empty-handed, he will <hi type="italic">in no wise cast them out.</hi> But, 2. More favour is implied than is expressed; when it is said that he will no cast them out the meaning is, He will receive them, and entertain them, and give them all that which they come to him for. As he will not refuse them at their first coming, so he will not afterwards, upon every displeasure, cast them out. <hi type="italic">His gifts and callings are without repentance.</hi> <div eID="gen27142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27143" type="x-p"/> [2.] That the Father will, without fail, bring all those to him in due time that were given him. In the federal transactions between the Father and the Son, relating to man's redemption, as the Son undertook for the justification, sanctification, and salvation, of all that should come to him ("Let me have them put into my hands, and then leave the management of them to me"), so the Father, the fountain and original of being, life, and grace, undertook to put into his hand all that were given him, and bring them to him. Now, <div eID="gen27143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27144" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He here <hi type="italic">assures</hi> us <hi type="italic">that</hi> this shall be done: <hi type="italic">All that the Father giveth me shall come to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.37">v. 37</reference>. Christ had complained (<reference osisRef="John.6.36">v. 36</reference>) of those who, though they had <hi type="italic">seen</hi> him, yet would not believe on him; and then he adds this, <div eID="gen27144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> For <hi type="italic">their</hi> conviction and awakening, plainly intimating that their not coming to him, and believing on him, if they persisted in it, would be a certain sign that they did not belong to the election of grace; for how can we think that God gave us to Christ if we give ourselves to the world and the flesh? <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.10">2 Pet. i. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27146" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> For <hi type="italic">his own</hi> comfort and encouragement: <hi type="italic">Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious.</hi> The election <hi type="italic">has obtained,</hi> and shall though multitudes be <hi type="italic">blinded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>. Though he lose many of his <hi type="italic">creatures,</hi> yet none of his <hi type="italic">charge: All that the Father gives him shall come to him</hi> notwithstanding. Here we have, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The election described: <hi type="italic">All that the father giveth me,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pan ho didosi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">every thing</hi> which the Father <hi type="italic">giveth to me;</hi> the persons of the elect, and all that belongs to them; all their services, all their interests. As all that he has is <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> so all that they have is <hi type="italic">his,</hi> and he speaks of them as his all: they were given him in full recompense of his undertaking. Not only all persons, but all things, are gathered together in Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>) and reconciled, <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col. i. 20</reference>. The giving of the chosen remnant to Christ is spoken of (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">v. 39</reference>) as a thing <hi type="italic">done;</hi> he <hi type="italic">hath given</hi> them. Here it is spoken of as a thing <hi type="italic">in the doing;</hi> he <hi type="italic">giveth them;</hi> because, <hi type="italic">when the first begotten was brought into the world,</hi> it should seem, there was a renewal of the grant; see <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">Heb. x. 5</reference>, &c. God was now about to <hi type="italic">give him the heathen for his inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>), to put him in possession of <hi type="italic">the desolate heritages</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa. xlix. 8</reference>), to <hi type="italic">divide him a portion with the great,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>. And though the Jews, who <hi type="italic">saw</hi> him, <hi type="italic">believed not</hi> on him, yet these (saith he) shall <hi type="italic">come to me;</hi> the other sheep, which are not of this fold, shall be <hi type="italic">brought,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.15-John.10.16">ch. x. 15, 16</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Acts.13.45-Acts.13.48">Acts xiii. 45-48</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The effect of it secured: <hi type="italic">They shall come to me.</hi> This is not in the nature of a <hi type="italic">promise,</hi> but a <hi type="italic">prediction,</hi> that as many as were in the counsel of God ordained to life shall be brought to life by being brought to Christ. They are <hi type="italic">scattered,</hi> are mingled among the nations, yet none of them shall be forgotten; not a grain of God's corn shall be lost, as is promised, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Amos ix. 9</reference>. They are by nature <hi type="italic">alienated</hi> from Christ, and averse to him, and yet <hi type="italic">they shall come.</hi> As God's omniscience is engaged for the finding of them all out, so is his omnipotence for the bringing of them all in. Not, They shall be <hi type="italic">driven,</hi> to me, but, They shall come freely, shall be made <hi type="italic">willing.</hi> <div eID="gen27146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27147" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He here <hi type="italic">acquaints</hi> us <hi type="italic">how</hi> it shall be done. How shall those who are given to Christ be brought to him? Two things are to be done in order to it:— <div eID="gen27147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27148" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Their <hi type="italic">understandings</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">enlightened;</hi> this is promised, <reference osisRef="John.6.45-John.6.46">v. 45, 46</reference>. It is written in the prophets, who spoke of these things before, <hi type="italic">And they shall be all taught of God;</hi> this we find, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Isa. liv. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">and Jer. xxxi. 34</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall all know me.</hi> Note, <div eID="gen27148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27149" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) In order to our <hi type="italic">believing in Jesus Christ,</hi> it is necessary that we be <hi type="italic">taught of God;</hi> that is, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] That there be a <hi type="italic">divine revelation made to us,</hi> discovering to us both what we are to believe concerning Christ and why we are to believe it. There are some things which <hi type="italic">even nature teaches,</hi> but to bring us to Christ there is need of a higher light. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] That there be a <hi type="italic">divine work wrought in us,</hi> enabling us to understand and receive these revealed truths and the evidence of them. God, in giving us reason, teaches us more than the <hi type="italic">beasts of the earth;</hi> but in giving us faith he teaches more than the <hi type="italic">natural man.</hi> Thus all the church's children, all that are <hi type="italic">genuine,</hi> are <hi type="italic">taught of God;</hi> he hath undertaken their education. <div eID="gen27149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27150" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It follows then, by way of inference from this, that <hi type="italic">every man</hi> that has <hi type="italic">heard and learned of the Father comes to Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.45">v. 45</reference>. [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] It is here implied that none will come to Christ but those that have <hi type="italic">heard</hi> and <hi type="italic">learned of the Father.</hi> We shall never be brought to Christ but under a divine conduct; except God by his grace enlighten our minds, inform our judgments, and rectify our mistakes, and not only <hi type="italic">tell</hi> us that we may <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> but teach us, that we may <hi type="italic">learn</hi> the truth as it is in Jesus, we shall never be brought to believe in Christ. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] That this <hi type="italic">divine teaching</hi> does so necessarily produce the <hi type="italic">faith of God's elect</hi> that we may conclude that those who do not <hi type="italic">come to Christ</hi> have never <hi type="italic">heard</hi> nor <hi type="italic">learned</hi> of the Father; for, if they had, doubtless they would have come to Christ. In vain do men pretend to be <hi type="italic">taught of God</hi> if they believe not in Christ, for he teaches no other lesson, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8-Gal.1.9">Gal. i. 8, 9</reference>. See how God deals with men as reasonable creatures, draws them with the <hi type="italic">cords of a man,</hi> opens the understanding first, and then by that, in a regular way, influences the inferior faculties; thus he comes in by the door, but Satan, as a robber, climbs up another way.
