But lest any should dream of a visible appearance of God the Father to the children of men (to teach them these things), and entertain any gross conceptions about hearing and learning of the Father, he adds (<reference osisRef="John.6.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Not that any man hath seen the Father;</hi> it is implied, nor <hi type="italic">can</hi> see him, with bodily eyes, or may expect to learn of him as Moses did, to whom he spoke <hi type="italic">face to face;</hi> but God, in enlightening men's eyes and teaching them, works in a spiritual way. The Father of spirits hath access to, and influence upon, men's spirits, undiscerned. The Father of spirits hath access to, and influence upon, men's spirits, undiscerned. Those that have not seen his face have felt his power. And yet there is one intimately acquainted with the Father, he <hi type="italic">who is of God,</hi> Christ himself, he hath <hi type="italic">seen the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jesus Christ is of God in a peculiar manner, God of God, light of light; not only sent of God, but begotten of God before all worlds. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is the prerogative of Christ to have <hi type="italic">seen the Father,</hi> perfectly to know him and his counsels. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Even that illumination which is preparative to faith is conveyed to us through Christ. Those that <hi type="italic">learn of the Father,</hi> forasmuch as they cannot see him themselves, must learn of Christ, who alone hath seen him. As all divine discoveries are made through Christ, so through him all divine powers are exerted. <div eID="gen27150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Their <hi type="italic">wills</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">bowed.</hi> If the soul of man had now its original rectitude there needed no more to influence the will than the illumination of the understanding; but in the depraved soul of fallen man there is a rebellion of the will against the right dictates of the understanding; a <hi type="italic">carnal mind,</hi> which is <hi type="italic">enmity</hi> itself to the divine light and law. It is therefore requisite that there be a work of grace wrought upon the will, which is here called <hi type="italic">drawing,</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">No man can come to me except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him.</hi> The Jews murmured at the doctrine of Christ; not only would not receive it themselves, but were angry that others did. Christ overheard their secret whisperings, and said (<reference osisRef="John.6.43">v. 43</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Murmur not among yourselves;</hi> lay not the fault of your dislike of my doctrine one upon another, as if it were because you find it generally distasted; no, it is owing to yourselves, and your own corrupt dispositions, which are such as amount to a <hi type="italic">moral impotency;</hi> your antipathies to the truths of God, and prejudices against them, are so strong that nothing less than a divine power can conquer them." And this is the case of all mankind: "<hi type="italic">No man can come to me,</hi> can persuade himself to come up to the terms of the gospel, <hi type="italic">except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="John.6.44">v. 44</reference>. Observe, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The nature of the work: It is <hi type="italic">drawing,</hi> which denotes not a <hi type="italic">force</hi> put upon the will, whereby of unwilling we are made willing, and a new bias is given to the soul, by which it inclines to God. This seems to be more than a <hi type="italic">moral suasion,</hi> for by that it is in the power to <hi type="italic">draw;</hi> yet it is not to be called a <hi type="italic">physical impulse,</hi> for it lies out of the road of <hi type="italic">nature;</hi> but he that <hi type="italic">formed the spirit of man within him</hi> by his creating power, and <hi type="italic">fashions the hearts of men</hi> by his providential influence, knows how to new-mould the soul, and to alter its bent and temper, and make it conformable to himself and his own will, without doing any wrong to its natural liberty. It is such a drawing as works not only a <hi type="italic">compliance,</hi> but a cheerful compliance, a complacency: <hi type="italic">Draw us, and we will run after thee.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The necessity of it: <hi type="italic">No man,</hi> in this weak and helpless state, can come to Christ without it. As we <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> do any natural action without the concurrence of <hi type="italic">common providence,</hi> so we cannot do any action morally good without the influence of <hi type="italic">special grace,</hi> in which the <hi type="italic">new man</hi> lives, and moves, and has its being, as much as the <hi type="italic">mere man</hi> has in the divine providence. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) The author of it: The <hi type="italic">Father who hath sent me.</hi> The Father, having sent Christ, will succeed him, for he would not send him on a fruitless errand. Christ having undertaken to bring souls to glory, God promised him, in order thereunto, to bring them to him, and so to give him possession of those to whom he had given him a right. God, having by promise given the kingdom of Israel to David, did at length <hi type="italic">draw the hearts</hi> of the people to him; so, having sent Christ to save souls, he sends souls to him to be saved by him. (<hi type="italic">d.</hi>) The crown and perfection of this work: And <hi type="italic">I will raise him up at the last day.</hi> This is four times mentioned in this discourse, and doubtless it includes all the intermediate and preparatory workings of divine grace. When he <hi type="italic">raises them up at the last day,</hi> he will put the <hi type="italic">last hand</hi> to his undertaking, will <hi type="italic">bring forth the topstone.</hi> If he undertakes this, surely he <hi type="italic">can</hi> do any thing, and will do every thing that is necessary in order to do it. Let our expectations be carried out towards a happiness reserved for the <hi type="italic">last day,</hi> when all the years of time shall be fully complete and ended. <div eID="gen27151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27152" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ, having thus spoken of himself as the <hi type="italic">bread of life,</hi> and of faith as <hi type="italic">the work of God,</hi> comes more particularly to show <hi type="italic">what of himself</hi> is this bread, namely, his flesh, and that to believe is to eat of that, <reference osisRef="John.6.51-John.6.58">v. 51-58</reference>, where he still prosecutes the metaphor of food. Observe, here, the <hi type="italic">preparation</hi> of this food: <hi type="italic">The bread that I will give is my flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>), <hi type="italic">the flesh of the Son of man and his blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.53">v. 53</reference>. <hi type="italic">His flesh is meat indeed, and his blood is drink indeed,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.55">v. 55</reference>. Observe, also, the <hi type="italic">participation</hi> of this food: We must <hi type="italic">eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.53">v. 53</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="John.6.54">v. 54</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whoso eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood;</hi> and the same words (<reference osisRef="John.6.56-John.6.57">v. 56, 57</reference>), he that <hi type="italic">eateth me.</hi> This is certainly a parable or figurative discourse, wherein the actings of the soul upon things spiritual and divine are represented by bodily actions about things sensible, which made the truths of Christ more intelligible to some, and less so to others, <reference osisRef="Mark.4.11-Mark.4.12">Mark iv. 11-12</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen27152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27153" type="x-p"/> (1.) Let us see how this discourse of Christ was liable to mistake and misconstruction, that <hi type="italic">men might see, and not perceive.</hi> [1.] It was misconstrued by the carnal <hi type="italic">Jews,</hi> to whom it was first delivered (<reference osisRef="John.6.52">v. 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">They strove among themselves;</hi> they whispered in each other's ears their dissatisfaction: <hi type="italic">How can this man give us his flesh to eat?</hi> Christ spoke (<reference osisRef="John.6.51">v. 51</reference>) of giving his flesh <hi type="italic">for us,</hi> to suffer and die; but they, without due consideration, understood it of his giving it <hi type="italic">to us,</hi> to be eaten, which gave occasion to Christ to tell them that, however what he said was otherwise intended, yet even that also of <hi type="italic">eating of his flesh</hi> was no such absurd thing (if rightly understood) as <hi type="italic">prima facie—in the first instance,</hi> they took it to be. [2.] It has been wretchedly misconstrued by the church of Rome for the support of their monstrous doctrine of transubstantiation, which gives the lie to our senses, contradicts the nature of a sacrament, and overthrows all convincing evidence. They, like these Jews here, understand it of a corporal and carnal eating of Christ's body, like Nicodemus, <reference osisRef="John.3.4">ch. iii. 4</reference>. The Lord's supper was not yet instituted, and therefore it could have no reference to that; it is a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> eating and drinking that is here spoken of, not a <hi type="italic">sacramental.</hi> [3.] It is misunderstood by many ignorant carnal people, who hence infer that, if they take the sacrament when they die, they shall certainly go to heaven, which, as it makes many that are weak causelessly uneasy if they want it, so it makes many that are wicked causelessly easy if they have it. Therefore, <div eID="gen27153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27154" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let us see how this discourse of Christ is to be understood. <div eID="gen27154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27155" type="x-p"/> [1.] What is meant by the <hi type="italic">flesh and blood of Christ.</hi> It is called (<reference osisRef="John.6.53">v. 53</reference>), <hi type="italic">The flesh of the Son of man, and his blood, his</hi> as Messiah and Mediator: the <hi type="italic">flesh and blood</hi> which he <hi type="italic">assumed</hi> in his incarnation (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>), and which he <hi type="italic">gave up</hi> in his <hi type="italic">death</hi> and <hi type="italic">suffering: my flesh which I will give</hi> to be crucified and slain. It is said to be <hi type="italic">given for the life of the world,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First, Instead</hi> of the <hi type="italic">life of the world,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">forfeited</hi> by sin, Christ gives his own flesh as a ransom or counterprice. Christ was our bail, bound <hi type="italic">body for body</hi> (as we say), and therefore <hi type="italic">his</hi> life must go for <hi type="italic">ours,</hi> that ours may be spared. <hi type="italic">Here am I, let these go their way. Secondly, In order to</hi> the <hi type="italic">life of the world,</hi> to purchase a <hi type="italic">general</hi> offer of eternal life to all the world, and the <hi type="italic">special</hi> assurances of it to all believers. So that the <hi type="italic">flesh and blood</hi> of the Son of man denote the Redeemer <hi type="italic">incarnate</hi> and <hi type="italic">dying;</hi> Christ and <hi type="italic">him crucified,</hi> and the redemption wrought out by him, with all the precious benefits of redemption: pardon of sin, acceptance with God, the adoption of sons, access to the throne of grace, the promises of the covenant, and eternal life; these are called <hi type="italic">the flesh and blood</hi> of Christ, 1. Because they are purchased by his flesh and blood, by the breaking of his body, and shedding of his blood. Well may the purchased privileges be denominated from the price that was paid for them, for it puts a value upon them; write upon them <hi type="italic">pretium sanguinis—the price of blood.</hi> 2. Because they are meat and drink to our souls. <hi type="italic">Flesh with the blood</hi> was prohibited (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen. ix. 4</reference>), but the privileges of the gospel are as flesh and blood to us, prepared for the nourishment of our souls. He had before compared himself to <hi type="italic">bread,</hi> which is necessary food; here to <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> which is delicious. It is a <hi type="italic">feast of fat things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>. The soul is satisfied with Christ as <hi type="italic">with marrow and fatness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Ps. lxiii. 5</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">meat indeed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink indeed; truly so,</hi> that is spiritually; so Dr. Whitby; as Christ is called the <hi type="italic">true vine;</hi> or <hi type="italic">truly meat,</hi> in opposition to the shows and shadows with which the world shams off those that feed upon it. In Christ and his gospel there is real supply, solid satisfaction; that is <hi type="italic">meat indeed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink indeed,</hi> which satiates and replenishes, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.25-Jer.31.26">Jer. xxxi. 25, 26</reference>. <div eID="gen27155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27156" type="x-p"/> [2.] What is meant by <hi type="italic">eating this flesh</hi> and <hi type="italic">drinking</hi> this <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> which is so necessary and beneficial; it is certain that is means neither more nor less than believing in Christ. As we partake of meat and drink by eating and drinking, so we partake of Christ and his benefits by faith: and <hi type="italic">believing in Christ</hi> includes these four things, which <hi type="italic">eating and drinking</hi> do:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> It implies an <hi type="italic">appetite</hi> to Christ. This spiritual eating and drinking begins with <hi type="italic">hungering</hi> and <hi type="italic">thirsting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">Matt. v. 6</reference>), earnest and importunate desires after Christ, not willing to take up with any thing short of an interest in him: "Give me Christ or else I die." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> An <hi type="italic">application</hi> of Christ to ourselves. Meat <hi type="italic">looked upon</hi> will not nourish us, but meat <hi type="italic">fed upon,</hi> and so made <hi type="italic">our own,</hi> and as it were <hi type="italic">one with us.</hi> We must so accept of Christ as to appropriate him to ourselves: <hi type="italic">my Lord, and my God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.28">ch. xx. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> A <hi type="italic">delight</hi> in Christ and his salvation. The doctrine of Christ crucified must be <hi type="italic">meat and drink</hi> to us, most pleasant and delightful. We must feast upon the dainties of the <hi type="italic">New Testament in the blood of Christ,</hi> taking as great a complacency in the methods which Infinite Wisdom has taken to redeem and save us as ever we did in the most needful supplies or grateful delights of nature. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> A <hi type="italic">derivation of nourishment</hi> from him and a dependence upon him for the support and comfort of our spiritual life, and the strength, growth, and vigour of the new man. To <hi type="italic">feed upon Christ</hi> is to do all <hi type="italic">in his name,</hi> in union with him, and by virtue drawn from him; it is to live upon him as we do upon our meat. How our bodies are nourished by our food we cannot describe, but that they are so we know and find; so it is with this spiritual nourishment. Our Saviour was so well pleased with this metaphor (as very significant and expressive) that, when afterwards he would institute some outward sensible signs, by which to represent our <hi type="italic">communicating</hi> of the benefits of his death, he chose those of <hi type="italic">eating</hi> and <hi type="italic">drinking,</hi> and made them <hi type="italic">sacramental</hi> actions. <div eID="gen27156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27157" type="x-p"/> (3.) Having thus explained the general meaning of this part of Christ's discourse, the particulars are reducible to two heads:— <div eID="gen27157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27158" type="x-p"/> [1.] The <hi type="italic">necessity</hi> of our <hi type="italic">feeding upon Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you have no life in you.</hi> That is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "It is a certain sign that you <hi type="italic">have no</hi> spiritual <hi type="italic">life</hi> in you if you have no <hi type="italic">desire</hi> towards Christ, nor <hi type="italic">delight</hi> in him." If the soul does not <hi type="italic">hunger</hi> and <hi type="italic">thirst,</hi> certainly it does not <hi type="italic">live:</hi> it is a sign that we are dead indeed if we are dead to such meat and drink as this. When <hi type="italic">artificial</hi> bees, that by curious springs were made to move to and fro, were to be <hi type="italic">distinguished</hi> from <hi type="italic">natural</hi> ones (they say), it was done by putting honey among them, which the natural bees only flocked to, but the artificial ones minded not, for <hi type="italic">they had no life in them. Secondly,</hi> "It is certain that you <hi type="italic">can have</hi> no spiritual life, unless you derive it from Christ by faith; separated from him you can do nothing." Faith in Christ is the <hi type="italic">primum vivens—the first living principle</hi> of grace; without it we have not the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> of <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> life, nor any title to eternal life: our bodies may as well live without meat as our souls without Christ. <div eID="gen27158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> [2.] The <hi type="italic">benefit</hi> and <hi type="italic">advantage</hi> of it, in two things:— <div eID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27160" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We shall be <hi type="italic">one with Christ,</hi> as our bodies are with our food when it is digested (<reference osisRef="John.6.56">v. 56</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that eats my flesh, and drinks my blood,</hi> that lives by faith in Christ crucified (it is spoken of as a continued act), he <hi type="italic">dwelleth in me, and I in him.</hi> By faith we have a close and intimate union with Christ; he is <hi type="italic">in us,</hi> and we <hi type="italic">in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.21-John.17.23">ch. xvii. 21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">1 John iii. 24</reference>. Believers dwell in Christ as their stronghold or city of refuge; Christ dwells in them as the master of the house, to rule it and provide for it. Such is the union between Christ and believers that he shares in their griefs, and they share in his graces and joys; he <hi type="italic">sups</hi> with them upon their bitter herbs, and <hi type="italic">they with him</hi> upon his <hi type="italic">rich dainties.</hi> It is an inseparable union, like that between the body and digested food, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Rom. viii. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.13">1 John iv. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen27160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27161" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We shall <hi type="italic">live,</hi> shall live eternally, <hi type="italic">by him,</hi> as our bodies live by our food. <div eID="gen27161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27162" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> We shall <hi type="italic">live by him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.57">v. 57</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father, so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me.</hi> We have here the series and order of the divine life. (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) God is the <hi type="italic">living Father,</hi> hath life in and of himself. <hi type="italic">I am that I am</hi> is his name for ever. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Jesus Christ, as Mediator, lives <hi type="italic">by the Father;</hi> he has life <hi type="italic">in himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.26">ch. v. 26</reference>), but he has it of the Father. He that sent him, not only qualified him with that life which was necessary to so great an undertaking, but constituted him the treasury of divine life to us; he breathed into the second Adam the breath of spiritual lives, as into the first Adam the breath of natural lives. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) True believers receive this divine life by virtue of their union with Christ, which is inferred from the union between the Father and the Son, as it is compared to it, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">ch. xvii. 21</reference>. For therefore <hi type="italic">he that eateth me,</hi> or feeds on me, <hi type="italic">even he shall live by me:</hi> those that live <hi type="italic">upon</hi> Christ shall live <hi type="italic">by</hi> him. The life of believers is <hi type="italic">had from Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">ch. i. 16</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">hid with Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col. iii. 4</reference>), we live by <hi type="italic">him</hi> as the members by the head, the branches by the root; because he lives, we shall live also. <div eID="gen27162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27163" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> We shall live <hi type="italic">eternally</hi> by him (<reference osisRef="John.6.54">v. 54</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood,</hi> as prepared in the gospel to be the food of souls, he <hi type="italic">hath eternal life,</hi> he hath it now, as <reference osisRef="John.6.40">v. 40</reference>. He has that in him which is eternal life begun; he has the earnest and foretaste of it, and the hope of it; he shall live <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.58">v. 58</reference>. His happiness shall run parallel with the longest line of eternity itself.

<div eID="gen27163" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with His Disciples; The Effect of Christ's Discourse; The Character of Judas.</title> <div sID="gen27164" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">60</hi> Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard <hi type="italic">this,</hi> said, This is a hard saying; who can hear it? <hi type="super">61</hi> When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, he said unto them, Doth this offend you? 62 <hi type="italic">What</hi> and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before? <hi type="super">63</hi> It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, <hi type="italic">they</hi> are spirit, and <hi type="italic">they</hi> are life. <hi type="super">64</hi> But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him. <hi type="super">65</hi> And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father. <hi type="super">66</hi> From that <hi type="italic">time</hi> many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. <hi type="super">67</hi> Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? <hi type="super">68</hi> Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life. <hi type="super">69</hi> And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God. <hi type="super">70</hi> Jesus answered them, Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil? <hi type="super">71</hi> He spake of Judas Iscariot <hi type="italic">the son</hi> of Simon: for he it was that should betray him, being one of the twelve. <div eID="gen27164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the effects of Christ's discourse. Some were offended and others edified by it; some driven <hi type="italic">from him</hi> and others brought nearer <hi type="italic">to him.</hi> <div eID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> I. To some it was a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> not only to the Jews, who were professed enemies to him and his doctrine, but even to many of <hi type="italic">his disciples,</hi> such as were disciples <hi type="italic">at large,</hi> who were his frequent hearers, and followed him <hi type="italic">in public;</hi> a mixed multitude, like those among Israel, that began all the discontents. Now here we have, <div eID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> 1. Their murmurings at the doctrine they heard (<reference osisRef="John.6.60">v. 60</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is a hard saying, who can hear it?</hi> (1.) They do not like it themselves: "What stuff is this? <hi type="italic">Eat the flesh, and drink the blood, of the Son of man!</hi> If it is to be understood figuratively, it is not intelligible; if literally, not practicable. What! must we turn cannibals? Can we not be religious, but we must be barbarous?" <hi type="italic">Si Christiani adorant quod comedunt</hi> (said Averroes), <hi type="italic">sit anima mea cum philosophis—If Christians adore what they eat, my mind shall continue with the philosophers.</hi> Now, when they found it a hard saying, if they had humbly begged of Christ to have <hi type="italic">declared unto them this parable,</hi> he would have opened it, and their understandings too; for <hi type="italic">the meek will he teach his way.</hi> But they were not willing to have Christ's sayings explained to them, because they would not lose <hi type="italic">this</hi> pretence for rejecting them—that they were <hi type="italic">hard sayings.</hi> (2.) They think it impossible that any one else should like it: "<hi type="italic">Who can hear it?</hi> Surely none can." Thus the scoffers at religion are ready to undertake that all the intelligent part of mankind concur with them. They conclude with great assurance that no <hi type="italic">man of sense</hi> will admit the doctrine of Christ, nor any <hi type="italic">man of spirit</hi> submit to his laws. Because they cannot bear to be so <hi type="italic">tutored,</hi> so <hi type="italic">tied up,</hi> themselves, they think none else can: <hi type="italic">Who can hear it?</hi> Thanks be to God, thousands have <hi type="italic">heard</hi> these sayings of Christ, and have found them not only easy, but pleasant, as their <hi type="italic">necessary food.</hi> <div eID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's animadversions upon their murmurings. <div eID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> (1.) He well enough knew their murmurings, <reference osisRef="John.6.61">v. 61</reference>. Their cavils were secret in their own breasts, or whispered among themselves in a corner. But, [1.] Christ <hi type="italic">knew</hi> them; he saw them, he heard them. Note, Christ takes notice not only of the bold and open <hi type="italic">defiances</hi> that are done to his name and glory by <hi type="italic">daring sinners,</hi> but of the secret slights that are put upon his doctrine by carnal professors; he knows that which the <hi type="italic">fool saith in his heart,</hi> and cannot for shame <hi type="italic">speak out;</hi> he observes how his doctrine is <hi type="italic">resented</hi> by those to whom it is <hi type="italic">preached;</hi> who <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> in it, and who <hi type="italic">murmur</hi> at it; who are reconciled to it, and bow before it, and who quarrel with it, and rebel against it, though ever so secretly. [2.] He knew it <hi type="italic">in himself,</hi> not by any information given him, nor any external indication of the thing, but by his own divine omniscience. He knew it not as the prophets, by a <hi type="italic">divine revelation</hi> made to him (that which the prophets desired to know was sometimes hid from them, as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.27">2 Kings iv. 27</reference>), but by a <hi type="italic">divine knowledge</hi> in him. He is that essential Word that <hi type="italic">discerns the thoughts of the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>. Thoughts are words to Christ; we should therefore take heed not only what we say and do, but what we think. <div eID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27170" type="x-p"/> (2.) He well enough knew how to answer them: "<hi type="italic">Doth this offend you?</hi> Is this a stumbling-block to you?" See how people by their own wilful mistakes create offences to themselves: they take offence where there is none given, and even make it where there is nothing to make it of. Note, We may justly wonder that so much offence should be taken at the doctrine of Christ for so little cause. Christ speaks of it here with wonder: "<hi type="italic">Doth this offend you?</hi>" Now, in answer to those who condemned his doctrine as intricate and obscure (<hi type="italic">Si non vis intelligi, debes negligi</hi>—<hi type="italic">If you are unwilling to be understood, you ought to be neglected</hi>), <div eID="gen27170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27171" type="x-p"/> [1.] He gives them a hint of his ascension into heaven, as that which would give an irresistible evidence of the truth of his doctrine (<reference osisRef="John.6.62">v. 62</reference>): <hi type="italic">What and if you shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before?</hi> And what then? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "If I should tell you of that, surely it would much more offend you, and you would think my pretensions too high indeed. If this be so hard a saying that you cannot hear it, how will you digest it when I tell you of my returning <hi type="italic">to</hi> heaven, whence I came down?" See <reference osisRef="John.3.12">ch. iii. 12</reference>. Those who stumble at smaller difficulties should consider how they will get over greater. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "When you see the Son of man ascend, this will much more offend you, for then my body will be less capable of being eaten by you in that gross sense wherein you now understand it;" so Dr. Whitby. Or, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> "When you see that, or hear it from those that shall see it, surely then you will be satisfied. You think I take too much upon me when I say, <hi type="italic">I came down from heaven,</hi> for it was with this that you quarrelled (<reference osisRef="John.6.42">v. 42</reference>); but will you think so when you see me return to heaven?" If he <hi type="italic">ascended,</hi> certainly he <hi type="italic">descended,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.9-Eph.4.10">Eph. iv. 9, 10</reference>. Christ did often refer himself thus to <hi type="italic">subsequent</hi> proofs, as <reference osisRef="John.1.50-John.1.51">ch. i. 50, 51</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.2.14">ii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">Matt. xii. 40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">xxvi. 64</reference>. Let us wait awhile, till the mystery of God shall be finished, and then we shall see that there was no reason to be offended at any of Christ's sayings. <div eID="gen27171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27172" type="x-p"/> [2.] He gives them a general key to this and all such parabolical discourses, teaching them that they are to be understood spiritually, and not after a corporal and carnal manner: <hi type="italic">It is the spirit that quickeneth, the flesh profiteth nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.63">v. 63</reference>. As it is in the natural body, the animal spirits quicken and enliven it, and without these the most nourishing food would profit nothing (what would the body be the better for bread, if it were not quickened and animated by the spirit), so it is with the soul. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The bare participation of ordinances, unless the Spirit of God work with them, and quicken the soul by them, <hi type="italic">profits nothing;</hi> the word and ordinances, if the Spirit works with them, are as food to a living man, if not, they are as food to a dead man. Even the flesh of Christ, the sacrifice for sin, will avail us nothing unless the blessed Spirit quicken our souls thereby, and enforce the powerful influences of his death upon us, till we by his grace are planted together in the likeness of it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The doctrine of eating Christ's flesh and drinking his blood, if it be understood literally, <hi type="italic">profits nothing,</hi> but rather leads us into mistakes and prejudices; but the spiritual sense or meaning of it quickens the soul, makes it <hi type="italic">alive</hi> and <hi type="italic">lively;</hi> for so it follows: <hi type="italic">The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life. To eat the flesh of Christ!</hi> this is a hard saying, but to believe that Christ died for me, to derive from that doctrine strength and comfort in my approaches to God, my oppositions to sin and preparations for a future state, this is the <hi type="italic">spirit and life</hi> of that saying, and, construing it thus, it is an excellent saying. The reason why men <hi type="italic">dislike</hi> Christ's sayings if because they <hi type="italic">mistake</hi> them. The literal sense of a parable does us no good, we are never the wiser for it, but the spiritual meaning is instructive. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The flesh profits nothing—those that <hi type="italic">are in the flesh</hi> (so some understand it), that are under the power of a carnal mind, <hi type="italic">profit not</hi> by Christ's discourses; but <hi type="italic">the Spirit quickeneth</hi>—those that have the Spirit, that are spiritual, are quickened and enlivened by them; for they are received <hi type="italic">ad modum recipientis—so as to correspond with the state of the receiver's mind.</hi> They found fault with Christ's sayings, whereas the fault was in themselves; it is only to <hi type="italic">sensual</hi> minds that spiritual things are <hi type="italic">senseless</hi> and <hi type="italic">sapless,</hi> spiritual minds <hi type="italic">relish</hi> them; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14-1Cor.2.15">1 Cor. ii. 14, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen27172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27173" type="x-p"/> [3.] He gives them an intimation of his <hi type="italic">knowledge of them,</hi> and that he had expected no better from them, though they called themselves his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.6.64-John.6.65">v. 64, 65</reference>. Now was fulfilled that of the prophet, speaking of Christ and his doctrine (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?</hi> Both these Christ here takes notice of. <div eID="gen27173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They did not <hi type="italic">believe his report:</hi> "There are <hi type="italic">some of you</hi> who said you would leave all to follow me who yet <hi type="italic">believe not;</hi>" and this was the reason why the <hi type="italic">word preached did not profit them,</hi> because it was <hi type="italic">not mixed with faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb. iv. 2</reference>. They did not believe him to be the Messiah, else they would have acquiesced in the doctrine he preached, and not have quarrelled with it, though there were some things in it <hi type="italic">dark, and hard to be understood. Oportet discentum credere—Young beginners in learning must take things upon their teacher's word.</hi> Note, 1. Among those who are <hi type="italic">nominal Christians,</hi> there are many who are <hi type="italic">real infidels.</hi> 2. The unbelief of hypocrites, before it discovers itself to the world, is naked and open before the eyes of Christ. He <hi type="italic">knew from the beginning</hi> who they were of the multitudes that followed him that <hi type="italic">believed,</hi> and who of the twelve should betray him; he knew <hi type="italic">from the beginning</hi> of their acquaintance with him, and attendance on him, when they were in the hottest pang of their zeal, who were sincere, as Nathanael (<reference osisRef="John.1.47">ch. i. 47</reference>), and who were not. Before they distinguished themselves by an overt act, he could infallibly distinguish <hi type="italic">who believed</hi> and who did not, whose love was <hi type="italic">counterfeit</hi> and whose <hi type="italic">cordial.</hi> We may gather hence, (1.) That the apostasy of those who have long made a plausible profession of religion is a certain proof of their constant hypocrisy, and that <hi type="italic">from the beginning they believed not,</hi> but is not a proof of the possibility of the total and final apostasy of any true believers: such revolts are not to be called the fall of real saints, but the discovery of pretended ones; see <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1 John ii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Stella cadens non stella fuit—The star that falls never was a star.</hi> (2.) That it is Christ's prerogative to <hi type="italic">know the heart;</hi> he knows who they are that <hi type="italic">believe not,</hi> but dissemble in their profession, and yet continues them room in his church, the use of his ordinances, and the credit of his name, and does not discover them in this world, unless they by their own wickedness discover themselves; because such is the constitution of his visible church, and the discovering day is yet to come. But, if we pretend to judge men's hearts, we step into Christ's throne, and anticipate his judgment. We are often deceived in men, and see cause to change our sentiments of them; but this we are sure of, that Christ knows all men, and <hi type="italic">his judgment is according to truth.</hi> <div eID="gen27174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27175" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The reason why they did not believe his report was because the <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord</hi> was not <hi type="italic">revealed</hi> to them (<reference osisRef="John.6.65">v. 65</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore said I unto you that no man can come to me, except it be given unto him of my Father;</hi> referring to <reference osisRef="John.6.44">v. 44</reference>. Christ therefore could not but know who believed and who did not, because faith is the gift and work of God, and all his Father's gifts and works could not but be known to him, for they all passed through his hands. There he had said that none could <hi type="italic">come to him, except the Father draw him;</hi> here he saith, <hi type="italic">except it be given him of my Father,</hi> which shows that God <hi type="italic">draws</hi> souls by giving them grace and strength, and a heart to come, without which, such is the moral impotency of man, in his fallen state, that he <hi type="italic">cannot come.</hi> <div eID="gen27175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> 3. We have here their final apostasy from Christ hereupon: <hi type="italic">From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.66">v. 66</reference>. When we admit into our minds hard thoughts of the word and works of Christ, and conceive a secret dislike, and are willing to hear insinuations tending to their reproach, we are then <hi type="italic">entering into temptation;</hi> it is as the letting forth of water; it is <hi type="italic">looking back,</hi> which, if infinite mercy prevent not, will end in <hi type="italic">drawing back;</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">Obsta principiis—Take heed of the beginnings</hi> of apostasy. (1.) See here the <hi type="italic">backsliding</hi> of these <hi type="italic">disciples. Many of them went back</hi> to their houses, and families, and callings, which they had left for a time to follow him; <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> one to his farm and another to his merchandise; <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> as Orpah did, to their people, and to their gods, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.15">Ruth i. 15</reference>. They had entered themselves in Christ's school, but they <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> did not only play truant for once, but took leave of him and his doctrine for ever. Note, The apostasy of Christ's disciples from him, though really a strange thing, yet has been such a common thing that we need not be surprised at it. Here were <hi type="italic">many</hi> that <hi type="italic">went back.</hi> It is often so; when some backslide many backslide with them; the disease is infectious. (2.) The occasion of this backsliding: <hi type="italic">From that time,</hi> from the time that Christ preached this comfortable doctrine, that he is the <hi type="italic">bread of life,</hi> and that those who by faith feed <hi type="italic">upon him</hi> shall live <hi type="italic">by him</hi> (which, one would think, should have engaged them to cleave more closely to him)—from <hi type="italic">that</hi> time they withdrew. Note, The corrupt and wicked heart of man often makes that an occasion of offence which is indeed matter of the greatest comfort. Christ foresaw that they would thus take offence at what he said, and yet he said it. That which is the undoubted word and truth of Christ must be faithfully delivered, whoever may be offended at it. Men's humours must be captivated to God's word, and not God's word accommodated to men's humours. (3.) The degree of their apostasy: <hi type="italic">They walked no more with him,</hi> returned no more to him and attended no more upon his ministry. It is hard for those who have been <hi type="italic">once enlightened,</hi> and have <hi type="italic">tasted the good word of God, if they fall away, to renew them again to repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">Heb. vi. 4-6</reference>. <div eID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27177" type="x-p"/> II. This discourse was to others a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life. Many went back,</hi> but, thanks be to God, all did not; even then the <hi type="italic">twelve</hi> stuck to him. Though the <hi type="italic">faith of some be overthrown,</hi> yet the <hi type="italic">foundation of God stands sure.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> 1. The affectionate question which Christ put to the twelve (<reference osisRef="John.6.67">v. 67</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will you also go away?</hi> He saith nothing to those who went back. <hi type="italic">If the unbelieving depart, let them depart;</hi> it was no great <hi type="italic">loss</hi> of those whom he never <hi type="italic">had;</hi> lightly come, lightly go; but he takes this occasion to speak to the twelve, to confirm them, and by trying their stedfastness the more to fix them: <hi type="italic">Will you also go away?</hi> (1.) "It is <hi type="italic">at your choice</hi> whether you will or no; if you will forsake me, now is the time, when so many do: it is an hour of temptation; if you will go back, go now." Note, Christ will detain none with him against their wills; his soldiers are volunteers, not pressed men. The twelve had now had time enough to try how they liked Christ and his doctrine, and that none of them might afterwards say that they were trepanned into discipleship, and if it were to do again they would not do it, he here allows them a power of revocation, and leaves them at their liberty; as <reference osisRef="Josh.25.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.15">Ruth i. 15</reference>. (2.) "It is <hi type="italic">at your peril</hi> if you do go away." If there was any secret inclination in the heart of any of them to depart from him, he stops it with this awakening question, "<hi type="italic">Wilt you also go away?</hi> Think not that you hang at as loose an end as they did, and may go away as easily as they could. They have not been so intimate with me as you have been, nor received so many favours from me; they are gone, but will <hi type="italic">you</hi> also go? Remember your character, and say, Whatever others do, we will never go away. <hi type="italic">Should such a man as I flee?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Neh.6.11">Neh. vi. 11</reference>. Note, The nearer we have been to Christ and the longer we have been with him, the more engagements we have laid ourselves under to him, the greater will be our sin if we desert him. (3.) "I have reason <hi type="italic">to think you will not.</hi> Will you go away? No, I have faster hold of you than so; <hi type="italic">I hope better things of you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.9">Heb. vi. 9</reference>), for <hi type="italic">you are they that have continued with me,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.22.28">Luke xxii. 28</reference>. When the apostasy of some is a grief to the Lord Jesus, the constancy of others is so much the more his honour, and he is pleased with it accordingly. Christ and believers know one another too well to part upon every displeasure. <div eID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> 2. The believing reply which Peter, in the name of the rest, made to this question, <reference osisRef="John.6.68-John.6.69">v. 68, 69</reference>. Christ put the question to them, as Joshua put Israel to their choice whom they would serve, with design to draw out from them a promise to adhere to him, and it had the like effect. <hi type="italic">Nay, but we will serve the Lord,</hi> Peter was upon all occasions the <hi type="italic">mouth of the rest,</hi> not so much because he had more of his Master's ear than they, but because he had more tongue of his own; and what he said was sometimes approved and sometimes reprimanded (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Matt. xvi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">23</reference>)—the common lot of those who are swift to speak. This here was well said, admirably well; and probably he said it by the direction, and with the express assent, of his fellow-disciples; at least he knew their mind, and spoke the sense of them all, and did not except Judas, for we must hope the best. <div eID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a good resolution to adhere to Christ, and so expressed as to intimate that they would not entertain the least thought of leaving him: "<hi type="italic">Lord, to whom shall we go?</hi> It were folly to go from thee, unless we knew where to better ourselves; no, Lord, we like our choice too well to change." Note, Those who leave Christ would do well to consider to whom they will go, and whether they can expect to find rest and peace any where but in him. See <reference osisRef="Ps.73.27-Ps.73.28">Ps. lxxiii. 27, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.9">Hos. ii. 9</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Whither shall we go?</hi> Shall we make our court to the world? It will certainly <hi type="italic">deceive</hi> us. Shall we return to sin? It will certainly <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> us. Shall we leave the <hi type="italic">fountain of living waters</hi> for <hi type="italic">broken cisterns?</hi>" The disciples resolve to continue their pursuit of life and happiness, and will have a guide to it, and will adhere to Christ as their guide, for they can never have a better. "Shall we go to the heathen philosophers, and become their disciples? They are become vain in their imaginations, and, professing themselves to be wise in other things, are become fools in religion. Shall we go to the scribes and Pharisees, and sit at their feet? What good can they do us who have made void the commandments of God by their traditions? Shall we go to Moses? He will send us back again to thee. Therefore, if ever we find the way to happiness, it must be in following thee." Note, Christ's holy religion appears to great advantage when it is compared with other institutions, for then it will be seen how far it excels them all. Let those who find fault with this religion find a better before they quit it. A divine teacher we must have; can we find a better than Christ? A divine revelation we cannot be without; if the scripture be not such a one, where else may we look for it? <div eID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a good reason for this resolution. It was not the inconsiderate resolve of a blind affection, but the result of mature deliberation. The disciples were resolved never to go away from Christ, <div eID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> [1.] Because of the <hi type="italic">advantage</hi> they promised themselves by him: <hi type="italic">Thou hast the words of eternal life.</hi> They themselves did not fully understand Christ's discourse, for as yet the doctrine of the cross was a riddle to them; but in the general they were satisfied that <hi type="italic">he had the words of eternal life,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the word of his doctrine showed the way to <hi type="italic">eternal life,</hi> set it before us, and directed us what to do, that we might inherit it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the word of his <hi type="italic">determination</hi> must confer eternal life. His <hi type="italic">having the words of eternal life</hi> is the same with his having <hi type="italic">power to give eternal life to as many as were given him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.2">ch. xvii. 2</reference>. He had in the foregoing discourse assured <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> to his followers; these disciples fastened upon this plain saying, and therefore resolved to stick to him, when the others overlooked this, and fastened upon the <hi type="italic">hard sayings,</hi> and therefore forsook him. Though we cannot account for every mystery, every obscurity, in Christ's doctrine, yet we know, in the general, that it is the word of eternal life, and therefore must live and die by it; for if we forsake Christ <hi type="italic">we forsake our own mercies.</hi> <div eID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> [2.] Because of the assurance they had concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.6.69">v. 69</reference>): <hi type="italic">We believe, and are sure, that thou art that Christ.</hi> if he be the promised Messiah, he must <hi type="italic">bring in an everlasting righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>), and therefore has the <hi type="italic">words of eternal life,</hi> for <hi type="italic">righteousness reigns to eternal life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.21">Rom. v. 21</reference>. observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> they believed: that this Jesus was the Messiah promised to the fathers and expected by them, and that he was not a mere man, but the Son of the living God, the same to whom God had said, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>. In times of temptation to apostasy it is good to have recourse to our first principles, and stick to them; and, if we faithfully abide by that which is <hi type="italic">past dispute,</hi> we shall be the better able both to <hi type="italic">find</hi> and to <hi type="italic">keep</hi> the truth in matters of doubtful disputation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">degree</hi> of their faith: it rose up to a full assurance: <hi type="italic">We are sure.</hi> We have known it <hi type="italic">by experience;</hi> this is the best knowledge. We should take occasion from others' wavering to be so much the more established, especially in that which is the present truth. When we have so strong a faith in the gospel of Christ as boldly to venture our souls <hi type="italic">upon it,</hi> knowing <hi type="italic">whom we have believed,</hi> then, and not till then, we shall be willing to venture every thing else for it. <div eID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27184" type="x-p"/> 3. The melancholy remark which our Lord Jesus made upon this reply of Peter's (<reference osisRef="John.6.70-John.6.71">v. 70, 71</reference>): <hi type="italic">Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?</hi> And the evangelist tells us whom he meant: <hi type="italic">he spoke of Judas Iscariot.</hi> Peter had undertaken for them all that they would be faithful to their Master. Now Christ does not condemn his charity (it is always good to hope the best), but he tacitly corrects his confidence. We must not be too sure concerning any. God knows those that are his; we do not. Observe here, (1.) Hypocrites and betrayers of Christ are no better than devils. Judas not only <hi type="italic">had</hi> a devil, but he <hi type="italic">was</hi> a devil. One of you is a <hi type="italic">false accuser;</hi> so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diabolos</hi></hi> sometimes signifies (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">2 Tim. iii. 3</reference>); and it is probable that Judas, when he sold his Master to the chief priests, represented him to them as a bad man, to justify himself in what he did. But I rather take it as we read it: <hi type="italic">He is a devil,</hi> a devil incarnate, a fallen apostle, as the devil a fallen angel. He is Satan, an adversary, an enemy to Christ. He is Abaddon, and Apollyon, a son of perdition. He was of his father the devil, did his lusts, was in his interests, as Cain, <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1 John iii. 12</reference>. Those whose bodies were possessed by the devil are never called <hi type="italic">devils</hi> (<hi type="italic">demoniacs,</hi> but not <hi type="italic">devils</hi>); but Judas, into whose <hi type="italic">heart</hi> Satan entered, and filled it, is called a <hi type="italic">devil.</hi> (2.) Many that are <hi type="italic">seeming</hi> saints are <hi type="italic">real</hi> devils. Judas had as fair an outside as many of the apostles; his venom was, like that of the serpent, covered with a fine skin. He <hi type="italic">cast out devils,</hi> and appeared an enemy to the devil's kingdom, and yet was himself a devil all the while. Not only he <hi type="italic">will be</hi> one shortly, but he <hi type="italic">is one</hi> now. It is <hi type="italic">strange,</hi> and to be wondered at; Christ speaks of it with wonder: <hi type="italic">Have not I?</hi> It is <hi type="italic">sad,</hi> and to be lamented, that ever Christianity should be made a cloak to diabolism. (3.) The disguises of hypocrites, however they may deceive men, and put a cheat upon them, cannot deceive Christ, for his piercing eye sees through them. He can call those <hi type="italic">devils</hi> that call themselves <hi type="italic">Christians,</hi> like the prophet's greeting to Jeroboam's wife, when she came to him in masquerade (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.6">1 Kings xiv. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam.</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">divine sight,</hi> far better than any <hi type="italic">double sight,</hi> can see spirits. (4.) There are those who are chosen by Christ to special services who yet prove false to him: <hi type="italic">I have chosen you</hi> to the <hi type="italic">apostleship,</hi> for it is expressly said that Judas was not chosen to eternal life (<reference osisRef="John.13.18">ch. xiii. 18</reference>), and yet one of <hi type="italic">you</hi> is a devil. Note, Advancement to places of honour and trust in the church is no certain evidence of saving grace. <hi type="italic">We have prophesied in thy name.</hi> (5.) In the most <hi type="italic">select</hi> societies on this side heaven it is no new thing to meet with those that are corrupt. Of the twelve that were chosen to an intimate conversation with an <hi type="italic">incarnate Deity,</hi> as great an honour and privilege as ever men were chosen to, one was an <hi type="italic">incarnate devil.</hi> The historian lays an emphasis upon this, that Judas was <hi type="italic">one of the twelve</hi> that were so dignified and distinguished. Let us not reject and unchurch the twelve because <hi type="italic">one of them is a devil,</hi> nor say that they are all cheats and hypocrites because one of them was so; let those that are so bear the blame, and not those who, while they are undiscovered, incorporate with them. There is a society within the veil into which no unclean thing shall enter, a church of first-born, in which are no <hi type="italic">false brethren.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.6"/> <div eID="gen27184" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27187" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27186" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with His Brethren; The Rumours Respecting Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand. 3 His brethren therefore said unto him, Depart hence, and go into Judæa, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest. <hi type="super">4</hi> For <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no man <hi type="italic">that</hi> doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, show thyself to the world. <hi type="super">5</hi> For neither did his brethren believe in him. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready. <hi type="super">7</hi> The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil. <hi type="super">8</hi> Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come. <hi type="super">9</hi> When he had said these words unto them, he abode <hi type="italic">still</hi> in Galilee. <hi type="super">10</hi> But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then the Jews sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he? <hi type="super">12</hi> And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people. <hi type="super">13</hi> Howbeit no man spake openly of him for fear of the Jews. <div eID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The reason given why Christ spent more of his time in Galilee than in Judea (<reference osisRef="John.7.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">because the Jews,</hi> the people in Judea and Jerusalem, sought to <hi type="italic">kill him,</hi> for curing the impotent man on the sabbath day, <reference osisRef="John.5.16">ch. v. 16</reference>. They thought to be the death of him, either by a popular tumult or by a legal prosecution, in consideration of which he kept at a distance in another part of the country, very much out of the lines of Jerusalem's communication. It is not said, He <hi type="italic">durst not,</hi> but, He <hi type="italic">would not,</hi> walk in Jewry; it was not through fear and cowardice that he declined it, but in <hi type="italic">prudence,</hi> because his hour was not yet come. Note, 1. Gospel light is justly <hi type="italic">taken away</hi> from those that endeavour to extinguish it. Christ will withdraw from those that drive him from them, will hide his face from those that spit in it, and justly shut up his bowels from those who spurn at them. 2. In times of imminent peril it is not only <hi type="italic">allowable,</hi> but <hi type="italic">advisable,</hi> to <hi type="italic">withdraw</hi> and <hi type="italic">abscond</hi> for our own safety and preservation, and to choose the service of those places which are least perilous, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">Matt. x. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> and not till <hi type="italic">then,</hi> we are called to expose and lay down our lives, when we cannot save them without sin. 3. If the providence of God casts persons of <hi type="italic">merit</hi> into places of obscurity and little note, it must not be thought strange; it was the lot of our Master himself. He who was fit to have sat in the highest of Moses's seats willingly walked in Galilee among the ordinary sort of people. Observe, He did not sit still in Galilee, nor bury himself alive there, but <hi type="italic">walked;</hi> he went about doing good. When we cannot do <hi type="italic">what</hi> and <hi type="italic">where</hi> we <hi type="italic">would,</hi> we must do <hi type="italic">what</hi> and <hi type="italic">where</hi> we <hi type="italic">can.</hi> <div eID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> II. The approach of the <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.2">v. 2</reference>), one of the three solemnities which called for the personal attendance of all the males at Jerusalem; see the institution of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Lev. xxiii. 34</reference>, &c., and the revival of it after a long disuse, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.14">Neh. viii. 14</reference>. It was intended to be both a <hi type="italic">memorial</hi> of the tabernacle state of Israel in the wilderness, and a <hi type="italic">figure</hi> of the tabernacle state of God's spiritual Israel in this world. This feast, which was instituted so many hundred years before, was still religiously observed. Note, Divine institutions are never antiquated, nor go out of date, by length of time: nor must wilderness mercies ever be forgotten. But it is called the <hi type="italic">Jews' feast,</hi> because it was now shortly to be <hi type="italic">abolished,</hi> as a mere Jewish thing, and left to them that <hi type="italic">served the tabernacle.</hi> <div eID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's discourse with his <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> some of his kindred, whether by his mother or his supposed father is not certain; but they were such as pretended to have an interest in him, and therefore interposed to advise him in his conduct. And observe, <div eID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> 1. Their ambition and vain-glory in urging him to make a more public appearance than he did: "<hi type="italic">Depart hence,</hi>" said they, "<hi type="italic">and go into Judea</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.3">v. 3</reference>), where thou wilt make a better figure than thou canst here." <div eID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> (1.) They give two reasons for this advice: [1.] That it would be an encouragement to those in and about Jerusalem who had a respect for him; for, expecting his temporal kingdom, the royal seat of which they concluded must be at Jerusalem, they would have had the disciples <hi type="italic">there</hi> particularly countenanced, and thought the time he spent among his Galilean disciples wasted and thrown away, and his miracles turning to no account unless those at Jerusalem saw them. Or, "That <hi type="italic">thy disciples,</hi> all of them in general, who will be gathered at Jerusalem to keep the feast, may <hi type="italic">see thy works,</hi> and not, as here, a few at one time and a few at another." [2.] That it would be for the advancement of his name and honour: <hi type="italic">There is no man that does any thing in secret</hi> if he himself <hi type="italic">seeks to be known</hi> openly. They took it for granted that Christ sought to make himself known, and therefore thought it absurd for him to conceal his miracles: "<hi type="italic">If thou do these things,</hi> if thou be so well able to gain the applause of the people and the approbation of the rulers by thy miracles, venture abroad, and <hi type="italic">show thyself to the world.</hi> Supported with these credentials, thou canst not fail of acceptance, and therefore it is high time to set up for an interest, and to think of being <hi type="italic">great.</hi>" <div eID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> (2.) One would not think there was any harm in this advice, and yet the evangelist noted it is an evidence of their infidelity: <hi type="italic">For neither did his brethren believe in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">v. 5</reference>), if they had, they would not have said this. Observe, [1.] It was an honour to be of the kindred of Christ, but no <hi type="italic">saving</hi> honour; they that hear his word and keep it are the kindred he values. Surely grace runs in no blood in the world, when not in that of Christ's family. [2.] It was a sign that Christ did not aim at any secular interest, for then his kindred would have struck in with him, and he would have secured them first. [3.] There were those who were akin to Christ according to the flesh who did believe in him (three of the twelve were <hi type="italic">his brethren</hi>), and yet others, as nearly allied to him as they, did not believe in him. Many that have the same external privileges and advantages do not make the same use of them. But, <div eID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> (3.) What was there amiss in the advice which they gave him? I answer, [1.] It was a piece of presumption for them to prescribe to Christ, and to teach him what measures to take; it was a sign that they <hi type="italic">did not believe him</hi> able to guide them, when they did not think him sufficient to guide himself. [2.] They discovered a great carelessness about his safety, when they would have him go to Judea, where they knew the Jews sought to kill him. Those that believed in him, and loved him, dissuaded him from Judea, <reference osisRef="John.11.8">ch. xi. 8</reference>. [3.] Some think they hoped that if his miracles were wrought at Jerusalem the Pharisees and rulers would try them, and discover some cheat in them, which would justify their unbelief. So. Dr. Whitby. [4.] Perhaps they were weary of his company in Galilee (for <hi type="italic">are not all these that speak Galileans?</hi>) and this was, in effect, a desire that he would <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts.</hi> [5.] They causelessly insinuate that he neglected his disciples, and denied them such a <hi type="italic">sight of his works</hi> as was necessary to the support of their faith. [6.] They tacitly reproach him as <hi type="italic">mean-spirited,</hi> that he durst not enter the lists with the great men, nor trust himself upon the stage of public action, which, if he had any courage and <hi type="italic">greatness of soul,</hi> he would do, and not sneak thus and skulk in a corner; thus Christ's humility, and his humiliation, and the small figure which his religion has usually made in the world, have been often turned to the reproach of both <hi type="italic">him</hi> and <hi type="italic">it.</hi> [7.] They seem to question the truth of the miracles he wrought, in saying, "<hi type="italic">If thou do these things,</hi> if they will bear the test of a public scrutiny in the courts above, produce them there." [8.] They think Christ altogether such a one as themselves, as subject as they to worldly policy, and as desirous as they to <hi type="italic">make a fair show in the flesh;</hi> whereas he sought not honour from men. [9.] Self was at the bottom of all; they hoped, if he would make himself as great as he might, they, being his kinsmen, should share in his honour, and have respect paid them for his sake. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Many carnal people go to public ordinances, to worship at the feast, only to <hi type="italic">show themselves,</hi> and all their care is to make a <hi type="italic">good appearance,</hi> to present themselves handsomely to the world. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Many that seem to seek Christ's honour do really therein seek their own, and make it serve a turn for themselves. <div eID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> 2. The prudence and humility of our Lord Jesus, which appeared in his answer to the advice his brethren gave him, <reference osisRef="John.7.6-John.7.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Though there were so many base insinuations in it, he answered them mildly. Note, Even that which is said without <hi type="italic">reason</hi> should be answered without <hi type="italic">passion;</hi> we should learn of our Master to reply with meekness even to that which is most <hi type="italic">impertinent</hi> and <hi type="italic">imperious,</hi> and, where it is easy to find much amiss, to seem not to see it, and wink at the affront. They expected Christ's company with them to the feast, perhaps hoping he would bear their charges: but here, <div eID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows the difference between himself and them, in two things:—[1.] His <hi type="italic">time</hi> was <hi type="italic">set,</hi> so was not <hi type="italic">theirs: My time is not yet come, but your time is always ready.</hi> Understand it of the time of his going up to the feast. It was an indifferent thing to them when they went, for they had nothing of moment to do either where they were, to <hi type="italic">detain</hi> them <hi type="italic">there,</hi> or where they were going, to <hi type="italic">hasten</hi> them <hi type="italic">thither;</hi> but every minute of Christ's time was precious, and had its own particular business allotted to it. He had some work yet to do in Galilee before he left the country: in the harmony of the gospels betwixt this <hi type="italic">motion</hi> made by his kindred and his <hi type="italic">going up</hi> to this feast comes in the story of his sending forth the seventy disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Luke x. 1</reference>, &c.), which was an affair of very great consequence; his time is <hi type="italic">not yet,</hi> for that must be done first. Those who live useless lives have <hi type="italic">their time always ready;</hi> they can go and come when they please. But those whose <hi type="italic">time</hi> is filled up with <hi type="italic">duty</hi> will often find themselves <hi type="italic">straitened,</hi> and they have <hi type="italic">not yet time</hi> for that which others can do <hi type="italic">at any time.</hi> Those who are made the servants of God, as all men are, and who have made themselves the servants of all, as all useful men have, must not expect not covet to be <hi type="italic">masters of their own time.</hi> The confinement of business is a thousand times better than the liberty of idleness. Or, it may be meant of the <hi type="italic">time</hi> of his appearing publicly at Jerusalem; Christ, who knows all men and all things, knew that the best and most proper time for it would be about the <hi type="italic">middle of the feast.</hi> We, who are ignorant and short-sighted, are apt to prescribe to him, and to think he should deliver his people, and so show himself now. The present time is <hi type="italic">our</hi> time, but he is fittest to judge, and, it may be, <hi type="italic">his time is not yet come;</hi> his people are not yet ready for deliverance, nor his enemies ripe for ruin; let us therefore wait with patience for <hi type="italic">his time,</hi> for all he does will be most glorious in its season. [2.] His <hi type="italic">life</hi> was <hi type="italic">sought,</hi> so was not <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.7">v. 7</reference>. They, in <hi type="italic">showing themselves</hi> to the world, did not expose themselves: "<hi type="italic">The world cannot hate you,</hi> for you are <hi type="italic">of the world,</hi> its children, its servants, and in with its interests; and no doubt the world will <hi type="italic">love its own;</hi>" see <reference osisRef="John.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>. Unholy souls, whom the holy God <hi type="italic">cannot love,</hi> the world that lies in wickedness <hi type="italic">cannot hate;</hi> but Christ, in showing himself to the world, laid himself open to the greatest danger; for <hi type="italic">me it hateth.</hi> Christ was not only <hi type="italic">slighted,</hi> as inconsiderable in the world (<hi type="italic">the world knew him not),</hi> but <hi type="italic">hated,</hi> as if he had been hurtful to the world; thus ill was he requited for his love to the world: reigning sin is a rooted antipathy and enmity to Christ. But why did the world hate Christ? What evil had he done to it? Had he, like Alexander, under colour of conquering it, laid it waste? "No, but because" (saith he) "<hi type="italic">I testify of it, that the works of it are evil.</hi>" Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The works of an evil world are <hi type="italic">evil works;</hi> as the tree is, so are the fruits: it is a dark world, and an apostate world, and its works are works of darkness and rebellion. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Our Lord Jesus, both by himself and by his ministers, did and will both discover and testify against the evil works of this wicked world. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a great uneasiness and provocation to the world to be convicted of the evil of its works. It is for the honour of virtue and piety that those who are impious and vicious do not care for hearing of it, for their own consciences make them <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> of the turpitude there is <hi type="italic">in</hi> sin and <hi type="italic">afraid</hi> of the punishment that follows <hi type="italic">after</hi> sin. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Whatever is <hi type="italic">pretended,</hi> the <hi type="italic">real</hi> cause of the world's enmity to the gospel is the testimony it bears against sin and sinners. Christ's witnesses by their doctrine and conversation <hi type="italic">torment</hi> those that dwell on the earth, and therefore are treated so barbarously, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. But it is better to incur the world's hatred, by testifying against its wickedness, than gain its good-will by going down the stream with it. <div eID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> (2.) He dismisses them, with a design to stay behind for some time in Galilee (<reference osisRef="John.7.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go you up to this feast, I go not up yet.</hi> [1.] He allows their going to the feast, though they were carnal and hypocritical in it. Note, Even those who go not to holy ordinances with right affections and sincere intentions must not be hindered nor discouraged from going; who knows but they may be wrought upon there? [2.] He denies them his company when they went to the feast, because they were carnal and hypocritical. Those who go to ordinances for ostentation, or to serve some secular purpose, go without Christ, and will speed accordingly. How sad is the condition of that man, though he reckon himself akin to Christ, to whom he saith, "<hi type="italic">Go up</hi> to such an ordinance, Go pray, Go hear the word, Go receive the sacrament, but <hi type="italic">I go not up</hi> with thee? <hi type="italic">Go thou</hi> and appear before God, but I will not appear <hi type="italic">for thee,</hi>" as <reference osisRef="Exod.33.1-Exod.33.3">Exod. xxxiii. 1-3</reference>. But, if the presence of Christ go not with us, to what purpose should we go up? <hi type="italic">Go you up, I go not up.</hi> When we are going to, or coming from, solemn ordinances, it becomes us to be careful what company we <hi type="italic">have</hi> and <hi type="italic">choose,</hi> and to avoid that which is vain and carnal, lest the coal of good affections be quenched by corrupt communication. <hi type="italic">I go not up yet to this feast;</hi> he does not say, I will not go up at all, but not yet. There may be reasons for deferring a particular duty, which yet must not be wholly omitted or laid aside; see <reference osisRef="Num.9.6-Num.9.11">Num. ix. 6-11</reference>. The reason he gives is, <hi type="italic">My time is not yet fully come.</hi> Note, Our Lord Jesus is very exact and punctual in knowing and keeping his time, and, as it was the time <hi type="italic">fixed,</hi> so it was the <hi type="italic">best</hi> time. <div eID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's continuance in Galilee till his <hi type="italic">full time</hi> was come, <reference osisRef="John.7.9">v. 9</reference>. He, saying these things to them (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tauta de eipon</hi></hi>) <hi type="italic">abode still in Galilee;</hi> because of this discourse he continued there; for, (1.) He would not be influenced by those who advised him to seek honour from men, nor go along with those who put him upon making a figure; he would not seem to countenance the temptation. (2.) He would not depart from his own purpose. He had said, upon a clear foresight and mature deliberation, that he would not go up yet to this feast, and therefore he abode still in Galilee. It becomes the followers of Christ thus to be <hi type="italic">steady,</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">use lightness.</hi> <div eID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> 4. His going up to the feast when his time was come. Observe, (1.) <hi type="italic">When</hi> he went: <hi type="italic">When his brethren were gone up.</hi> He would not go up <hi type="italic">with them,</hi> lest they should make a noise and disturbance, under pretence of <hi type="italic">showing him to the world;</hi> whereas it agreed both with the prediction and with his spirit not to <hi type="italic">strive nor cry,</hi> nor let his <hi type="italic">voice be heard in the streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.2">Isa. xlii. 2</reference>. But he went up <hi type="italic">after them.</hi> We may lawfully join in the same religious worship with those with whom we should yet decline an intimate acquaintance and converse; for the blessing of ordinances depends upon the grace of God, and not upon the grace of our fellow-worshippers. His carnal brethren went up <hi type="italic">first,</hi> and then he went. Note, In the external performances of religion it is possible that formal hypocrites may <hi type="italic">get the start</hi> of those that are sincere. Many come <hi type="italic">first to the temple</hi> who are brought thither by vain-glory, and go thence unjustified, as he, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>. It is not, Who comes <hi type="italic">first?</hi> that will be the question, but, Who comes <hi type="italic">fittest?</hi> If we bring our hearts <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> it is no matter who gets <hi type="italic">before us.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">How</hi> he went, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">os en krypto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a s if he were hiding himself: not openly, but as it were in secret,</hi> rather for fear of <hi type="italic">giving offence</hi> than of <hi type="italic">receiving injury.</hi> He went up to the feast, because it was an opportunity of honouring God and doing good; but he went up as it were in secret, because he would not provoke the government.
