The <hi type="italic">Holy Ghost</hi> was <hi type="italic">not yet given</hi> in such rivers of living water as should issue forth to water the whole earth, even the Gentile world, not in the <hi type="italic">gifts of tongues,</hi> to which perhaps this promise principally refers. [3.] That the reason why <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost was not given</hi> was because <hi type="italic">Jesus was not yet glorified. First,</hi> The death of Christ is sometimes called his glorification (<reference osisRef="John.13.31">ch. xiii. 31</reference>); for in his cross he conquered and triumphed. Now the gift of the Holy Ghost was purchased by the blood of Christ: this was the <hi type="italic">valuable consideration</hi> upon which the <hi type="italic">grant</hi> was grounded, and therefore till this <hi type="italic">price was paid</hi> (though many other gifts were bestowed upon its being <hi type="italic">secured</hi> to be paid) the Holy Ghost was not given. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There was not so much need of the Spirit, while Christ himself was here upon earth, as there was when he was gone, to supply the want of him. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The giving of the Holy Ghost was to be both an <hi type="italic">answer</hi> to Christ's <hi type="italic">intercession</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">ch. xiv. 16</reference>), and an <hi type="italic">act</hi> of his <hi type="italic">dominion;</hi> and therefore till he is glorified, and enters upon both these, the Holy Ghost is not given. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The conversion of the Gentiles was the glorifying of Jesus. When certain Greeks began to enquire after Christ, he said, <hi type="italic">Now is the Son of man glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>. Now the time when the gospel should be propagated in the nations was not yet come, and therefore there was as yet no occasion for the <hi type="italic">gift of tongues,</hi> that <hi type="italic">river of living water.</hi> But observe, though the Holy Ghost was not yet given, yet he was <hi type="italic">promised;</hi> it was now the great <hi type="italic">promise of the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.4">Acts i. 4</reference>. Though the gifts of Christ's grace are <hi type="italic">long deferred,</hi> yet they are <hi type="italic">well secured:</hi> and, while we are waiting for the good promise, we have the promise to live upon, which <hi type="italic">shall speak and shall not lie.</hi> <div eID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> II. The consequents of this discourse, what entertainment it met with; in general, it occasioned differences: <hi type="italic">There was a division among the people because of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.43">v. 43</reference>. There was a <hi type="italic">schism,</hi> so the word is; there were diversities of opinions, and those managed with heat and contention; various sentiments, and those such as set them at <hi type="italic">variance.</hi> Think we that Christ came to send peace, that all would unanimously embrace his gospel? No, the effect of the preaching of his gospel would be <hi type="italic">division,</hi> for, while some are <hi type="italic">gathered to it,</hi> others will be <hi type="italic">gathered against it;</hi> and this will put things into a <hi type="italic">ferment,</hi> as here; but this is no more the fault of the gospel than it is the fault of a wholesome medicine that it stirs up the <hi type="italic">peccant</hi> humours in the body, in order to the discharge of them. Observe what the debate was:— <div eID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> 1. Some were <hi type="italic">taken with him,</hi> and well affected to him: <hi type="italic">Many of the people, when they heard this saying,</hi> heard him with such compassion and kindness invite poor sinners to him, and with such authority engage to make them happy, that they could not but think highly of him. (1.) Some of them said, <hi type="italic">O, a truth this is the prophet,</hi> that prophet whom Moses spoke of to the fathers, who should be <hi type="italic">like unto him;</hi> or, This is <hi type="italic">the prophet</hi> who, according to the received notions of the Jewish church, is to be the harbinger and forerunner of the Messiah; or, <hi type="italic">This is truly a prophet,</hi> one divinely inspired and sent of God. (2.) Others went further, and said, <hi type="italic">This is the Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.41">v. 41</reference>), not the <hi type="italic">prophet</hi> of the Messiah, but the Messiah himself. The Jews had at this time a more than ordinary expectation of the Messiah, which made them ready to say upon every occasion, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there;</hi> and this seems to be only the effect of some such confused and floating notions which caught at the first appearance, for we do not find that these people became his disciples and followers; a good opinion of Christ is far short of a lively faith in Christ; many give Christ a good word that give him no more. These here said, <hi type="italic">This is the prophet,</hi> and <hi type="italic">this is the Christ,</hi> but could not persuade themselves to leave all and follow him; and so this their testimony to Christ was but a testimony <hi type="italic">against themselves.</hi> <div eID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> 2. Others were <hi type="italic">prejudiced against him.</hi> No sooner was this great truth started, that <hi type="italic">Jesus is the Christ,</hi> than immediately it was contradicted and argued against: and this one thing, that his rise and origin were (as they took it for granted) out of Galilee, was thought enough to answer all the arguments for his being the Christ. For, <hi type="italic">shall Christ come out of Galilee?</hi> Has not <hi type="italic">the scripture said that Christ comes of the seed of David?</hi> See here, (1.) A laudable knowledge of the scripture. They were so far in the right, that the Messiah was to be a <hi type="italic">rod out of the stem of Jesse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>), that out of Bethlehem should <hi type="italic">arise the Governor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>. This even the common people knew by the traditional expositions which their scribes gave them. Perhaps the people who had these scriptures so ready to object against Christ were not alike knowing in other parts of holy writ, but had had these put into their mouths by their leaders, to fortify their prejudices against Christ. Many that espouse some corrupt notions, and spend their zeal in defence of them, seem to be very ready in the scriptures, when indeed they know little more than those scriptures which they have been taught to <hi type="italic">pervert.</hi> (2.) A culpable ignorance of our Lord Jesus. They speak of it as certain and past dispute that <hi type="italic">Jesus was of Galilee,</hi> whereas by enquiring of himself, or his mother, or his disciples, or by consulting the genealogies of the family of David, or the register at Bethlehem, they might have known that he was the Son of David, and a native of Bethlehem; but <hi type="italic">this they willingly are ignorant of.</hi> Thus gross falsehoods in matters of fact, concerning persons and things, are often taken up by prejudiced and partial men, and great resolves founded upon them, even in the same place and the same age wherein the persons live and the things are done, while the truth might easily be found out. <div eID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> 3. Others were <hi type="italic">enraged against him,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">would have taken him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.44">v. 44</reference>. Though what he said was most sweet and gracious, yet they were exasperated against him for it. Thus did our Master suffer ill for saying and doing well. <hi type="italic">They would have taken him;</hi> they hoped somebody or other would seize him, and, if they had thought no one else would, they would have done it themselves. They <hi type="italic">would have taken him;</hi> but no man <hi type="italic">laid hands on him,</hi> being restrained by an invisible power, because his hour was not come. As the malice of Christ's enemies is always <hi type="italic">unreasonable,</hi> so sometimes the suspension of it is <hi type="italic">unaccountable.</hi>

<div eID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Officers' Testimony of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">45</hi> Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him? <hi type="super">46</hi> The officers answered, Never man spake like this man. <hi type="super">47</hi> Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived? <hi type="super">48</hi> Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? <hi type="super">49</hi> But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed. <hi type="super">50</hi> Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,) <hi type="super">51</hi> Doth our law judge <hi type="italic">any</hi> man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth? <hi type="super">52</hi> They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee? Search, and look: for out of Galilee ariseth no prophet. <hi type="super">53</hi> And every man went unto his own house. <div eID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> The chief priests and Pharisees are here in a close cabal, contriving how to suppress Christ; though this was the <hi type="italic">great day of the feast,</hi> they attended not the religious services of the day, but left them to the vulgar, to whom it was common for those great ecclesiastics to consign and turn over the business of devotion, while they thought themselves better employed in the affairs of church-policy. They sat in the council-chamber, expecting Christ to be brought a prisoner to them, as they had issued out warrants for apprehending him, <reference osisRef="John.7.32">v. 32</reference>. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> I. What passed between them and their own officers, who returned without him, <hi type="italic">re infecta</hi>—<hi type="italic">having done nothing.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> 1. The reproof they gave the officers for not executing the warrant they gave them: <hi type="italic">Why have you not brought him?</hi> He appeared publicly; the people were many of them disgusted, and would have assisted them in taking him; this was <hi type="italic">the last day of the feast,</hi> and they would not have such another opportunity; "why then did you neglect your duty?" It vexed them that those who were their own creatures, who depended on them, and on whom they depended, into whose minds they had instilled prejudices against Christ, should thus disappoint them. Note, Mischievous men fret that they cannot do the mischief they would, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.16">Neh. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason which the officers gave for the non-execution of their warrant: <hi type="italic">Never man spoke like this man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.46">v. 46</reference>. Now, (1.) This was a very great truth, that <hi type="italic">never any man spoke with</hi> that wisdom, and power, and grace, that convincing clearness, and that charming sweetness, wherewith Christ spoke; none of the prophets, no, not Moses himself. (2.) The very officers that were sent to take him were taken with him, and acknowledged this. Though they were probably men who had no quick sense of reason or eloquence, and certainly had no inclination to think well of Jesus, yet so much <hi type="italic">self-evidence</hi> was there in what Christ said that they could not but prefer him before all those that sat in Moses's seat. Thus Christ was preserved by the power God has upon the consciences even of bad men. (3.) They said this to their lords and masters, who could not endure to hear any thing that tended to the honour of Christ and yet could not avoid hearing this. Providence ordered it so that this should be said to them, that it might be a vexation in their sin and an aggravation of their sin. Their own officers, who could not be suspected to be biassed in favour of Christ, are witnesses against them. This testimony of theirs should have made them reflect upon themselves, with this thought, "Do we know what we are doing, when we are hating and persecuting one that speaks so admirably well?" <div eID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> 3. The Pharisees endeavour to secure their officers to their interest, and to beget in them prejudices against Christ, to whom they saw them begin to be well affected. They suggest two things:— <div eID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> (1.) That if they embrace the gospel of Christ they will <hi type="italic">deceive themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.47">v. 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">Are you also deceived?</hi> Christianity has, from its first rise, been represented to the world as a great cheat upon it, and they that embraced it as men <hi type="italic">deceived,</hi> then when they began to be <hi type="italic">undeceived.</hi> Those that looked for a Messiah in external pomp thought those deceived who believed in a Messiah that appeared in poverty and disgrace; but the event declares that none were ever more shamefully deceived, nor put a greater cheat upon themselves, than those who promised themselves worldly wealth and secular dominion with the Messiah. Observe what a <hi type="italic">compliment</hi> the Pharisees paid to these officers: "<hi type="italic">Are you also deceived?</hi> What! men of your sense, and thought, and figure; men that know better than to be imposed upon by every pretender and upstart teacher?" They endeavour to prejudice them against Christ by persuading them to think well of themselves. <div eID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they will <hi type="italic">disparage themselves.</hi> Most men, even in their religion, are willing to be governed by the example of those of the <hi type="italic">first rank;</hi> these officers therefore, whose preferments, such as they were, gave them a <hi type="italic">sense of honour,</hi> are desired to consider, <div eID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> [1.] That, if they become disciples of Christ, they go contrary to those who were persons of quality and reputation: "<hi type="italic">Have any of the rulers, or of the Pharisees, believed on him?</hi> You know they have not, and you ought to be bound up by their judgment, and to <hi type="italic">believe</hi> and <hi type="italic">do</hi> in religion according to the will of your superiors; will you be wiser than they?" Some of the rulers did embrace Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Matt. ix. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.53">ch. iv. 53</reference>), and more believed in him, but wanted courage to confess him (<reference osisRef="John.12.42">ch. xii. 42</reference>); but, when the interest of Christ runs low in the world, it is common for its adversaries to represent it as lower than really it is. But it was too true that few, very few, of them did. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The cause of Christ has seldom had rulers and Pharisees on its side. It needs not secular supports, nor proposes secular advantages, and therefore neither courts nor is courted by the great men of this world. <hi type="italic">Self-denial</hi> and the <hi type="italic">cross</hi> are hard lessons to <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and Pharisees. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> This has confirmed many in their prejudices against Christ and his gospel, that the rulers and Pharisees have been no friends to them. Shall <hi type="italic">secular</hi> men pretend to be more concerned about <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> things than spiritual men themselves, or to see further into religion than those who make its study their profession? If <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> do not believe in Christ, they that do believe in him will be the most singular, unfashionable, ungenteel people in the world, and quite out of the way of preferment; thus are people foolishly swayed by <hi type="italic">external motives</hi> in matters of <hi type="italic">eternal moment,</hi> are willing to be damned for fashion-sake, and to go to hell in compliment to the <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees.</hi> <div eID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> [2.] That they will link themselves with the despicable vulgar sort of people (<reference osisRef="John.7.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">But this people, who know not the law, are cursed,</hi> meaning especially those that were well-affected to the doctrine of Christ. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How scornfully and disdainfully they speak of them: <hi type="italic">This people.</hi> It is not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">laos</hi></hi>, this <hi type="italic">lay-people,</hi> distinguished from them that were the clergy, but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ochlos outos</hi></hi>, this <hi type="italic">rabble-people,</hi> this pitiful, scandalous, scoundrel people, whom they disdained to <hi type="italic">set with the dogs of their flock</hi> though God had set them with the lambs of his. If they meant the <hi type="italic">commonalty of the Jewish nation,</hi> they were the seed of Abraham, and in covenant with God, and not to be spoken of with such contempt. The church's common interests are betrayed when any one part of it studies to render the other mean and despicable. If they meant the <hi type="italic">followers of Christ,</hi> though they were generally persons of small figure and fortune, yet by owning Christ they discovered such a sagacity, integrity, and interest in the favours of Heaven, as made them truly great and considerable. Note, As the wisdom of God has often chosen base things, and things which are despised, so the folly of men has commonly debased and despised those whom God has chosen. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How unjustly they reproach them as ignorant of the word of God: <hi type="italic">They know not the law;</hi> as if none knew the law but those that knew it <hi type="italic">from them,</hi> and no scripture-knowledge were current but what came out of their mint; and as if none knew the law but such as were observant of their canons and traditions. Perhaps many of those whom they thus despised <hi type="italic">knew the law,</hi> and the prophets too, better than they did. Many a plain, honest, unlearned disciple of Christ, by meditation, experience, prayers, and especially obedience, attains to a more clear, sound, and useful knowledge of the word of God, than some great scholars with all their wit and learning. Thus David came to understand <hi type="italic">more than the ancients</hi> and <hi type="italic">all his teachers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. If the common people did not <hi type="italic">know the law,</hi> yet the chief priests and Pharisees, of all men, should not have upbraided them with this; for whose fault was it but theirs, who should have <hi type="italic">taught them better,</hi> but, instead of that, <hi type="italic">took away the key of knowledge?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.52">Luke xi. 52</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> How magisterially they pronounce sentence upon them: they are <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> hateful to God, and all wise men; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epikatartoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an execrable</hi> people. It is well that their saying they were cursed did not make them so, for the <hi type="italic">curse causeless shall not come.</hi> It is a usurpation of God's prerogative, as well as great uncharitableness, to say of any particular persons, much more of any body of people, that they are reprobates. We are unable to <hi type="italic">try,</hi> and therefore unfit to <hi type="italic">condemn,</hi> and our rule is, <hi type="italic">Bless, and curse not.</hi> Some think they meant no more than that the people were <hi type="italic">apt to be deceived</hi> and <hi type="italic">made fools of;</hi> but they use this odious word, They are <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> to express their own indignation, and to frighten their officers from having any thing to do with them; thus the language of hell, in our profane age, calls every thing that is displeasing <hi type="italic">cursed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">damned,</hi> and <hi type="italic">confounded.</hi> Now, for aught that appears, these officers had their convictions baffled and stifled by these suggestions, and they never enquire further after Christ; one word from a <hi type="italic">ruler</hi> or <hi type="italic">Pharisee</hi> will sway more with many than the true reason of things, and the great interests of their souls. <div eID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> II. What passed between them and Nicodemus, a member of their own body, <reference osisRef="John.7.50">v. 50</reference>, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> 1. The just and rational objection which Nicodemus made against their proceedings. Even in their corrupt and wicked sanhedrim God left not himself quite <hi type="italic">without</hi> witness against their enmity; nor was the vote against Christ carried <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente</hi>—<hi type="italic">unanimously.</hi>Observe, <div eID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> (1.) Who it was that appeared against them; it was Nicodemus, <hi type="italic">he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.50">v. 50</reference>. Observe, concerning him, [1.] That, though he had been with Jesus, and taken him for his teacher, yet he retained his place in the council, and his vote among them. Some impute this to his <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> and cowardice, and think it was his fault that he did not quit his place, but Christ had never said to him, <hi type="italic">Follow me,</hi> else he would have done as others that left all to follow him; therefore it seems rather to have been his <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> not immediately to throw up his place, because there he might have opportunity of serving Christ and his interest, and stemming the tide of the Jewish rage, which perhaps he did more than we are aware of. He might there be as Hushai among Absalom's counsellors, instrumental to <hi type="italic">turn their counsels into foolishness.</hi> Though we must in no case deny our Master, yet we may wait for an opportunity of confessing him to the best advantage. God has his remnant among all sorts, and many times finds, or puts, or makes, some good in the worst places and societies. There was Daniel in Nebuchadnezzar's court, and Nehemiah in Artaxerxes's. [2.] That though at first he came to Jesus <hi type="italic">by night,</hi> for fear of being known, and still continued in his post; yet, when there was occasion, he boldly appeared in defence of Christ, and opposed the whole council that were set against him. Thus many believers who at first were timorous, and ready to <hi type="italic">flee at the shaking of a leaf,</hi> have at length, by divine grace, grown courageous, and able to <hi type="italic">laugh at the shaking of a spear.</hi> Let none justify the disguising of their faith by the example of Nicodemus, unless, like him, they be ready upon the first occasion openly to appear in the cause of Christ, though they stand alone in it; for so Nicodemus did here, and <reference osisRef="John.19.39">ch. xix. 39</reference>. <div eID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he alleged against their proceedings (<reference osisRef="John.7.51">v. 51</reference>): <hi type="italic">Doth our law judge any man before it hear him</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">akouse par autou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">hear from himself</hi>) and <hi type="italic">know what he doeth?</hi> By no means, nor doth the law of any civilized nation allow it. Observe, [1.] He prudently argues from the principles of their own law, and an incontestable rule of justice, that no man is to be condemned <hi type="italic">unheard.</hi> Had he urged the excellency of Christ's doctrine or the evidence of his miracles, or repeated to them his divine discourse with him (<reference osisRef="John.3.1-John.3.21">ch. iii.</reference>), it had been but to <hi type="italic">cast pearls before swine,</hi> who would <hi type="italic">trample them under their feet,</hi> and would <hi type="italic">turn again and rend him;</hi> therefore he waives them. [2.] Whereas they had reproached the people, especially the followers of Christ, as <hi type="italic">ignorant of the law,</hi> he here tacitly retorts the charge upon themselves, and shows how ignorant they were of some of the first principles of the law, so unfit were they to give law to others. [3.] The law is here said to <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">know,</hi> when magistrates that govern and are governed by it <hi type="italic">judge,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">know;</hi> for they are the <hi type="italic">mouth of the law,</hi> and whatsoever they bind and loose according to the law is justly said to be bound and loosed by the law. [4.] It is highly fit that none should come under the <hi type="italic">sentence</hi> of the law, till they have first by a fair trial undergone the <hi type="italic">scrutiny</hi> of it. Judges, when they receive the complaints of the accuser, must always reserve in their minds room for the defence of the accused, for they have two ears, to remind them to hear both sides; this is said to be the manner of the Romans, <reference osisRef="Acts.25.18">Acts xxv. 18</reference>. The method of our law is <hi type="italic">Oyer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Terminer,</hi> first to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> and then to <hi type="italic">determine.</hi> [5.] Persons are to be judged, not by what is <hi type="italic">said</hi> of them, but by what they <hi type="italic">do. Our law</hi> will not ask what men's opinions are of them, or out-cries against them, but, What have they done? What <hi type="italic">overt-acts</hi> can they be convicted of? Sentence must be given, <hi type="italic">secundum allegata et probata—according to what is alleged and proved.</hi> Facts, and not faces, must be known in judgment; and the <hi type="italic">scale</hi> of justice must be used before the <hi type="italic">sword</hi> of justice. <div eID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> Now we may suppose that the motion Nicodemus made in the house upon this was, That Jesus should be desired to come and give them an account of himself and his doctrine, and that they should favour him with an impartial and unprejudiced hearing; but, though none of them could gainsay his maxim, none of them would second his motion. <div eID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> 2. What was said to this objection. Here is no direct reply given to it; but, when they could not resist the force of his argument, they fell foul upon him, and what was to seek in <hi type="italic">reason</hi> they made up in railing and reproach. Note, It is a sign of a bad cause when men cannot bear to <hi type="italic">hear reason,</hi> and take it as an affront to be reminded of its maxims. Whoever are <hi type="italic">against reason</hi> give cause to suspect that <hi type="italic">reason</hi> is <hi type="italic">against them.</hi> See how they taunt him: <hi type="italic">Art thou also of Galilee?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.52">v. 52</reference>. Some think he was well enough served for continuing among those whom he knew to be enemies to Christ, and for his speaking no more on the behalf of Christ than what he might have said on behalf of the greatest criminal-that he should not be condemned unheard. Had he said, "As for this Jesus, I have heard him myself, and know he is a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God,</hi> and you in opposing him fight against God," as he ought to have said, he could not have been more abused than he was for this feeble effort of his tenderness for Christ. As to what they said to Nicodemus, we may observe, <div eID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> (1.) How <hi type="italic">false</hi> the grounds of their arguing were, for, [1.] They suppose that Christ was of Galilee, and this was false, and if they would have been at the pains of an impartial enquiry they would have found it so. [2.] They suppose that because most of his disciples were Galileans they were all such, whereas he had abundance of disciples in Judea. [3.] They suppose that out of Galilee no prophet had <hi type="italic">risen,</hi> and for this appeal to Nicodemus's search; yet this was false too: Jonah was of Gath-hepher, Nahum an Elkoshite, both of Galilee. Thus do they <hi type="italic">make lies their refuge.</hi> <div eID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> (2.) How <hi type="italic">absurd</hi> their arguings were upon these grounds, such as were a shame to <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees.</hi> [1.] Is any man of worth and virtue ever the worse for the poverty and obscurity of his country? The Galileans were the seed of Abraham; barbarians and Scythians are the seed of Adam; and <hi type="italic">have we not all one Father?</hi> [2.] Supposing no prophet had risen out of Galilee, yet it is not impossible that any should arise thence. If Elijah was the first prophet of Gilead (as perhaps he was), and if the Gileadites were called <hi type="italic">fugitives,</hi> must it therefore be questioned whether he was a prophet or no? <div eID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27275" type="x-p"/> 3. The hasty adjournment of the court hereupon. They broke up the assembly in confusion, and with precipitation, and <hi type="italic">every man went to his own house.</hi> They met to take <hi type="italic">counsel together against the Lord and his Anointed,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">imagined a vain think;</hi> and not only he that sits in heaven laughed at them, but we may sit on earth and laugh at them too, to see all the policy of the close cabal broken to pieces with one plain honest word. They were not willing to hear Nicodemus, because they could not answer him. As soon as they perceived they had one such among them, they saw it was to no purpose to go on with their design, and therefore put off the debate to a more convenient season, when he was absent. Thus the counsel of the Lord is made to stand, in spite of the devices in the hearts of men.  <chapter eID="John.7"/> <div eID="gen27275" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27278" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27277" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Woman Taken in Adultery.</title> <div sID="gen27279" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Jesus went unto the mount of Olives. <hi type="super">2</hi> And early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came unto him; and he sat down, and taught them. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the scribes and Pharisees brought unto him a woman taken in adultery; and when they had set her in the midst, <hi type="super">4</hi> They say unto him, Master, this woman was taken in adultery, in the very act. <hi type="super">5</hi> Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou? <hi type="super">6</hi> This they said, tempting him, that they might have to accuse him. But Jesus stooped down, and with <hi type="italic">his</hi> finger wrote on the ground, <hi type="italic">as though he heard them not.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. <hi type="super">8</hi> And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they which heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> being convicted by <hi type="italic">their own</hi> conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. <hi type="super">10</hi> When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? <hi type="super">11</hi> She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more. <div eID="gen27279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27280" type="x-p"/> Though Christ was basely abused in the foregoing chapter, both by the rulers and by the people, yet here we have him still at Jerusalem, still in the temple. <hi type="italic">How often would he have gathered them!</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27281" type="x-p"/> I. His retirement in the evening out of the town (<reference osisRef="John.8.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He went unto the mount of olives;</hi> whether to some friend's house, or to some booth pitched there, now at the feast of tabernacles, is not certain; whether he rested there, or, as some think, continued all night in prayer to God, we are not told. But he went out of Jerusalem, perhaps because he had no friend there that had either kindness or courage enough to give him a night's lodging; while his persecutors had <hi type="italic">houses</hi> of their own to go to (<reference osisRef="John.7.53">ch. vii. 53</reference>), he could not so much as borrow a place to lay his head on, but what he must go a mile or two out of town for. He retired (as some think) because he would not expose himself to the peril of a popular tumult in the night. It is prudent to go out of the way of danger whenever we can do it without going out of the way of duty. In the day-time, when he had work to do in the temple, he willingly exposed himself, and was under special protection, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>. But in the night, when he had not work to do, he withdrew into the country, and sheltered himself there. <div eID="gen27281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27282" type="x-p"/> II. His return in the morning to the temple, and to his work there, <reference osisRef="John.8.2">v. 2</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27283" type="x-p"/> 1. What a diligent preacher Christ was: <hi type="italic">Early in the morning he came again, and taught.</hi> Though he had been teaching the day before, he taught again to-day. Christ was a constant preacher, in season and out of season. Three things were taken notice of here concerning Christ's preaching. (1.) The time: <hi type="italic">Early in the morning.</hi> Though he lodged out of town, and perhaps had spent much of the night in secret prayer, yet he came <hi type="italic">early.</hi> When a day's work is to be done for God and souls it is good to begin betimes, and take the day before us. (2.) The place: <hi type="italic">In the temple;</hi> not so much because it was a <hi type="italic">consecrated</hi> place (for then he would have chosen it at other times) as because it was now a <hi type="italic">place of concourse;</hi> and he would hereby countenance solemn assemblies for religious worship, and encourage people to come up to the temple, for he had not yet left it desolate. (3.) His posture: <hi type="italic">He sat down,</hi> and taught, as one having authority, and as one that intended to abide by it for some time. <div eID="gen27283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27284" type="x-p"/> 2. How diligently his preaching was attended upon: <hi type="italic">All the people came unto him;</hi> and perhaps many of them were the country-people, who were this day to return home from the feast, and were desirous to hear one sermon more from the mouth of Christ before they returned. They came to him, though he came early. They that <hi type="italic">seek him early shall find him.</hi> Though the rulers were displeased at those that came to hear him, yet they would come; and <hi type="italic">he taught them,</hi> though they were angry at <hi type="italic">him</hi> too. Though there were few or none among them that were persons of any figure, yet Christ bade them welcome, and taught them. <div eID="gen27284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27285" type="x-p"/> III. His dealing with those that brought to him the <hi type="italic">woman taken in adultery, tempting</hi> him. The scribes and Pharisees would not only not hear Christ patiently themselves, but they disturbed him when the people were attending on him. Observe here, <div eID="gen27285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27286" type="x-p"/> 1. The case proposed to him by the scribes and Pharisees, who herein contrived to pick a quarrel with him, and bring him into a snare, <reference osisRef="John.8.3-John.8.6">v. 3-6</reference>. <div eID="gen27286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27287" type="x-p"/> (1.) They set the prisoner to the bar (<reference osisRef="John.8.3">v. 3</reference>): they brought him <hi type="italic">a woman taken in adultery,</hi> perhaps now lately taken, during the time of the feast of tabernacles, when, it may be, their dwelling in booths, and their feasting and joy, might, by wicked minds, which corrupt the best things, be made occasions of sin. Those that were <hi type="italic">taken in adultery</hi> were by the Jewish law to be put to death, which the Roman powers allowed them the execution of, and therefore she was brought before the ecclesiastical court. Observe, She <hi type="italic">was taken in her adultery.</hi> Though adultery is a work of darkness, which the criminals commonly take all the care they can to conceal, yet sometimes it is strangely brought to light. Those that promise themselves secrecy in sin deceive themselves. The scribes and Pharisees bring her to Christ, and set her in the midst of the assembly, as if they would leave her wholly to the judgment of Christ, he having <hi type="italic">sat down,</hi> as a judge upon the bench. <div eID="gen27287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27288" type="x-p"/> (2.) They prefer an indictment against her: <hi type="italic">Master, this woman was taken in adultery,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.4">v. 4</reference>. Here they call him <hi type="italic">Master</hi> whom but the day before they had called a <hi type="italic">deceiver,</hi> in hopes with their flatteries to have ensnared him, as those, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20">Luke xx. 20</reference>. But, though men may be imposed upon with compliments, he that searches the heart cannot. <div eID="gen27288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27289" type="x-p"/> [1.] The crime for which the prisoner stands indicted is no less than adultery, which even in the patriarchal age, before the law of Moses, was looked upon as <hi type="italic">an iniquity to be punished by the judges,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.9-Job.31.11">Job xxxi. 9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.38.24">Gen. xxxviii. 24</reference>. The Pharisees, by their vigorous prosecution of this offender, seemed to have a great zeal against the sin, when it appeared afterwards that they themselves were not free from it; nay, they were within <hi type="italic">full of all uncleanness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.27-Matt.23.28">Matt. xxiii. 27, 28</reference>. Note, It is common for those that are indulgent to their own sin to be severe against the sins of others. <div eID="gen27289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27290" type="x-p"/> [2.] The proof of the crime was from the notorious evidence of the fact, an incontestable proof; she was <hi type="italic">taken in the act,</hi> so that there was no room left to plead not guilty. Had she not been taken in this act, she might have gone on to another, till her heart had been perfectly hardened; but sometimes it proves a mercy to sinners to have their sin brought to light, that they may <hi type="italic">do no more presumptuously.</hi> Better our sin should <hi type="italic">shame</hi> us than <hi type="italic">damn</hi> us, and be set in order before us for our conviction than for our condemnation. <div eID="gen27290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27291" type="x-p"/> (3.) They produce the statute in this case made and provided, and upon which she was indicted, <reference osisRef="John.8.5">v. 5</reference>. Moses in the law commanded <hi type="italic">that such should be stoned.</hi> Moses commanded that they should be <hi type="italic">put to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Lev. xx. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.22.22">Deut. xxii. 22</reference>), but not that they should be stoned, unless the adulteress was espoused, not married, or was a priest's daughter, <reference osisRef="Deut.22.21">Deut. xxii. 21</reference>. Note, Adultery is an exceedingly sinful sin, for it is the rebellion of a vile lust, not only against the command, but against the covenant, of our God. It is the violation of a divine institution in innocency, by the indulgence of one of the basest lusts of man in his degeneracy. <div eID="gen27291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27292" type="x-p"/> (4.) They pray his judgment in the case: "<hi type="italic">But what sayest thou,</hi> who pretendest to be a teacher come from God to repeal old laws and enact new ones? What hast thou to say in this case?" If they had asked this question in sincerity, with a humble desire to know his mind, it had been very commendable. Those that are entrusted with the administration of justice should look up to Christ for direction; but <hi type="italic">this they said tempting him, that they might have to accuse him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.6">v. 6</reference>. [1.] If he should confirm the sentence of the law, and let it take its course, they would censure him as inconsistent with himself (he having received publicans and harlots) and with the character of the Messiah, who should be meek, and have salvation, and proclaim a year of release; and perhaps they would accuse him to the Roman governor, for countenancing the Jews in the exercise of a judicial power. But, [2.] If he should acquit her, and give his opinion that the sentence should not be executed (as they expected he would), they would represent him, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As an enemy to the law of Moses, and as one that usurped an authority to correct and control it, and would confirm that prejudice against him which his enemies were so industrious to propagate, that he came to <hi type="italic">destroy the law and the prophets. Secondly,</hi> As a friend to sinners, and, consequently, a favourer of sin; if he should seem to connive at such wickedness, and let it go unpunished, they would represent him as countenancing it, and being a patron of offences, if he was a protector of offenders, than which no reflection could be more invidious upon one that professed the strictness, purity, and business of a prophet. <div eID="gen27292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27293" type="x-p"/> 2. The method he took to resolve this case, and so to break this snare. <div eID="gen27293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27294" type="x-p"/> (1.) He seemed to slight it, and turned a deaf ear to it: He <hi type="italic">stooped down, and wrote on the ground.</hi> It is impossible to tell, and therefore needless to ask, what he wrote; but this is the only mention made in the gospels of Christ's writing. Eusebius indeed speaks of his writing to Abgarus, king of Edessa. Some think they have a liberty of conjecture as to what he wrote here. Grotius says, It was some grave weighty saying, and that it was usual for wise men, when they were very thoughtful concerning any thing, to do so. Jerome and Ambrose suppose he wrote, <hi type="italic">Let the names of these wicked men be written in the dust.</hi> Others this, <hi type="italic">The earth accuses the earth, but the judgment is mine.</hi> Christ by this teaches us to be slow to speak when difficult cases are proposed to us, not quickly to shoot our bolt; and when provocations are given us, or we are bantered, to pause and consider before we reply; think twice before we speak once: <hi type="italic">The heart of the wise studies to answer.</hi> Our translation from some Greek copies, which add, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me prospoioumenos</hi></hi> (though most copies have it not), give this account of the reason of his writing on the ground, <hi type="italic">as though he heard them not.</hi> He did as it were look another way, to show that he was not willing to take notice of their address, saying, in effect, <hi type="italic">Who made me a judge or a divider?</hi> It is safe in many cases to be deaf to that which it is not safe to answer, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>. Christ would not have his ministers to be entangled in secular affairs. Let them rather employ themselves in any lawful studies, and fill up their time in writing on the ground (which nobody will heed), than busy themselves in that which does not belong to them. But, when Christ seemed as though he heard them not, he made it appear that he not only heard their words, but knew their thoughts. <div eID="gen27294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27295" type="x-p"/> (2.) When they importunately, or rather impertinently, pressed him for an answer, he turned the conviction of the prisoner upon the prosecutors, <reference osisRef="John.8.7">v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen27295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27296" type="x-p"/> [1.] They <hi type="italic">continued asking him,</hi> and his seeming not to take notice of them made them the more vehement; for now they thought sure enough that they had run him aground, and that he could not avoid the imputation of contradicting either the law of Moses, if he should acquit the prisoner, or his own doctrine of mercy and pardon, if he should condemn her; and therefore they pushed on their appeal to him with vigour; whereas they should have construed his disregard of them as a check to their design, and an intimation to them to desist, as they tendered their own reputation. <div eID="gen27296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27297" type="x-p"/> [2.] At last he put them all to shame and silence with one word: <hi type="italic">He lifted up himself,</hi> awaking as one out of sleep (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Ps. lxxviii. 65</reference>), and <hi type="italic">said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.</hi> <div eID="gen27297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Here Christ avoided the snare which they had laid for him, and effectually saved his own reputation. He neither reflected upon the law nor excused the prisoner's guilt, nor did he on the other hand encourage the prosecution or countenance their heat; see the good effect of consideration. When we cannot make our point by steering a direct course, it is good to fetch a compass. <div eID="gen27298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly, In the net which they spread is their own foot taken.</hi> They came with design to accuse him, but they were forced to accuse themselves. Christ owns it was fit the prisoner should be prosecuted, but appeals to their consciences whether they were fit to be the prosecutors. <div eID="gen27299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27300" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> He here refers to that rule which the law of Moses prescribed in the execution of criminals, that the <hi type="italic">hand of the witnesses must be first upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.7">Deut. xvii. 7</reference>), as in the stoning of Stephen, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.58">Acts vii. 58</reference>. The scribes and Pharisees were the witnesses against this woman. Now Christ puts it to them whether, according to their own law, they would dare to be the executioners. Durst they take away that life with their hands which they were now taking away with their tongues? would not their own consciences fly in their faces if they did? <div eID="gen27300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27301" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> He builds upon an uncontested maxim in morality, that it is very absurd for men to be zealous in punishing the offences of others, while they are every whit as guilty themselves, and they are not better than self-condemned who judge others, and yet themselves do the same thing: "If there be any of you who is <hi type="italic">without sin,</hi> without sin of this nature, that has not some time or other been guilty of fornication or adultery, let him cast the first stone at her." Not that magistrates, who are conscious of guilt themselves, should therefore connive at others' guilt. But therefore, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Whenever we find fault with others, we ought to reflect upon ourselves, and to be more severe against sin in ourselves than in others. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) We ought to be favourable, though not to the sins, yet to the persons, of those that offend, and to restore them with a <hi type="italic">spirit of meekness,</hi> considering ourselves and our own corrupt nature. <hi type="italic">Aut sumus, aut fuimus, vel possumus esse quod hic est—We either are, or have been, or may be, what he is.</hi> Let this restrain us from <hi type="italic">throwing stones</hi> at our brethren, and proclaiming their faults. <hi type="italic">Let him that is without sin</hi> begin such discourse as this, and then those that are truly humbled for their own sins will blush at it, and be glad to <hi type="italic">let it drop.</hi> (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Those that are any way obliged to animadvert upon the faults of others are concerned to look well to themselves, and keep themselves pure (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.5">Matt. vii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Qui alterum incusat probri, ipsum se intueri oportet.</hi> The snuffers of the tabernacle were of <hi type="italic">pure gold.</hi> <div eID="gen27301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27302" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> Perhaps he refers to the trial of the suspected wife by the jealous husband with the waters of jealousy. The man was to bring her to the priest (<reference osisRef="Num.5.15">Num. v. 15</reference>), as the scribes and Pharisees brought this woman to Christ. Now it was a received opinion among the Jews, and confirmed by experience, that if the husband who brought his wife to that trial had himself been at any time guilty of adultery, <hi type="italic">Aquæ non explorant ejus uxorem—The bitter water had no effect upon the wife.</hi> "Come then," saith Christ, "according to your own tradition will I judge you; if you are without sin, stand to the charge, and let the adulteress be executed; but if not, though she be guilty, while you that present her are equally so, according to your own rule she shall be free." <div eID="gen27302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27303" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> In this he attended to the great work which he came into the world about, and that was to bring sinners to repentance; not to destroy, but to save. He aimed to bring, not only the prisoner to repentance, by showing her his mercy, but the prosecutors too, by showing them their sins. They sought to ensnare him; he sought to convince and convert them. Thus <hi type="italic">the blood-thirsty hate the upright, but the just seek his soul.</hi> <div eID="gen27303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27304" type="x-p"/> [3.] Having given them this startling word, he left them to consider of it, <hi type="italic">and again stooped down, and wrote on the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.8">v. 8</reference>. As when they made their address he seemed to slight their question, so now that he had given them an answer he slighted their resentment of it, not caring what they said to it; nay, they needed not to make any reply; the matter was lodged in their own breasts, let them make the best of it there. Or, he would not seem to wait for an answer, lest they should on a sudden justify themselves, and then think themselves bound in honour to persist in it; but gives them time to pause, and to commune with their own hearts. God saith, <hi type="italic">I hearkened and heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>. Some Greek copies here read, He <hi type="italic">wrote on the ground,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">enos hekastou auton tas hamartias</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the sins of every one of them;</hi> this he could do, for he <hi type="italic">sets our iniquities before him;</hi> and this he will do, for he will <hi type="italic">set them in order</hi> before us too; he <hi type="italic">seals up our transgressions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.17">Job xiv. 17</reference>. But he does not write men's sins <hi type="italic">in the sand;</hi> no, they are written as with a <hi type="italic">pen of iron</hi> and the <hi type="italic">point of a diamond</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.1">Jer. xvii. 1</reference>), never to be forgotten till they are forgiven. <div eID="gen27304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27305" type="x-p"/> [4.] The scribes and Pharisees were so strangely thunderstruck with the words of Christ that they let fall their persecution of Christ, whom they durst no further tempt, and their prosecution of the woman, whom they durst no longer accuse (<reference osisRef="John.8.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They went out one by one.</hi> <div eID="gen27305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27306" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Perhaps his writing on the ground frightened them, as the hand-writing on the wall frightened Belshazzar. They concluded he was writing bitter things against them, writing their doom. Happy they who have no reason to be afraid of Christ's writing! <div eID="gen27306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27307" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What he said frightened them by sending them to their own consciences; he had <hi type="italic">shown them to themselves,</hi> and they were afraid if they should stay till he lifted up himself again his next word would show them to the world, and shame them before men, and therefore they thought it best to withdraw. They went out <hi type="italic">one by one,</hi> that they might go out <hi type="italic">softly,</hi> and not by a noisy flight disturb Christ; they went away by <hi type="italic">stealth,</hi> as <hi type="italic">people being ashamed steal away when they flee in battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.3">2 Sam. xix. 3</reference>. The order of their departure is taken notice of, <hi type="italic">beginning at the eldest,</hi> either because they were most guilty, or first aware of the danger they were in of being put to the blush; and if the eldest quit the field, and retreat ingloriously, no marvel if the younger follow them. Now see here, 1. The <hi type="italic">force</hi> of the word of Christ for the conviction of sinners: <hi type="italic">They who heard it were convicted by their own consciences.</hi> Conscience is God's deputy in the soul, and one word from him will set it on work, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>. Those that had been old in adulteries, and long fixed in a proud opinion of themselves, were here, even the oldest of them, startled by the word of Christ; even scribes and Pharisees, who were most conceited of themselves, are by the power of Christ's word made to retire with shame. 2. The <hi type="italic">folly</hi> of sinners under these convictions, which appears in these scribes and Pharisees. (1.) It is folly for those that are under convictions to make it their principal care to <hi type="italic">avoid shame,</hi> as Judah (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.23">Gen. xxxviii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">lest we be shamed.</hi> Our care should be more to save our souls than to save our credit. Saul evidenced his hypocrisy when he said, <hi type="italic">I have sinned, yet now honour me, I pray thee.</hi> There is no way to get the honour and comfort of penitents, but by taking the shame of penitents. (2.) It is folly for those that are under convictions to contrive how to <hi type="italic">shift off</hi> their convictions, and to get rid of them. The scribes and Pharisees had the wound <hi type="italic">opened,</hi> and now they should have been desirous to have it <hi type="italic">searched,</hi> and then it might have been <hi type="italic">healed,</hi> but this was the thing they <hi type="italic">dreaded</hi> and <hi type="italic">declined.</hi> (3.) It is folly for those that are under convictions to <hi type="italic">get away from Jesus Christ,</hi> as these here did, for he is the only one that can heal the wounds of conscience, and speak peace to us. Those that are convicted by their consciences will be condemned by their Judge, if they be not justified by their Redeemer; and will they then go from him? To whom will they go? <div eID="gen27307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27308" type="x-p"/> [5.] When the <hi type="italic">self-conceited</hi> prosecutors quitted the field, and <hi type="italic">fled for the same,</hi> the <hi type="italic">self-condemned</hi> prisoner stood her ground, with a resolution to abide by the judgment of our Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">Jesus was left alone</hi> from the company of the scribes and Pharisees, free from their molestations, <hi type="italic">and the woman standing in the midst</hi> of the assembly that were attending on Christ's preaching, where they set her, <reference osisRef="John.8.3">v. 3</reference>. She did not seek to make her escape, though she had opportunity for it; but her prosecutors had appealed unto Jesus, and to him she would go, on him she would wait for her doom. Note, Those whose cause is brought before our Lord Jesus will never have occasion to remove it into any other court, for he is the refuge of penitents. The law which accuses us, and calls for judgment against us, is by the gospel of Christ made to withdraw; its demands are answered, and its clamours silenced, by the blood of Jesus. Our cause is lodged in the gospel court; we are <hi type="italic">left with Jesus alone,</hi> it is with him only that we have now to deal, for to him all judgment is committed; let us therefore secure our interest in him, and we are made for ever. Let his gospel <hi type="italic">rule us,</hi> and it will infallibly <hi type="italic">save us.</hi> <div eID="gen27308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27309" type="x-p"/> [6.] Here is the conclusion of the trial, and the issue it was brought to: <hi type="italic">Jesus lifted up himself, and he saw none but the woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.10-John.8.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Though Christ may seem to take no notice of what is said and done, but leave it to the <hi type="italic">contending</hi> sons of men to <hi type="italic">deal it out among themselves,</hi> yet, when the hour of his judgment is come, he will no longer keep silence. When David had appealed to God, he prayed, <hi type="italic">Lift up thyself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Ps. vii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.2">and xciv. 2</reference>. The woman, it is likely, stood trembling at the bar, as one doubtful of the issue. Christ was <hi type="italic">without sin,</hi> and might cast the first stone; but though none more severe than he against sin, for he is infinitely just and holy, none more compassionate than he to sinners, for he is infinitely gracious and merciful, and this poor malefactor finds him so, now that she <hi type="italic">stands upon her deliverance.</hi> Here is the method of courts of judicature observed. <div eID="gen27309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The prosecutors are called: <hi type="italic">Where are those thine accusers? Hath no man condemned thee?</hi> Not but that Christ knew where they were; but he asked, that he might shame them, who declined his judgment, and encourage her who resolved to abide by it. St. Paul's challenge is like this, <hi type="italic">Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect?</hi> Where are those their accusers? The <hi type="italic">accuser of the brethren shall</hi> be fairly <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> and all indictments legally and regularly quashed. <div eID="gen27310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27311" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They do not appear when the question is asked: <hi type="italic">Hath no man condemned thee?</hi> She said, <hi type="italic">No man, Lord.</hi> She speaks respectfully to Christ, calls him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> but is silent concerning her prosecutors, says nothing in answer to that question which concerned them, <hi type="italic">Where are those thine accusers?</hi> She does not triumph in their retreat nor insult over them as witnesses against themselves, not against her. If we hope to be forgiven by our Judge, we must forgive our accusers; and if their accusations, how invidious soever, were the happy occasion of awakening our consciences, we may easily <hi type="italic">forgive them this wrong.</hi> But she answered the question which concerned herself, <hi type="italic">Has no man condemned thee?</hi> True penitents find it enough to give an account of themselves to God, and will not undertake to give an account of other people. <div eID="gen27311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The prisoner is therefore discharged: <hi type="italic">Neither do I condemn thee; go, and sin no more.</hi> Consider this, <div eID="gen27312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27313" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) As her discharge from the temporal punishment: "If they do not condemn thee to be <hi type="italic">stoned to death,</hi> neither <hi type="italic">do I.</hi>" Not that Christ came to disarm the magistrate of his sword of justice, nor that it is his will that capital punishments should not be inflicted on malefactors; so far from this, the administration of public justice is established by the gospel, and made subservient to Christ's kingdom: <hi type="italic">By me kings reign.</hi> But Christ would not condemn this woman, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Because it was <hi type="italic">none of his business;</hi> he was no judge nor divider, and therefore would not intermeddle in secular affairs. His <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> was <hi type="italic">not of this world. Tractent fabrilia fabri—Let every one act in his own province.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Because she was prosecuted by those that were more guilty than she and could not for shame insist upon their demand of justice against her. The law appointed the hands of the witnesses to be first upon the criminal, and afterwards the hands of all the people, so that if they fly off, and do not condemn her, the prosecution drops. The justice of God, in inflicting temporal judgments, sometimes takes notice of a <hi type="italic">comparative righteousness,</hi> and spares those who are otherwise obnoxious when the punishing of them would gratify those that are worse than they, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.26-Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 26, 27</reference>. But, when Christ dismissed her, it was with this caution, <hi type="italic">Go, and sin no more.</hi> Impunity emboldens malefactors, and therefore those who are guilty, and yet have found means to escape the edge of the law, need to double their watch, <hi type="italic">lest Satan get advantage;</hi> for the fairer the escape was, the fairer the warning was to go and sin no more. Those who help to save the life of a criminal should, as Christ here, help to save the soul with this caution. <div eID="gen27313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27314" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) As her discharge from the eternal punishment. For Christ to say, <hi type="italic">I do not condemn thee</hi> is, in effect, to say, <hi type="italic">I do forgive thee;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Son of man had power on earth to forgive sins,</hi> and could upon good grounds give this absolution; for as he knew the hardness and impenitent hearts of the prosecutors, and therefore said that which would confound them, so he knew the tenderness and sincere repentance of the prisoner, and therefore said that which would comfort her, as he did to that woman who was a sinner, such a sinner as this, who was likewise looked upon with disdain by a Pharisee (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.48">Luke vii. 48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.50">50</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee, go in peace.</hi> So here, <hi type="italic">Neither do I condemn thee.</hi> Note, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Those are truly happy whom Christ <hi type="italic">doth not condemn,</hi> for his discharge is a sufficient answer to all other challenges; they are all <hi type="italic">coram non judice—before an unauthorized judge.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Christ will not condemn those who, though they have sinned, will <hi type="italic">go and sin no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Ps. lxxxv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">Isa. lv. 7</reference>. He will not take the advantage he has against us for our former rebellions, if we will but lay down our arms and return to our allegiance. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Christ's favour to us in the remission of the sins that are past should be a prevailing argument with us to <hi type="italic">go and sin no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.1-Rom.6.2">Rom. vi. 1, 2</reference>. Will not Christ condemn thee? Go then and sin no more.

<div eID="gen27314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life. <hi type="super">13</hi> The Pharisees therefore said unto him, Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true. <hi type="super">14</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, Though I bear record of myself, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> my record is true: for I know whence I came, and whither I go; but ye cannot tell whence I come, and whither I go. <hi type="super">15</hi> Ye judge after the flesh; I judge no man. <hi type="super">16</hi> And yet if I judge, my judgment is true: for I am not alone, but I and the Father that sent me. <hi type="super">17</hi> It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true. <hi type="super">18</hi> I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then said they unto him, Where is thy Father? Jesus answered, Ye neither know me, nor my Father: if ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also. <hi type="super">20</hi> These words spake Jesus in the treasury, as he taught in the temple: and no man laid hands on him; for his hour was not yet come. <div eID="gen27315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27316" type="x-p"/> The rest of the chapter is taken up with debates between Christ and contradicting sinners, who cavilled at the most gracious words that proceeded out of his mouth. It is not certain whether these disputes were the same day that the adulteress was discharged; it is probable they were, for the evangelist mentions no other day, and takes notice (<reference osisRef="John.8.2">v. 2</reference>) how early Christ began that day's work. Though those Pharisees that accused the woman had absconded, yet there were other Pharisees (<reference osisRef="John.8.13">v. 13</reference>) to confront Christ, who had brass enough in their foreheads to keep them in countenance, though some of their party were put to such a shameful retreat; nay perhaps that made them the more industrious to pick quarrels with him, to retrieve, if possible, the reputation of their baffled party. In these verses we have, <div eID="gen27316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27317" type="x-p"/> I. A great doctrine laid down, with the application of it. <div eID="gen27317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27318" type="x-p"/> 1. The doctrine is, <hi type="italic">That Christ is the light of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then spoke Jesus again unto them;</hi> though he had spoken a great deal to them to little purpose, and what he had said was opposed, yet he <hi type="italic">spoke again,</hi> for he <hi type="italic">speaketh once, yea, twice.</hi> They had turned a deaf ear to what he said, and yet he <hi type="italic">spoke again to them,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">I am the light of the world.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ is the light of the world. One of the rabbies saith, <hi type="italic">Light</hi> is the name of the Messiah, as it is written, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.22">Dan. ii. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">And light dwelleth with him.</hi> God is light, and Christ is <hi type="italic">the image of the invisible God;</hi> God of gods, Light of lights. He was expected to be a <hi type="italic">light to enlighten the Gentiles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Luke ii. 32</reference>), and so the <hi type="italic">light of the world,</hi> and not of the Jewish church only. The visible light of the world is the sun, and Christ is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness.</hi> One sun enlightens the whole world, so does one Christ, and there needs no more. Christ in calling himself the light expresses, (1.) What he is in himself—most excellent and glorious. (2.) What he is to the world—the fountain of light, enlightening every man. What a dungeon would the world be without the sun! So would it be without Christ by whom <hi type="italic">light came into the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.19">ch. iii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen27318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27319" type="x-p"/> 2. The inference from this doctrine is, <hi type="italic">He that followeth me,</hi> as a traveller follows the light in a dark night, <hi type="italic">shall not walk in darkness,</hi> but <hi type="italic">shall have the light of life.</hi> If Christ be the light, then, (1.) It is our duty to <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> to submit ourselves to his guidance, and in every thing take directions from him, in the way that leads to happiness. Many follow <hi type="italic">false lights—ignes fatui,</hi> that lead them to destruction; but Christ is the <hi type="italic">true light.</hi> It is not enough to <hi type="italic">look at</hi> this light, and to <hi type="italic">gaze</hi> upon it, but we must follow it, believe in it, and walk in it, for it is a light to <hi type="italic">our feet,</hi> not <hi type="italic">our eyes</hi> only. (2.) It is the happiness of those who follow Christ that they <hi type="italic">shall not walk in darkness.</hi> They shall not be left destitute of those instructions in the way of truth which are necessary to keep them from destroying error, and those directions in the way of duty which are necessary to keep them from damning sin. They shall have the <hi type="italic">light of life,</hi> that knowledge and enjoyment of God which will be to them the light of spiritual life in this world and of everlasting life in the other world, where there will be no death nor darkness. Follow Christ, and we shall undoubtedly be happy in both worlds. Follow Christ, and we shall follow him to heaven. <div eID="gen27319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27320" type="x-p"/> II. The objection which the Pharisees made against this doctrine, and it was very trifling and frivolous: <hi type="italic">Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.13">v. 13</reference>. In this objection they went upon the suspicion which we commonly have of men's self-condemnation, which is concluded to be the native language of self-love, such as we are all ready to condemn in others, but few are willing to own in themselves. But in this case the objection was very unjust, for, 1. They made that his crime, and a diminution to the credibility of his doctrine, which in the case of one who introduced a divine revelation was necessary and unavoidable. Did not Moses and all the prophets bear witness of themselves when they avouched themselves to be God's messengers? Did not the Pharisees ask John Baptist, <hi type="italic">What sayest thou of thyself?</hi> 2. They overlooked the testimony of all the other witnesses, which corroborated the testimony he bore of himself. Had he only borne record of himself, his testimony had indeed been <hi type="italic">suspicious,</hi> and the belief of it might have been <hi type="italic">suspended;</hi> but his doctrine was attested by more than <hi type="italic">two or three</hi> credible <hi type="italic">witnesses,</hi> enough to <hi type="italic">establish every word</hi> of it. <div eID="gen27320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27321" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's reply to this objection, <reference osisRef="John.8.14">v. 14</reference>. He does not retort upon them as he might ("You profess yourselves to be devout and good men, but your witness is not <hi type="italic">true</hi>"), but plainly vindicates himself; and, though he had waived his own testimony (<reference osisRef="John.5.31">ch. v. 31</reference>), yet here he abides by it, that it did not derogate from the credibility of his other proofs, but was necessary to show the force of them. He is the light of the world, and it is the property of light to be self-evidencing. First principles prove themselves. He urges three things to prove that his testimony, though of himself, was true and cogent. <div eID="gen27321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27322" type="x-p"/> 1. That he was conscious to himself of his own authority, and abundantly satisfied in himself concerning it. He did not speak as one at uncertainty, nor propose a disputable notion, about which he himself hesitated, but <hi type="italic">declared a decree,</hi> and gave such an account of himself as he would <hi type="italic">abide by: I know whence I came, and whither I go.</hi> He was fully apprised of his own undertaking from first to last; knew whose errand he went upon, and what his success would be. He knew what he <hi type="italic">was</hi> before his manifestation to the world, and what he <hi type="italic">should be</hi> after; that he came <hi type="italic">from the Father,</hi> and was going <hi type="italic">to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.28">ch. xvi. 28</reference>), came <hi type="italic">from glory,</hi> and was going <hi type="italic">to glory,</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">ch. xvii. 5</reference>). This is the satisfaction of all good Christians, that though the world know them not, as it knew him not, yet they know whence their spiritual life comes, and whither it tends, and go upon sure grounds. <div eID="gen27322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27323" type="x-p"/> 2. That they are very incompetent judges of him, and of his doctrine, and not to be regarded. (1.) Because they were <hi type="italic">ignorant,</hi> willingly and resolvedly <hi type="italic">ignorant: You cannot tell whence I came, and whither I go.</hi> To what purpose is it to talk with those who know nothing of the matter, nor desire to know? He had told them of his coming from heaven and returning to heaven, but it was <hi type="italic">foolishness to them,</hi> they <hi type="italic">received it not;</hi> it was what the <hi type="italic">brutish man knows not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.92.6">Ps. xcii. 6</reference>. They took upon them to judge of that which they did not understand, which lay quite out of the road of their acquaintance. Those that despise Christ's dominions and dignities speak evil of what they <hi type="italic">know not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.8-Jude.1.10">Jude, v. 8, 10</reference>. (2.) Because they were <hi type="italic">partial</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">You judge after the flesh.</hi> When fleshly wisdom gives the rule of judgment, and outward appearances only are given in evidence, and the case decided according to them, then men <hi type="italic">judge after the flesh;</hi> and when the consideration of a secular interest turns the scale in judging of spiritual matters, when we judge in favour of that which pleases the carnal mind, and recommends us to a carnal world, we judge after the flesh; and the judgment cannot be right when the rule is wrong. The Jews judged of Christ and his gospel by outward appearances, and, because he appeared so mean, thought it impossible he should be the light of the world; as if the sun under a cloud were no sun. (3.) Because they were <hi type="italic">unjust</hi> and <hi type="italic">unfair</hi> towards him, intimated in this: "<hi type="italic">I judge no man;</hi> I neither make nor meddle with your political affairs, nor does my doctrine or practice at all intrench upon, or interfere with, your civil rights or secular powers." He thus <hi type="italic">judged no man.</hi> Now, if he did not <hi type="italic">war after the flesh,</hi> it was very unreasonable for them to <hi type="italic">judge him after the flesh,</hi> and to treat him as an offender against the civil government. Or, "<hi type="italic">I judge no man,</hi>" that is, "not now in my first coming, that is deferred till I come again," <reference osisRef="John.3.17">ch. iii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Prima dispensatio Christi medicinalis est, non judicialis—The first coming of Christ was for the purpose of administering, not justice, but medicine.</hi> <div eID="gen27323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27324" type="x-p"/> 3. That his testimony of himself was sufficiently supported and corroborated by the testimony of his Father <hi type="italic">with him and for him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">And yet, if I judge, my judgment is true.</hi> He did in his doctrine judge (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">ch. ix. 39</reference>), though not <hi type="italic">politically.</hi> Consider him then, <div eID="gen27324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27325" type="x-p"/> (1.) As a judge, and his own judgment was valid: "<hi type="italic">If I judge,</hi> I who have authority to execute judgments, I to whom all things are delivered, I who am the Son of God, and have the Spirit of God, if I judge, <hi type="italic">my judgment is true,</hi> of incontestable rectitude and uncontrollable authority, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.2">Rom. ii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">If</hi> I <hi type="italic">should judge,</hi> my judgment must be true, and then you would be condemned; but the judgment-day is not yet come, you are not yet to be condemned, but spared, and therefore now <hi type="italic">I judge no man;</hi>" so Chrysostom.
