Now that which makes his judgment unexceptionable is, [1.] His Father's concurrence with him: <hi type="italic">I am not alone, but I and the Father.</hi> He has the Father's concurring <hi type="italic">counsels</hi> to <hi type="italic">direct;</hi> as he was with the Father before the world in forming the counsels, so the Father was with him in the world in prosecuting and executing those counsels, and never left him <hi type="italic">inops consilii—without advice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa. xi. 2</reference>. All the <hi type="italic">counsels of peace</hi> (and of war too) <hi type="italic">were between them both,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>. He had also the Father's concurring power to authorize and confirm what he did; see <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">Ps. lxxxix. 21,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>. He did not act <hi type="italic">separately,</hi> but in his own name and his Father's, and <hi type="italic">by the authority aforesaid,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.17">ch. v. 17, and xiv. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.9-John.14.10">10</reference>. [2.] His Father's commission to him: "It is the Father that <hi type="italic">sent me.</hi>" Note, God will go along with those that he sends; see <reference osisRef="Exod.3.10">Exod. iii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">12</reference>: <hi type="italic">Come, and I will send thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">certainly I will be with thee.</hi> Now, if Christ had a <hi type="italic">commission</hi> from the Father, and the Father's <hi type="italic">presence</hi> with him in all his administrations, no doubt his <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> was <hi type="italic">true</hi> and valid; no exception lay <hi type="italic">against</hi> it, no appeal lay <hi type="italic">from</hi> it. <div eID="gen27325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27326" type="x-p"/> (2.) Look upon him as <hi type="italic">a witness,</hi> and now he appeared no otherwise (having not as yet taken the throne of judgment), and as such his testimony was true and unexceptionable; this he shows, <reference osisRef="John.8.17-John.8.18">v. 17, 18</reference>, where, <div eID="gen27326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27327" type="x-p"/> [1.] He quotes a maxim of the Jewish law, <reference osisRef="John.8.17">v. 17</reference>. That <hi type="italic">the testimony of two men is true.</hi> Not as if it were always true <hi type="italic">in itself,</hi> for many a time hand has been joined in hand to bear a <hi type="italic">false</hi> testimony, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.10">1 Kings xxi. 10</reference>. But it is allowed as sufficient evidence upon which to ground a verdict (<hi type="italic">verum dictum</hi>), and if nothing appear to the contrary it is taken for granted to be <hi type="italic">true.</hi> Reference is here had to that law (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.6">Deut. xvii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">At the mouth of two witnesses shall he that is worthy of death be put to death.</hi> And see <reference osisRef="Deut.9.15">Deut. ix. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.30">Num. xxxv. 30</reference>. It was in <hi type="italic">favour of life</hi> that in capital cases two witnesses wee required, as with us in case of treason. See <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen27327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27328" type="x-p"/> [2.] He applies this to the case in hand (<reference osisRef="John.8.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me bears witness of me.</hi> Behold two witnesses! Though in human courts, where two witnesses are required, the criminal or candidate is not admitted to be a witness for himself; yet in a matter purely divine, which can be proved only by a divine testimony, and God himself must be the witness, if the formality of two or three witnesses be insisted on, there can be no other than the eternal Father, the eternal Son of the Father, and the eternal Spirit. Now if the testimony of two distinct persons, that are <hi type="italic">men,</hi> and therefore may deceive or be deceived, is conclusive, much more ought the testimony of the Son of God concerning himself, backed with the testimony of his Father concerning him, to command assent; see <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">1 John v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.9-1John.5.11">9-11</reference>. Now this proves not only that the Father and the Son are two distinct persons (for their respective testimonies are here spoken of as the testimonies of two several persons), but that these two are one, not only one in their testimony, but equal in power and glory, and therefore the same in substance. St. Austin here takes occasion to caution his hearers against Sabellianism on the one hand, which confounded the persons in the Godhead, and Arianism on the other, which denied the Godhead of the Son and Spirit. <hi type="italic">Alius est filius, et alius pater, non tamed aliud, sed hoc ipsum est et pater, et filius, scilicet unus Deus est—The Son is one Person, and the Father is another; they do not, however, constitute two Beings, but the Father is the same Being that the Son is, that is, the only true God.</hi> Tract. 36, <hi type="italic">in</hi> Joann. Christ here speaks of himself and the Father as witnesses to the world, giving in evidence to the reason and conscience of the children of men, whom he deals with as men. And these witnesses <hi type="italic">to</hi> the world now will in the great day be witnesses <hi type="italic">against</hi> those that persist in unbelief, and <hi type="italic">their</hi> word will judge men. <div eID="gen27328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27329" type="x-p"/> This was the sum of the first conference between Christ and these carnal Jews, in the conclusion of which we are told how their tongues were let loose, and their hands tied. <div eID="gen27329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27330" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How their tongues were let loose (such was the malice of hell) to cavil at his discourse, <reference osisRef="John.8.19">v. 19</reference>. Though in what he said there appeared nothing of human policy or artifice, but a divine security, yet they set themselves to <hi type="italic">cross questions</hi> with him. None so incurably <hi type="italic">blind</hi> as those that resolve they <hi type="italic">will not see.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27331" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> How they evaded the <hi type="italic">conviction</hi> with a <hi type="italic">cavil: Then said they unto him, Where is thy Father?</hi> They might easily have understood, by the tenour of this and his other discourses, that when he spoke of his <hi type="italic">Father</hi> he meant no other than God himself; yet they pretend to understand him of a common person, and, since he appeals to his testimony, they bid him <hi type="italic">call his witness,</hi> and challenge him, if he can, to produce him: <hi type="italic">Where is thy Father?</hi> Thus, as Christ said of them (<reference osisRef="John.8.15">v. 15</reference>), they <hi type="italic">judge after the flesh.</hi> Perhaps they hereby intend a reflection upon the meanness and obscurity of his family: <hi type="italic">Where is thy Father,</hi> that he should be fit to give evidence in such a case as this? Thus they turned it off with a taunt, when they <hi type="italic">could not resist the wisdom and spirit with which he spoke.</hi> <div eID="gen27331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27332" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> How he evaded the <hi type="italic">cavil</hi> with a further <hi type="italic">conviction;</hi> he did not tell them where his Father was, but charged them with wilful ignorance: "<hi type="italic">You neither know me nor my Father.</hi> It is to no purpose to discourse to you about divine things, who talk of them as blind men do of colours. Poor creatures! you know nothing of the matter." (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) He charges them with ignorance of God: "<hi type="italic">You know not my Father.</hi>" In Judah was God known (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Ps. lxxvi. 1</reference>); they had some knowledge of him as the God that made the world, but their eyes were darkened that they could not see the light of his glory shining <hi type="italic">in the face of Jesus Christ.</hi> The <hi type="italic">little children</hi> of the Christian church <hi type="italic">know the Father,</hi> know him as a Father (<reference osisRef="1John.2.13">1 John ii. 13</reference>); but these rulers of the Jews did not, because they would not so know him. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) He shows them the true cause of their ignorance of God: <hi type="italic">If you had known me, you would have known my Father also.</hi> The reason why men are ignorant of God is because they are unacquainted with Jesus Christ. Did we know Christ, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] In knowing him we should know the Father, of whose person he is the express image, <reference osisRef="John.14.9">ch. xiv. 9</reference>. Chrysostom proves hence the Godhead of Christ, and his equality with his Father. We cannot say, "He that knows a man knows an angel," or, "He that knows a creature knows the Creator;" but he that knows Christ knows the Father. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] By him we should be instructed in the knowledge of God, and introduced into an acquaintance with him. If we <hi type="italic">knew Christ</hi> better, we should <hi type="italic">know the Father</hi> better; but, where the Christian religion is slighted and opposed, natural religion will soon be lost and laid aside. Deism makes way for atheism. Those become vain in their imaginations concerning God that will not learn of Christ. <div eID="gen27332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27333" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> See how their hands were tied, though their tongues were thus let loose; such was the power of Heaven to restrain the malice of hell. <hi type="italic">These words spoke Jesus,</hi> these bold words, these words of conviction and reproof, <hi type="italic">in the treasury,</hi> an apartment of the temple, where, to be sure, the chief priests, whose gain was their godliness, were mostly resident, attending the business of the revenue. Christ <hi type="italic">taught in the temple,</hi> sometimes in one part, sometimes in another, as he saw occasion. Now the priests who had so great a concern in the temple, and looked upon it as their <hi type="italic">demesne,</hi> might easily, with the assistance of the janizaries that were at their beck, either have seized him and exposed him to the rage of the mob, and that punishment which they called the <hi type="italic">beating of the rebels;</hi> or, at least, have <hi type="italic">silenced</hi> him, and stopped his mouth there, as Amos, though tolerated in the land of Judah, was forbidden to prophesy in the king's chapel, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.12-Amos.7.13">Amos, vii. 12, 13</reference>. Yet even <hi type="italic">in the temple,</hi> where they had him in their reach, <hi type="italic">no man laid hands on him,</hi> for <hi type="italic">his hour was not yet come.</hi> See here, 1. The restraint laid upon his persecutors by an invisible power; none of them durst meddle with him. God can set bounds to the wrath of men, as he does to the waves of the sea. Let us not therefore fear danger in the way of duty; for God hath Satan and all his instruments in a chain. 2. The reason of this restraint: <hi type="italic">His hour was not yet come.</hi> The frequent mention of this intimates how much the time of our departure out of the world depends upon the fixed counsel and decree of God. It <hi type="italic">will</hi> come, it is coming; not yet come, but it is at hand. Our enemies cannot hasten it any sooner, nor our friends delay it any longer, than the time appointed of the Father, which is very comfortable to every good man, who can look up and say with pleasure, <hi type="italic">My times are in thy hands;</hi> and better there than in our own. His hour was not yet come, because his work was not done, nor his testimony finished. To all God's purposes <hi type="italic">there is a time.</hi>

<div eID="gen27333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Then said Jesus again unto them, I go my way, and ye shall seek me, and shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then said the Jews, Will he kill himself? because he saith, Whither I go, ye cannot come. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he said unto them, Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world. <hi type="super">24</hi> I said therefore unto you, that ye shall die in your sins: for if ye believe not that I am <hi type="italic">he,</hi> ye shall die in your sins. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then said they unto him, Who art thou? And Jesus saith unto them, Even <hi type="italic">the same</hi> that I said unto you from the beginning. <hi type="super">26</hi> I have many things to say and to judge of you: but he that sent me is true; and I speak to the world those things which I have heard of him. <hi type="super">27</hi> They understood not that he spake to them of the Father. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then said Jesus unto them, When ye have lifted up the Son of man, then shall ye know that I am <hi type="italic">he,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I do nothing of myself; but as my Father hath taught me, I speak these things. <hi type="super">29</hi> And he that sent me is with me: the Father hath not left me alone; for I do always those things that please him. <hi type="super">30</hi> As he spake these words, many believed on him. <div eID="gen27334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27335" type="x-p"/> Christ here gives fair warning to the careless unbelieving Jews to consider what would be the consequence of their infidelity, that they might prevent it before it was too late; for he spoke words of terror as well as words of grace. Observe here, <div eID="gen27335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27336" type="x-p"/> I. The wrath threatened (<reference osisRef="John.8.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jesus said again unto them</hi> that which might be likely to do them good. He continued to teach, in kindness to those few who received his doctrine, though there were many that resisted it, which is an example to ministers to go on with their work, notwithstanding opposition, because a remnant shall be saved. Here Christ changes his voice; he had <hi type="italic">piped to them</hi> in the offers of his grace, and they <hi type="italic">had not danced;</hi> now he mourns to them in the denunciations of his wrath, to try if they would lament. He said, <hi type="italic">I go my way, and you shall seek me, and shall die in your sins. Whither I go you cannot come.</hi> Every word is terrible, and bespeaks spiritual judgments, which are the sorest of all judgments; worse than war, pestilence, and captivity, which the Old-Testament prophets denounced. Four things are here threatened against the Jews. <div eID="gen27336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27337" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's departure from them: <hi type="italic">I go my way,</hi> that is, "It shall not be long before I go; you need not take so much pains to drive me from you, I shall go of myself." They said to him, <hi type="italic">Depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of thy ways;</hi> and he takes them at their word; but woe to those from whom Christ departs. Ichabod, the glory is gone, our defence is departed, when Christ goes. Christ frequently warned them of his departure before he left them: he <hi type="italic">bade often farewell,</hi> as one <hi type="italic">loth to depart,</hi> and willing to be invited, and that would have them <hi type="italic">stir up themselves to take hold on him.</hi> <div eID="gen27337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27338" type="x-p"/> 2. Their enmity to the true Messiah, and their fruitless and infatuated enquiries after another Messiah when he was gone away, which were both their sin and their punishment: <hi type="italic">You shall seek me,</hi> which intimates either, (1.) Their <hi type="italic">enmity</hi> to the <hi type="italic">true Christ:</hi> "You shall seek to ruin my interest, by persecuting my doctrine and followers, with a fruitless design to root them out." This was a continual vexation and torment to themselves, made them incurably <hi type="italic">ill-natured,</hi> and brought <hi type="italic">wrath upon them</hi> (God's and their own) <hi type="italic">to the uttermost.</hi> Or, (2.) Their <hi type="italic">enquiries</hi> after <hi type="italic">false Christs:</hi> "You shall continue your expectations of the Messiah, and be the self-perplexing seekers of a Christ to come, when he is already come;" like the Sodomites, who, being struck with blindness, wearied themselves to find the door. See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.31-Rom.9.32">Rom. ix. 31, 32</reference>. <div eID="gen27338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27339" type="x-p"/> 3. Their final impenitency: <hi type="italic">You shall die in your sins.</hi> Here is an error in all our English Bibles, even the old bishops' translation, and that of Geneva (the Rhemists only excepted), for all the Greek copies have it in the singular number, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en te hamartia hymon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">in your sin,</hi> so all the Latin versions; and Calvin has a note upon the difference between this and <reference osisRef="John.8.24">v. 24</reference>, where it is plural, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tais hamartiais</hi></hi>, that here it is meant especially of the sin of unbelief, <hi type="italic">in hoc peccato vestro—in this sin of yours.</hi> Note, Those that live in unbelief are for ever undone if they die in unbelief. Or, it may be understood in general, <hi type="italic">You shall die in your iniquity,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.19">Ezek. iii. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.9">and xxxiii. 9</reference>. Many that have long lived in sin are, through grace, saved by a timely repentance from <hi type="italic">dying in sin;</hi> but for those who go out of this world of probation into that of retribution under the guilt of sin unpardoned, and the power of sin unbroken, there remaineth no relief: salvation itself cannot save them, <reference osisRef="Job.20.11">Job xx. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Ezek. xxxii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27340" type="x-p"/> 4. Their eternal separation from Christ and all happiness in him: <hi type="italic">Whither I go you cannot come.</hi> When Christ left the world, he went to a state of perfect happiness; he went to paradise. Thither he took the penitent thief with him, that did not die in his sins; but the impenitent not only <hi type="italic">shall not</hi> come to him, but they <hi type="italic">cannot;</hi> it is morally impossible, for heaven would not be heaven to those that die unsanctified and unmeet for it. You cannot come, because you have <hi type="italic">no right</hi> to enter into that Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.14">Rev. xxii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whither I go you cannot come,</hi> to fetch me thence, so Dr. Whitby; and the same is the comfort of all good Christians, that, when they get to heaven, they will be out of the reach of their enemies' malice. <div eID="gen27340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27341" type="x-p"/> II. The jest they made of this threatening. Instead of trembling at this word, they bantered it, and turned it into ridicule (<reference osisRef="John.8.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will he kill himself?</hi> See here, 1. What slight thoughts they had of Christ's threatenings; they could make themselves and one another merry with them, as those that mocked the messengers of the Lord, and turned the <hi type="italic">burden of the word of the Lord</hi> into a <hi type="italic">by-word,</hi> and <hi type="italic">precept upon precept, line upon line,</hi> into a merry song, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa. xxviii. 13</reference>. But <hi type="italic">be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong.</hi> 2. What ill thoughts they had of Christ's meaning, as if he had an inhuman design upon his own life, to avoid the indignities done him, like Saul. This is indeed (say they) to go whither we cannot follow him, for we will never <hi type="italic">kill ourselves.</hi> Thus they make him not only such a one as themselves, but worse; yet in the calamities brought by the Romans upon the Jews many of them in discontent and despair did kill themselves. They had put a much more favourable construction upon this word of his (<reference osisRef="John.7.34-John.7.35">ch. vii. 34, 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will he go to the dispersed among the Gentiles?</hi> But see how indulged malice grows more and more malicious. <div eID="gen27341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27342" type="x-p"/> III. The confirmation of what he had said. <div eID="gen27342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27343" type="x-p"/> 1. He had said, <hi type="italic">Whither I go you cannot come,</hi> and here he gives the reason for this (<reference osisRef="John.8.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">You are from beneath, I am from above; you are of this world, I am not of this world.</hi> You are <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek ton kato</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of those things which are beneath;</hi> noting, not so much their rise from beneath as their affection to these lower things: "You are <hi type="italic">in with these things,</hi> as those that belong to them; how can you come where I go, when your spirit and disposition are so directly contrary to mine?" See here, (1.) What the <hi type="italic">spirit of the Lord Jesus</hi> was—not of <hi type="italic">this world,</hi> but from <hi type="italic">above.</hi> He was perfectly dead to the wealth of the world, the ease of the body, and the praise of men, and was wholly taken up with divine and heavenly things; and none shall be with him but those who are <hi type="italic">born from above</hi> and have their <hi type="italic">conversation in heaven.</hi> (2.) How contrary to this <hi type="italic">their</hi> spirit was: "<hi type="italic">You are from beneath,</hi> and of this world." The Pharisees were of a carnal worldly spirit; and what communion could Christ have with them? <div eID="gen27343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27344" type="x-p"/> 2. He had said, <hi type="italic">You shall die in your sins,</hi> and here he stand to it: "Therefore I said, You shall die in your sins, because <hi type="italic">you are from beneath;</hi>" and he gives this further reason for it, <hi type="italic">If you believe not that I am he, you shall die in your sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.24">v. 24</reference>. See here, (1.) What we are required to believe: <hi type="italic">that I am he,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hoti ego eimi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that I am,</hi> which is one of God's names, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>. It was the Son of God that there said, <hi type="italic">Ehejeh asher Ehejeh—I will be what I will be;</hi> for the deliverance of Israel was but a figure of good things to come, but now he saith, "<hi type="italic">I am he;</hi> he that should come, he that you expect the Messias to be, that you would have me to be to you. I am more than the bare name of the Messiah; I do not only call myself so, but I <hi type="italic">am he.</hi>" True faith does not <hi type="italic">amuse</hi> the soul with an empty sound of words, but <hi type="italic">affects</hi> it with the doctrine of Christ's mediation, as a real thing that has real effects. (2.) How necessary it is that we believe this. If we have not this faith, <hi type="italic">we shall die in our sins;</hi> for the matter is so settled that without this faith, [1.] We cannot be saved from the power of sin while we live, and therefore shall certainly continue in it to the last. Nothing but the <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> of Christ's grace will be an argument powerful enough, and none but the <hi type="italic">Spirit</hi> of Christ's grace will be an agent powerful enough, to turn us from sin to God; and that Spirit is given, and that doctrine given, to be effectual to those only who believe in Christ: so that, if Satan be not by faith dispossessed, he has a lease of the soul for its life; if Christ do not cure us, our case is desperate, and we shall <hi type="italic">die in our sins.</hi> [2.] Without faith we cannot be saved from the punishment of sin when we die, for the <hi type="italic">wrath of God remains</hi> upon them that believe not, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>. Unbelief is the damning sin; it is a sin against the remedy. Now this implies the great gospel promise: <hi type="italic">If we believe that Christ is he,</hi> and receive him accordingly, <hi type="italic">we shall not die in our sins.</hi> The law saith absolutely to all, as Christ said (<reference osisRef="John.8.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">You shall die in your sins,</hi> for we are all guilty before God; but the gospel is a defeasance of the obligation upon condition of believing. The curse of the law is vacated and annulled to all that submit to the grace of the gospel. Believers die in Christ, in his love, in his arms, and so are saved from dying <hi type="italic">in their sins.</hi> <div eID="gen27344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27345" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is a further discourse concerning <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> occasioned by his requiring faith in himself as the condition of salvation, <reference osisRef="John.8.25-John.8.29">v. 25-29</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27346" type="x-p"/> 1. The question which the Jews put to him (<reference osisRef="John.8.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who art thou?</hi> This they asked tauntingly, and not with any desire to be instructed. He had said, You must believe that <hi type="italic">I am he.</hi> By his not saying expressly who he was, he plainly intimated that in his person he was such a one as could not be <hi type="italic">described</hi> by any, and in his office such a one as was <hi type="italic">expected</hi> by all that looked for redemption in Israel; yet this awful manner of speaking, which had so much significancy in it, they turned to his reproach, as if he knew not what to say of himself: "<hi type="italic">Who art thou,</hi> that we must with an implicit faith believe in thee, that thou art some mighty HE, we know not <hi type="italic">who</hi> or <hi type="italic">what,</hi> nor are <hi type="italic">worthy to know?</hi>" <div eID="gen27346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27347" type="x-p"/> 2. His answer to this question, wherein he directs them three ways for information:— <div eID="gen27347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27348" type="x-p"/> (1.) He refers them to <hi type="italic">what he had said</hi> all along: "Do you ask who I am? <hi type="italic">Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning.</hi>" The original here is a little intricate, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten archen ho ti kai lalo hymin</hi></hi> which some read thus: <hi type="italic">I am the beginning, which also I speak unto you.</hi> So Austin takes it. Christ is called <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Arche</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the beginning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col. i. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.8">Rev. i. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.6">xxi. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">iii. 14</reference>), and so it agrees with <reference osisRef="John.8.24">v. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">I am he.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Isa. xli. 4</reference>: <hi type="italic">I am the first, I am he.</hi> Those who object that it is the accusative case, and therefore not properly answering to <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tis ei</hi></hi>, must undertake to construe by grammar rules that parallel expression, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.8">Rev. i. 8</reference>, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho en</hi></hi>. But most interpreters agree with our version, Do you ask <hi type="italic">who I am?</hi> [1.] I am <hi type="italic">the same that I said to you from the beginning</hi> of time in the scriptures of the Old-Testament, the same that from the beginning was said to be <hi type="italic">the Seed of the woman, that should break the serpent's head,</hi> the same that in all the ages of the church was the Mediator of the covenant, and the faith of the patriarchs. [2.] <hi type="italic">From the beginning</hi> of my public ministry. The account he had already given of himself he resolved to <hi type="italic">abide by;</hi> he had declared himself to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.17">ch. v. 17</reference>), to be the Christ (<reference osisRef="John.4.26">ch. iv. 26</reference>), and the bread of life, and had proposed himself as the object of that faith which is necessary to salvation, and to this he refers them for an answer to their question. Christ is <hi type="italic">one with himself;</hi> what he had said from the beginning, he saith still. His is an <hi type="italic">everlasting gospel.</hi> <div eID="gen27348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27349" type="x-p"/> (2.) He refers them to his Father's judgment, and the instructions he had from him (<reference osisRef="John.8.26">v. 26</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have many things,</hi> more than you think of, <hi type="italic">to say, and</hi> in them <hi type="italic">to judge of you.</hi> But why should I trouble myself any further with you? I know very well that <hi type="italic">he who sent me is true,</hi> and will stand by me, and bear me out, for <hi type="italic">I speak to the world</hi> (to which I am sent as an ambassador) <hi type="italic">those things,</hi> all those and those only, <hi type="italic">which I have heard of him.</hi>" Here, <div eID="gen27349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27350" type="x-p"/> [1.] He suppresses his accusation of them. He had <hi type="italic">many things</hi> to charge them with, and many evidences to produce against them; but for the present he had said enough. Note, Whatever discoveries of sin are made to us, he that searches the heart has still more to judge of us, <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">1 John iii. 20</reference>. How much soever God reckons with sinners in this world there is still a further reckoning yet behind, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">Deut. xxxii. 34</reference>. Let us learn hence not to be forward to say all we can say, even against the worst of men; we may have many things to say, by way of censure, which yet it is better to leave <hi type="italic">unsaid,</hi> for what is it to us? <div eID="gen27350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27351" type="x-p"/> [2.] He enters his appeal against them to his Father: <hi type="italic">He that sent me.</hi> Here two things comfort him:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he had been <hi type="italic">true to his Father,</hi> and to the trust reposed in him: <hi type="italic">I speak to the world</hi> (for his gospel was to be preached to every creature) <hi type="italic">those things which I have heard of him.</hi> Being given for a <hi type="italic">witness to the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa. lv. 4</reference>), he was <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> a <hi type="italic">faithful witness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev. iii. 14</reference>. He did not <hi type="italic">conceal</hi> his doctrine, but spoke it <hi type="italic">to the world</hi> (being of common concern, it was to be of common notice); nor did he change or alter it, nor vary from the instructions he received from him that sent him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That his Father would be <hi type="italic">true to him;</hi> true to the promise that he would <hi type="italic">make his mouth like a sharp sword;</hi> true to his purpose concerning him, which was a <hi type="italic">decree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>); true to the threatenings of his wrath against those that should reject him. Though he should not <hi type="italic">accuse</hi> them to his Father, yet the Father, who sent him, would undoubtedly reckon with them, and would be <hi type="italic">true</hi> to what he had said (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.19">Deut. xviii. 19</reference>), that whosoever would not hearken to that prophet whom God would raise up <hi type="italic">he would require it of him.</hi> Christ would not accuse them; "for," saith he, "he that sent me is true, and will pass judgment on them, though I should not demand judgment against them." Thus, when he <hi type="italic">lets fall</hi> the present prosecution, he <hi type="italic">binds them over</hi> to the judgment-day, when it will be too late to dispute what they will not now be persuaded to believe. <hi type="italic">I, as a deaf man, heard not; for thou wilt hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">15</reference>. Upon this part of our Saviour's discourse the evangelist has a melancholy remark (<reference osisRef="John.8.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">They understood not that he spoke to them of the Father.</hi> See here, 1. The power of Satan to blind the minds of those who believe not. Though Christ spoke so plainly of God as his Father in heaven, yet they did not understand whom he meant, but thought he spoke of some father he had in Galilee. Thus the plainest things are riddles and parables to those who are resolved to hold fast their prejudices; day and night are alike to the blind. 2. The reason why the threatenings of the word make so little impression upon the minds of sinners; it is because they understand not whose the wrath is that is revealed in them. When Christ told them of the truth of him that sent him, as a warning to them to prepare for his judgment, which is <hi type="italic">according to truth,</hi> they slighted the warning, because they understood not to whose judgment it was that they made themselves obnoxious. <div eID="gen27351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27352" type="x-p"/> (3.) He refers them to <hi type="italic">their own convictions</hi> hereafter, <reference osisRef="John.8.28-John.8.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. He finds they will not understand him, and therefore adjourns the trial till further evidence should come in; they that <hi type="italic">will not see shall see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. Now observe here, <div eID="gen27352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27353" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">What</hi> they should ere long be <hi type="italic">convinced of: "You shall know that I am he,</hi> that Jesus is the true Messiah. Whether you will own it or no before men, you shall be made to know it in your own consciences, the convictions of which, though you may <hi type="italic">stifle,</hi> yet you cannot <hi type="italic">baffle: that I am he,</hi> not that you represent me to be, but he that I preach myself to be, he that should come!" Two things they should be convinced of, in order to this:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he did nothing <hi type="italic">of himself,</hi> not of himself as man, of himself alone, of himself without the Father, with whom he was <hi type="italic">one.</hi> He does not hereby derogate from his own inherent power, but only denies their charge against him as a <hi type="italic">false prophet;</hi> for of false prophets it is said that they prophesied <hi type="italic">out of their own hearts,</hi> and followed <hi type="italic">their own spirits. Secondly,</hi> That as <hi type="italic">his Father taught him</hi> so he <hi type="italic">spoke these things,</hi> that he was not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">autodidaktos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">self-taught,</hi> but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theodidaktos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">taught of God.</hi> The doctrine he preached was the counterpart of the counsels of God, with which he was intimately acquainted; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kathos edidaxe, tauta lalo</hi></hi>—I speak those things, not only <hi type="italic">which</hi> he taught me, but <hi type="italic">as</hi> he taught me, with the same divine power and authority. <div eID="gen27353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27354" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">When</hi> they should be convinced of this: <hi type="italic">When you have lifted up the Son of man,</hi> lifted him up upon the cross, as the brazen serpent upon the pole (<reference osisRef="John.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>), as the sacrifices under the law (for Christ is the great sacrifice), which, when they were offered, were said to be <hi type="italic">elevated,</hi> or <hi type="italic">lifted up;</hi> hence the burnt-offerings, the most ancient and honourable of all, were called <hi type="italic">elevations</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gnoloth</hi> from <hi type="italic">Gnolah, asendit—he ascended</hi>), and in many other offerings they used the significant ceremony of <hi type="italic">heaving</hi> the sacrifice up, and <hi type="italic">moving</hi> it before the Lord; thus was Christ <hi type="italic">lifted up.</hi> Or the expression denotes that his death was his exaltation. They that put him to death thought thereby for ever to have <hi type="italic">sunk</hi> him and his interest, but it proved to be the advancement of both, <reference osisRef="John.12.24">ch. xii. 24</reference>. When the Son of man was <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> the Son of man was <hi type="italic">glorified.</hi> Christ had called his dying his <hi type="italic">going away;</hi> here he calls it his being lifted <hi type="italic">up;</hi> thus the death of the saints, as it is their departure out of this world, so it is their advancement to a better. Observe, He speaks of those he is now talking with as the <hi type="italic">instruments</hi> of his death: when <hi type="italic">you have lifted up the Son of man;</hi> not that they were to be the <hi type="italic">priests</hi> to offer him up (no, that was his own act, he <hi type="italic">offered up himself</hi>), but they would be his betrayers and murderers; see <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. They <hi type="italic">lifted him up</hi> to the cross, but then he lifted up himself to his Father. Observe with what tenderness and mildness Christ here speaks to those who he certainly knew would put him to death, to teach us not to hate or seek the hurt of any, though we may have reason to think they hate us and seek our hurt. Now, Christ speaks of his death as that which would be a powerful conviction of the infidelity of the Jews. <hi type="italic">When you have lifted up the Son of man, then shall you know</hi> this. And why then? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because careless and unthinking people are often taught the worth of mercies by the want of them, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Luke xvii. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The guilt of their sin in putting Christ to death would so awaken their consciences that they would be put upon serious enquiries after a Saviour, and then would know that Jesus was he who alone could save them. And so it proved, when, being told that with wicked hands they had <hi type="italic">crucified and slain</hi> the Son of God, they cried out, <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> and were made to know assuredly that this Jesus was <hi type="italic">Lord and Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Acts ii. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> There would be such signs and wonders attending his death, and the <hi type="italic">lifting of him up</hi> from death in his resurrection, as would give a stronger proof of his being the Messiah than any that had been yet given: and multitudes were hereby brought to believe that Jesus is the Christ, who had before contradicted and opposed him. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> By the death of Christ the pouring out of the Spirit was purchased, who would convince the world that <hi type="italic">Jesus is he,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.7-John.16.8">ch. xvi. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The judgments which the Jews brought upon themselves, by putting Christ to death, which filled up the measure of their iniquity, were a sensible conviction to the most hardened among them that <hi type="italic">Jesus was he.</hi> Christ had often foretold that desolation as the just punishment of their invincible unbelief, and <hi type="italic">when it came to pass (lo, it did come</hi>) they could not but know that the great <hi type="italic">prophet had been among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.33">Ezek. xxxiii. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen27354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27355" type="x-p"/> [3.] What supported our Lord Jesus in the mean time (<reference osisRef="John.8.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that sent me is with me,</hi> in my whole undertaking; <hi type="italic">for the Father</hi> (the fountain and first spring of this affair, from whom as its great cause and author it is derived) <hi type="italic">hath not left me alone,</hi> to manage it myself, hath not deserted the business nor me in the prosecution of it, for <hi type="italic">do I always those things that please him.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen27355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27356" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The assurance which Christ had of his Father's <hi type="italic">presence</hi> with him, which includes both a divine <hi type="italic">power</hi> going along with him to <hi type="italic">enable</hi> him for his work, and a divine <hi type="italic">favour</hi> manifested to him to <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> him in it. <hi type="italic">He that sent me is with me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">Ps. lxxxix. 21</reference>. This greatly <hi type="italic">emboldens</hi> our faith in Christ and our reliance upon his word that he had, and knew he had, his Father with him, to <hi type="italic">confirm the word of his servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>. The King of kings accompanied his own ambassador, to attest his mission and assist his management, and <hi type="italic">never left him alone,</hi> either solitary or weak; it also <hi type="italic">aggravated</hi> the wickedness of those that opposed him, and was an intimation to them of the <hi type="italic">premunire</hi> they ran themselves into by resisting him, for thereby they were found <hi type="italic">fighters against God.</hi> How easily soever they might think to crush him and run him down, let them know he had one to back him with whom it is the greatest madness that can be to <hi type="italic">contend.</hi> <div eID="gen27356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27357" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The ground of this assurance: <hi type="italic">For I do always those things that please him.</hi> That is, 1. That great affair in which our Lord Jesus was <hi type="italic">continually</hi> engaged was an affair which the <hi type="italic">Father that sent him</hi> was highly <hi type="italic">well pleased with.</hi> His whole undertaking is called the <hi type="italic">pleasure of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>), because of the counsels of the eternal mind about it, and the complacency of the eternal mind in it. 2. His management of that affair was in nothing <hi type="italic">displeasing</hi> to his Father; in executing his commission he punctually observed all his instructions, and did in nothing vary from them. No mere man since the fall could say such a word as this (for <hi type="italic">in many things we offend all</hi>) but our Lord Jesus never offended his Father in any thing, but, as became him, he <hi type="italic">fulfilled all righteousness.</hi> This was necessary to the validity and value of the sacrifice he was to offer up; for if he had in any thing <hi type="italic">displeased</hi> the Father himself, and so had had any sin of his own to answer for, the Father could not have been pleased with him as a propitiation for our sins; but such a priest and such a sacrifice became us as was perfectly pure and spotless. We may likewise learn hence that God's servants may <hi type="italic">then</hi> expect God's presence with them when they <hi type="italic">choose</hi> and do <hi type="italic">those things that please him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4-Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27358" type="x-p"/> V. Here is the good effect which this discourse of Christ's had upon some of his hearers (<reference osisRef="John.8.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">As he spoke these words many believed on him.</hi> Note, 1. Though multitudes perish in their unbelief, yet there is a remnant according to the election of grace, who <hi type="italic">believe to the saving of the soul.</hi> If Israel, the whole body of the people, <hi type="italic">be not gathered,</hi> yet there are those of them in whom Christ will be <hi type="italic">glorious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa. xlix. 5</reference>. This the apostle insists upon, to reconcile the Jews' rejection with the <hi type="italic">promises made unto their fathers.</hi> There is a remnant, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. 2. The words of Christ, and particularly his <hi type="italic">threatening</hi> words, are made effectual by the grace of God to bring in poor souls to believe in him. When Christ told them that if they <hi type="italic">believed not</hi> they should <hi type="italic">die in their sins,</hi> and never get to heaven, they thought it was time to look about them, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">18</reference>. 3. Sometimes there is a <hi type="italic">wide door opened,</hi> and an <hi type="italic">effectual</hi> one, even where they are <hi type="italic">many adversaries.</hi> Christ will carry on his work, though <hi type="italic">the heathen rage.</hi> The gospel sometimes gains great victories where it meets with great opposition. Let this encourage God's ministers to preach the gospel, though it be with <hi type="italic">much contention,</hi> for they shall not <hi type="italic">labour in vain.</hi> Many may be <hi type="italic">secretly</hi> brought home to God by those endeavours which are openly contradicted and cavilled at by men of corrupt minds. Austin has an affectionate ejaculation in his lecture upon these words: <hi type="italic">Utinam et, me loquenti, multi credant; non in me, sed mecum in eo—I wish that when I speak, many may believe, not on me, but with me on him.</hi>

<div eID="gen27358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27359" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, <hi type="italic">then</hi> are ye my disciples indeed; <hi type="super">32</hi> And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. <hi type="super">33</hi> They answered him, We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free? <hi type="super">34</hi> Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the Son abideth ever. <hi type="super">36</hi> If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed. <hi type="super">37</hi> I know that ye are Abraham's seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you. <div eID="gen27359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> We have in these verses, <div eID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> I. A comfortable doctrine laid down concerning the <hi type="italic">spiritual liberty</hi> of Christ's disciples, intended for the encouragement of <hi type="italic">those</hi> Jews <hi type="italic">that believed.</hi> Christ, knowing that his doctrine began to work upon some of his hearers, and perceiving that virtue had gone out of him, turned his discourse from the proud Pharisees, and addressed himself to those <hi type="italic">weak</hi> believers. When he had denounced wrath against those that were hardened in unbelief, then he spoke comfort to those few feeble <hi type="italic">Jews that believed in him.</hi> See here, <div eID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> 1. How graciously the Lord Jesus looks to those that <hi type="italic">tremble at his word,</hi> and are ready to receive it; he has something to say to those who have hearing ears, and will not pass by those who set themselves in his way, without speaking to them. <div eID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> 2. How carefully he cherishes the beginnings of grace, and meets those that are coming towards him. These <hi type="italic">Jews that believed</hi> were yet but <hi type="italic">weak;</hi> but Christ did not therefore cast them off, for he <hi type="italic">gathers the lambs in his arms.</hi> When faith is in its infancy, he has <hi type="italic">knees</hi> to <hi type="italic">prevent it, breasts</hi> for it to <hi type="italic">suck,</hi> that it may not <hi type="italic">die from the womb.</hi> In what he said to them, we have two things, which he saith to all that should at any time believe:— <div eID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> (1.) The character of a true disciple of Christ: <hi type="italic">If you continue in my word, then are you my disciples indeed.</hi> When they <hi type="italic">believed on him,</hi> as the great prophet, they gave up themselves to be <hi type="italic">his disciples.</hi> Now, at their entrance into his school, he lays down this for a settled rule, that he would own none for his disciples but those that <hi type="italic">continued in his word.</hi> [1.] It is implied that there are many who profess themselves Christ's disciples who are not his <hi type="italic">disciples indeed,</hi> but only in show and name. [2.] It highly concerns those that are not <hi type="italic">strong in faith</hi> to see to it that they be <hi type="italic">sound in the faith,</hi> that, though not disciples of the highest form, they are nevertheless <hi type="italic">disciples indeed.</hi> [3.] Those who seem willing to be Christ's disciples ought to be told that they had as good never come to him, unless they come with a resolution by his grace to abide by him. Let those who have thoughts of covenanting with Christ have no thoughts of reserving a power of revocation. Children are sent to school, and bound apprentices, only for a <hi type="italic">few years;</hi> but those only are Christ's who are willing to be bound to him <hi type="italic">for the term of life.</hi> [4.] Those only that <hi type="italic">continue in Christ's word</hi> shall be accepted as his <hi type="italic">disciples indeed,</hi> that adhere to his word in every instance without partiality, and abide by it to the end without apostasy. It is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">menein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to dwell</hi> in Christ's word, as a man does at home, which is his centre, and rest, and refuge. Our converse with the word and conformity to it must be constant. If we continue disciples to the last, then, and not otherwise, we approve ourselves <hi type="italic">disciples indeed.</hi> <div eID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> (2.) The privilege of a true disciple of Christ. Here are two precious promises made to those who thus approve themselves disciples indeed, <reference osisRef="John.8.32">v. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> [1.] "<hi type="italic">You shall know the truth,</hi> shall know all that truth which it is needful and profitable for you to know, and shall be more confirmed in the belief of it, shall know the certainty of it." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Even those who are true believers, and disciples indeed, yet may be, and are, much in the dark concerning many things which they should know. God's children are but children, and understand and speak as children. Did we not need to be taught, we should not need to be disciples. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a very great privilege to <hi type="italic">know the truth,</hi> to know the particular truths which we are to believe, in their mutual dependences and connections, and the grounds and reasons of our belief,—to know what is truth and what proves it to be so. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a gracious promise of Christ, to all who continue in his word, that they shall know the truth as far as is needful and profitable for them. Christ's scholars are sure to be well taught. <div eID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">The truth shall make you free;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The truth which Christ teaches tends to make men free, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. Justification makes us free from the guilt of sin, by which we were <hi type="italic">bound over</hi> to the judgment of God, and <hi type="italic">bound under</hi> amazing fears; sanctification makes us free from the bondage of corruption, by which we were <hi type="italic">restrained</hi> from that service which is perfect freedom, and <hi type="italic">constrained</hi> to that which is perfect slavery. Gospel truth frees us from the yoke of the ceremonial law, and the more grievous burdens of the traditions of the elders. It makes us <hi type="italic">free from</hi> our spiritual enemies, free <hi type="italic">in</hi> the service of God, free <hi type="italic">to</hi> the privileges of sons, and free <hi type="italic">of</hi> the Jerusalem which is from above, which is free. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The knowing, entertaining, and believing, of this truth does actually <hi type="italic">make us free,</hi> free from prejudices, mistakes, and false notions, than which nothing more <hi type="italic">enslaves</hi> and <hi type="italic">entangles</hi> the soul, free from the dominion of lust and passion; and restores the soul to the government of itself, by reducing it into obedience to its Creator. The mind, by admitting the truth of Christ in the light and power, is vastly enlarged, and has scope and compass given it, is greatly elevated and raised above things of sense, and never acts with so true a liberty as when it acts under a divine command, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2 Cor. iii. 17</reference>. The enemies of Christianity pretend to <hi type="italic">free thinking,</hi> whereas really those are the freest reasonings that are guided by faith, and those are men of <hi type="italic">free thought</hi> whose thoughts are captivated and brought into obedience to Christ. <div eID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> II. The offence which the carnal Jews took at this doctrine, and their objection against it. Though it was a doctrine that brought glad tidings of liberty to the captives, yet they cavilled at it, <reference osisRef="John.8.33">v. 33</reference>. The Pharisees grudged this comfortable word to those that believed, the standers by, who had <hi type="italic">no part nor lot in this matter;</hi> they thought themselves reflected upon and affronted by the gracious charter of liberty granted to those that believed, and therefore with a great deal of pride and envy they answered him, "<hi type="italic">We Jews are Abraham's seed,</hi> and therefore are <hi type="italic">free-born,</hi> and have not lost our birthright-freedom; <hi type="italic">we were never in bondage to any man; how sayest thou then,</hi> to us <hi type="italic">Jews, You shall be made free?</hi>" See here, <div eID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> 1. What it was that they were grieved at; it was an <hi type="italic">innuendo</hi> in those words, <hi type="italic">You shall be made free,</hi> as if the Jewish church and nation were in some sort of bondage, which reflected on the Jews in general, and as if all that did not believe in Christ continued in that bondage, which reflected on the Pharisees in particular. Note, The privileges of the faithful are the envy and vexation of unbelievers, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> 2. What it was that they alleged against it; whereas Christ intimated that they needed to be made free, they urge, (1.) "We are Abraham's seed, and Abraham was a <hi type="italic">prince and a great man;</hi> though we live in Canaan, we are not descended from Canaan, nor under his doom, <hi type="italic">a servant of servants shall he be;</hi> we hold in <hi type="italic">frank-almoign—free alms,</hi> and not in <hi type="italic">villenage—by a servile tenure.</hi>" It is common for a sinking decaying family to boast of the glory and dignity of its ancestors, and to borrow honour from that name to which they repay disgrace; so the Jews here did. But this was not all. Abraham was in covenant with God, and his children by his right, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. Now that covenant, no doubt, was a free charter, and invested them with privileges not consistent with a state of slavery, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. And therefore they thought they had no occasion with so <hi type="italic">great a sum</hi> as they reckoned faith in Christ to be <hi type="italic">to obtain this freedom,</hi> when they were thus free-born. Note, It is the common fault and folly of those that have pious parentage and education to trust to their privilege and boast of it, as if it would atone for the want of real holiness. They were Abraham's seed, but what would this avail them, when we find one in hell that could call Abraham father? Saving benefits are not, like common privileges, conveyed by <hi type="italic">entail</hi> to us and our issue, nor can a title to heaven be made by <hi type="italic">descent,</hi> nor may we claim as <hi type="italic">heirs at law,</hi> by making out our pedigree; our title is purely by purchase, not our own but our Redeemer's for us, under certain provisos and limitations, which if we do not observe it will not avail us to be Abraham's seed. Thus many, when they are pressed with the necessity of regeneration, turn it off with this, <hi type="italic">We are the church's children;</hi> but they are not all Israel that are of Israel. (2.) <hi type="italic">We were never in bondage to any man.</hi> Now observe, [1.] How false this allegation was. I wonder how they could have the assurance to say a thing in the face of a congregation which was so notoriously <hi type="italic">untrue.</hi> Were not the seed of Abraham in bondage to the Egyptians? Were they not often in bondage to the neighbouring nations in the time of the judges? Were they not seventy years captives in Babylon? Nay, were they not at this time tributaries to the Romans, and, though not in a <hi type="italic">personal,</hi> yet in a <hi type="italic">national</hi> bondage to them, and groaning to be made free? And yet, to confront Christ, they have the impudence to say, <hi type="italic">We were never in bondage.</hi> Thus they would expose Christ to the ill-will both of the Jews, who were very jealous for the honour of their liberty, and of the Romans, who would not be thought to enslave the nations they conquered. [2.] How foolish the application was. Christ had spoken of a liberty wherewith the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> would make them free, which must be meant of a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> liberty, for truth as it is the <hi type="italic">enriching,</hi> so it is the <hi type="italic">enfranchising</hi> of the mind, and the <hi type="italic">enlarging</hi> of that from the captivity of error and prejudice; and yet they plead against the offer of <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> liberty that they were never in <hi type="italic">corporal</hi> thraldom, as if, because they were never in bondage to any <hi type="italic">man,</hi> they were never in bondage to any <hi type="italic">lust.</hi> Note, Carnal hearts are sensible of no other grievances than those that molest the body and injure their secular affairs. Talk to them of encroachments upon their civil liberty and property,—tell them of waste committed upon their lands, or damage done to their houses,—and they understand you very well, and can give you a sensible answer; the thing touches them and affects them. But discourse to them of the bondage of sin, a captivity to Satan, and a liberty by Christ,—tell them of wrong done to their precious souls, and the hazard of their eternal welfare,—and <hi type="italic">you bring certain strange things to their ears;</hi> they say of it (as those did, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.49">Ezek. xx. 49</reference>), <hi type="italic">Doth he not speak parables?</hi> This was much like the blunder Nicodemus made about being <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> <div eID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27371" type="x-p"/> III. Our Saviour's vindication of his doctrine from these objections, and the further explication of it, <reference osisRef="John.8.34-John.8.37">v. 34-37</reference>, where he does these four things:— <div eID="gen27371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27372" type="x-p"/> 1. He shows that, notwithstanding their civil liberties and their visible church-membership, yet it was possible that they might be in a state of bondage (<reference osisRef="John.8.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whosoever commits sin,</hi> though he be of Abraham's seed, and was never in bondage to any man, is the servant of sin. Observe, Christ does not upbraid them with the falsehood of their plea, or their present bondage, but further explains what he had said for their edification. Thus ministers should with meekness instruct those that oppose them, that they may <hi type="italic">recover themselves,</hi> not with passion provoke them to entangle themselves yet more. Now here, <div eID="gen27372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27373" type="x-p"/> (1.) The preface is very solemn: <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> an awful asseveration, which our Saviour often used, to command a reverent attention and a ready assent. The style of the prophets was, <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord,</hi> for they were <hi type="italic">faithful as servants;</hi> but Christ, being a Son, speaks in his own name: <hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> I the <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> the faithful witness; he pawns his veracity upon it. "I say it to you, who boast of your relation to Abraham, as if that would save you." <div eID="gen27373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27374" type="x-p"/> (2.) The truth is of universal concern, though here delivered upon a particular occasion: <hi type="italic">Whosoever commits sin is the servant of sin,</hi> and sadly needs to be made free. A state of sin is a state of bondage. [1.] See who it is on whom this brand is fastened—on him that <hi type="italic">commits sin,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pas ho poion hamartian</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">every one that makes sin.</hi> There is not a <hi type="italic">just man</hi> upon earth, that <hi type="italic">lives, and sins not;</hi> yet every one that sins is not a servant of sin, for then God would have no servants; but he that <hi type="italic">makes sin,</hi> that <hi type="italic">makes choice</hi> of sin, prefers the way of wickedness before the way of holiness (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.16-Jer.44.17">Jer. xliv. 16, 17</reference>),—that <hi type="italic">makes a covenant</hi> with sin, enters into league with it, and <hi type="italic">makes a marriage</hi> with it,—that <hi type="italic">makes contrivances</hi> of sin, <hi type="italic">makes provision</hi> for the flesh, and devises iniquity,—and that <hi type="italic">makes a custom</hi> of sin, who walks after the flesh, and <hi type="italic">makes a trade</hi> of sin. [2.] See what the brand is which Christ fastens upon those that thus <hi type="italic">commit sin.</hi> He stigmatizes them, gives them a mark of servitude. They are <hi type="italic">servants of sin,</hi> imprisoned under the guilt of sin, under an arrest, in hold for it, <hi type="italic">concluded under sin,</hi> and they are subject to the power of sin. He is a <hi type="italic">servant of sin,</hi> that is, he makes himself so, and is so accounted; he has <hi type="italic">sold himself to work wickedness;</hi> his lusts give law to him, he is at their beck, and is not his own master. He does the work of sin, supports its interest, and accepts its wages, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.16">Rom. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27375" type="x-p"/> 2. He shows them that, being in a state of bondage, their having a place in the house of God would not entitle them to the inheritance of sons; for (<reference osisRef="John.8.35">v. 35</reference>) <hi type="italic">the servant,</hi> though he be in the house for awhile, yet, being but a <hi type="italic">servant, abideth not in the house for ever.</hi> Services (we say) are no inheritances, they are but <hi type="italic">temporary,</hi> and not for a <hi type="italic">perpetuity; but the son</hi> of the family abideth ever. Now, (1.) This points primarily at the rejection of the Jewish church and nation. Israel had been <hi type="italic">God's son,</hi> his <hi type="italic">first-born;</hi> but they wretchedly degenerated into a <hi type="italic">servile</hi> disposition, were enslaved to the world and the flesh, and therefore, though by virtue of their birthright they thought themselves secure of their church membership, Christ tells them that having thus made themselves servants they should not <hi type="italic">abide in the house for ever.</hi> Jerusalem, by opposing the gospel of Christ, which proclaimed liberty, and adhering to the Sinai-covenant, which gendered to bondage, after its term was <hi type="italic">expired</hi> came to be <hi type="italic">in bondage with her children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.24-Gal.4.25">Gal. iv. 24, 25</reference>), and therefore was unchurched and disfranchised, her charter seized and taken away, and she was cast out as the son of the bond-woman, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.14">Gen. xxi. 14</reference>. Chrysostom gives this sense of this place: "Think not to be made free from sin by the rites and ceremonies of the law of Moses, for Moses was but a servant, and had not that perpetual authority in the church which the Son had; but, if the Son make you free, it is well," <reference osisRef="John.8.36">v. 36</reference>. But, (2.) It looks further, to the rejection of all that are the <hi type="italic">servants of sin,</hi> and receive not the <hi type="italic">adoption</hi> of the <hi type="italic">sons of God;</hi> though those unprofitable servants may be in God's house awhile, as retainers to his family, yet there is a day coming when the children of the <hi type="italic">bond-woman</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">free</hi> shall be distinguished. True believers only, who are the children of the promise and of the covenant, are accounted free, and shall abide for ever in the house, as Isaac: they shall have a <hi type="italic">nail</hi> in the holy place on earth (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>) and <hi type="italic">mansions</hi> in the holy place in heaven, <reference osisRef="John.14.2">ch. xiv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27376" type="x-p"/> 3. He shows them the way of deliverance out of the state of bondage into the <hi type="italic">glorious liberty of the children of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Rom. viii. 21</reference>. The case of those that are the servants of sin is sad, but thanks be to God it is not helpless, it is not hopeless. As it is the privilege of all the sons of the family, and their dignity above the servants, that they abide in the house for ever; so he who is <hi type="italic">the Son,</hi> the first-born among many brethren, and the heir of all things, has a power both of manumission and of adoption (<reference osisRef="John.8.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed.</hi> Note, <div eID="gen27376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27377" type="x-p"/> (1.) Jesus Christ in the gospel offers us <hi type="italic">our freedom;</hi> he has authority and power to <hi type="italic">make free.</hi> [1.] To <hi type="italic">discharge prisoners;</hi> this he does <hi type="italic">in justification,</hi> by making satisfaction for <hi type="italic">our guilt</hi> (on which the gospel offer is grounded, which is to all a conditional <hi type="italic">act of indemnity,</hi> and to all true believers, upon their believing, an absolute <hi type="italic">charter of pardon</hi>), and for <hi type="italic">our debts,</hi> for which we were by the law arrested and in execution. Christ, as our surety, or rather our <hi type="italic">bail</hi> (for he was not originally bound <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> but upon our insolvency bound <hi type="italic">for us</hi>), compounds with the creditor, answers the demands of injured justice with more than an <hi type="italic">equivalent,</hi> takes the <hi type="italic">bond</hi> and <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> into his own hands, and gives them up <hi type="italic">cancelled</hi> to all that by faith and repentance give him (if I may so say) a <hi type="italic">counter-security</hi> to save his honour harmless, and so they are <hi type="italic">made free;</hi> and from the debt, and every part thereof, they are for ever acquitted, exonerated, and discharged, and a general release is sealed of all actions and claims; while against those who refuse to come up to these terms the securities lie still in the Redeemer's hands, in full force. [2.] He has a power to rescue <hi type="italic">bond-slaves,</hi> and this he does in <hi type="italic">sanctification;</hi> by the powerful arguments of his gospel, and the powerful operations of his Spirit, he breaks the power of corruption in the soul, rallies the scattered forces of reason and virtue, and fortifies God's interest against sin and Satan, and so the soul is made free. [3.] He has a power to <hi type="italic">naturalize strangers and foreigners,</hi> and this he does in <hi type="italic">adoption.</hi> This is a further act of grace; we are not only forgiven and healed, but <hi type="italic">preferred;</hi> there is a charter of privileges as well as pardon; and thus the Son makes us free <hi type="italic">denizens</hi> of the kingdom of priests, the holy nation, the new Jerusalem. <div eID="gen27377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27378" type="x-p"/> (2.) Those whom Christ makes free are <hi type="italic">free indeed.</hi> It is not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alethos</hi></hi>, the word used (<reference osisRef="John.8.31">v. 31</reference>) for disciples <hi type="italic">indeed, but</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ontos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">really.</hi> It denotes, [1.] The truth and certainty of the promise, the liberty which the Jews boasted of was an <hi type="italic">imaginary</hi> liberty; they boasted of a <hi type="italic">false gift;</hi> but the liberty which Christ gives is a certain thing, it is real, and has real effects. The servants of sin promise themselves liberty, and fancy themselves free, when they have broken religion's bands asunder; but they cheat themselves. None are <hi type="italic">free indeed</hi> but those whom Christ <hi type="italic">makes free.</hi> [2.] It denotes the singular excellency of the freedom promised; it is a freedom that deserves the name, in comparison with which all other liberties are no better than slaveries, so much does it turn to the honour and advantage of those that are <hi type="italic">made free</hi> by it. It is a <hi type="italic">glorious</hi> liberty. It is that which <hi type="italic">is</hi> (so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ontos</hi></hi> signifies); it is <hi type="italic">substance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>); while the things of the world are shadows, things that <hi type="italic">are not.</hi> <div eID="gen27378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27379" type="x-p"/> 4. He applies this to these unbelieving cavilling Jews, in answer to their boasts of relation to Abraham (<reference osisRef="John.8.37">v. 37</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I know</hi> very well <hi type="italic">that you are Abraham's seed, but now you seek to kill me,</hi> and therefore have forfeited the honour of your relation to Abraham, <hi type="italic">because my word hath no place in you.</hi>" Observe here, <div eID="gen27379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27380" type="x-p"/> (1.) The dignity of their extraction admitted: "<hi type="italic">I know that you are Abraham's seed,</hi> every one knows it, and it is your honour." He grants them what was true, and in what they said that was false (that they were <hi type="italic">never</hi> in bondage to any) he does not <hi type="italic">contradict</hi> them, for he studied to <hi type="italic">profit</hi> them, and not to <hi type="italic">provoke</hi> them, and therefore said that which would please them: <hi type="italic">I know that you are Abraham's seed.</hi> They boasted of their descent from <hi type="italic">Abraham,</hi> as that which <hi type="italic">aggrandized</hi> their names, and made them exceedingly honourable; whereas really it did but <hi type="italic">aggravate</hi> their crimes, and make them exceedingly sinful. Out of their own mouths will he judge vain-glorious hypocrites, who boast of their parentage and education: "Are you Abraham's seed? Why then did you not tread in the steps of his faith and obedience?" <div eID="gen27380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27381" type="x-p"/> (2.) The inconsistency of their practice with this dignity: <hi type="italic">But you seek to kill me.</hi> They had attempted it several times, and were now designing it, which quickly appeared (<reference osisRef="John.8.59">v. 59</reference>), when they <hi type="italic">took up stones to cast at him.</hi> Christ knows all the wickedness, not only which men do, but which they seek, and design, and endeavour to do. To seek to kill any innocent man is a crime black enough, but to <hi type="italic">compass and imagine</hi> the death of him that was King of kings was a crime the heinousness of which we want words to express. <div eID="gen27381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27382" type="x-p"/> (3.) The reason of this inconsistency. Why were they that were Abraham's seed so very inveterate against Abraham's promised seed, in whom they and <hi type="italic">all the families of the earth</hi> should be <hi type="italic">blessed?</hi> Our Saviour here tells them, It is because <hi type="italic">my word hath no place in you,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou chorei en hymin</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">Non capit in vobis,</hi> so the Vulgate. "My word <hi type="italic">does not take with you,</hi> you have no inclination to it, no relish of it, other things are more taking, more pleasing." Or, "It does not <hi type="italic">take hold of you,</hi> it has no power over you, makes no impression upon you." Some of the critics read it, <hi type="italic">My word does not penetrate into you;</hi> it descended as the rain, but it came upon them as the rain upon the rock, which it runs off, and did not soak into their hearts, as the rain upon the ploughed ground. The Syriac reads it, "<hi type="italic">Because you do not acquiesce in my word;</hi> you are not persuaded of the truth of it, nor pleased with the goodness of it." Our translation is very significant: <hi type="italic">It has no place in you.</hi> They <hi type="italic">sought to kill him,</hi> and so effectually to <hi type="italic">silence</hi> him, not because he had done they any harm, but because they could not bear the convincing, commanding power of his word. Note, [1.] The words of Christ ought to have a place in us, the innermost and uppermost place,—a <hi type="italic">dwelling</hi> place, as a man at home, and not as a stranger or sojourner,—a <hi type="italic">working</hi> place; it must have room to operate, to work sin out of us, and to work grace in us; it must have a <hi type="italic">ruling</hi> place, its place must be <hi type="italic">upon the throne,</hi> it must dwell in us richly. [2.] There are many that make a profession of religion in whom <hi type="italic">the word of</hi> Christ has no place; they will not <hi type="italic">allow</hi> it a place, for they do not like it; Satan does all he can to <hi type="italic">displace</hi> it; and other things possess the place it should have in us. [3.] Where the word of God has no place no good is to be expected, for room is left there for all wickedness. If the unclean spirit find the heart empty of Christ's word, he <hi type="italic">enters in, and dwells there.</hi>

<div eID="gen27382" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27383" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> I speak that which I have seen with my Father: and ye do that which ye have seen with your father. <hi type="super">39</hi> They answered and said unto him, Abraham is our father. Jesus saith unto them, If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham. <hi type="super">40</hi> But now ye seek to kill me, a man that hath told you the truth, which I have heard of God: this did not Abraham. <hi type="super">41</hi> Ye do the deeds of your father. Then said they to him, We be not born of fornication; we have one Father, <hi type="italic">even</hi> God. <hi type="super">42</hi> Jesus said unto them, If God were your Father, ye would love me: for I proceeded forth and came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me. <hi type="super">43</hi> Why do ye not understand my speech? <hi type="italic">even</hi> because ye cannot hear my word. 44 Ye are of <hi type="italic">your</hi> father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it. <hi type="super">45</hi> And because I tell <hi type="italic">you</hi> the truth, ye believe me not. <hi type="super">46</hi> Which of you convinceth me of sin? And if I say the truth, why do ye not believe me? <hi type="super">47</hi> He that is of God heareth God's words: ye therefore hear <hi type="italic">them</hi> not, because ye are not of God. <div eID="gen27383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27384" type="x-p"/> Here Christ and the Jews are still at issue; he sets himself to convince and convert them, while they still set themselves to contradict and oppose him. <div eID="gen27384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27385" type="x-p"/> I.
