He here traces the difference between his sentiments and theirs to a different rise and origin (<reference osisRef="John.8.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">I speak that which I have seen with my Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">you</hi> do <hi type="italic">what you have seen with your father.</hi> Here are two fathers spoken of, according to the two families into which the sons of men are divided—God and the devil, and without controversy these are contrary the one to the other. <div eID="gen27385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27386" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> was from <hi type="italic">heaven;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">copied</hi> out of the <hi type="italic">counsels</hi> of infinite wisdom, and the kind intentions of eternal love. (1.) <hi type="italic">I speak that which I have seen.</hi> The discoveries Christ has made to us of God and another world are not grounded upon guess and hearsay, but upon ocular inspection; so that he was thoroughly <hi type="italic">apprized</hi> of the nature, and <hi type="italic">assured</hi> of the truth, of all he said. He that is given to be a witness to the people is an eye-witness, and therefore unexceptionable. (2.) It is what I have seen <hi type="italic">with my Father.</hi> The doctrine of Christ is not a plausible hypothesis, supported by probable arguments, but it is an exact counterpart of the incontestable truths lodged in the eternal mind. It was not only what he had <hi type="italic">heard from</hi> his Father, but what he had <hi type="italic">seen with him</hi> when <hi type="italic">the counsel of peace was between them both.</hi> Moses spoke what he heard from God, but he might not see the face of God; Paul had been in the third heaven, but what he had seen there he could not, he must not, utter; for it was Christ's prerogative to have <hi type="italic">seen</hi> what he <hi type="italic">spoke,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> what he had <hi type="italic">seen.</hi> <div eID="gen27386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27387" type="x-p"/> 2. Their <hi type="italic">doings</hi> were from hell: "<hi type="italic">You do that which you have seen with your father.</hi> You do, by your own works, father yourselves, for it is evident whom you resemble, and therefore easy to find out your origin." As a child that is trained up with his father learns his father's words and fashions, and grows like him by an affected imitation as well as by a natural image, so these Jews, by their malicious opposition to Christ and the gospel, made themselves as like the devil as if they had industriously set him before them for their pattern. <div eID="gen27387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> II. He takes off and answers their vain-glorious boasts of relation to Abraham and to God as their fathers, and shows the vanity and falsehood of their pretensions. <div eID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27389" type="x-p"/> 1. They pleaded relation to Abraham, and he replies to this plea. <hi type="italic">They said, Abraham is our father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.39">v. 39</reference>. In this they intended, (1.) To do honour to themselves, and to make themselves look great. They had forgotten the mortification given them by that acknowledgement prescribed them (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deut. xxvi. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">A Syrian ready to perish was my father;</hi> and the charge exhibited against their degenerate ancestors (whose steps they trod in, and not those of the first founder of the family), <hi type="italic">Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother a Hittite,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.3">Ezek. xvi. 3</reference>. As it is common for those families that are sinking and going to decay to boast most of their pedigree, so it is common for those churches that are corrupt and depraved to value themselves upon their antiquity and the eminence of their first planters. <hi type="italic">Fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium—We have been Trojans, and there once was Troy.</hi> (2.) They designed to cast an odium upon Christ as if he reflected upon the patriarch Abraham, in speaking of their father as one they had learned evil from. See how they sought an occasion to quarrel with him. Now Christ overthrows this plea, and exposes the vanity of it by a plain and cogent argument: "Abraham's children will do the works of Abraham, but you do not do Abraham's works, therefore you are not Abraham's children." <div eID="gen27389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> [1.] The proposition is plain: "<hi type="italic">If you were Abraham's children,</hi> such children of Abraham as could claim an interest in the covenant made with him and his seed, which would indeed put an honour upon you, then you would <hi type="italic">do the works of Abraham,</hi> for to those only of Abraham's house who <hi type="italic">kept the way of the Lord,</hi> as Abraham did, would God <hi type="italic">perform what he had spoken,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>. Those only are reckoned the seed of Abraham, to whom the promise belongs, who <hi type="italic">tread in the steps</hi> of his faith and obedience, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.12">Rom. iv. 12</reference>. Though the Jews had their genealogies, and kept them exact, yet they could not by them make out their relation to Abraham, so as to take the benefit of the old entail (<hi type="italic">performam doni—according to the form of the gift</hi>), unless they walked in the same spirit; good women's relation to Sarah is proved only by this—<hi type="italic">whose daughters you are as long as you do well,</hi> and no longer, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">1 Pet. iii. 6</reference>. Note, Those who would approve themselves Abraham's seed must not only be of Abraham's faith, but do Abraham's works (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.21-Jas.2.22">James ii. 21, 22</reference>),—must come at God's call, as he did,—must resign their dearest comforts to him,—must be strangers and sojourners in this world,—must keep up the worship of God in their families, and always walk before God in their uprightness; for these were the works of Abraham. <div eID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> [2.] The assumption is evident likewise: <hi type="italic">But you do not do</hi> the works of Abraham, for <hi type="italic">you seek to kill me, a man that has told you the truth, which I have heard of God; this did not Abraham,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.40">v. 40</reference>. <div eID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He shows them what their work was, their present work, which they were now about; they <hi type="italic">sought to kill him;</hi> and three things are intimated as an aggravation of their intention:—1. They were so <hi type="italic">unnatural</hi> as to seek the life of <hi type="italic">a man,</hi> a man like themselves, bone of their bone, and flesh of their flesh, who had done them no harm, nor given them any provocation. You <hi type="italic">imagine mischief against a man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Ps. lxii. 3</reference>. 2. They were so <hi type="italic">ungrateful</hi> as to seek the life of one who had <hi type="italic">told them the truth,</hi> had not only done them no injury, but had done them the greatest kindness that could be; had not only not imposed upon them with a lie, but had instructed them in the most necessary and important truths; <hi type="italic">was he therefore become their enemy?</hi> 3. They were so <hi type="italic">ungodly</hi> as to seek the life of one who told them the truth <hi type="italic">which he had heard from God,</hi> who was a messenger sent from God to them, so that their attempt against him was <hi type="italic">quasi deicidium—an act of malice against God.</hi> This was their work, and they persisted in it. <div eID="gen27392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He shows them that this did not become the children of Abraham; for <hi type="italic">this did not Abraham.</hi> 1. "He did nothing like this." He was famous for his humanity, witness his rescue of the captives; and for his piety, witness his obedience to the heavenly vision in many instances, and some tender ones. Abraham believed God; they were obstinate in unbelief: Abraham followed God; they fought against him; so that he would be <hi type="italic">ignorant of them, and would not acknowledge them,</hi> they were so unlike him, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.16">Isa. lxiii. 16</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.17">Jer. xxii. 15-17</reference>. 2. "He would not have done thus if he had lived now, or I had lived then." <hi type="italic">Hoc Abraham non fecisset—He would not have done this;</hi> so some read it. We should thus reason ourselves out of any way of wickedness; would Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob have done so? We cannot expect to be <hi type="italic">ever with them,</hi> if we be <hi type="italic">never like them.</hi> <div eID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> [3.] The conclusion follows of course (<reference osisRef="John.8.41">v. 41</reference>): "Whatever your boasts and pretensions be, you are not Abraham's children, but father yourselves upon another family (<reference osisRef="John.8.41">v. 41</reference>); there is <hi type="italic">a father whose deeds you do,</hi> whose spirit you are of, and whom you resemble." He does not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> say plainly that he means the devil, till they by their continued cavils forced him so to explain himself, which teaches us to treat even bad men with civility and respect, and not to be forward to say that <hi type="italic">of</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">to</hi> them, which, though <hi type="italic">true,</hi> sounds <hi type="italic">harsh.</hi> He tried whether they would suffer their own consciences to infer from what he said that they were the devil's children; and it is better to hear it from them now that we are called to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> that is, to change our father and change our family, by changing our spirit and way, than to hear it from Christ in the great day. <div eID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27395" type="x-p"/> 2. So far were they from owning their unworthiness of relation to Abraham that they pleaded relation to God himself as their Father: "We are <hi type="italic">not born of fornication,</hi> we are not bastards, but legitimate sons; <hi type="italic">we have one Father, even God.</hi>" <div eID="gen27395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27396" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some understand this literally. They were not the sons of the bondwoman, as the Ishmaelites were; nor begotten in incest, as the Moabites and Ammonites were (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>); nor were they a spurious brood in Abraham's family, but Hebrews of the Hebrews; and, being born in <hi type="italic">lawful</hi> wedlock, they might call God <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> who instituted that honourable estate in innocency; for a legitimate seed, not tainted with divorces nor the plurality of wives, is called a <hi type="italic">seed of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.15">Mal. ii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen27396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27397" type="x-p"/> (2.) Others take it figuratively. They begin to be aware now that Christ spoke of a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> not a <hi type="italic">carnal</hi> father, of the father of their religion; and so, <div eID="gen27397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27398" type="x-p"/> [1.] They deny themselves to be a generation of idolaters: "We are <hi type="italic">not born of fornication,</hi> are not the children of idolatrous parents, nor have been bred up in idolatrous worships." Idolatry is often spoken of as spiritual <hi type="italic">whoredom,</hi> and idolaters as <hi type="italic">children of whoredoms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.4">Hosea ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3">Isa. lvii. 3</reference>. Now, if they meant that they were not the posterity of idolaters, the allegation was false, for no nation was more addicted to idolatry than the Jews before the captivity; if they meant no more than that they themselves were not idolaters, what then? A man may be free from idolatry, and yet perish in another iniquity, and be shut out of Abraham's covenant. <hi type="italic">If thou commit no idolatry</hi> (apply it to this spiritual fornication), yet if thou kill thou art become a <hi type="italic">transgressor</hi> of the covenant. A rebellious prodigal son will be disinherited, though he be not <hi type="italic">born of fornication.</hi> <div eID="gen27398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27399" type="x-p"/> [2.] They boast themselves to be true worshippers of the true God. We have not many fathers, as the heathens had, <hi type="italic">gods many and lords many,</hi> and yet were without God, as <hi type="italic">filius populi—a son of the people,</hi> has many fathers and yet none certain; no, <hi type="italic">the Lord our God is one Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">one Father,</hi> and therefore it is well with us. Note, Those flatter themselves, and put a damning cheat upon their own souls, who imagine that their professing the true religion and worshipping the true God will save them, though they worship not God in spirit and in truth, nor are true to their profession. Now our Saviour gives a full answer to this fallacious plea (<reference osisRef="John.8.42-John.8.43">v. 42, 43</reference>), and proves, by two arguments, that they had no right to call God Father. <div eID="gen27399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27400" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They did not love Christ: <hi type="italic">If God were your Father, you would love me.</hi> He had disproved their relation to Abraham by their going about to kill him (<reference osisRef="John.8.40">v. 40</reference>), but here he disproves their relation to God by their not loving and owning him. A man may pass for a <hi type="italic">child</hi> of Abraham if he do not appear an enemy to Christ by gross sin; but he cannot approve himself a child of God unless he be a faithful friend and follower of Christ. Note, All that have God for their Father have a true love to Jesus Christ, and esteem of his person, a grateful sense of his love, a sincere affection to his cause and kingdom, a complacency in the salvation wrought out by him and in the method and terms of it, and a care to keep his commandments, which is the surest evidence of our love to him. We are here in a state of probation, upon our trial how we will conduct ourselves towards our Maker, and accordingly it will be with us in the state of retribution. God has taken various methods to prove us, and this was one: he sent his Son into the world, with sufficient proofs of his sonship and mission, concluding that all that called him Father would <hi type="italic">kiss his Son,</hi> and bid <hi type="italic">him</hi> welcome who was the first-born among many brethren; see <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1 John v. 1</reference>. By this our adoption will be proved or disproved—Did we love Christ, or no? <hi type="italic">If any man do not,</hi> he is so far from being a child of God that he is <hi type="italic">anathema,</hi> accursed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1 Cor. xvi. 22</reference>. Now our Saviour proves that if they were God's children they would <hi type="italic">love him;</hi> for, saith he, I proceeded <hi type="italic">forth and came from God.</hi> They will love him; for, 1. He was the <hi type="italic">Son of God: I proceeded forth from God.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Exelthon</hi></hi> this means his divine <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exeleusis</hi></hi>, or origin from the Father, by the communication of the divine essence, and also the union of the divine <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos</hi></hi> to his human nature; so Dr. Whitby. Now this could not but recommend him to the affections of all that were <hi type="italic">born of God.</hi> Christ is called the <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> because, being the beloved of the Father, he is certainly the beloved of all the saints, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>. 2. He was <hi type="italic">sent of God,</hi> came from him as an ambassador to the world of mankind. He did not <hi type="italic">come of himself,</hi> as the false prophets, who had not either their <hi type="italic">mission</hi> or their <hi type="italic">message</hi> from God, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jer. xxiii. 21</reference>. Observe the emphasis he lays upon this: <hi type="italic">I came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me.</hi> He had both his credentials and his instructions from God; he came to <hi type="italic">gather together in one the children of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.51">ch. xi. 51</reference>), to bring <hi type="italic">many sons to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. And would not all God's children embrace with both arms a messenger sent from their Father on <hi type="italic">such</hi> errands? But these Jews made it appear that they were nothing akin to God, by their want of affection to Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen27400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They did not understand him. It was a sign they did not belong to God's family that they did not understand the language and dialect of the family: <hi type="italic">You do not understand my speech</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.43">v. 43</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten lalian ten emen</hi></hi>. Christ's speech was divine and heavenly, but intelligible enough to those that were acquainted with the voice of Christ in the Old Testament. Those that had made the word of the Creator familiar to them needed no other key to the dialect of the Redeemer; and yet these Jews make strange of the doctrine of Christ, and find knots in it, and I know not what stumbling stones. Could a Galilean be known by his speech? An Ephraimite by his <hi type="italic">sibboleth?</hi> And would any have the confidence to call God Father to whom the Son of God was a barbarian, even when he spoke the will of God in the words of the Spirit of God? Note, Those who are not acquainted with the divine speech have reason to fear that they are strangers to the divine nature. Christ spoke the words of God (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">ch. iii. 34</reference>) in the dialect of the kingdom of God; and yet they, who pretended to belong to the kingdom, understood not the idioms and properties of it, but like strangers, and rude ones too, ridiculed it. And the reason why they did not understand Christ's speech made the matter much worse: <hi type="italic">Even because you cannot hear my word,</hi> that is, "You cannot persuade yourselves to hear it attentively, impartially, and without prejudice, as it should be heard." The meaning of this <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> is an obstinate <hi type="italic">will not;</hi> as the Jews could not hear Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Acts vii. 57</reference>) nor Paul, <reference osisRef="Acts.23.22">Acts xxiii. 22</reference>. Note, The rooted antipathy of men's corrupt hearts to the doctrine of Christ is the true reason of their ignorance of it, and of their errors and mistakes about it. They do not like it nor love it, and therefore they will not understand it; like Peter, who pretended he <hi type="italic">knew not what the damsel said</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.70">Matt. xxvi. 70</reference>), when in truth he knew not what to say to it. <hi type="italic">You cannot hear my words,</hi> for you have <hi type="italic">stopped your ears</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4-Ps.58.5">Ps. lviii. 4, 5</reference>), and God, in a way of righteous judgment, <hi type="italic">has made your ears heavy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa. vi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27402" type="x-p"/> III. Having thus disproved their relation both to Abraham and to God, he comes next to tell them plainly whose children they were: <hi type="italic">You are of your father the devil,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.44">v. 44</reference>. If they were not God's children, they were the devil's, for God and Satan divide the world of mankind; the devil is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> said to <hi type="italic">work in the children of disobedience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>. All wicked people are the devil's children, <hi type="italic">children of Belial</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2 Cor. vi. 15</reference>), the serpent's seed (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>), children of the wicked one, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Matt. xiii. 38</reference>. They partake of his nature, bear his image, obey his commands, and follow his example. Idolaters <hi type="italic">said to a stock, Thou art our father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jer. ii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27403" type="x-p"/> This is a high charge, and sounds very harsh and horrid, that any of the children of men, especially the church's children, should be called <hi type="italic">children of the devil,</hi> and therefore our Saviour fully proves it. <div eID="gen27403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27404" type="x-p"/> 1. By a general argument: <hi type="italic">The lusts of your father you will do,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">thelete poiein</hi></hi>. (1.) "You <hi type="italic">do</hi> the devil's lusts, the lusts which he would have you to fulfil; you gratify and please him, and comply with his temptation, and are <hi type="italic">led captive by him at his will:</hi> nay, you do those lusts which the devil himself fulfils." Fleshly lusts and worldly lusts the devil tempts men to; but, being a spirit, he cannot fulfil them himself. The peculiar lusts of the devil are <hi type="italic">spiritual wickedness;</hi> the lusts of the intellectual powers, and their corrupt reasonings; pride and envy, and wrath and malice; enmity to that which is good, and enticing others to that which is evil; these are lusts which the devil fulfils, and those who are under the dominion of these lusts resemble the devil, as the child does the parent. The more there is of contemplation, and contrivance, and secret complacency, in sin, the more it resembles the <hi type="italic">lusts of the devil.</hi> (2.) You <hi type="italic">will do</hi> the devil's lusts. The more there is of the <hi type="italic">will</hi> in these lusts, the more there is of the devil in them. When sin is committed <hi type="italic">of choice</hi> and not by surprise, with <hi type="italic">pleasure</hi> and not with reluctancy, when it is persisted in with a daring presumption and a desperate resolution, like theirs that said, <hi type="italic">We have loved strangers and after them we will go,</hi> then the sinner <hi type="italic">will</hi> do the devil's lusts. "The lusts of your father you <hi type="italic">delight to do;</hi>" so Dr. Hammond; they are rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel. <div eID="gen27404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27405" type="x-p"/> 2. By two particular instances, wherein they manifestly resembled the devil—<hi type="italic">murder</hi> and <hi type="italic">lying.</hi> The devil is an enemy to life, because God is the God of life and life is the happiness of man; and an enemy to truth, because God is the God of truth and truth is the bond of human society. <div eID="gen27405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> (1.) He was <hi type="italic">a murderer from the beginning,</hi> not from his own beginning, for he was created an angel of light, and had a first estate which was pure and good, but from the beginning of his apostasy, which was soon after the creation of man. He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anthropoktonos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">homicida, a man-slayer.</hi> [1.] He was a <hi type="italic">hater of man,</hi> and so in affection an disposition a murderer of him. He has his name, <hi type="italic">Satan,</hi> from <hi type="italic">sitnah—hatred.</hi> He maligned God's image upon man, envied his happiness, and earnestly desired his ruin, was an avowed enemy to the whole race. [2.] He was man's tempter to <hi type="italic">that</hi> sin which brought death into the world, and so he was effectually the murderer of all mankind, which in Adam had but <hi type="italic">one neck.</hi> He was a murderer of souls, <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> them into sin, and by it <hi type="italic">slew them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">Rom. vii. 11</reference>), poisoned man with the forbidden fruit, and, to aggravate the matter, made him his own murderer. Thus he was not only <hi type="italic">at</hi> the beginning, but <hi type="italic">from</hi> the beginning, which intimates that thus he <hi type="italic">has been</hi> ever since; as he began, so he continues, the murderer of men by his temptations. The great tempter is the great destroyer. The Jews called the devil <hi type="italic">the angel of death.</hi> [3.] He was the first wheel in the first murder that ever was committed by Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother, <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1 John iii. 12</reference>. If the devil had not been very strong in Cain, he could not have done such an unnatural thing as to kill his own brother. Cain killing his brother by the instigation of the devil, the devil is called the <hi type="italic">murderer,</hi> which does not speak Cain's personal guilt the less, but the devil's the more, whose torments, we have reason to think, will be the greater, when the time comes, for all that wickedness into which he has drawn men. See what reason we have to <hi type="italic">stand</hi> upon our guard <hi type="italic">against the wiles of the devil,</hi> and never to hearken to him (for he is a murderer, and certainly aims to do us mischief, even when he <hi type="italic">speaks fair</hi>), and to wonder that he who is the murderer of the children of men should yet be, by their own consent, so much their master. Now herein these Jews were followers of him, and were murderers, like him; murderers of souls, which they led blindfold into the ditch, and made the <hi type="italic">children of hell;</hi> sworn enemies of Christ, and now ready to be his betrayers and murderers, for the same reason that Cain killed Abel. These Jews were that <hi type="italic">seed of the serpent</hi> that were to <hi type="italic">bruise the heel</hi> of the <hi type="italic">seed of the woman; Now you seek to kill me.</hi> <div eID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was <hi type="italic">a liar.</hi> A lie is opposed to truth (<reference osisRef="1John.2.21">1 John ii. 21</reference>), and accordingly the devil is here described to be, <div eID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27408" type="x-p"/> [1.] An enemy to truth, and therefore to Christ. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is a <hi type="italic">deserter,</hi> from the truth; he <hi type="italic">abode not in the truth,</hi> did not continue in the purity and rectitude of his nature wherein he was created, but left his first state; when he degenerated from goodness, he departed from truth, for his apostasy was founded in a lie. The angels were the <hi type="italic">hosts of the Lord;</hi> those that fell were not <hi type="italic">true</hi> to their commander and sovereign, they were not to be <hi type="italic">trusted,</hi> being charged with folly and defection, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job iv. 18</reference>. By <hi type="italic">the truth</hi> here we may understand the revealed will of God concerning the salvation of man by Jesus Christ, the truth which Christ was now preaching, and which the Jews opposed; herein they did <hi type="italic">like their father the devil,</hi> who, <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> the honour put upon the human nature in the <hi type="italic">first Adam,</hi> and <hi type="italic">foreseeing</hi> the much greater honour intended in the <hi type="italic">second Adam,</hi> would not be reconciled to that counsel of God, nor <hi type="italic">stand in the truth</hi> concerning it, but, from a spirit of pride and envy, set himself to resist it, and to thwart the designs of it; and so did these Jews here, as his children and agents. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">destitute</hi> of the truth: <hi type="italic">There is no truth in him.</hi> His interest in the world is supported by lies and falsehoods, and there is no truth, nothing you can confide in, in him, nor in any thing he says or does. The notions he propagates concerning good and evil are false and erroneous, his proofs are lying wonders, his temptations are all cheats; he has great knowledge of the truth, but having no affection to it, but on the contrary being a sworn enemy to it, he is said to have <hi type="italic">no truth in him.</hi> <div eID="gen27408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27409" type="x-p"/> [2.] He is a friend and patron of lying: <hi type="italic">When he speaketh a lie he speaketh of his own.</hi> Three things are here said of the devil with reference to the sin of lying:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he is <hi type="italic">a liar;</hi> his oracles were lying oracles, his prophets lying prophets, and the images in which he was worshipped <hi type="italic">teachers of lies.</hi> He tempted our first parents with a downright lie. All his temptations are carried on by lies, calling <hi type="italic">evil good and good evil,</hi> and promising impunity in sin; he knows them to be lies, and suggests them with an intention to deceive, and so to destroy. When he now <hi type="italic">contradicted</hi> the gospel, in the scribes and Pharisees, it was by lies; and when afterwards he <hi type="italic">corrupted it,</hi> in the <hi type="italic">man of sin,</hi> it was by strong delusions, and a great complicated lie. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That when he <hi type="italic">speaks a lie</hi> he <hi type="italic">speaks of his own,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek ton idion</hi></hi>. It is the proper <hi type="italic">idiom</hi> of his language; of <hi type="italic">his own,</hi> not of God; his Creator never put it into him. When men speak a lie they borrow it from the devil, <hi type="italic">Satan fills their hearts to lie</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.3">Acts v. 3</reference>); but when the devil speaks a lie the <hi type="italic">model</hi> of it is of his own framing, the motives to it are from himself, which bespeaks the desperate depth of wickedness into which those apostate spirits are sunk; as in their first defection they had no tempter, so their sinfulness is still their own. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That he is the <hi type="italic">father of it,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">autou</hi></hi>. 1. He is the father of every <hi type="italic">lie;</hi> not only of the lies which he himself suggests, but of those which others speak; he is the author and founder of all lies. When men speak lies, they speak from him, and as his mouth; they come originally from him, and bear his image. 2. He is the father of <hi type="italic">every liar;</hi> so it may be understood. God made men with a disposition to truth. It is congruous to reason and natural light, to the order of our faculties and the laws of society, that we should speak truth; but the devil, the author of sin, the spirit that works in the children of disobedience, has so corrupted the nature of man that the wicked are said to be <hi type="italic">estranged from the womb, speaking lies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Ps. lviii. 3</reference>); he has taught them <hi type="italic">with their tongues to use deceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13">Rom. iii. 13</reference>. He is the father of liars, who begat them, who trained them up in the <hi type="italic">way of lying,</hi> whom they resemble and obey, and with whom all <hi type="italic">liars</hi> shall have their portion for ever. <div eID="gen27409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27410" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ, having thus proved all murderers and all liars to be the devil's children, leaves it to the consciences of his hearers to say, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man.</hi> But he comes in the <reference osisRef="John.8.45-John.8.58">following verses</reference> to assist them in the application of it to themselves; he does not call them <hi type="italic">liars,</hi> but shows them that they were <hi type="italic">no friends to truth,</hi> and therein resembled him who <hi type="italic">abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him.</hi> Two things he charges upon them:— <div eID="gen27410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27411" type="x-p"/> 1. That they would not <hi type="italic">believe the word of truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.45">v. 45</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hoti ten aletheian lego, ou pisteuete moi</hi></hi>. <div eID="gen27411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27412" type="x-p"/> (1.) Two ways it may be taken;—[1.] "Though I tell you the truth, yet you will not believe me (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hoti</hi></hi>), <hi type="italic">that I do so.</hi>" Though he gave abundant proof of his commission from God, and his affection to the children of men, yet they would not believe that he told them the truth. Now was <hi type="italic">truth fallen in the street,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.14-Isa.59.15">Isa. lix. 14, 15</reference>. The greatest truths with some gained not the least credit; for they <hi type="italic">rebelled against the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.13">Job xxiv. 13</reference>. Or, [2.] <hi type="italic">Because I tell you the truth</hi> (so we read it) therefore <hi type="italic">you believe me not.</hi> They would not receive him, nor entertain him as a prophet, because he told them some unpleasing truths which they did not care to hear, told them the truth concerning themselves and their own case, showed them their faces in a glass that would not flatter them; therefore they would not believe a word he said. Miserable is the case of those to whom the light of divine truth is become a torment. <div eID="gen27412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27413" type="x-p"/> (2.) Now, to show them the unreasonableness of their infidelity, he condescends to put the matter to this fair issue, <reference osisRef="John.8.46">v. 46</reference>. He and they being contrary, either he was in an error or they were. Now take it either way. <div eID="gen27413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27414" type="x-p"/> [1.] If <hi type="italic">he</hi> were in an error, why did they not convince him? The falsehood of <hi type="italic">pretended</hi> prophets was discovered either by the <hi type="italic">ill tendency</hi> of their doctrines (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.2">Deut. xiii. 2</reference>), or by the <hi type="italic">ill tenour</hi> of their conversation: <hi type="italic">You shall know them by their fruits;</hi> but (saith Christ) <hi type="italic">which of you,</hi> you of the sanhedrim, that take upon you to judge of prophets, <hi type="italic">which of you convinceth me of sin?</hi> They accused him of some of the worst of crimes—gluttony, drunkenness, blasphemy, sabbath-breaking, confederacy with Satan, and what not. But their accusations were malicious groundless calumnies, and such as every one that knew him knew to be <hi type="italic">utterly false.</hi> When they had done their utmost by trick and artifice, subornation and perjury, to prove some crime upon him, the very judge that condemned him owned he <hi type="italic">found no fault in him.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sin</hi> he here challenges them to convict him of is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> An inconsistent doctrine. They had heard his testimony; could they show any thing in it absurd or unworthy to be believed, any contradiction either of himself or of the scriptures, or any corruption of truth or manners insinuated by his doctrine? <reference osisRef="John.18.20">ch. xviii. 20</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> An incongruous conversation: "Which of you can justly charge me with any thing, in word or deed, unbecoming a prophet?" See the wonderful condescension of our Lord Jesus, that he demanded not credit any further than the allowed motives of credibility supported his demands. See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.5 Jer.2.31">Jer. ii. 5, 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mic. vi. 3</reference>. Ministers may hence learn, 1. To <hi type="italic">walk</hi> so <hi type="italic">circumspectly</hi> as that it may not be in the power of their most strict observers to convince them of sin, <hi type="italic">that the ministry be not blamed.</hi> The only way not to be convicted of sin is not to sin. 2. To be willing to <hi type="italic">admit a scrutiny;</hi> though we are confident in many things that we are in the right, yet we should be willing to have it tried whether we be not in the wrong. See <reference osisRef="Job.6.24">Job vi. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen27414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27415" type="x-p"/> [2.] If <hi type="italic">they</hi> were in an error, why were they not convinced by him? "<hi type="italic">If I say the truth, why do you not believe me?</hi> If you cannot convince me of error, you must own that I <hi type="italic">say the truth,</hi> and why do you not then <hi type="italic">give me credit?</hi> Why will you not deal with me upon trust?" Note, If men would but enquire into the reason of their infidelity, and examine why they do not believe that which they cannot gainsay, they would find themselves reduced to such absurdities as they could not but be ashamed of; for it will be found that the reason why we believe not in Jesus Christ is because we are not willing to part with our sins, and deny ourselves, and serve God faithfully; that we are not of the Christian religion, because we would not indeed be of any, and unbelief of our Redeemer resolves itself into a downright rebellion against our Creator. <div eID="gen27415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27416" type="x-p"/> 2. Another thing charged upon them is that they would not hear the words of God (<reference osisRef="John.8.47">v. 47</reference>), which further shows how groundless their claim of relation to God was. Here is, <div eID="gen27416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27417" type="x-p"/> (1.) A doctrine laid down: <hi type="italic">He that is of God heareth God's words;</hi> that is, [1.] He is <hi type="italic">willing</hi> and <hi type="italic">ready</hi> to hear them, is sincerely desirous to know what the mind of God is, and cheerfully embraces whatever he knows to be so. God's words have such an authority over, and such an agreeableness with all that are born of God, that they meet them, as the child Samuel did, with, <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth.</hi> Let the word of the Lord come. [2.] He <hi type="italic">apprehends</hi> and <hi type="italic">discerns</hi> them, he so hears them as to perceive the <hi type="italic">voice of God</hi> in them, which the natural man does not, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. He that is of God is <hi type="italic">soon aware</hi> of the discoveries he makes of himself of the <hi type="italic">nearness of his name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.1">Ps. lxxv. 1</reference>), as they of the family know the master's tread, and the master's knock, and <hi type="italic">open to him immediately</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.36">Luke xii. 36</reference>), as the sheep know the voice of their shepherd from that of a stranger, <reference osisRef="John.10.4-John.10.5">ch. x. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.2.8">Cant. ii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen27417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27418" type="x-p"/> (2.) The application of this doctrine, for the conviction of these unbelieving Jews: <hi type="italic">You therefore hear them not;</hi> that is, "You heed not, you understand not, you believe not, the words of God, nor care to hear them, <hi type="italic">because you are not of God.</hi> Your being thus deaf and dead to the words of God is a plain evidence that you are <hi type="italic">not of God.</hi>" It is in his word that God manifests himself and is present among us; we are therefore reckoned to be well or ill affected to his word; see <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. iv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.6">1 John iv. 6</reference>. Or, their not being of God was the reason why they did not profitably <hi type="italic">hear the words of God,</hi> which Christ spoke; they did not understand and believe him, not because the things themselves were obscure or wanted evidence, but because the hearers were <hi type="italic">not of God,</hi> were not born again. If the word of the kingdom do not bring forth fruit, the blame is to be laid upon the soil, not upon the seed, as appears by the parable of the sower, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.3">Matt. xiii. 3</reference>.

<div eID="gen27418" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27419" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">48</hi> Then answered the Jews, and said unto him, Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil? <hi type="super">49</hi> Jesus answered, I have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me. <hi type="super">50</hi> And I seek not mine own glory: there is one that seeketh and judgeth. <div eID="gen27419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27420" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The malice of hell breaking out in the base language which the unbelieving Jews gave to our Lord Jesus. Hitherto they had cavilled at his doctrine, and had made invidious remarks upon it; but, having shown themselves uneasy when he complained (<reference osisRef="John.8.43">v. 43</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.8.47">47</reference>) that they would not hear him, now at length they fall to downright railing, <reference osisRef="John.8.48">v. 48</reference>. They were not the common people, but, as it should seem, the scribes and Pharisees, the men of consequence, who, when they saw themselves convicted of an obstinate infidelity, scornfully turned off the conviction with this: <hi type="italic">Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil?</hi> See here, see it and wonder, see it and tremble, <div eID="gen27420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27421" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the blasphemous character commonly given of our Lord Jesus among the wicked Jews, to which they refer. (1.) That he was a Samaritan, that is, that he was an enemy to their church and nation, one that they hated and could not endure. Thus they exposed him to the ill will of the people, with whom you could not put a man into a worse name than to call him <hi type="italic">a Samaritan.</hi> If he had been a Samaritan, he had been punishable, by the <hi type="italic">beating of the rebels</hi> (as they called it), for coming into the temple. They had often enough called him <hi type="italic">a Galilean—a mean man;</hi> but as if that were not enough, though it contradicted the other, they will have him a <hi type="italic">Samaritan—a bad man.</hi> The Jews to this day call the Christians, in reproach, <hi type="italic">Cuthæi-Samaritans.</hi> Note, Great endeavours have in all ages been used to make good people odious by putting them under black characters, and it is easy to run that down with a crowd and a cry which is once put into an ill name. Perhaps because Christ justly inveighed against the pride and tyranny of the priests and elders, they hereby suggest that he aimed at the ruin of their church, in aiming at its reformation, and was <hi type="italic">falling away</hi> to the Samaritans. (2.) That <hi type="italic">he had a devil.</hi> Either, [1.] That he was <hi type="italic">in league with the devil.</hi> Having reproached his doctrine as tending to Samaritanism, here they reflect upon his miracles as done in combination with Beelzebub. Or, rather [2.] That he was possessed with a devil, that he was a melancholy man, whose brain was <hi type="italic">clouded,</hi> or a mad man, whose brain was <hi type="italic">heated,</hi> and that which he said was no more to be believed than the extravagant rambles of a distracted man, or one in a delirium. Thus the divine revelation of those things which are above the discovery of reason have been often branded with the charge of enthusiasm, and the prophet was called a <hi type="italic">mad fellow,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.11">2 Kings ix. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Hosea ix. 7</reference>. The inspiration of the Pagan oracles and prophets was indeed a frenzy, and those that had it were for the time beside themselves; but that which was truly <hi type="italic">divine</hi> was not so. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is justified of her children,</hi> as wisdom indeed. <div eID="gen27421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> 2. How they undertook to justify this character, and applied it to the present occasion: <hi type="italic">Say we not well that thou art so?</hi> One would think that his excellent discourses should have altered their opinion of him, and have made them recant; but, instead of this, their hearts were more hardened and their prejudices confirmed. They value themselves on their enmity to Christ, as if they had never spoken <hi type="italic">better</hi> than when they spoke the worst they could of Jesus Christ. Those have arrived at the highest pitch of wickedness who avow their impiety, repeat what they should retract, and justify themselves in that for which they ought to condemn themselves. It is bad to say and do ill, but it is worse to <hi type="italic">stand to it;</hi> I do <hi type="italic">well to be angry.</hi> When Christ spoke with so much boldness against the sins of the great men, and thereby incensed them against him, those who were sensible of no interest but what is secular and sensual concluded him <hi type="italic">beside himself,</hi> for they thought none but a madman would lose his preferment, and hazard his life, for his religion and conscience. <div eID="gen27422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> II. The meekness and mercifulness of Heaven shining in Christ's reply to this vile calumny, <reference osisRef="John.8.49-John.8.50">v. 49, 50</reference>. <div eID="gen27423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27424" type="x-p"/> 1. He denies their charge against him: <hi type="italic">I have not a devil;</hi> as Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.25">Acts xxvi. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am not mad.</hi> The imputation is unjust; "I am neither actuated by a devil, nor in compact with one;" and this he evidenced by what he did against the devil's kingdom. He takes no notice of their calling him a <hi type="italic">Samaritan,</hi> because it was a calumny that disproved itself, it was a personal reflection, and not worth taking notice of: but saying he had a devil reflected on his commission, and therefore he answered that. St. Augustine gives this gloss upon his not saying any thing to their calling him a Samaritan—that he was indeed that good Samaritan spoken of in the parable, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.33">Luke x. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen27424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> 2. He asserts the sincerity of his own intentions: But <hi type="italic">I honour my Father.</hi> They suggested that he took undue honours to himself, and derogated from the honour due to God only, both which he <hi type="italic">denies</hi> here, in saying that he made it his business to honour his Father, and him only. It also proves that he <hi type="italic">had not a devil;</hi> for, if he had, he would not honour God. Note, Those who can truly way that they make it their constant care to honour God are sufficiently armed against the censures and reproaches of men. <div eID="gen27425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27426" type="x-p"/> 3. He complains of the wrong they did him by their calumnies: <hi type="italic">You do dishonour me.</hi> By this it appears that, as man, he had a tender sense of the disgrace and indignity done him; reproach was a sword in his bones, and yet he underwent it for our salvation. It is the will of God that <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son,</hi> yet there are many that <hi type="italic">dishonour him;</hi> such a contradiction is there in the carnal mind to the will of God. Christ honoured his Father so as never man did, and yet was himself dishonoured so as never man was; for, though God has promised that those who honour him he will honour, he never promised that men should honour them. <div eID="gen27426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27427" type="x-p"/> 4. He clears himself from the imputation of vain glory, in saying this concerning himself, <reference osisRef="John.8.50">v. 50</reference>. See here, (1.) His <hi type="italic">contempt</hi> of worldly honour: <hi type="italic">I seek not mine own glory.</hi> He did not aim at this in what he had said of himself or against his persecutors; he did not court the applause of men, nor covet preferment in the world, but industriously declined both. He did not <hi type="italic">seek his own glory</hi> distinct from his Father's, nor had any separate interest of his own. For men to <hi type="italic">search their own glory</hi> is <hi type="italic">not glory</hi> indeed (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.27">Prov. xxv. 27</reference>), but rather their shame to be so much <hi type="italic">out in their aim.</hi> This comes in here as a reason why Christ made so light of their reproaches: "<hi type="italic">You do dishonour me,</hi> but cannot disturb me, shall not disquiet me, for I <hi type="italic">seek not my own glory.</hi>" Note, Those who are dead to men's praise can safely bear their contempt. (2.) His <hi type="italic">comfort</hi> under worldly dishonour: <hi type="italic">There is one that seeketh and judgeth.</hi> In two things Christ made it appear that he <hi type="italic">sought not his own glory;</hi> and here he tells us what satisfied him as to both. [1.] He did not <hi type="italic">court</hi> men's respect, but was indifferent to it, and in reference to this he saith, "<hi type="italic">There is one that seeketh,</hi> that will secure and advance, my interest in the esteem and affections of the people, while I am in no care about it." Note, God will seek <hi type="italic">their</hi> honour that do not seek <hi type="italic">their own;</hi> for before honour is humility. [2.] He did not <hi type="italic">revenge</hi> men's affronts, but was unconcerned at them, and in reference to this he saith, "<hi type="italic">There is one that judgeth,</hi> that will vindicate my honour, and severely reckon with those that trample upon it." Probably he refers here to the judgments that were coming upon the nation of the Jews for the indignities they did to the Lord Jesus. See <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13-Ps.37.15">Ps. xxxvii. 13-15</reference>. <hi type="italic">I heard not, for thou wilt hear.</hi> If we undertake to judge for ourselves, whatever damage we sustain, our recompence is in our own hands; but if we be, as we ought to be, humble appellants and patient expectants, we shall find, to our comfort, <hi type="italic">there is one that judgeth.</hi>

<div eID="gen27427" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees</title> <div sID="gen27428" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">51</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, If a man keep my saying, he shall never see death. <hi type="super">52</hi> Then said the Jews unto him, Now we know that thou hast a devil. Abraham is dead, and the prophets; and thou sayest, If a man keep my saying, he shall never taste of death. <hi type="super">53</hi> Art thou greater than our father Abraham, which is dead? and the prophets are dead: whom makest thou thyself? <hi type="super">54</hi> Jesus answered, If I honour myself, my honour is nothing: it is my Father that honoureth me; of whom ye say, that he is your God: <hi type="super">55</hi> Yet ye have not known him; but I know him: and if I should say, I know him not, I shall be a liar like unto you: but I know him, and keep his saying. <hi type="super">56</hi> Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and was glad. 57 Then said the Jews unto him, Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham? <hi type="super">58</hi> Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am. <hi type="super">59</hi> Then took they up stones to cast at him: but Jesus hid himself, and went out of the temple, going through the midst of them, and so passed by. <div eID="gen27428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27429" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen27429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27430" type="x-p"/> I. The doctrine of the immortality of believers laid down, <reference osisRef="John.8.51">v. 51</reference>. It is ushered in with the usual solemn preface, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you,</hi> which commands both attention and assent, and this is what he says, <hi type="italic">If a man keep my sayings, he shall never see death.</hi> Here we have, 1. The <hi type="italic">character</hi> of a believer: he is one that <hi type="italic">keeps the sayings</hi> of the Lord Jesus, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ton logon ton emon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">my word;</hi> that <hi type="italic">word of mine</hi> which I have delivered to you; this we must not only <hi type="italic">receive,</hi> but <hi type="italic">keep;</hi> not only <hi type="italic">have,</hi> but <hi type="italic">hold.</hi> We must keep it in mind and memory, keep it in love and affection, so keep it as in nothing to violate it or go contrary to it, keep it <hi type="italic">without spot</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1 Tim. vi. 14</reference>), keep it as a trust committed to us, keep in it as our way, keep to it as our rule. 2. The <hi type="italic">privilege</hi> of a believer: <hi type="italic">He shall by no means see death for ever;</hi> so it is in the original. Not as if the bodies of believers were secured from the stroke of death. No, even the <hi type="italic">children of the Most High</hi> must <hi type="italic">die like men,</hi> and the followers of Christ have been, more than other men, in deaths often, and <hi type="italic">killed all the day long;</hi> how then is this promise made good that they <hi type="italic">shall not see death?</hi> Answer, (1.) The property of death is so altered to them that they do not see it as death, they do not see the terror of death, it is quite taken off; their sight does not <hi type="italic">terminate</hi> in death, as theirs does who <hi type="italic">live by sense;</hi> no, they look so clearly, so comfortably, through death, and beyond death, and are so taken up with their state on the other side death, that they overlook death, and <hi type="italic">see it not.</hi> (2.) The power of death is so broken that though there is no remedy, but they must see <hi type="italic">death,</hi> yet they shall not see death <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> shall not be always shut up under its arrests, the day will come when <hi type="italic">death shall be swallowed up in victory.</hi> (3.) They are perfectly delivered from <hi type="italic">eternal death,</hi> shall not be <hi type="italic">hurt of the second death.</hi> That is the death especially meant here, that death which is <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> which is opposed to everlasting life; this they shall never see, for they shall <hi type="italic">never come into condemnation;</hi> they shall have their everlasting lot where there will be <hi type="italic">no more death,</hi> where they <hi type="italic">cannot die any more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Luke xx. 36</reference>. Though now they cannot avoid seeing death, and tasting it too, yet they shall shortly be there where it will be <hi type="italic">seen no more for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.14.13">Exod. xiv. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen27430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27431" type="x-p"/> II. The Jews cavil at this doctrine. Instead of laying hold of this precious promise of immortality, which the nature of man has an ambition of (who is there that does not love life, and dread the sight of death?) they lay hold of this occasion to reproach him that makes them so kind an offer: <hi type="italic">Now we know that thou hast a devil.</hi> Abraham <hi type="italic">is dead.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27432" type="x-p"/> 1. Their <hi type="italic">railing: "Now we know that thou hast a devil,</hi> that thou art a madman; thou ravest, and sayest thou knowest not what." See how these swine trample underfoot the precious pearls of gospel promises. If now at last they had evidence to prove him <hi type="italic">mad,</hi> why did they say (<reference osisRef="John.8.48">v. 48</reference>), before they had that proof, <hi type="italic">Thou hast a devil?</hi> But this is the method of malice, first to <hi type="italic">fasten</hi> an invidious charge, and then to <hi type="italic">fish</hi> for evidence of it: <hi type="italic">Now we know that thou hast a devil.</hi> If he had not abundantly proved himself a <hi type="italic">teacher come from God,</hi> his promises of immortality to his credulous followers might justly have been ridiculed, and charity itself would have imputed them to a crazed fancy; but his doctrine was evidently divine, his miracles confirmed it, and the Jews' religion taught them to expect such a prophet, and to believe in him; for them therefore thus to reject him was to abandon that promise to which their <hi type="italic">twelve tribes hoped to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.27">Acts xxvi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen27432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27433" type="x-p"/> 2. Their <hi type="italic">reasoning,</hi> and the colour they had to <hi type="italic">run him down</hi> thus. In short, they look upon him as guilty of an insufferable piece of arrogance, in making himself greater than <hi type="italic">Abraham and the prophets: Abraham is dead,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the prophets,</hi> they are dead too; very true, by the same token that these Jews were the genuine offspring of those that killed them. Now, (1.) It is true that Abraham and the prophets were great men, great in the favour of God, and great in the esteem of all good men. (2.) It is true that they <hi type="italic">kept God's sayings,</hi> and were obedient to them; and yet, (3.) It is true that they <hi type="italic">died;</hi> they never pretended to <hi type="italic">have,</hi> much less to <hi type="italic">give,</hi> immortality, but every one in his own order was <hi type="italic">gathered to his people.</hi> It was their honour that they <hi type="italic">died in faith,</hi> but die they must. Why should a good man be afraid to die, when Abraham is dead, and the prophets are dead? They have <hi type="italic">tracked</hi> the way through that darksome valley, which should reconcile us to death and help to take off the terror of it. Now they think Christ talks madly, when he saith, <hi type="italic">If a man keep my sayings, he shall never taste death. Tasting</hi> death means the same thing with <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> it; and well may death be represented as grievous to <hi type="italic">several</hi> of the senses, which is the destruction of them <hi type="italic">all.</hi> Now their arguing goes upon two mistakes:—[1.] They understood Christ of an immortality in this world, and this was a mistake. In the sense that Christ spoke, it was not true that <hi type="italic">Abraham and the prophets were dead,</hi> for God is still the <hi type="italic">God of Abraham</hi> and the <hi type="italic">God of the holy prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.6">Rev. xxii. 6</reference>); now God is not the God of the dead, but of the living; therefore Abraham and the prophets are still alive, and, as Christ meant it, they had not <hi type="italic">seen</hi> nor <hi type="italic">tasted</hi> death. [2.] They thought none could be greater than Abraham and the prophets, whereas they could not but know that the Messiah would be greater than Abraham or any of the prophets; they did virtuously, but he excelled them all; nay, they borrowed their greatness from him. It was the honour of Abraham that he was the Father of the Messiah, and the honour of the prophets that they testified beforehand concerning him: so that he certainly <hi type="italic">obtained a</hi> far <hi type="italic">more excellent name than they.</hi> Therefore, instead of inferring from Christ's making himself greater than Abraham that he had a <hi type="italic">devil,</hi> they should have inferred from his proving himself so (by doing the works which neither Abraham nor the prophets ever did) that he was the Christ; but their eyes were blinded. They scornfully asked, <hi type="italic">Whom makest thou thyself?</hi> As if he had been guilty of pride and vain-glory; whereas he was so far from making himself greater than he was that he now drew a veil over his own glory, emptied himself, and made himself less than he was, and was the greatest example of humility that ever was. <div eID="gen27433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27434" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's reply to this cavil; still he vouchsafes to reason with them, that every mouth may be stopped. No doubt he could have struck them dumb or dead upon the spot, but this was the <hi type="italic">day of his patience.</hi> <div eID="gen27434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27435" type="x-p"/> 1. In his answer he insists not upon his own testimony concerning himself, but waives it as not sufficient nor conclusive (<reference osisRef="John.8.54">v. 54</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I honour myself, my honour is nothing,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ean ego doxazo</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">if I glorify myself.</hi> Note, Self-honour is no honour; and the affectation of glory is both the forfeiture and the defeasance of it: it is <hi type="italic">not glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.27">Prov. xxv. 27</reference>), but so great a reproach that there is no sin which men are more industrious to hide than this; even he that most affects praise would not be thought to do it. Honour of our own creating is a mere chimera, has nothing in it, and therefore is called <hi type="italic">vain-glory.</hi> Self-admirers are self-<hi type="italic">deceivers.</hi> Our Lord Jesus was not one that <hi type="italic">honoured himself,</hi> as they represented him; he was <hi type="italic">crowned</hi> by him who is the fountain of honour, and glorified not himself to be made a high priest, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.4-Heb.5.5">Heb. v. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27436" type="x-p"/> 2. He refers himself to <hi type="italic">his</hi> Father, God; and to <hi type="italic">their</hi> father, Abraham. <div eID="gen27436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27437" type="x-p"/> (1.) To his Father, <hi type="italic">God: It is my Father that honoureth me.</hi> By this he means, [1.] That he <hi type="italic">derived</hi> from his Father all the honour he now claimed; he had commanded them to believe in him, to follow him, and to keep his word, all which put an honour upon him; but it was the Father that <hi type="italic">laid help</hi> upon him, that <hi type="italic">lodged</hi> all <hi type="italic">fulness</hi> in him, that sanctified him, and sealed him, and sent him into the world to receive all the honours due to the Messiah, and this justified him in all these demands of respect. [2.] That he <hi type="italic">depended</hi> upon his Father for all the honour he further <hi type="italic">looked for.</hi> He courted not the applauses of the age, but despised them; for his eye and heart were upon the glory which the Father had promised him, and <hi type="italic">which he had with the Father before the world was.</hi> He aimed at an advancement with which the Father was to <hi type="italic">exalt him, a name</hi> he was to <hi type="italic">give him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.8-Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 8, 9</reference>. Note, Christ and all that are his depend upon God for their honour; and he that is sure of honour where he is known cares not though he be slighted where he is in disguise. Appealing thus often to his Father, and his Father's testimony of him, which yet the Jews did not admit nor give credit to, <div eID="gen27437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He here takes occasion to show the reason of <hi type="italic">their</hi> incredulity, notwithstanding <hi type="italic">this</hi> testimony—and this was their <hi type="italic">unacquaintedness</hi> with God; as if he had said, "But why should I talk to you of my Father's honouring me, when he is one you know nothing of? You <hi type="italic">say of him that he is your God, yet you have not known him.</hi>" Here observe, <div eID="gen27438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27439" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> The profession they made of relation to God: "<hi type="italic">You say that he is your God,</hi> the God you have chosen, and are in covenant with; you say that you are Israel; but all are not so indeed that are of Israel," <reference osisRef="Rom.9.6">Rom. ix. 6</reference>. Note, Many pretend to have an interest in God, and say that he is <hi type="italic">theirs,</hi> who yet have no just cause to say so. Those who called themselves the <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord,</hi> having <hi type="italic">profaned the excellency of Jacob,</hi> did but trust in lying words. What will it avail us to say, He is <hi type="italic">our God,</hi> if we be not in sincerity <hi type="italic">his people,</hi> nor such as he will own? Christ mentions here their profession of relation to God, as that which was an aggravation of their unbelief. All people will honour those whom their God honours; but these Jews, who said that the Lord was their God, studied how to put the utmost disgrace upon one upon whom their God put honour. Note, The Profession we make of a covenant relation to God, and an interest in him, if it be not improved <hi type="italic">by us</hi> will be improved <hi type="italic">against us.</hi> <div eID="gen27439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27440" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Their ignorance of him, and estrangement from him, notwithstanding this profession: <hi type="italic">Yet you have not known him.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) <hi type="italic">You know him not at all.</hi> These Pharisees were so taken up with the study of their traditions concerning things foreign and trifling that they never minded the most needful and useful knowledge; like the false prophets of old, who <hi type="italic">caused people to forget God's name by their dreams,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.27">Jer. xxiii. 27</reference>. Or, (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) <hi type="italic">You know him not aright,</hi> but mistake concerning him; and this is as bad as not knowing him at all, or worse. Men may be able to dispute subtly concerning God, and yet may think him such a one as themselves, and <hi type="italic">not know him.</hi> You say that he is <hi type="italic">yours,</hi> and it is natural to us to desire to know <hi type="italic">our own,</hi> yet you <hi type="italic">know him not.</hi> Note, There are many who <hi type="italic">claim-kindred</hi> to God who yet have no acquaintance with him. It is only the name of God which they have learned to talk of, and to hector with; but for the nature of God, his attributes and perfections, and relations to his creatures, they know nothing of the matter; we <hi type="italic">speak this to their shame,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.34">1 Cor. xv. 34</reference>. Multitudes satisfy themselves, but deceive themselves, with a titular relation to an <hi type="italic">unknown God.</hi> This Christ charges upon the Jews here, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] To show how vain and groundless their pretensions of relation to God were. "You say that he is yours, but you give yourselves the lie, for it is plain that you do not know him;" and we reckon that a cheat is effectually convicted if it be found that he is ignorant of the persons he pretends alliance to. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] To show the true reason why they were not wrought upon by Christ's doctrine and miracles. They knew not God; and therefore perceived not the image of God, nor the voice of God in Christ. Note, The reason why men receive not the <hi type="italic">gospel of Christ</hi> is because they have not the <hi type="italic">knowledge of God.</hi> Men <hi type="italic">submit not to the righteousness of Christ</hi> because they are <hi type="italic">ignorant of God's righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Rom. x. 3</reference>. They that know not God, and obey not the gospel of Christ, are put together, <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen27440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27441" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He gives them the reason of <hi type="italic">his</hi> assurance that his Father would <hi type="italic">honour</hi> him and <hi type="italic">own him: But I know him;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">I know him;</hi> which bespeaks, not only his <hi type="italic">acquaintance</hi> with him, having lain in his bosom, but his <hi type="italic">confidence</hi> in him, to stand by him, and bear him out in his whole undertaking; as was prophesied concerning him (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7-Isa.50.8">Isa. l. 7, 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">I know</hi> that I shall not be ashamed, for he is near that justifies; and as Paul, "<hi type="italic">I know whom I have believed</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>), I know him to be faithful, and powerful, and heartily engaged in the cause which I know to be his <hi type="italic">own.</hi>" Observe, 1. How he <hi type="italic">professes</hi> his knowledge of his Father, with the greatest certainty, as one that was neither afraid nor ashamed to own it: <hi type="italic">If I should say I know him not, I should be a liar like unto you.</hi> He would not deny his relation to God, to humour the Jews, and to avoid their reproaches, and prevent further trouble; nor would he retract what he had said, nor confess himself either deceived or a deceiver; if he should, he would be found a false witness against God and himself. Note, Those who disown their religion and relation to God, as Peter, are liars, as much as hypocrites are, who pretend to know him, when they do not. See <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13-1Tim.6.14">1 Tim. vi. 13, 14</reference>. Mr. Clark observes well, upon this, that it is a great sin to deny God's grace in us. 2. How he <hi type="italic">proves</hi> his knowledge of his Father: <hi type="italic">I know him and keep his sayings,</hi> or <hi type="italic">his word.</hi> Christ, as man, was obedient to the moral law, and, as Redeemer, to the mediatorial law; and in both he kept <hi type="italic">his Father's</hi> word, and <hi type="italic">his own word</hi> with the Father. Christ requires of us (<reference osisRef="John.8.51">v. 51</reference>) that we <hi type="italic">keep his sayings;</hi> and he has set before us a copy of obedience, a copy without a blot: he <hi type="italic">kept his Father's sayings;</hi> well might he who <hi type="italic">learned obedience</hi> teach it; see <reference osisRef="Heb.5.8-Heb.5.9">Heb. v. 8, 9</reference>. Christ by this evinced that he knew the Father. Note, The best proof of our acquaintance with God is our obedience to him. Those only know God aright that keep his word; it is a ruled case, <reference osisRef="1John.2.3">1 John ii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Hereby we know that we know him</hi> (and do not only fancy it), <hi type="italic">if we keep his commandments.</hi> <div eID="gen27441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27442" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ refers them to <hi type="italic">their</hi> father, whom they boasted so much of a relation to, and that was Abraham, and this closes the discourse. <div eID="gen27442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27443" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ asserts Abraham's prospect of him, and respect to him: <hi type="italic">Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it, and was glad,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.56">v. 56</reference>. And by this he proves that he was not at all out of the way when he <hi type="italic">made himself greater than Abraham.</hi> Two things he here speaks of as instances of that patriarch's respect to the promised Messiah:— <div eID="gen27443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The ambition he had to <hi type="italic">see his day: He rejoiced,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">egalliasto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he leaped at it.</hi> The word, though it commonly signifies <hi type="italic">rejoicing,</hi> must here signify a transport of <hi type="italic">desire</hi> rather than of <hi type="italic">joy,</hi> for otherwise the latter part of <reference osisRef="John.8.56">the verse</reference> would be a tautology; he <hi type="italic">saw it, and was glad.</hi> He <hi type="italic">reached out,</hi> or <hi type="italic">stretched himself forth,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">see my day;</hi> as Zaccheus, that ran before, and climbed the tree, <hi type="italic">to see Jesus.</hi> The notices he had received of the Messiah to come had raised in him an expectation of something <hi type="italic">great,</hi> which he earnestly longed to know more of. The dark intimation of that which is considerable puts men upon enquiry, and makes them earnestly ask <hi type="italic">Who?</hi> and <hi type="italic">What?</hi> and <hi type="italic">Where?</hi> and <hi type="italic">When?</hi> and <hi type="italic">How?</hi> And thus the prophets of the Old Testament, having a general idea of a grace that should <hi type="italic">come, searched diligently</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1 Pet. i. 10</reference>), and Abraham was as industrious herein as any of them. God told him of a land that he would give his posterity, and of the wealth and honour he designed them (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.14">Gen. xv. 14</reference>); but he never <hi type="italic">leaped</hi> thus to see that day, as he did to see the day of the Son of man. He could not look with so much indifferency upon the promised <hi type="italic">seed</hi> as he did upon the promised land; <hi type="italic">in that</hi> he was, but <hi type="italic">to the other</hi> he could not be, contentedly a stranger. Note, Those who rightly know any thing of Christ cannot but be earnestly desirous to know more of him. Those who discern the dawning of the light of the Sun of righteousness cannot but wish to see his rising. The mystery of redemption is that which <hi type="italic">angels desire to look into,</hi> much more should we, who are more immediately concerned in it. Abraham desired to see Christ's day, though it was at a great distance; but this degenerate seed of his discerned not his day, nor bade it welcome when it came. The appearing of Christ, which gracious souls love and long for, carnal hearts dread and loathe. <div eID="gen27444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27445" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The satisfaction he had in what he did see of it: <hi type="italic">He saw it, and was glad.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27446" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> How God gratified the pious desire of Abraham; he longed to see Christ's day, and he <hi type="italic">saw it.</hi> Though he saw it not so plainly, and fully, and distinctly as we now see it under the gospel, yet he saw something of it, more <hi type="italic">afterwards</hi> than he did at first. Note, To him that has, and to him that asks, shall be given; to him that uses and improves what he has, and that desires and prays for more of the knowledge of Christ, God will give more. But how did Abraham see Christ's day? (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Some understand it of the sight he had of it in the other world. The separate soul of Abraham, when the veil of flesh was rent, saw the mysteries of the kingdom of God in heaven. Calvin mentions this sense of it, and does not much disallow it. Note, The longings of gracious souls after Jesus Christ will be fully satisfied when they come to heaven, and not till then. But, (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It is more commonly understood of some sight he had of <hi type="italic">Christ's day</hi> in this world. They that <hi type="italic">received not the promises,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">saw them afar off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.13">Heb. xi. 13</reference>. Balaam saw Christ, but not <hi type="italic">now,</hi> not <hi type="italic">nigh.</hi> There is room to conjecture that Abraham had some vision of Christ and his day, for his own private satisfaction, which is not, nor must be, recorded in his story, like that of Daniel's, which must be <hi type="italic">shut up, and sealed unto the time of the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Dan. xii. 4</reference>. Christ knew what Abraham saw better than Moses did. But there are divers things recorded in which Abraham saw more of that which he longed to see than he did when the promise was first made to him. He saw in Melchizedek one <hi type="italic">made like unto the Son of God,</hi> and a priest for ever; he saw an appearance of Jehovah, attended with two angels, in the plains of Mamre. In the prevalency of his intercession for Sodom he saw a specimen of Christ's intercession; in the casting out of Ishmael, and the establishment of the covenant with Isaac, he saw a figure of the gospel day, which is Christ's day; for these things were an allegory. In offering Isaac, and the ram instead of Isaac, he saw a double type of the great sacrifice; and his calling the place <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh—It shall be seen,</hi> intimates that he saw something more in it than others did, which time would produce; and in making his servant <hi type="italic">put his hand under his thigh,</hi> when he swore, he had a regard to the Messiah. <div eID="gen27446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> How <hi type="italic">Abraham</hi> entertained these discoveries of Christ's day, and bade them welcome: <hi type="italic">He saw, and was glad.</hi> He was glad of what he <hi type="italic">saw</hi> of God's favour to himself, and glad of what he <hi type="italic">foresaw</hi> of the mercy God had in store for the world. Perhaps this refers to Abraham's laughing when God assured him of a son by Sarah (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.16-Gen.17.17">Gen. xvii. 16, 17</reference>), for that was not a laughter of distrust as Sarah's but of joy; in that promise he saw Christ's day, and it <hi type="italic">filled him with joy unspeakable.</hi> Thus he embraced the promises. Note, A believing sight of Christ and his day will put gladness into the heart.
