No joy like the joy of faith; we are never acquainted with true pleasure till we are acquainted with Christ. <div eID="gen27447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27448" type="x-p"/> [2.] The Jews cavil at this, and reproach him for it (<reference osisRef="John.8.57">v. 57</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham?</hi> Here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They suppose that if Abraham saw him and his day he also had seen Abraham, which yet was not a necessary <hi type="italic">innuendo,</hi> but this turn of his words would best serve to expose him; yet it was true that Christ had seen Abraham, and had talked with him as a man talks with his friend. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They suppose it a very absurd thing for him to pretend to have seen Abraham, who was <hi type="italic">dead</hi> so many ages before he was born. The state of the dead is an <hi type="italic">invisible</hi> state; but here they ran upon the old mistake, understanding that corporally which Christ spoke spiritually. Now this gave them occasion to <hi type="italic">despise his youth,</hi> and to upbraid him with it, as if he were <hi type="italic">but of yesterday, and knew</hi> nothing: <hi type="italic">Thou art not yet fifty years old.</hi> They might as well have said, <hi type="italic">Thou art not forty;</hi> for he was now but thirty-two or thirty-three years old. As to this, Irenæus, one of the first fathers, with this passage supports the tradition which he says he had from some that had conversed with St. John, that our Saviour lived to be fifty years old, which he contends for, <hi type="italic">Advers. Hæres.</hi> lib. 2, cap. 39, 40. See what little credit is to be given to tradition; and, as to this here, the Jews spoke <hi type="italic">at random;</hi> some year they would mention, and therefore pitched upon one that they thought he was far enough short of; he did not look to be forty, but they were sure he could not be fifty, much less contemporary with Abraham. Old age is reckoned to begin at fifty (<reference osisRef="Num.4.47">Num. iv. 47</reference>), so that they meant no more than this, "Thou art not to be reckoned an old man; many of us are much thy seniors, and yet pretend not to have seen Abraham." Some think that his countenance was so altered, with grief and watching, that, together with the gravity of his aspect, it made him look like a man of fifty years old: <hi type="italic">his visage was so marred,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa. lii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen27448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27449" type="x-p"/> [3.] Our Saviour gives an effectual answer to this cavil, by a solemn assertion of his own seniority even to Abraham himself (<reference osisRef="John.8.58">v. 58</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> I do not only say it in private to my own disciples, who will be sure to say as I say, but <hi type="italic">to you</hi> my enemies and persecutors; I say it to your faces, take it how you will: <hi type="italic">Before Abraham was, I am;</hi>" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prin Abraam genesthai, ego eimi</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">Before Abraham was made or born, I am.</hi> The change of the word is observable, and bespeaks Abraham a creature, and himself the Creator; well therefore might he make himself <hi type="italic">greater</hi> than Abraham. <hi type="italic">Before Abraham he was, First,</hi> As God. <hi type="italic">I am,</hi> is the name of God (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>); it denotes his self-existence; he does not say, <hi type="italic">I was,</hi> but <hi type="italic">I am,</hi> for he is the first and the last, immutably the same (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.8">Rev. i. 8</reference>); thus he was not only before Abraham, but before <hi type="italic">all worlds,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">Prov. viii. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As Mediator. He was the appointed Messiah, long before Abraham; the <hi type="italic">Lamb slain from the foundation of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Rev. xiii. 8</reference>), the channel of conveyance of light, life, and love from God to man. This supposes his divine nature, that he is the same in himself from eternity (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">Heb. xiii. 8</reference>), and that he is the same to man ever since the fall; he was made of God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, to Adam, and Abel, and Enoch, and Noah, and Shem, and all the patriarchs that lived and died by faith in him before Abraham was born. Abraham was the root of the Jewish nation, the rock out of which they were hewn. If Christ was before Abraham, his doctrine and religion were no novelty, but were, in the substance of them, prior to Judaism, and ought to take place of it. <div eID="gen27449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27450" type="x-p"/> [4.] This great word ended the dispute <hi type="italic">abruptly,</hi> and put a period to it: they could bear to hear no more from him, and he needed to say no more to them, having witnessed this good confession, which was sufficient to support all his claims. One would think that Christ's discourse, in which shone so much both of grace and glory, should have captivated them all; but their inveterate prejudice against the holy spiritual doctrine and law of Christ, which were so contrary to their pride and worldliness, baffled all the methods of conviction. Now was fulfilled that prophecy (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.1-Mal.3.2">Mal. iii. 1, 2</reference>), that when the messenger of the covenant should <hi type="italic">come to his temple</hi> they <hi type="italic">would not abide the day of his coming,</hi> because he would be <hi type="italic">like a refiner's fire.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27451" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How they were <hi type="italic">enraged</hi> at Christ for what he said: <hi type="italic">They took up stones to cast at him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.59">v. 59</reference>. Perhaps they looked upon him as a blasphemer, and such were indeed to be stoned (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.16">Lev. xxiv. 16</reference>); but they must be first legally tried and convicted. Farewell justice and order if every man pretend to execute a law at his pleasure. Besides, they had said but just now that he was a distracted crack-brained man, and if so it was against all reason and equity to punish him as a malefactor for what he said. <hi type="italic">They took up stones.</hi> Dr. Lightfoot will tell you how they came to have stones so ready in the temple; they had workmen at this time repairing the temple, or making some additions, and the pieces of stone which they hewed off served for this purpose. See here the desperate power of sin and Satan in and over the children of disobedience. Who would think that ever there should be such wickedness as this in men, such an open and daring rebellion against one that undeniably proved himself to be the Son of God? Thus every one has a stone to throw at his holy religion, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.22">Acts xxviii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen27451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How he made his <hi type="italic">escape</hi> out of their hands. 1. He <hi type="italic">absconded;</hi> Jesus <hi type="italic">hid himself;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ekrybe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he was hid,</hi> either by the crowd of those that wished well to him, to shelter him (he that ought to have been upon a throne, high and lifted up, is content to be <hi type="italic">lost in a crowd</hi>); or perhaps he concealed himself behind some of the walls or pillars of the temple (<hi type="italic">in the secret of his tabernacle he shall hide me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 5</reference>); or by a divine power, casting a mist before their eyes, he made himself invisible to them. <hi type="italic">When the wicked rise a man is hidden,</hi> a wise and good man, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.12">Prov. xxviii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.28">28</reference>. Not that Christ was afraid or ashamed to stand by what he had said, but his <hi type="italic">hour was not yet come,</hi> and he would countenance the flight of his ministers and people in times of persecution, when they are called to it. The Lord hid Jeremiah and Baruch, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jer. xxxvi. 26</reference>. 2. He <hi type="italic">departed,</hi> he <hi type="italic">went out of the temple,</hi> going <hi type="italic">through the midst of them,</hi> undiscovered, and <hi type="italic">so passed by.</hi> This was not a cowardly inglorious flight, nor such as argued either guilt or fear. It was foretold concerning him that he should not fail nor be discouraged, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa. xlii. 4</reference>. But, (1.) It was an instance of his power over his enemies, and that they could do no more against him than he gave them leave to do; by which it appears that when afterwards he was taken in their pits he <hi type="italic">offered himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.18">ch. x. 18</reference>. They now thought they had made sure of him and yet he <hi type="italic">passed through the midst</hi> of them, either their eyes being blinded or their hands tied, and thus he left them to fume, like a lion <hi type="italic">disappointed of his prey.</hi> (2.) It was an instance of his prudent provision for his own safety, when he knew that his work was not done, nor his testimony finished; thus he gave an example to his own rule, <hi type="italic">When they persecute you in one city flee to another;</hi> nay, if occasion be, to a <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> for so Elijah did (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.3-1Kgs.19.4">1 Kings xix. 3, 4</reference>), and the woman, the church, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">Rev. xii. 6</reference>. When they took up loose stones to throw at Christ, he could have commanded the fixed stones, which did <hi type="italic">cry out of the wall</hi> against them, to avenge his cause, or the earth to open and swallow them up; but he chose to accommodate himself to the state he was in, to make the example imitable by the prudence of his followers, without a miracle. (3.) It was a righteous deserting of those who (worse than the Gadarenes, who <hi type="italic">prayed him to depart</hi>) stoned him from among them. Christ will not long stay with those who bid him be gone. Christ did again visit the temple after this; as one <hi type="italic">loth to depart,</hi> he <hi type="italic">bade oft farewell;</hi> but at last he abandoned it for ever, and left it <hi type="italic">desolate.</hi> Christ now <hi type="italic">went through</hi> the midst of the Jews, and none of them courted his stay, nor stirred up himself to take hold of him, but were even content to let him go. Note, God never forsakes any till they have first provoked him to withdraw, and will have none of him. Calvin observes that these chief priests, when they had driven Christ out of the temple, valued themselves on the possession they kept of it: "But," says he, "those deceive themselves who are proud of a church or temple which Christ has forsaken." <hi type="italic">Longe falluntur, cum templum se habere putant Deo vacuum.</hi> When Christ left them it is said that he passed by silently and unobserved; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paregen houtos</hi></hi>, so that they were not aware of him. Note, Christ's departures from a church, or a particular soul, are often <hi type="italic">secret,</hi> and not soon taken notice of. As <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God comes not,</hi> so it <hi type="italic">goes not, with observation.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Judg.16.20">Judg. xvi. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Samson wist not that the Lord was departed from him.</hi> Thus it was with these forsaken Jews, God left them, and they never missed him.  <chapter eID="John.8"/> <div eID="gen27452" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27455" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27454" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sight Given to One Born Blind.</title> <div sID="gen27456" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And as <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> passed by, he saw a man which was blind from <hi type="italic">his</hi> birth. <hi type="super">2</hi> And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? <hi type="super">3</hi> Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. <hi type="super">4</hi> I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work. 5 As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. 6 When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay, <hi type="super">7</hi> And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing. <div eID="gen27456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27457" type="x-p"/> We have here sight given to a poor beggar that had been blind from his birth. Observe, <div eID="gen27457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27458" type="x-p"/> I. The notice which our Lord Jesus took of the piteous case of this poor blind man (<reference osisRef="John.9.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">As Jesus passed by he saw a man which was blind from his birth.</hi> The first words seem to refer to the last of the foregoing chapter, and countenance the opinion of those who in the harmony place this story immediately after that. There it was said, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paregen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he passed by,</hi> and here, without so much as repeating him name (though our translators supply it) <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kai parago</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">and as he passed by.</hi> 1. Though the Jews had so basely abused him, both by word and deed gave him the highest provocation imaginable, yet he did not miss any opportunity of doing good among them, nor take up a resolution, as justly he might have done, never to have favoured them with any good offices. The cure of this blind man was a kindness to <hi type="italic">the public,</hi> enabling him to work for his living who before was a charge and burden to the neighbourhood. It is noble, and generous, and Christ-like, to be willing to <hi type="italic">serve the public,</hi> even when we are slighted and disobliged by them, or think ourselves so. Though he was in his flight from a threatening danger, and escaping for his life, yet he willingly halted and staid awhile to show mercy to this poor man. We make more haste than good speed when we out-run opportunities of doing good. 3. When the Pharisees drove Christ from them, he went to this poor blind beggar. Some of the ancients make this a figure of the bringing of the gospel to the Gentiles, <hi type="italic">who sat in darkness,</hi> when the Jews had rejected it, and driven it from them. 4. Christ took this poor blind man in his way, and cured him <hi type="italic">in transitu—as he passed by.</hi> Thus should we take occasions of doing good, even as we <hi type="italic">pass by,</hi> wherever we are. <div eID="gen27458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27459" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) The condition of this poor man was very sad. He was <hi type="italic">blind,</hi> and had been so <hi type="italic">from his birth.</hi> If the light is sweet, how melancholy must it needs be for a man, all his days, <hi type="italic">to eat in darkness!</hi> He that is <hi type="italic">blind</hi> has no <hi type="italic">enjoyment</hi> of the light, but he that is <hi type="italic">born blind</hi> has no <hi type="italic">idea</hi> of it. Methinks such a one would give a great deal to have his curiosity satisfied with but one day's sight of light and colours, shapes and figures, though he were never to see them more. <hi type="italic">Why is</hi> the <hi type="italic">light</hi> of life <hi type="italic">given to one that is in this misery,</hi> that is deprived of the light of the sun, <hi type="italic">whose way is</hi> thus <hi type="italic">hid, and whom God hath</hi> thus <hi type="italic">hedged in?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.20">Job iii. 20-23</reference>. Let us bless God that it was not our case. The eye is one of the most curious parts of the body, its structure exceedingly nice and fine. In the formation of animals, it is said to be the first part that appears distinctly discernible. What a mercy is it that there was no miscarriage in the making of ours! Christ cured many that were blind by disease or accident, but here he cured one that was <hi type="italic">born blind.</hi> [1.] That he might give an instance of his power to help in the most desperate cases, and to relieve when none else can. [2.] That he might give a <hi type="italic">specimen</hi> of the work of his grace upon the souls of sinners, which gives sight to those that were by nature blind. <div eID="gen27459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27460" type="x-p"/> (2.) The compassions of our Lord Jesus towards him were very tender. He <hi type="italic">saw him;</hi> that is, he took cognizance of his case, and looked upon him with concern. When God is about to work deliverance, he is said to see <hi type="italic">the affliction;</hi> so Christ saw this poor man. Others saw him, but not as he did. This poor man could not see Christ, but Christ saw him, and anticipated both his prayers and expectations with a surprising cure. Christ is often found of those that seek him not, nor see him, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa. lxv. 1</reference>. And, if we know or apprehend any thing of Christ, it is because we were first <hi type="italic">known of him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>) and <hi type="italic">apprehended</hi> by him, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">Phil. iii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen27460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27461" type="x-p"/> II. The discourse between Christ and his disciples concerning this man. When he <hi type="italic">departed out of the temple</hi> they went along with him: for these were they that <hi type="italic">continued with him in his temptations,</hi> and followed him whithersoever he went; and they lost nothing by their adherence to him, but gained experience abundantly. Observe, <div eID="gen27461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27462" type="x-p"/> 1. The question which the disciples put to their Master upon this blind man's case, <reference osisRef="John.9.2">v. 2</reference>. When Christ looked upon him, they had an eye to him too; Christ's compassion should kindle ours. It is probable that Christ told them this poor man was born blind, or they knew it by common fame; but they did not move Christ to heal him. Instead of this, they started a very odd question concerning him: <hi type="italic">Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?</hi> Now this question of theirs was, <div eID="gen27462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Uncharitably censorious.</hi> They take it for granted that this extraordinary calamity was the punishment of some uncommon wickedness, and that this man was a sinner above all men that dwelt at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.4">Luke xiii. 4</reference>. For the <hi type="italic">barbarous people</hi> to infer, <hi type="italic">Surely this man is a murderer,</hi> was not so strange; but it was <hi type="italic">inexcusable</hi> in them, who knew the scriptures, who had read that <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all,</hi> and knew that it was adjudged in Job's case that the greatest sufferers are not <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> to be looked upon as the greatest sinners. The grace of repentance calls our own afflictions <hi type="italic">punishments,</hi> but the grace of charity calls the afflictions of others <hi type="italic">trials,</hi> unless the contrary is very evident. <div eID="gen27463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27464" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was <hi type="italic">unnecessarily curious.</hi> Concluding this calamity to be inflicted for some very heinous crime, they ask, <hi type="italic">Who were the criminals, this man or his parents?</hi> And what was this to them? Or what good would it do them to know it? We are apt to be more inquisitive concerning other people's sins than concerning our own; whereas, it is more our concern to know wherefore God contends with us than wherefore he contends with others; for to judge ourselves is our sin. They enquire, [1.] Whether this man was punished thus for some sin of his own, either committed or foreseen before his birth. Some think that the disciples were tainted with the Pythagorean notion of the <hi type="italic">pre-existence</hi> of souls, and their <hi type="italic">transmigration</hi> from one body to another. Was this man's soul condemned to the dungeon of this blind body to punish it for some great sin committed in another body which it had before animated? The Pharisees seem to have had the same opinion of his case when they said, <hi type="italic">Thou wast altogether born in sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.34">v. 34</reference>), as if all those, and those only, were born in sin whom nature had <hi type="italic">stigmatized.</hi> Or, [2.] Whether he was punished for the wickedness of his parents, which God sometimes <hi type="italic">visits upon the children.</hi> It is a good reason why parents should take heed of sin, lest their children smart for it when they are gone. Let not us thus be cruel to our own, as the <hi type="italic">ostrich in the wilderness.</hi> Perhaps the disciples asked this, not as believing that this was the punishment of some actual sin of his own or his parents, but Christ having intimated to another patient that his sin was the cause of this impotency (<reference osisRef="John.5.14">ch. v. 14</reference>), "Master," say they, "whose sin is the cause of this impotency?" Being at a loss what construction to put upon this providence, they desire to be informed. The equity of God's dispensations is always certain, for <hi type="italic">his righteousness is as the great mountains,</hi> but not always to be accounted for, for his <hi type="italic">judgments are a great deep.</hi> <div eID="gen27464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27465" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's answer to this question. He was always <hi type="italic">apt to teach,</hi> and to rectify his disciples' mistakes. <div eID="gen27465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27466" type="x-p"/> (1.) He gives the reason of this poor man's blindness: "<hi type="italic">Neither has this man sinned nor his parents,</hi> but he was born blind, and has continued so to this day, that now at last <hi type="italic">the works of God should be made manifest in him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="John.9.3">v. 3</reference>. Here Christ, who perfectly knew the secret springs of the divine counsels, told them two things concerning such uncommon calamities:—[1.] That they are not always inflicted as punishments of sin. The sinfulness of the whole race of mankind does indeed justify God in all the miseries of human life; so that those who have the least share of them must say that God is <hi type="italic">kind,</hi> and those who have the largest share must not say that he is <hi type="italic">unjust;</hi> but many are made much more <hi type="italic">miserable</hi> than others in this life who are not at all more <hi type="italic">sinful.</hi> Not but that this man was a sinner, and his parents sinners, but is was not any uncommon guilt that God had an eye to in inflicting this upon him. Note, We must take heed of judging any to be great sinners merely because they are great sufferers, lest we be found, not only <hi type="italic">persecuting those whom God has smitten</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>), but accusing those whom he has justified, and <hi type="italic">condemning</hi> those for whom <hi type="italic">Christ died,</hi> which is daring and dangerous, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.33-Rom.8.34">Rom. viii. 33, 34</reference>. [2.] That they are sometimes intended purely <hi type="italic">for the glory of God,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">manifesting of his works.</hi> God has a sovereignty over all his creatures and an exclusive right in them, and may make them serviceable to his glory in such a way as he thinks fit, in doing or suffering; and if God be glorified, either by us or in us, we were not made <hi type="italic">in vain.</hi> This man was <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> and it was worth while for him to be so, and to continue thus long dark, <hi type="italic">that the works of God might be manifest in him.</hi> That is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the <hi type="italic">attributes of God</hi> might be made manifest in him: his justice in making sinful man liable to such grievous calamities; his ordinary power and goodness in supporting a poor man under such a grievous and tedious affliction, especially that his extraordinary power and goodness might be manifested in curing him. Note, The difficulties of providence, otherwise unaccountable, may be resolved into this—God intends in them to <hi type="italic">show himself,</hi> to declare his glory, to make himself to be taken notice of. Those who regard him not in the ordinary course of things are sometimes alarmed by things extraordinary. How contentedly then may a good man be a <hi type="italic">loser in his comforts,</hi> while he is sure that thereby God will be one way or other a <hi type="italic">gainer in his glory! Secondly,</hi> That the counsels of God concerning the Redeemer might be manifested in him. He was <hi type="italic">born blind</hi> that our Lord Jesus might have the honour of <hi type="italic">curing him,</hi> and might therein prove himself sent of God to be the true light to the world. Thus the fall of man was permitted, and the <hi type="italic">blindness</hi> that followed it, that the works of God might be manifest in <hi type="italic">opening the eyes of the blind.</hi> It was now a great while since this man was born blind, and yet it never appeared till now <hi type="italic">why</hi> he was so. Note, The intentions of Providence commonly do not appear till a great while after the event, perhaps <hi type="italic">many years</hi> after. The sentences in the book of providence are sometimes <hi type="italic">long,</hi> and you must read a great way before you can apprehend the sense of them. <div eID="gen27466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27467" type="x-p"/> (2.) He gives the reason of his own forwardness and readiness to help and heal him, <reference osisRef="John.9.4-John.9.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. It was not for ostentation, but in pursuance of his undertaking: <hi type="italic">I must work the works of him that sent me</hi> (of which this is one), <hi type="italic">while it is day,</hi> and working time; <hi type="italic">the night cometh,</hi> the period of that day, <hi type="italic">when no man can work.</hi> This is not only a reason why Christ was constant in doing good to the souls and bodies of men, but why particularly he did this, though it was the sabbath day, on which works of necessity might be done, and he proves this to be a work of necessity. <div eID="gen27467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> [1.] It was his Father's will: <hi type="italic">I must work the works of him that sent me.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The Father, when he sent his Son into the world, gave him <hi type="italic">work to do;</hi> he did not come into the world to take state, but to do business; whom God sends he employs, for he sends none to be idle. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The works Christ had to do were the <hi type="italic">works of him that sent him,</hi> not only appointed <hi type="italic">by him,</hi> but done <hi type="italic">for him;</hi> he was a worker together with God. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He was pleased to lay himself under the strongest obligations to do the business he was sent about: I <hi type="italic">must work.</hi> He <hi type="italic">engaged his heart,</hi> in the covenant of redemption, to <hi type="italic">draw near,</hi> and <hi type="italic">approach</hi> to God as Mediator, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. Shall we be willing to be <hi type="italic">loose,</hi> when Christ was willing to be <hi type="italic">bound? Fourthly,</hi> Christ, having laid himself under obligations to do his work, laid out himself with the utmost vigour and industry in his work. He <hi type="italic">worked the works</hi> he had to do; did <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ergazesthai ta erga</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">made a business of that which was his business.</hi> It is not enough to look at our work, and talk over it, but we must work it. <div eID="gen27468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27469" type="x-p"/> [2.] Now was his opportunity: I must work <hi type="italic">while it is day,</hi> while the time lasts which is appointed to work in, and while the light lasts which is given to work by. Christ himself had <hi type="italic">his day. First,</hi> All the business of the <hi type="italic">mediatorial kingdom</hi> was to be done within the limits of time, and in this world; for at the end of the world, when time shall be no more, the <hi type="italic">kingdom shall be delivered up to God, even the Father,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mystery of God finished. Secondly,</hi> all the work he had to do <hi type="italic">in his own person</hi> here on earth was to be done <hi type="italic">before his death;</hi> the time of his living in this world is <hi type="italic">the day</hi> here spoken of. Note, The time of our life is our day, in which it concerns us to do the <hi type="italic">work of the day.</hi> Day-time is the proper season for work (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.22-Ps.104.23">Ps. civ. 22, 23</reference>); during the day of life we must be busy, not waste <hi type="italic">day-time,</hi> nor play by <hi type="italic">day-light;</hi> it will be time enough to rest when our day is done, for it is <hi type="italic">but a day.</hi> <div eID="gen27469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27470" type="x-p"/> [3.] The period of his opportunity was at hand, and therefore he would be busy; <hi type="italic">The night comes when no man can work.</hi> Note, The consideration of our death approaching should quicken us to improve all the opportunities of life, both for doing and getting good. <hi type="italic">The night comes,</hi> it will come certainly, may come suddenly, is coming nearer and nearer. We cannot compute how nigh our sun is, it may go down at noon; nor can we promise ourselves a twilight between the day of life and the night of death. When the night comes we <hi type="italic">cannot work,</hi> because the light afforded us to work by is <hi type="italic">extinguished;</hi> the grave is a land of darkness, and our work cannot be done <hi type="italic">in the dark.</hi> And, besides, our time allotted us for our work will then have <hi type="italic">expired;</hi> when our Master tied us to duty he tied us to time too; when night comes, <hi type="italic">call the labourers;</hi> we must then <hi type="italic">show our work,</hi> and receive according to the things done. In the world of retribution we are no longer probationers; it is too late to <hi type="italic">bid</hi> when the inch of candle is <hi type="italic">dropped.</hi> Christ uses this as an argument with himself to be diligent, though he had no opposition from within to struggle with; much more need have we to work upon our hearts these and the like considerations to quicken us. <div eID="gen27470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27471" type="x-p"/> [4.] His business in the world was to enlighten it (<reference osisRef="John.9.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">As long as I am in the world,</hi> and that will not be long, <hi type="italic">I am the light of the world.</hi> He had said this before, <reference osisRef="John.8.12">ch. viii. 12</reference>. He is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> that has not only light in his wings for those that can see, but healing in his wings, or beams, for those that are blind and cannot see, therein far exceeding in virtue that great light which rules <hi type="italic">by day.</hi> Christ would cure this blind man, the representative of a blind world, because he came to be <hi type="italic">the light of the world,</hi> not only to give <hi type="italic">light,</hi> but to give <hi type="italic">sight.</hi> Now this gives us, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A great <hi type="italic">encouragement</hi> to come to him, as a guiding, quickening, refreshing light. To whom should we look but to him? Which way should we turn our eyes, but to the light? We partake of the sun's light, and so we may of Christ's grace, without money and without price. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A good <hi type="italic">example</hi> of usefulness in the world. What Christ saith of himself, he saith of his disciples: <hi type="italic">You are lights in the world,</hi> and, if so, <hi type="italic">Let your light shine.</hi> What were candles made for but to burn? <div eID="gen27471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27472" type="x-p"/> III. The manner of the cure of the blind man, <reference osisRef="John.9.6-John.9.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. The circumstances of the miracle are singular, and no doubt significant. <hi type="italic">When he had thus spoken</hi> for the instruction of his disciples, and the opening of their understandings, he addressed himself to the opening of the blind man's eyes. He did not defer it till he could do it either more privately, for his greater safety, or more publicly, for his greater honour, or till the sabbath was past, when it would give less offence. What good we have opportunity of doing we should do quickly; he that will never do a good work till there is nothing to be objected against it will leave many a good work for ever undone, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>. In the cure observe, <div eID="gen27472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27473" type="x-p"/> 1. The preparation of the eye-salve. Christ <hi type="italic">spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle.</hi> He could have cured him with a word, as he did others, but he chose to do it in this way to show that he is not <hi type="italic">tied</hi> to any method. He made clay of his own spittle, because there was no water near; and he would teach us not to be nice or curious, but, when we have at any time occasion, to be willing to take up with that which is <hi type="italic">next hand,</hi> if it will but serve the turn. Why should we <hi type="italic">go about</hi> for that which may as well be had and done a <hi type="italic">nearer way?</hi> Christ's making use of his own spittle intimates that there is healing virtue in every thing that belongs to Christ; clay made of Christ's spittle was much more precious than the balm of Gilead. <div eID="gen27473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27474" type="x-p"/> 2. The application of it to the place: <hi type="italic">He anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.</hi> Or, as the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">He spread</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epechrise</hi></hi>), <hi type="italic">he daubed the clay upon the eyes of the blind man,</hi> like a tender physician; he did it himself with his own hand, though the patient was a beggar. Now Christ did this, (1.) To magnify his power in making a blind man to see by that method which one would think more likely to make a seeing man blind. Daubing clay on the eyes would <hi type="italic">close them</hi> up, but never <hi type="italic">open them.</hi> Note, The power of God often works by contraries; and he makes men feel their own blindness before he gives them sight. (2.) To give an intimation that it was his mighty hand, the very same that at first made man out of <hi type="italic">the clay;</hi> for by him God <hi type="italic">made the worlds,</hi> both the great world, and man the little world. Man was <hi type="italic">formed out of the clay,</hi> and moulded like the clay, and here Christ used the same materials to give sight to the body that at first he used to give being to it. (3.) To represent and typify the healing and opening of the eyes of the mind by the grace of Jesus Christ. The design of the gospel is to <hi type="italic">open men's eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 18</reference>. Now the eye-salve that does the work is of Christ's preparing; it is made up, not as this, of his spittle, but of his blood, the blood and water that came out of his pierced side; we must come to Christ for <hi type="italic">the eye-salve,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>. He only is <hi type="italic">able,</hi> and he only is <hi type="italic">appointed,</hi> to make it up, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 18</reference>. The means used in this work are very weak and unlikely, and are made effectual only by the power of Christ; when a dark world was to be enlightened, and nations of blind souls were to have their eyes opened, God chose the <hi type="italic">foolish things, and weak, and despised,</hi> for the doing of it. And the method Christ takes is first to make men feel themselves blind, as this poor man did whose eyes were daubed with clay, and then to give them sight. Paul in his conversion was <hi type="italic">struck blind</hi> for three days, and then the <hi type="italic">scales fell from his eyes.</hi> The way prescribed for getting spiritual wisdom is, <hi type="italic">Let a man become a fool, that he may be wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. We must be made uneasy with our blindness, as this man here, and then healed. <div eID="gen27474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> 3. The directions given to the patient, <reference osisRef="John.9.7">v. 7</reference>. His physician said to him, <hi type="italic">Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.</hi> Not that this washing was needful to effect the cure; but, (1.) Christ would hereby try his obedience, and whether he would with an implicit faith obey the orders of one he was so much a stranger to. (2.) He would likewise try how he stood affected to the tradition of the elders, which taught, and perhaps had taught him (for many that are <hi type="italic">blind</hi> are very knowing), that it was not lawful to wash the eyes, no not with spittle medicinally, on the sabbath day, much less to go to a pool of water to wash them. (3.) He would hereby represent the method of spiritual healing, in which, though the effect is owing purely to his power and grace, there is duty to be done by us. Go, search the scriptures, attend upon the ministry, converse with the wise; this is like washing in the pool of Siloam. Promised graces must be expected in the way of instituted ordinances. The waters of baptism were to those who had been trained up in darkness like the pool of Siloam, in which they might not only wash and be clean, but <hi type="italic">wash, and have their eyes opened.</hi> Hence they that were baptized are said to be <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">photisthentes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">enlightened;</hi> and the ancients called baptism <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">photismos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">illumination.</hi> Concerning the pool of Siloam observe, [1.] That it was supplied with water from mount Zion, so that these were the <hi type="italic">waters of the sanctuary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">Ps. xlvi. 4</reference>), living waters, which were <hi type="italic">healing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">Ezek. xlvii. 9</reference>. [2.] That the waters of Siloam had of old signified the throne and kingdom of the house of David, pointing at the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa. viii. 6</reference>), and the Jews who <hi type="italic">refused the waters of Shiloah,</hi> Christ's doctrine and law, and rejoiced in the tradition of the elders. Christ would try this man, whether he would cleave to the waters of Siloam or no. [3.] The evangelist takes notice of the signification of the name, its being interpreted <hi type="italic">sent.</hi> Christ is often called the <hi type="italic">sent of God,</hi> the Messenger of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal. iii. 1</reference>); so that when Christ sent him to the pool of Siloam he did in effect send him to himself; for Christ is <hi type="italic">all in all</hi> to the healing of souls. Christ as a prophet directs us to himself as a priest. <hi type="italic">Go, wash in the fountain opened,</hi> a fountain of life, not a <hi type="italic">pool.</hi> <div eID="gen27475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> 4. The patient's obedience to these directions: <hi type="italic">He went his way therefore,</hi> probably led by some friend or other; or perhaps he was so well acquainted with Jerusalem that he could find the way himself. Nature often supplies the want of sight with an uncommon sagacity; and <hi type="italic">he washed his eyes;</hi> probably the disciples, or some stander by, informed him that he who bade him do it was that Jesus whom he had heard so much of, else he would not have gone, at his bidding, on that which looked so much like a fool's errand; in confidence of Christ's power, as well as in obedience to his command, he went, and washed. <div eID="gen27476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> 5. The cure effected: <hi type="italic">He came seeing.</hi> There is more glory in this concise narrative, <hi type="italic">He went</hi> and <hi type="italic">washed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">came seeing,</hi> than in Cæsar's <hi type="italic">Veni, vidi, vici—I came, I saw, I conquered.</hi> When the clay was <hi type="italic">washed off</hi> from his eyes, all the other impediments were removed with it; so when the pangs and struggles of the new birth are over, and the pains and terrors of conviction past, the bands of sin fly off with them, and a glorious light and liberty succeed. See here an instance, (1.) Of the power of Christ. What cannot <hi type="italic">he</hi> do who could not only do <hi type="italic">this,</hi> but do it <hi type="italic">thus?</hi> With a lump of clay laid on either eye, and washed off again, he couched those cataracts immediately which the most skilful oculist, with the finest instrument and the most curious hand, could not remove. No doubt this is <hi type="italic">he that should come,</hi> for by him the blind receive their sight. (2.) It is an instance of the virtue of faith and obedience. This man let Christ do what <hi type="italic">he</hi> pleased, and did what he appointed him to do, and so was cured. Those that would be healed by Christ must be ruled by him. He <hi type="italic">came back</hi> from the pool to his neighbours and acquaintance, wondering and wondered at; he came <hi type="italic">seeing.</hi> This represents the benefit gracious souls find in attending on instituted ordinances, according to Christ's appointment; they have gone to the pool of Siloam weak, and have come away strengthened; have gone doubting, and come away satisfied; have gone mourning, and come away rejoicing; have gone trembling, and come away triumphing; have gone <hi type="italic">blind,</hi> and come away <hi type="italic">seeing,</hi> come away singing, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa. lii. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen27477" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sight Given to One Born Blind.</title> <div sID="gen27478" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The neighbours therefore, and they which before had seen him that he was blind, said, Is not this he that sat and begged? <hi type="super">9</hi> Some said, This is he: others <hi type="italic">said,</hi> He is like him: <hi type="italic">but</hi> he said, I am <hi type="italic">he.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore said they unto him, How were thine eyes opened? <hi type="super">11</hi> He answered and said, A man that is called Jesus made clay, and anointed mine eyes, and said unto me, Go to the pool of Siloam, and wash: and I went and washed, and I received sight. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then said they unto him, Where is he? He said, I know not. <div eID="gen27478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27479" type="x-p"/> Such a wonderful event as the giving of sight to a man born blind could not but be the talk of the town, and many heeded it no more than they do other town-talk, that is but nine days' wonder; but here we are told what the neighbours said of it, for the confirmation of the matter of fact. That which at first was not believed without <hi type="italic">scrutiny</hi> may afterwards be admitted without <hi type="italic">scruple.</hi> Two things are debated in this conference about it:— <div eID="gen27479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> I. Whether this was the same man that had before been blind, <reference osisRef="John.9.8">v. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen27480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> 1. The neighbours that lived near the place where he was born and bred, and knew that he had been blind, could not but be amazed when they saw that he had his eye-sight, had it on a sudden, and perfectly; and they said, <hi type="italic">Is not this he that sat and begged?</hi> It seems, this blind man was a common beggar, being disabled to work for his living; and so discharged from the obligation of the law, that if <hi type="italic">any would not work, neither should he eat.</hi> When he could not go about, he <hi type="italic">sat;</hi> if we cannot <hi type="italic">work</hi> for God, we must <hi type="italic">sit still</hi> quietly for him. When he could not labour, his parents not being able to maintain him, he <hi type="italic">begged.</hi> Note, Those who cannot otherwise subsist must not, like the unjust steward, be <hi type="italic">ashamed to beg;</hi> let no man be ashamed of anything but sin. There are some common beggars that are objects of charity, that should be distinguished; and we must not let the bees starve for the sake of the drones or wasps that are among them. As to this man, (1.) It was well ordered by Providence that he on whom this miracle was wrought should be a common beggar, and so generally known and remarkable, by which means the truth of the miracle was better attested, and there were more to witness against those infidel Jews who would not believe <hi type="italic">that he had been blind</hi> than if he had been maintained in his father's house. (2.) It was the greater instance of Christ's condescension that he seemed (as I may say) to take more pains about the cure of a common beggar than of others. When it was for the advantage of his miracles that they should be wrought on those that were remarkable, he pitched upon those that were made so by their poverty and misery; not by their dignity. <div eID="gen27481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27482" type="x-p"/> 2. In answer to this inquiry, (1.) Some said, <hi type="italic">This is he,</hi> the very same man; and these are witnesses to the truth of the miracle, for they had long known him stone-blind. (2.) Others, who could not think it possible that a man born blind should thus on a sudden receive his sight, for that reason, and no other, said, <hi type="italic">He is not he, but is like him,</hi> and so, by their confession, if it be he, it is a great miracle that is wrought upon him. Hence we may take occasion to think, [1.] Of the wisdom and power of Providence in ordering such a universal variety of the faces of men and women, so that no two are so alike but that they may be distinguished, which is necessary to society, and commerce, and the administration of justice. And, [2.] Of the wonderful change which the converting grace of God makes upon some who before were very wicked and vile, but are thereby so universally and visibly altered that one would not take them to be the same persons. <div eID="gen27482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27483" type="x-p"/> 3. This controversy was soon decided by the man himself: <hi type="italic">He said, I am he,</hi> the very man that so lately sat and begged; "I am he that was blind, and was an object of the charity of men, but now see, and am a monument of the mercy and grace of God." We do not find that the neighbours appealed to him in this matter, but he, hearing the debate, interposed, and put an end to it. It is a piece of justice we owe to our neighbours to rectify their mistakes, and to set things before them, as far as we are able, in a true light. Applying it spiritually, it teaches us that those who are savingly enlightened by the grace of God should be ready to own what they were before that blessed change was wrought, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13-1Tim.1.14">1 Tim. i. 13, 14</reference>. <div eID="gen27483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27484" type="x-p"/> II. How he came to have his eyes opened, <reference osisRef="John.9.10-John.9.12">v. 10-12</reference>. They will now turn aside, and <hi type="italic">see this great sight,</hi> and enquire further concerning it. He did not <hi type="italic">sound a trumpet</hi> when he did these alms, nor perform his cures <hi type="italic">upon a stage;</hi> and yet, like a city upon a hill, they could not be hid. Two things these neighbours enquire after:— <div eID="gen27484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27485" type="x-p"/> 1. The manner of the cure: <hi type="italic">How were thine eyes opened?</hi> The works of the Lord being great, they ought to be <hi type="italic">sought out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">Ps. cxi. 2</reference>. It is good to observe the way and method of God's works, and they will appear the more wonderful. We may apply it spiritually; it is strange that blind eyes should be opened, but more strange when we consider how they are opened; how weak the means are that are used, and how strong the opposition that is conquered. In answer to this enquiry the poor man gives them a plain and full account of the matter: <hi type="italic">A man that is called Jesus made clay,—and I received sight.</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, Those who have experienced special instances of God's power and goodness, in temporal or spiritual things, should be ready upon all occasions to communicate their experiences, for the glory of God and the instruction and encouragement of others. See David's collection of his experiences, his own and others', <reference osisRef="Ps.34.4-Ps.34.6">Ps. xxxiv. 4-6</reference>. It is a debt we owe to our benefactor, and to our brethren. God's favours are lost <hi type="italic">upon</hi> us, when they are lost <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> and go no further. <div eID="gen27485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27486" type="x-p"/> 2. The author of it (<reference osisRef="John.9.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where is he?</hi> Some perhaps asked this question out of curiosity. "Where is he, that we may see him?" A man that did such cures as these might well be a show, which one would go a good way for the sight of. Others, perhaps, asked out of ill-will. "Where is he, that we may <hi type="italic">seize</hi> him?" There was a proclamation out for the discovering and apprehending of him (<reference osisRef="John.11.57">ch. xi. 57</reference>); and the unthinking crowd, in spite of all reason and equity, will have ill thoughts of those that are put into an ill name. Some, we hope, asked this question out of <hi type="italic">good-will.</hi> "Where is he, that we may be acquainted with him? Where is he, that we may come to him, and share in the favours he is so free of?" In answer to this, he could say nothing: <hi type="italic">I know not.</hi> As soon as Christ had sent him to the pool of Siloam, it should seem, he withdrew immediately (as he did, <reference osisRef="John.5.13">ch. v. 13</reference>), and did not stay till the man returned, as if he either doubted of the effect or waited for the man's thanks. Humble souls take more pleasure in <hi type="italic">doing good</hi> than in hearing of it again; it will be time enough to hear of it in the <hi type="italic">resurrection of the just.</hi> The man had never seen Jesus, for by the time that he had gained his sight he had lost his Physician; and he asked, it is probable, <hi type="italic">Where is he?</hi> None of all the new and surprising objects that presented themselves could be so grateful to him as one sight of Christ, but as yet he knew no more of him than that he was called, and rightly called, <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour.</hi> Thus in the work of grace wrought upon the soul we see the change, but see not the hand that makes it; for the way of the Spirit is like that of the wind, which thou hearest the sound of, but canst not tell <hi type="italic">whence it comes nor whither it goes.</hi>

<div eID="gen27486" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cavilling of the Pharisees; The Cavilling of the Pharisees Refuted.</title> <div sID="gen27487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> They brought to the Pharisees him that aforetime was blind. <hi type="super">14</hi> And it was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and opened his eyes. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then again the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. He said unto them, He put clay upon mine eyes, and I washed, and do see. 16 Therefore said some of the Pharisees, This man is not of God, because he keepeth not the sabbath day. Others said, How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles? And there was a division among them. <hi type="super">17</hi> They say unto the blind man again, What sayest thou of him, that he hath opened thine eyes? He said, He is a prophet. <hi type="super">18</hi> But the Jews did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and received his sight, until they called the parents of him that had received his sight. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they asked them, saying, Is this your son, who ye say was born blind? how then doth he now see? <hi type="super">20</hi> His parents answered them and said, We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind: 21 But by what means he now seeth, we know not; or who hath opened his eyes, we know not: he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself. <hi type="super">22</hi> These <hi type="italic">words</hi> spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. <hi type="super">23</hi> Therefore said his parents, He is of age; ask him. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then again called they the man that was blind, and said unto him, Give God the praise: we know that this man is a sinner. <hi type="super">25</hi> He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner <hi type="italic">or no,</hi> I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see. <hi type="super">26</hi> Then said they to him again, What did he to thee? how opened he thine eyes? <hi type="super">27</hi> He answered them, I have told you already, and ye did not hear: wherefore would ye hear <hi type="italic">it</hi> again? will ye also be his disciples? <hi type="super">28</hi> Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple; but we are Moses' disciples. <hi type="super">29</hi> We know that God spake unto Moses: <hi type="italic">as for</hi> this <hi type="italic">fellow,</hi> we know not from whence he is. <hi type="super">30</hi> The man answered and said unto them, Why herein is a marvellous thing, that ye know not from whence he is, and <hi type="italic">yet</hi> he hath opened mine eyes. <hi type="super">31</hi> Now we know that God heareth not sinners: but if any man be a worshipper of God, and doeth his will, him he heareth. <hi type="super">32</hi> Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind. <hi type="super">33</hi> If this man were not of God, he could do nothing. <hi type="super">34</hi> They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out. <div eID="gen27487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27488" type="x-p"/> One would have expected that such a miracle as Christ wrought upon the blind man would have settled his reputation, and silenced and shamed all opposition, but it had the contrary effect; instead of being embraced as a prophet for it, he is prosecuted as a criminal. <div eID="gen27488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27489" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the information that was given in to the Pharisees concerning this matter: <hi type="italic">They brought to the Pharisees him that aforetime was blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.13">v. 13</reference>. They brought him to the great sanhedrim, which consisted chiefly of Pharisees, at least the Pharisees in the sanhedrim were most active against Christ. 1. Some think that those who brought this man to the Pharisees did it with a <hi type="italic">good design,</hi> to show them that this Jesus, whom they persecuted, was not what they represented him, but really a great man, and one that gave considerable proofs of a divine mission. What hath convinced us of the truth and excellency of religion, and hath removed our prejudices against it, we should be forward, as we have opportunity, to offer to others for their conviction. 2. It should seem, rather, that they did it with an <hi type="italic">ill design,</hi> to exasperate the Pharisees the more against Christ, and there was no need of this, for they were bitter enough of themselves. They brought him with such a suggestion as that in <reference osisRef="John.11.47-John.11.48">ch. xi. 47, 48</reference>, <hi type="italic">If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him.</hi> Note, Those rulers that are of a persecuting spirit shall never want ill instruments about them, that will blow the coals, and make them worse. <div eID="gen27489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27490" type="x-p"/> II. The ground which was pretended for this information, and the colour given to it. That which is good was never maligned but under the imputation of something evil. And the crime objected here (<reference osisRef="John.9.14">v. 14</reference>) was that <hi type="italic">it was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and opened his eyes.</hi> The profanation of the sabbath day is certainly wicked, and gives a man a very ill character; but the traditions of the Jews had made that to be a violation of the law of the sabbath which was far from being so. Many a time this matter was contested between Christ and the Jews, that it might be settled for the benefit of the church in all ages. But it may be asked, "Why would Christ not only work miracles on the sabbath day, but work them in such a manner as he knew would give offence to the Jews? When he had healed the impotent man, why should he bid him carry his bed? Could he not have cured this blind man without making clay?" I answer, 1. He would not seem to yield to the usurped power of the scribes and Pharisees. Their government was illegal, their impositions were arbitrary, and their zeal for the rituals consumed the substantials of religion; and therefore Christ would not <hi type="italic">give place</hi> to them, <hi type="italic">by subjection, no not for an hour.</hi> Christ was made under the law of God, but not under their law. 2. He did it that he might, both by word and action, expound the law of the fourth commandment, and vindicate it from their corrupt glosses, and so teach us that a weekly sabbath is to be <hi type="italic">perpetually</hi> observed in the church, one day in seven (for what need was there to explain that law, if it must be presently abrogated?) and that it is not to be so <hi type="italic">ceremonially</hi> observed by us as it was by the Jews? Works of necessity and mercy are allowed, and the sabbath-rest to be kept, not so much for its own sake as in order to the sabbath-work. 3. Christ chose to work his cures on the sabbath day to dignify and sanctify the day, and to intimate that spiritual cures should be wrought mostly on the Christian sabbath day. How many blind eyes have been opened by the preaching of the gospel, that blessed eye-salve, on the Lord's day! How many impotent souls cured on that day! <div eID="gen27490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27491" type="x-p"/> III. The trial and examination of this matter by the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="John.9.15">v. 15</reference>. So much passion, prejudice, and ill-humour, and so little reason, appear here, that the discourse is nothing but crossing questions. One would think, when a man in these circumstances was brought before them, they would have been so taken up in admiring the miracle, and congratulating the happiness of the poor man, that they could not have been peevish with him. But their enmity to Christ had divested them of all manner of humanity, and divinity too. Let us see how they teased this man. <div eID="gen27491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27492" type="x-p"/> 1. They interrogated him concerning the cure itself. <div eID="gen27492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27493" type="x-p"/> (1.) They doubted whether he had indeed been <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> and demanded proof of that which even the prosecutors had acknowledged (<reference osisRef="John.9.18">v. 18</reference>): They <hi type="italic">did not believe,</hi> that is, they would not, that he was <hi type="italic">born blind.</hi> Men that seek occasion to quarrel with the clearest truths may find it if they please; and they that resolve to <hi type="italic">hold fast deceit</hi> will never want a handle to hold it by. This was not a prudent caution, but a prejudiced infidelity. However, it was a good way that they took for the clearing of this: <hi type="italic">They called the parents of the man who had received his sight.</hi> This they did in hopes to disprove the miracle. These parents were poor and timorous, and if they had said that they could not be sure that this was their son, or that it was only some weakness or dimness in his sight that he had been born with, which if they had been able to get help for him might have been cured long since, or had otherwise prevaricated, for fear of the court, the Pharisees had gained their point, had robbed Christ of the honour of this miracle, which would have lessened the reputation of all the rest. But God so ordered and overruled this counsel of theirs that it turned to the more effectual proof of the miracle, and left them under a necessity of being either convinced or confounded. Now in this part of the examination we have, <div eID="gen27493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27494" type="x-p"/> [1.] The questions that were put to them (<reference osisRef="John.9.19">v. 19</reference>): They <hi type="italic">asked them</hi> in an imperious threatening way, "<hi type="italic">Is this your son?</hi> Dare you swear to it? <hi type="italic">Do you say he was born blind?</hi> Are you sure of it? Or did he but pretend to be so, to have an excuse for his begging? <hi type="italic">How then doth he now see?</hi> That is impossible, and therefore you had better unsay it." Those who cannot bear the light of truth do all they can to <hi type="italic">eclipse</hi> it, and hinder the discovery of it. Thus the <hi type="italic">managers of evidence,</hi> or mismanagers rather, lead witnesses out of the way, and teach them how to conceal or disguise the truth, and so involve themselves in a double guilt, like that of Jeroboam, who sinned, and made Israel to sin. <div eID="gen27494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27495" type="x-p"/> [2.] Their answers to these interrogatories, in which, <div eID="gen27495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27496" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They fully attest that which they could safely say in this matter; <hi type="italic">safely,</hi> that is, upon their own knowledge, and <hi type="italic">safely,</hi> that is, without running themselves into a <hi type="italic">premunire</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">We know that this is our son</hi> (for they were daily conversant with him, and had such a natural affection to him as the true mother had, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.26">1 Kings iii. 26</reference>, which made them know it was <hi type="italic">their own</hi>); and we know that he was <hi type="italic">born blind.</hi> They had reason to know it, inasmuch as it had cost them many a sad thought, and many a careful troublesome hour, about him. How often had they looked upon him with grief, and lamented their child's blindness more than all the burdens and inconveniences of their poverty, and wished he had never been born, rather than be born to such an uncomfortable life! Those who are ashamed of their children, or any of their relations, because of their bodily infirmities, may take a reproof from <hi type="italic">these</hi> parents, who freely owned, This is <hi type="italic">our son,</hi> though he was <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> and lived upon alms. <div eID="gen27496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They cautiously decline giving any evidence concerning his cure; partly because they were not themselves eye-witnesses of it, and could say nothing to it <hi type="italic">of their own knowledge;</hi> and partly because they found it was a <hi type="italic">tender point,</hi> and would not bear to be meddled with. And therefore, having owned that he was <hi type="italic">their son</hi> and was <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> further these deponents say not. <div eID="gen27497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27498" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Observe how warily they express themselves (<reference osisRef="John.9.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">By what means he now seeth we know not,</hi> or <hi type="italic">who has opened his eyes we know not,</hi> otherwise than by <hi type="italic">hearsay;</hi> we can give no account either by what means or by whose hand it was done." See how the wisdom of this world teaches men to <hi type="italic">trim</hi> the matter in critical junctures. Christ was accused as a sabbath-breaker, and as an imposter. Now these parents of the blind man, though they were not eye-witnesses of the cure, were yet fully assured of it, and were bound in gratitude to have borne their testimony to the honour of the Lord Jesus, who had done their son so great a kindness; but they had not courage to do it, and then thought it might serve to atone for their not appearing in favour of him that they said nothing to his prejudice; whereas, in the day of trial, he that is not <hi type="italic">apparently</hi> for Christ is justly looked upon as <hi type="italic">really against</hi> him, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.23">Luke xi. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.8.38">Mark viii. 38</reference>. That they might not be further urged in this matter, they refer themselves and the court to him: <hi type="italic">He is of age, ask him, he shall speak for himself.</hi> This implies that while children are not of age (while they are <hi type="italic">infants,</hi> such as cannot speak) it is incumbent upon their parents to <hi type="italic">speak for them,</hi> speak to God for them in prayer, speak to the church for them in baptism; but, when they are of age, it is fit that they should be asked whether they be willing to stand to that which their parents did for them, and let them speak for themselves. This man, though he was <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> seems to have been of quick understanding above many, which enabled him to speak for himself better than his friends could speak for him. Thus God often by a kind providence makes up in the mind what is wanting in the body, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23-1Cor.12.24">1 Cor. xii. 23, 24</reference>. His parents turning them over to him was only to save themselves from trouble, and expose him; whereas they that had so great an interest in his <hi type="italic">mercies</hi> had reason to embark with him in his <hi type="italic">hazards</hi> for the honour of that Jesus who had done so much for them. <div eID="gen27498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27499" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> See the reason why they were so cautious (<reference osisRef="John.9.22-John.9.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because they feared the Jews.</hi> It was not because they would put an honour upon their son, by making him his own advocate, or because they would have the matter cleared by the <hi type="italic">best hand,</hi> but because they would shift trouble off from themselves, as most people are in care to do, no matter on whom they throw it. Near is my friend, and near is my child, and perhaps near is my religion, but <hi type="italic">nearer is myself—Proximus egomet mihi.</hi> But Christianity teaches another lesson, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.24">1 Cor. x. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.8.6">Esth. viii. 6</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen27499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27500" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The <hi type="italic">late law</hi> which the sanhedrim had made. It was agreed and enacted by their authority that, if any man within their jurisdiction did <hi type="italic">confess</hi> that Jesus <hi type="italic">was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27501" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The crime designed to be punished, and so prevented, by this statute, and that was embracing Jesus of Nazareth as the promised Messiah, and manifesting this by any overt-act, which amounted to a confessing of him. They themselves did expect a Messiah, but they could by no means bear to think that this Jesus should be he, nor admit the question whether he were or no, for two reasons:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because his precepts were all so contrary to their traditional <hi type="italic">laws.</hi> The spiritual worship he prescribed overthrew their formalities; nor did any thing more effectually destroy their singularity and narrow-spiritedness than that universal charity which he taught; humility and mortification, repentance and self-denial, were lessons new to them, and sounded harsh and strange in their ears. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because his promises and appearances were so contrary to their traditional hopes. They expected a Messiah in outward pomp and splendour, that should not only free the nation from the Roman yoke, but advance the grandeur of the sanhedrim, and make all the members of it princes and peers: and now to hear of a Messiah whose outward circumstances were all mean and poor, whose first appearance and principal residence were in Galilee, a despised province, who never made his court to them, nor sought their favour, whose followers were neither sword-men nor gown-men, nor any men of honour, but contemptible fishermen, who proposed and promised no redemption but from sin, no consolation of Israel but what is spiritual and divine, and at the same time bade his followers expect the cross, and count upon persecution; this was such a reproach to all the ideas they had formed and filled the minds of their people with, such a blow to their power and interest, and such a disappointment to all their hopes, that they could never be reconciled to it, nor so much as give it a fair or patient hearing, but, right or wrong, it must be <hi type="italic">crushed.</hi> <div eID="gen27501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27502" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The penalty to be inflicted for this crime. If any should own himself a disciple of Jesus, he should be deemed and taken as an apostate from the faith of the Jewish church, and a rebel and traitor against the government of it, and should therefore be <hi type="italic">put out of the synagogue,</hi> as one that had rendered himself unworthy of the honours, and incapable of the privileges, of their church; he should be excommunicated, and expelled the commonwealth of Israel. Nor was this merely an ecclesiastical censure, which a man that made no conscience of their authority might slight, but it was, in effect, an <hi type="italic">outlawry,</hi> which excluded a man from civil commerce and deprived him of his liberty and property. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ's holy religion, from its first rise, has been opposed by penal laws made against the professors of it; as if men's consciences would otherwise <hi type="italic">naturally</hi> embrace it, this unnatural force has been put upon them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The church's artillery, when the command of it has fallen into ill hands, has often been turned against itself, and ecclesiastical censures have been made to serve a carnal secular interest. It is no new thing to see those cast out of the synagogue that were the greatest ornaments and blessings of it, and to hear those that expelled them say, <hi type="italic">The Lord be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>. Now of this edict it is said, 1. That the Jews had agreed it, or <hi type="italic">conspired</hi> it. Their consultation and communion herein were a perfect conspiracy against the crown and dignity of the Redeemer, against the Lord and his Anointed. 2. That they had already agreed it. Though he had been but a few months in any public character among them, and, one would think, in so short a time could not have made them jealous of him, yet thus early were they aware of his growing interest, and already agreed to do their utmost to suppress it. He had lately made his escape out of the temple, and, when they saw themselves baffled in their attempts to take him, they presently took this course, to make it penal for any body to own him. Thus unanimous and thus expeditious are the enemies of the church, and their counsels; but he that <hi type="italic">sits in heaven laughs at them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">has them in derision,</hi> and so may we. <div eID="gen27502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27503" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The influence which this law had upon the parents of the blind man. They declined saying any thing of Christ, and shuffled it off to their son, <hi type="italic">because they feared the Jews.</hi> Christ had incurred the frowns of the government to do their son a kindness, but they would not incur them to do him any honour. Note, <hi type="italic">The fear of man brings a snare</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">Prov. xxix. 25</reference>), and often makes people deny and disown Christ, and his truths and ways, and act against their consciences. Well, the parents have thus disentangled themselves, and are discharged from any further attendance; let us now go on with the examination of the man himself; the doubt of the Pharisees, whether he was <hi type="italic">born blind,</hi> was put out of doubt <hi type="italic">by them;</hi> and therefore, <div eID="gen27503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27504" type="x-p"/> (2.) They enquired of <hi type="italic">him</hi> concerning the <hi type="italic">manner of the cure,</hi> and made their remarks upon it, <reference osisRef="John.9.15-John.9.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27505" type="x-p"/> [1.] The same question which his neighbours had put to him <hi type="italic">now again the Pharisees asked him, how he had received his sight.</hi> This they enquired not with any sincere desire to find out the truth, by tracing the report to the original, but with a desire to find an occasion against Christ; for, if the man should relate the matter fully, they would prove Christ a sabbath-breaker; if he should vary from his former story, they would have some colour to suspect the whole to be a collusion. <div eID="gen27505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27506" type="x-p"/> [2.] The same answer, in effect, which he had before given to his neighbours, he here repeats to the Pharisees: <hi type="italic">He put clay upon mine eyes, and I washed, and do see.</hi> He does not here speak of the making of the clay, for indeed he had not seen it made. That circumstance was not essential, and might give the Pharisees most occasion against him, and therefore he waives it. In the former account he said, <hi type="italic">I washed, and received sight;</hi> but lest they should think it was only a glimpse for the present, which a heated imagination might fancy itself to have, he now says, "<hi type="italic">I do see:</hi> it is a complete and lasting cure." <div eID="gen27506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27507" type="x-p"/> [3.] The remarks made upon this story were very different, and occasioned a debate in the court, <reference osisRef="John.9.16">v. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27508" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some took this occasion to censure and condemn Christ for what he had done. Some of the Pharisees said, <hi type="italic">This man is not of God,</hi> as he pretends, <hi type="italic">because he keepeth not the sabbath day.</hi> 1. The doctrine upon which this censure is grounded is very true—that those <hi type="italic">are not of God</hi>—those pretenders to prophecy not <hi type="italic">sent of God,</hi> those pretenders to saintship not <hi type="italic">born of God</hi>—who do not <hi type="italic">keep the sabbath day.</hi> Those that are of God will <hi type="italic">keep the commandments of God;</hi> and this is his commandment, that we sanctify the sabbath. Those that are of God keep up communion with God, and delight to hear from him, and speak to him, and therefore will observe the sabbath, which is a day appointed for intercourse with heaven. The sabbath is called a <hi type="italic">sign,</hi> for the sanctifying of it is a sign of a sanctified heart, and the profaning of it a sign of a profane heart. But, 2. The application of it to our Saviour is very unjust, for he did religiously observe the sabbath day, and never in any instance violated it, never did otherwise than <hi type="italic">well</hi> on the sabbath day. He did not keep the sabbath according to the tradition of the elders and the superstitious observances of the Pharisees, but he kept it according to the command of God, and therefore, no doubt, he was of God, and his miracles proved him to be <hi type="italic">Lord also of the sabbath day.</hi> Note, much unrighteous and uncharitable judging is occasioned by men's making the rules of religion more strict than God has made them, and adding their own fancies to God's appointments, as the Jews here, in the case of sabbath-sanctification. We ourselves may forbear such and such things, on the sabbath day, as we find a distraction to us, and we do well, but we must not therefore tie up others to the same strictness.
