Every thing that we take for a rule of practice must not presently be made a rule of judgment. <div eID="gen27508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27509" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Others spoke in his favour, and very pertinently urged, <hi type="italic">How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles?</hi> It seems that even in this <hi type="italic">council of the ungodly</hi> there were some that were capable of a <hi type="italic">free thought,</hi> and were witnesses for Christ, even in the midst of his enemies. The matter of fact was plain, that this was a true miracle, the more it was searched into the more it was cleared; and this brought his former similar works to mind, and gave occasion to speak magnificently of them, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">toiauta semeia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">such great signs,</hi> so many, so evident. And the inference from it is very natural: Such things as these could never be done by a <hi type="italic">man that is a sinner,</hi> that is, not by any mere man, in his own name, and by his own power; or, rather, not by one that is a cheat or an imposter, and in that sense a a sinner; such a one may indeed show some <hi type="italic">signs and lying wonders,</hi> but not such signs and true wonders as Christ wrought. How could a man produce such divine credentials, if he had not a divine commission? Thus there was a <hi type="italic">division among them, a schism,</hi> so the word is; they clashed in their opinion, a warm debate arose, and the <hi type="italic">house divided</hi> upon it. Thus God defeats the counsels of his enemies by dividing them; and by such testimonies as these given against the malice of persecutors, and the rubs they meet with, their designs against the church are sometimes rendered ineffectual and always inexcusable. <div eID="gen27509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27510" type="x-p"/> 2. After their enquiry concerning the cure, we must observe their enquiry concerning the <hi type="italic">author</hi> of it. And here observe, <div eID="gen27510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27511" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the man said of him, in answer to their enquiry. They ask him (<reference osisRef="John.9.17">v. 17</reference>), "<hi type="italic">What sayest thou of him, seeing that he has opened thine eyes?</hi> What dost thou think of his doing this? And what idea hast thou of him that did it?" If he should speak <hi type="italic">slightly</hi> of Christ, in answer to this, as he might be tempted to do, to please them, now that he was in their hands, as his parents had done—if he should say, "I know not what to make of him; he may be a conjuror for aught I know, or some mountebank"—they would have triumphed in it. Nothing confirms Christ's enemies in their enmity to him so much as the slights put upon him by those that have passed for his friends. But, if he should speak honourably of Christ, they would prosecute him upon their new law, which did not except, no, not his own patient; they would make him an example, and so deter others from applying to Christ for cures, for which, though they came cheap from Christ, yet they would make them pay dearly. Or perhaps Christ's friends proposed to have the man's own sentiments concerning his physician, and were willing to know, since he appeared to be a sensible man, what he thought of him. Note, Those whose eyes Christ has opened know best what to say of him, and have great reason, upon all occasions, to say well of him. What think we of Christ? To this question the poor man makes a short, plain, and direct answer: "<hi type="italic">He is a prophet,</hi> he is one inspired and sent of God to preach, and work miracles, and deliver to the world a divine message." There had been no prophets among the Jews for three hundred years; yet they did not conclude that they should have no more, for they knew that he was yet to come who should <hi type="italic">seal up vision and prophecy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. It should seem, this man had not any thoughts that Christ was the Messiah, the great prophet, but one of the same rank with the other prophets. The woman of Samaria concluded he was <hi type="italic">a prophet</hi> before she had any thought of his being the Messiah (<reference osisRef="John.4.19">ch. iv. 19</reference>); so this blind man thought well of Christ according to the light he had, though he did not think well enough of him; but, being faithful in what he had already attained to, God revealed even <hi type="italic">that</hi> unto him. This poor blind beggar had a clearer judgment of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God, and saw further into the proofs of a divine mission, than the <hi type="italic">masters in Israel,</hi> that assumed an authority to judge of prophets. <div eID="gen27511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27512" type="x-p"/> (2.) What they said of him, in reply to the man's testimony. Having in vain attempted to invalidate the evidence of the fact, and finding that indeed a <hi type="italic">notable miracle was wrought,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">could not deny it,</hi> they renew their attempt to banter it, and run it down, and do all they can to shake the good opinion the man had of him that opened his eyes, and to convince him that Christ was a bad man (<reference osisRef="John.9.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give God the praise, we know that this man is a sinner.</hi> Two ways this is understood: [1.] By way of <hi type="italic">advice,</hi> to take heed of ascribing the praise of his cure to a sinful man, but to give it all to God, to whom it was due. Thus, under colour of zeal for the honour of God, they rob Christ of his honour, as those do who will not worship Christ as God, under pretence of zeal for this great truth, that there is but one God to be worshipped; whereas this is his declared will, that all men should <hi type="italic">honour the Son even as they honour the Father;</hi> and in confessing that Christ is Lord we <hi type="italic">give glory to God the Father.</hi> When God makes use of men that are sinners as instruments of good to us, we must <hi type="italic">give God the glory,</hi> for every creature is that to us which he makes it to be; and yet there is gratitude owing to the instruments. It was a good word, <hi type="italic">Give God the praise,</hi> but here it was ill used; and there seems to be this further in it, "This man is <hi type="italic">a sinner,</hi> a <hi type="italic">bad man,</hi> and therefore give the praise so much the more to God, who could work by such an instrument." [2.] By way of <hi type="italic">adjuration;</hi> so some take it. "We know (though thou dost not, who hast but lately come, as it were, into a new world) that this man is <hi type="italic">a sinner,</hi> a great impostor, and cheats the country; this we are sure of, therefore <hi type="italic">give God praise</hi>" (as Joshua said to Achan) "by making an ingenuous confession of the fraud and collusion which we are confident there is in this matter; in God's name, man, tell the truth." Thus is God's name abused in papal inquisitions, when by oaths, <hi type="italic">ex officio,</hi> they extort accusations of <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> from the <hi type="italic">innocent,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">others</hi> from the <hi type="italic">ignorant.</hi> See how basely they speak of the Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">We know that this man is a sinner,</hi> is a man of sin. In which we may observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their insolence and pride. They would not have it thought, when they asked the man what he thought of him, that they needed information; nay, they know very well that he is a sinner, and nobody can convince them of the contrary. He had challenged them to their faces (<reference osisRef="John.8.46">ch. viii. 46</reference>) to <hi type="italic">convince him of sin,</hi> and they had nothing to say; but now behind his back they speak of him as a malefactor, convicted upon the notorious evidence of the fact. Thus false accusers make up in confidence what is wanting in proof. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The injury and indignity hereby done to the Lord Jesus. When he became man, he took upon him the form not only of a <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> but of a <hi type="italic">sinner</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>), and passed for a sinner in common with the rest of mankind. Nay, he was represented as a sinner of the first magnitude, a sinner above all men; and, being <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> he despised even this shame. <div eID="gen27512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27513" type="x-p"/> 3. The debate that arose between the Pharisees and this poor man concerning Christ. They say, <hi type="italic">He is a sinner;</hi> he says, <hi type="italic">He is a prophet.</hi> As it is an encouragement to those who are concerned for the cause of Christ to hope that it shall never be lost for want of witnesses, when they find a poor blind beggar picked up from the way-side, and made a witness for Christ, to the faces of his most impudent enemies; so it is an encouragement to those who are called out to witness for Christ to find with what prudence and courage this man managed his defence, according to the promise, <hi type="italic">It shall be given you in that same hour what you shall speak.</hi> Though he had never seen Jesus, he had felt his grace. Now in the parley between the Pharisees and this poor man we may observe three steps:— <div eID="gen27513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27514" type="x-p"/> (1.) He sticks to the certain matter of fact the evidence of which they endeavour to shake. That which is doubtful is best resolved into that which is plain, and therefore, [1.] He adheres to that which to himself at least, and to his own satisfaction, was past dispute (<reference osisRef="John.9.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Whether he be a sinner or no I know not,</hi> I will not now stand to dispute, nor need I, the matter is plain, and though I should altogether hold my peace would speak for itself;" or, as it might better be rendered, "<hi type="italic">If he be a sinner, I know it not,</hi> I see no reason to say so, but the contrary; for this <hi type="italic">one thing I know,</hi> and can be more sure of than you can be of that of which you are so confident, <hi type="italic">that whereas I was blind, now I see,</hi> and therefore must not only say that he has been a good friend to me, but that he is a <hi type="italic">prophet;</hi> I am both able and bound to speak well of him." Now here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He tacitly reproves their great assurance of the ill character they gave of the blessed Jesus: "You say that you <hi type="italic">know</hi> him to be a <hi type="italic">sinner;</hi> I, who know him as well as you do, cannot give any such character." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He boldly relies upon his own experience of the power and goodness of the holy Jesus, and resolves to abide by it. There is no disputing against experience, nor arguing a man out of his senses; here is one that is properly an eyewitness of the power and grace of Christ, though he had never seen him. Note, As Christ's mercies are most valued by those that have felt the want of them, that have been blind and now see, so the most powerful and durable affections to Christ are those that arise from an experimental knowledge of him, <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.20">Acts iv. 20</reference>. The poor man does not here give a nice account of the method of the cure, nor pretend to describe it <hi type="italic">philosophically,</hi> but in short, <hi type="italic">Whereas I was blind, now I see.</hi> Thus in the work of grace in the soul, though we cannot tell when and how, by what instruments and by what steps and advances, the blessed change was wrought, yet we may take the comfort of it if we can say, through grace, "<hi type="italic">Whereas I was blind, now I see.</hi> I did live a carnal, worldly, sensual life, but, thanks be to God, it is now otherwise with me," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>. [2.] They endeavour to baffle and stifle the evidence by a needless repetition of their enquiries into it (<reference osisRef="John.9.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">What did he to thee? How opened he thine eyes?</hi> They asked these questions, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because they wanted something to say, and would rather speak <hi type="italic">impertinently</hi> than seem to be silenced or run a-ground. Thus eager disputants, that resolve they will have the last word, by such vain repetitions, to avoid the shame of being silenced, make themselves accountable for many idle words. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because they hoped, by putting the man upon repeating his evidence, to catch him tripping in it, or wavering, and then they would think they had gained a good point. <div eID="gen27514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27515" type="x-p"/> (2.) He upbraids them with their obstinate infidelity and invincible prejudices, and they revile him as a disciple of Jesus, <reference osisRef="John.9.27-John.9.29">v. 27-29</reference>, where the man is more bold with them and they are more sharp upon him than before. <div eID="gen27515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27516" type="x-p"/> [1.] The man boldly upbraids them with their wilful and unreasonable opposition to the evidence of this miracle, <reference osisRef="John.9.27">v. 27</reference>. He would not gratify them with a repetition of the story, but bravely replied, <hi type="italic">I have told you already, and you did not hear, wherefore would you hear it again, will you also be his disciples?</hi> Some think that he spoke <hi type="italic">seriously,</hi> and really expecting that they would be convinced. "He had many disciples, I will be one, will you also come in among them?" Some zealous young Christians see so much reason for religion that they are ready to think every one will presently be on their mind. But it rather seems to be spoken <hi type="italic">ironically: "Will you be his disciples?</hi> No, I know you abhor the thoughts of it; why then should you desire to hear that which will either make you his disciples or leave you inexcusable if you be not?" Those that wilfully shut their eyes against the light, as these Pharisees here did, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Make themselves contemptible and base, as these here did, who were justly exposed by this poor man for denying the conclusion, when they had nothing to object against either of the premises. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They forfeit all the benefit of further instructions and means of knowledge and conviction: they that have been told once, and <hi type="italic">would not hear,</hi> why should they be told it again? <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jer. li. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Matt.10.14">Matt. x. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They hereby <hi type="italic">receive the grace of God in vain.</hi> This implied in that, "<hi type="italic">Will you be his disciples?</hi> No, you resolve you will not; why then would you hear it again, only that you may be his accusers and persecutors?" Those who will not see cause to embrace Christ, and join with his followers, yet, one would think, should see cause enough not to hate and persecute him and them. <div eID="gen27516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27517" type="x-p"/> [2.] For this they scorn and revile him, <reference osisRef="John.9.28">v. 28</reference>. When they could not resist the wisdom and spirit by which he spoke, they broke out into a passion, and scolded him, began to call names, and give him ill language. See what Christ's faithful witnesses must expect from the adversaries of his truth and cause; let them count upon <hi type="italic">all manner of evil</hi> to be said of them, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.11">Matt. v. 11</reference>. The method commonly taken by unreasonable man is to make out with railing what is wanting in truth and reason. <div eID="gen27517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27518" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They taunted this man for his affection to Christ; they said, <hi type="italic">Thou art his disciple,</hi> as if that were reproach enough, and they could not say worse of him. "We scorn to be his disciples, and will leave that preferment to thee, and such scoundrels as thou art." They do what they can to put Christ's religion in an ill name, and to represent the profession of it as a contemptible scandalous thing. They <hi type="italic">reviled him.</hi> The Vulgate reads it, <hi type="italic">maledixerunt eum—they cursed him;</hi> and what was their curse? It was this, <hi type="italic">Be thou his disciple.</hi> "May such a curse" (saith St. Augustine here) "ever be on us and on our children!" If we take our measures of credit and disgrace from the sentiment or rather clamours of a blind deluded world, we shall <hi type="italic">glory in our shame,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">ashamed of our glory.</hi> They had no reason to call this man a <hi type="italic">disciple of</hi> Christ, he had neither seen him nor heard him preach, only he had spoken favourably of a kindness Christ had done him, and this they could not bear. <div eID="gen27518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They gloried in their relation to Moses as their Master: "<hi type="italic">We are Moses's disciples,</hi> and do not either need or desire any other teacher." Note, 1. Carnal professors of religion are very apt to trust to, and be proud of, the dignities and privileges of their profession, while they are strangers to the principles and powers of their religion. These Pharisees had before boasted of their good parentage: <hi type="italic">We are Abraham's seed;</hi> here they boast of their good education, <hi type="italic">We are Moses's disciples;</hi> as if these would save them. 2. It is sad to see how much one part of religion is opposed, under colour of zeal for another part. There was a perfect harmony between Christ and Moses; Moses prepared for Christ, and Christ perfected Moses, so that they might be disciples of Moses, and become the disciples of Christ too; and yet they here put them in opposition, nor could they have persecuted Christ but under the shelter of the abused name of Moses. Thus those who gainsay the doctrine of free grace value themselves as promoters of man's duty, <hi type="italic">We are Moses's disciples;</hi> while, on the other hand, those that cancel the obligation of the law value themselves as the assertors of free grace, and as if none were the disciples of Jesus but they; whereas, if we rightly understand the matter, we shall see God's grace and man's duty meet together and kiss and befriend each other. <div eID="gen27519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They gave some sort of reason for their adhering to Moses against Christ (<reference osisRef="John.9.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">We know that God spoke unto Moses; as for this fellow, we know not whence he is.</hi> But did they not know that among other things which God spoke unto Moses this was one, that they must expect another prophet, and further revelation of the mind of God? yet, when our Lord Jesus, pursuant to what God said to Moses, did appear, and gave sufficient proofs of his being that prophet, under pretence of sticking to the old religion, and the established church, they not only forfeited, but forsook, their own mercies. In this argument of theirs observe, 1. How impertinently they allege, in defence of their enmity to Christ, that which none of his followers ever denied: <hi type="italic">We know that God spoke unto Moses,</hi> and, thanks be to God, we know it too, more plainly to Moses than to any other of the prophets; but what then? God spoke to Moses, and does it therefore follow that Jesus is an impostor? Moses was a prophet also? Moses spoke honourably of Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.5.46">ch. v. 46</reference>), and Jesus spoke honourably of Moses (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.29">Luke xvi. 29</reference>); they were both faithful in the same house of God, Moses as a servant, Christ as a Son; therefore their pleading Moses' divine warrant in opposition to Christ's was an artifice, to make unthinking people believe it was as certain that Jesus was a false prophet as that Moses was a true one; whereas they were both true. 2. How absurdly they urge their ignorance of Christ as a reason to justify their contempt of him: <hi type="italic">As for this fellow.</hi> Thus scornfully do they speak of the blessed Jesus, as if they did not think it worth while to charge their memories with a name so inconsiderable; they express themselves with as much disdain of the Shepherd of Israel as if he had not been worthy to be <hi type="italic">set with the dogs of their flock: As for this fellow,</hi> this sorry fellow, <hi type="italic">we know not whence he is.</hi> They looked upon themselves to have the key of knowledge, that none must preach without a license first had and obtained from them, under the seal of their court. They expected that all who set up for teachers should apply to them, and give them satisfaction, which this Jesus had never done, never so far owned their power as to ask their leave, and therefore they concluded him an intruder, and one that came not in by the door: <hi type="italic">They knew not whence</hi> nor what <hi type="italic">he was,</hi> and therefore concluded him a <hi type="italic">sinner;</hi> whereas those we know little of we should judge charitably of; but proud and narrow souls will think none good but themselves, and those that are in their interest. It was not long ago that the Jews had made the contrary to this an objection against Christ (<reference osisRef="John.7.27">ch. vii. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">We know this man whence he is, but when Christ comes no man knows whence he is.</hi> Thus they could with the greatest assurance either affirm or deny the same thing, according as they saw it would serve their turn. They <hi type="italic">knew not whence he was;</hi> and whose fault was that? (1.) It is certain that they ought to have enquired. The Messiah was to appear about this time, and it concerned them to look about them, and examine every indication; but these priests, like those, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer. ii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">said not, Where is the Lord?</hi> (2.) It is certain that they might have known whence he was, might not only have known, by searching the register, that he was born in Bethlehem; but by enquiring into his doctrine, miracles, and conversation, they might have known that he was sent of God, and had better orders, a better commission, and far better instructions, than any they could give him. See the absurdity of infidelity. Men will not know the doctrine of Christ because they are resolved they will not believe it, and then pretend they do not believe it because they do not know it. Such ignorance and unbelief, which support one another, aggravate one another. <div eID="gen27520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27521" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reasons with them concerning this matter, and they excommunicate him. <div eID="gen27521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27522" type="x-p"/> [1.] The poor man, finding that he had reason on his side, which they could not answer, grows more bold, and, in prosecution of his argument, is very close upon them. <div eID="gen27522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He wonders at their obstinate infidelity (<reference osisRef="John.9.30">v. 30</reference>); not at all daunted by their frowns, nor shaken by their confidence, he bravely answered, "<hi type="italic">Why, herein is a marvelous thing,</hi> the strangest instance of wilful ignorance that ever was heard of among men that pretend to sense, that <hi type="italic">you know not whence he is,</hi> and yet he has opened mine eyes." Two things he wonders at:—1. That they should be strangers to a man so <hi type="italic">famous.</hi> He that could open the eyes of the blind must certainly be a considerable man, and worth taking notice of. The Pharisees were inquisitive men, had a large correspondence and acquaintance, thought themselves the eyes of the church and its watchmen, and yet that they should talk as if they thought it below them to take cognizance of such a man as this, and have conversation with him, this is a strange thing indeed. There are many who pass for learned and knowing men, who understand business, and can talk sensibly in other things, who yet are ignorant, to a wonder, of the doctrine of Christ, who have no concern, no, not so much as a curiosity, to acquaint themselves with that which the <hi type="italic">angels desire to look into.</hi> 2. That they should question the divine mission of one that had undoubtedly wrought a divine miracle. When they said, <hi type="italic">We know not whence he is,</hi> they meant, "We know not any proof that his doctrine and ministry are from heaven." "Now this is strange," saith the poor man, "that the miracle wrought upon me has not convinced you, and put the matter out of doubt,—that you, whose education and studies give you advantages above others of discerning the things of God, should thus shut your eyes against the light." It is a <hi type="italic">marvelous work and wonder, when the wisdom of the wise thus perisheth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Isa. xxix. 14</reference>), that they deny the truth of that of which they cannot gainsay the evidence. Note, (1.) The unbelief of those who enjoy the means of knowledge and conviction is indeed a marvelous thing, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.6">Mark vi. 6</reference>. (2.) Those who have themselves experienced the power and grace of the Lord Jesus do especially wonder at the wilfulness of those who reject him, and, having such good thoughts of him themselves, are amazed that others have not. Had Christ opened the eyes of the Pharisees, they would not have doubted his being a prophet. <div eID="gen27523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27524" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He argues strongly against them, <reference osisRef="John.9.31-John.9.33">v. 31-33</reference>. They had determined concerning Jesus that he was not of God (<reference osisRef="John.9.16">v. 16</reference>), but was a <hi type="italic">sinner</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.24">v. 24</reference>), in answer to which the man here proves not only that he was <hi type="italic">not a sinner</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.31">v. 31</reference>), but that he was <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.33">v. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen27524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27525" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> He argues here, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) With great knowledge. Though he could not read a letter of the book, he was well acquainted with the scripture and the things of God; he had wanted the sense of seeing, yet had well improved that of hearing, by which faith cometh; yet this would not have served him if he had not had an extraordinary presence of God with him, and special aids of his Spirit, upon this occasion. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) With great zeal for the honour of Christ, whom he could not endure to hear run down, and evil spoken of. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) With great boldness, and courage, and undauntedness, not terrified by the proudest of his adversaries. Those that are ambitious of the favours of God must not be afraid of the frowns of men. "See here," saith Dr. Whitby, "a blind man and unlearned judging more rightly of divine things than the whole learned council of the Pharisees, whence we learn that we are not always to be led by the authority of councils, popes, or bishops; and that it is not absurd for laymen sometimes to vary from their opinions, these overseers being sometimes guilty of great oversights." <div eID="gen27525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> His argument may be reduced into form, somewhat like that of David, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18-Ps.66.20">Ps. lxvi. 18-20</reference>. The proposition in David's argument is, <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart, God will not hear me;</hi> here it is to the same purport, <hi type="italic">God heareth not sinners:</hi> the assumption there is, <hi type="italic">But verily God hath heard me;</hi> here it is, Verily God hath heard Jesus, he hath been honoured with the doing of that which was never done before: the conclusion there is to the honour, <hi type="italic">Blessed be God;</hi> here to the honour of the Lord Jesus, He is <hi type="italic">of God.</hi> <div eID="gen27526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27527" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) He lays it down for an undoubted truth that none but good men are the favourites of heaven (<reference osisRef="John.9.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now we know,</hi> you know it as well as I, <hi type="italic">that God heareth not sinners;</hi> but <hi type="italic">if any man be a worshipper of God, and does his will, him he heareth.</hi> Here, <div eID="gen27527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27528" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The assertions, rightly understood, are true. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Be it spoken to the terror of the wicked, <hi type="italic">God heareth not sinners,</hi> that is, such sinners as the Pharisees meant when they said of Christ, <hi type="italic">He is a sinner,</hi> one that, under the shelter of God's name, advanced the devil's interest. This bespeaks no discouragement to repenting returning sinners, but to those that go on still in their trespasses, that make their prayers not only consistent with, but subservient to, their sins, as the hypocrites do; God will not <hi type="italic">hear</hi> them, he will not own them, nor give an answer of peace to their prayers. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Be it spoken to the comfort of the righteous, <hi type="italic">If any man be a worshipper of God, and does his will, him he heareth.</hi> Here is, 1. The complete character of a good man: he is one that <hi type="italic">worships God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">does his will;</hi> he is constant in his devotions at set times, and regular in his conversation at all times. He is one that makes it his business to glorify his Creator by the solemn adoration of his name and a sincere obedience to his will and law; both must go together. 2. The unspeakable comfort of such a man: him <hi type="italic">God hears;</hi> hears his complaints, and relieves him; hears his appeals, and rights him; hears his praises, and accepts them; hears his prayers, and answers them, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.15">Ps. xxxiv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen27528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27529" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The application of these truths is very pertinent to prove that he, at whose word such a divine power was put forth as cured one born blind, was not a bad man, but, having manifestly such an interest in the holy God as that he <hi type="italic">heard him always</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.9.31-John.9.32">ch. ix. 31, 32</reference>), was certainly a holy one. <div eID="gen27529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27530" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) He magnifies the miracles which Christ had wrought, to strengthen the argument the more (<reference osisRef="John.9.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind.</hi> This is to show either, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] That it was a true miracle, and above the power of nature; it was never heard that any man, by the use of natural means, had cured one that was <hi type="italic">born blind;</hi> no doubt, this man and his parents had been very inquisitive into cases of this nature, whether any such had been helped, and could hear of none, which enabled him to speak this with the more assurance. Or, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] That it was an extraordinary miracle, and beyond the precedents of former miracles; neither Moses nor any of the prophets, though they did great things, ever did such things as this, wherein divine power and divine goodness seem to strive which should outshine. Moses wrought miraculous plagues, but Christ wrought miraculous cures. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The wondrous works of the Lord Jesus were such as the like had never been done before. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It becomes those who have received mercy from God to magnify the mercies they have received, and to speak honourably of them; not that thereby glory may redound to themselves, and they may seem to be extraordinary favourites of Heaven, but that God may have so much the more glory. <div eID="gen27530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27531" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) He therefore concludes, <hi type="italic">If this man were not of God, he could do nothing,</hi> that is, nothing extraordinary, no such thing as <hi type="italic">this;</hi> and therefore, no doubt, he is <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> notwithstanding his nonconformity to your traditions in the business of the sabbath day. Note, What Christ did on earth sufficiently demonstrated what he was in heaven; for, if he had not been sent of God, he could not have wrought such miracles. It is true the man of sin comes with <hi type="italic">lying wonders,</hi> but not with real miracles; it is likewise supposed that a false prophet might, by divine permission, give a <hi type="italic">sign or a wonder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.2">Deut. xiii. 1, 2</reference>), yet the case is so put as that it would carry with it its own confutation, for it is to enforce a temptation to serve other gods, which was to set God <hi type="italic">against himself.</hi> It is true, likewise, that many wicked people have in Christ's name done many wonderful works, which did not prove those that wrought them to be of God, but him in whose name they were wrought. We may each of us know by this whether we are of God or no: <hi type="italic">What do we?</hi> What do we for God, for our souls, in working out our salvation? What do we more than others? <div eID="gen27531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27532" type="x-p"/> [2.] The Pharisees, finding themselves unable either to answer his reasonings or to bear them, fell foul upon him, and with a great deal of pride and passion broke off the discourse, <reference osisRef="John.9.34">v. 34</reference>. Here we are told, <div eID="gen27532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27533" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What they <hi type="italic">said.</hi> Having nothing to reply to his argument, they reflected upon his person: <hi type="italic">Thou wast altogether born in sin, and dost thou teach us?</hi> They take that amiss which they had reason to take kindly, and are cut to the heart with rage by that which should have pricked them to the heart with penitence. Observe, 1. How they despised him, and what a severe censure they passed upon him: "<hi type="italic">Thou wast not only born in sin,</hi> as every man is, but altogether so, wholly corrupt, and bearing about with thee in thy body as well as in thy soul the marks of that corruption; thou wast one whom nature <hi type="italic">stigmatized.</hi>" Had he still continued blind, it had been barbarous to upbraid him with it, and thence to gather that he was more deeply tainted with sin than other people; but it was most unjust to take notice of it now that the cure had not only rolled away the reproach of his blindness, but had <hi type="italic">signalized</hi> him as a favourite of Heaven. Some take it thus: "Thou hast been a common beggar, and such are too often common sinners, and thou hast, no doubt, been as bad as any of them;" whereas by his discourse he had proved the contrary, and had evinced a deep tincture of piety. But when proud imperious Pharisees resolve to run a man down, any thing shall serve for a pretence. 2. How they <hi type="italic">disdain</hi> to learn of him, or to receive instruction from him: <hi type="italic">Dost thou teach us?</hi> A mighty emphasis must be laid here upon <hi type="italic">thou</hi> and <hi type="italic">us.</hi> "What! wilt <hi type="italic">thou,</hi> a silly sorry fellow, ignorant and illiterate, that hast not seen the light of the sun a day to an end, a beggar by the way-side, of the very dregs and refuse of the town, wilt thou pretend to teach <hi type="italic">us,</hi> that are the sages of the law and grandees of the church, that sit in Moses's chair and are masters in Israel?" Note, Proud men scorn to be taught, especially by their inferiors, whereas we should never think ourselves too old, nor too wise, nor too good, to learn. Those that have much wealth would have more; and why not those that have much knowledge? And those are to be valued by whom we may improve in learning. What a poor excuse was this for the Pharisees' infidelity, that it would be a disparagement to them to be instructed, and informed, and convinced, by such a silly fellow as this!

<div eID="gen27533" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Address to the Man that Had Been Blind.</title> <div sID="gen27534" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said unto him, Dost thou believe on the Son of God? <hi type="super">36</hi> He answered and said, Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him? <hi type="super">37</hi> And Jesus said unto him, Thou hast both seen him, and it is he that talketh with thee. <hi type="super">38</hi> And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him. <div eID="gen27534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27535" type="x-p"/> In these verses we may observe, <div eID="gen27535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27536" type="x-p"/> I. The tender care which our Lord Jesus took of this poor man (<reference osisRef="John.9.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">When Jesus heard that they had cast him out</hi> (for it is likely the town rang of it, and everybody cried out shame upon them for it), then he <hi type="italic">found him,</hi> which implies his seeking him and looking after him, that he might encourage and comfort him, 1. Because he had, to the best of his knowledge, spoken so very well, so bravely, so boldly, in defence of the Lord Jesus. Note, Jesus Christ will be sure to stand by his witnesses, and own those that own him and his truth and ways. Earthly princes neither do, nor can, take cognizance of all that vindicate them and their government and administration; but our Lord Jesus knows and observes all the faithful testimonies we bear to him at any time, and a book of remembrance is written, and it shall redound not only to our credit hereafter, but our comfort now. 2. Because the Pharisees had cast him out and abused him. Besides the common regard which the righteous Judge of the world has to those who suffer wrongfully (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.6">Ps. ciii. 6</reference>), there is a particular notice taken of those that suffer in the cause of Christ and for the testimony of a good conscience. Here was one poor man suffering for Christ, and he took care that as his afflictions abounded his consolations should <hi type="italic">much more abound.</hi> Note, (1.) Though persecutors may exclude good men from their communion, yet they cannot exclude them from communion with Christ, nor put them out of the way of his visits. Happy are they who have a friend from whom men cannot debar them. (2.) Jesus Christ will graciously find and receive those who for his sake are unjustly rejected and cast out by men. He will be a hiding place to his outcasts, and appear, to the joy of those whom their brethren hated and cast out. <div eID="gen27536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27537" type="x-p"/> II. The comfortable converse Christ had with him, wherein he brings him acquainted with the consolation of Israel. He had well improved the knowledge he had, and now Christ gives him further instruction; for he that is faithful in a little shall be entrusted with more, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.12">Matt. xiii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen27537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27538" type="x-p"/> 1. Our Lord Jesus examines his faith: "<hi type="italic">Dost thou believe on the Son of God?</hi> Dost thou give credit to the promises of the Messiah? Dost thou expect his coming, and art thou ready to receive and embrace him when he is manifested to thee?" This was that faith of the Son of God by which the saints lived before his manifestation. Observe, (1.) The Messiah is here called the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and so the Jews had learned to call him from the prophecies, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">lxxxix. 27</reference>. See <reference osisRef="John.1.49">ch. i. 49</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou art the Son of God,</hi> that is, the true Messiah. Those that expected the temporal kingdom of the Messiah delighted rather in calling him the <hi type="italic">Son of David,</hi> which gave more countenance to that expectation, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.42">Matt. xxii. 42</reference>. But Christ, that he might give us an idea of his kingdom, as purely spiritual and divine, calls himself the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and rather <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> in general than of David in particular. (2.) The desires and expectations of the Messiah, which the Old-Testament saints had, guided by and grounded upon the promise, were graciously interpreted and accepted as their believing on the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> This faith Christ here enquires after: <hi type="italic">Dost thou believe?</hi> Note, The great thing which is now required of us (<reference osisRef="1John.3.23">1 John iii. 23</reference>), and which will shortly be enquired after concerning us, is our <hi type="italic">believing on the Son of God,</hi> and by this we must stand or fall for ever. <div eID="gen27538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27539" type="x-p"/> 2. The poor man solicitously enquires concerning the Messiah he was to believe in, professing his readiness to embrace him and close with him (<reference osisRef="John.9.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is he, Lord, that I may believe on him?</hi> (1.) Some think he did know that Jesus, who cured him, was the Son of God, but did not know which was Jesus, and therefore, supposing this person that talked with him to be a follower of Jesus, desired him to do him the favour to direct him to his master; not that he might satisfy his curiosity with the sight of him, but that he might the more firmly believe in him, and profess his faith, and <hi type="italic">know whom he had believed.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Song.5.6-Song.5.7">Cant. v. 6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.3.2-Song.3.3">iii. 2, 3</reference>. It is Christ only that can direct us to himself. (2.) Others think he did know that this person who talked with him was Jesus, the same that cured him, whom he believed a great and good man and a prophet, but did not yet know that he was the Son of God and the true Messiah. "Lord, I believe there is a Christ to come; thou who hast given me bodily sight, tell me, O tell me, who and where this Son of God is." Christ's question intimated that the Messiah was come, and was now among them, which he presently takes the hint of, and asks, <hi type="italic">Where is he, Lord?</hi> The question was rational and just: <hi type="italic">Who is he, Lord, that I may believe on him?</hi> For how could he believe in one of whom he had not heard; the work of ministers is to tell us <hi type="italic">who the Son of God is,</hi> that we may believe on him, <reference osisRef="John.20.31">ch. xx. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen27539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27540" type="x-p"/> 3. Our Lord Jesus graciously reveals himself to him as that Son of God on whom he must believe: <hi type="italic">Thou hast both seen him, and it is he that talketh with thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.37">v. 37</reference>. Thou needest not go far to find out the Son of God, <hi type="italic">Behold the Word is nigh thee.</hi> We do not find that Christ did thus expressly, and in so many words, reveal himself to any other as to this man here and to the woman of <hi type="italic">Samaria: I that speak unto thee am he.</hi> He left others to find out by arguments who he was, but to these weak and foolish things of the world he chose to manifest himself, so as not to the <hi type="italic">wise and prudent.</hi> Christ here describes himself to this man by two things, which express his great favour to him:— (1.) <hi type="italic">Thou hast seen him;</hi> and he was much indebted to the Lord Jesus for opening his eyes, that he might see him. Now he was made sensible, more than ever, what an unspeakable mercy it was to be cured of his blindness, that he might see the Son of God, a sight which rejoiced his heart more than that of the <hi type="italic">light of this world.</hi> Note, The Greatest comfort of bodily eyesight is its serviceableness to our faith and the interests of our souls. How contentedly might this man have returned to his former blindness, like old Simeon, now that his eyes had <hi type="italic">seen God's salvation!</hi> If we apply this to the opening of the eyes of the mind, it intimates that spiritual sight is given principally for this end, that we may see Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>. Can we say that by faith we have seen Christ, seen him in his beauty and glory, in his ability and willingness to save, so seen him as to be satisfied concerning him, to be satisfied in him? Let us give him the praise, who opened our eyes. (2.) <hi type="italic">It is he that talketh with thee;</hi> and he was indebted to Christ for condescending to do this. He was not only favoured with a sight of Christ, but was admitted into fellowship and communion with him. Great princes are willing to be <hi type="italic">seen</hi> by those whom yet they will not vouchsafe to <hi type="italic">talk with.</hi> But Christ, by his word and Spirit, talks with those whose desires are towards him, and in talking with them manifests himself to them, as he did to the two disciples, when he talked their hearts warm, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">Luke xxiv. 32</reference>. Observe, This poor man was solicitously enquiring after the Saviour, when at the same time he saw him, and was talking with him. Note, Jesus Christ is often nearer the souls that seek him than they themselves are aware of. Doubting Christians are sometimes saying, <hi type="italic">Where is the Lord?</hi> and fearing that they are cast out from his sight when at the same time it is he that <hi type="italic">talks with them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">puts strength into them.</hi> <div eID="gen27540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27541" type="x-p"/> 4. The poor man readily entertains this surprising revelation, and, in a transport of joy and wonder, he said, <hi type="italic">Lord, I believe, and he worshipped him.</hi> (1.) He professed his faith in Christ: <hi type="italic">Lord, I believe thee to be the Son of God.</hi> He would not dispute any thing that <hi type="italic">he</hi> said who had shown such mercy to him, and wrought such a miracle for him, nor doubt of the truth of a doctrine which was confirmed by such signs. Believing with the heart, he thus confesses with the mouth; and now the bruised reed was become a cedar. (2.) He paid his homage to him: <hi type="italic">He worshipped him,</hi> not only gave him the civil respect due to a great man, and the acknowledgments owing to a kind benefactor, but herein gave him divine honour, and worshipped him as the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> manifested in the flesh. None but God is to be worshipped; so that in worshipping Jesus he owned him to be God. Note, True faith will show itself in a humble adoration of the Lord Jesus. Those who believe in him will see all the reason in the world to worship him. We never read any more of this man; but, it is very likely, from henceforth he became a constant follower of Christ.

<div eID="gen27541" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Address to the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27542" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">39</hi> And Jesus said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind. <hi type="super">40</hi> And <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the Pharisees which were with him heard these words, and said unto him, Are we blind also? <hi type="super">41</hi> Jesus said unto them, If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth. <div eID="gen27542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27543" type="x-p"/> Christ, having spoken comfort to the poor man that was persecuted, here speaks conviction to his persecutors, a specimen of the distributions of trouble and rest at the great day, <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6-2Thess.1.7">2 Thess. i. 6, 7</reference>. Probably this was not immediately after his discourse with the man, but he took the next opportunity that offered itself to address the Pharisees. Here is, <div eID="gen27543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27544" type="x-p"/> I. The account Christ gives of his design in coming into the world (<reference osisRef="John.9.39">v. 39</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For judgment I am</hi> come to order and administer the great affairs of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God among men,</hi> and am invested with a judicial power in order thereunto, to be executed in conformity to the wise counsels of God, and in pursuance of them." What Christ spoke, he spoke not as a preacher in the pulpit, but as a king upon the throne, and a judge upon the bench. <div eID="gen27544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27545" type="x-p"/> 1. His business into the world was <hi type="italic">great;</hi> he came to keep the assizes and general goal-delivery. He came <hi type="italic">for judgment,</hi> that is, (1.) To preach a doctrine and a law which would try men, and effectually discover and distinguish them, and would be completely fitted, in all respects, to be the rule of government now and of judgment shortly. (2.) To put a difference between men, by revealing the thoughts of many hearts, and laying open men's true characters, by this one test, whether they were well or ill affected to him. (3.) To change the face of government in his church, to abolish the Jewish economy, to take down that fabric, which, though erected for the time by the hand of God himself, yet by lapse of time was antiquated, and by the incurable corruptions of the managers of it was become rotten and dangerous, and to erect a new building by another model, to institute new ordinances and offices, to abrogate Judaism and enact Christianity; <hi type="italic">for</hi> this <hi type="italic">judgment he came into the world,</hi> and it was a great revolution. <div eID="gen27545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27546" type="x-p"/> 2. This great truth he explains by a metaphor borrowed from the miracle which he had lately wrought. That <hi type="italic">those who see not might see, and that those who see might be made blind.</hi> Such a difference of Christ's coming is often spoken of; to some his gospel is a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life,</hi> to others of <hi type="italic">death unto death.</hi> (1.) This is applicable to nations and people, that the Gentiles, who had long been destitute of the light of divine revelation, might see it; and the Jews, who had long enjoyed it, might have the things of their peace hid from their eyes, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Hos. i. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">ii. 23</reference>. The Gentiles see a great light, while blindness is <hi type="italic">happened unto Israel,</hi> and their <hi type="italic">eyes are darkened.</hi> (2.) To particular sons. Christ came into the world, [1.] Intentionally and designedly to give sight to those that were spiritually blind; by his word to reveal the object, and by his Spirit to heal the organ, that many precious souls might be turned <hi type="italic">from darkness to light.</hi> He came <hi type="italic">for judgment,</hi> that is, to set those at liberty from their dark prison that were willing to be released, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. [2.] Eventually, and in the issue, <hi type="italic">that those who see might be made blind;</hi> that those who have a high conceit of their own wisdom, and set up that in contradiction to divine revelation, might be sealed up in ignorance and infidelity. The preaching of the cross was foolishness, and an infatuating thing, to those who by wisdom <hi type="italic">knew not God.</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">came into the world for</hi> this <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> to administer the affairs of a spiritual kingdom, seated in men's minds. Whereas, in the Jewish church, the blessings and judgments of God's government were mostly temporal, now the method of administration should be changed; and as the good subjects of his kingdom should be blessed with spiritual blessings in heavenly things, such as arise from a due illumination of the mind, so the rebels should be punished with spiritual plagues, not war, famine, and pestilence, as formerly, but such as arise from a <hi type="italic">judicial infatuation,</hi> hardness of heart, terror of conscience, strong delusions, vile affections. In this way Christ will <hi type="italic">judge between cattle and cattle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Ezek. xxxiv. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.22">22</reference>. <div eID="gen27546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27547" type="x-p"/> II. The Pharisees' cavil at this. They were <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> not desirous to learn any good from him, but to form evil against him; and they said, <hi type="italic">Are we blind also?</hi> When Christ said that <hi type="italic">those who saw</hi> should by his coming be made blind, they apprehended that he meant them, who were the <hi type="italic">seers</hi> of the people, and valued themselves on their <hi type="italic">insight</hi> and <hi type="italic">foresight.</hi> "Now," say they, "we know that the common people are blind; but <hi type="italic">are we blind also?</hi> What we? The rabbin, the doctors, the learned in the laws, the graduates in the schools, <hi type="italic">are we blind too?</hi>" This is <hi type="italic">scandalum magnatum—a libel on the great.</hi> Note, Frequently those that need reproof most, and deserve it best, though they have wit enough to discern a <hi type="italic">tacit</hi> one, have not grace enough to bear a <hi type="italic">just</hi> one. These Pharisees took this reproof for a reproach, as those lawyers (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.45">Luke xi. 45</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Are we blind also?</hi> Darest thou say that we are blind, whose judgment every one has such a veneration for, values, and yields to?" Note, Nothing fortifies men's corrupt hearts more against the convictions of the word, nor more effectually repels them, than the good opinion, especially if it be a high opinion, which others have of them; as if all that had gained applause with men must needs obtain acceptance with God, than which nothing is more false and deceitful, for God sees not as man sees. <div eID="gen27547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27548" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's answer to this cavil, which, if it did not convince them, yet silenced them: <hi type="italic">If you were blind you should have no sin; but now you say, We see, therefore your sin remaineth.</hi> They gloried that they were not blind, as the common people, were not so credulous and manageable as they, but would <hi type="italic">see with their own eyes,</hi> having abilities, as they thought, sufficient for their own guidance, so that they needed not any body to lead them. This very thing which they gloried in, Christ here tells them, was their shame and ruin. For, <div eID="gen27548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27549" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">If you were blind, you would have no sin.</hi> (1.) "If you had been really ignorant, your sin had not been so deeply aggravated, nor would you have had so much sin to answer for as now you have. If you were blind, as the poor Gentiles are, and many of your own poor subjects, from whom you have taken the key of knowledge, you would have had comparatively <hi type="italic">no sin.</hi>" The times of ignorance God <hi type="italic">winked at;</hi> invincible ignorance, though it does not justify sin, excuses it, and lessens the guilt. It will be more tolerable with those that perish for lack of vision than with those that <hi type="italic">rebel against the light.</hi> (2.) "If you had been sensible of your own blindness, if when you would see nothing else you could have seen the need of one to lead you, you would soon have accepted Christ as your guide, and then you would <hi type="italic">have had no sin,</hi> you would have submitted to an evangelical righteousness, and have been put into a justified state." Note, Those that are convinced of their disease are in a fair way to be cured, for there is not a greater hindrance to the salvation of souls than self-sufficiency. <div eID="gen27549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27550" type="x-p"/> 2. "<hi type="italic">But now you say, We see;</hi> now that you have knowledge, and are instructed out of the law, your sin is highly aggravated; and now that you have a conceit of that knowledge, and think you see your way better than any body can show it you, <hi type="italic">therefore your sin remains,</hi> your case is desperate, and your disease incurable." And as those are most blind who <hi type="italic">will not see,</hi> so their blindness is most dangerous who fancy they do see. No patients are so hardly managed as those in a frenzy who say that they are <hi type="italic">well,</hi> and nothing ails them. The sin of those who are self-conceited and self-confident <hi type="italic">remains,</hi> for they reject the gospel of grace, and therefore the guilt of their sin remains unpardoned; and they forfeit the Spirit of grace, and therefore the power of their sin remains unbroken. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a wise man in his own conceit?</hi> Hearest thou the Pharisees say, <hi type="italic">We see? There is more hope of a fool,</hi> of a publican and a harlot, than of such.  <chapter eID="John.9"/> <div eID="gen27550" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27553" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27552" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Good Shepherd.</title> <div sID="gen27554" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. <hi type="super">2</hi> But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. <hi type="super">3</hi> To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him: for they know his voice. <hi type="super">5</hi> And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers. <hi type="super">6</hi> This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep. <hi type="super">8</hi> All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them. <hi type="super">9</hi> I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture. <hi type="super">10</hi> The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have <hi type="italic">it</hi> more abundantly. <hi type="super">11</hi> I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. <hi type="super">12</hi> But he that is a hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep. <hi type="super">13</hi> The hireling fleeth, because he is a hireling, and careth not for the sheep. <hi type="super">14</hi> I am the good shepherd, and know my <hi type="italic">sheep,</hi> and am known of mine. <hi type="super">15</hi> As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep. <hi type="super">16</hi> And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, <hi type="italic">and</hi> one shepherd. <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. 18 No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father. <div eID="gen27554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27555" type="x-p"/> It is not certain whether this discourse was at the <hi type="italic">feast of dedication</hi> in the winter (spoken of <reference osisRef="John.10.22">v. 22</reference>), which may be taken as the date, not only of what follows, but of what goes before (that which countenances this is, that Christ, in his discourse there, carries on the metaphor of the sheep, <reference osisRef="John.10.26-John.10.27">v. 26, 27</reference>, whence it seems that that discourse and this were at the same time); or whether this was a continuation of his parley with the Pharisees, in the close of the foregoing chapter. The Pharisees supported themselves in their opposition to Christ with this principle, that they were the <hi type="italic">pastors of the church,</hi> and that Jesus, having no commission from them, was an intruder and an impostor, and therefore the people were bound in duty to stick to <hi type="italic">then,</hi> against <hi type="italic">him.</hi> In opposition to this, Christ here describes who were the false shepherds, and who the true, leaving them to infer what they were. <div eID="gen27555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27556" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the parable or similitude proposed (<reference osisRef="John.10.1-John.10.5">v. 1-5</reference>); it is borrowed from the custom of that country, in the management of their sheep. Similitudes, used for the illustration of divine truths, should be taken from those things that are most familiar and common, that the things of God be not clouded by that which should clear them. The preface to this discourse is solemn: <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you,—Amen, amen.</hi> This vehement asseveration intimates the certainty and weight of what he said; we find <hi type="italic">amen</hi> doubled in the church's praises and prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.13">Ps. xli. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.19">lxxii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.52">lxxxix. 52</reference>. If we would have our <hi type="italic">amens</hi> accepted in heaven, let Christ's <hi type="italic">amens</hi> be prevailing on earth; his repeated <hi type="italic">amens.</hi> <div eID="gen27556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27557" type="x-p"/> 1. In the parable we have, (1.) The evidence of a thief and robber, that comes to do mischief to the flock, and damage to the owner, <reference osisRef="John.10.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">He enters not by the door,</hi> as having no lawful cause of entry, but <hi type="italic">climbs up some other way,</hi> at a window, or some breach in the wall. How industrious are wicked people to do mischief! What plots will they lay, what pains will they take, what hazards will they run, in their wicked pursuits! This should shame us out of our slothfulness and cowardice in the service of God. (2.) The character that distinguishes the rightful owner, who has a property in the sheep, and a care for them: <hi type="italic">He enters in by the door,</hi> as one having authority (<reference osisRef="John.10.2">v. 2</reference>), and he comes to do them some good office or other, to <hi type="italic">bind up that which is broken,</hi> and <hi type="italic">strengthen that which is sick,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16">Ezek. xxxiv. 16</reference>. Sheep need man's care, and, in return for it, are serviceable to man (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>); they clothe and feed those by whom they are coted and fed. (3.) The ready entrance that the shepherd finds: <hi type="italic">To him the porter openeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.3">v. 3</reference>. Anciently they had their sheepfolds within the outer gates of their houses, for the greater safety of their flocks, so that none could come to them the right way, but such as the porter opened to or the master of the house gave the keys to. (4.) The care he takes and the provision he makes for his sheep. The <hi type="italic">sheep hear his voice,</hi> when he speaks familiarly to them, when they come into the fold, as men now do to their dogs and horses; and, which is more, he <hi type="italic">calls his own sheep by name,</hi> so exact is the notice he takes of them, the account he keeps of them; and he leads them our from the fold to the green pastures; and (<reference osisRef="John.10.4-John.10.5">v. 4, 5</reference>) when he <hi type="italic">turns them out</hi> to graze he does not drive them, but (such was the custom in those times) he goes before them, to prevent any mischief or danger that might meet them, and they, being used to it, <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> and are safe. (5.) The strange attendance of the sheep upon the shepherd: <hi type="italic">They know his voice,</hi> so as to discern his mind by it, and to distinguish it from that of a stranger (for <hi type="italic">the ox knows his owner,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa. i. 3</reference>), and <hi type="italic">a stranger will they not follow,</hi> but, as suspecting some ill design, will flee from him, not <hi type="italic">knowing his voice,</hi> but that it is not the voice of their own shepherd. This is the parable; we have the key to it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.31">Ezek. xxxiv. 31</reference>: <hi type="italic">You my flock are men, and I am your God.</hi> <div eID="gen27557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27558" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us observe from this parable, (1.) That good men are fitly compared to sheep. Men, as creatures depending on their Creator, are called the <hi type="italic">sheep of his pasture.</hi> Good men, as new creatures, have the good qualities of sheep, <hi type="italic">harmless</hi> and inoffensive as sheep; <hi type="italic">meek</hi> and quiet, without noise; <hi type="italic">patient</hi> as sheep under the hand both of the shearer and of the butcher; <hi type="italic">useful</hi> and profitable, tame and tractable, to the shepherd, and <hi type="italic">sociable</hi> one with another, and much used in sacrifices. (2.) The church of God in the world is a <hi type="italic">sheepfold,</hi> into which the <hi type="italic">children of God</hi> that were scattered abroad are <hi type="italic">gathered together</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">ch. xi. 52</reference>), and in which they are united and incorporated; it is a good fold, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">Ezek. xxxiv. 14</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mic. ii. 12</reference>. This fold is well fortified, for God himself is as a <hi type="italic">wall of fire about it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zech. ii. 5</reference>. (3.) This sheepfold lies much exposed to thieves and robbers; crafty seducers that debauch and deceive, and cruel persecutors that destroy and devour; <hi type="italic">grievous wolves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Acts xx. 29</reference>); thieves that would steal Christ's sheep from him, to sacrifice them to devils, or steal their food from them, that they might perish for lack of it; <hi type="italic">wolves</hi> in sheep's clothing, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.15">Matt. vii. 15</reference>. (4.) The great Shepherd of the sheep takes wonderful care of the flock and of all that belong to it. God is the great Shepherd, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Ps. xxiii. 1</reference>. He knows those that are his calls them by name, marks them for himself, leads them out to fat pastures, makes them both feed and rest there, speaks comfortably to them, guards them by his providence, guides them by his Spirit and word, and goes before them, <hi type="italic">to set them in the way of his steps.</hi> (5.) The under-shepherds, who are entrusted to feed the flock of God, ought to be careful and faithful in the discharge of that trust; magistrates must defend them, and protect and advance all their secular interests; ministers must serve them in their spiritual interests, must <hi type="italic">feed their souls</hi> with the word of God faithfully opened and applied, and with gospel ordinances duly administered, <hi type="italic">taking the oversight of them.</hi> They must <hi type="italic">enter by the door</hi> of a regular ordination, and to such <hi type="italic">the porter will open;</hi> the Spirit of Christ will <hi type="italic">set before them an open door,</hi> give them authority in the church, and assurance in their own bosoms. They must know the members of their flocks by name, and watch over them; must lead them into the pastures of public ordinances, preside among them, be their mouth to God and God's to them; and in their conversation must be examples to the believers. (6.) Those who are truly the sheep of Christ will be very observant of their Shepherd, and very cautious and shy of strangers. [1.] <hi type="italic">They follow their Shepherd,</hi> for they <hi type="italic">know his voice,</hi> having both a discerning ear, and an obedient heart. [2.] <hi type="italic">They flee from a stranger,</hi> and dread following him, because they know not his voice. It is dangerous following those in whom we discern not the <hi type="italic">voice of Christ,</hi> and who would draw us from <hi type="italic">faith in him</hi> to <hi type="italic">fancies concerning him.</hi> And those who have experienced the power and efficacy of divine truths upon their souls, and have the savour and relish of them, have a wonderful sagacity to discover Satan's wiles, and to discern between good and evil. <div eID="gen27558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27559" type="x-p"/> II. The Jew's ignorance of the drift and meaning of this discourse (<reference osisRef="John.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jesus spoke this parable</hi> to them, this figurative, but wise, elegant, and instructive discourse, <hi type="italic">but they understood not what the things were which he spoke unto them,</hi> were not aware whom he meant by the <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers</hi> and whom by the <hi type="italic">good Shepherd.</hi> It is the sin and shame of many who hear the word of Christ that they do not understand it, and they do not because they will not, and because they will <hi type="italic">mis-understand it.</hi> They have no acquaintance with, nor taste of, the things themselves, and therefore do not understand the parables and comparisons with which they are illustrated. The Pharisees had a great conceit of their own knowledge, and could not bear that it should be questioned, and yet they had not sense enough to <hi type="italic">understand the things that Jesus spoke of;</hi> they were above their capacity. Frequently the greatest pretenders to knowledge are most ignorant in the things of God. <div eID="gen27559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27560" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's explication of this parable, opening the particulars of it fully. Whatever difficulties there may be in the sayings of the Lord Jesus, we shall find him ready to explain himself, if we be but willing to understand him. We shall find one scripture expounding another, and the <hi type="italic">blessed Spirit</hi> interpreter to the <hi type="italic">blessed Jesus.</hi> Christ, in the parable, had distinguished the shepherd from the robber by this, that he <hi type="italic">enters in by the door.</hi> Now, in the explication of the parable, he makes himself to be both <hi type="italic">the door</hi> by which the shepherd enters and the shepherd that enters in by the door. Though it may be a solecism in rhetoric to make the same person to be both the <hi type="italic">door</hi> and the <hi type="italic">shepherd,</hi> it is no solecism in divinity to make Christ to have his authority from himself, as he has life in himself; and <hi type="italic">himself</hi> to <hi type="italic">enter by his own blood,</hi> as the door, <hi type="italic">into the holy place.</hi> <div eID="gen27560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27561" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ is <hi type="italic">the door.</hi> This he saith to those who pretended to <hi type="italic">seek for righteousness,</hi> but, like the Sodomites, <hi type="italic">wearied themselves to find the door,</hi> where it was not to be found. He saith it to the Jews, who would be thought God's only sheep, and to the Pharisees, who would be thought their only shepherds: <hi type="italic">I am the door</hi> of the sheepfold; the door of the church. <div eID="gen27561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27562" type="x-p"/> (1.) In general, [1.] He is as a <hi type="italic">door shut,</hi> to keep out thieves and robbers, and such as are not fit to be admitted. The shutting of the door is the securing of the house; and what greater security has the church of God than the interposal of the Lord Jesus, and his wisdom, power, and goodness, betwixt it and all its enemies? [2.] He is as a <hi type="italic">door open</hi> for passage and communication. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By Christ, as the door, we have our first admission into the flock of God, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">ch. xiv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We go in and out in a religious conversation, assisted by him, accepted in him; walking up and down in his name, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.12">Zech. x. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> By him God comes to his church, visits it, and communicates himself to it. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> By him, as the door, the sheep are at last admitted into the heavenly kingdom, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">Matt. xxv. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen27562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27563" type="x-p"/> (2.) More particularly, <div eID="gen27563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27564" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ is the door of <hi type="italic">the shepherds,</hi> so that none who come not in by him are to be accounted <hi type="italic">pastors,</hi> but (according to the rule laid down, <reference osisRef="John.10.1">v. 1</reference>) <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers</hi> (though they pretended to be <hi type="italic">shepherds</hi>); but the <hi type="italic">sheep did not hear them.</hi> This refers to all those that had the character of shepherds in <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> whether magistrates or ministers, that exercised their office without any regard to the Messiah, or any other expectations of him than what were suggested by their own carnal interest. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The character given of them: they are <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.8">v. 8</reference>); all that <hi type="italic">went before him,</hi> not in time, many of them were faithful shepherds, but all that <hi type="italic">anticipated</hi> his commission, and went before he sent them (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jer. xxiii. 21</reference>), that assumed a precedency and superiority above him, as the antichrist is said to <hi type="italic">exalt himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2 Thess. ii. 4</reference>. "The scribes, and Pharisees, and chief priests, <hi type="italic">all, even as many as have come before me,</hi> that have endeavoured to forestal my interest, and to prevent my gaining any room in the minds of people, by prepossessing them with prejudices against me, they are <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers,</hi> and steal those hearts which they have no title to, defrauding the right owner of his property." They condemned our Saviour as a thief and a robber, because he did not come in by them as the door, nor take out a license from them; but he shows that they ought to have received their commission from him, to have been admitted by him, and to have come after him, and because they did not, but stepped <hi type="italic">before him,</hi> they were <hi type="italic">thieves and robbers.</hi> They would not come in as his disciples, and therefore were condemned as usurpers, and their pretended commissions vacated and superseded. Note, Rivals with Christ are robbers of his church, however they pretend to be <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> nay, <hi type="italic">shepherds of shepherds. Secondly,</hi> The care taken to preserve the sheep from them: <hi type="italic">But the sheep did not hear them.</hi> Those that had a true savour of piety, that were spiritual and heavenly, and sincerely devoted to God and godliness, could by no means approve of the traditions of the elders, nor relish their formalities. Christ's disciples, without any particular instructions from their Master, made no conscience of eating with unwashen hands, or plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day; for nothing is more opposite to true Christianity than Pharisaism is, nor any thing more disrelishing to a soul truly devout than their hypocritical devotions. <div eID="gen27564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27565" type="x-p"/> [2.] Christ is the door of <hi type="italic">the sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">By me</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">di emou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">through me</hi> as the door) <hi type="italic">if any man enter into the sheepfold,</hi> as one of the flock, he <hi type="italic">shall be saved;</hi> shall not only by safe from thieves and robbers, but he shall be happy, he <hi type="italic">shall go in and out.</hi> Here are, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Plain directions how to come into the fold: we must come in <hi type="italic">by Jesus Christ</hi> as the door. By faith in him, as the great Mediator between God and man, we come into covenant and communion with God. There is no entering into God's church but by coming into Christ's church; nor are any looked upon as members of the kingdom of God among men but those that are willing to submit to the grace and government of the Redeemer. We must now enter by the <hi type="italic">door of faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.27">Acts xiv. 27</reference>), since the door of <hi type="italic">innocency</hi> is shut against us, and that <hi type="italic">pass</hi> become unpassable, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Precious promises to those who observe this direction. 1.
