We have here Martha's creed, the good confession she witnessed, the same with that for which Peter was commended (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.16-Matt.16.17">Matt. xvi. 16, 17</reference>), and it is the <hi type="italic">conclusion of the whole matter.</hi> <div eID="gen27697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27698" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Here is the <hi type="italic">guide of her faith,</hi> and that is the word of Christ; without any alteration, exception, or proviso, she takes it entire as Christ had said it: <hi type="italic">Yea, Lord,</hi> whereby she subscribes to the truth of all and every part of that which Christ had promised, in his own sense: <hi type="italic">Even so.</hi> Faith is an echo to divine revelation, returns the same words, and resolves to abide by them: <hi type="italic">Yea, Lord, As the word did make it so I believe and take it,</hi> said queen Elizabeth. <div eID="gen27698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27699" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">ground of her faith,</hi> and that is the authority of Christ; she believes <hi type="italic">this</hi> because she believes that he who saith it is Christ. She has recourse to the foundation for the support of the superstructure. <hi type="italic">I believe,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pepisteuka</hi></hi>, "<hi type="italic">I have believed</hi> that thou art Christ, and therefore <hi type="italic">I do believe this.</hi>" Observe here, <div eID="gen27699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> What she believed and confessed concerning Jesus; three things, all to the same effect:— (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) That he was the Christ, or Messiah, promised and expected under this name and notion, the <hi type="italic">anointed one.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) That he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God;</hi> so the Messiah was called (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>), not by office only, but by nature. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) That it was <hi type="italic">he who should come</hi> into the world, the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho erchomenos</hi></hi>. That blessing of blessings which the church had for so many ages waited for as <hi type="italic">future,</hi> she embraced as <hi type="italic">present.</hi> <div eID="gen27700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> What she inferred hence, and what she alleged this for. If she admits this, that Jesus is the Christ, there is no difficulty in believing that he is the resurrection and the life; for if he be the Christ, then, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) He is the fountain of light and truth, and we may take all his sayings for faithful and divine, upon his own word. If he be the Christ, he is that prophet whom we are to hear <hi type="italic">in all things.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) He is the fountain of life and blessedness, and we may therefore depend upon his ability as well as upon his veracity. How shall bodies, turned to dust, <hi type="italic">live again?</hi> How shall souls, clogged and clouded as ours are, <hi type="italic">live for ever?</hi> We could not believe this, but that we believe him that undertakes it to be <hi type="italic">the Son of God,</hi> who has life <hi type="italic">in himself,</hi> and has it for us. <div eID="gen27701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27702" type="x-p"/> 2. The interview between Christ and Mary the other sister. And here observe, <div eID="gen27702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27703" type="x-p"/> (1.) The notice which Martha gave her of Christ's coming (<reference osisRef="John.11.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">When she had so said,</hi> as one that needed to say no more, <hi type="italic">she went her way,</hi> easy in her mind, and <hi type="italic">called Mary her sister.</hi> [1.] Martha, having received instruction and comfort from Christ herself, called her sister to share with her. Time was when Martha would have drawn Mary from Christ, to come and help her in <hi type="italic">much serving</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.40">Luke x. 40</reference>); but, to make her amends for this, here she is industrious to draw her to Christ. [2.] She called her <hi type="italic">secretly,</hi> and whispered it in her ear, because there was company by, Jews, who were no friends to Christ. The saints are called <hi type="italic">into the fellowship of Jesus Christ</hi> by an invitation that is secret and distinguishing, given to them and not to others; they have meat to eat that the world knows not of, joy that a stranger does not intermeddle with. [3.] She called her by order from Christ; he bade her <hi type="italic">go call her sister.</hi> This call that is <hi type="italic">effectual,</hi> whoever brings it, is sent by Christ. <hi type="italic">The Master is come, and calleth for thee. First,</hi> She calls Christ <hi type="italic">the Master,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">didaskalos</hi></hi>, a <hi type="italic">teaching master;</hi> by that title he was commonly called and known among them. Mr. George Herbert took pleasure in calling Christ, <hi type="italic">my Master. Secondly,</hi> She triumphs in his arrival: <hi type="italic">The Master is come.</hi> He whom we have long wished and waited for, <hi type="italic">he is come, he is come;</hi> this was the best cordial in the present distress. "Lazarus is gone, and our comfort in him is gone; but the <hi type="italic">Master is come,</hi> who is better than the dearest friend, and has that in him which will abundantly make up all our losses. He is come who is our <hi type="italic">teacher,</hi> who will teach us how to get good by our sorrow (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Ps. xciv. 12</reference>), who will <hi type="italic">teach,</hi> and so comfort." <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> She invites her sister to go and meet him: "<hi type="italic">He calls for thee,</hi> enquires what is become of thee, and would have thee sent for." Note, When Christ our Master comes, he <hi type="italic">calls for us.</hi> He comes in his word and ordinances, calls us to them, calls us by them, calls us to himself. He calls for thee in particular, for thee <hi type="italic">by name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Ps. xxvii. 8</reference>); and, if he call thee, he will cure thee, he will comfort thee. <div eID="gen27703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27704" type="x-p"/> (2.) The haste which Mary made to Christ upon this notice given her (<reference osisRef="John.11.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">As soon as she heard</hi> this good news, that the <hi type="italic">Master was come,</hi> she <hi type="italic">arose quickly,</hi> and came to him. She little thought how near he was to her, for he is often nearer to them that mourn in Zion than they are aware of; but, when she knew how near he was, she started up, and in a transport of joy ran to meet him. The least intimation of Christ's gracious approaches is enough to a lively faith, which stands ready to take the hint, and answer the first call. When Christ was come, [1.] She did not consult the decorum of her mourning, but, forgetting ceremony, and the common usage in such cases, she ran through the town, to meet Christ. Let no nice punctilios of decency and honour deprive us at any time of opportunities of conversing with Christ. [2.] She did not consult her neighbours, the Jews that were <hi type="italic">with her, comforting her;</hi> she left them all, to come to him, and did not only not ask their advice, but not so much as ask their leave, or beg their pardon for her rudeness. <div eID="gen27704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27705" type="x-p"/> (3.) We are told (<reference osisRef="John.11.30">v. 30</reference>) where she found the Master; he was not yet come into Bethany, but was at the town's end, <hi type="italic">in that place where Martha met him.</hi> See here, [1.] Christ's love to his work. He staid near the place where the grave was, that he might be ready to go to it. He would not go into the town, to <hi type="italic">refresh himself</hi> after the fatigue of his journey, till he had done the work he came to do; nor would he go into the town, lest it should look like ostentation, and a design to levy a crowd to be spectators of the miracle. [2.] Mary's love to Christ; still she <hi type="italic">loved much.</hi> Though Christ had seemed unkind in his delays, yet she could take nothing amiss from him. Let us go thus to Christ <hi type="italic">without the camp,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">Heb. xiii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen27705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27706" type="x-p"/> (4.) The misconstruction which the Jews that were with Mary made of her going away so hastily (<reference osisRef="John.11.31">v. 31</reference>): They said, <hi type="italic">She goes to the grave, to weep there.</hi> Martha bore up better under this affliction than Mary did, who was a woman of a tender and sorrowful spirit; such was her natural temper. Those that are so have need to watch against melancholy, and ought to be pitied and helped. These comforters found that their formalities did her no service, but that she hardened herself in sorrow: and therefore concluded when she went out, and turned that way, it was to go <hi type="italic">to the grave</hi> and <hi type="italic">weep there.</hi> See, [1.] What often is the folly and fault of mourners; they contrive how to aggravate their own grief, and to make bad worse. We are apt in such cases to take a strange pleasure in our own pain, and to say, <hi type="italic">We do well</hi> to be passionate in our grief, even unto death; we are apt to fasten upon those things that aggravate the affliction, and what good does this do us, when it is our duty to reconcile ourselves to the will of God in it? Why should mourners go to the grave to weep there, when they sorrow not as those that have no hope? Affliction of itself is grievous; why should we make it more so? [2.] What is the wisdom and duty of comforters; and that is, to prevent as much as may be, in those who grieve inordinately, the revival of the sorrow, and to divert it. Those Jews that followed Mary were thereby led to Christ, and became the witnesses of one of his most glorious miracles. It is good cleaving to Christ's friends in their sorrows, for thereby we may come to know him better. <div eID="gen27706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27707" type="x-p"/> (5.) Mary's address to our Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.11.32">v. 32</reference>): She came, attended with her train of comforters, and <hi type="italic">fell down at his feet,</hi> as one overwhelmed with a passionate sorrow, and said with many tears (as appears <reference osisRef="John.11.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died,</hi> as Martha said before, for they had often said it to one another. Now here, [1.] Her posture is very humble and submissive: <hi type="italic">She fell down at his feet,</hi> which was more than Martha did, who had a greater command of her passions. She fell down not as a sinking mourner, but fell down at his feet as a humble petitioner. This Mary had sat <hi type="italic">at Christ's feet to hear his word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.39">Luke x. 39</reference>), and here we find her there on another errand. Note, Those that in a day of peace place themselves at Christ's feet, to receive instructions from him, may with comfort and confidence in a day of trouble cast themselves at his feet with hope to find favour with him. She <hi type="italic">fell at his feet,</hi> as one submitting to his will in what was done, and referring herself to his good-will in what was now to be done. When we are in affliction we must cast ourselves at Christ's feet in a penitent sorrow and self-abasement for sin, and a patient resignation of ourselves to the divine disposal. Mary's casting herself at Christ's feet was in token of the profound respect and veneration she had for him. Thus subjects were wont to give honour to their kings and princes; but, our Lord Jesus not appearing in secular glory as an earthly prince, those who by this posture of adoration gave honour to him certainly looked upon him as more than man, and intended hereby to give him divine honour. Mary hereby made profession of the Christian faith as truly as Martha did, and in effect said, <hi type="italic">I believe that thou art the Christ; bowing the knee to</hi> Christ, and <hi type="italic">confessing him with the tongue,</hi> are put together as equivalent, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.11">Rom. xiv. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.10-Phil.2.11">Phil. ii. 10, 11</reference>. This she did in presence of <hi type="italic">the Jews</hi> that attended her, who, though friends to her and her family, yet were bitter enemies to Christ; yet in their sight she fell at Christ's feet, as one that was neither ashamed to own the veneration she had for Christ nor afraid of disobliging her friends and neighbours by it. Let them resent it as they pleased, she falls at his feet; and, if this be to be vile, she will be yet more vile; see <reference osisRef="Song.8.1">Cant. viii. 1</reference>. We serve a Master of whom we have no reason to be ashamed, and whose acceptance of our services is sufficient to balance the reproach of men and all their revilings. [2.] Her address is very pathetic: <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.</hi> Christ's delay was designed for the best, and proved so; yet both the sisters very indecently <hi type="italic">cast the same in his teeth,</hi> and in effect charge him with the death of their brother. This repeated challenge he might justly have resented, might have told them he had something else to do than to be at their beck and to attend them; he must come when his business would permit him: but not a word of this; he considered the circumstances of their affliction, and that losers think they may have leave to speak, and therefore overlooked the rudeness of this welcome, and gave us an example of mildness and meekness in such cases. Mary added no more, as Martha did; but it appears, by what follows, that what she fell short in words she made up in tears; she said less than Martha, but wept more; and tears of devout affection have a voice, a loud prevailing voice, in the ears of Christ; no rhetoric like this.

<div eID="gen27707" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ at the Grave of Lazarus; The Resurrection of Lazarus.</title> <div sID="gen27708" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, <hi type="super">34</hi> And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. <hi type="super">35</hi> Jesus wept. <hi type="super">36</hi> Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him! <hi type="super">37</hi> And some of them said, Could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died? <hi type="super">38</hi> Jesus therefore again groaning in himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it. <hi type="super">39</hi> Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been <hi type="italic">dead</hi> four days. <hi type="super">40</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God? <hi type="super">41</hi> Then they took away the stone <hi type="italic">from the place</hi> where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up <hi type="italic">his</hi> eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. <hi type="super">42</hi> And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that they may believe that thou hast sent me. <hi type="super">43</hi> And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. <hi type="super">44</hi> And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go. <div eID="gen27708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27709" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. Christ's tender <hi type="italic">sympathy</hi> with his afflicted friends, and the share he took to himself in their sorrows, which appeared three ways:— <div eID="gen27709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27710" type="x-p"/> 1. By the inward groans and troubles of his spirit (<reference osisRef="John.11.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jesus saw Mary weeping</hi> for the loss of a loving brother, and the <hi type="italic">Jews that came with her weeping</hi> for the loss of a good neighbour and friend; when he saw what a <hi type="italic">place of weepers,</hi> a <hi type="italic">bochim,</hi> this was, <hi type="italic">he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled.</hi> See here, <div eID="gen27710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27711" type="x-p"/> (1.) The griefs of the sons of men represented in the tears of Mary and her friends. What an emblem was here of this world, this vale of tears! Nature itself teaches us to weep over our dear relations, when they are removed by death; Providence thereby calls to <hi type="italic">weeping and mourning.</hi> It is probable that Lazarus's estate devolved upon his sisters, and was a considerable addition to their fortunes; and in such a case people say, now-a-days, though they cannot wish their relations dead (that is, they do not say they do), yet, if they were dead, they would not wish them alive again; but these sisters, whatever they got by their brother's death, heartily wished him alive again. Religion teaches us likewise to <hi type="italic">weep with them that weep,</hi> as these Jews wept with Mary, considering that we ourselves also <hi type="italic">are in the body.</hi> Those that truly love their friends will share with them in their joys and griefs; for what is friendship but a communication of affections? <reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job xvi. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27712" type="x-p"/> (2.) The grace of the Son of God and his compassion towards those that are in misery. <hi type="italic">In all their afflictions he is afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa. lxiii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.10.16">Judg. x. 16</reference>. When Christ saw them all in tears, <div eID="gen27712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27713" type="x-p"/> [1.] He <hi type="italic">groaned in the spirit.</hi> He suffered himself to be tempted (as we are when we are disturbed by some great affliction), <hi type="italic">yet without sin.</hi> This was an expression, either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of his displeasure at the inordinate grief of those about him, as <reference osisRef="Mark.5.39">Mark v. 39</reference>: "<hi type="italic">Why make ye this ado and weep?</hi> What a hurry is here! does this become those that believe in a God, a heaven, and another world?" Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of his feeling sense of the calamitous state of human lie, and the power of death, to which fallen man is subject. Having now to make a vigorous attack upon death and the grave, he thus stirred up himself to the encounter, <hi type="italic">put on the garments of vengeance,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his fury it upheld him;</hi> and that he might the more resolutely undertake the redress of our grievances, and the cure of our griefs, he was pleased to make himself sensible of the weight of them, and under the burden of them he now <hi type="italic">groaned in spirit.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It was an expression of his kind sympathy with his friends that were in sorrow. Here was the sounding of the bowels, the mercies which the afflicted church so earnestly solicits, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa. lxiii. 15</reference>. Christ not only seemed concerned, but he <hi type="italic">groaned in the spirit;</hi> he was inwardly and sincerely affected with the case. David's pretended friends counterfeited sympathy, to disguise their enmity (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.6">Ps. xli. 6</reference>); but we must learn of Christ to have our love and sympathy <hi type="italic">without dissimulation.</hi> Christ's was a deep and hearty sigh. <div eID="gen27713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27714" type="x-p"/> [2.] He was <hi type="italic">troubled.</hi> He <hi type="italic">troubled himself;</hi> so the phrase is, very significantly. He had all the passions and affections of the human nature, for in all things he must <hi type="italic">be like to his brethren;</hi> but he had a perfect command of them, so that they were never <hi type="italic">up,</hi> but <hi type="italic">when</hi> and <hi type="italic">as</hi> they were called; he was never troubled, but when he <hi type="italic">troubled himself,</hi> as he saw cause. He often <hi type="italic">composed</hi> himself to trouble, but was never discomposed or disordered by it. He was voluntary both in his passion and in his compassion. He had power to lay down his grief, and power to take it again. <div eID="gen27714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27715" type="x-p"/> 2. His concern for them appeared by his <hi type="italic">kind enquiry</hi> after the poor remains of his deceased friend (<reference osisRef="John.11.34">v. 34</reference>): Where <hi type="italic">have you laid him?</hi> He knew where he was laid, and yet asks, because, (1.) He would thus express himself as <hi type="italic">a man,</hi> even when he was going to exert the power of a God. Being found in fashion as a man, he accommodates himself to the way and manner of the sons of men: <hi type="italic">Non nescit, sed quasi nescit—He is not ignorant, but he makes as if he were,</hi> saith Austin here. (2.) He enquired where the grave was, lest, if he had gone straight to it of his own knowledge, the unbelieving Jews should have thence taken occasion to suspect a collusion between him and Lazarus, and a trick in the case. Many expositors observe this from Chrysostom. (3.) He would thus divert the grief of his mourning friends, by raising their expectations of something great; as if he had said, "I did not come hither with an address of condolence, to mingle a few fruitless insignificant tears with yours; no, I have other work to do; come, let us adjourn to the grave, and go about our business there." Note, A serious address to our work is the best remedy against inordinate grief. (4.) He would hereby intimate to us the special care he takes of the bodies of the saints while they lie in the grave; he takes notice <hi type="italic">where they are laid,</hi> and will look after them. There is not only a covenant with the dust, but a guard upon it. <div eID="gen27715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27716" type="x-p"/> 3. It appeared by <hi type="italic">his tears.</hi> Those about him did not tell him where the body was buried, but desired him to <hi type="italic">come and see,</hi> and led him directly to the grave, that his eye might yet more affect his heart with the calamity. <div eID="gen27716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27717" type="x-p"/> (1.) As he was going to the grave, as if he had been following the corpse thither, <hi type="italic">Jesus wept,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.35">v. 35</reference>. A very short verse, but it affords many useful instructions. [1.] That Jesus Christ was really and truly man, and partook with the children, not only of flesh and blood, but of a human soul, susceptible of the impressions of joy, and grief, and other affections. Christ gave this proof of his humanity, in both senses of the word; that, as a man, he could weep, and, as a merciful man, he <hi type="italic">would weep,</hi> before he gave this proof of his divinity. [2.] That he was <hi type="italic">a man of sorrows,</hi> and <hi type="italic">acquainted with grief,</hi> as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 3</reference>. We never read that he laughed, but more than once we have him in tears. Thus he shows not only that a mournful state will consist with the love of God, but that those who sow to the Spirit must sow in tears. [3.] Tears of compassion well become Christians, and make them most to resemble Christ. It is a relief to those who are in sorrow to have their friends sympathize with them, especially such a friend as their Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen27717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27718" type="x-p"/> (2.) Different constructions were put upon Christ's weeping. [1.] Some made a kind and candid interpretation of it, and what was very natural (<reference osisRef="John.11.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!</hi> They seem to wonder that he should have so strong an affection for one to whom he was not related, and with whom he had not had any long acquaintance, for Christ spent most of his time in Galilee, a great way from Bethany. It becomes us, according to this example of Christ, to show our love to our friends, both living and dying. We must sorrow for our brethren that sleep in Jesus as those that are full of love, though not void of hope; as the <hi type="italic">devout men</hi> that buried Stephen, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.2">Acts viii. 2</reference>. Though our tears profit not the dead, they embalm their memory. These tears were indications of his particular love to Lazarus, but he has given proofs no less evident of his love to all the saints, in that he died for them. When he only dropped a tear over Lazarus, they said, <hi type="italic">See how he loved him!</hi> Much more reason have we to say so, for whom he hath laid down his life: <hi type="italic">See how he loved us! Greater love has no man than this</hi> [2.] Others made a peevish unfair reflection upon it, as if these tears bespoke his inability to help his friend (<reference osisRef="John.11.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind,</hi> have prevented the death of Lazarus? Here it is slyly insinuated, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the death of Lazarus being (as it seemed by his tears) a great grief to him, if he could have prevented it he would, and therefore because he <hi type="italic">did not</hi> they incline to think that he <hi type="italic">could not;</hi> as, when he was dying, they concluded that he could not, because he did not, save himself, and <hi type="italic">come down from the cross;</hi> not considering that divine power is always directed in its operations by divine wisdom, not merely according to his will, but according to the counsel of his will, wherein it becomes us to acquiesce. If Christ's friends, whom he loves, die,—if his church, whom he loves, be persecuted and afflicted,—we must not impute it to any defect either in his power or love, but conclude that it is because he sees it for the best. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That therefore it might justly be questioned whether he did indeed <hi type="italic">open the eyes of the blind,</hi> that is, whether it was not a sham. His not working this miracle they thought enough to invalidate the former; at least, it should seem that he had limited power, and therefore not a divine one. Christ soon convinced these <hi type="italic">whisperers,</hi> by raising Lazarus from the dead, which was the greater work, that he could have prevented his death, but therefore did not because he would glorify himself the more. <div eID="gen27718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's approach to the grave, and the preparation that was made for working this miracle. <div eID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27720" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ repeats his groans upon his coming near the grave (<reference osisRef="John.11.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">Again groaning in himself, he comes to the grave:</hi> he groaned, (1.) Being displeased at the unbelief of those who spoke doubtingly of his power, and blamed him for not preventing the death of Lazarus; he was <hi type="italic">grieved for the hardness of their hearts.</hi> He never groaned so much for his own pains and sufferings as for the sins and follies of men, particularly Jerusalem's, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>. (2.) Being affected with the fresh lamentations which, it is likely, the mourning sisters made when they came near the grave, more passionately and pathetically than before, his tender spirit was sensibly touched with their wailings. (3.) Some think that he <hi type="italic">groaned in spirit</hi> because, to gratify the desire of his friends, he was to bring Lazarus again into this sinful troublesome world, from that rest into which he was newly entered; it would be a kindness to Martha and Mary, but it would be to him like thrusting one out to a stormy sea again who was newly got into a safe and quiet harbour. If Lazarus had been let alone, Christ would quickly have gone to him into the other world; but, being restored to life, Christ quickly left him behind in this world. (4.) Christ groaned as one that would affect himself with the calamitous state of the human nature, as subject to death, from which he was now about to redeem Lazarus. Thus he stirred up himself to take hold on God in the prayer he was to make, that he might <hi type="italic">offer it up with strong crying,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. Ministers, when they are sent by the preaching of the gospel to raise dead souls, should be much affected with the deplorable condition of those they preach to and pray for, and groan in themselves to think of it. <div eID="gen27720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27721" type="x-p"/> 2. The grave wherein Lazarus lay is here described: <hi type="italic">It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it.</hi> The graves of the common people, probably, were dug as ours are; but persons of distinction were, as with us, interred in vaults, so Lazarus was, and such was the sepulchre in which Christ was buried. Probably this fashion was kept up among the Jews, in imitation of the patriarchs, who buried their dead in the cave of Machpelah, <reference osisRef="Gen.23.19">Gen. xxiii. 19</reference>. This care taken of the dead bodies of their friends intimates their expectation of their resurrection; they reckoned the solemnity of the funeral ended when the stone was rolled to the grave, or, as here, <hi type="italic">laid upon it,</hi> like that on the mouth of the den into which Daniel was cast (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.17">Dan. vi. 17</reference>), that the <hi type="italic">purpose might not be changed;</hi> intimating that the dead are separated from the living, and gone the <hi type="italic">way whence they shall not return.</hi> This stone was probably a <hi type="italic">gravestone,</hi> with an inscription upon it, which the Greeks called <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mnemeion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a memorandum,</hi> because it is both a <hi type="italic">memorial</hi> of the dead and a <hi type="italic">memento</hi> to the living, putting them in remembrance of that which we are all concerned to remember. It is called by the Latins, <hi type="italic">Monumentum, &#224; monendo,</hi> because it gives <hi type="italic">warning.</hi> <div eID="gen27721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27722" type="x-p"/> 3. Orders are given to remove the stone (<reference osisRef="John.11.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take away the stone.</hi> He would have this stone removed that all the standersby might see the body lie dead in the sepulchre, and that way might be made for its coming out, and it might appear to be a true body, and not a <hi type="italic">ghost</hi> or <hi type="italic">spectre.</hi> He would have some of the servants to remove it, that they might be witnesses, by the smell of the putrefaction of the body, and that therefore it was truly dead. It is a good step towards the raising of a soul to spiritual life when the stone is taken away, when prejudices are removed and got over, and way made for the word to the heart, that it may do its work there, and say what it has to say. <div eID="gen27722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27723" type="x-p"/> 4. An objection made by Martha against the opening of the grave: <hi type="italic">Lord, by this time he stinketh,</hi> or <hi type="italic">is become noisome, for he has been dead four days,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tetartaios gar esti</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">quatriduanus est;</hi> he is <hi type="italic">four days old</hi> in the other world; a citizen and inhabitant of the grave of four days' standing. Probably Martha perceived the body to smell, as they were removing the stone, and therefore cried out thus. <div eID="gen27723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27724" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is easy to observe hence the nature of human bodies: four days are but a little while, yet what a great change will this time make with the body of man, if it be but so long <hi type="italic">without food,</hi> much more if so long <hi type="italic">without life!</hi> Dead bodies (saith Dr. Hammond) after a revolution of the humours, which is completed in seventy-two hours, naturally tend to putrefaction; and the Jews say that by the fourth day after death the body is so altered that one cannot be sure it is such a person; so Maimonides in Lightfoot. Christ rose the third day because he was not to <hi type="italic">see corruption.</hi> <div eID="gen27724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27725" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is not so easy to say what was Martha's design in saying this. [1.] Some think she said it in a due tenderness, and such as decency teaches to the dead body; now that it began to putrefy, she did not care it should be thus publicly shown and made a spectacle of. [2.] Others think she said it out of a concern for Christ, lest the smell of the dead body should be <hi type="italic">offensive</hi> to him. That which is very noisome is compared to an open sepulchre, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Ps. v. 9</reference>. If there were any thing noisome she would not have her Master near it; but he was none of those tender and delicate ones that cannot bear as ill smell; if he had, he would not have visited the world of mankind, which sin had made a perfect dunghill, altogether noisome, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">Ps. xiv. 3</reference>. [3.] It should seem, by Christ's answer, that it was the language of her unbelief and distrust: "Lord, it is too late now to attempt any kindness to him; his body begins to rot, and it is impossible that this putrid carcase should <hi type="italic">live.</hi>" She gives up his case as helpless and hopeless, there having been no instances, either of late or formerly, of any raised to life after they had begun to see corruption. When <hi type="italic">our bones are dried,</hi> we are ready to say, <hi type="italic">Our hope is lost.</hi> Yet this distrustful word of hers served to make the miracle both the more evident and the more illustrious; by this it appeared that he was truly dead, and not in a trance; for, though the posture of a dead body might be counterfeited, the smell could not. Her suggesting that it <hi type="italic">could not be done</hi> puts the more honour upon him that <hi type="italic">did it.</hi> <div eID="gen27725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27726" type="x-p"/> 5. The gentle reproof Christ gave to Martha for the weakness of her faith (<reference osisRef="John.11.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">Said I not unto thee that if thou wouldest believe thou shouldest see the glory of God?</hi> This word of his to her was not before recorded; it is probable that he said it to her when she had said (<reference osisRef="John.11.27">v. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lord, I believe:</hi> and it is enough that it is recorded here, where it is repeated. Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus has given us all the assurances imaginable that a sincere faith shall at length be crowned with a blessed vision: "If thou believe, thou shalt see God's glorious appearances for thee in this world, and to thee in the other world." If we will take Christ's word, and rely on his power and faithfulness, we shall see the glory of God, and be happy in the sight. (2.) We have need to be often reminded of these <hi type="italic">sure mercies</hi> with which our Lord Jesus hath encouraged us. Christ does not give a direct answer to what Martha had said, nor any particular promise of what he would do, but orders her to keep hold of the general assurances he had already given: <hi type="italic">Only believe.</hi> We are apt to forget what Christ has spoken, and need him to put us in mind of it by his Spirit: "<hi type="italic">Said I not unto thee</hi> so and so? And dost thou think that he will ever unsay it?" <div eID="gen27726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27727" type="x-p"/> 6. The opening of the grave, in obedience to Christ's order, notwithstanding Martha's objection (<reference osisRef="John.11.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then they took away the stone.</hi> When Martha was satisfied, and had waived her objection, <hi type="italic">then</hi> they proceeded. If we will see the glory of God, we must let Christ take his own way, and not <hi type="italic">prescribe</hi> but <hi type="italic">subscribe</hi> to him. <hi type="italic">They took away the stone,</hi> and this was all they could do; Christ only could <hi type="italic">give life.</hi> What man can do is but to <hi type="italic">prepare the way of the Lord,</hi> to fill the valleys, and level the hills, and, as here, to <hi type="italic">take away the stone.</hi> <div eID="gen27727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27728" type="x-p"/> III. The miracle itself wrought. The spectators, invited by the rolling away of the stone, gathered about the grave, not to commit <hi type="italic">dust to dust, earth to earth,</hi> but to receive dust from the dust, and earth from the earth again; and, their expectations being raised, our Lord Jesus addresses himself to his work. <div eID="gen27728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27729" type="x-p"/> 1. He applies himself to his <hi type="italic">living Father in heaven,</hi> so he had called him (<reference osisRef="John.6.17">ch. vi. 17</reference>), and so eyes him here. <div eID="gen27729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27730" type="x-p"/> (1.) The gesture he used was very significant: <hi type="italic">He lifted up his eyes,</hi> an outward expression of the elevation of his mind, and to show those who stood by whence he derived his power; also to set us an example; this outward sign is hereby recommended to our practice; see <reference osisRef="John.17.1">ch. xvii. 1</reference>. Look how those will answer it who profanely ridicule it; but that which is especially charged upon us hereby is to <hi type="italic">lift up our hearts</hi> to God in the heavens; what is prayer, but the ascent of the soul to God, and the directing of its affections and motions heavenward? He <hi type="italic">lifted up</hi> his eyes, as looking above, looking beyond the grave where Lazarus lay, and overlooking all the difficulties that arose thence, that he might have his eyes fixed upon the divine omnipotence; to teach us to do as Abraham, who considered not <hi type="italic">his own body now dead, nor the deadness of Sarah's womb,</hi> never took these into his thoughts, and so gained such a degree of faith as not to <hi type="italic">stagger at the promise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.20">Rom. iv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen27730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27731" type="x-p"/> (2.) His address to God was with great assurance, and such a confidence as became him: <hi type="italic">Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.</hi> <div eID="gen27731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27732" type="x-p"/> [1.] He has here taught us, by his own example, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In prayer to call God Father, and to draw nigh to him as children to a father, with a humble reverence, and yet with a holy boldness. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In our <hi type="italic">prayers</hi> to <hi type="italic">praise him,</hi> and, when we come to beg for further mercy, thankfully to acknowledge former favours. Thanksgivings, which bespeak <hi type="italic">God's glory</hi> (not <hi type="italic">our own,</hi> like the Pharisee's God, <hi type="italic">I thank thee</hi>), are decent forms into which to put our supplications. <div eID="gen27732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27733" type="x-p"/> [2.] But our Saviour's thanksgiving here was intended to express the unshaken assurance he had of the effecting of this miracle, which he had in his own power to do in concurrence with his Father: "<hi type="italic">Father, I thank thee</hi> that my will and thine are in this matter, as always, the same." Elijah and Elisha raised the dead, as servants, by <hi type="italic">entreaty;</hi> but Christ, as a Son, by <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> having life in himself, and power to quicken whom he would; and he speaks of this as his own act (<reference osisRef="John.11.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">I go, that I may awake him;</hi> yet he speaks of it as what he had obtained by prayer, for his Father <hi type="italic">heard him:</hi> probably he put up the prayer for it when he <hi type="italic">groaned in spirit</hi> once and again (<reference osisRef="John.11.33">v. 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.38">38</reference>), in a <hi type="italic">mental</hi> prayer, with groanings which could not be <hi type="italic">uttered.</hi> <div eID="gen27733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27734" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ speaks of this miracle as an answer to prayer, 1. Because he would thus <hi type="italic">humble himself;</hi> though he was a Son, yet <hi type="italic">learned he this obedience,</hi> to ask and receive. His mediatorial crown was granted him upon request, though it is <hi type="italic">of right,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.5">and ch. xvii. 5</reference>. He prays for the glory he had before the world was, though, having never forfeited it, he might have demanded it. 2. Because he was pleased thus to <hi type="italic">honour prayer,</hi> making it the key wherewith even he unlocked the treasures of divine power and grace. Thus he would teach us in prayer, by the lively exercise of faith, to <hi type="italic">enter into the holiest.</hi> <div eID="gen27734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ, being assured that his prayer was answered, professes, <div eID="gen27735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27736" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> His thankful acceptance of this answer: <hi type="italic">I thank thee that thou hast heard me.</hi> Though the miracle was not yet wrought, yet the prayer was answered, and he triumphs before the victory. No other can pretend to such an assurance as Christ had; yet we may by faith in the promise have a prospect of mercy before it be actually given in, and may rejoice in that prospect, and give God thanks for it. In David's devotions, the same psalm which begins with prayer for a mercy closes with thanksgivings for it. Note, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Mercies in answer to prayer ought in a special manner to be acknowledged with thankfulness. Besides the grant of the mercy itself, we are to value it as a great favour to have our poor prayers taken notice of. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) We ought to <hi type="italic">meet</hi> the first appearances of the return of prayer with early thanksgivings. As God <hi type="italic">answers</hi> us with mercy, even <hi type="italic">before we call,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hears while we are yet speaking,</hi> so we should answer him with praise even before he grants, and give him thanks while he is yet speaking good words and comfortable words. <div eID="gen27736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> His cheerful assurance of a ready answer at any time (<reference osisRef="John.11.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">And I know that thou hearest me always.</hi> Let none think that this was some uncommon favour granted him now, such as he never had before, nor should ever have again; no, he had the same divine power going along with him in his whole undertaking, and undertook nothing but what he knew to be agreeable to the counsel of God's will. "I <hi type="italic">gave thanks</hi>" (saith he) "for being heard in this, because I am sure to be heard in every thing." See here, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The interest our Lord Jesus had in heaven; the Father <hi type="italic">heard him always,</hi> he had access to the Father upon every occasion, and success with him in every errand. And we may be sure that his interest is not the less for his going to heaven, which may encourage us to depend upon his intercession, and put all our petitions into his hand, for we are sure that him the Father <hi type="italic">hears always.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The confidence he had of that interest: <hi type="italic">I knew it.</hi> He did not in the least hesitate or doubt concerning it, but had an entire satisfaction in his own mind of the Father's complacency in him and concurrence with him in every thing. We cannot have such a particular assurance as he had; but this we know, that <hi type="italic">whatsoever we ask according to his will he heareth us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.14-1John.5.15">1 John v. 14, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen27737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27738" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> But why should Christ give this public intimation of his obtaining this miracle by prayer? He adds, It is <hi type="italic">because of the people who stand by, that they may believe that thou hast sent me;</hi> for <hi type="italic">prayer may preach.</hi> 1. It was to obviate the objections of his enemies, and their reflections. It was blasphemously suggested by the Pharisees, and their creatures, that he wrought his miracles by compact with the devil; now, to evidence the contrary, he openly made his address to God, using <hi type="italic">prayers,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">charms,</hi> not <hi type="italic">peeping and muttering</hi> as those did that used <hi type="italic">familiar spirits</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>), but, with elevated eyes and voice professing his communication with Heaven, and dependence on Heaven. 2. It was to corroborate the faith of those that were well inclined to him: <hi type="italic">That they may believe that thou hast sent me,</hi> not to destroy men's lives, but to save them. Moses, to show that God sent him, made the earth open and swallow men up (<reference osisRef="Num.16.31">Num. xvi. 31</reference>); Elijah, to show that God sent him, made fire come from heaven and devour men; for the law was a dispensation of terror and death but Christ proves his mission by raising to life one that was dead. Some give this sense: had Christ declared his doing it freely by his own power, some of his weak disciples, who as yet understood not his divine nature, would have thought he took too much upon him, and have been stumbled at it. These <hi type="italic">babes</hi> could not bear that <hi type="italic">strong meat,</hi> therefore he chooses to speak of his power as received and derived he speaks self-denyingly of himself, that he might speak the more plainly to us. <hi type="italic">Non ita respexit ad swam dignitatem atque ad nostram salutem</hi>—<hi type="italic">In what he said, he consulted not so much his dignity as our salvation.</hi>—Jansenius. <div eID="gen27738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27739" type="x-p"/> 2. He now applies himself to his <hi type="italic">dead friend in the earth.</hi> He <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice, Lazarus come forth.</hi> <div eID="gen27739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27740" type="x-p"/> (1.) He could have raised Lazarus by a silent exertion of his power and will, and the indiscernible operations of the Spirit of life; but he did it by a call, a loud call, <div eID="gen27740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27741" type="x-p"/> [1.] To be significant of the power then put forth for the raising of Lazarus, how he <hi type="italic">created this new thing;</hi> he <hi type="italic">spoke, and it was done.</hi> He cried aloud, to signify the greatness of the work, and of the power employed in it, and to excite himself as it were to this attack upon the gates of death, as soldiers engage with a shout. Speaking to Lazarus, it was proper to <hi type="italic">cry with a loud voice;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The soul of Lazarus, which was to be called back, was at a distance, not hovering about the grave, as the Jews fancied, but removed to Hades, the world of spirits; now it is natural to speak loud when we call to those at a distance. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The body of Lazarus, which was to be called up, was <hi type="italic">asleep,</hi> and we usually speak loud when we would awake any out of sleep. He cried with a loud voice that the scripture might be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa. xlv. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth.</hi> <div eID="gen27741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27742" type="x-p"/> [2.] To be typical of other works of wonder, and particularly other resurrections, which the power of Christ was to effect. This loud call was a figure, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of the gospel call, by which dead souls were to be brought out of the grave of sin, which resurrection Christ had formerly spoken of (<reference osisRef="John.5.25">ch. v. 25</reference>), and of his word as the means of it (<reference osisRef="John.6.63">ch. vi. 63</reference>), and now he gives a specimen of it. By his word, he saith to souls, <hi type="italic">Live, yea, he</hi> saith to them, <hi type="italic">Live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Arise from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Eph. v. 14</reference>. The spirit of life from God entered into those that had been dead and dry bones, when Ezekiel prophesied over them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.10">Ezek. xxxvii. 10</reference>. Those who infer from the commands of the word to <hi type="italic">turn and live</hi> that man has a power of his own to convert and regenerate himself might as well infer from this call to Lazarus that he had a power to raise himself to life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of the sound of the archangel's trumpet at the last day, with which they that sleep in the dust shall be awakened and summoned before the great tribunal, when Christ shall <hi type="italic">descend with a shout, a call, or command,</hi> like this here, <hi type="italic">Come forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">Ps. l. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall call</hi> both <hi type="italic">to the heavens</hi> for their souls, <hi type="italic">and to the earth</hi> for their bodies, <hi type="italic">that he may judge his people.</hi> <div eID="gen27742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27743" type="x-p"/> (2.) This <hi type="italic">loud call</hi> was but <hi type="italic">short,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">mighty through God</hi> to the battering down of the strongholds of the grave. [1.] He calls him by name, Lazarus, as we call those by their names whom we would awake out of a fast sleep. God said to Moses, as a mark of his favour, <hi type="italic">I know thee by name.</hi> The naming of him intimates that the same individual person that died shall rise again at the last day. He that <hi type="italic">calls the stars by their names</hi> can distinguish by name his stars that are in the dust of the earth, and will lose none of them. [2.] He calls him <hi type="italic">out of the grave,</hi> speaking to him as if he were already alive, and had nothing to do but to come out of his grave. He does not say unto him, <hi type="italic">Live;</hi> for he himself must give life; but he saith to him, <hi type="italic">Move,</hi> for when by the grace of Christ we live spiritually we must stir up ourselves to <hi type="italic">move;</hi> the grave of sin and this world is no place for those whom Christ has quickened, and therefore they must <hi type="italic">come forth.</hi> [3.] The event was according to the intention: <hi type="italic">He that was dead came forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.44">v. 44</reference>. Power went along with the word of Christ to reunite the soul and the body of Lazarus, and then he came forth. The miracle is described, not by its invisible springs, to satisfy our curiosity, but by its visible effects, to conform our faith. Do any ask where the soul of Lazarus was during the four days of its separation? We are not told, but have reason to think it was in paradise; <hi type="italic">in joy and felicity;</hi> but you will say, "Was it not then really an unkindness to it to cause it to return into the prison of the body?" And if it were, yet, being for the honour of Christ and the serving of the interests of his kingdom, it was no more an injury to him than it was to St. Paul to continue in the flesh when he knew that to depart to Christ was so much better. If any ask whether Lazarus, after he was raised, could give an account or description of his soul's removal out of the body or return to it, or what he saw in the other world, I suppose both those changes were so unaccountable to himself that he must say with Paul, <hi type="italic">Whether in the body or out of the body, I cannot tell;</hi> and of what he saw and heard, that it was not lawful nor possible to express it. In a world of sense we cannot frame to ourselves, much less communicate to others, any adequate ideas of the world of spirits and the affairs of that world. Let us not covet to be wise above what is written, and this is all that is written concerning the resurrection of that Lazarus, that <hi type="italic">he that was dead came forth.</hi> Some have observed that though we read of many who were raised from the dead, who no doubt conversed familiarly with men afterwards, yet the scripture has not recorded one word spoken by any of them, except by our Lord Jesus only. <div eID="gen27743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27744" type="x-p"/> (3.) This miracle was wrought, [1.] <hi type="italic">Speedily.</hi> Nothing intervenes between the command, <hi type="italic">Come forth,</hi> and the effect, <hi type="italic">He came forth; dictum factum—no sooner said than done;</hi> let there be life, and there was life. Thus the change in the resurrection will be <hi type="italic">in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">1 Cor. xv. 52</reference>. The almighty power that can do it can do it in an instant: <hi type="italic">Then shalt thou call and I will answer;</hi> will come at the call, as Lazarus, <hi type="italic">Here am I.</hi> [2.] <hi type="italic">Perfectly.</hi> He was so thoroughly revived that he got up out of his grave as strongly as ever he got up out of his bed, and returned not only to life, but health. He was not raised to serve a present turn, but to live as other men. [3.] With this additional miracle, as some reckon it, that he came out of his grave, though he was fettered with his grave-clothes, with which he was <hi type="italic">bound hand and foot,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his face bound about with a napkin</hi> (for so the manner of the Jews was to bury); and he came forth in the same dress wherein he was buried, that it might appear that it was he himself and not another, and that he was not only alive, but strong, and able to walk, after a sort, even in his grave-clothes. The <hi type="italic">binding of his face with a napkin</hi> proved that he had been really dead, for otherwise, in less than so many days' time, that would have smothered him. And the standers-by, in unbinding him, would <hi type="italic">handle him, and see him, that it was he himself,</hi> and so be witnesses of the miracle. Now see here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How little we carry away with us, when we leave the world—only a winding-sheet and a coffin; there is no change of raiment in the grave, nothing but a single suit of grave-clothes. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What condition we shall be in in the grave. What <hi type="italic">wisdom or device</hi> can there be where the eyes are hoodwinked, or what working where the hands and feet are fettered? And so it will be in the grave, whither we are going. Lazarus being <hi type="italic">come forth,</hi> hampered and embarrassed with his grave-clothes, we may well imagine that those about the grave were exceedingly surprised and frightened at it; we should be so if we should see a dead body rise; but Christ, to make the thing familiar, sets them to work: "<hi type="italic">Loose him,</hi> slacken his grave-clothes, that they may serve for day-clothes till he comes to his house, and then he will go himself, so clad, without guide or supporter to his own house." As, in the Old Testament, the translations of Enoch and Elias were sensible demonstrations of an invisible and future state, the one about the middle of the patriarchal age, the other of the Mosaic economy, so the resurrection of Lazarus, in the New Testament, was designed for the confirmation of the doctrine of the resurrection.

<div eID="gen27744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Consultation of the Pharisees; The Prophecy of Caiaphas; A Conspiracy against Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">45</hi> Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on him. <hi type="super">46</hi> But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done. <hi type="super">47</hi> Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles. <hi type="super">48</hi> If we let him thus alone, all <hi type="italic">men</hi> will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation. <hi type="super">49</hi> And one of them, <hi type="italic">named</hi> Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all, <hi type="super">50</hi> Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not. <hi type="super">51</hi> And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; <hi type="super">52</hi> And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad. <hi type="super">53</hi> Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death. <hi type="super">54</hi> Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews; but went thence unto a country near to the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim, and there continued with his disciples. <hi type="super">55</hi> And the Jews' passover was nigh at hand: and many went out of the country up to Jerusalem before the passover, to purify themselves. <hi type="super">56</hi> Then sought they for Jesus, and spake among themselves, as they stood in the temple, What think ye, that he will not come to the feast? <hi type="super">57</hi> Now both the chief priests and the Pharisees had given a commandment, that, if any man knew where he were, he should show <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that they might take him. <div eID="gen27745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27746" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the consequences of this glorious miracle, which were as usual; to some it was a savour of life unto life, to others of death unto death. <div eID="gen27746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27747" type="x-p"/> I. Some were invited by it, and induced to believe. Many of the Jews, when they <hi type="italic">saw the things that Jesus did, believed on him,</hi> and well they might, for it was an incontestable proof of his divine mission. They had often heard of his miracles, and yet evaded the conviction of them, by calling in question the matter of fact; but now that they had themselves seen this done their unbelief was conquered, and they yielded at last. But <hi type="italic">blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.</hi> The more we see of Christ the more cause we shall see to love him and confide in him. These were some of those Jews that came to Mary, to comfort her. When we are doing good offices to others we put ourselves in the way of receiving favours from God, and have opportunities of getting good when we are doing good. <div eID="gen27747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27748" type="x-p"/> II. Others were irritated by it, and hardened in their unbelief. <div eID="gen27748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27749" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">informers</hi> were so (<reference osisRef="John.11.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">Some of them,</hi> who were eye-witnesses of the miracle, were so far from being convinced that they <hi type="italic">went to the Pharisees,</hi> whom they knew to be his implacable enemies, and <hi type="italic">told them what things Jesus had done;</hi> not merely as a matter of news worthy their notice, much less as an inducement to them to think more favourably of Christ, but with a spiteful design to excite those who needed no spur the more vigorously to prosecute him. Here is a strange instance, (1.) Of a most <hi type="italic">obstinate infidelity,</hi> refusing to yield to the most powerful means of conviction; and it is hard to imagine how they could evade the force of this evidence, but that the <hi type="italic">god of this world</hi> had <hi type="italic">blinded their minds.</hi> (2.) Of a most <hi type="italic">inveterate enmity.</hi> If they would not be satisfied that he was to be believed in as the Christ, yet one would think they should have been mollified, and persuaded not to persecute him; but, if the water be not sufficient to <hi type="italic">quench</hi> the fire, it will <hi type="italic">inflame</hi> it. They told <hi type="italic">what Jesus had done,</hi> and told no more than what was true; but their malice gave a tincture of diabolism to their information equal to that of <hi type="italic">lying;</hi> perverting what is true is as bad as forging what is false. <hi type="italic">Doeg</hi> is called a <hi type="italic">false, lying,</hi> and <hi type="italic">deceitful tongue</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.2-Ps.52.4">Ps. lii. 2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.120.2-Ps.120.3">cxx. 2, 3</reference>), though what he said was <hi type="italic">true.</hi> <div eID="gen27749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27750" type="x-p"/> 2. The judges, the leaders, the <hi type="italic">blind leaders,</hi> of the people were no less exasperated by the report made to them, and here we are told what they did. <div eID="gen27750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27751" type="x-p"/> (1.) A special council is called and held (<reference osisRef="John.11.47">v. 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then gathered the chief priests and Pharisees a council,</hi> as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">The rulers take counsel together against the Lord.</hi> Consultations of the sanhedrim were intended for the public good; but here, under colour of this, the greatest injury and mischief are done to the people. The things that belong to the nation's peace were hid from the eyes of those that were entrusted with its counsels. This council was called, not only for joint advice, but for mutual irritation; that as iron sharpens iron, and as coals are to burning coals and wood to fire, so they might exasperate and inflame one another with enmity and rage against Christ and his doctrine. <div eID="gen27751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27752" type="x-p"/> (2.) The case is proposed, and shown to be weighty and of great consequence. <div eID="gen27752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27753" type="x-p"/> [1.] The matter to be debated was what course they should take with this Jesus, to stop the growth of his interest; they said <hi type="italic">What do we? For this man doeth many miracles.</hi> The information given about the raising of Lazarus was produced, and the <hi type="italic">men, brethren, and fathers</hi> were called in to help as solicitously as if a formidable enemy had been with an army in the heart of their country. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They own the truth of Christ's miracles, and that he had wrought many of them; they are therefore witnesses against themselves, for they acknowledge his credentials and yet deny his commission. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They consider what is to be done, and chide themselves that they have not done something sooner effectually to crush him. They do not take it at all into their consideration whether they shall not receive him and own him as the Messiah, though they profess to expect him, and Jesus gave pregnant proofs of his being so; but they take it for granted that he is an enemy, and as such is to be run down: "<hi type="italic">What do we?</hi> Have we no care to support our church? Is it nothing to us that a doctrine so destructive to our interest spreads thus? Shall we tamely yield up the ground we have got in the affections of the people? Shall we see our authority brought into contempt, and the craft by which we get our living ruined, and not bestir ourselves? What have we been doing all this while? And what are we now thinking of? Shall we be always talking, and bring nothing to pass?" <div eID="gen27753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27754" type="x-p"/> [2.] That which made this matter weighty was the peril they apprehended their church and nation to be in from the Romans (<reference osisRef="John.11.48">v. 48</reference>): "If we do not silence him, and take him off, <hi type="italic">all men will believe on him;</hi> and, this being the setting up of a new king, the Romans will take umbrage at it, <hi type="italic">and will come</hi> with an army, and <hi type="italic">take away our place and nation,</hi> and therefore it is no time to trifle." See what an opinion they have, <div eID="gen27754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of their own <hi type="italic">power.</hi> They speak as if they thought Christ's progress and success in his work depended upon their connivance; as if he could not go on to work miracles, and make disciples, unless they <hi type="italic">let him alone;</hi> as if it were in their power to conquer him who had conquered death, or as if they could <hi type="italic">fight against God,</hi> and prosper. But he that sits in heaven laughs at the fond conceit which impotent malice has of its own omnipotence. <div eID="gen27755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27756" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of their own <hi type="italic">policy.</hi> They fancy themselves to be men of mighty insight and foresight, and great sagacity in their moral prognostications. <div eID="gen27756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27757" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> They take on them to prophecy that, in a little time, if he have liberty to go on, <hi type="italic">all men will believe on him,</hi> hereby owning, when it was to serve their purpose, that his doctrine and miracles had a very convincing power in them, such as could not be resisted, but that all men would become his proselytes and votaries. Thus do they now make his interest formidable, though, to serve another turn, these same men strove to make it contemptible, <reference osisRef="John.7.48">ch. vii. 48</reference>, <hi type="italic">Have any of the rulers believed on him?</hi> This was the thing they were afraid of, that men would <hi type="italic">believe on him,</hi> and then all their measures were broken. Note, The success of the gospel is the dread of its adversaries; if souls be saved, they are undone. <div eID="gen27757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27758" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> They foretel that if the generality of the nation be <hi type="italic">drawn after him,</hi> the rage of the Romans will be <hi type="italic">drawn upon them.</hi> They <hi type="italic">will come and take away our place;</hi> the country in general, especially Jerusalem, or the temple, the <hi type="italic">holy place,</hi> and <hi type="italic">their</hi> place, their darling, their idol; or, their <hi type="italic">preferments</hi> in the temple, their <hi type="italic">places</hi> of power and trust. Now it was true that the Romans had a very jealous eye upon them, and knew they wanted nothing but power and opportunity to shake off their yoke. It was likewise true that if the Romans should pour an army in upon them it would be very hard for them to make any head against it; yet here appeared a cowardice which one would not have found in the priests of the Lord if they had not by their wickedness forfeited their interest in God and all good men. Had they kept their integrity, they needed not to have feared the Romans; but they speak like a dispirited people, as the men of Judah when they basely said to Samson, <hi type="italic">Knowest thou not that the Philistines rule over us?</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.15.11">Judg. xv. 11</reference>. When men lose their piety they lose their courage. But, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) It was false that there was any danger of the Romans' being irritated against their nation by the progress of Christ's gospel, for it was no way <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings nor provinces,</hi> but highly beneficial. The Romans had no jealousy at all of his growing interest; for he taught men to give tribute to Cæsar, and not to <hi type="italic">resist evil,</hi> but to take up the cross. The Roman governor, at his trial, could <hi type="italic">find no fault in him.</hi> There was more danger of the Romans' being incensed against the Jewish nation by the priests than by Christ. Note, Pretended fears are often the colour of malicious designs. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Had there really been some danger of displeasing the Romans by tolerating Christ's preaching, yet this would not justify their hating and persecuting a good man. Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The enemies of Christ and his gospel have often coloured their enmity with a seeming care for the <hi type="italic">public good</hi> and the <hi type="italic">common safety,</hi> and, in order to this, have branded his prophets and ministers as troublers of Israel, and men that <hi type="italic">turn the world upside down.</hi> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Carnal policy commonly sets up <hi type="italic">reasons of state,</hi> in opposition to <hi type="italic">rules of justice.</hi> When men are concerned for their own wealth and safety more than for truth and duty, it is wisdom from beneath, which is <hi type="italic">earthly, sensual, and devilish.</hi> But see what was the issue; they pretended to be afraid that their tolerating Christ's gospel would bring desolation upon them by the Romans, and therefore, <hi type="italic">right or wrong,</hi> set themselves against it; but it proved that their persecuting the gospel brought upon them that which they feared, filled up the measure of their iniquity, and the Romans came and <hi type="italic">took away their place and nation,</hi> and their place <hi type="italic">knows them no more.</hi> Note, That calamity, which we seek to escape by sin we take the most effectual course to bring upon our own heads; and those who think by opposing Christ's kingdom to secure or advance their own secular interest will find Jerusalem a more <hi type="italic">burdensome stone</hi> than they think it is, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zech. xii. 3</reference>. The <hi type="italic">fear of the wicked it shall come upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">Prov. x. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen27758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27759" type="x-p"/> (3.) Caiaphas makes a malicious but mystical speech in the council on this occasion. <div eID="gen27759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27760" type="x-p"/> [1.] The <hi type="italic">malice</hi> of it appears evident at first view, <reference osisRef="John.11.49-John.11.50">v. 49, 50</reference>. He, being the high priest, and so president of the council, took upon him to decide the matter before it was debated: "<hi type="italic">You know nothing at all,</hi> your hesitating betrays your ignorance, for it is not a thing that will bear a dispute, it is soon determined, if you consider that received maxim, <hi type="italic">That it is expedient for us that one man should die for the people.</hi>" Here, <div eID="gen27760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The counsellor was Caiaphas, who was <hi type="italic">high priest that same year.</hi> The high priesthood was by divine appointment settled upon the heir male of the house of Aaron, for and during the term of his natural life, and then to his heir male; but in those degenerate times it was become, though not an annual office, like a consulship, yet frequently changed, as they could make an interest with the Roman powers. Now it happened that <hi type="italic">this year</hi> Caiaphas wore the mitre. <div eID="gen27761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27762" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The drift of the advice was, in short, this, That some way or other must be found out to put Jesus to death. We have reason to think that they strongly suspected him to be indeed the Messiah; but his doctrine was so contrary to their darling traditions and secular interest, and his design did so thwart their notions of the Messiah's kingdom, that they resolve, be he who he will, he must be put to death. Caiaphas does not say, Let him be silenced, imprisoned, banished, though amply sufficient for the <hi type="italic">restraint</hi> of one they thought dangerous; but <hi type="italic">die he must.</hi> Note, Those that have set themselves against Christianity have commonly divested themselves of humanity, and been infamous for cruelty. <div eID="gen27762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27763" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> This is plausibly insinuated, with all the subtlety as well as malice of the old serpent. 1. He suggests his own sagacity, which we must suppose him as high priest to excel in, though the <hi type="italic">Urim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thummim</hi> were long since lost. How scornfully does he say, "<hi type="italic">You know nothing,</hi> who are but common priests; but you must give me leave to see further into things than you do!" Thus it is common for those in authority to impose their corrupt dictates by virtue of that; and, because they <hi type="italic">should be</hi> the wisest and best, to expect that every body should believe they <hi type="italic">are so.</hi> 2. He takes it for granted that the case is plain and past dispute, and that those are very ignorant who do not see it to be so. Note, Reason and justice are often run down with a high hand. <hi type="italic">Truth is fallen in the streets,</hi> and, when it is down, down with it; and <hi type="italic">equity cannot enter,</hi> and, when it is out, out with it, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.14">Isa. lix. 14</reference>. 3. He insists upon a maxim in politics, That the welfare of communities is to be preferred before that of particular persons. <hi type="italic">It is expedient for us</hi> as priests, whose all lies at stake, that <hi type="italic">one man die for the people.</hi> Thus far it holds true, that it is <hi type="italic">expedient,</hi> and more than so, it is truly <hi type="italic">honourable,</hi> for a man to hazard his life in the service of his country (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1 John iii. 16</reference>); but to put an innocent man to death under colour of consulting the public safety is the devil's policy. Caiaphas craftily insinuates that the greatest and best man, though <hi type="italic">major singulis—greater than any one individual,</hi> is <hi type="italic">minor universis—less than the collected mass,</hi> and ought to think his life well spent, nay well lost, to save his country from ruin. But what is this to the murdering of one that was evidently a great blessing under pretence of preventing an imaginary mischief to the country? The case ought to have been put thus: Was it expedient for them to bring upon themselves and upon their nation the guilt of blood, a prophet's blood, for the securing of their civil interests from a danger which they had no just reason to be afraid of? Was it expedient for them to drive God and their glory from them, rather than venture the Romans' displeasure, who could do them no harm if they had God on their side? Note, Carnal policy, which steers only by secular considerations, while it thinks to <hi type="italic">save all</hi> by sin, <hi type="italic">ruins all</hi> at last. <div eID="gen27763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27764" type="x-p"/> [2.] The <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> that was in this counsel of Caiaphas does not appear at first view, but the evangelist leads us into it (<reference osisRef="John.11.51-John.11.52">v. 51, 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">This spoke he not of himself,</hi> it was not only the language of his own enmity and policy, but in these words he prophesied, though he himself was not aware of it, <hi type="italic">that Jesus should die for that nation.</hi> Here is a precious comment upon a pernicious text; the counsel of cursed Caiaphas so construed as to fall in with the counsels of the blessed God. Charity teaches us to put the most favourable construction upon men's words and actions that they will fear; but piety teaches us to make a good improvement of them, even contrary to that for which they were intended. If wicked men, in what they <hi type="italic">do</hi> against us, <hi type="italic">are God's hand</hi> to humble and reform us, why may they not in what they say against us be God's mouth to instruct and convince us? But in this of Caiaphas there was an extraordinary direction of Heaven prompting him to say that which was capable of a very sublime sense. As the hearts of all men are in God's hand, so are their tongues. Those are deceived who say, "<hi type="italic">Our tongues are our own,</hi> so that either we <hi type="italic">may</hi> say what we will, and are not accountable to God's judgment, or we <hi type="italic">can</hi> say what we will, and are not restrainable by his providence and power." Balaam could not say what he would, when he came to curse Israel, nor Laban when he pursued Jacob. <div eID="gen27764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27765" type="x-p"/> (4.) The evangelist explains and enlarges upon Caiaphas's words. <div eID="gen27765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27766" type="x-p"/> [1.] He explains what he said, and shows how it not only was, but was intended to be, accommodated to an excellent purpose.
