He did not <hi type="italic">speak it of himself.</hi> As it was an artifice to stir up the council against Christ, he spoke it of himself, or of the devil rather; but as it was an <hi type="italic">oracle,</hi> declaring it the purpose and design of God by the death of Christ to save God's spiritual Israel from sin and wrath, he did not speak it of himself, for he knew nothing of the matter, he <hi type="italic">meant not so, neither did his heart think so,</hi> for nothing was in his heart but to destroy and cut off, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen27766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27767" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He <hi type="italic">prophesied,</hi> and those that prophesied did not, in their prophesying, <hi type="italic">speak of themselves.</hi> But is Caiaphas also among the prophets? He is so, <hi type="italic">pro h&#226;c vice—this once,</hi> though a bad man, and an implacable enemy to Christ and his gospel. Note, 1. God can and often does make wicked men instruments to serve his own purposes, even contrary to their own intentions; for he has them not only <hi type="italic">in a chain,</hi> to restrain them from doing the mischief they would, but <hi type="italic">in a bridle,</hi> to lead them to do the service they would not. 2. Words of prophecy in the mouth are no infallible evidence of a principle of grace in the heart. <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?</hi> will be rejected as a frivolous plea. <div eID="gen27767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27768" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He prophesied, <hi type="italic">being high priest that year;</hi> not that his being high priest did at all dispose or qualify him to be a prophet; we cannot suppose the pontifical mitre to have first inspired with prophecy the basest head that ever wore it; but, 1. Being high priest, and therefore of note and eminence in the conclave, God was pleased to put this significant word into his mouth rather than into the mouth of any other, that it might be the more observed or the non-observance of it the more aggravated. The apophthegms of great men have been thought worthy of special regard: <hi type="italic">A divine sentence is in the lips of the king;</hi> therefore this divine sentence was put into the lips of the high priest, that even out of his mouth this word might be established, That Christ died for <hi type="italic">the good of the nation,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">for any iniquity in his hands.</hi> He happened to be high priest that year which was fixed to be the <hi type="italic">year of the redeemed,</hi> when Messiah the prince <hi type="italic">must be cut off, but not for himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>), and he must own it. 2. Being high priest <hi type="italic">that year,</hi> that famous year, in which there was to be such a plentiful effusion of the Spirit, more than had ever been yet, according to the prophecy (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.28-Joel.2.29">Joel ii. 28, 29</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Acts.2.17">Acts ii. 17</reference>), some drops of the blessed shower light upon Caiaphas, as the crumbs (says Dr. Lightfoot) of the children's bread, which fall from the table among the dogs. This year was the year of the expiration of the Levitical priesthood; and out of the mouth of him who was that year high priest was extorted an implicit resignation of it to him who should not (as they had done for many ages) offer beasts for that nation, but offer himself, and so make an end of the <hi type="italic">sin-offering.</hi> This resignation he made <hi type="italic">inwittingly,</hi> as Isaac gave the blessing to Jacob. <div eID="gen27768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27769" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The matter of his prophecy was <hi type="italic">that Jesus should die for that nation,</hi> the very thing to which all the prophets bore witness, who <hi type="italic">testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>), that the death of Christ must be the life and salvation of Israel; he meant by <hi type="italic">that nation</hi> those in it that obstinately adhered to Judaism, but God meant those in it that would receive the doctrine of Christ, and become followers of him, all believers, the spiritual seed of Abraham. The death of Christ, which Caiaphas was now projecting, proved the ruin of that interest in the nation of which he intended it should be the security and establishment, for it brought wrath upon them to the uttermost; but it proved the advancement of that interest of which he hoped it would have been the ruin, for Christ, being lifted up from the earth, drew all men unto him. It is a great thing that is here prophesied: That Jesus should <hi type="italic">die,</hi> die for others, not only <hi type="italic">for their good,</hi> but <hi type="italic">in their stead, dies for that nation,</hi> for they had the first offer made them of salvation by his death. If the whole nation of the Jews had unanimously believed in Christ, and received his gospel, they had been not only saved eternally, but saved as a nation from their grievances. The fountain was first <hi type="italic">opened to the house of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zech. xiii. 1</reference>. He so died for <hi type="italic">that nation</hi> as that <hi type="italic">the whole nation should not perish,</hi> but that <hi type="italic">a remnant should be saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27770" type="x-p"/> [2.] The evangelist enlarges upon this word of Caiaphas (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">v. 52</reference>), <hi type="italic">not for that nation only,</hi> how much soever it thought itself the darling of Heaven, but <hi type="italic">that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27771" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The persons Christ died for: <hi type="italic">Not for the nation</hi> of the Jews <hi type="italic">only</hi> (it would have been comparatively but <hi type="italic">a light thing</hi> for the Son of God to go through so vast an undertaking only to restore the <hi type="italic">preserved of Jacob,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the outcasts of Israel</hi>); no, he must be <hi type="italic">salvation to the ends of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">Isa. xlix. 6</reference>. He must die for <hi type="italic">the children of God that were scattered abroad.</hi> 1. Some understand it of the children of God that were then <hi type="italic">in being,</hi> scattered abroad in the Gentile world, <hi type="italic">devout men</hi> of every nation (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.5">Acts ii. 5</reference>), that <hi type="italic">feared God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.2">Acts x. 2</reference>), and worshipped him (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Acts xvii. 4</reference>), proselytes of the gate, who served the God of Abraham, but submitted not to the ceremonial law of Moses, persons that had a savour of natural religion, but were <hi type="italic">dispersed</hi> in the nations, had no solemn assemblies of their own, nor any peculiar profession to unite in or distinguish themselves by. Now Christ died to incorporate these in one great society, to be denominated from him and governed by him; and this was the setting up of a standard, to which all that had a regard to God and a concern for their souls might have recourse, and under which they might enlist themselves. 2. Others take in with these all that belong to the election of grace, who are called the children of God, though not yet born, because they are <hi type="italic">predestinated to the adoption of children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Eph. i. 5</reference>. Now these are <hi type="italic">scattered abroad</hi> in several <hi type="italic">places of the earth,</hi> out of all kindreds and tongues (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>), and in several <hi type="italic">ages of the world,</hi> to the end of time; there are those that <hi type="italic">fear him throughout all generations,</hi> to all these he had an eye in the atonement he made by his blood; as he prayed, so he died, for <hi type="italic">all that should believe on him.</hi> <div eID="gen27771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27772" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The purpose and intention of his death concerning those persons; he died to <hi type="italic">gather in</hi> those who wandered, and to <hi type="italic">gather together in one</hi> those who were scattered; to invite those to him who were at a distance from him, and to unite those in him who were at a distance from each other. Christ's dying is, 1. The great <hi type="italic">attractive of our hearts;</hi> for this end he is lifted up, to draw men to him. The conversion of souls is the gathering to them in to Christ as their ruler and refuge, as the doves to their windows; and he died to effect this. By dying he purchased them to himself, and the gift of the Holy Ghost for them; his love in dying for us is the great loadstone of our love. 2. The great <hi type="italic">centre of our unity.</hi> He gathers them together <hi type="italic">in one,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>. They are one with him, one body, one spirit, and one with each other in him. All the saints in all places and ages meet in Christ, as all the members in the head, and all the branches in the root. Christ by the merit of his death recommended all the saints in <hi type="italic">one</hi> to the grace and favour <hi type="italic">of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.11-Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 11-13</reference>), and by the motive of his death recommends them all severally to the love and affection one of another, <reference osisRef="John.13.34">ch. xiii. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen27772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27773" type="x-p"/> (5.) The result of this debate is a resolve of the council to put Jesus to death (<reference osisRef="John.11.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">From that day they took counsel together, to put him to death.</hi> They now understood one another's minds, and so each was fixed in his own, that Jesus must die; and, it should seem, a committee was appointed to sit, <hi type="italic">de die in diem—daily,</hi> to consider of it, to consult about it, and to receive proposals for effecting it. Note, The wickedness of the wicked ripens by degrees, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">James i. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">Ezek. vii. 10</reference>. Two considerable advances were now made in their accursed design against Christ. [1.] What before they had thought of <hi type="italic">severally</hi> now they <hi type="italic">jointly</hi> concurred in, and so strengthened the hands one of another in this wickedness, and proceeded with the greater assurance. Evil men confirm and encourage themselves and one another in evil practices, by comparing notes; men of corrupt minds bless themselves when they find others of <hi type="italic">the same mind:</hi> then the wickedness which before seemed impracticable appears not only possible, but easy to be effected, <hi type="italic">vis unita fortior—energies, when united, become more efficient.</hi> [2.] What before they wished done, but <hi type="italic">wanted a colour for,</hi> now they are furnished with a plausible pretence to justify themselves in, which will serve, if not to take off the guilt (that is the least of their care), yet to take off the odium, and so satisfy, if not the personal, yet the political conscience, as some subtly distinguish. Many will go on very securely in doing an evil thing as long as they have but something to say in excuse for it. Now this resolution of theirs to put him to death, right or wrong, proves that all the formality of a trial, which he afterwards underwent, was but show and pretence; they were before determined what to do. <div eID="gen27773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27774" type="x-p"/> (6.) Christ hereupon absconded, knowing very well what was the vote of their close cabal, <reference osisRef="John.11.54">v. 54</reference>. <div eID="gen27774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27775" type="x-p"/> [1.] He suspended his public appearances: <hi type="italic">He walked no more openly among the Jews,</hi> among the inhabitants of Judea, who were properly called Jews, especially those at Jerusalem; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou periepatei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he did not walk up and down</hi> among them, did not go from place to place, preaching and working miracles with the freedom and openness that he had done, but while he staid in Judea, he was there <hi type="italic">incognito.</hi> Thus the chief priests put the light of Israel <hi type="italic">under a bushel.</hi> <div eID="gen27775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27776" type="x-p"/> [2.] He withdrew into an obscure part of the country, so obscure that the name of the town he retired to is scarcely met with any where else. He went to a country <hi type="italic">near the wilderness,</hi> as if he were driven out from among men, or rather wishing, with Jeremiah, that he might have in the wilderness a <hi type="italic">lodging place of way-faring men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 2</reference>. He entered into a city called Ephraim, some think Ephratah, that is, Bethlehem, where he was born, and which bordered upon the wilderness of Judah; others think Ephron, or Ephraim, mentioned <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2 Chron. xiii. 19</reference>. Thither his disciples went with him; neither would they leave him in solitude, nor would he leave them in danger. There he continued, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dietribe</hi></hi>, there he <hi type="italic">conversed,</hi> he knew how to improve this time of retirement in private conversation, when he had not an opportunity of preaching publicly. He <hi type="italic">conversed with his disciples,</hi> who were his family, when he was forced from the temple, and his <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diatribai</hi></hi>, or <hi type="italic">discourses</hi> there, no doubt, were very edifying. We must do the good we can, when we cannot do the good we would. But why would Christ abscond now? It was not because he either feared the power of his enemies or distrusted his own power; he had many ways to save himself, and was neither averse to suffering nor unprepared for it; but he retired, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To put a mark of his displeasure upon Jerusalem and the people of the Jews. They rejected him and his gospel; justly therefore did he remove himself and his gospel from them. The prince of <hi type="italic">teachers</hi> was now <hi type="italic">removed into a corner</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa. xxx. 20</reference>); there was <hi type="italic">no open vision</hi> of him; and it was a sad presage of that thick darkness which was shortly to come upon Jerusalem, because she knew not the day of her visitation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To render the cruelty of his enemies against him the more inexcusable. If that which was grievous to them, and thought dangerous to the public, was his <hi type="italic">public appearance,</hi> he would try whether their anger would be turned away by his retirement into privacy; when David had fled to Gath, Saul was satisfied, and sought no more for him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.4">1 Sam. xxvii. 4</reference>. But it was the <hi type="italic">life,</hi> the precious life, that these wicked men hunted after. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> His hour was <hi type="italic">not yet come,</hi> and therefore he declined danger, and did it in a way common to men, both to warrant and encourage the flight of his servants in time of persecution and to comfort those who are forced from their usefulness, and buried alive in privacy and obscurity; <hi type="italic">the disciple is not better than his Lord. Fourthly,</hi> His retirement, for awhile, was to make his return into Jerusalem, when his hour was come, the more remarkable and illustrious. This swelled the acclamations of joy with which his well-wishers welcomed him at his next public appearance, when he rode triumphantly into the city. <div eID="gen27776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27777" type="x-p"/> (7.) The strict enquiry made for him during his recess, <reference osisRef="John.11.55-John.11.57">v. 55-57</reference>. <div eID="gen27777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27778" type="x-p"/> [1.] The occasion of it was the approach of the passover, at which they expected his presence, according to custom (<reference osisRef="John.11.55">v. 55</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Jews' passover was nigh at hand;</hi> a festival which shone bright in their calendar, and which there was great expectation of for some time before. This was Christ's fourth and last passover, since he entered upon his public ministry, and it might truly be said (as, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.18">2 Chron. xxxv. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">There never was such a passover in Israel,</hi> for in it <hi type="italic">Christ our passover was sacrificed for us.</hi> Now the passover being at hand, <hi type="italic">many went out</hi> of all parts of <hi type="italic">the country to Jerusalem, to purify themselves.</hi> This was either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A <hi type="italic">necessary purification</hi> of those who had contracted any ceremonial pollution; they came to be sprinkled with the <hi type="italic">water of purification,</hi> and to perform the other rites of cleansing according to the law, for they might not eat the passover in their uncleanness, <reference osisRef="Num.9.6">Num. ix. 6</reference>. Thus before our gospel passover we must renew our repentance, and by faith wash in the blood of Christ, and so <hi type="italic">compass God's altar.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A <hi type="italic">voluntary purification,</hi> or self-sequestration, by fasting and prayer, and other religious exercises, which many that were more devout than their neighbours spent some time in before the passover, and chose to do it at Jerusalem, because of the advantage of the temple-service. Thus must we by solemn preparation set bounds about the mount on which we expect to meet with God. <div eID="gen27778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27779" type="x-p"/> [2.] The enquiry was very solicitous: <hi type="italic">They said, What think you, that he will not come to the feast?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.56">v. 56</reference>. <div eID="gen27779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27780" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some think this was said by those who wished well to him, and expected his coming, that they might hear his doctrine and see his miracles. Those who came early out of the country, that they might purify themselves, were very desirous to meet with Christ, and perhaps came up the sooner with that expectation, and therefore <hi type="italic">as they stood in the temple,</hi> the place of their purification, they enquired what news of Christ? Could any body give them hopes of seeing him? If there were those, and those of the most devout people, and best affected to religion, who showed this respect to Christ, it was a check to the enmity of the chief priests, and a witness against them. <div eID="gen27780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27781" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It should rather seem that they were his enemies who made this enquiry after him, who wished for an opportunity to lay hands on him. They, seeing the town begin to fill with devout people out of the country, wondered they did not find him among them. When they should have been assisting those that came to purify themselves, according to the duty of their place, they were plotting against Christ. How miserably degenerate was the Jewish church, when the priests of the Lord were become like the priests of the calves, a <hi type="italic">snare upon Mizpeh, and a net spread upon Tabor,</hi> and were <hi type="italic">profound to make slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.1-Hos.5.2">Hos. v. 1, 2</reference>),—when, instead of keeping the feast with unleavened bread, they were themselves soured with the leaven of the worst malice! Their asking, <hi type="italic">What think you? Will he not come up to the feast?</hi> implies, 1. An invidious reflection upon Christ, as if he would omit his attendance on the feast of the Lord for fear of exposing himself. If others, through irreligion, be absent, they are not animadverted upon; but if Christ be absent, for his own preservation (for God will have mercy, and not sacrifice), it is turned to his reproach, as it was to David's that his seat was empty at the feast, though Saul wanted him only that he might have an opportunity of nailing him to the wall with his javelin, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.25-1Sam.20.27">1 Sam. xx. 25-27</reference>, &c. It is sad to see holy ordinances prostituted to such unholy purposes. 2. A fearful apprehension that they had of missing their game: "<hi type="italic">Will he not come up to the feast?</hi> If he do not, our measures are broken, and we are all undone; for there is no sending a pursuivant into the country, to fetch him up." <div eID="gen27781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27782" type="x-p"/> [3.] The orders issued out by the government for the apprehending of him were very strict, <reference osisRef="John.11.57">v. 57</reference>. The great sanhedrim issued out a proclamation, strictly charging and requiring that if any person in city or country <hi type="italic">knew where he was</hi> (pretending that he was a criminal, and had fled from justice) they should show it, that he might be taken, probably promising a reward to any that would discover him, and imposing a penalty on such as harboured him; so that hereby he was represented to the people as an obnoxious dangerous man, an outlaw, whom any one might have a blow at. Saul issued out such a proclamation for the apprehending of David, and Ahab of Elijah. See, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How intent they were upon this prosecution, and how indefatigably they laboured in it, now at a time when, if they had had any sense of religion and the duty of their function, they would have found something else to do. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How willing they were to involve others in the guilt with them; if any man were capable of betraying Christ, they would have him think himself bound to do it. Thus was the interest they had in the people abused to the worst purposes. Note, It is an aggravation of the sins of wicked rulers that they commonly make those that are under them instruments of their unrighteousness. But notwithstanding this proclamation, though doubtless many knew where he was, yet such was his interest in the affections of some, and such God's hold of the consciences of others, that he continued undiscovered, for the <hi type="italic">Lord hid him.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.11"/> <div eID="gen27782" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen27785" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27784" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mary Anoints Christ's Feet; Hypocrisy of Judas; Indignation of the Chief Priests.</title> <div sID="gen27786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Jesus six days before the passover came to Bethany, where Lazarus was which had been dead, whom he raised from the dead. <hi type="super">2</hi> There they made him a supper; and Martha served: but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him. 3 Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment. 4 Then saith one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, Simon's <hi type="italic">son,</hi> which should betray him, <hi type="super">5</hi> Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor? 6 This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein. 7 Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. <hi type="super">8</hi> For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always. <hi type="super">9</hi> Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus' sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead. <hi type="super">10</hi> But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death; <hi type="super">11</hi> Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus. <div eID="gen27786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27787" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen27787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27788" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">kind visit</hi> our Lord Jesus paid to his friends at Bethany, <reference osisRef="John.12.1">v. 1</reference>. He came up out of the country, <hi type="italic">six days before the passover,</hi> and took up at Bethany, a town which, according to the computation of our metropolis, lay so near Jerusalem as to be within the bills of mortality. He lodged here with his friend Lazarus, whom he had lately <hi type="italic">raised from the dead.</hi> His coming to Bethany now may be considered, <div eID="gen27788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27789" type="x-p"/> 1. As a preface to the passover he intended to celebrate, to which reference is made in assigning the date of his coming: <hi type="italic">Six days before the passover.</hi> Devout men set time apart before, to prepare themselves for that solemnity, and thus it became our Lord Jesus to <hi type="italic">fulfil all righteousness.</hi> Thus he has set us an example of solemn self-sequestration, before the solemnities of the gospel passover; let us hear the voice crying, <hi type="italic">Prepare ye the way of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen27789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27790" type="x-p"/> 2. As a voluntary exposing of himself to the fury of his enemies; now that his hour was at hand he came within their reach, and freely offered himself to them, though he had shown them how easily he could evade all their snares. Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus was voluntary in his sufferings; his life was not <hi type="italic">forced</hi> from him, but <hi type="italic">resigned: Lo, I come.</hi> As the strength of his persecutors could not overpower him, so their subtlety could not surprise him, but he died because he would. (2.) As there is a time when we are allowed to shift for our own preservation, so there is a time when we are called to hazard our lives in the cause of God, as St. Paul, when he <hi type="italic">went bound in the Spirit to Jerusalem.</hi> <div eID="gen27790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27791" type="x-p"/> 3. As an instance of his kindness to his friends at Bethany, whom he loved, and from whom he was shortly to be taken away. This was a farewell visit; he came to take leave of them, and to leave with them words of comfort against the day of trial that was approaching. Note, Though Christ depart for a time from his people, he will give them intimations that he departs in love, and not in anger. Bethany is here described to be the town <hi type="italic">where Lazarus was, whom he raised from the dead.</hi> The miracle wrought here put a new honour upon the place, and made it remarkable. Christ came hither to observe what improvement was made of this miracle; for where Christ works wonders, and shows signal favours, he looks after them, to see whether the intention of them be answered. Where he has sown plentifully, he observes whether it comes up again. <div eID="gen27791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27792" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">kind entertainment</hi> which his friends there gave him: They <hi type="italic">made him a supper</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.2">v. 2</reference>), a great supper, a feast. It is queried whether this was the same with that which is recorded, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.6">Matt. xxiv. 6</reference>, &c., in the house of Simon. Most commentators think it was; for the substance of the story and many of the circumstances agree; but that comes in after what was said <hi type="italic">two days</hi> before the passover, whereas this was done <hi type="italic">six days</hi> before; nor is it likely that Martha should serve in any house but her own; and therefore I incline with Dr. Lightfoot to think them different: that in Matthew on the third day of the passover week, but this the seventh day of the week before, being the Jewish sabbath, the night before he rode in triumph into Jerusalem; that in the house of Simon; this of Lazarus. These two being the most public and solemn entertainments given him in Bethany, Mary probably graced them <hi type="italic">both</hi> with this token of her respect; and what she <hi type="italic">left</hi> of her ointment this first time, when she spent but a <hi type="italic">pound</hi> of it (<reference osisRef="John.12.3">v. 3</reference>), she used that second time, when she <hi type="italic">poured it all out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.3">Mark xiv. 3</reference>. Let us see the account of this entertainment. 1. They <hi type="italic">made him a supper;</hi> for with them, ordinarily, supper was the best meal. This they did in token of their respect and gratitude, for a feast is made for <hi type="italic">friendship;</hi> and that they might have an opportunity of free and pleasant conversation with him, for a feast is made for <hi type="italic">fellowship.</hi> Perhaps it is in allusion to this and the like entertainments given to Christ in the days of his flesh that he promises, to such as open the door of their hearts to him, that he will <hi type="italic">sup with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>. 2. Martha <hi type="italic">served;</hi> she herself waited at table, in token of her great respect to the Master. Though a person of some quality, she did not think it below her to <hi type="italic">serve,</hi> when Christ sat at meat; nor should we think it a dishonour or disparagement to us to stoop to any service whereby Christ may be honoured. Christ had formerly reproved Martha for being <hi type="italic">troubled with much serving.</hi> But she did not therefore leave off serving, as some, who, when they are reproved for one extreme, peevishly run into another; no, still she <hi type="italic">served;</hi> not as then at a distance, but <hi type="italic">within hearing</hi> of Christ's gracious words, reckoning those happy who, as the queen of Sheba said concerning Solomon's servants, stood continually before him, to hear his wisdom; better be a <hi type="italic">waiter</hi> at Christ's table than a <hi type="italic">guest</hi> at the table of a prince. 3. Lazarus was <hi type="italic">one of those that sat at meat.</hi> It proved the truth of his resurrection, as it did of Christ's, that there were those who did <hi type="italic">eat and drink with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.41">Acts x. 41</reference>. Lazarus did not retire into a <hi type="italic">wilderness</hi> after his resurrection, as if, when he had made a visit to the other world, he must ever after be a hermit in this; no, he conversed familiarly with people, as others did. He <hi type="italic">sat at meat,</hi> as a monument of the miracle Christ had wrought. Those whom Christ has <hi type="italic">raised up</hi> to a spiritual life are made to <hi type="italic">sit together with him.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Eph.2.5-Eph.2.6">Eph. ii. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen27792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27793" type="x-p"/> III. The particular respect which Mary showed him, above the rest, in anointing his feet with sweet ointment, <reference osisRef="John.12.3">v. 3</reference>. She had a <hi type="italic">pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly,</hi> which probably she had by her for her own use; but the death and resurrection of her brother had quite weaned her from the use of all such things, and with this she <hi type="italic">anointed the feet of Jesus,</hi> and, as a further token of her reverence for him and negligence of herself, she <hi type="italic">wiped them with her hair,</hi> and this was taken notice of by all that were present, for <hi type="italic">the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Prov.27.16">Prov. xxvii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27794" type="x-p"/> 1. Doubtless she intended this as a token of her love to Christ, who had given real tokens of his love to her and her family; and thus she studies what she shall render. Now by this her love to Christ appears to have been, (1.) A <hi type="italic">generous</hi> love; so far from sparing necessary charges in his service, she is as ingenious to <hi type="italic">create</hi> an occasion of expense in religion as most are to avoid it. If she had any thing more valuable than another, that must be brought out for the honour of Christ. Note, Those who love Christ truly love him so much better than this world as to be willing to lay out the best they have for him. (2.) A <hi type="italic">condescending</hi> love; she not only bestowed her ointment upon Christ, but with her own hands poured it upon him, which she might have ordered one of her servants to have done; nay, she did not, as usual, anoint his <hi type="italic">head</hi> with it, but his <hi type="italic">feet.</hi> True love, as it does not spare charges, so it does not spare pains, in honouring Christ. Considering what Christ has done and suffered for us, we are very ungrateful if we think any service too hard to do, or too mean to stoop to, whereby he may <hi type="italic">really</hi> be glorified. (3.) A <hi type="italic">believing</hi> love; there was faith working by this love, faith in Jesus as the Messiah, the Christ, the Anointed, who, being both priest and king, was anointed as Aaron and David were. Note, <hi type="italic">God's Anointed</hi> should be <hi type="italic">our Anointed.</hi> Has God poured on him the oil of gladness above his fellows? Let us pour on him the ointment of our best affections above all competitors. By consenting to Christ as <hi type="italic">our</hi> king, we must comply with God's designs, appointing him <hi type="italic">our head</hi> whom he has appointed, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Hos. i. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen27794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27795" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">filling of the house</hi> with the pleasant <hi type="italic">odour of the ointment</hi> may intimate to us, (1.) That those who entertain Christ in their hearts and houses bring a sweet odour into them; Christ's presence brings with it an ointment and <hi type="italic">perfume which rejoice the heart.</hi> (2.) Honours done to Christ are comforts to all his friends and followers; they are to God and good men an offering of a <hi type="italic">sweet-smelling savour.</hi> <div eID="gen27795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27796" type="x-p"/> IV. Judas's dislike of Mary's compliment, or token of her respect to Christ, <reference osisRef="John.12.4-John.12.5">v. 4, 5</reference>, where observe, <div eID="gen27796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> 1. The person that carped at it was Judas, <hi type="italic">one of his disciples;</hi> not one of their nature, but only one of their number. It is possible for the worst of men to lurk under the disguise of the best profession; and there are many who pretend to stand in relation to Christ who really have no kindness for him. Judas was an apostle, a preacher of the gospel, and yet one that discouraged and checked this instance of pious affection and devotion. Note, It is sad to see the life of religion and holy zeal frowned upon and discountenanced by such as are bound by their office to assist and encourage it. But this was he that should <hi type="italic">betray Christ.</hi> Note, Coldness of love to Christ, and a secret contempt of serious piety, when they appear in professors of religion, are sad presages of a final apostasy. Hypocrites, by less instances of worldliness, discover themselves to be ready for a compliance with greater temptations. <div eID="gen27797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> 2. The pretence with which he covered his dislike (<reference osisRef="John.12.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why was not this ointment,</hi> since it was designed for a pious use, sold for three hundred pence" (8<hi type="italic">l.</hi> 10<hi type="italic">s.</hi> of our money), "and <hi type="italic">given to the poor?</hi>" (1.) Here is a foul iniquity gilded over with a specious and plausible pretence, for Satan transforms himself into an angel of light. (2.) Here is worldly wisdom passing a censure upon pious zeal, as guilty of imprudence and mismanagement. Those who value themselves upon their <hi type="italic">secular policy,</hi> and undervalue others for their <hi type="italic">serious piety,</hi> have more in them of the spirit of Judas than they would be thought to have. (3.) Here is charity to the poor made a colour for opposing a piece of piety to Christ, and secretly made a cloak for covetousness. Many excuse themselves from <hi type="italic">laying out</hi> in charity under pretence of <hi type="italic">laying up</hi> for charity: whereas, if the clouds be full of rain, they will <hi type="italic">empty themselves.</hi> Judas asked, <hi type="italic">Why was it not given to the poor?</hi> To which it is easy to answer, Because it was better bestowed upon the Lord Jesus. Note, We must not conclude that those do no acceptable piece of service who do not do it in our way, and just as we would have them; as if every thing must be adjudged imprudent and unfit which does not take its measures from us and our sentiments. Proud men think all ill-advised who do not advise with them. <div eID="gen27798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> 3. The detection and discovery of Judas's hypocrisy herein, <reference osisRef="John.12.6">v. 6</reference>. Here is the evangelist's remark upon it, by the direction of him who <hi type="italic">searches the heart: This he said, not that he cared for the poor,</hi> as he pretended, <hi type="italic">but because he was a thief, and had the bag.</hi> <div eID="gen27799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> (1.) It did not come from a principle of charity: <hi type="italic">Not that he cared for the poor.</hi> He had no compassion towards them, no concern for them: what were the poor to him any further than he might serve his own ends by being overseer of the poor? Thus some warmly contend for the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of the church, as others for its <hi type="italic">purity,</hi> when perhaps it may be said, Not that they care for the church; it is all one to them whether its <hi type="italic">true interest</hi> sink or swim, but under the pretence of this they are advancing themselves. Simeon and Levi pretended zeal for circumcision, <hi type="italic">not that they cared</hi> for the seal of the covenant, any more than Jehu for the Lord of hosts, when he said, <hi type="italic">Come see my zeal.</hi> <div eID="gen27800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27801" type="x-p"/> (2.) It did come from a principle of covetousness. The truth of the matter was, this ointment being designed for his Master, he would rather have had it in money, to be put in the common stock with which he was entrusted, and then he knew what to do with it. Observe, <div eID="gen27801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27802" type="x-p"/> [1.] Judas was treasurer of Christ's household, whence some think he was called <hi type="italic">Iscariot,</hi> the <hi type="italic">bag-bearer. First,</hi> See what <hi type="italic">estate</hi> Jesus and his disciples had to live upon. It was but <hi type="italic">little;</hi> they had neither farms nor merchandise, neither barns nor storehouses, only a <hi type="italic">bag;</hi> or, as some think the word signifies, a <hi type="italic">box,</hi> or <hi type="italic">coffer,</hi> wherein they kept just enough for their subsistence, giving the overplus, if any were, to the poor; this they carried about with them, wherever they went. <hi type="italic">Omnia mea mecum porto—I carry all my property about me.</hi> This bag was supplied by the contributions of good people, and the Master and his disciples had all <hi type="italic">in common;</hi> let this lessen our esteem of worldly wealth, and deaden us to the punctilios of state and ceremony, and reconcile us to a mean and despicable way of living, if this be our lot, that it was our Master's lot; for our sakes he <hi type="italic">became poor. Secondly,</hi> See who was the <hi type="italic">steward</hi> of the little they had; it was Judas, he was purse-bearer. It was his office to receive and pay, and we do not find that he gave any account what markets he made. He was appointed to this office, either, 1. Because he was the least and lowest of all the disciples; it was not Peter nor John that was made steward (though it was a place of trust and profit), but Judas, the meanest of them. Note, Secular employments, as they are a digression, so they are a degradation to a minister of the gospel; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.4">1 Cor. vi. 4</reference>. The prime-ministers of state in Christ's kingdom refused to be concerned in the revenue, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.2">Acts vi. 2</reference>. 2. Because he was desirous of the place. He loved in his heart to be fingering money, and therefore had the moneybag committed to him, either, (1.) As a kindness, to please him, and thereby oblige him to be true to his Master. Subjects are sometimes disaffected to the government because disappointed of their preferment; but Judas had no cause to complain of this; the bag he chose, and the bag he had. Or, (2.) In judgment upon him, to punish him for his secret wickedness; that was put into his hands which would be a snare and trap to him. Note, Strong inclinations to sin within are often justly punished with strong temptations to sin without. We have little reason to be fond of the bag, or proud of it, for at the best we are but stewards of it; and it was Judas, one of an ill character, and born to be hanged (pardon the expression), that was steward of the bag. <hi type="italic">The prosperity of fools destroys them.</hi> <div eID="gen27802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27803" type="x-p"/> [2.] Being trusted with the bag, he was <hi type="italic">a thief,</hi> that is, he had a thievish disposition. The reigning love of money is <hi type="italic">heart-theft</hi> as much as anger and revenge are <hi type="italic">heart-murder.</hi> Or perhaps he had been really guilty of embezzling his Master's stores, and converting to his own use what was given to the public stock. And some conjecture that he was now contriving to fill his pockets, and then run away and leave his Master, having heard him speak so much of troubles approaching, to which he could by no means reconcile himself. Note, Those to whom the management and disposal of public money is committed have need to be governed by steady principles of justice and honesty, that no blot cleave to their hands; for though some make a jest of cheating the government, or the church, or the country, if cheating be <hi type="italic">thieving,</hi> and, communities being more considerable than particular persons, if robbing them be the greater sin, the guilt of theft and the portion of thieves will be found no jesting matter. Judas, who had betrayed his trust, soon after betrayed his Master. <div eID="gen27803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27804" type="x-p"/> V. Christ's justification of what Mary did (<reference osisRef="John.12.7-John.12.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let her alone.</hi> Hereby he intimated his acceptance of her kindness (though he was perfectly mortified to all the delights of sense, yet, as it was a token of her goodwill, he signified himself well-pleased with it), and his care that she should not be molested in it: <hi type="italic">Pardon her,</hi> so it may be read; "excuse her this once, if it be an error it is an error of her love." Note, Christ would not have those censured nor discouraged who sincerely design to please him, though in their honest endeavours there be not all the discretion that may be, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.3">Rom. xiv. 3</reference>. Though we would not do as they do, yet <hi type="italic">let them alone.</hi> For Mary's justification, <div eID="gen27804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27805" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ puts a favourable construction upon what she did, which those that condemned it were not aware of: <hi type="italic">Against the day of my burying she has kept this.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">She has reserved this for the day of my embalming;</hi> so Dr. Hammond. "You do not grudge the ointment used for the embalming of your dead friends, nor say that it should be sold, and given to the poor. Now this anointing either was so <hi type="italic">intended,</hi> or at least may be so <hi type="italic">interpreted;</hi> for the day of my burying is now at hand, and she has anointed a body that is already <hi type="italic">as good as dead.</hi>" Note, (1.) Our Lord Jesus thought much and often of his own death and burial; it would be good for us to do so too. (2.) Providence does often so open a door of opportunity to good Christians, and the Spirit of grace does so open their hearts, that the expressions of their pious zeal prove to be more <hi type="italic">seasonable,</hi> and more <hi type="italic">beautiful,</hi> than any foresight of their own could make them. (3.) The grace of Christ puts kind comments upon the pious words and actions of good people, and not only makes the best of what is amiss, but makes the most of what is good. <div eID="gen27805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27806" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives a sufficient answer to Judas's objection, <reference osisRef="John.12.8">v. 8</reference>. (1.) It is so ordered in the kingdom of Providence that <hi type="italic">the poor we have always with us,</hi> some or other that are proper objects of charity (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">Deut. xv. 11</reference>); such there will be as long as there are in this lapsed state of mankind so much folly and so much affliction. (2.) It is so ordered in the kingdom of grace that the church should not always have the bodily presence of Jesus Christ: "<hi type="italic">Me you have not always,</hi> but only nor for a little time." Note, We need wisdom, when two duties come in competition, to know which to give the preference to, which must be determined by the circumstances. Opportunities are to be improved, and those opportunities first and most vigorously which are likely to be of the shortest continuance, and which we see most speedily hastening away. That good duty which may be done <hi type="italic">at any time</hi> ought to give way to that which cannot be done but <hi type="italic">just now.</hi> <div eID="gen27806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27807" type="x-p"/> VI. The public notice which was taken of our Lord Jesus here at this supper in Bethany (<reference osisRef="John.12.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Much people of the Jews knew that he was there,</hi> for he was the talk of the town, and <hi type="italic">they came</hi> flocking thither; the more because he had lately absconded, and now broke out as the sun from behind a dark cloud. 1. They came to see Jesus, whose name was very much magnified, and made considerable by the late miracle he had wrought in raising Lazarus. They came, not to hear him, but to gratify their curiosity with a sight of him here at Bethany, fearing he would not appear publicly, as he used to do, this passover. They came, not to seize him, or inform against him, though the government had prosecuted him to an outlawry, but to see him and show him respect. Note, There are some in whose affections Christ will have an interest, in spite of all the attempts of his enemies to misrepresent him. It being known where Christ was, multitudes came to him. Note, Where the king is there is the court; where Christ is there will the <hi type="italic">gathering of the people be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.37">Luke xvii. 37</reference>. 2. They came to see Lazarus and Christ together, which was a very inviting sight. Some came for the confirmation of their faith in Christ, to have the story perhaps from Lazarus's own mouth. Others came only for the gratifying of their curiosity, that they might say they had seen a man who had been dead and buried, and yet lived again; so that Lazarus served for a <hi type="italic">show,</hi> these holy-days, to those who, like the Athenians, spent their time in telling and hearing new things. Perhaps some came to put curious questions to Lazarus about the state of the dead, to ask what news from the other world; we ourselves have sometimes said, it may be, We would have gone a great way for one hour's discourse with Lazarus. But if any came on this errand it is probable that Lazarus was silent, and gave them no account of his voyage; at least, the scripture is silent, and gives us no account of it; and we must not covet to be wise above what is written. But our Lord Jesus was present, who was a much fitter person for them to apply to than Lazarus; for if we hear not Moses and the prophets, Christ and the apostles, if we heed not what they tell us concerning another world, neither should we be persuaded though Lazarus rose from the dead. We have a more sure word of prophecy. <div eID="gen27807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27808" type="x-p"/> VII. The indignation of the chief priests at the growing interest of our Lord Jesus, and their plot to crush it (<reference osisRef="John.12.10-John.12.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): They <hi type="italic">consulted</hi> (or decreed) <hi type="italic">how they might put Lazarus also to death,</hi> because that <hi type="italic">by reason of him</hi> (of what was done to him, not of any thing he said or did) <hi type="italic">many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.</hi> Here observe, <div eID="gen27808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> 1. How vain and unsuccessful their attempts against Christ had hitherto been. They had done all they could to alienate the people from him, and exasperate them against him, and yet many of the Jews, their neighbours, their creatures, their admirers, were so overcome by the convincing evidence of Christ's miracles that they <hi type="italic">went away</hi> from the interest and party of the priests, went off from obedience to their tyranny, <hi type="italic">and believed on Jesus;</hi> and it was by reason of Lazarus; his resurrection put life into their faith, and convinced them that this Jesus was undoubtedly the Messiah, and had life in himself, and power to give life. This miracle confirmed them in the belief of his other miracles, which they had heard he wrought in Galilee: what was impossible to him that could raise the dead? <div eID="gen27809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> 2. How absurd and unreasonable this day's vote was—that Lazarus must be put to death. This is an instance of the most brutish rage that could be; they were like a <hi type="italic">wild bull in a net,</hi> full of fury, and laying about them without any consideration. It was a sign that they <hi type="italic">neither feared God nor regarded man.</hi> For, (1.) If they had feared God, they would not have done such an act of defiance to him. God will have Lazarus to live by miracle, and they will have him to die by malice. They cry, <hi type="italic">Away with such a fellow, it is not fit he should live,</hi> when God had so lately sent him back to the earth, declaring it highly fit he should live; what was this but <hi type="italic">walking contrary to God?</hi> They would put Lazarus to death, and challenge almighty power to raise him again, as if they could contend with God, and try titles with the King of kings. Who has the keys of death and the grave, he or they? <hi type="italic">O cæca malitia! Christus qui suscitare potuit mortuum, non possit occisum.—Blind malice, to suppose that Christ, who could raise one that had died a natural death, could not raise one that had been slain!</hi>—Augustine in loc. Lazarus is singled out to be the object of their special hatred, because God has distinguished him by the tokens of his peculiar love, as if they had made a league offensive and defensive with death and hell, and resolved to be severe upon all deserters. One would think that they should rather have consulted how they might have joined in friendship with Lazarus and his family, and by their mediation have reconciled themselves to this Jesus whom they had persecuted; but the god of this world had <hi type="italic">blinded their minds.</hi> (2.) If they had regarded man, they would not have done such an act of injustice to Lazarus, an innocent man, to whose charge they could not pretend to lay any crime. What bands are strong enough to hold those who can so easily break through the most sacred ties of common justice, and violate the maxims which even nature itself teaches? But the support of their own tyranny and superstition was thought sufficient, as in the church of Rome, not only to justify, but to consecrate the greatest villanies, and make them meritorious.

<div eID="gen27810" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Entrance into Jerusalem</title> <div sID="gen27811" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> On the next day much people that were come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, 13 Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written, <hi type="super">15</hi> Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt. <hi type="super">16</hi> These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they had done these things unto him. <hi type="super">17</hi> The people therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of his grave, and raised him from the dead, bare record. <hi type="super">18</hi> For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle. <hi type="super">19</hi> The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him. <div eID="gen27811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27812" type="x-p"/> This story of Christ's riding in triumph to Jerusalem is recorded by all the evangelists, as worthy of special remark; and in it we may observe, <div eID="gen27812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27813" type="x-p"/> I. The respect that was paid to our Lord Jesus by the common people, <reference osisRef="John.12.12-John.12.13">v. 12, 13</reference>, where we are told, <div eID="gen27813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27814" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they were that paid him this respect: <hi type="italic">much people,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ochlos polys</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a great crowd</hi> of those that came up to the feast; not the inhabitants of Jerusalem, but the country people that came from remote parts to worship at the feast; the nearer the temple of the Lord, the further from the Lord of the temple. They were such as <hi type="italic">came up to the feast.</hi> (1.) Perhaps they had been Christ's hearers in the country, and great admirers of him there, and therefore were forward to testify their respect to him at Jerusalem, where they knew he had many enemies. Note, Those that have a true value and veneration for Christ will neither be ashamed nor afraid to own him before men in any instance whereby they may do him honour. (2.) Perhaps they were those more <hi type="italic">devout Jews</hi> that came up to the feast some time before, to purify themselves, that were more inclined to religion than their neighbours, and these were they that were so forward to honour Christ. Note, The more regard men have to God and religion in general, the better disposed they will be to entertain Christ and his religion, which is not destructive but perfective of all previous discoveries and institutions. They were not the rulers, nor the great men, that went out to meet Christ, but the commonalty; some would have called them a mob, a rabble: but Christ has chosen the weak and foolish things (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1 Cor. i. 27</reference>), and is honoured more by the multitude than by the magnificence of his followers; for he values men by their souls, not their names and titles of honour. <div eID="gen27814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27815" type="x-p"/> 2. On what occasion they did it: <hi type="italic">They heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.</hi> They had enquired for him (<reference osisRef="John.11.55-John.11.56">ch. xi. 55, 56</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will he not come up to the feast?</hi> And now they hear he is coming; for none that seek Christ seek in vain. Now when they heard he was coming, they bestirred themselves, to give him an agreeable reception. Note, Tidings of the approach of Christ and his kingdom should awaken us to consider what is the work of the day, that it may be done in the day. Israel must prepare to meet <hi type="italic">their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Amos iv. 12</reference>), and the virgins to <hi type="italic">meet the bridegroom.</hi> <div eID="gen27815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27816" type="x-p"/> 3. In what way they expressed their respect; they had not the keys of the city to present to him, nor the sword nor mace to carry before him, none of the city music to compliment him with, but such as they had they gave him; and even this despicable crowd was a faint resemblance of that glorious company which John saw <hi type="italic">before the throne, and before the Lamb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9-Rev.7.10">Rev. vii. 9, 10</reference>. Though these were not before the throne, they were before the Lamb, the paschal Lamb, who now, according to the usual ceremony, four days before the feast, was set apart to be sacrificed for us. There it is said of that celestial choir, <div eID="gen27816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27817" type="x-p"/> (1.) That they had palms in their hands, and so had these <hi type="italic">branches of palm-trees.</hi> The palm-tree has ever been an emblem of victory and triumph; Cicero calls one that had won many prizes <hi type="italic">plurimarum palmarum homo—a man of many palms.</hi> Christ was now by his death to conquer principalities and powers, and therefore it was fit that he should have the victor's palm borne before him; though he was but girding on the harness, yet he could boast as though he had put it off. But this was not all; the carrying of palm-branches was part of the ceremony of the feast of tabernacles (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev. xxiii. 40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.8.15">Neh. viii. 15</reference>), and their using this expression of joy in the welcome given to our Lord Jesus intimates that all the feasts pointed at his gospel, had their accomplishment in it, and particularly that of the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zech. xiv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27818" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice, saying, Salvation to our God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">Rev. vii. 10</reference>); so did these here, they shouted before him, as is usual in popular welcomes, <hi type="italic">Hosanna, blessed is the king of Israel, that comes in the name of the Lord;</hi> and <hi type="italic">hosanna</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">salvation.</hi> It is quoted from <reference osisRef="Ps.118.25-Ps.118.26">Ps. cxviii. 25, 26</reference>. See how well acquainted these common people were with the scripture, and how pertinently they apply it to the Messiah. High thoughts of Christ will be best expressed in scripture-words. Now in their acclamations, [1.] They acknowledge our Lord Jesus to be the king of Israel, that comes <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord.</hi> Though he went now in poverty and disgrace, yet, contrary to the notions their scribes had given them of the Messiah, they own him to be a king, which bespeaks both his dignity and honour, which we must adore; and his dominion and power, to which we must submit. They own him to be, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A rightful king, coming in <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>), sent of God, not only as a prophet, but as a king. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The promised and long-expected king, Messiah the prince, for he is <hi type="italic">king of Israel.</hi> According to the light they had, they proclaimed him king of Israel in the streets of Jerusalem; and, they themselves being Israelites, hereby they avouched him for their king. [2.] They heartily wish well to his kingdom, which is the meaning of hosanna; let the king of Israel prosper, as when Solomon was crowned they cried, <hi type="italic">God save king Solomon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1 Kings i. 39</reference>. In crying hosanna they prayed for three things:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That his kingdom might come, in the light and knowledge of it, and in the power and efficacy of it. God speed the gospel plough. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it might conquer, and be victorious over all opposition, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That it might continue. Hosanna is, <hi type="italic">Let the king live for ever;</hi> though his kingdom may be disturbed, let it never be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 17</reference>. [3.] They bid him welcome into Jerusalem: "<hi type="italic">Welcome is he that cometh;</hi> we are heartily glad to see him; <hi type="italic">come in thou blessed of the Lord;</hi> and well may we attend with our blessings him who meets us with his." This welcome is like that (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.7-Ps.24.9">Ps. xxiv. 7-9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lift up your heads, O ye gates.</hi> Thus we must every one of us bid Christ welcome into our hearts, that is, we must praise him, and be well pleased in him. As we should be highly pleased with the being and attributes of God, and his relation to us, so we should be with the person and offices of the Lord Jesus, and his meditation between us and God. Faith saith, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh.</hi> <div eID="gen27818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27819" type="x-p"/> II. The posture Christ puts himself into for receiving the respect that was paid him (<reference osisRef="John.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had found,</hi> or procured, <hi type="italic">a young ass,</hi> he <hi type="italic">sat thereon.</hi> It was but a poor sort of figure he made, he alone upon an ass, and a crowd of people about him shouting <hi type="italic">Hosanna.</hi> 1. This was much more of state than he used to take; he used to travel on foot, but now was mounted. Though his followers should be willing to take up with mean things, and not affect any thing that looks like grandeur, yet they are allowed to use the service of the inferior creatures, according as God in his providence gives particular possession of those things over which, by his covenant with Noah and his sons, he has given to man a general dominion. 2. Yet it was much less of state than the great ones of the world usually take. If he would have made a public entry, according to the state of a man of high degree, he should have rode in a chariot like that of Solomon's (<reference osisRef="Song.3.9-Song.3.10">Cant. iii. 9, 10</reference>), with <hi type="italic">pillars of silver,</hi> the <hi type="italic">bottom of gold,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">covering of purple;</hi> but, if we judge according to the fashion of this world, to be introduced thus was rather a disparagement than any honour to the king of Israel, for it seemed as if he would look great, and knew not how. His kingdom was not of this world, and therefore came not with outward pomp. He was now humbling himself, but in his exalted state John sees him in a vision <hi type="italic">on a white horse, with a bow and a crown.</hi> <div eID="gen27819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> III. The fulfilling of the scripture in this: <hi type="italic">As it is written, Fear not, daughter of Sion,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.15">v. 15</reference>. This is quoted from <reference osisRef="Zech.9.19">Zech. ix. 19</reference>. To him bore all the prophets witness, and particularly to this concerning him. <div eID="gen27820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> 1. It was foretold that Zion's king should come, should come <hi type="italic">thus, sitting on an ass's colt;</hi> even this minute circumstance was foretold, and Christ took care it should be punctually fulfilled. Note, (1.) Christ is Zion's king; the holy hill of Zion was of old destined to be the metropolis or royal city of the Messiah. (2.) Zion's king does and will look after her, and come to her; though for a short time he retires, in due time he returns. (3.) Though he comes but slowly (an ass is slow-paced), yet he comes surely, and with such expressions of humility and condescension as greatly encourage the addresses and expectations of his loyal subjects. Humble supplicants may reach to speak with him. If this be a discouragement to Zion, that her king appears in no greater state or strength, let her know that though he comes to her riding on an ass's colt, yet he goes forth against her enemies riding <hi type="italic">on the heavens for her help,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">Deut. xxxiii. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen27821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> 2. The daughter of Zion is therefore called upon to <hi type="italic">behold her king,</hi> to take notice of him and his approaches; behold and wonder, for he comes with observation, though not with outward show, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fear not.</hi> In the prophecy, Zion is told to rejoice greatly, and to shout, but here it is rendered, <hi type="italic">Fear not.</hi> Unbelieving fears are enemies to spiritual joys; if they be cured, if they be conquered, joy will come of course; Christ comes to his people to <hi type="italic">silence</hi> their fears. If the case be so that we cannot reach to the exultations of joy, yet we should labour to get from under the oppressions of fear. <hi type="italic">Rejoice greatly;</hi> at least, <hi type="italic">fear not.</hi> <div eID="gen27822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> IV. The remark made by the evangelist respecting the disciples (<reference osisRef="John.12.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They understood not at first</hi> why Christ did this, and how the scripture was fulfilled; but when <hi type="italic">Jesus was glorified,</hi> and thereupon the Spirit poured out, then they remembered that <hi type="italic">these things were written of him</hi> in the Old Testament, and that they and others had, in pursuance thereof, <hi type="italic">done these things to him.</hi> <div eID="gen27823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27824" type="x-p"/> 1. See here the imperfection of the disciples in their infant state; even <hi type="italic">they understood not these things at first.</hi> They did not consider, when they fetched the ass and set him thereon, that they were performing the ceremony of the inauguration of Zion's king. Now observe, (1.) The scripture is often fulfilled by the agency of those who have not themselves an eye to the scripture in what they do, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>. (2.) There are many excellent things, both in the word and providence of God, which the disciples themselves do not at first understand: not at their first acquaintance with the things of God, while they <hi type="italic">see men as trees walking;</hi> not at the first proposal of the things to their view and consideration. That which afterwards is clear was at first dark and doubtful. (3.) It well becomes the disciples of Christ, when they are grown up to maturity in knowledge, frequently to reflect upon the follies and weaknesses of their first beginning, that free grace may have the glory of their proficiency, and they may have compassion on the ignorant. <hi type="italic">When I was a child, I spoke as a child.</hi> <div eID="gen27824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27825" type="x-p"/> 2. See here the improvement of the disciples in their adult state. Though they had been children, they were not always so, but went on to perfection. Observe, <div eID="gen27825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27826" type="x-p"/> (1.) When they understood it: <hi type="italic">When Jesus was glorified;</hi> for, [1.] Till then they did not rightly apprehend the nature of his kingdom, but expected it to appear in external pomp and power, and therefore knew not how to apply the scriptures which spoke of it to so mean an appearance. Note, The right understanding of the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, of its powers, glories, and victories, would prevent our misinterpreting and misapplying the scriptures that speak of it. [2.] Till then the Spirit was not poured out, who was to lead them into all truth. Note, The disciples of Christ are enabled to understand the scriptures by the same Spirit that indited the scriptures. <hi type="italic">The spirit of revelation is</hi> to all the saints a <hi type="italic">spirit of wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.17-Eph.1.18">Eph. i. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen27826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27827" type="x-p"/> (2.) How they understood it; they compared the prophecy with the event, and put them together, that they might mutually receive light from each other, and so they came to understand both: <hi type="italic">Then remembered they that these things were written of him</hi> by the prophets, consonant to which they were done to him. Note, Such an admirable harmony there is between the word and works of God that the remembrance of what is written will enable us to understand what is done, and the observation of what is done will help us to understand what is written. <hi type="italic">As we have heard, so have we seen.</hi> The scripture is every day fulfilling. <div eID="gen27827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27828" type="x-p"/> V. The reason which induced the people to pay this respect to our Lord Jesus upon his coming into Jerusalem, though the government was so much set against him. It was because of the illustrious miracle he had lately wrought in raising Lazarus. <div eID="gen27828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> 1. See here what account and what assurance they had of this miracle; no doubt, the city rang of it, the report of it was in all people's mouths. But those who considered it as a proof of Christ's mission, and a ground of their faith in him, that they might be well satisfied of the matter of fact, traced the report to those who were eye-witnesses of it, that they might <hi type="italic">know the certainty</hi> of it by the utmost evidence the thing was capable of: <hi type="italic">The people therefore that</hi> stood by <hi type="italic">when he called Lazarus</hi> out of his grave, being found out and examined, <hi type="italic">bore record,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.17">v. 17</reference>. They unanimously averred the thing to be true, beyond dispute or contradiction, and were ready, if called to it, to depose it upon oath, for so much is implied in the word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Emartyrei</hi></hi>. Note, The truth of Christ's miracles was evidenced by incontestable proofs. It is probable that those who had seen this miracle did not only assert it to those who asked them, but published it unasked, that this might add to the triumphs of this solemn day; and Christ's coming in now from Bethany, where it was done, would put them in mind of it. Note, Those who wish well to Christ's kingdom should be forward to proclaim what they know that may redound to his honour. <div eID="gen27829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> 2. What improvement they made of it, and what influence it had upon them (<reference osisRef="John.12.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">For this cause,</hi> as much as any other, <hi type="italic">the people met him.</hi> (1.) Some, out of curiosity, were desirous to see one that had done such a wonderful work. Many a good sermon he had preached in Jerusalem, which drew not such crowds after him as this one miracle did. But, (2.) Others, out of conscience, studied to do him honour, as one sent of God. This miracle was reserved for one of the last, that it might confirm those which went before, and might gain him this honour just before his sufferings; Christ's works were all not only <hi type="italic">well done</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.7">Mark vii. 7</reference>) but <hi type="italic">well timed.</hi> <div eID="gen27830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> VI. The indignation of the Pharisees at all this; some of them, probably, saw, and they all soon heard of, Christ's public entry. The committee appointed to find out expedients to crush him thought they had gained their point when he had retired unto privacy, and that he would soon be forgotten in Jerusalem, but they now rage and fret when they see they imagined but a <hi type="italic">vain thing.</hi> 1. They own that they had got no ground against him; it was plainly to be perceived that they <hi type="italic">prevailed nothing.</hi> They could not, with all their insinuations, alienate the people's affections from him, nor with their menaces restrain them from showing their affection to him. Note, Those who oppose Christ, and fight against his kingdom, will be made to perceive that they prevail nothing. God will accomplish his own purposes in spite of them, and the little efforts of their impotent malice. <hi type="italic">You prevail nothing,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk opheleite</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">you profit nothing.</hi> Note, There is nothing got by opposing Christ. 2. They own that he had got ground: <hi type="italic">The world is gone after him;</hi> there is a vast crowd attending him, a <hi type="italic">world of people:</hi> an hyperbole common in most languages. Yet here, like Caiaphas, ere they were aware, they prophesied that <hi type="italic">the world would go after him;</hi> some of all sorts, some from all parts; nations shall be discipled. But to what intent was this said? (1.) Thus they <hi type="italic">express</hi> their own vexation at the growth of his interest; their envy makes them fret. If the <hi type="italic">horn of the righteous be exalted with honour, the wicked see it, and are grieved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.9-Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 9, 10</reference>); considering how great these Pharisees were, and what abundance of respect was paid them, one would think they needed not grudge Christ so inconsiderable a piece of honour as was now done him; but proud men would monopolize honour, and have none share with them, like Haman. (2.) Thus they excite themselves and one another, to a more vigorous carrying on of the war against Christ. As if they should say, "Dallying and delaying thus will never do. We must take some other and more effectual course, to put a stop to this infection; it is time to try our utmost skill and force, before the grievance grows past redress." Thus the enemies of religion are made more resolute and active by being baffled; and shall its friends be disheartened with every disappointment, who know its cause is righteous and will at last be victorious?

<div eID="gen27831" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Certain Greeks Desire to See Jesus; The Recompence of Christ's Servants.</title> <div sID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast: <hi type="super">21</hi> The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus. <hi type="super">22</hi> Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified. <hi type="super">24</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. <hi type="super">25</hi> He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal. <hi type="super">26</hi> If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will <hi type="italic">my</hi> Father honour. <div eID="gen27832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> Honour is here paid to Christ by certain Greeks that enquired or him with respect. We are not told what day of Christ's last week this was, probably not the same day he rode into Jerusalem (for that day was taken up in public work), but a day or two after. <div eID="gen27833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27834" type="x-p"/> I. We are told who they were that paid this honour to our Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">Certain Greeks among</hi> the people who <hi type="italic">came up to worship at the feast,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.20">v. 20</reference>. Some think they were <hi type="italic">Jews of the dispersion,</hi> some of the twelve tribes that were scattered among the Gentiles, and were called <hi type="italic">Greeks,</hi> Hellenist Jews; but others think they were Gentiles, those whom they called <hi type="italic">proselytes of the gate,</hi> such as the eunuch and Cornelius. Pure natural religion met with the best assistance among the Jews, and therefore those among the Gentiles who were piously inclined joined with them in their solemn meetings, as far as was allowed them. There were devout worshippers of the true God even among those that were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel. It was in the latter ages of the Jewish church that there was this flocking of the Gentiles to the temple at Jerusalem,—a happy presage of the taking down of the partition-wall between Jews and Gentiles. The forbidding of the priests to accept of any oblation or sacrifice from a Gentile (which was done by Eleazar the son of Ananias, the high priest), Josephus says, was one of those things that brought the Romans upon them, <hi type="italic">War</hi> 2. 409-410. Though these Greeks, if uncircumcised, were not admitted to eat the passover, yet they came to <hi type="italic">worship at the feast.</hi> We must thankfully use the privileges we have, though there may be others from which we are shut out. <div eID="gen27834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27835" type="x-p"/> II.
