Christ foretold that Judas would betray him when there was no ground to suspect such a thing, and so proved himself the eternal Word, which is a <hi type="italic">discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.</hi> The prophecies of the New Testament concerning the apostasy of the latter times (which we have, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.17">2 Thess. ii.</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv.</reference>, and in the Apocalypse) being evidently accomplished is a proof that those writings were divinely inspired, and confirms our faith in the whole canon of scripture. 2. By this application of the types and prophecies of the Old Testament to himself, he proved himself to be the true Messiah, to whom <hi type="italic">all the prophets bore witness.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">it was written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer,</hi> and he suffered just as it was written, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.25-Luke.24.26">Luke xxiv. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.28">ch. viii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen27976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> III. He gives a word of encouragement to his apostles, and all his ministers whom he employs in his service (<reference osisRef="John.13.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me.</hi> The purport of these words is the same with what we have in other scriptures, but it is not easy to make out their coherence here. Christ had told his disciples that they must humble and abase themselves. "Now," saith he, "though there may be those that will despise you for your condescension, yet there will be those that will do you honour, and shall be honoured for so doing." Those who know themselves dignified by Christ's commission may be content to be vilified in the world's opinion. Or, he intended to silence the scruples of those who, because there was a traitor among the apostles, would be shy of receiving any of them; for, if one of them was false to his Master, to whom would any of them be true? <hi type="italic">Ex uno disce omnes—They are all alike.</hi> No, as Christ will think never the worse of them for Judas's crime, so he will stand by them, and own them, and will raise up such as shall receive them. Those that had received Judas when he was a preacher, and perhaps were converted and edified by his preaching, were never the worse, nor should reflect upon it with any regret, though he afterwards proved a traitor; for he was one whom Christ sent. We cannot know what men are, much less what they will be, but those who appear to be sent of Christ we must receive, till the contrary appear. Though some, by entertaining strangers, have entertained robbers unawares, yet we must still be hospitable, for thereby some have entertained angels. The abuses put upon our charity, though ordered with ever so much discretion, will neither justify our uncharitableness, nor lose us the reward of our charity. 1. We are here encouraged to receive ministers as <hi type="italic">sent of Christ: "He that receiveth whomsoever I send,</hi> though weak and poor, and subject to like passions as others (for as the law, so the gospel, <hi type="italic">makes men priests that have infirmity</hi>), yet if he deliver my message, and be regularly called and appointed to do so, and as an officer give himself to the word and prayer, he that entertains him shall be owned as a friend of mine." Christ was now leaving the world, but he would leave an order of men to be his agents, to deliver his word, and those who receive <hi type="italic">this,</hi> in the light and love of it, receive <hi type="italic">him.</hi> To believe the doctrine of Christ, and obey his law, and accept the salvation offered upon the terms proposed; this is receiving those whom Christ sends, and it is <hi type="italic">receiving Christ Jesus the Lord</hi> himself. 2. We are here encouraged to receive Christ as sent of God: <hi type="italic">He that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">receiveth me,</hi> that receiveth Christ in his ministers, receiveth the Father also, for they come upon his errand likewise, baptizing in the name of the Father, as well as of the Son. Or, in general, <hi type="italic">He that receiveth me</hi> as his prince and Saviour receiveth <hi type="italic">him that sent me</hi> as his portion and felicity. Christ was sent of God, and in embracing his religion we embrace the <hi type="italic">only true</hi> religion. <div eID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ more particularly notifies to them the plot which one of their number was now hatching against him (<reference osisRef="John.13.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">When Jesus had thus said</hi> in general, to prepare them for a more particular discovery, he was <hi type="italic">troubled in spirit,</hi> and showed it by some gesture or sign, and <hi type="italic">he testified,</hi> he solemnly declared it (<hi type="italic">cum animo testandi—with the solemnity of a witness on oath), "One of you shall betray me;</hi> one of you my apostles and constant followers." None indeed could be said to <hi type="italic">betray</hi> him but those in whom he reposed a confidence, and who were the witnesses of his retirements. This did not determine Judas to the sin by any fatal necessity; for, though the event did follow according to the prediction, yet not from the prediction. Christ is not the author of sin; yet as to this heinous sin of Judas, 1. Christ foresaw it; for even that which is secret and future, and hidden from the eyes of all living, naked and open before the eyes of Christ. He <hi type="italic">knows what is in men</hi> better than they do themselves (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings viii. 12</reference>), and therefore sees what will be done by them. <hi type="italic">I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. 2. He foretold it, not only for the sake of the rest of the disciples, but for the sake of Judas himself, that he might take warning, and recover himself out of the snare of the devil. Traitors proceed not in their plots when they find they are discovered; surely Judas, when he finds that his Master knows his design, will retreat in time; if not, it will aggravate his condemnation. 3. He spoke of it with a manifest concern; he was <hi type="italic">troubled in spirit</hi> when he mentioned it. He had often spoken of his own sufferings and death, without any such trouble of spirit as he here manifested when he spoke of the ingratitude and treachery of Judas. This touched him in a tender part. Note, The falls and miscarriages of the disciples of Christ are a great trouble of spirit to their Master; the sins of Christians are the grief of Christ. "What! <hi type="italic">One of you betray me?</hi> You that have received from me such distinguishing favours; you that I had reason to think would be firm to me, that have professed such a respect for me; what iniquity have you found in me that one of you should betray me?" This went to his heart, as the undutifulness of children grieves those who have <hi type="italic">nourished and brought them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa. i. 2</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> V. The disciples quickly take the alarm. They knew their Master would neither deceive them nor jest with them; and therefore <hi type="italic">looked one upon another,</hi> with a manifest concern, <hi type="italic">doubting of whom he spake.</hi> 1. By looking one upon another they evinced the trouble they were in upon this notice given them; it struck such a horror upon them that they knew not well which way to look, nor what to say. They saw their Master troubled, and therefore they were troubled. This was at a feast where they were cheerfully entertained; but hence we must be taught to rejoice with trembling, and as though we rejoiced not. When David wept for his son's rebellion, all his followers wept with him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. xv. 30</reference>); so Christ's disciples here. Note, That which grieves Christ is, and should be, a grief to all that are his, particularly the scandalous miscarriages of those that are called by his name: <hi type="italic">Who is offended, and I burn not?</hi> 2. Hereby they endeavoured to <hi type="italic">discover</hi> the traitor. They looked wistfully in one another's face, to see who blushed, or, by some disorder in the countenance, manifested guilt in the heart, upon this notice; but, while those who were faithful had their consciences so clear that they could <hi type="italic">lift up their faces without spot,</hi> he that was false had his conscience so seared that he was not ashamed, neither could he blush, and so no discovery could be made in this way. Christ thus perplexed his disciples for a time, and put them into confusion, that he might <hi type="italic">humble them, and prove them,</hi> might excite in them a jealousy of themselves, and an indignation at the baseness of Judas. It is good for us sometimes to be put to a gaze, to be put to a pause. <div eID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> VI. The disciples were solicitous to get their Master to explain himself, and to tell them particularly whom he meant; for nothing but this can put them out of their present pain, for each of them thought he had as much reason to suspect himself as any of his brethren; now, <div eID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> 1. Of all the disciples John was most fit to ask, because he was the favourite, and sat next his Master (<reference osisRef="John.13.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was leaning on Jesus's bosom one of the disciples whom Jesus loved.</hi> It appears that this was John, by comparing <reference osisRef="John.21.20">ch. xxi. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.21.24">24</reference>. Observe, (1.) The particular kindness which Jesus had for him; he was known by this periphrasis, that he was <hi type="italic">the disciple whom Jesus loved.</hi> He loved them all (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">v. 1</reference>), but John was particularly dear to him. His name signifies <hi type="italic">gracious.</hi> Daniel, who was honoured with the revelations of the Old Testament, as John of the New, was <hi type="italic">a man greatly beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Dan. ix. 23</reference>. Note, Among the disciples of Christ some are dearer to him than others. (2.) His place and posture at this time: He was <hi type="italic">leaning on Jesus's bosom.</hi> Some say that it was the fashion in those countries to sit at meat in a leaning posture, so that the second lay in the bosom of the first, and so on, which does not seem probable to me, for in such a posture as this they could neither eat nor drink conveniently; but, whether this was the case or not, John now <hi type="italic">leaned on Christ's bosom,</hi> and it seems to be an extraordinary expression of endearment used at this time. Note, There are some of Christ's disciples whom he lays in his bosom, who have more free and intimate communion with him than others. The Father loved the Son, and laid him <hi type="italic">in his bosom</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), and believers are in like manner one with Christ, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">ch. xvii. 21</reference>. This honour all the saints shall have shortly in the bosom of Abraham. Those who lay themselves at Christ's feet, he will lay in his bosom. (3.) Yet he conceals his name, because he himself was the penman of the story. He put this instead of his name, to show that he was pleased with it; it is his title of honour, that he was <hi type="italic">the disciple whom Jesus loved,</hi> as in David's and Solomon's court there was one that was the <hi type="italic">king's friend;</hi> yet he does not put his name down, to show that he was not proud of it, nor would seem to boast of it. Paul in a like case saith, <hi type="italic">I knew a man in Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> 2. Of all the disciples Peter was most forward to know, <reference osisRef="John.13.24">v. 24</reference>. Peter, sitting at some distance, beckoned to John, by some sign or other, to ask. Peter was generally the leading man, most apt to put himself forth; and, where men's natural tempers lead them to be thus bold in answering and asking, if kept under the laws of humility and wisdom, they make men very serviceable. God gives his gifts variously; but that the forward men in the church may not think too well of themselves, nor the modest be discouraged, it must be noted that it was not Peter, but John, that was the beloved disciple. Peter was desirous to know, not only that he might be sure it was not he, but that, knowing who it was, they might withdraw from him, and guard against him, and, if possible, prevent his design. It were a desirable thing, we should think, to know who in the church will deceive us; yet let this suffice—Christ knows, though we do not. The reason why Peter did not himself ask was because John had a much fairer opportunity, by the advantage of his seat at table, to whisper the question into the ear of Christ, and to receive a like private answer. It is good to improve our interest in those that are near to Christ, and to engage their prayers for us. Do we know any that we have reason to think lie in Christ's bosom? Let us beg of them to speak a good word for us. <div eID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> 3. The question was asked accordingly (<reference osisRef="John.13.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">He then, lying at the breast of Jesus,</hi> and so having the convenience of whispering with him, <hi type="italic">saith unto him, Lord, who is it?</hi> Now here John shows, (1.) A regard to his fellow-disciple, and to the motion he made. Though Peter had not the honour he had at this time, yet he did not therefore disdain to take the hint and intimation he gave him. Note, Those who lie in Christ's bosom may often learn from those who lie at his feet something that will be profitable for them, and be reminded of that which they did not of themselves think of. John was willing to gratify Peter herein, having so fair an opportunity for it. As every one hath received the gift, so let him minister the same for a common good, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.6">Rom. xii. 6</reference>. (2.) A reverence of his Master. Though he whispered this in Christ's ear, yet he called him Lord; the familiarity he was admitted to did not at all lessen his respect for his Master. It becomes us to use a reverence in expression, and to observe a decorum even in our secret devotions, which no eye is a witness to, as well as in public assemblies. The more intimate communion gracious souls have with Christ, the more sensible they are of his worthiness and their own unworthiness, as <reference osisRef="Gen.18.27">Gen. xviii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ gave a speedy answer to this question, but whispered it in John's ear; for it appears (<reference osisRef="John.13.29">v. 29</reference>) that the rest were still ignorant of the matter. <hi type="italic">He it is to whom I shall give a sop,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">psomion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a morsel, a crust, when I have dipped it</hi> in the sauce. And <hi type="italic">when he had dipped the sop,</hi> John strictly observing his motion, <hi type="italic">he gave it to Judas;</hi> and Judas took it readily enough, not suspecting the design of it, but glad of a savoury bit, to make up his mouth with. (1.) Christ notified the traitor by a sign. He could have told John by name who he was (The adversary and enemy is that wicked Judas, he is the traitor, and none but he); but thus he would exercise the observation of John, and intimate what need his ministers have of a spirit of discerning; for the false brethren we are to stand upon our guard against are not made known to us by words, but by signs; they are to be known to us by <hi type="italic">their fruits,</hi> by <hi type="italic">their spirits;</hi> it requires great diligence and care to form a right judgment upon them. (2.) That sign was a sop which Christ gave him, a very proper sign, because it was the fulfilling of the scripture (<reference osisRef="John.13.18">v. 18</reference>) that the traitor should be one that <hi type="italic">ate bread with him,</hi> that was at this time a fellow-commoner with him. It had likewise a significancy in it, and teaches us, [1.] That Christ sometimes gives sops to traitors; worldly riches, honours, and pleasures are sops (if I may so speak), which Providence sometimes gives into the hands of wicked men. Judas perhaps thought himself a favourite because he had the sop, like Benjamin at Joseph's table, a mess by himself; thus the prosperity of fools, like a stupifying sop, helps to <hi type="italic">destroy them.</hi> [2.] That we must not be outrageous against those whom we know to be very malicious against us. Christ carved to Judas as kindly as to any at the table, though he knew he was then plotting his death. <hi type="italic">If thine enemy hunger, feed him;</hi> this is to do as Christ does. <div eID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> VII. Judas himself, instead of being convinced hereby of his wickedness, was the more confirmed in it, and the warning given him was to him a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> for it follows, <div eID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> 1. The devil hereupon took possession of him (<reference osisRef="John.13.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">After the sop, Satan entered into him:</hi> not to make him melancholy, nor drive him distracted, which was the effect of his possessing some; not to hurry him into the fire, nor into the water; happy had it been for him if that had been the worst of it, or if with the swine he had been choked in the sea; but Satan entered into him to possess him with a prevailing prejudice against Christ and his doctrine, and a contempt of him, as one whose life was of small value, to excite in him a covetous desire of the wages of unrighteousness and a resolution to stick at nothing for the obtaining of them. But, <div eID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> (1.) Was not Satan in him before? How then is it said that now <hi type="italic">Satan entered into him?</hi> Judas was all along a devil (<reference osisRef="John.6.70">ch. vi. 70</reference>), a son of perdition, but now Satan gained a more full possession of him, had a <hi type="italic">more abundant entrance</hi> into him. His purpose to betray his Master was now ripened into a fixed resolution; now he returned with seven other spirits more wicked than himself, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.26">Luke xi. 26</reference>. Note, [1.] Though the devil is in every wicked man that does his works (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>), yet sometimes he enters more manifestly and more powerfully than at other times, when he puts them upon some enormous wickedness, which humanity and natural conscience startle at. [2.] Betrayers of Christ have much of the devil in them. Christ speaks of the sin of Judas as greater than that of any of his persecutors. <div eID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> (2.) How came Satan to enter into him <hi type="italic">after the sop?</hi> Perhaps he was presently aware that it was the discovery of him, and it made him desperate in his resolutions. Many are made worse by the gifts of Christ's bounty, and are confirmed in their impenitency by that which should have led them to repentance. The <hi type="italic">coals of fire heaped upon their heads,</hi> instead of melting them, harden them. <div eID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ hereupon dismissed him, and delivered him up to his own heart's lusts: <hi type="italic">Then said Jesus unto him, What thou doest, do quickly.</hi> This is not to be understood as either advising him to his wickedness or warranting him in it; but either, (1.) As abandoning him to the conduct and power of Satan. Christ knew that Satan had entered into him, and had peaceable possession; and now he gives him up as hopeless. The various methods Christ had used for his conviction were ineffectual; and therefore, "What thou doest thou wilt do quickly; if thou art resolved to ruin thyself, go on, and take what comes." Note, When the evil spirit is willingly admitted, the good Spirit justly withdraws. Or, (2.) As challenging him to do his worst: "Thou art plotting against me, put thy plot in execution and welcome, the sooner the better, I do not fear thee, I am ready for thee." Note, our Lord Jesus was very forward to suffer and die for us, and was impatient of delay in the perfecting of his undertaking. Christ speaks of Judas's betraying him as a thing he was now doing, though he was only purposing it. Those who are contriving and designing mischief are, in God's account, doing mischief. <div eID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27990" type="x-p"/> 3. Those that were at table understood not what he meant, because they did not hear what he whispered to John (<reference osisRef="John.13.28-John.13.29">v. 28, 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">No man at table,</hi> neither the disciples nor any other of the guests, except John, <hi type="italic">knew for what intent</hi> he spoke this to him. (1.) They did not suspect that Christ said it to Judas as a traitor, because it did not enter into their heads that Judas was such a one, or would prove so. Note, It is an excusable dulness in the disciples of Christ not to be quick-sighted in their censures. Most are ready enough to say, when they hear harsh things spoken in general, Now such a one is meant, and now such a one; but Christ's disciples were so well taught to love one another that they could not easily learn to suspect one another; <hi type="italic">charity thinks no evil.</hi> (2.) They therefore took it for granted that he said it to him as a trustee, or treasurer of the household, giving him order for the laying out of some money. Their surmises in this case discover to us for what uses and purposes our Lord Jesus commonly directed payments out of that little stock he had, and so teach us how to honour the Lord with our substance. They concluded something was to be laid out, either, [1.] In works of piety: <hi type="italic">Buy those things that we have need of against the feast.</hi> Though he borrowed a room to eat the passover in, yet he bought in provision for it. That is to be reckoned well bestowed which is laid out upon <hi type="italic">those things we have need of</hi> for the maintenance of God's ordinances among us; and we have the less reason to grudge that expense now because our gospel-worship is far from being so chargeable as the legal worship was. [2.] Or in works of charity: <hi type="italic">That he should give something to the poor.</hi> By this it appears, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That our Lord Jesus, though he lived upon alms himself (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Luke viii. 3</reference>), yet gave alms to the poor, a little out of a little. Though he might very well be excused, not only because he was poor himself, but because he did so much good in other ways, curing so many <hi type="italic">gratis;</hi> yet, to set us an example, he gave, for the relief of the poor, out of that which he had for the subsistence of his family; see <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the time of a religious feast was thought a proper time for works of charity. When he celebrated the passover he ordered something for the poor. When we experience God's bounty to us, this should make us bountiful to the poor. <div eID="gen27990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27991" type="x-p"/> 4. Judas hereupon sets himself vigorously to pursue his design against him: He <hi type="italic">went away.</hi> Notice is taken, <div eID="gen27991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27992" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of his speedy departure: <hi type="italic">He went out presently,</hi> and quitted the house, [1.] For fear of being more plainly discovered to the company, for, if he were, he expected they would all fall upon him, and be the death of him, or at least of his project. [2.] He went out as one weary of Christ's company and the society of his apostles. Christ needed not to expel him, he expelled himself. Note, Withdrawing from the communion of the faithful is commonly the first overt-act of a backslider, and the beginning of an apostasy. [3.] <hi type="italic">He went out</hi> to prosecute his design, to look for those with whom he was to make his bargain, and to settle the agreement with them. Now that Satan had got into him he hurried him on with precipitation, lest he should see his error and repent of it. <div eID="gen27992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> (2.) Of the time of his departure: <hi type="italic">It was night.</hi> [1.] Though it was night, an unseasonable time for business, yet, Satan having entered into him, he made no difficulty of the coldness and darkness of the night. This should shame us out of our slothfulness and cowardice in the service of Christ, that the devil's servants are so earnest and venturous in his service. [2.] Because it was night, and this gave him advantage of privacy and concealment. He was not willing to be <hi type="italic">seen</hi> treating with the chief priests, and therefore chose the dark night as the fittest time for such works of darkness. Those whose deeds are evil love darkness rather than light. See <reference osisRef="Job.24.13">Job xxiv. 13</reference>, &c.

<div eID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Departure Predicted.</title> <div sID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Therefore, when he was gone out, Jesus said, Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him. 32 If God be glorified in him, God shall also glorify him in himself, and shall straightway glorify him. <hi type="super">33</hi> Little children, yet a little while I am with you. Ye shall seek me: and as I said unto the Jews, Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you. <hi type="super">34</hi> A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. 35 By this shall all <hi type="italic">men</hi> know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another. <div eID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> This and what follows, to the end of <reference osisRef="John.13.31-John.14.33">ch. xiv.</reference>, was Christ's table-talk with his disciples. When supper was done, Judas went out; but what did the Master and his disciples do, whom he left sitting at table? They applied themselves to profitable discourse, to teach us as much as we can to make conversation with our friends at table serviceable to religion. Christ begins this discourse. The more forward we are humbly to promote that communication which is good, and to the use of edifying, the more like we are to Jesus Christ. Those especially that by their place, reputation, and gifts, <hi type="italic">command the company,</hi> to whom <hi type="italic">men give ear,</hi> ought to use the interest they have in other respects as an opportunity of doing them good. Now our Lord Jesus discourses with them (and probably discourses much more largely than is here recorded), <div eID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the great mystery of his own death and sufferings, about which they were as yet so much in the dark that they could not persuade themselves to expect the thing itself, much less did they understand the meaning of it; and therefore Christ gives them such instructions concerning it as made the offence of the cross to cease. Christ did not begin this discourse till Judas was gone out, for he was a false brother. The presence of wicked people is often a hindrance to good discourse. When Judas <hi type="italic">was gone out,</hi> Christ said, <hi type="italic">now is the Son of man glorified;</hi> now that Judas is discovered and discarded, who was a spot in their love-feast and a scandal to their family, <hi type="italic">now is the Son of man glorified.</hi> Note, Christ is glorified by the purifying of Christian societies: corruptions in his church are a reproach to him; the purging out of those corruptions rolls away the reproach. Or, rather, now Judas was gone to set the wheels a-going, in order to his being put to death, and the thing was likely to be effected shortly: <hi type="italic">Now is the Son of man glorified,</hi> meaning, <hi type="italic">Now he is crucified.</hi> <div eID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is something which Christ instructs them in, concerning his sufferings, that was very <hi type="italic">comforting.</hi> <div eID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he should himself be glorified in them. Now the Son of man is to be exposed to the greatest ignominy and disgrace, to be despitefully used to the last degree, and dishonoured both by the cowardice of his friends and the insolence of his enemies; yet <hi type="italic">now he is glorified;</hi> For, [1.] Now he is to obtain a glorious victory over Satan and all the powers of darkness, to spoil them, and triumph over them. He is now <hi type="italic">girding on the harness,</hi> to take the field against these adversaries of God and man, with as great an assurance as if he had <hi type="italic">put it off.</hi> [2.] Now he is to work out a glorious deliverance for his people, by his death to reconcile them to God, and bring in an everlasting righteousness and happiness for them; to shed that blood which is to be an inexhaustible fountain of joys and blessings to all believers. [3.] Now he is to give a glorious example of self-denial and patience under the cross, courage and contempt of the world, zeal for the glory of God, and love to the souls of men, such as will make him to be for ever admired and had in honour. Christ had been glorified in many miracles he had wrought, and yet he speaks of his being glorified <hi type="italic">now</hi> in his sufferings, as if that were more than all his other glories in his humble state. <div eID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> (2.) That God the Father should be glorified in them. The sufferings of Christ were, [1.] The satisfaction of God's justice, and so God was glorified in them. Reparation was thereby made with great advantage for the wrong done him in his honour by the sin of man. The ends of the law were abundantly answered, and the glory of his government effectually asserted and maintained. [2.] They were the manifestation of his holiness and mercy. The attributes of God shine brightly in creation and providence, but much more in the work of redemption; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1 Cor. i. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>. God is love, and herein he hath commended his love. <div eID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he should himself be greatly glorified after them, in consideration of God's being greatly glorified by them, <reference osisRef="John.13.32">v. 32</reference>. Observe how he enlarges upon it. [1.] He is sure that God will glorify him; and those whom God glorifies are glorious indeed. Hell and earth set themselves to vilify Christ, but God resolved to glorify him, and he did it. He glorified him in his sufferings by the amazing signs and wonders, both in heaven and earth, which attended them, and extorted even from his crucifiers an acknowledgment that he was the Son of God. But especially after his sufferings he glorified him, when he set him <hi type="italic">at his own right hand,</hi> gave him a <hi type="italic">name above every name.</hi> [2.] That he will glorify him <hi type="italic">in himself</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en heauto</hi></hi>. Either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In Christ himself. He will glorify him in his own person, and not only in his kingdom among men. This supposes his speedy resurrection. A common person may be honoured after his death, in his memory or posterity, but Christ was honoured in <hi type="italic">himself.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">secondly,</hi> in God himself. God will glorify him <hi type="italic">with himself,</hi> as it is explained, <reference osisRef="John.17.5">ch. xvii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall sit down with the Father upon his throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>. This is true glory. [3.] That he will glorify him straightway. He looked upon the joy and glory set before him, not only as great, but as near; and his sorrows and sufferings short and soon over. Good services done to earthly princes often remain long unrewarded; but Christ had his preferments presently. It was but forty hours (or not so much) from his death to his resurrection, and forty days thence to his ascension, so that it might well be said that he was <hi type="italic">straightway glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Ps. xvi. 10</reference>. [4.] All this in consideration of God's being glorified in and by his sufferings: <hi type="italic">Seeing God is glorified in him,</hi> and receives honour from his sufferings, God shall in like manner glorify him in himself, and give honour to him. Note, <hi type="italic">first,</hi> In the exaltation of Christ there was a regard had to his humiliation, and a reward given for it. <hi type="italic">Because he humbled himself, therefore God highly exalted him.</hi> If the Father be so great a gainer in his glory by the death of Christ, we may be sure that the Son shall be no loser in his. See the covenant between them, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those who mind the business of glorifying God no doubt shall have the happiness of being glorified with him. <div eID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is something that Christ instructs them in, concerning his sufferings, which was <hi type="italic">awakening,</hi> for as yet they were slow of heart to understand it (<reference osisRef="John.13.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Little children, yet a little while I am with you,</hi> &c. Two things Christ here suggests, to quicken his disciples to improve their present opportunities; two serious words:— <div eID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> (1.) That his stay in this world, to be with them here, they would find to be very short. <hi type="italic">Little children.</hi> This compellation does not bespeak so much their weakness as his tenderness and compassion; he speaks to them with the affection of a father, now that he is about to leaven them, and to leave blessings with them. Know this, then, that <hi type="italic">yet a little while I am with you.</hi> Whether we understand this as referring to his death or his ascension it comes much to one; he had but a little time to spend with them, and therefore, [1.] Let them improve the advantage they now had. If they had any good question to ask, if they would have any advice, instruction, or comfort, let them speak quickly; for <hi type="italic">yet a little while I am with you.</hi> We must make the best of the helps we have for our souls while we have them, because we shall not have them long; they will be taken from us, or we from them. [2.] Let them not doat upon his bodily presence, as if their happiness and comfort were bound up in that; no, they must think of living without it; not be always little children, but go alone, without their nurses. Ways and means are appointed but for a <hi type="italic">little while,</hi> and are not to be rested in, but pressed through to our rest, to which they have a reference. <div eID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> (2.) That their following him to the other world, to be with him there, they would find to be very difficult. What he had said to the Jews (<reference osisRef="John.7.34">ch. vii. 34</reference>) he saith to his disciples; for they have need to be quickened by the same considerations that are propounded for the convincing and awakening of sinners. Christ tells them here, [1.] That when he was gone they would feel the want of him; <hi type="italic">You shall seek me,</hi> that is "you shall wish you had me again with you." We are often taught the worth of mercies by the want of them. Though the presence of the Comforter yielded them real and effectual relief in straits and difficulties, yet it was not such a <hi type="italic">sensible</hi> satisfaction as his bodily presence would have been to those who had been used to it. But observe, Christ said to the Jews, You shall seek me and <hi type="italic">not find me;</hi> but to the disciples he only saith, <hi type="italic">You shall seek me,</hi> intimating that though they should not find his bodily presence any more than the Jews, yet they should find that which was tantamount, and should not seek in vain. When they sought his body in the sepulchre, though they did not find it, yet they sought to good purpose. [2.] That whither he went they <hi type="italic">could not come,</hi> which suggests to them high thoughts of him, who was going to an invisible inaccessible world, to dwell in that <hi type="italic">light which none can approach unto;</hi> and also low thoughts of themselves, and serious thoughts of their future state. Christ tells them that they could not follow him (as Joshua told the people that they could not serve the Lord) only to quicken them to so much the more diligence and care. They could not follow him to his cross, for they had not courage and resolution; it appeared that they could not when they all forsook him and fled. Nor could they follow him to his crown, for they had not a sufficiency of their own, nor were their work and warfare yet finished. <div eID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> II. He discourses with them concerning the great duty of brotherly love (<reference osisRef="John.13.34-John.13.35">v. 34, 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall love one another.</hi> Judas was now gone out, and had proved himself a false brother; but they must not therefore harbour such jealousies and suspicions one of another as would be the bane of love: though there was one Judas among them, yet they were not all Judases. Now that the enmity of the Jews against Christ and his followers was swelling to the height, and they must expect such treatment as their Master had, it concerned them by brotherly love to strengthen one another's hands. Three arguments for mutual love are here urged:— <div eID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> 1. The command of their Master (<reference osisRef="John.13.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">A new commandment I give unto you.</hi> He not only commends it as amiable and pleasant, not only counsels it as excellent and profitable, but commands it, and makes it one of the fundamental laws of his kingdom; it goes a-breast with the command of believing in Christ, <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">1 John iii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.22">1 Pet. i. 22</reference>. It is the command of our ruler, who has a right to give law to us; it is the command of our Redeemer, who gives us this law in order to the curing of our spiritual diseases and the preparing of us for our eternal bliss. It is <hi type="italic">a new commandment;</hi> that is, (1.) It is a renewed commandment; it was a commandment <hi type="italic">from the beginning</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.7">1 John ii. 7</reference>), as old as the law of nature, it was the second great commandment of the law of Moses; yet, because it is also one of the great commandments of the New Testament, of Christ the new Lawgiver, it is called a new commandment; it is like an old book in a new edition corrected and enlarged. This commandment has been so corrupted by the traditions of the Jewish church that when Christ revived it, and set it in a true light, it might well be called a <hi type="italic">new commandment.</hi> Laws of revenge and retaliation were so much in vogue, and self-love had so much the ascendant, that the law of brotherly love was forgotten as obsolete and out of date; so that as it came from Christ new, it was new to the people. (2.) It is an excellent command, as a <hi type="italic">new song</hi> is an excellent song, that has an uncommon gratefulness in it. (3.) It is an everlasting command; so strangely new as to be always so; as the <hi type="italic">new covenant,</hi> which shall never decay (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>); it shall be new to eternity, when faith and hope are antiquated. (4.) As Christ gives it, it is <hi type="italic">new.</hi> Before it was, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour;</hi> now it is, You shall love <hi type="italic">one another;</hi> it is pressed in a more winning way when it is thus pressed as mutual duty owing to one another. <div eID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> 2. The example of their Saviour is another argument for brotherly love: <hi type="italic">As I have loved you.</hi> It is this that makes it a <hi type="italic">new commandment</hi>—that this rule and reason of <hi type="italic">love (as I have loved you</hi>) is perfectly new, and such as had been hidden from ages and generations. Understand this, (1.) Of all the instances of Christ's love to his disciples, which they had already experienced during the time he went in and out among them. He spoke kindly to them, concerned himself heartily for them, and for their welfare, instructed, counselled, and comforted them, prayed with them and for them, vindicated them when they were accused, took their part when they were run down, and publicly owned them to be dearer to him that his <hi type="italic">mother, or sister, or brother.</hi> He reproved them for what was amiss, and yet compassionately bore with their failings, excused them, made the best of them, and passed by many an oversight. Thus he <hi type="italic">had</hi> loved them, and just now washed their feet; and thus they <hi type="italic">must</hi> love one another, and love <hi type="italic">to the end.</hi> Or, (2.) It may be understood of the special instance of love to all his disciples which he was now about to give, in laying down his life for them. <hi type="italic">Greater love hath no man than this,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.13">ch. xv. 13</reference>. Has he thus loved us all? Justly may he expect that we should be loving to one another. Not that we are capable of doing any thing of the <hi type="italic">same nature</hi> for each other (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.7">Ps. xlix. 7</reference>), but we must love one another in some respects after the <hi type="italic">same manner;</hi> we must set this before us as our copy, and take directions from it. Our love to one another must be free and ready, laborious and expensive, constant and persevering; it must be love <hi type="italic">to the souls</hi> one of another. We must also love one another from <hi type="italic">this motive,</hi> and upon this consideration—because Christ has loved us. See <reference osisRef="Rom.15.1 Rom.15.3 Eph.5.2 Eph.5.25 Phil.2.1-Phil.2.5">Rom. xv. 1, 3; Eph. v. 2, 25; Phil. ii. 1-5</reference>. <div eID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> 3. The reputation of their profession (<reference osisRef="John.13.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another.</hi> Observe, We must have love, not only show love, but have it in the root and habit of it, and have it when there is not any present occasion to show it; have it <hi type="italic">ready.</hi> "Hereby it will appear that you are indeed my followers by following me in this." Note, Brotherly love is the badge of Christ's disciples. By this he knows them, by this they may know themselves (<reference osisRef="1John.2.14">1 John ii. 14</reference>), and by this others may know them. This is the livery of his family, the distinguishing character of his disciples; this he would have them <hi type="italic">noted for,</hi> as that wherein they excelled all others—their loving one another. This was what their Master was famous for; all that ever heard of him have heard of his love, his great love; and therefore, if you see any people more affectionate one to another than what is common, say, "Certainly these are the followers of Christ, they have been with Jesus." Now by this it appears, (1.) That the heart of Christ was very much upon it, that his disciples <hi type="italic">should love one another.</hi> In this they must be <hi type="italic">singular;</hi> whereas the way of the world is to be <hi type="italic">every one for himself,</hi> they should be hearty for one another. He does not say, <hi type="italic">By this shall men know</hi> that you are my disciples—if you <hi type="italic">work miracles,</hi> for a worker of miracles is but a cypher without charity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.2">1 Cor. xiii. 1, 2</reference>); but <hi type="italic">if you love one another</hi> from a principle of self-denial and gratitude to Christ. This Christ would have to be the <hi type="italic">proprium</hi> of his religion, the principal note of the true church. (2.) That it is the true honour of Christ's disciples to excel in brotherly love. Nothing will be more effectual than this to recommend them to the esteem and respect of others. See what a powerful attractive it was, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46-Acts.2.47">Acts ii. 46, 47</reference>. Tertullian speaks of it as the glory of the primitive church that the Christians were known by their affection to one another. Their adversaries took notice of it, and said, <hi type="italic">See how these Christians love one another,</hi> Apol. cap. 39. (3.) That, if the followers of Christ do not love one another, they not only cast an unjust reproach upon their profession, but give just cause to suspect their own sincerity. <hi type="italic">O Jesus! are these thy Christians,</hi> these passionate, malicious, spiteful, ill-natured people? <hi type="italic">Is this thy son's coat?</hi> When our brethren stand in need of help from us, and we have an opportunity of being service able to them, when they differ in opinion and practice from us, or are any ways rivals with or provoking to us, and so we have an occasion to condescend and forgive, in such cases as this it will be known whether we have this badge of Christ's disciples.

<div eID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Self-Confidence.</title> <div sID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> Simon Peter said unto him, Lord, whither goest thou? Jesus answered him, Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now; but thou shalt follow me afterwards. <hi type="super">37</hi> Peter said unto him, Lord, why cannot I follow thee now? I will lay down my life for thy sake. <hi type="super">38</hi> Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice. <div eID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> I. Peter's curiosity, and the check given to that. <div eID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> 1. Peter's question was bold and blunt (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lord, whither goest thou?</hi> referring to what Christ had said (<reference osisRef="John.13.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whither I go, you cannot come.</hi> The practical instructions Christ had given them concerning brotherly love he overlooks, and asks no questions upon them, but fastens upon that concerning which Christ purposely kept them in the dark. Note, It is a common fault among us to be more inquisitive concerning things secret, which belong to God only, than concerning things <hi type="italic">revealed, which belong to us and our children,</hi> more desirous to have our curiosity gratified than our consciences directed, to know what is done in heaven than what we may do to get thither. It is easy to observe it in the converse of Christians, how soon a discourse of that which is plain and edifying is dropped, and no more said to it, the subject is exhausted; which in a matter of doubtful disputation runs into an endless strife of words. <div eID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's answer was instructive. He did not gratify him with any particular account of the world he was going to, nor ever foretold his glories and joys so distinctly as he did his sufferings, but said what he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">v. 36</reference>): Let this suffice, <hi type="italic">thou canst not follow me now, but shalt follow me hereafter,</hi> (1.) We may understand it of his following him to the cross: "Thou hast not yet strength enough of faith and resolution to drink of my cup;" and it appeared so by his cowardice when Christ was suffering. For this reason, when Christ was seized, he provided for the safety of his disciples. <hi type="italic">Let these go their way,</hi> because they could not <hi type="italic">follow him now.</hi> Christ considers the frame of his disciples, and will not cut out for them that work and hardship which they are not as yet fit for; the day shall be as the strength is. Peter, though designed for martyrdom, cannot follow Christ now, not being come to his full growth, but he <hi type="italic">shall follow</hi> him <hi type="italic">hereafter;</hi> he shall be crucified at last, like his Master. Let him not think that because he escapes suffering now he shall never suffer. From our missing the cross once, we must not infer that we shall never meet it; we may be reserved for greater trials than we have yet known. (2.) We may understand it of his following him to the crown. Christ was now going to his glory, and Peter was very desirous to go with him: "No," saith Christ, "<hi type="italic">thou canst not follow me now,</hi> thou art not yet ripe for heaven, nor hast thou finished thy work on earth. The forerunner must <hi type="italic">first enter to prepare a place</hi> for thee, but <hi type="italic">thou shalt follow me afterwards,</hi> after thou hast fought the good fight, and at the time appointed." Note, Believers must not expect to be glorified as soon as they are effectually called, for there is a wilderness between the Red Sea and Canaan. <div eID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> II. Peter's confidence, and the check given to that. <div eID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> 1. Peter makes a daring protestation of his constancy. He is not content to be left behind, but asks, "<hi type="italic">Lord why cannot I follow thee now?</hi> Dost thou question my sincerity and resolution? I promise thee, if there be occasion, <hi type="italic">I will lay down my life for thy sake.</hi>" Some think Peter had a conceit, as the Jews had in a like case (<reference osisRef="John.7.35">ch. vii. 35</reference>), that Christ was designing a journey or voyage into some remote country, and that he declared his resolution to go along with him wherever he went; but, having heard his Master so often speak of his own sufferings, surely he could not understand him any otherwise than of his going away by death; and he resolves as Thomas did that he will <hi type="italic">go and die with him;</hi> and better die with him than live without him. See here, (1.) What an affectionate love Peter had to our Lord Jesus: "<hi type="italic">I will lay down my life for thy sake,</hi> and I can do no more." I believe Peter spoke as he thought, and though he was inconsiderate he was not insincere, in his resolution. Note, Christ should be dearer to us than our own lives, which therefore, when we are called to it, we should be willing to lay down for his sake, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>. (2.) How ill he took it to have it questioned, intimated in that expostulation, "<hi type="italic">Lord, why cannot I follow thee now?</hi> Dost thou suspect my fidelity to thee?" <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">1 Sam. xxix. 8</reference>. Note, It is with regret that true love hears its own sincerity arraigned, as <reference osisRef="John.21.17">ch. xxi. 17</reference>. Christ had indeed said that one of them was a devil, but he was discovered, and gone out, and therefore Peter thinks he may speak with the more assurance of his own sincerity; "Lord, I am resolved I will never leave thee, and therefore <hi type="italic">why cannot I follow thee?</hi>" We are apt to think that we can do any thing, and take it amiss to be told that this and the other we cannot do, whereas without Christ we can do nothing. <div eID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28015" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ gives him a surprising prediction of his inconstancy, <reference osisRef="John.13.38">v. 38</reference>. Jesus Christ knows us better than we know ourselves, and has many ways of discovering those to themselves whom he loves, and will hide pride from. (1.) He upbraids Peter with his confidence: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake?</hi> Me thinks, he seems to have said this with a smile: "Peter, thy promises are too large, too lavish to be relied on; thou dost not consider with what reluctancy and struggle a life is laid down, and what a hard task it is to die; not so soon done as said." Christ hereby puts Peter upon second thoughts, not that he might retract his resolution, or recede from it, but that he might insert into it that necessary proviso, "Lord, <hi type="italic">thy grace enabling me,</hi> I will lay down my life for thy sake." "Wilt thou undertake to die for me? What! thou that trembledst to walk upon the water to me? What! thou that, when sufferings were spoken of, criedst out, <hi type="italic">Be it far from thee, Lord?</hi> It was an easy thing to leave thy boats and nets to follow me, but not so easy to lay down thy life." His Master himself struggled when it came to his, and <hi type="italic">the disciple is not greater than his Lord.</hi> Note, It is good for us to shame ourselves out of our presumptuous confidence in ourselves. Shall a bruised reed set up for a pillar, or a sickly child undertake to be a champion? What a fool am I to talk so big. (2.) He plainly foretels his cowardice in the critical hour. To stop the mouth of his boasting, lest Peter should say it again, Yea Master, that I will, Christ solemnly asserts it with, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto thee, the cock shall not crow till thou hast denied me thrice.</hi> He does not say as afterwards, <hi type="italic">This night,</hi> for it seems to have been two nights before the passover; but, "Shortly thou wilt have denied me thrice within the space of one night; nay, within so short a space as between the first and last crowing of the cock: <hi type="italic">The cock shall not crow,</hi> shall not have crowed his crowing out, till thou has again and again denied me, and that for fear of suffering." The crowing of the cock is mentioned, [1.] To intimate that the trial in which he would miscarry thus should be in the night, which was an improbable circumstance, but Christ's foretelling it was an instance of his infallible foresight. [2.] Because the crowing of the cock was to be the occasion of his repentance, which of itself would not have been if Christ had not put this into the prediction. Christ not only foresaw that Judas would betray him though he only in heart designed it, but he foresaw that Peter would deny him though he did not design it, but the contrary. He knows not only the wickedness of sinners, but the weakness of saints. Christ told Peter, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he would deny him, would renounce and abjure him: "Thou wilt not only not follow me still, but wilt be ashamed to own that ever thou didst follow me." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he would do this not once only by a hasty slip of the tongue, but after he had paused would repeat it a second and third time; and it proved too true. We commonly give it as a reason why the prophecies of scripture are expressed darkly and figuratively, because, if they did <hi type="italic">plainly</hi> describe the event, the accomplishment would thereby either be defeated or necessitated by a fatality inconsistent with human liberty; and yet this plain and express prophecy of Peter's denying Christ did neither, nor did in the least make Christ accessary to Peter's sin. But we may well imagine what a mortification it was to Peter's confidence of his own courage to be told this, and to be told it in such a manner that he durst not contradict it, else he would have said as Hazael, <hi type="italic">What! is thy servant a dog?</hi> This could not but fill him with confusion. Note, The most secure are commonly the least safe; and those most shamefully betray their own weakness that most confidently presume upon their own strength, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.12">1 Cor. x. 12</reference>.  <chapter eID="John.13"/> <div eID="gen28015" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28018" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28017" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28019" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. <hi type="super">2</hi> In my Father's house are many mansions: if <hi type="italic">it were</hi> not <hi type="italic">so,</hi> I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. <hi type="super">3</hi> And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, <hi type="italic">there</hi> ye may be also. <div eID="gen28019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28020" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen28020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28021" type="x-p"/> I. A general caution which Christ gives to his disciples against <hi type="italic">trouble of heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled.</hi> They now began to be troubled, were entering into this temptation. Now here see, <div eID="gen28021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28022" type="x-p"/> 1. How Christ took notice of it. Perhaps it was apparent in their looks; it was said (<reference osisRef="John.13.22">ch. xiii. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">They looked one upon another</hi> with anxiety and concern, and Christ looked upon them all, and observed it; at least, it was intelligible to the Lord Jesus, who is acquainted with all our secret undiscovered sorrows, with the wound that bleeds inwardly; he knows not only how we are afflicted, but how we stand affected under our afflictions, and how near they lie to our hearts; he takes cognizance of all the trouble which his people are at any time in danger of being overwhelmed with; <hi type="italic">he knows our souls in adversity.</hi> Many things concurred to trouble the disciples now. <div eID="gen28022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28023" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ had just told them of the unkindness he should receive from some of them, and this troubled them all. Peter, no doubt, looked very sorrowful upon what Christ said to him, and all the rest were sorry for him and for themselves too, not knowing whose turn it should be to be told next of some ill thing or other they should do. As to this, Christ comforts them; though a godly jealousy over ourselves is of great use to keep us humble and watchful, yet it must not prevail to the disquieting of our spirits and the damping of our holy joy. <div eID="gen28023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28024" type="x-p"/> (2.) He had just told them of his own departure from them, that he should not only go away, but go away in a cloud of sufferings. They must shortly hear him loaded with reproaches, and these will be <hi type="italic">as a sword in their bones;</hi> they must see him barbarously abused and put to death, and this also will be a sword piercing <hi type="italic">through their own souls,</hi> for they had loved him, and chosen him, and left all to follow him. When we now look upon Christ pierced, we cannot but <hi type="italic">mourn and be in bitterness,</hi> though we see the glorious issue and fruit of it; much more grievous must the sight be to them, who could then look no further. If Christ depart from them [1.] They will think themselves shamefully disappointed; for they looked that this had been he that should have delivered Israel, and should have set upon his kingdom in secular power and glory, and, in expectation of this, had lost all to follow him. Now, if he leave the world in the same circumstances of meanness and poverty in which he had lived, and worse, they are quite defeated. [2.] They will think themselves sadly deserted and exposed. They knew by experience what little presence of mind they had in difficult emergencies, that they could count upon nothing but being ruined and run down if they part with their Master. Now, in reference to all these, <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled.</hi> Here are three words, upon any of which the emphasis may significantly be laid. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Upon the word <hi type="italic">troubled,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me tarassestho</hi></hi>. Be not so troubled as to be put into a hurry and confusion, <hi type="italic">like the troubled sea when</hi> it cannot rest. He does not say, "Let not your hearts be sensible of the griefs, or sad because of them" but, "Be not ruffled and discomposed, be not cast down and disquieted," <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Ps. xlii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Upon the word <hi type="italic">heart:</hi> "Though the nation and city be troubled, though your little family and flock be troubled, yet <hi type="italic">let not your heart be troubled.</hi> Keep possession of your own souls when you can keep possession of nothing else." The heart is the main fort; whatever you do, keep trouble from this, keep this with <hi type="italic">all diligence.</hi> The spirit must <hi type="italic">sustain the infirmity,</hi> therefore, see that this be not <hi type="italic">wounded. Thirdly,</hi> Upon the word <hi type="italic">your:</hi> "You that are my disciples and followers, my redeemed, chosen, sanctified ones, however others are overwhelmed with the sorrows of this present time, be not you so, for you know better; let <hi type="italic">the sinners in Zion</hi> tremble, but let the <hi type="italic">sons of Zion be joyful in their king.</hi>" Herein Christ's disciples should <hi type="italic">do more than others,</hi> should keep their minds quiet, when every thing else is unquiet. <div eID="gen28024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28025" type="x-p"/> 2. The remedy he prescribes against this trouble of mind, which he saw ready to prevail over them; in general, <hi type="italic">believe</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pisteuete</hi></hi>. (1.) Some read it in both parts imperatively, "<hi type="italic">Believe in God,</hi> and his perfections and providence, <hi type="italic">believe also in me,</hi> and my mediation. Build with confidence upon the great acknowledged principles of natural religion: that there is a God, that he is most holy, wise, powerful, and good; that he is the governor of the world, and has the sovereign disposal of all events; and comfort yourselves likewise with the peculiar doctrines of that holy religion which I have taught you." But, (2.) We read the former as an acknowledgment that they did believe in God, for which he commends them: "But, if you would effectually provide against a stormy day, <hi type="italic">believe also in me.</hi>" Through Christ we are brought into covenant with God, and become interested in his favour and promise, which otherwise as sinners we must despair of, and the remembrance of God would have been our trouble; but, by believing in Christ as the Mediator between God and man, our belief in God becomes comfortable; and this is the will of God, that <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son as they honour the Father,</hi> by believing in the Son as they believe in the Father. Those that rightly believe in God will believe in Jesus Christ, whom he has made known to them; and believing in God through Jesus Christ is an excellent means of keeping trouble from the heart. The joy of faith is the best remedy against the griefs of sense; it is a remedy with a promise annexed to it; <hi type="italic">the just shall live by faith;</hi> a remedy with a <hi type="italic">probatum est</hi> annexed to it. <hi type="italic">I had fainted unless I had believed.</hi> <div eID="gen28025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28026" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a particular direction to act faith upon the promise of eternal life, <reference osisRef="John.14.2-John.14.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He had directed them to trust to God, and to trust in him; but what must they trust God and Christ for? Trust them for a happiness to come when this body and this world shall be no more, and for a happiness to last as long as the immortal soul and the eternal world shall last. Now this is proposed as a sovereign cordial under all the troubles of this present time, to which there is that in the happiness of heaven which is admirably adapted and accommodated. The saints have encouraged themselves with this in their greatest extremities, <hi type="italic">That heaven would make amends for all.</hi> Let us see how this is suggested here. <div eID="gen28026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28027" type="x-p"/> 1. Believe and consider that really there is such a happiness: <hi type="italic">In my Father's house there are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.2">v. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen28027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28028" type="x-p"/> (1.) See under what notion the happiness of heaven is here represented: as <hi type="italic">mansions,</hi> many mansions in Christ's Father's house. [1.] Heaven is a house, not a tent or tabernacle; it is <hi type="italic">a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.</hi> [2.] It is a Father's house: <hi type="italic">my Father's house;</hi> and his Father is our Father, to whom he was now ascending; so that in right of their elder brother all true believers shall be welcome to that happiness as to their home. It is his house who is King of kings and Lord of lords, dwells in light, and inhabits eternity. [3.] There are <hi type="italic">mansions</hi> there; that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Distinct dwellings, an apartment for each. Perhaps there is an allusion to the priests' chambers that were about the temple. In heaven there are accommodations for particular saints; though all shall be swallowed up in God, yet our individuality shall not be lost there; every Israelite had his lot in Canaan, and every elder <hi type="italic">a seat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Rev. iv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Durable dwellings. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Monai</hi></hi>, from <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mneio</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">maneo, abiding places.</hi> The house itself is lasting; our estate in it is not for a term of years, but a perpetuity. Here we are as in an inn; in heaven we shall gain a settlement. The disciples had quitted their houses to attend Christ, who had not where to lay his head, but the mansions in heaven will make them amends. [4.] There are <hi type="italic">many</hi> mansions, for there are many sons to be brought to glory, and Christ exactly knows their number, nor will be straitened for room by the coming of more company than he expects. He had told Peter that he should follow him (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">ch. xiii. 36</reference>), but let not the rest be discouraged, in heaven there are mansions for them <hi type="italic">all. Rehoboth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.26.22">Gen. xxvi. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen28028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28029" type="x-p"/> (2.) See what assurance we have of the reality of the happiness itself, and the sincerity of the proposal of it to us: "<hi type="italic">If it were not so, I would have told you.</hi> If you had deceived yourselves, when you quitted your livelihoods, and ventured your lives for me, in prospect of a happiness future and unseen, I would soon have undeceived you." The assurance is built, [1.] Upon the veracity of his word. It is implied, "If there were not such a happiness, valuable and attainable, I would not have told you that there was." [2.] Upon the sincerity of his affection to them. As he is true, and would not impose upon them himself, so he is kind, and would not suffer them to be imposed upon. If either there were no such mansions, or none designed for them, who had left all to follow him, he would have given them timely notice of the mistake, that they might have made an honourable retreat to the world again, and have made the best they could of it. Note, Christ's good-will to us is a great encouragement to our hope in him. He loves us too well, and means us too well, to disappoint the expectations of his own raising, or to leave those to be of all men most miserable who have been of him most observant. <div eID="gen28029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28030" type="x-p"/> 2. Believe and consider that the design of Christ's going away was to prepare a place in heaven for his disciples. "You are grieved to think of my going away, whereas I go on your errand, <hi type="italic">as the forerunner; I am to enter for you.</hi>" He went to prepare a place for us; that is, (1.) To take possession for us, as our advocate or attorney, and so to secure our title as indefeasible. Livery of seisin was given to Christ, for the use and behoof of all that should believe on him. (2.) To make provision for us as our friend and father. The happiness of heaven, though prepared <hi type="italic">before the foundation of the world,</hi> yet must be further fitted up for man in his fallen state. It consisting much in the presence of Christ there, it was therefore necessary that he should <hi type="italic">go before,</hi> to enter into that glory which his disciples were to share in. Heaven would be an <hi type="italic">unready</hi> place for a Christian if Christ were not there. He went to prepare a table for them, to prepare thrones for them, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Luke xxii. 30</reference>. Thus Christ declares the fitness of heaven's happiness for the saints, for whom it is prepared. <div eID="gen28030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28031" type="x-p"/> 3. Believe and consider that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he would certainly come again in due time, to fetch them to that blessed place which he was now going to possess for himself and prepare for them (<reference osisRef="John.14.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I go and prepare a place for you,</hi> if this be the errand of my journey, you may be sure, when every thing is ready, <hi type="italic">I will come again, and receive you to myself,</hi> so that you shall follow me hereafter, <hi type="italic">that where I am there you may be also.</hi>" Now these are comfortable words indeed. (1.) That Jesus Christ will come again; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">erchomai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I do come,</hi> intimating the certainty of it, that he will come and that he is daily coming. We say, We are coming, when we are busy in preparing for our coming, and so he is; all he does has a reference and tendency to his second coming. Note, The belief of Christ's second coming, of which he has given us the assurance, is an excellent preservative against trouble of heart, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Phil. iv. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.8">James v. 8</reference>. (2.) That he will come again to receive all his faithful followers to himself. He sends for them privately at death, and gathers them one by one; but they are to make their public entry in solemn state all together at the last day, and then Christ himself will come to receive them, to conduct them in the abundance of his grace, and to welcome them in the abundance of his love. He will hereby testify the utmost respect and endearment imaginable. The coming of Christ is in order to our <hi type="italic">gathering together unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2 Thess. ii. 1</reference>. (3.) <hi type="italic">That where he is there they shall be also.</hi> This intimates, what many other scriptures declare, that the quintessence of heaven's happiness is being with Christ <hi type="italic">there,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.24">ch. xvii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Phil. i. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">1 Thess. iv. 17</reference>. Christ speaks of his being there as now present, <hi type="italic">that where I am;</hi> where I am to be shortly, where I am to be eternally; there you shall be shortly, there you shall be eternally: not only <hi type="italic">there,</hi> in the same place; but <hi type="italic">here,</hi> in the same state: not only spectators of his glory, as the three disciples on the mount, but sharers in it. (4.) That this may be inferred from his <hi type="italic">going to prepare a place</hi> for us, for his preparations shall not be in vain. He will not build and furnish lodgings, and let them stand empty. He will be the finisher of that of which he is the author. If he has prepared the place for us, he will prepare us for it, and in due time put us in possession of it. As the resurrection of Christ is the assurance of our resurrection, so his ascension, victory, and glory, are an assurance of ours.

<div eID="gen28031" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know. 5 Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way? <hi type="super">6</hi> Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. <hi type="super">7</hi> If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him. <hi type="super">8</hi> Philip saith unto him, Lord, show us the Father, and it sufficeth us. <hi type="super">9</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou <hi type="italic">then,</hi> Show us the Father? <hi type="super">10</hi> Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works. <hi type="super">11</hi> Believe me that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works' sake. <div eID="gen28032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28033" type="x-p"/> Christ, having set the happiness of heaven before them as the end, here shows them himself as the way to it, and tells them that they were better acquainted both with the end they were to aim at and with the way they were to walk in than they thought they were: <hi type="italic">You know,</hi> that is, 1. "You may know; it is none of the <hi type="italic">secret things</hi> which belong not to you, but one of the <hi type="italic">things revealed;</hi> you <hi type="italic">need not ascend into heaven,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">go down into the deep,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the word is nigh you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.6-Rom.10.8">Rom. x. 6-8</reference>), level to you." 2. "You do know; you know that which is the home and which is the way, though perhaps not as the home and as the way. You have been told it, and cannot but know, if you would recollect and consider it." Note, Jesus Christ is willing to make the best of his people's knowledge, though they are weak and defective in it. He knows the good that is in them better than they do themselves, and is certain that they have that knowledge, and faith, and love, of which they themselves are not sensible, or not certain. <div eID="gen28033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28034" type="x-p"/> This word of Christ gave occasion to two of his disciples to address themselves to him, and he answers them both. <div eID="gen28034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28035" type="x-p"/> I. Thomas enquired concerning the way (<reference osisRef="John.14.5">v. 5</reference>), without any apology for contradicting his Master. <div eID="gen28035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28036" type="x-p"/> 1. He said, "<hi type="italic">Lord, we know not whither thou goest,</hi> to what place or what state, <hi type="italic">and how can we know the way</hi> in which we must follow thee? We can neither guess at it, nor enquire it out, but must still be at a loss." Christ's testimony concerning their knowledge made them more sensible of their ignorance, and more inquisitive after further light. Thomas here shows more modesty than Peter, who thought he could follow Christ now. Peter was the more solicitous to know <hi type="italic">whither Christ went.</hi> Thomas here, though he complains that he did not know this, yet seems more solicitous to know <hi type="italic">the way.</hi> Now, (1.) His confession of his ignorance was commendable enough. If good men be in the dark, and know but in part, yet they are willing to own their defects. But, (2.) The cause of his ignorance was culpable. They knew not whither Christ went, because they dreamed of a temporal kingdom in external pomp and power, and doted upon this, notwithstanding what he had said again and again to the contrary. Hence it was that, when Christ spoke of going away and their following him, their fancy ran upon his going to some remarkable city or other, Bethlehem, or Nazareth, or Capernaum, or some of the cities of the Gentiles, as David to Hebron, there to be anointed king, and <hi type="italic">to restore the kingdom to Israel;</hi> and which way this place lay, where these castles in the air were to be built, east, west, north, or south, they could not tell, and therefore knew not the way. Thus still we think ourselves more in the dark than we need be concerning the future state of the church, because we expect its worldly prosperity, whereas it is spiritual advancement that the promise points at. Had Thomas understood, as he might have done, that Christ was going to the invisible world, the world of spirits, to which spiritual things only have a reference, he would not have said, <hi type="italic">Lord, we do not know the way.</hi> <div eID="gen28036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28037" type="x-p"/> II.
