Now to this complaint of their ignorance, which included a desire to be taught, Christ gives a full answer, <reference osisRef="John.14.6-John.14.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Thomas had enquired both whither he went and what was the way, and Christ answers both these enquiries and makes good what he had said, that they would have needed no answer if they had understood themselves aright; for they knew him, and he was the way; they knew the Father, and he was the end; and therefore, <hi type="italic">whither I go you know, and the way you know.</hi> Believe in God as the end, and in me as the way (<reference osisRef="John.14.1">v. 1</reference>), and you do all you should do. <div eID="gen28037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28038" type="x-p"/> (1.) He speaks of himself as the way, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">v. 6</reference>. Dost thou <hi type="italic">not know the way? I am the way,</hi> and I only, for <hi type="italic">no man comes to the Father but by me.</hi> Great things Christ here saith of himself, showing us, <div eID="gen28038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28039" type="x-p"/> [1.] The nature of his mediation: He is <hi type="italic">the way, the truth, and the life.</hi> <div eID="gen28039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Let us consider these first distinctly. 1. Christ is <hi type="italic">the way, the highway</hi> spoken of, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. Christ was his own way, for by <hi type="italic">his own blood he entered into the holy place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb. ix. 12</reference>), and he is our way, for we enter by him. By his doctrine and example he teaches us our duty, by his merit and intercession he procures our happiness, and so he is the way. In him God and man meet, and are brought together. We could not get to the tree of life in the way of innocency; but Christ is another way to it. By Christ, as the way an intercourse is settled and kept up between heaven and earth; the angels of God ascend and descend; our prayers go to God, and his blessings come to us by him; this is <hi type="italic">the way that leads to rest, the good old way.</hi> The disciples followed him, and Christ tells them that they followed the road, and, while they continued following him, they would never be out of their way. 2. He is <hi type="italic">the truth.</hi> (1.) As truth is opposed to figure and shadow. Christ is the substance of all the Old-Testament types, which are therefore said to be <hi type="italic">figures of the true,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>. Christ is <hi type="italic">the true manna</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">ch. vi. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">the true tabernacle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">Heb. viii. 2</reference>. (2.) As truth is opposed to falsehood and error; the doctrine of Christ is true doctrine. When we enquire for truth, we need learn no more than <hi type="italic">the truth as it is in Jesus.</hi> (3.) As truth is opposed to fallacy and deceit; he is true to all that trust in him, as true as truth itself, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2 Cor. i. 20</reference>. 3. He is <hi type="italic">the life;</hi> for we are <hi type="italic">alive unto God</hi> only in and <hi type="italic">through Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.11">Rom. vi. 11</reference>. Christ formed in us is that to our souls which our souls are to our bodies. Christ is <hi type="italic">the resurrection and the life.</hi> <div eID="gen28040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28041" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Let us consider these jointly, and with reference to each other. Christ is <hi type="italic">the way, the truth, and the life;</hi> that is, 1. He is the beginning, the middle, and the end. In him we must set out, go on, and finish. As <hi type="italic">the truth,</hi> he is the guide of our way; as <hi type="italic">the life,</hi> he is the end of it. 2. He is <hi type="italic">the true and living way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.20">Heb. x. 20</reference>); there are <hi type="italic">truth and life</hi> in the way, as well as at the end of it. 3. He is <hi type="italic">the true way to life,</hi> the only true way; other ways may seem right, but the end of them is <hi type="italic">the way of death.</hi> <div eID="gen28041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28042" type="x-p"/> [2.] The necessity of his mediation: <hi type="italic">No man cometh to the Father but by me.</hi> Fallen man must come to God as a Judge, but cannot come to him as a Father, otherwise than by Christ as Mediator. We cannot perform the duty of coming to God, by repentance and the acts of worship, without the Spirit and grace of Christ, nor obtain the happiness of coming to God as our Father without his merit and righteousness; he is the <hi type="italic">high priest of our profession,</hi> our advocate. <div eID="gen28042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28043" type="x-p"/> (2.) He speaks of his Father as the end (<reference osisRef="John.14.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you had known me</hi> aright, <hi type="italic">you would have known my Father also; and henceforth,</hi> by the glory you have seen in me and the doctrine you have heard from me, <hi type="italic">you know him and have seen him.</hi>" Here is, [1.] A tacit rebuke to them for their dulness and carelessness in not acquainting themselves with Jesus Christ, though they had been his constant followers and associates: <hi type="italic">If you had known me—.</hi> They knew him, and yet did not know him so well as they might and should have known him. They knew him to be the Christ, but did not follow on to know God in him. Christ had said to the Jews (<reference osisRef="John.8.19">ch. viii. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">If you had known me, you would have known my Father also;</hi> and here the same to his disciples; for it is hard to say which is more strange, the wilful ignorance of those that are enemies to the light, or the defects and mistakes of <hi type="italic">the children of light,</hi> that have had such opportunities of knowledge. If they had known Christ aright, they would have known that his kingdom is spiritual, and <hi type="italic">not of this world;</hi> that <hi type="italic">he came down from heaven,</hi> and therefore must return <hi type="italic">to heaven;</hi> and then they would have known his Father also, would have known whither he designed to go, when he said, <hi type="italic">I go to the Father,</hi> to a glory in the other world, not in this. If we knew Christianity better, we should better know natural religion. [2.] A favourable intimation that he was well satisfied concerning their sincerity, notwithstanding the weakness of their understanding: "<hi type="italic">And henceforth,</hi> from my giving you this hint, which will serve as a key to all the instructions I have given you hitherto, let me tell you, <hi type="italic">you know him, and have seen him,</hi> inasmuch as you know me, and have seen me;" for in the face of Christ we see the glory of God, as we see a father in his son that resembles him. Christ tells his disciples that they were not so ignorant as they seemed to be; for, though <hi type="italic">little children,</hi> yet they had known the Father, <reference osisRef="1John.2.13">1 John ii. 13</reference>. Note, Many of the disciples of Christ have more knowledge and more grace than they think they have, and Christ takes notice of, and is well pleased with, that good in them which they themselves are not aware of; for those that know God do not all at once know that they know him, <reference osisRef="1John.2.3">1 John ii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen28043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28044" type="x-p"/> II. Philip enquired concerning the Father (<reference osisRef="John.14.8">v. 8</reference>), and Christ answered him, <reference osisRef="John.14.9-John.14.11">v. 9-11</reference>, where observe, <div eID="gen28044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28045" type="x-p"/> 1. Philip's request for some extraordinary discovery of the Father. He was not so forward to speak as some others of them were, and yet, from an earnest desire of further light, he cries out, <hi type="italic">Show us the Father.</hi> Philip listened to what Christ said to Thomas, and fastened upon the last words, <hi type="italic">You have seen him.</hi> "Nay," says Philip, "that is what we want, that is what we would have: <hi type="italic">Show us the Father and it sufficeth us.</hi>" (1.) This supposes an earnest desire of acquaintance with God as a Father. The petition is, "<hi type="italic">Show us the Father;</hi> give us to know him in that relation to us;" and this he begs, not for himself only, but for the rest of the disciples. The plea is, <hi type="italic">It sufficeth us.</hi> He not only professes it himself, but will pass his word for his fellow-disciples. Grant us but one sight of the Father, and we have enough. Jansenius saith, "Though Philip did not mean it, yet the Holy Ghost, by his mouth, designed here to teach us that the satisfaction and happiness of a soul consist in the vision and fruition of God," <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Ps. xvi. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">xvii. 15</reference>. In the knowledge of God the understanding rests, and is at the summit of its ambition; in the knowledge of God as our Father the soul is satisfied; a sight of the Father is a heaven upon earth, fills us <hi type="italic">with joy unspeakable.</hi> (2.) As Philip speaks it here, it intimates that he was not satisfied with such a discovery of the Father as Christ thought fit to give them, but he would prescribe to him, and press upon him, something further and no less than some visible appearance of <hi type="italic">the glory of God,</hi> like that to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">Exod. xxxiii. 22</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">the elders of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.24.9-Exod.24.11">Exod. xxiv. 9-11</reference>. "Let us see the Father with our bodily eyes, as we see thee, <hi type="italic">and it sufficeth us;</hi> we will trouble thee with no more questions, <hi type="italic">Whither goest thou?</hi>" And so it manifests not only the weakness of his faith, but his ignorance of the gospel way of manifesting <hi type="italic">the Father,</hi> which is spiritual, and not sensible. Such a sight of God, he thinks, would <hi type="italic">suffice</hi> them, and yet those who did thus see him were not <hi type="italic">sufficed,</hi> but soon <hi type="italic">corrupted themselves, and made a graven image.</hi> Christ's institutions have provided better for the confirmation of our faith than our own inventions would. <div eID="gen28045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28046" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's reply, referring him to the discoveries already made of the Father, <reference osisRef="John.14.9-John.14.11">v. 9-11</reference>. <div eID="gen28046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28047" type="x-p"/> (1.) He refers him to what he had seen, <reference osisRef="John.14.9">v. 9</reference>. He upbraids him with his ignorance and inadvertency: "<hi type="italic">Have I been so long time with you,</hi> now above three years intimately conversant with you, <hi type="italic">and yet hast thou not known me, Philip?</hi> Now, <hi type="italic">he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?</hi> Wilt thou ask for that which thou hast already?" Now here, <div eID="gen28047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28048" type="x-p"/> [1.] He reproves him for two things: <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For not improving his acquaintance with Christ, as he might have done, to a clear and distinct knowledge of him: "<hi type="italic">Hast thou not known me, Philip,</hi> whom thou hast followed so long, and conversed with so much?" Philip, the first day he came to him, declared that he knew him to be the Messiah (<reference osisRef="John.1.45">ch. i. 45</reference>), and yet to this day did <hi type="italic">not know the Father</hi> in him. Many that have good knowledge in the scripture and divine things fall short of the attainments justly expected from them, for want of compounding the ideas they have, and going on to perfection. Many know Christ, who yet do not know what they might know of him, nor see what they should see in him. That which aggravated Philip's dulness was that he had so long an opportunity of improvement: <hi type="italic">I have been so long time with thee.</hi> Note, The longer we enjoy the means of knowledge and grace, the more inexcusable we are if we be found defective in grace and knowledge. Christ expects that our proficiency should be in some measure according to our standing, that we should not be always babes. Let us thus reason with ourselves: "Have I been so long a hearer of sermons, a student in the scripture, a scholar in the school of Christ, and yet so weak in <hi type="italic">the knowledge of Christ,</hi> and so unskilful in <hi type="italic">the word of righteousness?</hi>" <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He reproves him for his infirmity in the prayer made, <hi type="italic">Show us the Father.</hi> Note, Herein appears much of the weakness of Christ's disciples that they <hi type="italic">know not what to pray for as they ought</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom. viii. 26</reference>), but often <hi type="italic">ask amiss</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.3">Jam. iv. 3</reference>), for that which either is not promised or is already bestowed in the sense of the promise, as here. <div eID="gen28048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28049" type="x-p"/> [2.] He instructs him, and gives him a maxim which not only in general magnifies Christ and leads us to the knowledge of God in him, but justifies what Christ had said (<reference osisRef="John.14.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">You know the Father, and have seen him;</hi> and answered what Philip had asked, <hi type="italic">Show us the Father.</hi> Why, saith Christ, the difficulty is soon over, for <hi type="italic">he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. First,</hi> All that saw <hi type="italic">Christ in the flesh</hi> might <hi type="italic">have seen the Father</hi> in him, if Satan had not <hi type="italic">blinded their minds,</hi> and kept them from a sight of Christ, as <hi type="italic">the image of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. iv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> All that saw Christ by faith did <hi type="italic">see the Father</hi> in him, though they were not suddenly aware that they did so. In the light of Christ's doctrine they saw God as <hi type="italic">the father of lights;</hi> in the miracles they saw God <hi type="italic">as the God of power, the finger of God.</hi> The holiness of God shone in the spotless purity of Christ's life, and his grace in all the acts of grace he did. <div eID="gen28049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28050" type="x-p"/> (2.) He refers him to what he had reason to believe (<reference osisRef="John.14.10-John.14.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me,</hi> and therefore that in <hi type="italic">seeing me</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">seen the Father?</hi> Hast thou not believed this? If not, take my word for it, and believe it now." <div eID="gen28050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28051" type="x-p"/> [1.] See here what it is which we are to believe: <hi type="italic">That I am in the Father, and the Father in me;</hi> that is, as he had said (<reference osisRef="John.10.30">ch. x. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">I and my Father are one.</hi> He speaks of the Father and himself as two persons, and yet so one as never any two were or can be. In knowing Christ as <hi type="italic">God of God, light of light, very God of very God, begotten, not made,</hi> and as <hi type="italic">being of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made,</hi> we know the Father; and in seeing him thus we see the Father. In Christ we behold more of <hi type="italic">the glory of God</hi> than Moses did at Mount Horeb. <div eID="gen28051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28052" type="x-p"/> [2.] See here what inducements we have to believe this; and they are two:—We must believe it, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For his word's sake: <hi type="italic">The words that I speak to you, I speak not of myself.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.7.16">ch. vii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">My doctrine is not mine.</hi> What he said seemed to them careless as <hi type="italic">the word of man,</hi> speaking his own thought at his own pleasure; but really it was the wisdom of God that indited it and the will of God that enforced it. <hi type="italic">He spoke not of himself</hi> only, but the mind of God according to the eternal counsels. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> For his works' sake: <hi type="italic">The Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth them;</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">believe me for their sake.</hi> Observe, 1. The Father is said to <hi type="italic">dwell</hi> in him <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho en emoi menon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he abideth in me,</hi> by the inseparable union of the divine and human nature: never had God such a temple to dwell in on earth as <hi type="italic">the body of the Lord Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.2.21">ch. ii. 21</reference>. Here was the true Shechinah, of which that in the tabernacle was but a type. <hi type="italic">The fulness of the Godhead dwelt in him bodily,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col. ii. 9</reference>. The Father so dwells in Christ that in him he may <hi type="italic">be found,</hi> as a man where he dwells. <hi type="italic">Seek ye the Lord, seek</hi> him in Christ, and <hi type="italic">he will be found,</hi> for in him he dwells. 2. <hi type="italic">He doeth the works.</hi> Many words of power, and works of mercy, Christ did, and the Father did them in him; and the work of redemption in general was God's own work. 3. We are bound to believe this, <hi type="italic">for the very works' sake.</hi> As we are to believe the being and perfections of God for the sake of the works of creation, which declare his glory; so we are to believe the revelation of God to man in Jesus Christ for the sake of the works of the Redeemer, those mighty works which, by showing forth themselves (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.2">Matt. xiv. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Show forth him, and God in him.</hi> Note, Christ's miracles are proofs of his divine mission, not only for the conviction of infidels, but for the confirmation of the faith of his own disciples, <reference osisRef="John.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.36">v. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.37">x. 37</reference>.

<div eID="gen28052" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28053" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater <hi type="italic">works</hi> than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father. 13 And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. <hi type="super">14</hi> If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen28053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28054" type="x-p"/> The disciples, as they were full of grief to think of parting with their Master, so they were full of care what would become of themselves when he was gone; while he was with them, he was a support to them, kept them in countenance, kept them in heart; but, if he leave them, they will be <hi type="italic">as sheep having no shepherd,</hi> an easy prey to those who seek to run them down. Now, to silence these fears, Christ here assures them that they should be clothed with powers sufficient to bear them out. As Christ has <hi type="italic">all power,</hi> they, in his name, should have great <hi type="italic">power, both in heaven and in earth.</hi> <div eID="gen28054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28055" type="x-p"/> I. Great power on earth (<reference osisRef="John.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that believeth on me</hi> (as I know you do), <hi type="italic">the works that I do shall he do also.</hi> This does not weaken the argument Christ had taken from his works, to prove himself one with the Father (that others should do as <hi type="italic">great works</hi>), but rather strengthens it; for the miracles which the apostles wrought were <hi type="italic">wrought in his name,</hi> and <hi type="italic">by faith in him;</hi> and this magnifies his power more than any thing, that he not only wrought miracles himself, but gave power to others to do so too. <div eID="gen28055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28056" type="x-p"/> 1. Two things he assures them of:— <div eID="gen28056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28057" type="x-p"/> (1.) That they should be enabled to do such works as he had done, and that they should have a more ample power for the doing of them than they had had when he first sent them forth, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.8">Matt. x. 8</reference>. Did Christ <hi type="italic">heal the sick, cleanse the leper, raise the dead?</hi> So should they. Did he convince and convert sinners, and draw multitudes to him? So should they. Though he should depart, the work should not cease, nor fall to the ground, but should be carried on as vigorously and successfully as ever; and it is still in the doing. <div eID="gen28057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28058" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they should do <hi type="italic">greater works than these.</hi> [1.] In the kingdom of nature they should work greater miracles. No miracle is little, but some to our apprehension seem greater than others. Christ had healed with the hem of his garment, but Peter with his shadow (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.15">Acts v. 15</reference>), Paul by the handkerchief that had touched him, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.12">Acts xix. 12</reference>. Christ wrought miracles for two or three years in one country, but his followers wrought miracles in his name for many ages in divers countries. <hi type="italic">You shall do greater works,</hi> if there be occasion, for the glory of God. <hi type="italic">The prayer of faith,</hi> if at any time it had been necessary, would have <hi type="italic">removed mountains.</hi> [2.] In the kingdom of grace. They should obtain greater victories by the gospel than had been obtained while Christ was upon earth. The truth is, the captivating of so great a part of the world to Christ, under such outward disadvantages, was the miracle of all. I think this refers especially to <hi type="italic">the gift of tongues;</hi> this was the immediate effect of the <hi type="italic">pouring out of the Spirit,</hi> which was a constant miracle upon the mind, in which words are framed, and which was made to serve so glorious an intention as that of spreading the gospel to all nations <hi type="italic">in their own language.</hi> This was a greater <hi type="italic">sign to them that believed not</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1 Cor. xiv. 22</reference>), and more powerful for their conviction, than any other miracle whatever. <div eID="gen28058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28059" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason Christ gives for this is, <hi type="italic">Because I go unto my Father,</hi> (1.) "<hi type="italic">Because I go,</hi> it will be requisite that you should have such a power, lest the work suffer damage by my absence." (2.) "<hi type="italic">Because I go to the Father,</hi> I shall be in a capacity to furnish you with such a power, for <hi type="italic">I go to the Father, to send the Comforter,</hi> from whom <hi type="italic">you shall receive power,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Acts i. 8</reference>. The wonderful works which they did in Christ's name were part of the glories of his exalted state, <hi type="italic">when he ascended on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen28059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28060" type="x-p"/> II. Great <hi type="italic">power in heaven: "Whatsoever you shall ask, that will I do</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.14.13-John.14.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), as Israel, who was a prince with God. Therefore you shall do such mighty works, because you have such an interest in me, and I in <hi type="italic">my Father.</hi>" Observe, <div eID="gen28060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28061" type="x-p"/> 1. In what way they were to keep up communion with him, and derive power from him, when he was gone to the Father—by prayer. When dear friends are to be removed to a distance from each other, they provide for the settling of a correspondence; thus, when Christ was going to his Father, he tells his disciples how they might write to him upon every occasion, and send their epistles by a safe and ready way of conveyance, without danger of miscarrying, or lying by the way: "Let me hear from you by prayer, <hi type="italic">the prayer of faith,</hi> and you shall hear from me by the Spirit." This was the old way of intercourse with Heaven, ever since <hi type="italic">men began to call upon the name of the Lord;</hi> but Christ by his death has laid it more open, and it is still open to us. Here is, (1.) Humility prescribed: <hi type="italic">You shall ask.</hi> Though they had quitted all for Christ, they could demand nothing of him as a debt, but must be humble supplicants, beg or starve, beg or perish. (2.) Liberty allowed: "Ask any thing, any thing that is good and proper for you; any thing, provided you know what you ask, you may ask; you may ask for assistance in your work, for a mouth and wisdom, for preservation out of the hands of your enemies, for power to work miracles when there is occasion, for the success of the ministry in the conversion of souls; ask to be informed, directed, vindicated." Occasions vary, but they shall be welcome to the throne of grace upon every occasion. <div eID="gen28061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28062" type="x-p"/> 2. In what name they were to present their petitions: <hi type="italic">Ask in my name.</hi> To ask in Christ's name is, (1.) To plead his merit and intercession, and to depend upon that plea. The Old-Testament saints had an eye to this when they prayed <hi type="italic">for the Lord's sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.17">Dan. ix. 17</reference>), and <hi type="italic">for the sake of the anointed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.9">Ps. lxxxiv. 9</reference>), but Christ's mediation is brought to a clearer light by the gospel, and so we are enabled more expressly to <hi type="italic">ask in his name.</hi> When Christ dictated the Lord's prayer, this was not inserted, because they did not then so fully understand this matter as they did afterwards, when the Spirit was poured out. If we ask <hi type="italic">in our own name,</hi> we cannot expect to speed, for, being strangers, we have <hi type="italic">no name</hi> in heaven; being sinners, we have an <hi type="italic">ill name</hi> there; but Christ's is a good name, well known in heaven, and very precious. (2.) It is to aim at his glory and to seek this as our highest end in all our prayers. <div eID="gen28062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28063" type="x-p"/> 3. What success they should have in their prayers: "What you ask, <hi type="italic">that will I do,</hi>" <reference osisRef="John.14.13">v. 13</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="John.14.14">v. 14</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I will do it.</hi> You may be sure I will: not only it shall be done, I will see it done, or give orders for the doing of it, but <hi type="italic">I will do it;</hi>" for he has not only the interest of an intercessor, but the power of a sovereign prince, who <hi type="italic">sits at the right hand of God,</hi> the hand of action, and has the doing of all in the kingdom of God. By faith in his name we may have what we will for the asking. <div eID="gen28063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28064" type="x-p"/> 4. For what reason their prayers should speed so well: <hi type="italic">That the Father may be glorified in the Son.</hi> That is, (1.) This they ought to aim at, and have their eye upon, in asking. In this all our desires and prayers should meet as in their centre; to this they must all be directed, that God in Christ may be honoured by our services, and in our salvation. <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name</hi> is an answered prayer, and is put first, because, if the heart be sincere in this, it does in a manner <hi type="italic">consecrate</hi> all the other petitions. (2.) This Christ will aim at in granting, and for the sake of this will do what they ask, that hereby the glory of the Father in the Son may be manifested. The wisdom, power, and goodness of God were magnified in the Redeemer when by a power derived from him, and exerted in his name and for his service, his apostles and ministers were enabled to do such great things, both in the proofs of their doctrine and in the successes of it.

<div eID="gen28064" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28065" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> If ye love me, keep my commandments. <hi type="super">16</hi> And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; 17 <hi type="italic">Even</hi> the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. <div eID="gen28065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28066" type="x-p"/> Christ not only proposes such things to them as were the matter of their comfort, but here promises to send the Spirit, whose office it should be to be their Comforter, to <hi type="italic">impress</hi> these things upon them. <div eID="gen28066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28067" type="x-p"/> I. He premises to this a memento of duty (<reference osisRef="John.14.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">If you love me, keep my commandments.</hi> Keeping the commandments of Christ is here put for the practice of godliness in general, and for the faithful and diligent discharge of their office as apostles in particular. Now observe, 1. When Christ is comforting them, he bids them <hi type="italic">keep his commandments;</hi> for we must not expect comfort but in the way of duty. The same word (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parakaleo</hi></hi>) signifies both to exhort and to comfort. 2. When they were in care what they should do, now that their Master was leaving them, and what would become of them now, he bids them <hi type="italic">keep his commandments,</hi> and then nothing could come amiss to them. In difficult times our care concerning the events of the day should be swallowed up in a care concerning the duty of the day. 3. When they were showing their love to Christ by their grieving to think of his departure, and the sorrow which filled their hearts upon the foresight of that, he bids them, if they would show their love to him, do it, not by these weak and feminine passions, but by their conscientious care to perform their trust, and by a universal obedience to his commands; this is better than sacrifice, better than tears. <hi type="italic">Lovest thou me? Feed my lambs.</hi> 4. When Christ has given them precious promises, of the answer of their prayers and the coming of the Comforter, he lays down this as a limitation of the promises, "Provided you keep my commandments, from a principle of love to me." Christ will not be an advocate for any but those that will be ruled and advised by him as their counsel. Follow the conduct of the Spirit, and you shall have the comfort of the Spirit. <div eID="gen28067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28068" type="x-p"/> II. He promises this great and unspeakable blessing to them, <reference osisRef="John.14.16-John.14.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. <div eID="gen28068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28069" type="x-p"/> 1. It is promised that they shall have <hi type="italic">another comforter.</hi> This is the great New-Testament promise (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.4">Acts i. 4</reference>), as that of the Messiah was of the Old Testament; a promise adapted to the present distress of the disciples, who were in sorrow, and needed a comforter. Observe here, <div eID="gen28069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28070" type="x-p"/> (1.) The blessing promised: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">allon parakleton</hi></hi>. The word is used only here in these discourses of Christ's, and <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1 John ii. 1</reference>, where we translate it an <hi type="italic">advocate.</hi> The Rhemists, and Dr. Hammond, are for retaining the <hi type="italic">Greek</hi> word <hi type="italic">Paraclete;</hi> we read, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.31">Acts ix. 31</reference>, of the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paraklesis tou hagiou pneumatos</hi></hi>, the <hi type="italic">comfort of the Holy Ghost,</hi> including his whole office as a paraclete. [1.] You shall have another <hi type="italic">advocate.</hi> The office of the Spirit was to be Christ's advocate with them and others, to plead his cause, and take care of his concerns, on earth; to be <hi type="italic">vicarius Christi—Christ's Vicar,</hi> as one of the ancients call him; and to be their advocate with their opposers. When Christ was with them he spoke for them as there was occasion; but now that he is leaving them they shall not be run down, the Spirit of the Father shall speak in them, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19-Matt.10.20">Matt. x. 19, 20</reference>. And the cause cannot miscarry that is pleaded by such an advocate. [2.] You shall have another <hi type="italic">master</hi> or <hi type="italic">teacher,</hi> another <hi type="italic">exhorter.</hi> While they had Christ with them he excited and exhorted them to their duty; but now that he is going he leaves one with them that shall do this as effectually, though silently. Jansenius thinks the most proper word to render it by is a <hi type="italic">patron,</hi> one that shall both instruct and protect you. [3.] Another <hi type="italic">comforter.</hi> Christ was expected as the consolation of Israel. One of the names of the Messiah among the Jews was <hi type="italic">Menahem—the Comforter.</hi> The Targum calls the days of the Messiah <hi type="italic">the years of consolation.</hi> Christ comforted his disciples when he was with them, and now that he was leaving them in their greatest need he promises them <hi type="italic">another.</hi> <div eID="gen28070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28071" type="x-p"/> (2.) The giver of this blessing: <hi type="italic">The Father</hi> shall give him, <hi type="italic">my Father</hi> and <hi type="italic">your Father;</hi> it includes both. The same that gave the Son to be our Saviour will give his Spirit to be our comforter, pursuant to the same design. The Son is said to send the Comforter (<reference osisRef="John.15.26">ch. xv. 26</reference>), but the Father is the prime agent. <div eID="gen28071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28072" type="x-p"/> (3.) How this blessing is procured—by the intercession of the Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">I will pray the Father.</hi> He said (<reference osisRef="John.14.14">v. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">I will do it;</hi> here he saith, <hi type="italic">I will pray for it,</hi> to show not only that he is both God and man, but that he is both king and priest. As priest he is ordained for men to make intercession, as king he is authorized by the Father to execute judgment. When Christ saith, <hi type="italic">I will pray the Father,</hi> it does not suppose that the Father is unwilling, or must be importuned to it, but only that the gift of the Spirit is a fruit of Christ's mediation, purchased by his merit, and taken out by his intercession. <div eID="gen28072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28073" type="x-p"/> (4.) The continuance of this blessing: <hi type="italic">That he may abide with you for ever.</hi> That is, [1.] "<hi type="italic">With you,</hi> as long as you live. You shall never know the want of a comforter, nor lament his departure, as you are now lamenting mine." Note, It should support us under the loss of those comforts which were designed us for a time that there are everlasting consolations provided for us. It was not expedient that Christ should be with them for ever, for they who were designed for public service, must not always live a college-life; they must disperse, and therefore a comforter that would be with them all, in all places alike, wheresoever dispersed and howsoever distressed, was alone fit to be with them for ever. [2.] "With your successors, when you are gone, to the end of time; your successors in Christianity, in the ministry." [3.] If we take <hi type="italic">for ever</hi> in its utmost extent, the promise will be accomplished in those consolations of God which will be the eternal joy of all the saints, <hi type="italic">pleasures for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen28073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28074" type="x-p"/> 2. This comforter is the <hi type="italic">Spirit of truth, whom you know,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.16-John.14.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. They might think it impossible to have a comforter equivalent to him who is the Son of God: "Yea," saith Christ, "you shall have the Spirit of God, who is equal in power and glory with the Son." <div eID="gen28074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28075" type="x-p"/> (1.) The comforter promised is <hi type="italic">the Spirit,</hi> one who should do his work in a spiritual way and manner, inwardly and invisibly, by working on men's spirits. <div eID="gen28075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28076" type="x-p"/> (2.) "He is the <hi type="italic">Spirit of truth.</hi>" He will be true to you, and to his undertaking for you, which he will perform to the utmost. He will <hi type="italic">teach you the truth,</hi> will enlighten your minds with the knowledge of it, will strengthen and confirm your belief of it, and will increase your love to it. The Gentiles by their idolatries, and the Jews by their traditions, were led into gross errors and mistakes; but the Spirit of truth shall not only <hi type="italic">lead you into all truth,</hi> but others by your ministry. Christ is the truth, and he is the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit that he was anointed with. <div eID="gen28076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28077" type="x-p"/> (3.) He is one <hi type="italic">whom the world cannot receive;</hi> but <hi type="italic">you know him. Therefore he abideth with you.</hi> [1.] The disciples of Christ are here distinguished from the world, for they are chosen and called out of the world that lies in wickedness; they are the children and heirs of another world, not of this. [2.] It is the misery of those that are invincibly devoted to the world that they <hi type="italic">cannot receive</hi> the Spirit of truth. The spirit <hi type="italic">of the world</hi> and <hi type="italic">of God</hi> are spoken of as directly contrary the one to the other (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1 Cor. ii. 12</reference>); for where the spirit of the world has the ascendant, the Spirit of God is excluded. Even the <hi type="italic">princes of this world,</hi> though, as princes, they had advantages of knowledge, yet, as princes of this world, they laboured under invincible prejudices, so that they knew not <hi type="italic">the things of the Spirit of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. [3.] Therefore men <hi type="italic">cannot receive the Spirit of truth</hi> because they <hi type="italic">see him not, neither know him.</hi> The comforts of the Spirit are <hi type="italic">foolishness to them,</hi> as much as ever the cross of Christ was, and the great things of the gospel, like those of the law, are counted as a strange thing. These are judgments far above out of their sight. Speak to the children of this world of the operations of the Spirit, and you are as a barbarian to them. [4.] The best knowledge of the Spirit of truth is that which is got by experience: <hi type="italic">You know him, for he dwelleth with you.</hi> Christ had dwelt with them, and by their acquaintance with him they could not but know <hi type="italic">the Spirit of truth.</hi> They had themselves been endued with the Spirit in some measure. What enabled them to leave all to follow Christ, and to continue with him in his temptations? What enabled them to preach the gospel, and work miracles, but the Spirit dwelling in them? The experiences of the saints are the explications of the promises; paradoxes to others are axioms to them. [5.] Those that have an experimental acquaintance with the Spirit have a comfortable assurance of his continuance: He <hi type="italic">dwelleth with you, and shall be in you,</hi> for the blessed Spirit doth not use to shift his lodging. Those that know him know how to value him, invite him and bid him welcome; and therefore he shall be in them, as the light in the air, as the sap in the tree, as the soul in the body. Their communion with him shall be intimate, and their union with him inseparable. [6.] The gift of the Holy Ghost is a peculiar gift, bestowed upon the disciples of Christ in a distinguishing way—them, and not the world; it is to them <hi type="italic">hidden manna,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">white stone.</hi> No comforts comparable to those which make no show, make no noise. This is the favour God bears to his chosen; it is the <hi type="italic">heritage of those that fear his name.</hi>

<div eID="gen28077" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28078" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you. <hi type="super">19</hi> Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also. <hi type="super">20</hi> At that day ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you. <hi type="super">21</hi> He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. <hi type="super">22</hi> Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world? <hi type="super">23</hi> Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him. <hi type="super">24</hi> He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father's which sent me. <div eID="gen28078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28079" type="x-p"/> When friends are parting, it is a common request they make to each other, "Pray let us hear from you as often as you can:" this Christ engaged to his disciples, that out of sight they should not be out of mind. <div eID="gen28079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28080" type="x-p"/> I. He promises that he would continue his care of them (<reference osisRef="John.14.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will not leave you orphans,</hi> or <hi type="italic">fatherless;</hi> for, though I leave you, yet I leave you this comfort, <hi type="italic">I will come to you.</hi>" His departure from them was that which grieved them; but it was not so bad as they apprehended, for it was neither total nor final. 1. Not total. "Though I leave you without my bodily presence, yet I do not leave you without comfort." Though children, and left <hi type="italic">little,</hi> yet they had received the adoption of sons, and his Father would be their Father, with whom those who otherwise would be fatherless find mercy. Note, The case of true believers, though sometimes it may be sorrowful, is never comfortless, because they are never orphans: for God is their Father, who is an <hi type="italic">everlasting Father.</hi> 2. Not final: <hi type="italic">I will come to you,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">erchomai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I do come;</hi> that is, (1.) "I will come speedily to you at my resurrection, I will not be long away, but will be with you again in a little time." He had often said, <hi type="italic">The third day I will rise again.</hi> (2.) "I will be coming daily to you in my Spirit;" in the tokens of his love, and visits of his grace, he is still coming. (3.) "I will come certainly at the end of time; surely I will come quickly to introduce you into the joy of your Lord." Note, The consideration of Christ's coming to us saves us from being comfortless in his removals from us; for, if he <hi type="italic">depart for a season,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">that we may receive him for ever.</hi> Let this moderate our grief, <hi type="italic">The Lord is at hand.</hi> <div eID="gen28080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28081" type="x-p"/> II. He promises that they should continue their acquaintance with him and interest in him (<reference osisRef="John.14.19-John.14.20">v. 19, 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet a little while, and the world sees me no more,</hi> that is, Now I am no more in the world. After his death, <hi type="italic">the world saw him no more,</hi> for, though he rose to life, he never <hi type="italic">showed himself to all the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.41">Acts x. 41</reference>. The malignant world thought they had seen enough of him, and <hi type="italic">cried, Away with him; crucify him;</hi> and so shall their doom be; they shall see him no more. Those only that see Christ with an eye of faith shall see him for ever. The world sees him no more till his second coming; but his disciples have communion with him in his absence. <div eID="gen28081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28082" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">You see me,</hi> and shall continue to see me, when <hi type="italic">the world sees me no more.</hi> They saw him with their bodily eyes after his resurrection, for he showed himself to them <hi type="italic">by many infallible proofs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Acts i. 8</reference>. And <hi type="italic">then were the disciples glad when they saw the Lord.</hi> They saw him with an eye of faith after his ascension, sitting at God's right hand, as Lord of all; saw that in him which the world saw not. <div eID="gen28082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28083" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also.</hi> That which grieved them was, that their Master was dying, and they counted upon nothing else but to die with him. No, saith Christ, (1.) <hi type="italic">I live;</hi> this the great God glories in, <hi type="italic">I live,</hi> saith the Lord, and Christ saith the same; not only, I shall live, as he saith of them, but, I do live; for he has <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lives for evermore.</hi> We are not comfortless, while <hi type="italic">we know that our Redeemer lives.</hi> (2.) Therefore <hi type="italic">you shall live also.</hi> Note, The life of Christians is bound up in the life of Christ; as sure and as long as he lives, those that by faith are united to him shall live also; they shall live spiritually, a divine life in communion with God. This life is hid with Christ; if the head and root live, the members and branches live also. They shall <hi type="italic">live eternally;</hi> their bodies shall rise in the virtue of Christ's resurrection; it will be well with them in the world to come. It cannot but be well with all that are his, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen28083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28084" type="x-p"/> 3. You shall have the assurance of this (<reference osisRef="John.14.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">At that day,</hi> when I am glorified, when the Spirit is poured out, <hi type="italic">you shall know</hi> more clearly and certainly than you do now that <hi type="italic">I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.</hi> (1.) These glorious mysteries will be fully known in heaven; <hi type="italic">At that day,</hi> when I shall receive you to myself, you shall know perfectly that which now you <hi type="italic">see through a glass darkly.</hi> Now it appears not <hi type="italic">what we shall be,</hi> but then it will appear what we were. (2.) They were more fully known after the pouring out of the Spirit upon the apostles; at that day divine light should shine, and their eyes should see more clearly, their knowledge should greatly advance and increase then, would become more extensive and more distinct, and like the blind man's at the second touch of Christ's hand, who at first only <hi type="italic">saw men as trees walking.</hi> (3.) They are known by all that receive the Spirit of truth, to their abundant satisfaction, for in the knowledge of this is founded their <hi type="italic">fellowship with the Father</hi> and <hi type="italic">his Son Jesus Christ.</hi> They know, [1.] That <hi type="italic">Christ is in the Father,</hi> is one with the Father, by their experience of what he has wrought for them and in them; they find what an admirable consent and harmony there is between Christianity and natural religion, that that is grafted into this, and so they know that Christ <hi type="italic">is in the Father.</hi> [2.] That Christ is in them; experienced Christians know by the Spirit that Christ abides in them, <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">1 John iii. 24</reference>. [3.] That they are in Christ, for the relation is mutual, and equally near on both sides, Christ in them and they in Christ, which speaks an intimate and inseparable union; in the virtue of which it is that <hi type="italic">because he lives they shall live also.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Union with Christ is the life of believers; and their relation to him, and to God through him, is their felicity. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The knowledge of this union is their unspeakable joy and satisfaction; they were now in Christ, and he in them, but he speaks of it as a further act of grace that they should know it, and have the comfort of it. An interest in Christ and the knowledge of it are sometimes separated. <div eID="gen28084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28085" type="x-p"/> III. He promises that he would love them, and manifest himself to them, <reference osisRef="John.14.21-John.14.24">v. 21-24</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen28085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28086" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they are whom Christ will look upon, and accept, as lovers of him; those that <hi type="italic">have his commandments, and keep them.</hi> By this Christ shows that the kind things he here said to his disciples were intended not for those only that were <hi type="italic">now</hi> his <hi type="italic">followers,</hi> but for all that should <hi type="italic">believe in him through their word.</hi> Here is, (1.) The duty of those who claim the dignity of being disciples. Having Christ's commandments, we must keep them; as Christians in name and profession we have Christ's commandments, we have them sounding in our ears, written before our eyes, we have the knowledge of them; but this is not enough; would we approve ourselves Christians indeed, we must keep them. Having them in our heads, we must keep them in our hearts and lives. (2.) The dignity of those that do the duty of disciples. They are looked upon by Christ to be such as love him. Not those that have the greatest wit and know how to talk for him, but those that <hi type="italic">keep his commandments.</hi> Note, The surest evidence of our love to Christ is obedience to the laws of Christ. Such is the love of a subject to his sovereign, a dutiful, respectful, obediential love, a conformity to his will, and satisfaction in his wisdom. <div eID="gen28086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28087" type="x-p"/> 2. What returns he will make to them for their love; rich returns; there is no love lost upon Christ. (1.) They shall have the Father's love: <hi type="italic">He that loveth me shall be loved of my Father.</hi> We could not love God if he did not first, out of his good-will to us, give us his grace to love him; but there is a love of complacency promised to those that do love God, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Prov. viii. 17</reference>. He loves them, and lets them know that he loves them, smiles upon them, and embraces them. God so loves the Son as to love all those that love him. (2.) They shall have Christ's love: <hi type="italic">And I will love him,</hi> as God-man, as Mediator. God will love him as a Father, and I will love him as a brother, an elder brother. The Creator will love him, and be the felicity of his being; the Redeemer will love him, and be the protector of his well-being. In the nature of God, nothing shines more brightly than this, that <hi type="italic">God is love.</hi> And in the undertaking of Christ nothing appears more glorious than this, that <hi type="italic">he loved us.</hi> Now both these loves are the crown and comfort, the <hi type="italic">grace and glory,</hi> which shall be to all those that <hi type="italic">love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity.</hi> Christ was now leaving his disciples, but promises to continue his love to them; for he not only retains a kindness for believers, though absent, but is doing them kindness while absent, for he bears them on his heart, and ever lives interceding for them. (3.) They shall have the comfort of that love: <hi type="italic">I will manifest myself to him.</hi> Some understand it of Christ's showing himself alive to his disciples after his resurrection; but, being promised to all that <hi type="italic">love him and keep his commandments,</hi> it must be construed so as to extend to them. There is a spiritual manifestation of Christ and his love made to all believers. When he enlightens their minds to know his love, and the dimensions of it (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.18-Eph.3.19">Eph. iii. 18, 19</reference>), enlivens their graces, and draws them into exercise, and thus enlarges their comforts in himself—when he clears up the evidences of their interest in him, and gives them tokens of his love, experience of his tenderness, and earnests of his kingdom and glory,—then he manifests himself to them; and Christ is manifested to none but those to whom he is pleased to manifest himself. <div eID="gen28087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28088" type="x-p"/> 3. What occurred upon Christ's making this promise. <div eID="gen28088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28089" type="x-p"/> (1.) One of the disciples expresses his wonder and surprise at it, <reference osisRef="John.14.22">v. 22</reference>. Observe, [1.] Who it was that said this—<hi type="italic">Judas, not Iscariot.</hi> Judah, or Judas, was a famous name; the most famous tribe in Israel was that of Judah; two of Christ's disciples were of that name: one of them was the traitor, the other was the brother of James (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.16">Luke vi. 16</reference>), one of those that were akin to Christ, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.55">Matt. xiii. 55</reference>. He is called <hi type="italic">Lebbeus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thaddeus,</hi> was the penman of the last of the epistles, which in our translation, for distinction's sake, we call <hi type="italic">the epistle of Jude.</hi> This was he that spoke here. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There was a very good man, and a very bad man, called by the same name; for names commend us not to God, nor do they make men worse. Judas the apostle was never the worse, nor Judas the apostate ever the better, for being namesakes. But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The evangelist carefully distinguishes between them; when he speaks of this pious Judas, he adds, <hi type="italic">not Iscariot.</hi> Take heed of mistaking; let us not confound the precious and the vile. [2.] What he said—<hi type="italic">Lord how is it?</hi> which intimates either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the weakness of his understanding. So some take it. He expected the temporal kingdom of the Messiah, that it should appear in external pomp and power, such as all the world would wonder after. "How, then," thinks he, "should it be confined to us only?" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ti gegonen</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">what is the matter</hi> now, that thou wilt not show thyself openly as is expected, that <hi type="italic">the Gentiles may come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising?</hi>" Note, We create difficulties to ourselves by mistaking the nature of Christ's kingdom, as if it were of this world. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> as expressing the strength of his affections, and the humble and thankful sense he had of Christ's distinguishing favours to them: <hi type="italic">Lord, how is it?</hi> He is amazed at the condescensions of divine grace, as David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>. What is there in us to deserve so great a favour? Note, 1. Christ's manifesting himself to his disciples is done in a distinguishing way-to them, and <hi type="italic">not to the world</hi> that <hi type="italic">sits in darkness;</hi> to the <hi type="italic">base,</hi> and not to the <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> and <hi type="italic">noble;</hi> to <hi type="italic">babes,</hi> and not to the <hi type="italic">wise</hi> and <hi type="italic">prudent.</hi> Distinguishing favours are very obliging; considering who are passed by, and who are pitched upon. 2. It is justly <hi type="italic">marvellous in our eyes;</hi> for it is unaccountable, and must be resolved into free and sovereign grace. <hi type="italic">Even so, Father, because it seemed good unto thee.</hi> <div eID="gen28089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28090" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ, in answer hereto, explains and confirms what he had said, <reference osisRef="John.14.23-John.14.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. He overlooks what infirmity there was in what Judas spoke, and goes on with his comforts. <div eID="gen28090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28091" type="x-p"/> [1.] He further explains the condition of the promise, which was loving him, and keeping his commandments. And, as to this, he shows what an inseparable connection there is between love and obedience; love is the root, obedience is the fruit. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Where a sincere love to Christ is in the heart, there will be obedience: "<hi type="italic">If a man love me</hi> indeed, that love will be such a commanding constraining principle in him, that, no question, he will <hi type="italic">keep my words.</hi>" Where there is true love to Christ there is a value for his favour, a veneration for his authority, and an entire surrender of the whole man to his direction and government. Where love is, duty follows of course, is easy and natural, and flows from a principle of gratitude. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> On the other hand, where there is no true love to Christ there will be no care to obey him: <hi type="italic">He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.24">v. 24</reference>. This comes in here as a discovery of those that <hi type="italic">do not love Christ;</hi> whatever they pretend, certainly those do not love him that believe not his truths, and obey not his laws, to whom Christ's sayings are but as idle tales, which he heeds not, or hard sayings, which he likes not. It is also a reason why Christ will not manifest himself to the world that doth not <hi type="italic">love him,</hi> because they put this affront upon him, not to <hi type="italic">keep his sayings;</hi> why should Christ be familiar with those that will be strange to him? <div eID="gen28091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28092" type="x-p"/> [2.] He further explains the promise (<reference osisRef="John.14.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">If a man thus love me, I will manifest myself to him. First, My Father will love him;</hi> this he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.14.21">v. 21</reference>), and here repeats it for the confirming of our faith; because it is hard to imagine that the great god should make those the objects of his love that had made themselves <hi type="italic">vessels of his wrath.</hi> Jude wondered that Christ should <hi type="italic">manifest himself to them;</hi> but this answers it, "If my Father love you, why should not I be free with you?" <hi type="italic">Secondly, We will come unto him, and make our abode with him.</hi> This explains the meaning of Christ's manifesting himself to him, and magnifies the favour. 1. Not only,<hi type="italic">I will,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">We will, I and the Father,</hi> who, in this, <hi type="italic">are one.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.14.9">v. 9</reference>. The light and love of God are communicated to man in the light and love of the Redeemer, so that wherever Christ is formed the image of God is stamped. 2. Not only, "<hi type="italic">I will show myself to him</hi> at a distance," but, "<hi type="italic">We will come to him,</hi> to be near him, to be with him," such are the powerful influences of divine graces and comforts upon the souls of those that love Christ in sincerity. 3. Not only, "I will give him a transient view of me, or make him a short and running visit," but, <hi type="italic">We will take up our abode with him</hi> which denotes complacency in him and constancy to him. God will not only love obedient believers, but he will take a pleasure in loving them, will rest in love to them, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zeph. iii. 17</reference>. He will be with them as at his home. <div eID="gen28092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28093" type="x-p"/> [3.] He gives a good reason both to bind us to observe the condition and encourage us to depend upon the promise. <hi type="italic">The word which you hear is not mine, but his that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.24">v. 24</reference>. To this purport he had often spoken (<reference osisRef="John.7.16">ch. vii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.28">viii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.44">xii. 44</reference>), and here it comes in very pertinently. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the stress of duty is laid upon the precept of Christ as our rule, and justly, for that word of Christ which we are to keep is the Father's word, and his will the Father's will. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The stress of our comfort is laid upon the promise of Christ. But forasmuch as, in dependence upon that promise, we must deny ourselves, and take up our cross, and quit all, it concerns us to enquire whether the security be sufficient for us to venture our all upon; and this satisfies us that it is, that the promise is not Christ's bare word, but the Father's which sent him, which therefore we may rely upon.

<div eID="gen28093" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28094" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> These things have I spoken unto you, being <hi type="italic">yet</hi> present with you. <hi type="super">26</hi> But the Comforter, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. <hi type="super">27</hi> Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. <div eID="gen28094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28095" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ here comforts his disciples with:— <div eID="gen28095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28096" type="x-p"/> I. That they should be under the tuition of his Spirit, <reference osisRef="John.14.25-John.14.26">v. 25, 26</reference>, where we may observe, <div eID="gen28096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28097" type="x-p"/> 1. The reflection Christ would have them make upon the instructions he had given them: <hi type="italic">These things have I spoken unto you</hi> (referring to all the good lessons he had taught them, since they entered themselves into his school), <hi type="italic">being yet present with you.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That what he had said he did not retract nor unsay, but ratify it, or stand to it. What he had spoken he had spoken, and would abide by it. (2.) That he had improved the opportunity of his bodily presence with them to the utmost: "As long as I have been yet present with them, you know I have lost no time." Note, When our teachers are about to be removed from us we should call to mind what they have spoken, <hi type="italic">being yet present with us.</hi> <div eID="gen28097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28098" type="x-p"/> 2. The encouragement given them to expect another teacher, and that Christ would find out a way of speaking to them after his departure from them, <reference osisRef="John.14.26">v. 26</reference>. He had told them before that the Father would give them this other comforter (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">v. 16</reference>), and here he returns to speak of it again; for as the promise of the Messiah had been, so the promise of the Spirit now was, the consolation of Israel. Two things he here tells them further concerning the sending of the Holy Ghost:— <div eID="gen28098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28099" type="x-p"/> (1.) On whose account he should be sent: "The Father will send him <hi type="italic">in my name;</hi> that is, for <hi type="italic">my sake,</hi> at my special instance and request:" or, "as my agent and representative." He came in his Father's name, as his ambassador: the Spirit comes in his name, as resident in his absence, to carry on his undertaking, and to ripen things for his second coming. Hence he is called <hi type="italic">the Spirit of Christ,</hi> for he pleads his cause, and does his work. <div eID="gen28099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28100" type="x-p"/> (2.) On what errand he should be sent; two things he shall do:—[1.] <hi type="italic">He shall teach you all things,</hi> as a Spirit of wisdom and revelation Christ was a teacher to his disciples; if he leave them now that they have made so little proficiency, what will become of them? Why, the Spirit shall teach them, shall be their standing tutor. He shall teach them all things necessary for them either to learn themselves, or to teach others. For those that would teach the things of God must first themselves be taught of God; this is the Spirit's work. See <reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa. lix. 21</reference>. [2.] <hi type="italic">He shall bring all things to your remembrance whatsoever I have said unto you.</hi> Many a good lesson Christ had taught them, which they had forgotten, and which would be to seek when they had occasion for it. Many things they did not retain the remembrance of, because they did not rightly understand the meaning of them. The Spirit shall not teach them a new gospel, but bring to their minds that which they had been taught, by leading them into the understanding of it. The apostles were all of them to preach, and some of them to write, the things that Jesus did and taught, to transmit them to distant nations and future ages; now, if they had been left to themselves herein, some needful things might have been forgotten, others misrepresented, through the treachery of their memories; therefore the Spirit is promised to enable them truly to relate and record what Christ said unto them. And to all the saints the Spirit of grace is given to be a remembrancer, and to him by faith and prayer we should commit the keeping of what we hear and know. <div eID="gen28100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28101" type="x-p"/> II. That they should be under the influence of his peace (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Peace I leave with you.</hi> When Christ was about to leave the world he <hi type="italic">made his will.</hi> His soul he committed to his Father; his body he bequeathed to Joseph, to be decently interred; his clothes fell to the soldiers; his mother he left to the care of John: but what should he leave to his poor disciples, that had left all for him? Silver and gold he had none; but he left them that which was infinitely better, <hi type="italic">his peace.</hi> <hi type="italic">"I leave you,</hi> but I leave <hi type="italic">my peace</hi> with you. I not only give you a title to it, but put you in possession of it." He did not part in anger, but in love; for this was his farewell, <hi type="italic">Peace I leave with you,</hi> as a dying father leaves portions to his children; and this is a <hi type="italic">worthy portion.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28102" type="x-p"/> 1. The legacy that is here bequeathed <hi type="italic">Peace, my peace.</hi> Peace is put for all good, and Christ has left us all needful good, all that is really and truly good, as all the purchased promised good. Peace is put for reconciliation and love; the peace bequeathed is peace with God, peace with one another; peace <hi type="italic">in our own bosoms</hi> seems to be especially meant; a tranquillity of mind arising from a sense of our justification before God. It is the counterpart of our pardons, and the composure of our minds. This Christ calls <hi type="italic">his</hi> peace, for he is himself our peace, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>. It is the peace he purchased for us and preached to us, and on which the angels congratulated men at his birth, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Luke ii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen28102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28103" type="x-p"/> 2. To whom this legacy is bequeathed: "To you, my disciples and followers, that will be exposed to trouble, and have need of peace; to you that are the sons of peace, and are qualified to receive it." This legacy was left to them as the representatives of the church, to them and their successors, to them and all true Christians in all ages. <div eID="gen28103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28104" type="x-p"/> 3. In what manner it is left: <hi type="italic">Not as the world giveth, give I unto you.</hi> That is, (1.) "I do not compliment you with <hi type="italic">Peace be unto you;</hi> no, it is not a mere formality, but a real blessing." (2.) "The peace I give is of such a nature that the smiles of the world cannot give it, nor the frowns of the world take it away." Or, (3.) "The gifts I give to you are not such as this world gives to its children and votaries, to whom it is kind." The world's gifts concern only the body and time; Christ's gifts enrich the soul for eternity: the world gives lying vanities, and that which will cheat us; Christ gives substantial blessings, which will never fail us: the world gives and takes; Christ gives a good part that shall <hi type="italic">never be taken away.</hi> (4.) The peace which Christ gives is infinitely more valuable than that which the world gives. The world's peace begins in ignorance, consists with sin, and ends in endless troubles; Christ's peace begins in grace, consists with no allowed sin, and ends at length in everlasting peace. As is the difference between a killing lethargy and a reviving refreshing sleep, such is the difference between Christ's peace and the world's. <div eID="gen28104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28105" type="x-p"/> 4. What use they should make of it: <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled,</hi> for any evils past or present, <hi type="italic">neither let it be afraid</hi> of any evil to come. Note, Those that are interested in the covenant of grace, and entitled to the peace which Christ gives, ought not to yield to overwhelming griefs and fears. This comes in here as the conclusion of the whole matter; he had said (<reference osisRef="John.14.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled,</hi> and here he repeats it as that for which he had now given sufficient reason.

<div eID="gen28105" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28106" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come <hi type="italic">again</hi> unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I. <hi type="super">29</hi> And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe. <hi type="super">30</hi> Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me. <hi type="super">31</hi> But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do. Arise, let us go hence. <div eID="gen28106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28107" type="x-p"/> Christ here gives his disciples another reason why their hearts should not be troubled for his going away; and that is, because his heart was not. And here he tells them what it was that enabled him to endure the cross and despise the shame, that they might <hi type="italic">look unto him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">run with patience.</hi> He comforted himself, <div eID="gen28107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28108" type="x-p"/> I. That, though he went away, he should <hi type="italic">come again: "You have heard how I have said,</hi> and now I say it again, <hi type="italic">I go away, and come again.</hi>" Note, What we have heard of the doctrine of Christ, especially concerning his second coming, we have need to be told again and again. When we are under the power of any transport of passion, grief, or fear, or care, we forget that Christ will come again. See <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Phil. iv. 5</reference>. Christ encouraged himself with <hi type="italic">this,</hi> in his sufferings and death, that he should <hi type="italic">come again,</hi> and the same should comfort us in our departure at death; we go away to come again; the leave we take of our friends at that parting is only a good night, not a final farewell. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13-1Thess.4.14">1 Thess. iv. 13, 14</reference>. <div eID="gen28108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28109" type="x-p"/> II. That he <hi type="italic">went to his Father: "If you loved me,</hi> as by your sorrow you say you do, <hi type="italic">you would rejoice</hi> instead of mourning, because, though I leave you, yet I said, <hi type="italic">I go unto the Father,</hi> not only mine, but yours, which will be my advancement and your advantage; for <hi type="italic">my Father is greater than I.</hi>" Observe here, 1. It is matter of joy to Christ's disciples that he is gone to the Father, to take possession for orphans, and make intercession for transgressors. His departure had a bright side as well as a dark side. Therefore he sent this message after his resurrection (<reference osisRef="John.20.17">ch. xx. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">I ascend to my Father and your Father,</hi> as most comfortable. 2. The reason of this is, because <hi type="italic">the Father is greater than he,</hi> which, if it be a proper proof of that for which it is alleged (as no doubt it is), must be understood thus, that his state with his Father would be much more excellent and glorious than his present state; his returning to his Father (so Dr. Hammond) would be the advancing of him to a much higher condition than that which he was now in. Or thus, His going to the Father himself, and bringing all his followers to him there, was the ultimate end of his undertaking, and therefore greater than the means. Thus Christ raises the thoughts and expectations of his disciples to something greater than that in which now they thought all their happiness bound up. The kingdom of the Father, wherein he shall be all in all, will be greater than the mediatorial kingdom. 3. The disciples of Christ should show that they love him by their rejoicing in the glories of his exaltation, rather than by lamenting the sorrows of his humiliation, and rejoicing that he is gone to his Father, where he would be, and where we shall be shortly with him. Many that love Christ, let their love run out in a wrong channel; they think if they love him they must be continually in pain because of him; whereas those that love him should <hi type="italic">dwell at ease</hi> in him, should <hi type="italic">rejoice in Christ Jesus.</hi> <div eID="gen28109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28110" type="x-p"/> III. That his going away, compared with the prophecies which went before of it, would be a means of confirming the faith of his disciples (<reference osisRef="John.14.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have told you before it come to pass</hi> that I must die and rise again, and ascend to the Father, and send the Comforter, <hi type="italic">that, when it is come to pass, you might believe.</hi>" See this reason, <reference osisRef="John.13.19">ch. xiii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.4">xvi. 4</reference>. Christ told his disciples of his death, though he knew it would both puzzle them and grieve them, because it would afterwards redound to the confirmation of their faith in two things:—1. That he who foretold these things had a divine prescience, and knew beforehand what day would bring forth. When St. Paul was going to Jerusalem, he <hi type="italic">knew not the things that did abide him there,</hi> but Christ did. 2. That the things foretold were according to the divine purpose and designation, not sudden resolves, but the counterparts of an eternal counsel. Let them therefore not be troubled at that which would be for the confirmation of their faith, and so would redound to their real benefit; for the <hi type="italic">trial of our faith</hi> is very precious, though it cost us present <hi type="italic">heaviness, through manifold temptations,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1 Pet. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28111" type="x-p"/> IV. That he was sure of a victory over Satan, with whom he knew he was to have a struggle in his departure (<reference osisRef="John.14.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Henceforth I will not talk much with you,</hi> having not much to say, but what may be adjourned to the pouring out of the Spirit." He had a great deal of good talk with them after this (<reference osisRef="John.15.1-John.16.33">ch. xv. and xvi.</reference>), but, in comparison with what he had said, it was not much. His time was now short, and he therefore spoke largely to them now, because the opportunity would soon be over. Note, We should always endeavour to talk to the purpose, because perhaps we may not have time to talk much. We know not how soon our breath may be stopped, and therefore should be always breathing something that is good. When we come to be sick and die, perhaps we may not be capable of talking much to those about us; and therefore what good counsel we have to give them, let us give it while we are in health. One reason why he would not talk much with them was because he had now other work to apply himself to: <hi type="italic">The prince of this world comes.</hi> He called the devil the <hi type="italic">prince of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.31">ch. xii. 31</reference>. The disciples dreamed of their Master being the prince of this world, and they worldly princes under him.
