But Christ tells them that the <hi type="italic">prince of this world</hi> was his enemy, and so were the <hi type="italic">princes of this world,</hi> that were actuated and ruled by him, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. But <hi type="italic">he has nothing in me.</hi> Observe here, 1. The prospect Christ had of an approaching conflict, not only with men, but with the powers of darkness. The devil had set upon him with his temptations (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11">Matt. iv.</reference>), had offered him the <hi type="italic">kingdoms of this world,</hi> if he would hold them as tributary to him, with an eye to which Christ calls him, in disdain, <hi type="italic">the prince of this world. Then the devil departed from him for a season;</hi> "But now," says Christ, "I see him rallying again, preparing to make a furious onset, and so to gain by terrors that which he could not gain by allurements;" to frighten from his undertaking, when he could not entice from it. Note, The foresight of a temptation gives us great advantage in our resistance of it; for, being fore-warned, we should be fore-armed. While we are here, we may see Satan continually coming against us, and ought therefore to be always upon our guard. 2. The assurance he had of good success in the conflict: <hi type="italic">He hath nothing in me,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk echei ouden</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He hath nothing at all.</hi> (1.) There was no guilt in Christ to give authority to <hi type="italic">the prince of this world</hi> in his terrors. The devil is said to have <hi type="italic">the power of death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>); the Jews called him <hi type="italic">the angel of death,</hi> as an executioner. Now Christ having done no evil, Satan had no legal power against him, and therefore, though he prevailed to crucify him, he could not prevail to terrify him; though he hurried him to death, yet not to despair. When Satan comes to disquiet us, he has something in us to perplex us with, for we have all sinned; but, when he would disturb Christ, he found no occasion against him. (2.) There was no corruption in Christ, to give advantage to <hi type="italic">the prince of this world</hi> in his temptations. He could not crush his undertaking by drawing him to sin, because there was nothing sinful in him, nothing irregular for his temptations to fasten upon, no tinder for him to strike fire into; such was the spotless purity of his nature that he was above the possibility of sinning. The more Satan's interest in us is crushed and decays, the more comfortably may we expect sufferings and death. <div eID="gen28111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28112" type="x-p"/> V. That his departure was in compliance with, and obedience to, his Father. Satan could not force his life from him, and yet he would die: <hi type="italic">that the world may know that I love the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.31">v. 31</reference>. We may take this, <div eID="gen28112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28113" type="x-p"/> 1. As confirming what he had often said, that his undertaking, as Mediator, was a demonstration to the world, (1.) Of his compliance with the Father; hereby it appeared that he loved the Father. As it was an evidence of his love to man that he died for his salvation, so it was of his love to God that he died for his glory and the accomplishing of his purposes. Let the world know that between the Father and the Son there is not love lost. <hi type="italic">As the Father loved the Son, and gave all things into his hands;</hi> so <hi type="italic">the Son loved the Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gave his spirit into his hand.</hi> (2.) Of his obedience to his Father: "<hi type="italic">As the Father gave me commandment, even so I</hi> did—did the thing commanded me in the manner commanded." Note, The best evidence of our love to the Father is our doing as he hath given us commandment. As Christ loved the Father, and obeyed him, <hi type="italic">even to the death,</hi> so we must love Christ, and obey him. Christ's eye to the Father's commandment, obliging him to suffer and die, bore him up with cheerfulness, and overcame the reluctancies of nature; this took off the offence of the cross, that what he did was by order from the Father. The command of God is sufficient to bear us out in that which is most disputed by others, and therefore should be sufficient to bear us up in that which is most difficult to ourselves: <hi type="italic">This is the will of him</hi> that made me, <hi type="italic">that sent me.</hi> <div eID="gen28113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28114" type="x-p"/> 2. As concluding what he had now said; having brought it to this, here he leaves it: <hi type="italic">that the world may know that I love the Father.</hi> You shall see how cheerfully I can meet the appointed cross: "<hi type="italic">Arise, let us go hence</hi> to the garden;" so some; or, to <hi type="italic">Jerusalem.</hi> When we talk of troubles at a distance, it is easy to say, <hi type="italic">Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest;</hi> but when it comes to the pinch, when an unavoidable cross lies in the way of duty, then to say, "<hi type="italic">Arise, let us go</hi> to meet it," instead of going out of our way to miss it, this lets <hi type="italic">the world know that we love the Father.</hi> If this discourse was at the close of the passover-supper, it should seem that at these words he arose from the table, and retired into the drawing-room, where he might the more freely carry on the discourse with his disciples in the following chapters, and pray with them. Dr. Goodwin's remark upon this is, that Christ mentioning the great motive of his sufferings, his Father's commandment, was in all haste to go forth to suffer and die, was afraid of slipping the time of Judas's meeting him: <hi type="italic">Arise,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">let us go hence</hi> but he looks upon the glass, as it were, sees it not quite out, and therefore sits down again, and preaches another sermon. Now, (1.) In these words he gives his disciples an encouragement to follow him. He does not say, <hi type="italic">I must go;</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Let us go.</hi> He calls them out to no hardships but what he himself goes before them in as their leader. They had promised they would not desert him: "Come," says he, "<hi type="italic">let us go</hi> then; let us see how you will make the words good." (2.) He gives them an example, teaching them at all times, especially in suffering times, to sit loose to all things here below, and often to think and speak of leaving them. Though we sit easy, and in the midst of the delights of an agreeable conversation, yet we must not think of being here always: <hi type="italic">Arise, let us go hence.</hi> If it was at the close of the paschal and eucharistical supper, it teaches us that the solemnities of our communion with God are not to be constant in this world. When we sit down under Christ's shadow with delight, and say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here;</hi> yet we must think of rising and going hence; going down from the mount.  <chapter eID="John.14"/> <div eID="gen28114" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28117" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28116" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ the True Vine.</title> <div sID="gen28118" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. <hi type="super">2</hi> Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every <hi type="italic">branch</hi> that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you. <hi type="super">4</hi> Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. <hi type="super">5</hi> I am the vine, ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. <hi type="super">6</hi> If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the fire, and they are burned. <hi type="super">7</hi> If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you. <hi type="super">8</hi> Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples. <div eID="gen28118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28119" type="x-p"/> Here Christ discourses concerning the fruit, <hi type="italic">the fruits of the Spirit,</hi> which his disciples were to bring forth, under the similitude of a vine. Observe here, <div eID="gen28119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28120" type="x-p"/> I. The doctrine of this similitude; what notion we ought to have of it. <div eID="gen28120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28121" type="x-p"/> 1. That Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the vine, the true vine.</hi> It is an instance of the humility of Christ that he is pleased to speak of himself under low and humble comparisons. He that is <hi type="italic">the Sun of righteousness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the bright and morning Star,</hi> compares himself to a <hi type="italic">vine.</hi> The church, which is Christ mystical, is a vine (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">Ps. lxxx. 8</reference>), so is Christ, who is the church seminal. Christ and his church are thus set forth. (1.) He is <hi type="italic">the vine,</hi> planted in the vineyard, and not a spontaneous product; planted in the earth, for his is <hi type="italic">the Word made flesh.</hi> The vine has an unsightly unpromising outside; and Christ had <hi type="italic">no form nor comeliness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Isa. liii. 2</reference>. The vine is a spreading plant, and Christ will be known as <hi type="italic">salvation to the ends of the earth.</hi> The fruit of the vine honours God and cheers man (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.13">Judg. ix. 13</reference>), so does the fruit of Christ's mediation; it is <hi type="italic">better than gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">Prov. viii. 19</reference>. (2.) He is <hi type="italic">the true vine,</hi> as truth is opposed to pretence and counterfeit; he is really a fruitful plant, a plant of renown. He is not like that wild vine which deceived those who gathered of it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.39">2 Kings iv. 39</reference>), but a true vine. Unfruitful trees are said to <hi type="italic">lie</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.17">Hab. iii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">marg.</hi>), but Christ is a vine that will not deceive. Whatever excellency there is in any creature, serviceable to man, it is but a shadow of that grace which is in Christ for his people's good. He is that true vine typified by Judah's vine, which enriched him with the blood of the grape (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen. xlix. 11</reference>), by Joseph's vine, the branches of which <hi type="italic">ran over the wall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen. xlix. 22</reference>), by Israel's vine, under which he <hi type="italic">dwelt safely,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1 Kings iv. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen28121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28122" type="x-p"/> 2. That believers are branches of this vine, which supposes that Christ is the root of the vine. The root is unseen, and our <hi type="italic">life is hid with Christ;</hi> the root bears the tree (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.18">Rom. xi. 18</reference>), diffuses sap to it, and is all in all to its flourishing and fruitfulness; and in Christ are all supports and supplies. The branches of the vine are many, some on one side of the house or wall, others on the other side; yet, meeting in the root, are all but one vine; thus all good Christians, though in place and opinion distant from each other, yet meet in Christ, the centre of their unity. Believers, like the branches of the vine, are weak, and insufficient to stand of themselves, but as they are borne up. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.2">Ezek. xv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen28122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28123" type="x-p"/> 3. That <hi type="italic">the Father is the husbandman,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">georgos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the land-worker.</hi> Though <hi type="italic">the earth is the Lord's,</hi> it yields him no fruit unless he work it. God has not only a propriety in, but a care of, the vine and all the branches. He <hi type="italic">hath planted, and watered, and gives the increase;</hi> for <hi type="italic">we are God's husbandry,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1 Cor. iii. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.2-Isa.27.3">xxvii. 2, 3</reference>. He had an eye upon Christ, the root, and upheld him, and made him to flourish <hi type="italic">out of a dry ground.</hi> He has an eye upon all the branches, and prunes them, and watches over them, that nothing hurt them. Never was any husbandman so wise, so watchful, about his vineyard, as God is about his church, which therefore must needs prosper. <div eID="gen28123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28124" type="x-p"/> II. The duty taught us by this similitude, which is to <hi type="italic">bring forth fruit,</hi> and, in order to this, to <hi type="italic">abide</hi> in Christ. <div eID="gen28124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28125" type="x-p"/> 1. We must be fruitful. From a vine we look for grapes (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 2</reference>), and from a Christian we look for Christianity; this is the <hi type="italic">fruit,</hi> a Christian temper and disposition, a Christian life and conversation, Christian devotions and Christian designs. We must honour God, and do good, and exemplify the purity and power of the religion we profess; and this is bearing fruit. The disciples here must be fruitful, as Christians, in all <hi type="italic">the fruits of righteousness,</hi> and as apostles, in diffusing the savour of the knowledge of Christ. To persuade them to this, he urges, <div eID="gen28125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28126" type="x-p"/> (1.) The doom of the unfruitful (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">v. 2</reference>): They are <hi type="italic">taken away.</hi> [1.] It is here intimated that there are many who pass for <hi type="italic">branches</hi> in Christ who yet do <hi type="italic">not bear fruit.</hi> Were they really united to Christ by faith, they would bear fruit; but being only tied to him by the thread of an outward profession, though they seem to be branches, they will soon be seen to be dry ones. Unfruitful professors are unfaithful professors; professors, and no more. It might be read, <hi type="italic">Every branch that beareth not fruit in me,</hi> and it comes much to one; for those that do not bear fruit in Christ, and in his Spirit and grace, are as if they bore no fruit at all, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Hos. x. 1</reference>. [2.] It is here threatened that they shall be <hi type="italic">taken away,</hi> in justice to them and in kindness to the rest of the branches. From him that has not real union with Christ, and fruit produced thereby, <hi type="italic">shall be taken away even that which he seemed to have,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.8.18">Luke viii. 18</reference>. Some think this refers primarily to Judas. <div eID="gen28126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28127" type="x-p"/> (2.) The promise made to the fruitful: <hi type="italic">He purgeth them, that they may bring forth more fruit.</hi> Note, [1.] Further fruitfulness is the blessed reward of forward fruitfulness. The first blessing was, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful;</hi> and it is still a great blessing. [2.] Even fruitful branches, in order to their further fruitfulness, have need of purging or pruning; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kathairei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he taketh away that which is superfluous</hi> and luxuriant, which hinders its growth and fruitfulness. The best have that in them which is peccant, <hi type="italic">aliquid amputandum—something which should be taken away;</hi> some notions, passions, or humours, that want to be purged away, which Christ has promised to do by his word, and Spirit, and providence; and these shall be taken off by degrees in the proper season. [3.] The purging of fruitful branches, in order to their greater fruitfulness, is the care and work of the great husbandman, for his own glory. <div eID="gen28127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28128" type="x-p"/> (3.) The benefits which believers have by the doctrine of Christ, the power of which they should labour to exemplify in a fruitful conversation: <hi type="italic">Now you are clean,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.3">v. 3</reference>. [1.] Their society was clean, now that Judas was expelled by that word of Christ, <hi type="italic">What thou doest, do quickly;</hi> and till they were got clear of him <hi type="italic">they were not all clean.</hi> The word of Christ is a distinguishing word, and separates <hi type="italic">between the precious and the vile;</hi> it will purify <hi type="italic">the church of the first-born</hi> in the great dividing day. [2.] They were each of them clean, that is, sanctified, by the truth of Christ (<reference osisRef="John.17.17">ch. xvii. 17</reference>); that faith by which they received the word of Christ <hi type="italic">purified their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">Acts xv. 9</reference>. The Spirit of grace by the word refined them from the dross of the world and the flesh, and purged out of them <hi type="italic">the leaven of the scribes and Pharisees,</hi> from which, when they saw their inveterate rage and enmity against their Master, they were now pretty well cleansed. Apply it to all believers. The word of Christ is spoken to them; there is a cleansing virtue in that word, as it works grace, and works out corruption. It cleanses as fire cleanses the gold from its dross, and as physic cleanses the body from its disease. We then evidence that we are cleansed by the word when we <hi type="italic">bring forth fruit unto holiness.</hi> Perhaps here is an allusion to the law concerning vineyards in Canaan; the fruit of them was as unclean, and uncircumcised, the first three years after it was planted, and <hi type="italic">the fourth year it</hi> was to <hi type="italic">be holiness of praise unto the Lord;</hi> and then it was clean, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23-Lev.19.24">Lev. xix. 23, 24</reference>. The disciples had now been three years under Christ's instruction; and <hi type="italic">now you are clean.</hi> <div eID="gen28128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28129" type="x-p"/> (4.) The glory that will redound to God by our fruitfulness, with the comfort and honour that will come to ourselves by it, <reference osisRef="John.15.8">v. 8</reference>. If we <hi type="italic">bear much fruit,</hi> [1.] Herein our Father will be glorified. The fruitfulness of the apostles, as such, in the diligent discharge of their office, would be to the glory of God in the conversion of souls, and the offering of them up to him, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Rom. xv. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">16</reference>. The fruitfulness of all Christians, in a lower or narrower sphere, is to the glory of God. By the eminent good works of Christians many are brought to <hi type="italic">glorify our Father who is in heaven.</hi> [2.] So shall we be Christ's disciples indeed, approving ourselves so, and making it to appear that we are really what we call ourselves. So shall we both evidence our discipleship and adorn it, and be to our Master <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise,</hi> and a glory, that is, disciples indeed, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>. So shall we be owned by our Master in the great day, and have the reward of disciples, a share <hi type="italic">in the joy of our Lord.</hi> And the more fruit we bring forth, the more we abound in that which is good, the more he is glorified. <div eID="gen28129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28130" type="x-p"/> 2. In order to our fruitfulness, we must abide in Christ, must keep up our union with him by faith, and do all we do in religion in the virtue of that union. Here is, <div eID="gen28130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28131" type="x-p"/> (1.) The duty enjoined (<reference osisRef="John.15.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Abide in me, and I in you.</hi> Note, It is the great concern of all Christ's disciples constantly to keep up a dependence upon Christ and communion with him, habitually to adhere to him, and actually to derive supplies from him. Those that are come to Christ must abide in him: "<hi type="italic">Abide in me,</hi> by faith; <hi type="italic">and I in you,</hi> by my Spirit; <hi type="italic">abide in me,</hi> and then fear not but I will <hi type="italic">abide in you;</hi>" for the communion between Christ and believers never fails on his side. We must abide in Christ's word by a regard to it, and it in us as a <hi type="italic">light to our feet.</hi> We must abide in Christ's merit as our righteousness and plea, and it in us as our support and comfort. The knot of the branch abides in the vine, and the sap of the vine abides in the branch, and so there is a constant communication between them. <div eID="gen28131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28132" type="x-p"/> (2.) The necessity of our abiding in Christ, in order to our fruitfulness (<reference osisRef="John.15.4-John.15.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You cannot bring forth fruit, except you abide in me;</hi> but, if you do, you <hi type="italic">bring forth much fruit; for,</hi> in short, <hi type="italic">without me,</hi> or separate from me, <hi type="italic">you can do nothing.</hi>" So necessary is it to our comfort and happiness that we be fruitful, that the best argument to engage us to abide in Christ is, that otherwise we cannot be fruitful. [1.] Abiding in Christ is necessary in order to our doing much good. He that is constant in the exercise of faith in Christ and love to him, that lives upon his promises and is led by his Spirit, <hi type="italic">bringeth forth much fruit,</hi> he is very serviceable to God's glory, and his own account in the great day. Note, Union with Christ is a noble principle, productive of all good. A life of faith in the Son of God is incomparably the most excellent life a man can live in this world; it is regular and even, pure and heavenly; it is useful and comfortable, and all that answers the end of life. [2.] It is necessary to our doing any good. It is not only a means of cultivating ad increasing what good there is already in us, but it is the root and spring of all good: "<hi type="italic">Without me you can do nothing:</hi> not only no great thing, <hi type="italic">heal the sick, or raise the dead,</hi> but nothing." Note, We have as necessary and constant a dependence upon the grace of the Mediator for all the actions of the spiritual and divine life as we have upon the providence of the Creator for all the actions of the natural life; for, as to both, it is in the divine power <hi type="italic">that we live, move, and have our being.</hi> Abstracted from the merit of Christ, we can do nothing towards our justification; and from the Spirit of Christ nothing towards our sanctification. <hi type="italic">Without Christ we can do nothing</hi> aright, nothing that will be fruit pleasing to God or profitable to ourselves, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2 Cor. iii. 5</reference>. We depend upon Christ, not only as the vine upon the wall, for support; but, as the branch on the root, for sap. <div eID="gen28132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28133" type="x-p"/> (3.) The fatal consequences of forsaking Christ (<reference osisRef="John.15.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">If any man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch.</hi> This is a description of the fearful state of hypocrites that are <hi type="italic">not in Christ,</hi> and of apostates that <hi type="italic">abide not in Christ.</hi> [1.] They are cast forth as dry and withered branches, which are plucked off because they cumber the tree. It is just that those should have no benefit by Christ who think they have no need of him; and that those who reject him should be rejected by him. Those that abide not in Christ shall be abandoned by him; they are left to themselves, to fall into scandalous sin, and then are justly cast out of the communion of the faithful. [2.] They are withered, as a branch broken off from the tree. Those that abide not in Christ, though they may flourish awhile in a plausible, at least a passable profession, yet in a little time wither and come to nothing. Their parts and gifts wither; their zeal and devotion wither; their credit and reputation wither; their hopes and comforts wither, <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.13">Job viii. 11-13</reference>. Note, Those that bear no fruit, after while will bear no leaves. <hi type="italic">How soon is that fig-tree withered away</hi> which Christ has cursed! [3.] <hi type="italic">Men gather them.</hi> Satan's agents and emissaries pick them up, and make an easy prey of them. Those that fall off from Christ presently fall in with sinners; and the sheep that wander from Christ's fold, the devil stands ready to seize them for himself. When the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul, an evil spirit possessed him. [4.] They <hi type="italic">cast them into the fire,</hi> that is, they are cast into the fire; and those who seduce them and draw them to sin do in effect cast them there; for they <hi type="italic">make them children of hell.</hi> Fire is the fittest place for withered branches, for they are good for nothing else, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.2-Ezek.15.4">Ezek. xv. 2-4</reference>. [5.] <hi type="italic">They are burned;</hi> this follows of course, but it is here added very emphatically, and makes the threatening very terrible. They will not be consumed in a moment, like <hi type="italic">thorns under a pot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Eccl. vii. 6</reference>), but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kaietai</hi></hi>, they are burning for ever in a fire, which not only cannot be quenched, but will never spend itself. This comes of quitting Christ, this is the end of barren trees. Apostates are <hi type="italic">twice dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>), and when it is said, <hi type="italic">They are cast into the fire and are burned,</hi> it speaks as if they were twice damned. Some apply men's gathering them to the ministry of the angels in the great day, when they shall gather out of Christ's kingdom all things that offend, and shall <hi type="italic">bundle the tares for the fire.</hi> <div eID="gen28133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28134" type="x-p"/> (4.) The blessed privilege which those have that <hi type="italic">abide in Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.15.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">If my words abide in you, you shall ask what you will</hi> of my Father in my name, <hi type="italic">and it shall be done.</hi> See here, [1.] How our union with Christ is maintained—by the word: <hi type="italic">If you abide in me;</hi> he had said before, <hi type="italic">and I in you;</hi> here he explains himself, <hi type="italic">and my words abide in you;</hi> for it is in the word that Christ is set before us, and offered to us, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6-Rom.10.8">Rom. x. 6-8</reference>. It is in the word that we receive and embrace him; and so where the <hi type="italic">word of Christ dwells richly</hi> there Christ dwells. If the word be our constant guide and monitor, if it be in us as at home, then we abide in Christ, and he in us. [2.] How our communion with Christ is maintained—by prayer: <hi type="italic">You shall ask what you will, and it shall be done to you.</hi> And what can we desire more than to have what we will for the asking? Note, Those that abide in Christ as their heart's delight shall have, through Christ, their heart's desire. If we have Christ, we shall want nothing that is good for us. Two things are implied in this promise:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That if we abide in Christ, and his word in us, we shall not ask any thing but what is proper to be done for us. The promises abiding in us lie ready to be turned into prayers; and the prayers so regulated cannot but speed. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That if we <hi type="italic">abide in Christ and his word</hi> we shall have such an interest in God's favour and Christ's mediation that we shall have an answer of peace to all our prayers.

<div eID="gen28134" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Love to His Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen28135" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love. <hi type="super">10</hi> If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love. <hi type="super">11</hi> These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> your joy might be full. <hi type="super">12</hi> This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you. <hi type="super">13</hi> Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. 14 Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you. 15 Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you. <hi type="super">16</hi> Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you. <hi type="super">17</hi> These things I command you, that ye love one another. <div eID="gen28135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28136" type="x-p"/> Christ, who is love itself, is here discoursing concerning love, a fourfold love. <div eID="gen28136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28137" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the Father's love to him; and concerning this he here tells us, 1. That the Father did love him (<reference osisRef="John.15.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Father hath loved me.</hi> He loved him as Mediator: <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> He was the Son of his love. He loved him, and gave <hi type="italic">all things into his hand;</hi> and yet so <hi type="italic">loved the world</hi> as to deliver him up for us all. When Christ was entering upon his sufferings he comforted himself with this, that his Father loved him. Those whom God loves as a Father may despise the hatred of all the world. 2. That he abode in his Father's love, <reference osisRef="John.15.10">v. 10</reference>. He continually loved his Father, and was beloved of him. Even when he was made sin and a curse for us, and <hi type="italic">it pleased the Lord to bruise him,</hi> yet he abode in his Father's love. See <reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">Ps. lxxxix. 33</reference>. Because he continued to love his Father, he went cheerfully through his sufferings, and therefore his Father continued to love him. 3. That therefore he abode in his Father's love because he kept his Father's law: <hi type="italic">I have kept my Father's commandments,</hi> as Mediator, and so <hi type="italic">abide in his love.</hi> Hereby he showed that he continued to love his Father, that he went on, and went through, with his undertaking, and therefore the Father continued to love him. His soul <hi type="italic">delighted in him,</hi> because he <hi type="italic">did not fail, nor was discouraged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1-Isa.42.4">Isa. xlii. 1-4</reference>. We having broken the law of creation, and thereby thrown ourselves out of the love of God; Christ satisfied for us by obeying the law of redemption, and so he abode in his love, and restored us to it. <div eID="gen28137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28138" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning his own love to his disciples. Though he leaves them, he loves them. And observe here, <div eID="gen28138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28139" type="x-p"/> 1. The pattern of this love: <hi type="italic">As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you.</hi> A strange expression of the condescending grace of Christ! As the Father loved him, who was most worthy, he loved them, who were most unworthy. The Father loved him as his Son, and he loves them as his children. <hi type="italic">The Father gave all things into his hand;</hi> so, with himself, <hi type="italic">he freely giveth us all things.</hi> The Father loved him as Mediator, as head of the church, and the great trustee of divine grace and favour, which he had not for himself only, but for the benefit of those for whom he was entrusted; and, says he, "I have been a faithful trustee. As the Father has committed his love to me, so I transmit it to you." Therefore the Father was well pleased with him, that he might be well pleased with us in him; and loved him, that in him, as beloved, he might <hi type="italic">make us accepted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28140" type="x-p"/> 2. The proofs and products of this love, which are four:— <div eID="gen28140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28141" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ loved his disciples, for he laid down his life for them (<reference osisRef="John.15.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Greater</hi> proof of <hi type="italic">love hath no man</hi> to show <hi type="italic">than this,</hi> to <hi type="italic">lay down his life for his friend.</hi> And this is the love wherewith <hi type="italic">Christ hath loved us,</hi> he is our <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antipsychos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">bail for us,</hi> body for body, life for life, though he knew our insolvency, and foresaw how much the engagement would cost him. Observe here, [1.] The extent of the love of the children of men to one another. The highest proof of it is laying down one's life for a friend, to save his life, and perhaps there have been some such heroic achievements of love, more than <hi type="italic">plucking out one's own eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.15">Gal. iv. 15</reference>. If <hi type="italic">all that a man has he will give for his life,</hi> he that gives this for his friend gives all, and can give no more; this may sometimes be our duty, <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1 John iii. 16</reference>. Paul was ambitious of the honour (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>); and <hi type="italic">for a good man some will even dare to die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.7">Rom. v. 7</reference>. It is love in the highest degree, which is <hi type="italic">strong as death.</hi> [2.] The excellency of the love of Christ beyond all other love. He has not only equaled, but exceeded, the most illustrious lovers. Others have laid down their lives, content that they should be taken from them; but Christ gave up his, was not merely passive, but made it his own act and deed. The life which others have laid down has been but of equal value with the life for which it was laid down, and perhaps less valuable; but Christ is infinitely more worth than ten thousand of us. Others have thus laid down their lives for their friends, but Christ laid down his for us <hi type="italic">when we were enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">Rom. v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Plusquam ferrea aut lapidea corda esse oportet, quæ non emolliet tam incomparabilis divini amoris suavitas—Those hearts must be harder than iron or stone which are not softened by such incomparable sweetness of divine love.</hi>—Calvin. <div eID="gen28141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28142" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ loved his disciples, for he took them into a covenant of friendship with himself, <reference osisRef="John.15.14-John.15.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. "If you approve yourselves by your obedience my disciples indeed, <hi type="italic">you are my friends,</hi> and shall be treated as friends." Note, The followers of Christ are the friends of Christ, and he is graciously pleased to call and account them so. Those that do the duty of his servants are admitted and advanced to the dignity of his friends. David had one servant in his court, and Solomon one in his, that was in a particular manner <hi type="italic">the king's friend</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.37">2 Sam. xv. 37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.5">1 Kings iv. 5</reference>); but this honour have all Christ's servants. We may in some particular instance befriend a stranger; but we espouse all the interests of a friend, and concern ourselves in all his cares: thus Christ takes believers to be his friends. He visits them and converses with them as his friends, bears with them and makes the best of them, is afflicted in their afflictions, and takes pleasure in their prosperity; he pleads for them in heaven and takes care of all their interests there. Have friends but one soul? He that is joined to the Lord is <hi type="italic">one spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.17">1 Cor. vi. 17</reference>. Though they often show themselves unfriendly, he is a friend that loves at all times. Observe how endearingly this is expressed here. [1.] He will not <hi type="italic">call them servants,</hi> though they call him <hi type="italic">Master</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lord.</hi> Those that would be like Christ in humility must not take a pride in insisting upon all occasions on their authority and superiority, but remember that their servants are their fellow-servants. But, [2.] He will <hi type="italic">call them his friends;</hi> he will not only love them, but will let them know it; for <hi type="italic">in his tongue is the law of kindness.</hi> After his resurrection he seems to speak with more affectionate tenderness of and to his disciples than before. <hi type="italic">Go to my brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.17">ch. xx. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Children, have you any meat?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.21.5">ch. xxi. 5</reference>. But observe, though Christ called <hi type="italic">them his friends,</hi> they called themselves <hi type="italic">his servants:</hi> Peter, <hi type="italic">a servant of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. i. 1</reference>), and so James, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>. The more honour Christ puts upon us, the more honour we should study to do him; the higher in his eyes, the lower in our own. <div eID="gen28142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28143" type="x-p"/> (3.) Christ loved his disciples, for he was very free in communicating his mind to them (<reference osisRef="John.15.15">v. 15</reference>): "Henceforth you shall not be kept so much in the dark as you have been, like <hi type="italic">servants</hi> that are only told their present work; but, when the Spirit is poured out, you shall know your Master's designs as <hi type="italic">friends. All things that I have heard of my Father I have declared unto you.</hi>" As to the secret will of God, there are many things which we must be content not to know; but, as to the revealed will of God, Jesus Christ has faithfully handed to us what he received of the Father, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. The great things relating to man's redemption Christ declared to his disciples, that they might declare them to others; they were the men of his counsel, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.11">Matt. xiii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen28143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28144" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ loved his disciples, for he chose and ordained them to be the prime instruments of his glory and honour in the world (<reference osisRef="John.15.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have chosen you, and ordained you,</hi> His love to them appeared, <div eID="gen28144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28145" type="x-p"/> [1.] In their election, their election to their apostleship (<reference osisRef="John.6.70">ch. vi. 70</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have chosen you twelve.</hi> It did not begin on their side: <hi type="italic">You have not chosen me,</hi> but I first <hi type="italic">chose you.</hi> Why were they admitted to such an intimacy with him, employed in such an embassy for him, and endued with such power from on high? It was not owing to their wisdom and goodness in choosing him for their Master, but to his favour and grace in choosing them for his disciples. It is fit that Christ should have the choosing of his own ministers; still he does it by his providence and Spirit. Though ministers make that holy calling their own choice, Christ's choice is prior to theirs and directs and determines it. Of all that are chosen to grace and glory it may be said, They have not chosen Christ, but he had chosen them, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen28145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28146" type="x-p"/> [2.] In their ordination: <hi type="italic">I have ordained you;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hetheka hymas</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">I have put you</hi> into the ministry (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1 Tim. i. 12</reference>), put you into commission." By this it appeared that he took them for his friends when he crowned their heads with such an honour, and filled their hands with such a trust. It was a mighty confidence he reposed in them, when he made them his ambassadors to negotiate the affairs of his kingdom in this lower world, and the prime ministers of state in the administration of it. The treasure of the gospel was committed to them, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it might be propagated: that you should go, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hina hymeis hypagete</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">that you should go as under a yoke</hi> or burden, for the ministry is a work, and you that go about it must resolve to undergo a great deal; <hi type="italic">that you may go</hi> from place to place all the world over, and <hi type="italic">bring forth fruit.</hi>" They were ordained, not to sit still, but to go about, to be diligent in their work, and to lay out themselves unweariedly in doing good. They were ordained, not to beat the air, but to be instrumental in God's hand for the bringing of nations into obedience to Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.13">Rom. i. 13</reference>. Note, Those whom Christ ordains should and shall be fruitful; should labour, and shall not labour in vain. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it might be perpetuated; that the fruit may remain, that the good effect of their labours may continue in the world from generation to generation, to the end of time. The church of Christ was not to be a short-lived thing, as many of the sects of the philosophers, that were a nine days' wonder; it did not <hi type="italic">come up in a night,</hi> nor should it <hi type="italic">perish in a night,</hi> but be as the days of heaven. The sermons and writings of the apostles are transmitted to us, and we at this day are built upon that foundation, ever since the Christian church was first founded by the ministry of the apostles and seventy disciples; as one generation of ministers and Christians has passed away, still another has come. By virtue of that great charter (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Matt. xxviii. 19</reference>), Christ has a church in the world, which, as our lawyers say of bodies corporate, does <hi type="italic">not die,</hi> but lives in a succession; and thus <hi type="italic">their fruit remains</hi> to this day, and shall do while the earth remains. <div eID="gen28146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28147" type="x-p"/> [3.] His love to them appeared in the interest they had at the throne of grace: <hi type="italic">Whatsoever you shall ask of my Father, in my name, he will give it you.</hi> Probably this refers in the first place to the power of working miracles which the apostles were clothed with, which was to be drawn out by prayer. "Whatever gifts are necessary to the furtherance of your labours, whatever help from heaven you have occasion for at any time, it is but ask and have." Three things are here hinted to us for our encouragement in prayer, and very encouraging they are. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That we have a God to go to who is a Father; Christ here calls him <hi type="italic">the Father,</hi> both mine and yours; and the Spirit in the word and in the heart teaches us to cry, <hi type="italic">Abba, Father. Secondly,</hi> That we come in a good name. Whatever errand we come upon to the throne of grace according to God's will, we may with a humble boldness mention Christ's name in it, and plead that we are related to him, and he is concerned for us. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That an answer of peace is promised us. What you come for shall be given you. This great promise made to that great duty keeps up a comfortable and gainful intercourse between heaven and earth. <div eID="gen28147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28148" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning the disciples' love to Christ, enjoined in consideration of the great love wherewith he had loved them. Three things he exhorts them to:— <div eID="gen28148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28149" type="x-p"/> 1. To continue in his love, <reference osisRef="John.15.9">v. 9</reference>. "Continue in your love to me, and in mine to you." Both may be taken in. We must place our happiness in the continuance of Christ's love to us, and make it our business to give continued proofs of our love to Christ, that nothing may tempt us to withdraw from him, or provoke him to withdraw from us. Note, All that love Christ should continue in their love to him, that is, be always loving him, and taking all occasions to show it, and love to the end. The disciples were to go out upon service for Christ, in which they would meet with many troubles; but, says Christ, "<hi type="italic">Continue in my love.</hi> Keep up your love to me, and then all the troubles you meet with will be easy; love made seven years' hard service easy to Jacob. Let not the troubles you meet with for Christ's sake quench your love to Christ, but rather quicken it. <div eID="gen28149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28150" type="x-p"/> 2. To let his joy remain in them, and fill them, <reference osisRef="John.15.11">v. 11</reference>. This he designed in those precepts and promises given them. <div eID="gen28150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28151" type="x-p"/> (1.) That his joy might remain in them. The words are so placed, in the original, that they may be read either, [1.] That <hi type="italic">my joy in you may remain.</hi> If they bring forth much fruit, and continue in his love, he will continue to rejoice in them as he had done. Note, Fruitful and faithful disciples are the joy of the Lord Jesus; he <hi type="italic">rests in his love</hi> to them, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zeph. iii. 17</reference>. As there is a transport of joy in heaven in the conversion of sinners, so there is a remaining joy in the perseverance of saints. Or, [2.] That <hi type="italic">my joy,</hi> that is, your joy in me, <hi type="italic">may remain.</hi> It is the will of Christ that his disciples should constantly and continually rejoice in him, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">Phil. iv. 4</reference>. The joy of the hypocrite is but for a moment, but the joy of those who abide in Christ's love is a continual feast. The word of the Lord enduring for ever, the joys that flow from it, and are founded on it, do so too. <div eID="gen28151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28152" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">That your joy might be full;</hi> not only that you might be full of joy, but that your joy in me and in my love may rise higher and higher, till it come to perfection, when you <hi type="italic">enter into the joy of your Lord.</hi>" Note, [1.] Those and those only that have Christ's joy remaining in them have their joy full; worldly joys are empty, soon surfeit but never satisfy. It is only wisdom's joy that will fill the soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Ps. xxxvi. 8</reference>. [2.] The design of Christ in his world is to <hi type="italic">fill the joy</hi> of his people; see <reference osisRef="1John.1.4">1 John i. 4</reference>. This and the other he hath said, that our joy might be fuller and fuller, and perfect at last. <div eID="gen28152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28153" type="x-p"/> 3. To evidence their love to him by keeping his commandments: "<hi type="italic">If you keep my commandments, you shall abide in my love,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.10">v. 10</reference>. This will be an evidence of the fidelity and constancy of your love to me, and then you may be sure of the continuance of my love to you." Observe here, (1.) The promise "<hi type="italic">You shall abide in my love</hi> as in a dwelling place, at home in Christ's love; as in a resting place, at ease in Christ's love; as in a stronghold, safe in it. <hi type="italic">You shall abide in my love,</hi> you shall have grace and strength to persevere in loving me." If the same hand that first shed abroad the love of Christ in our hearts did not keep us in that love, we should not long abide in it, but, through the love of the world, should go <hi type="italic">out of love</hi> with Christ himself. (2.) The condition of the promise: <hi type="italic">If you keep my commandments.</hi> The disciples were to keep Christ's commandments, not only by a constant conformity to them themselves, but by a faithful delivery of them to others; they were to keep them as trustees, in whose hands that great <hi type="italic">depositum</hi> was lodged, for they were to <hi type="italic">teach all things that Christ had commanded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">This commandment</hi> they must <hi type="italic">keep without spot</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1 Tim. vi. 14</reference>), and thus they must show that they abide in his love. <div eID="gen28153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28154" type="x-p"/> To induce them to keep his commandments, he urges, [1.] His own example: <hi type="italic">As I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love.</hi> Christ submitted to the law of mediation, and so preserved the honour and comfort of it, to teach us to submit to the laws of the Mediator, for we cannot otherwise preserve the honour and comfort of our relation to him. [2.] The necessity of it to their interest in him (<reference osisRef="John.15.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You are my friends if you do whatsoever I command you</hi> and not otherwise." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those only will be accounted Christ's faithful friends that approve themselves his obedient servants; for those that will not have him to reign over them shall be treated as his enemies. <hi type="italic">Idem velle et idem nolle ea demum vera est amicitia—Friendship involves a fellowship of aversions and attachments.</hi>—Sallust. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is universal obedience to Christ that is the only acceptable obedience; to obey him in every thing that he commands us, not <hi type="italic">excepting,</hi> much less <hi type="italic">excepting against,</hi> any command. <div eID="gen28154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28155" type="x-p"/> IV. Concerning the <hi type="italic">disciples' love one to another,</hi> enjoined as an evidence of their love to Christ, and a grateful return for his love to them. We must keep his commandments, and this is his commandment, that we <hi type="italic">love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.12-John.15.17">v. 12, and again, v. 17</reference>. No one duty of religion is more frequently inculcated, nor more pathetically urged upon us, by our Lord Jesus, than that of mutual love, and for good reason. 1. It is here recommended by Christ's pattern (<reference osisRef="John.15.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">as I have loved you.</hi> Christ's love to us should direct and engage our love to each other; in this manner, and from this motive, we should love one another, as, and because, Christ has loved us. He here specifies some of the expressions of his love to them; he called them friends, communicated his mind to them, was ready to give them what they asked. <hi type="italic">Go you and do likewise.</hi> 2. It is required by his precept. He interposes his authority, has made it one of the statute-laws of his kingdom. Observe how differently it is expressed in <reference osisRef="John.15.12-John.15.17">these two verses</reference>, and both very emphatic. (1.) <hi type="italic">This is my commandment</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.15.12">v. 12</reference>), as if this were the most necessary of all the commandments. As under the law the prohibition of idolatry was the commandment more insisted on than any other, foreseeing the people's addictedness to that sin, so Christ, foreseeing the addictedness of the Christian church to uncharitableness, has laid most stress upon this precept. (2.) <hi type="italic">These things I command you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.17">v. 17</reference>. He speaks as if he were about to give them many things in charge, and yet names this only, <hi type="italic">that you love one another;</hi> not only because this includes many duties, but because it will have a good influence upon all.

<div eID="gen28155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Hatred and Persecution Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen28156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before <hi type="italic">it hated</hi> you. <hi type="super">19</hi> If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you. <hi type="super">20</hi> Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also. <hi type="super">21</hi> But all these things will they do unto you for my name's sake, because they know not him that sent me. <hi type="super">22</hi> If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin. <hi type="super">23</hi> He that hateth me hateth my Father also. <hi type="super">24</hi> If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father. <hi type="super">25</hi> But <hi type="italic">this cometh to pass,</hi> that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause. <div eID="gen28156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28157" type="x-p"/> Here Christ discourses concerning <hi type="italic">hatred,</hi> which is the character and genius of the devil's kingdom, as love is of the kingdom of Christ. Observe here, <div eID="gen28157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28158" type="x-p"/> I. Who they are in whom this hatred is found—the world, the children of this world, as distinguished from the children of God; those who are in the interests of the god of this world, whose image they bear, and whose power they are subject to; all those, whether Jews or Gentiles, who would not come into the church of Christ, which he audibly called, and visibly separates from this evil world. The calling of these <hi type="italic">the world</hi> intimates, 1. Their number; there were a world of people that opposed Christ and Christianity. Lord, how were they increased that troubled the Son of David! I fear, if we should put it to the vote between Christ and Satan, Satan would out-poll us quite. 2. Their confederacy and combination; these numerous hosts are embodied, and are as one, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">Ps. lxxxiii. 5</reference>. Jews and Gentiles, that could agree in nothing else, agreed to persecute Christ's minister. 3. Their spirit and disposition; they are <hi type="italic">men of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.13-Ps.16.14">Ps. xvi. 13, 14</reference>), wholly devoted to this world and the things of it, and never thinking of another world. The people of God, though they are taught to hate the sins of sinners, yet not their persons, but to love and do good to all men. A malicious, spiteful, envious spirit, is not the spirit of Christ, but of the world. <div eID="gen28158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28159" type="x-p"/> II. Who are they against whom this hatred is levelled-against the disciples of Christ, against Christ himself, and against the Father. <div eID="gen28159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28160" type="x-p"/> 1. The world hates the disciples of Christ: <hi type="italic">The world hateth you</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.15.19">v. 19</reference>); and he speaks of it as that which they must expect and count upon, <reference osisRef="John.15.18">v. 18</reference>, as <reference osisRef="1John.3.13">1 John iii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen28160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28161" type="x-p"/> (1.) Observe how this comes in here. [1.] Christ had expressed the great kindness he had for them as friends; but, lest they should be puffed up with this, there was given them, as there was to Paul, a <hi type="italic">thorn in the flesh,</hi> that is, as it is explained there, reproaches and persecutions for Christ's sake, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2 Cor. xii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">10</reference>. [2.] He had appointed them their work, but tells them what hardships they should meet with in it, that it might not be a surprise to them, and that they might prepare accordingly. [3.] He had charged them to <hi type="italic">love one another,</hi> and need enough they had to love one another, for the world would hate them; to be kind to one another, for they would have a great deal of unkindness and ill-will from those that were without. "Keep peace among yourselves, and this will fortify you against the world's quarrels with you." Those that are in the midst of enemies are concerned to hold together. <div eID="gen28161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28162" type="x-p"/> (2.) Observe what is here included. <div eID="gen28162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28163" type="x-p"/> [1.] The world's enmity against the followers of Christ: it <hi type="italic">hateth them.</hi> Note, Whom Christ blesseth the world curseth. The favourites and heirs of heaven have never been the darlings of this world, since the old enmity was put between the seed of the woman and of the serpent. Why did Cain hate Abel, but <hi type="italic">because his works were righteous?</hi> Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing; Joseph's brethren hated him because his father loved him; Saul hated David because <hi type="italic">the Lord was with him;</hi> Ahab hated Micaiah because of his prophecies; such are the causeless causes of the world's hatred. <div eID="gen28163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28164" type="x-p"/> [2.] The fruits of that enmity, two of which we have here, <reference osisRef="John.15.20">v. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They will persecute you, because they hate you, for hatred is a restless passion. It is the common lot of those who will live godly in Christ Jesus to <hi type="italic">suffer persecution,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.12">2 Tim. iii. 12</reference>. Christ foresaw what ill usage his ambassadors would meet with in the world, and yet, for the sake of those few that by their ministry were to be called out of the world, he sent them forth as sheep in the midst of wolves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Another fruit of their enmity is implied, that they would reject their doctrine. When Christ says, <hi type="italic">If they have kept my sayings, they will keep yours,</hi> he means, They will keep yours, and regard yours, no more than they have regarded and kept mine. Note, The preachers of the gospel cannot but take the despising of their message to be the greatest injury that can be done to themselves; as it was a great affront to Jeremiah to say, <hi type="italic">Let us not give heed to any of his words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer. xviii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen28164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28165" type="x-p"/> [3.] The causes of that enmity. The world will hate them, <div eID="gen28165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because they do not belong to it (<reference osisRef="John.15.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you were of the world,</hi> of its spirit, and in its interests, if you were carnal and worldly, <hi type="italic">the world would love you</hi> as its own; but, because you are called out of the world, it hates you, and ever will." Note, 1. We are not to wonder if those that are devoted to the world are caressed by it as its friends; most men <hi type="italic">bless the covetous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Ps. x. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.18">xlix. 18</reference>. 2. Nor are we to wonder if those that are delivered from the world are maligned by it as its enemies; when Israel is rescued out of Egypt, the Egyptians will pursue them. Observe, The reason why Christ's disciples are not of the world is not because they have by their own wisdom and virtue distinguished themselves from the world, but because Christ hath chosen them out of it, to set them apart for himself; and this is the reason why the world hates them; for, (1.) The glory which by virtue of this choice they are designed for sets them above the world, and so makes them the objects of its envy. The saints shall judge the world, and the upright have dominion, and therefore they are hated. (2.) The grace which by virtue of this choice they are endued with sets them against the world; they swim against the stream of the world, and are not conformed to it; they witness against it, and are not conformed to it. This would support them under all the calamities which the world's hatred would bring upon them, that they were hated because they were the choice and the chosen ones of the Lord Jesus, and were not of the world. Now, [1.] This was no just cause for the world's hatred of them. If we do any thing to make ourselves hateful, we have reason to lament it; but, if men hate us for that for which they should love and value us, we have reason to pity them, but no reason to perplex ourselves. Nay, [2.] This was just cause for their own joy. He that is hated because he is rich and prospers cares not who has the vexation of it, while he has the satisfaction of it. <div eID="gen28166" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen28167"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28168"/>—Populus me sibilat, at mihi plaudo<l eID="gen28168" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28169"/>Ipse domi—<l eID="gen28169" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28170"/>—Let them hiss on, he cries,<l eID="gen28170" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28171"/>While in my own opinion fully blessed. <hi type="italic">Timon in Hor.</hi><l eID="gen28171" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen28167"/> <div sID="gen28172" type="x-p"/> Much more may those hug themselves whom the world hates, but whom Christ loves. <div eID="gen28172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "Another cause of the world's hating you will be because you do belong to Christ (<reference osisRef="John.15.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">For my name's sake.</hi>" Here is the core of the controversy; whatever is pretended, this is the ground of the quarrel, they hate Christ's disciples because they <hi type="italic">bear his name,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bear up his name</hi> in the world. Note, 1. It is the character of Christ's disciples that they stand up for his name. The name into which they were baptized is that which they will live and die by. 2. It has commonly been the lot of those that appear for Christ's name to suffer for so doing, to suffer many things, and hard things, <hi type="italic">all these things.</hi> It is matter of comfort to the greatest sufferers if they suffer for Christ's name's sake. <hi type="italic">If you be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are you</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1 Pet. iv. 14</reference>), happy indeed, considering not only the honour that is imprinted upon those sufferings (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Acts v. 41</reference>), but the comfort that is infused into them, and especially the crown of glory which those sufferings lead to. <hi type="italic">If we suffer with Christ,</hi> and for Christ, <hi type="italic">we shall reign with him.</hi> <div eID="gen28173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> After all, it is the world's ignorance that is the true cause of its enmity to the disciples of Christ (<reference osisRef="John.15.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because they know not him that sent me.</hi> 1. They know not God. If men had but a due acquaintance with the very first principles of natural religion, and did but know God, though they did not embrace Christianity, yet they could not hate and persecute it. Those have no knowledge who eat up God's people, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Ps. xiv. 4</reference>. 2. They know not God as he that sent our Lord Jesus, and authorized him to be the great Mediator of the peace. We do not rightly know God if we do not know him in Christ, and those who persecute those whom he sends make it to appear that they know not that he was sent of God. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen28174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28175" type="x-p"/> 2. The world hates Christ himself. And this is spoken of here for two ends:— <div eID="gen28175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28176" type="x-p"/> (1.) To mitigate the trouble of his followers, arising from the world's hatred, and to make it the less strange, and the less grievous (<reference osisRef="John.15.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">You know that it hated me before you,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proton hymon</hi></hi>. We read it as signifying priority of time; he began in the bitter cup of suffering, and then left us to pledge him; but it may be read as expressing his superiority over them: "<hi type="italic">You know</hi> that it hated me, <hi type="italic">your first,</hi> your chief and captain, your leader and commander." [1.] If Christ, who excelled in goodness, and was perfectly innocent and universally beneficent, was hated, can we expect that any virtue or merit of ours should screen us from malice? [2.] If our Master, the founder of our religion, met with so much opposition in the planting of it, his servants and followers can look for no other in propagating and professing it. For this he refers them (<reference osisRef="John.15.20">v. 20</reference>) to his own word, at their admission into discipleship: <hi type="italic">Remember the word that I said unto you.</hi> It would help us to understand Christ's latter sayings to compare them with his former sayings. Nor would any thing contribute more to the making of us easy than remembering the words of Christ, which will expound his providences. Now in this word there is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> A plain truth: <hi type="italic">The servant is not greater than his Lord.</hi> This he had said to them. <reference osisRef="Matt.10.24">Matt. x. 24</reference>. Christ is our Lord, and therefore we must diligently attend all his motions, and patiently acquiesce in all his disposals, for the servant is inferior to his lord. The plainest truths are sometimes the strongest arguments for the hardest duties; Elihu answers a multitude of Job's murmurings with this one self-evident truth, that God is greater than man, <reference osisRef="Job.33.12">Job xxxiii. 12</reference>. So here is, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A proper inference drawn from it: "<hi type="italic">If they have persecuted men,</hi> as you have seen, and are likely to see much more, <hi type="italic">they will also persecute you;</hi> you may expect it and count upon it: for," 1. "You will do the same that I have done to provoke them; you will reprove them for their sins, and call them to repentance, and give them strict rules of holy living, which they will not bear." 2. "You cannot do more than I have done to oblige them; after so great an instance, let none wonder if they suffer ill for doing well." He adds, "<hi type="italic">If they have kept my sayings, they will keep yours also;</hi> as there have been a few, and but a few, that have been wrought upon by my preaching, so there will be by yours a few, and but a few." Some give another sense of this, making <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eteresan</hi></hi> to be put for <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pareteresan</hi></hi>. "If they have lain in wait for my sayings, with a design to ensnare me, they will in like manner lie in wait to entangle you in your talk." <div eID="gen28176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28177" type="x-p"/> (2.) To aggravate the wickedness of this unbelieving world, and to discover its exceeding sinfulness; to hate and persecute the apostles was bad enough, but in them to hate and persecute Christ himself was much worse. The world is generally in an ill name in scripture, and nothing can put it into a worse name than this, that it hated Jesus Christ. There is a world of people that are haters of Christ. Two things he insists upon to aggravate the wickedness of those that hated him:— <div eID="gen28177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28178" type="x-p"/> [1.] That there was the greatest reason imaginable why they should love him; men's good words and good works usually recommend them; now as to Christ, <div eID="gen28178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28179" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His words were such as merited their love (<reference osisRef="John.15.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I had not spoken unto them,</hi> to court their love, <hi type="italic">they had not had sin,</hi> their opposition had not amounted to a hatred of me, their sin had been comparatively no sin. But now that I have said so much to them to recommend myself to their best affections they have no pretence, no excuse for their sin." Observe here, 1. The advantage which those have that enjoy the gospel; Christ in it comes and speaks to them; he spoke in person to the men of that generation, and is still speaking to us by our Bibles and ministers, and as one that has the most unquestionable authority over us, and affection for us. Every word of his is pure, carries with it a commanding majesty, and yet a condescending tenderness, able, one would think, to charm the deafest adder. 2. The excuse which those have that enjoy not the gospel: "<hi type="italic">If I had not spoken to them,</hi> if they had ever heard of Christ and of salvation by him, <hi type="italic">they had not had sin.</hi>" (1.) Not this kind of sin. They had not been chargeable with a contempt of Christ if he had not come and made a tender of his grace to them. As <hi type="italic">sin is not imputed where there is no law,</hi> so unbelief is not imputed where there is no gospel; and, where it is imputed, it is thus far the only damning sin, that, being a sin against the remedy, other sin would not damn if the guilt of them were not bound on with this. (2.) Not such a degree of sin. If they had not had the gospel among them, their other sins had not been so bad; for the <hi type="italic">times of ignorance God winked at,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.47-Luke.12.48">Luke xii. 47, 48</reference>. 3. The aggravated guilt which those lie under to whom Christ has <hi type="italic">come and spoken in vain,</hi> whom he has called and invited in vain, with whom he has reasoned and pleaded in vain; <hi type="italic">They have no cloak for their sin;</hi> they are altogether inexcusable, and in the judgment day will be speechless, and will not have a word to say for themselves. Note, The clearer and fuller the discoveries are which are made to us of the grace and truth of Jesus Christ, the more is said to us that is convincing and endearing, the greater is our sin if we do not love him and believe in him. The word of Christ strips sin of its cloak, that it may appear sin. <div eID="gen28179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His works were such as merited their love, as well as his words (<reference osisRef="John.15.24">v. 24</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I had not done among them,</hi> in their country, and before their eyes, such works as <hi type="italic">no other man ever did, they had not had sin;</hi> their unbelief and enmity had been excusable, and they might have had some colour to say that my word was not to be credited, if not otherwise confirmed;" but he produced satisfactory proofs of his divine mission, <hi type="italic">works which no other man did.</hi> Note, 1. As the Creator demonstrates his power and Godhead by his works (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Rom. i. 20</reference>), so doth the Redeemer. His miracles, his mercies, works of wonder and works of grace, prove him sent of God, and sent on a kind errand. 2. Christ's works were such as <hi type="italic">no man ever did.</hi> No common person that had not a commission from heaven, and God with him, could work miracles, <reference osisRef="John.3.2">ch. iii. 2</reference>. And no prophet ever wrought such miracles, so many, so illustrious. Moses and Elias wrought miracles as servants, by a derived power; but Christ, as a Son, by his own power. This was it that amazed the people, that with authority he commanded diseases and devils (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.27">Mark i. 27</reference>); they owned they never saw the like, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.12">Mark ii. 12</reference>. They were all good works, works of mercy; and this seems especially intended here, for he is upbraiding them with this, that they hated him. One that was so universally useful, more than ever any man was, one would think, should have been universally beloved, and yet even he is hated. 3. The works of Christ enhance the guilt of sinners' infidelity and enmity to him, to the last degree of wickedness and absurdity. If they had only heard his words, and not seen his works,—if we had only his sermons upon record, and not his miracles, unbelief might have pleaded want of proof; but now it has no excuse. Nay, the rejecting of Christ, both by them and us, has in it the sin, not only of obstinate unbelief, but of base ingratitude. They saw Christ to be most amiable, and studious to do them a kindness; yet they hated him, and studied to do him mischief. And we see in his word that great love wherewith he loved us, and yet are not wrought upon by it. <div eID="gen28180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28181" type="x-p"/> [2.] That there was no reason at all why they should hate him. Some that at one time will say and do that which is recommending, yet at another time will say and do that which is provoking and disobliging; but our Lord Jesus not only did much to merit men's esteem and good-will, but never did any thing justly to incur their displeasure; this he pleads by quoting a scripture for it (<reference osisRef="John.15.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This comes to pass,</hi> this unreasonable hatred of me, and of my disciples for my sake, <hi type="italic">that the word might be fulfilled which is written in their law</hi>" (that is, in the Old Testament, which is a law, and was received by them as a law), "<hi type="italic">They hated me without a cause;</hi>" this David speaks of himself as a type of Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Ps. xxxv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">lxix. 4</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those that hate Christ hate him without any just cause; enmity to Christ is unreasonable enmity. We think those deserve to be hated that are haughty and froward, but Christ is meek and lowly, compassionate and tender; those also that under colour of complaisance are malicious, envious, and revengeful, but Christ devoted himself to the service of those that used him, nay, and of those that abused him; toiled for others' ease, and impoverished himself to enrich us. Those we think hateful that are <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings and provinces,</hi> and disturbers of the public peace; but Christ, on the contrary, was the greatest blessing imaginable to his country, and yet was hated. He testified indeed that <hi type="italic">their works were evil,</hi> with a design to make them good, but to hate him for this cause was to hate him without cause. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Herein the scripture was fulfilled, and the antitype answered the type. Saul and his courtiers hated David without cause, for he had been serviceable to him with his harp, and with his sword; Absalom and his party hated him, though to him he had been an indulgent father, and to them a great benefactor. Thus was the Son of David hated, and hunted most unjustly. Those that hated Christ did not design there in to fulfil the scripture; but God, in permitting it, had that in his eye; and it confirms our faith in Christ as the Messiah that even this was foretold concerning him, and, being foretold, was accomplished in him. And we must not think it strange or hard if it have a further accomplishment in us. We are apt to justify our complaints of injuries done us with this, that they are causeless, whereas the more they are so the more they are like the sufferings of Christ, and may be the more easily borne. <div eID="gen28181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28182" type="x-p"/> 3. In Christ the world hates God himself; this is twice said here (<reference osisRef="John.15.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hateth me,</hi> though he thinks his hatred goes no further, yet really he <hi type="italic">hates my Father also.</hi> And again, <reference osisRef="John.15.24">v. 24</reference>, They have <hi type="italic">seen and hated both me and my Father.</hi> Note, (1.) There are those that hate God, notwithstanding the beauty of his nature and the bounty of his providence; they are enraged at his justice, as the devils that believe it and tremble, are vexed at his dominion, and would gladly <hi type="italic">break his bands asunder.</hi> Those who cannot bring themselves to deny that there is a God, and yet wish there were none, they see and hate him. (2.) Hatred of Christ will be construed and adjudged hatred of God, for he is in his person his Father's express image, and in his office his great agent and ambassador. God will have all men to honour the Son as they honour the Father, and therefore what entertainment the Son has, that the Father has. Hence it is easy to infer that those who are enemies to the Christian religion, however they may cry up natural religion, are really enemies to all religion. Deists are in effect atheists, and those that ridicule the light of the gospel would, if they could, extinguish even natural light, and shake off all obligations of conscience and the fear of God.
