Let an unbelieving malignant world know that their enmity to the gospel of Christ will be looked upon in the great day as an enmity to the blessed God himself; and let all that suffer for righteousness' sake, according to the will of God, take comfort from this; if God himself be hated in them, and struck at through him, they need not be either ashamed of their cause or afraid of the issue.

<div eID="gen28182" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Comforter Announced.</title> <div sID="gen28183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me: <hi type="super">27</hi> And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning. <div eID="gen28183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28184" type="x-p"/> Christ having spoken of the great opposition which his gospel was likely to meet with in the world, and the hardships that would be put upon the preachers of it, lest any should fear that they and it would be run down by that violent torrent, he here intimates to all those that were well-wishers to his cause and interest what effectual provision was made for supporting it, both by the principal testimony of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="John.15.26">v. 26</reference>), and the subordinate testimony of the apostles (<reference osisRef="John.15.27">v. 27</reference>), and testimonies are the proper supports of truth. <div eID="gen28184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28185" type="x-p"/> I. It is here promised that the blessed Spirit shall maintain the cause of Christ in the world, notwithstanding the opposition it should meet with. Christ, when he was reviled, committed his injured cause to his Father, and did not lose by his silence, for the Comforter came, pleaded it powerfully, and carried it triumphantly. "<hi type="italic">When the Comforter</hi> or Advocate <hi type="italic">is come, who proceedeth from the Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">whom I will send</hi> to supply the want of my bodily presence, <hi type="italic">he shall testify of me</hi> against those that <hi type="italic">hate me without cause.</hi>" We have more in <reference osisRef="John.15.26">this verse</reference> concerning the Holy Ghost than in any one verse besides in the Bible; and, being baptized into his name, we are concerned to acquaint ourselves with him as far as he is revealed. <div eID="gen28185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28186" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is an account of him in his essence, or subsistence rather. He is <hi type="italic">the Spirit of truth, who proceedeth from the Father.</hi> Here, (1.) He is spoken of as a distinct person; not a quality or property, but a person under the proper name of a <hi type="italic">Spirit,</hi> and proper title of the <hi type="italic">Spirit of truth,</hi> a title fitly given him where he is brought in testifying. (2.) As a divine person, that <hi type="italic">proceedeth from the Father,</hi> by out-goings that were of old, <hi type="italic">from everlasting.</hi> The spirit or breath of man, called the <hi type="italic">breath of life,</hi> proceeds from the man, and by it modified he delivers his mind, by it invigorated he sometimes exerts his strength to <hi type="italic">blow out</hi> what he would extinguish, and <hi type="italic">blow up</hi> what he would excite. Thus the blessed Spirit is the emanation of divine light, and the energy of divine power. The rays of the sun, by which it dispenses and diffuses its light, heat, and influence, proceed from the sun, and yet are one with it. The <hi type="italic">Nicene</hi> Creed says, The Spirit <hi type="italic">proceedeth from the Father and the Son,</hi> for he is called the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal. iv. 6</reference>. And the Son is here said to <hi type="italic">send him.</hi> The Greek church chose rather to say, <hi type="italic">from the Father by the Son.</hi> <div eID="gen28186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28187" type="x-p"/> 2. In his mission. (1.) He will come in a more plentiful effusion of his gifts, graces, and powers, than had ever yet been. Christ had been long the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho erchomenos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he that should come;</hi> now the blessed Spirit is so. (2.) <hi type="italic">I will send him to you from the Father.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">ch. xiv. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will pray the Father, and he shall send you the Comforter,</hi> which bespeaks the Spirit to be the fruit of the intercession Christ makes within the veil: here he says, <hi type="italic">I will send him,</hi> which bespeaks him to be the fruit of his dominion within the veil. The Spirit was sent, [1.] By Christ as Mediator, now <hi type="italic">ascended on high to give gifts unto men,</hi> and all power being given to him. [2.] From the Father: "Not only from heaven, my Father's house" (the Spirit was given in a <hi type="italic">sound from heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Acts ii. 2</reference>), "but according to my Father's will and appointment, and with his concurring power and authority." [3.] To the apostles to instruct them in their preaching, enable them for working, and carry them through their sufferings. He was given to them and their successors, both in Christianity and in the ministry; to them and their seed, and their seed's seed, according to that promise, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa. lix. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen28187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28188" type="x-p"/> 3. In his office and operations, which are two:—(1.) One implied in the title given to him; he is the <hi type="italic">Comforter,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Advocate.</hi> An advocate for Christ, to maintain his cause against the world's infidelity, a comforter to the saints against the world's hatred. (2.) Another expressed: <hi type="italic">He shall testify of me.</hi> He is not only an advocate, but a witness for Jesus Christ; he is one of the three that <hi type="italic">bear record in heaven,</hi> and the first of the three that <hi type="italic">bear witness on earth.</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.7-1John.5.8">1 John v. 7, 8</reference>. He instructed the apostles, and enabled them to work miracles; he indited the scriptures, which are the standing witnesses that <hi type="italic">testify of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.39">ch. v. 39</reference>. The power of the ministry is derived from the Spirit, for he qualifies ministers; and the power of Christianity too, for he sanctifies Christians, and in both testifies of Christ. <div eID="gen28188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28189" type="x-p"/> II. It is here promised that the apostles also, by the Spirit's assistance, should have the honour of being Christ's witnesses (<reference osisRef="John.15.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">And you also shall bear witness</hi> of me, being competent witnesses, for <hi type="italic">you have been with</hi> me from the beginning of my ministry. Observe here, <div eID="gen28189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28190" type="x-p"/> 1. That the apostles were appointed to be witnesses for Christ in the world. When he had said, <hi type="italic">The Spirit shall testify,</hi> he adds, <hi type="italic">And you also shall bear witness.</hi> Note, The Spirit's working is not to supersede, but to engage and encourage ours. Though the Spirit testify, ministers also must bear their testimony, and people attend to it; for the Spirit of grace witnesses and works by the means of grace. The apostles were the first witnesses that were called in the famous trial between Christ and the prince of this world, which issued in the ejectment of the intruder. This intimates, (1.) The work cut out for them; they were to attest the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, concerning Christ, for the recovering of his just right, and the maintaining of his crown and dignity. Though Christ's disciples fled when they should have been witnesses for him upon his trial before the high priest and Pilate, yet after the Spirit was poured out upon them they appeared courageous in vindication of the cause of Christ against the accusations it was loaded with. The truth of the Christian religion was to be proved very much by the evidence of matter of fact, especially Christ's resurrection, of which the apostles were in a particular manner chosen witnesses (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.41">Acts x. 41</reference>), and they bore their testimony accordingly, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.15">Acts iii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.32">v. 32</reference>. Christ's ministers are his witnesses. (2.) The honour put upon them hereby—that they should be <hi type="italic">workers together with God.</hi> "The <hi type="italic">Spirit shall testify of me,</hi> and you also, under the conduct of the Spirit, and in concurrence with the Spirit (who will preserve you from mistaking in that which you relate on your own knowledge, and will inform you of that which you cannot know but by revelation), <hi type="italic">shall bear witness.</hi>" This might encourage them against the hatred and contempt of the world, that Christ had honoured them, and would own them. <div eID="gen28190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28191" type="x-p"/> 2. That they were qualified to be so: <hi type="italic">You have been with me from the beginning.</hi> They not only heard his public sermons, but had constant private converse with him. He <hi type="italic">went about doing good,</hi> and, while others saw the wonderful and merciful works that he did in their own town and country only, those that went about with him were witnesses of them all. They had likewise opportunity of observing the unspotted purity of his conversation, and could witness for him that they never saw in him, nor heard from him, any thing that had the least tincture of human frailty. Note. (1.) We have great reason to receive the record which the apostles gave of Christ, for they did not speak by hearsay, but what they had the greatest assurance of imaginable, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.16 1John.1.1 1John.1.3">2 Pet. i. 16; 1 John i. 1, 3</reference>. (2.) Those are best able to bear witness for Christ that have themselves been with him, by faith, hope, and love, and by living a life of communion with God in him. Ministers must first learn Christ, and then preach him. Those speak best of the things of God that speak experimentally. It is particularly a great advantage to have been acquainted with Christ <hi type="italic">from the beginning,</hi> to understand all things from the <hi type="italic">very first,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Luke i. 3</reference>. To have been with him from the beginning of our days. An early acquaintance and constant converse with the gospel of Christ will make a man like a good householder.  <chapter eID="John.15"/> <div eID="gen28191" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28194" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28193" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Persecution Foretold; The Expediency of Christ's Departure.</title> <div sID="gen28195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These things have I spoken unto you, that ye should not be offended. <hi type="super">2</hi> They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service. <hi type="super">3</hi> And these things will they do unto you, because they have not known the Father, nor me. 4 But these things have I told you, that when the time shall come, ye may remember that I told you of them. And these things I said not unto you at the beginning, because I was with you. <hi type="super">5</hi> But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou? <hi type="super">6</hi> But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart. <div eID="gen28195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28196" type="x-p"/> Christ dealt faithfully with his disciples when he sent them forth on his errands, for he told them the worst of it, that they might sit down and count the cost. He had told them in the chapter before to expect the world's hatred; now here in these verses, <div eID="gen28196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28197" type="x-p"/> I. He gives them a reason why he alarmed them thus with the expectation of trouble: <hi type="italic">These things have I spoken unto you, that you should not be offended,</hi> or <hi type="italic">scandalized,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. The disciples of Christ are apt to be offended at the cross; and the offence of the cross is a dangerous temptation, even to good men, to turn back from the ways of God, or turn aside out of them, or drive on heavily in them; to quit either their integrity or their comfort. It is not for nothing that a suffering time is called <hi type="italic">an hour of temptation.</hi> 2. Our Lord Jesus, by giving us notice of trouble, designed to take off the terror of it, that it might not be a surprise to us. Of all the adversaries of our peace, in this world of troubles, none insult us more violently, nor put our troops more into disorder, than disappointment does; but we can easily welcome a guest we expect, and <hi type="italic">being fore-warned are fore-armed—Præmoniti, præmuniti.</hi> <div eID="gen28197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28198" type="x-p"/> II. He foretels particularly what they should suffer (<reference osisRef="John.16.2">v. 2</reference>): "Those that have power to do it shall <hi type="italic">put you out of their synagogues;</hi> and this is not the worst, <hi type="italic">they shall kill you." Ecce duo-gladii—Behold two swords</hi> drawn against the followers of the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen28198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28199" type="x-p"/> 1. The sword of ecclesiastical censure; this is drawn against them by the Jews, for they were the only pretenders to church-power. They shall <hi type="italic">cast you out of their synagogues;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aposynagogous poiesousin hymas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they shall make you excommunicates.</hi> (1.) "They shall cast you out of the particular synagogues you were members of." At first, they scourged them in their synagogues as contemners of the law (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.17">Matt. x. 17</reference>), and at length cast them out as incorrigible. (2.) "They shall cast you out of the congregation of Israel in general, the national church of the Jews; shall debar you from the privileges of that, put you into the condition of an outlaw," <hi type="italic">qui caput gerit lupinum—to be knocked on the head, like another wolf;</hi> "they will look upon you as Samaritans, as heathen men and publicans." <hi type="italic">Interdico tibi aqua et igne—I forbid you the use of water and fire.</hi> And were it not for the penalties, forfeitures, and incapacities, incurred hereby, it would be no injury to be thus driven out of a house infected and falling. Note, It has often been the lot of Christ's disciples to be unjustly excommunicated. Many a good truth has been branded with an anathema, and many a child of God <hi type="italic">delivered to Satan.</hi> <div eID="gen28199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28200" type="x-p"/> 2. The sword of civil power: "The time cometh, <hi type="italic">the hour is come;</hi> now things are likely to be worse with you than hitherto they have been; when you are expelled as heretics, they will <hi type="italic">kill you, and think they do God service,</hi> and others will think so too." (1.) You will find them really cruel: They will <hi type="italic">kill you.</hi> Christ's sheep have been accounted as sheep for the slaughter; the twelve apostles (we are told) were all put to death, except John. Christ had said (<reference osisRef="John.15.27">ch. xv. 27</reference>), You shall <hi type="italic">bear witness,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">martyreite</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">you shall be martyrs,</hi> shall seal the truth with your blood, your heart's blood. (2.) You will find them <hi type="italic">seemingly conscientious;</hi> they will think they do God service; they will seem <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">latreian prospherein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to offer a good sacrifice</hi> to God; as those that cast out God's servants of old, and said, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>. Note, [1.] It is possible for those that are real enemies to God's service to pretend a mighty zeal for it. The devil's work has many a time been done in God's livery, and one of the most mischievous enemies Christianity ever had sits <hi type="italic">in the temple of God.</hi> Nay, [2.] It is common to patronise an enmity to religion with a color of duty to God, and service to his church. God's people have suffered the greatest hardships from conscientious persecutors. Paul verily thought he <hi type="italic">ought to do</hi> what he did <hi type="italic">against the name of Jesus.</hi> This does not at all lessen the sin of the persecutors, for villanies will never be consecrated by putting the name of God to them; but it does enhance the sufferings of the persecuted, to die under the character of being enemies to God; but there will be a resurrection of names as well as of bodies at the great day. <div eID="gen28200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28201" type="x-p"/> III. He gives them the true reason of the world's enmity and rage against them (<reference osisRef="John.16.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">These things will they do unto you,</hi> not because you have done them any harm, but <hi type="italic">because they have not known the Father, nor me.</hi> Let this comfort you, that none will be your enemies but the worst of men." Note, 1. Many that pretend to know God are wretchedly ignorant of him. Those that pretend to <hi type="italic">do him service</hi> thought they knew him, but it was a wrong notion they had of him. Israel transgressed the covenant, and yet cried, <hi type="italic">My God, we know thee.</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1-Hos.8.2">Hos. viii. 1, 2</reference>. 2. Those that are ignorant of Christ cannot have any right knowledge of God. In vain do men pretend to know God and religion, while they slight Christ and Christianity. 3. Those are very ignorant indeed of God and Christ that think it an acceptable piece of service to persecute good people. Those that know Christ know that he <hi type="italic">came not into the world to destroy men's lives, but to save them;</hi> that he rules by the power of truth and love, not of fire and sword. Never was such a persecuting church as that which makes <hi type="italic">ignorance the mother of devotion.</hi> <div eID="gen28201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28202" type="x-p"/> IV. He tells them why he gave them notice of this now, and why not sooner. <div eID="gen28202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28203" type="x-p"/> 1. Why he told them of it now (<reference osisRef="John.16.4">v. 4</reference>), not to discourage them, or add to their present sorrow; nor did he tell them of their danger that they might contrive how to avoid it, but that "when <hi type="italic">the time shall come</hi> (and you may be sure it will come), you may <hi type="italic">remember that I told you.</hi>" Note, When suffering times come it will be of use to us to remember what Christ has told us of sufferings. (1.) That our belief of Christ's foresight and faithfulness may be confirmed; and, (2.) That the trouble may be the less grievous, for we were told of it before, and we took up our profession in expectation of it, so that it ought not to be a surprise to us, nor looked upon as a wrong to us. As Christ in his sufferings, so his followers in theirs, should have an eye to the <hi type="italic">fulfilling of the scripture.</hi> <div eID="gen28203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28204" type="x-p"/> 2. Why he did not tell them of it sooner: "<hi type="italic">I spoke not this to you from the beginning</hi> when you and I came to be first acquainted, because <hi type="italic">I was with you.</hi>" (1.) While he was with them, he bore the shock of the world's malice, and stood in the front of the battle; against him the powers of darkness levelled all their force, not against <hi type="italic">small or great,</hi> but only against the <hi type="italic">king of Israel,</hi> and therefore he did not need to say so much to them of suffering, because it did not fall much to their share; but we do find that from the beginning he bade them prepare for sufferings; and therefore, (2.) It seems rather to be meant of the promise of <hi type="italic">another comforter.</hi> This he had said little of to them <hi type="italic">at the beginning,</hi> because he was himself with them to instruct, guide, and comfort them, and then they needed not the promise of the Spirit's extraordinary presence. The children of the bride-chamber would not have so much need of a comforter till the bridegroom should be <hi type="italic">taken away.</hi> <div eID="gen28204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28205" type="x-p"/> V. He expresses a very affectionate concern for the present sadness of his disciples, upon occasion of what he had said to them (<reference osisRef="John.16.5-John.16.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now</hi> I am to be no longer with you, but <hi type="italic">go my way to him that sent me,</hi> to repose there, after this fatigue; and <hi type="italic">none of you asketh me,</hi> with any courage, <hi type="italic">Whither goest thou?</hi> But, instead of enquiring after that which would comfort you, you pore upon that which looks melancholy, and <hi type="italic">sorrow has filled your heart.</hi>" <div eID="gen28205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28206" type="x-p"/> 1. He had told them that he was about to leave them: <hi type="italic">Now I go my way.</hi> He was not driven away by force, but voluntarily departed; his life was not extorted from him, but deposited by him. He went <hi type="italic">to him that sent him,</hi> to give an account of his negotiation. Thus, when we depart out of this world, we <hi type="italic">go to him that sent us</hi> into it, which should make us all solicitous to live to good purposes, remembering we have a commission to execute, which must be returned at a certain day. <div eID="gen28206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28207" type="x-p"/> 2. He had told them what hard times they must suffer when he was gone, and that they must not expect such an easy quiet life as they had had. Now, if these were the legacies he had to leave to them, who had <hi type="italic">left all</hi> for him, they would be tempted to think they had made a sorry bargain of it, and were, for the present, in a consternation about it, in which their master sympathizes with them, yet blames them, (1.) That they were careless of the means of comfort, and did not stir up themselves to seek it: <hi type="italic">None of you asks me, Whither goest thou?</hi> Peter had started this question (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">ch. xiii. 36</reference>), and Thomas had seconded it (<reference osisRef="John.14.5">ch. xiv. 5</reference>), but they did not pursue it, they did not take the answer; they were in the dark concerning it, and did not enquire further, nor seek for fuller satisfaction; they did not continue seeking, continue knocking. See what a compassionate teacher Christ is, and how condescending to the weak and ignorant. Many a teacher will not endure that the learner should ask the same question twice; if he cannot take a thing quickly, let him go without it; but our Lord Jesus knows how to deal with babes, that must be taught with <hi type="italic">precept upon precept.</hi> If the disciples here would have found that his going away was for his advancement, and therefore his departure from them should not inordinately trouble them (for why should they be against his preferment?) and for their advantage, and therefore their sufferings for him should not inordinately trouble them; for a sight of <hi type="italic">Jesus at the right hand of God</hi> would be an effectual support to them, as it was to Stephen. Note, A humble believing enquiry into the design and tendency of the darkest dispensations of Providence would help to reconcile us to them, and to grieve the less, and fear the less, because of them; it will silence us to ask, Whence came they? but will abundantly satisfy us to ask, Whither go they? for we know they <hi type="italic">work for good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Rom. viii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen28207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28208" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they were too intent, and pored too much, upon the occasions of their grief: <hi type="italic">Sorrow has filled their hearts.</hi> Christ had said enough to fill them with joy (<reference osisRef="John.15.11">ch. xv. 11</reference>); but by looking at that only which made against them, and overlooking that which made for them, they were so full of sorrow that there was no room left for joy. Note, It is the common fault and folly of melancholy Christians to dwell upon the dark side of the cloud, to meditate nothing but terror, and turn a deaf ear to <hi type="italic">the voice of joy and gladness.</hi> That which filled the disciples' hearts with sorrow, and hindered the operation of the cordials Christ administered, was too great an affection to this present life. They were big with hopes of their Master's external kingdom and glory, and that they should shine and reign with him: and now, instead of that, to hear of nothing but bonds and afflictions, this filled them with sorrow. Nothing is a greater prejudice to our joy in God than <hi type="italic">the love of the world;</hi> and <hi type="italic">the sorrow of the world,</hi> the consequence of it.

<div eID="gen28208" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Expediency of Christ's Departure; The Promise of the Spirit.</title> <div sID="gen28209" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you. <hi type="super">8</hi> And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment: <hi type="super">9</hi> Of sin, because they believe not on me; <hi type="super">10</hi> Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more; <hi type="super">11</hi> Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged. <hi type="super">12</hi> I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now. <hi type="super">13</hi> Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall he speak: and he will show you things to come. <hi type="super">14</hi> He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall show <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto you. <hi type="super">15</hi> All things that the Father hath are mine: therefore said I, that he shall take of mine, and shall show <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto you. <div eID="gen28209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28210" type="x-p"/> As it was usual with the Old Testament prophets to comfort the church in its calamities with the promise of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa. ix. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.6">Mic. v. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zech. iii. 8</reference>); so, the Messiah being come, the promise of the Spirit was the great cordial, and is still. <div eID="gen28210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28211" type="x-p"/> Three things we have here concerning <hi type="italic">the Comforter's coming:</hi>— <div eID="gen28211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28212" type="x-p"/> I. That Christ's departure was absolutely necessary to the Comforter's coming, <reference osisRef="John.16.7">v. 7</reference>. The disciples were so loth to believe this that Christ saw cause to assert it with a more than ordinary solemnity: <hi type="italic">I tell you the truth.</hi> We may be confident of <hi type="italic">the truth</hi> of everything that Christ told us; he has no design to impose upon us. Now, to make them easy, he here tells them, <div eID="gen28212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28213" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, <hi type="italic">It was expedient for them that he should go away.</hi> This was strange doctrine, but if it was true it was comfortable enough, and showed them how absurd their sorrow was. <hi type="italic">It is expedient,</hi> not only for me, but <hi type="italic">for you</hi> also, <hi type="italic">that I go away;</hi> though they did not see it, and are loth to believe it, so it is. Note, (1.) Those things often seem grievous to us that are really expedient for us; and particularly our going away when we have finished our course. (2.) Our Lord Jesus is always for that which is most expedient for us, whether we think so or no. He deals not with us according to the folly of our own choice, but graciously over-rules it, and gives us the physic we are loth to take, because he knows it is good for us. <div eID="gen28213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28214" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">It was therefore expedient</hi> because it was in order to the sending of the Spirit. Now observe, <div eID="gen28214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28215" type="x-p"/> (1.) That Christ's going was in order to the Comforter's coming. <div eID="gen28215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28216" type="x-p"/> [1.] This is expressed negatively: <hi type="italic">If I go not away, the Comforter will not come.</hi> And why not? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> So it was settled in the divine counsels concerning this affair, and the measure must not be altered; <hi type="italic">shall the earth be forsaken for them?</hi> He that gives freely may recall one gift before he bestows another, while we would fondly hold all. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is congruous enough that the ambassador extraordinary should be recalled, before the envoy come, that is constantly to reside. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The sending of the Spirit was to be the fruit of Christ's purchase, and that purchase was to be made by his death, which was his going away. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It was to be an answer to his intercession within the veil. See <reference osisRef="John.14.16">ch. xiv. 16</reference>. Thus must this gift be both paid for, and prayed for, by our Lord Jesus, that we might learn to put the greater value upon it. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The great argument the Spirit was to use in convincing the world must be Christ's ascension into heaven, and his welcome here. See <reference osisRef="John.16.10">v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.39">and ch. vii. 39</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The disciples must be weaned from his bodily presence, which they were too apt to dote upon, before they were duly prepared to receive the spiritual aids and comforts of a new dispensation. <div eID="gen28216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28217" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is expressed positively: <hi type="italic">If I depart I will send him to you;</hi> as though he had said, "Trust me to provide effectually that you shall be no loser by my departure." The glorified Redeemer is not unmindful of his church on earth, nor will ever leave it without its necessary supports. Though he <hi type="italic">departs, he sends the Comforter,</hi> nay, he departs on purpose to send him. Thus still, though one generation of ministers and Christians depart, another is raised up in their room, for Christ will maintain his own cause. <div eID="gen28217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28218" type="x-p"/> (2.) That the presence of Christ's Spirit in his church is so much better, and more desirable, than his bodily presence, that it was really expedient for us that he should go away, to send the Comforter. His corporal presence could be put in one place at one time, but his Spirit is every where, in all places, at all times, wherever <hi type="italic">two or three are gathered in his name.</hi> Christ's bodily presence draws men's eyes, his Spirit draws their hearts; that was <hi type="italic">the letter</hi> which <hi type="italic">kills,</hi> his <hi type="italic">Spirit gives life.</hi> <div eID="gen28218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28219" type="x-p"/> II. That the coming of <hi type="italic">the Spirit</hi> was absolutely necessary to the carrying on of Christ's interests on earth (<reference osisRef="John.16.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">And when he is come,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">elthon ekeinos</hi></hi>. He that is sent is willing of himself to come, and at his first coming he will do this, <hi type="italic">he will reprove,</hi> or, as the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">he will convince the world,</hi> by your ministry, concerning <hi type="italic">sin, righteousness, and judgment.</hi> <div eID="gen28219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28220" type="x-p"/> 1. See here what the office of the Spirit is, and on what errand he is sent. (1.) To <hi type="italic">reprove.</hi> The Spirit, by the word and conscience, is a reprover; ministers are reprovers by office, and by them the Spirit reproves. (2.) To <hi type="italic">convince.</hi> It is a law-term, and speaks the office of the judge in summing up the evidence, and setting a matter that has been long canvassed in a clear and true light. He shall <hi type="italic">convince,</hi> that is, "He shall put to silence the adversaries of Christ and his cause, by discovering and demonstrating the falsehood and fallacy of that which they have maintained, and the truth and certainty of that which they have opposed." Note, Convincing work is the Spirit's work; he can do it effectually, and none but he; man may open the cause, but it is the Spirit only that can open the heart. The Spirit is called the <hi type="italic">Comforter</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.7">v. 7</reference>), and here it is said, <hi type="italic">He shall convince.</hi> One would think this were cold comfort, but it is the method the Spirit takes, first to convince, and then to comfort; first to lay open the wound, and then to apply healing medicines. Or, taking conviction more generally, for a demonstration of what is right, it intimates that the Spirit's comforts are solid, and grounded upon truth. <div eID="gen28220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28221" type="x-p"/> 2. See who they are whom he is to reprove and convince: <hi type="italic">The world,</hi> both Jew and Gentile. (1.) He shall give the world the most powerful means of conviction, for the apostles shall go into all the world, backed by the Spirit, to preach the gospel, fully proved. (2.) He shall sufficiently provide for the taking off and silencing of the objections and prejudices of the world against the gospel. Many an infidel was <hi type="italic">convinced of all and judged of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24">1 Cor. xiv. 24</reference>. (3.) He shall effectually and savingly convince many in the world, some in every age, in every place, in order to their conversion to the faith of Christ. Now this was an encouragement to the disciples, in reference to the difficulties they were likely to meet with, [1.] That they should see good done, Satan's kingdom <hi type="italic">fall like lightning,</hi> which would be their joy, as it was his. Even this malignant world the Spirit shall work upon; and the conviction of sinners is the comfort of faithful ministers. [2.] That this would be the fruit of their services and sufferings, these should contribute very much to this good work. <div eID="gen28221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28222" type="x-p"/> 3. See what the Spirit shall convince the world of. <div eID="gen28222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28223" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Of sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">because they believe not on me.</hi> [1.] The Spirit is sent to convince sinners of sin, not barely to tell them of it; in conviction there is more than this; it is to prove it upon them, and force them to own it, as they (<reference osisRef="John.8.9">ch. viii. 9</reference>) that were <hi type="italic">convicted of their own consciences. Make them to know their abominations.</hi> The Spirit convinces of the fact of sin, that we have done so and so; of the fault of sin, that we have done ill in doing so; of the folly of sin, that we have acted against right reason, and our true interest; of the filth of sin, that by it we are become odious to God; of the fountain of sin, the corrupt nature; and lastly, of the fruit of sin, that the end thereof is death. The Spirit demonstrates the depravity and degeneracy of the whole world, that all the world is guilty before God. [2.] The Spirit, in conviction, fastens especially upon the sin of unbelief, their not believing in Christ, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As the great reigning sin. There was, and is, a world of people, that believe not in Jesus Christ, and they are not sensible that it is their sin. Natural conscience tells them that murder and theft are sin; but it is a supernatural work of the spirit to convince them that it is a sin to suspend their belief of the gospel, and to reject the salvation offered by it. Natural religion, after it has given us its best discoveries and directions, lays and leaves us under this further obligation, that whatever divine revelation shall be made to us at any time, with sufficient evidence to prove it divine, we accept it, and submit to it. This law those transgress who, when <hi type="italic">God speaketh to us by his Son, refuse him that speaketh;</hi> and therefore it is sin. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As the great ruining sin. Every sin is so in its own nature; no sin is so to them that believe in Christ; so that it is unbelief that damns sinners. It is because of this that they cannot <hi type="italic">enter into rest,</hi> that they cannot <hi type="italic">escape the wrath of God;</hi> it is a sin against the remedy. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> As that which is at the bottom of all sin; so Calvin takes it. The Spirit shall convince the world that the true reason why sin reigns among them is because they are not by faith united to Christ. <hi type="italic">Ne putimus vel guttam unam rectitudinis sine Christo nobis inesse—Let us not suppose that, apart from Christ, we have a drop of rectitude.</hi>—Calvin. <div eID="gen28223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28224" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and you see me no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.10">v. 10</reference>. We may understand this, [1.] Of Christ's personal righteousness. He shall convince the world that Jesus of Nazareth was Christ the righteous (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1 John ii. 1</reference>), as the centurion owned (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.47">Luke xxiii. 47</reference>), <hi type="italic">Certainly this was a righteous man.</hi> His enemies put him under the worst of characters, and multitudes were not or would not be convinced but that he was a bad man, which strengthened their prejudices against his doctrine; but he is <hi type="italic">justified by the spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>), he is proved to be a <hi type="italic">righteous man,</hi> and not, a deceiver; and then the point is in effect gained; for he is either the great Redeemer or a great cheat; but a cheat we are sure he is not. Now by what medium or argument will the Spirit convince men of the sincerity of the Lord Jesus? Why, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their <hi type="italic">seeing him no more</hi> will contribute something towards the removal of their prejudices; they shall see him no more <hi type="italic">in the likeness of sinful flesh, in the form of a servant,</hi> which made them slight him. Moses was more respected after his removal than before. But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His <hi type="italic">going to the Father</hi> would be a full conviction of it. The coming of the Spirit, according to the promise, was a proof of Christ's exaltation to God's <hi type="italic">right hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.33">Acts ii. 33</reference>), and this was a demonstration of his righteousness; for the holy God would never set a deceiver at his right hand. [2.] Of Christ's righteousness communicated to us for our justification and salvation; that everlasting righteousness which Messiah was to bring in, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The Spirit shall convince men of this righteousness. Having by convictions of sin shown them their need of a righteousness, lest this should drive them to despair he will show them where it is to be had, and how they may, upon their believing, be acquitted from guilt, and accepted as righteous in God's sight. It was hard to convince those of this righteousness that <hi type="italic">went about to establish their own</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Rom. x. 3</reference>), but the Spirit will do it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Christ's ascension is the great argument proper to convince men of this righteousness: <hi type="italic">I go to the Father, and,</hi> as an evidence of my welcome with him, <hi type="italic">you shall see me no more.</hi> If Christ had left any part of his undertaking unfinished, he had been sent back again; but now that we are sure he is <hi type="italic">at the right hand of God,</hi> we are sure of being justified through him. <div eID="gen28224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28225" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.11">v. 11</reference>. Observe here, [1.] The devil, <hi type="italic">the prince of this world,</hi> was judged, was discovered to be a great deceiver and destroyer, and as such judgment was entered against him, and execution in part done. He was cast out of the Gentile world when his oracles were silenced and his altars deserted, cast out of the bodies of many in Christ's name, which miraculous power continued long in the church; he was cast out of the souls of people by the grace of God working with the gospel of Christ; he <hi type="italic">fell as lightning from heaven.</hi> [2.] This is a good argument wherewith the Spirit convinces the world of judgment, that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of inherent holiness and sanctification, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.18">Matt. xii. 18</reference>. By <hi type="italic">the judgment of the prince of this world,</hi> it appears that Christ is stronger than Satan, and can disarm and dispossess him, and set up his throne upon the ruin of his. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of a new and better dispensation of things. He shall show that Christ's errand into the world was to set things to right in it, and to introduce times of reformation and regeneration; and he proves it by this, that <hi type="italic">the prince of this world,</hi> the great master of misrule, is judged and expelled. All will be well when his power is broken who made the mischief. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Of the power and dominion of the Lord Jesus. He shall convince the world that <hi type="italic">all judgment is committed to him,</hi> and that he is the <hi type="italic">Lord of all,</hi> which is evident by this, that he has judged the prince of this world, has broken <hi type="italic">the serpent's head, destroyed him that had the power of death, and spoiled principalities;</hi> if Satan be thus subdued by Christ, we may be sure no other power can stand before him. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Of the final day of judgment: all the obstinate enemies of Christ's gospel and kingdom shall certainly be reckoned with at last, for the devil, their ringleader, is judged. <div eID="gen28225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28226" type="x-p"/> III. That the coming of the Spirit would be of unspeakable advantage to the disciples themselves. The Spirit has work to do, not only on the enemies of Christ, to convince and humble them, but upon his servants and agents, to instruct and comfort them; and therefore it was <hi type="italic">expedient for them that he should go away.</hi> <div eID="gen28226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28227" type="x-p"/> 1. He intimates to them the tender sense he had of their present weakness (<reference osisRef="John.16.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have yet many things to say unto you</hi> (not which should have been said, but which he could and would have said), <hi type="italic">but you cannot bear them now.</hi> See what a teacher Christ is. (1.) None like him for copiousness; when he has said much, he has still many things more to say; treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in him, if we be not straitened in ourselves. (2.) None like him for compassion; he would have told them more of <hi type="italic">the things pertaining to the kingdom of God,</hi> particularly of the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, but they could not bear it, it would have confounded and stumbled them, rather than have given them any satisfaction. When, after his resurrection, they spoke to him of <hi type="italic">restoring the kingdom to Israel,</hi> he referred them to <hi type="italic">the coming of the Holy Ghost,</hi> by which they should receive power to bear those discoveries which were so contrary to the notions they had received that they could not <hi type="italic">bear them now.</hi> <div eID="gen28227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28228" type="x-p"/> 2. He assures them of sufficient assistances, by the pouring out of the Spirit. They were now conscious to themselves of great dulness, and many mistakes; and what shall they do now their master is leaving them? "<hi type="italic">But when he, the Spirit of Truth, is come,</hi> you will be easy, and all will be well." Well indeed; for he shall undertake to guide the apostles, and glorify Christ. <div eID="gen28228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28229" type="x-p"/> (1.) To guide the apostles. He will take care, <div eID="gen28229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28230" type="x-p"/> [1.] That they do not miss their way: <hi type="italic">He will guide you;</hi> as the camp of Israel was guided through the wilderness by <hi type="italic">the pillar of cloud and fire.</hi> The Spirit guided their tongues in speaking, and their pens in writing, to secure them from mistakes. The Spirit is given us to be our guide (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.14">Rom. viii. 14</reference>), not only to show us the way, but to go along with us, by his continued aids and influences. <div eID="gen28230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28231" type="x-p"/> [2.] That they do not come short of their end: <hi type="italic">He will guide them into all truth,</hi> as the skilful pilot guides the ship into the port it is bound for. To be led <hi type="italic">into a truth</hi> is more than barely to know it; it is to be intimately and experimentally acquainted with it; to be piously and strongly affected with it; not only to have the notion of it in our heads, but the relish and savour and power of it in our hearts; it denotes a gradual discovery of truth shining more and more: "He shall lead you by those truths that are plain and easy to those that are more difficult." But how into <hi type="italic">all truth?</hi> The meaning is, <div eID="gen28231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Into the whole truth relating to their embassy; whatever was needful or useful for them to know, in order to the due discharge of their office, they should be fully instructed in it; what truths they were to teach others the Spirit would teach them, would give them the understanding of, and enable them both to explain and to defend. <div eID="gen28232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28233" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Into nothing but the truth. All that <hi type="italic">he shall guide you into</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1 John ii. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">the anointing is truth.</hi> In the following words he proves both these:—1. "The Spirit shall teach nothing but the truth, <hi type="italic">for he shall not speak of himself</hi> any doctrine distinct from mine, <hi type="italic">but whatsoever he shall hear,</hi> and knows to be the mind of the Father, <hi type="italic">that,</hi> and that only, <hi type="italic">shall he speak.</hi>" This intimates, (1.) That the testimony of the Spirit, in the word and by the apostles, is what we may rely upon. The <hi type="italic">Spirit</hi> knows <hi type="italic">and searches all things, even the deep things of God,</hi> and the apostles received that Spirit (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10-1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 10, 11</reference>), so that we may venture our souls upon the Spirit's word. (2.) That the testimony of the Spirit always concurs with the word of Christ, <hi type="italic">for he does not speak of himself,</hi> has no separate interest or intention of his own, but, as in essence so in records, he <hi type="italic">is one with the Father and the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">1 John v. 7</reference>. Men's word and spirit often disagree, but the eternal Word and the eternal Spirit never do. 2. "He shall teach you all truth, and keep back nothing that is profitable for you, for <hi type="italic">he will show you things to come.</hi>" The Spirit was in the apostles a Spirit of prophecy; it was foretold that he should be so (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joel ii. 28</reference>), and he was so. <hi type="italic">The Spirit showed them things to come,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Acts.11.28">Acts xi. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.23">xx. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.11">xxi. 11</reference>. The Spirit spoke of the apostasy of the <hi type="italic">latter times,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1 Tim. iv. 1</reference>. John, when he was in the Spirit had <hi type="italic">things to come</hi> shown him in vision. Now this was a great satisfaction to their own minds, and of use to them in their conduct, and was also a great confirmation of their mission. Jansenius has a pious note upon this: We should not grudge that the Spirit does not <hi type="italic">show us things to come</hi> in this world, as he did to the apostles; let it suffice that the Spirit in the word hath <hi type="italic">shown us things to come</hi> in the other world, which are our chief concern. <div eID="gen28233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28234" type="x-p"/> (2.) The Spirit undertook to glorify Christ, <reference osisRef="John.16.14-John.16.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. [1.] Even the sending of the Spirit was the glorifying of Christ. God the Father glorified him in heaven, and the Spirit glorified him on earth. It was the honour of the Redeemer that the Spirit was both sent in his name and sent on his errand, to carry on and perfect his undertaking. All the gifts and graces of the Spirit, all the preaching and all the writing of the apostles, under the influence of the Spirit, the tongues, and miracles, were to glorify Christ. [2.] The Spirit glorified Christ by leading his followers into <hi type="italic">the truth as it is in Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Eph. iv. 21</reference>. He assures them, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> that the Spirit should communicate the things of Christ to them: <hi type="italic">He shall receive of mine, and shall show it unto you.</hi> As in essence <hi type="italic">he proceeded from the Son,</hi> so in influence and operation he derived from him. <hi type="italic">He shall take</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek tou emou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of that which is mine.</hi> All that the Spirit shows us, that is, applies to us, for our instruction and comfort, all that he gives us for our strength and quickening, and all that he secures and seals to us, did all belong to Christ, and was had and received from him. All was his, for he bought it, and paid dearly for it, and therefore he had reason to call it his own; his, for he first received it; it was given him as the head of the church, to be communicated by him to all his members. The Spirit came not to erect a new kingdom, but to advance and establish the same kingdom that Christ had erected, to maintain the same interest and pursue the same design; those therefore that pretend to the Spirit, and vilify Christ, give themselves the lie, for he came to glorify Christ. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That herein the things of God should be communicated to us. Lest any should think that the receiving of this would not make them much the richer, he adds, <hi type="italic">All things that the Father hath are mine.</hi> As God, all that self-existent light and self-sufficient happiness which <hi type="italic">the Father has,</hi> he has; as Mediator, <hi type="italic">all things are delivered to him of the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>); all that <hi type="italic">grace and truth</hi> which God designed to show us he lodged in the hands of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col. i. 19</reference>. Spiritual blessings in heavenly things are given by the Father to the Son for us, and the Son entrusts the Spirit to convey them to us. Some apply it to that which goes just before: <hi type="italic">He shall show you things to come,</hi> and so it is explained by <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>. God gave <hi type="italic">it to Christ, and he signified it to John, who wrote what the Spirit said,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>.

<div eID="gen28234" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Departure and Return; Sorrow and Joy Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen28235" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to the Father. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then said <hi type="italic">some</hi> of his disciples among themselves, What is this that he saith unto us, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me: and, Because I go to the Father? <hi type="super">18</hi> They said therefore, What is this that he saith, A little while? we cannot tell what he saith. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him, and said unto them, Do ye enquire among yourselves of that I said, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me? <hi type="super">20</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy. <hi type="super">21</hi> A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world. <hi type="super">22</hi> And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you. <div eID="gen28235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28236" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus, for the comfort of his sorrowful disciples, here promises that he would visit them again. <div eID="gen28236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28237" type="x-p"/> I. Observe the intimation he gave them of the comfort he designed them, <reference osisRef="John.16.16">v. 16</reference>. Here he tells them, <div eID="gen28237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28238" type="x-p"/> 1. That they should now shortly lose the sight of him: <hi type="italic">A little while, and you</hi> that have seen me so long, and still desire to <hi type="italic">see me, shall not see me;</hi> and therefore, if they had any good question to ask him, they must ask quickly, for he was now taking his leave of them. Note, It is good to consider how near to a period our seasons of grace are, that we may be quickened to improve them while they are continued. Now our eyes see our teachers, see the days <hi type="italic">of the Son of man;</hi> but, perhaps, yet a <hi type="italic">little while, and we shall not see them.</hi> They lost the sight of Christ, (1.) At his death, when he withdrew from this world, and never after showed himself openly in it. The most that death does to our Christian friends is to take them out of our sight, not out of being, not out of bliss, but out of all relation to us, only out of sight, and then not out of mind. (2.) At his ascension, when he withdrew from them (from those who, after his resurrection, had for some time conversed with him), <hi type="italic">out of their sight; a cloud received</hi> him, and, though they looked up steadfastly after him, <hi type="italic">they saw him no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.9-Acts.1.10">Acts i. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.12">2 Kings ii. 12</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">2 Cor. v. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen28238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28239" type="x-p"/> 2. That yet they should speedily recover the sight of him; <hi type="italic">Again a little while, and you shall see me,</hi> and therefore you ought not to <hi type="italic">sorrow as those that have no hope.</hi> His farewell was not a final farewell; they should see him again, (1.) At his resurrection, soon after his death, when <hi type="italic">he showed himself alive,</hi> by many infallible proofs, and this in a very little while, not forty hours. See <reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Hos. vi. 2</reference>. (2.) By the pouring out of the Spirit, soon after his ascension, which scattered the mists of ignorance and mistake they were almost lost in, and gave them a much clearer insight into the mysteries of Christ's gospel than they had yet had. The Spirit's coming was Christ's visit to his disciples, not a transient but a permanent one, and such a visit as abundantly retrieved the sight of him. (3.) At his second coming. They saw him again as they removed one by one to him at death, and they shall see him together at the end of time, when <hi type="italic">he shall come in the clouds, and every eye shall see him.</hi> It might be truly said of this that it was but <hi type="italic">a little while, and they should see him;</hi> for what are the days of time, to the days of eternity? <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8-2Pet.3.9">2 Pet. iii. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen28239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28240" type="x-p"/> 3. He assigns the reason: "<hi type="italic">Because I go to the Father;</hi> and therefore," (1.) "I must leave you for a time, because my business calls me to the upper world, and you must be content to spare me, for really my business is yours." (2.) "Therefore you shall see me again shortly, for the Father will not detain me to your prejudice. If I go upon your errand, you shall see me again as soon as my business is done, as soon as is convenient." <div eID="gen28240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28241" type="x-p"/> It should seem, all this refers rather to his going away at death, and return at his resurrection, than his going away at the ascension, and his return at the end of time; for it was his death that was their grief, not his ascension (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.52">Luke xxiv. 52</reference>), and between his death and resurrection it was indeed a <hi type="italic">little while.</hi> And it may be read, not, <hi type="italic">yet a little while</hi> (it is not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eti mikron</hi></hi>, as it is <reference osisRef="John.12.35">ch. xii. 35</reference>), but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mikron</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for a little while you shall not see me,</hi> namely, the three days of his lying in the grave; and again, <hi type="italic">for a little while you shall see me,</hi> namely, the forty days between his resurrection and ascension. Thus we may say of our ministers and Christian friends, <hi type="italic">Yet a little while, and we shall not see them,</hi> either they must leave us or we must leave them, but it is certain that we must part shortly, and yet not part for ever. It is but a good night to those whom we hope to see with <hi type="italic">joy in the morning.</hi> <div eID="gen28241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28242" type="x-p"/> II. The perplexity of the disciples upon the intimation given them; they were at a loss what to make of it (<reference osisRef="John.16.17-John.16.18">v. 17, 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">Some of them said,</hi> softly, <hi type="italic">among themselves,</hi> either some of the weakest, that were least able, or some of the most inquisitive, that were most desirous, to understand him, <hi type="italic">What is this that he saith to us?</hi> Though Christ had often spoken to this purport before, yet still they were in the dark; though <hi type="italic">precept be upon precept,</hi> it is in vain, unless God gave the understanding. Now see here, 1. The disciples' weakness, in that they could not understand so plain a saying, to which Christ had already given them a key, having told them so often in plain terms that he should <hi type="italic">be killed, and the third day rise again;</hi> yet, say they, <hi type="italic">We cannot tell what he saith;</hi> for, (1.) <hi type="italic">Sorrow had filled their heart,</hi> and made them unapt to receive the impressions of comfort. The darkness of ignorance and the darkness of melancholy commonly increase and thicken one another; mistakes cause griefs, and then griefs confirm mistakes. (2.) The notion of Christ's secular kingdom was so deeply rooted in them that they could make no sense at all of those sayings of his which they knew not how to reconcile with that notion. When we think the scripture must be made to agree with the false ideas we have imbibed, no wonder that we complain of difficulty; but when our reasonings are captivated to revelation, the matter becomes easy. (3.) It should seem, that which puzzled them was the <hi type="italic">little while.</hi> If he must go at least, yet they could not conceive how he should leave them quickly, when his stay hitherto had been so short, and so little while, comparatively. Thus it is hard for us to represent to ourselves that change as near which yet we know will come certainly, and may come suddenly. When we are told, <hi type="italic">Yet a little while</hi> and we must go hence, <hi type="italic">yet a little while</hi> and we must <hi type="italic">give up our account,</hi> we know not how to digest it; for we always took the vision to be <hi type="italic">for a great while to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">Ezek. xii. 27</reference>. 2. Their willingness to be instructed. When they were at a loss about the meaning of Christ's words, they conferred together upon it, and asked help of one another. By mutual converse about divine things we both borrow the light of others and improve our own. Observe how exactly they repeat Christ's words. Though we cannot fully solve every difficulty we meet with in scripture, yet we must not therefore throw it by, but revolve what we cannot explain, and wait <hi type="italic">till God shall reveal even this unto us.</hi> <div eID="gen28242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28243" type="x-p"/> III. The further explication of what Christ had said. <div eID="gen28243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28244" type="x-p"/> 1. See here <hi type="italic">why</hi> Christ explained it (<reference osisRef="John.16.19">v. 19</reference>); because he <hi type="italic">knew they were desirous to ask him,</hi> and designed it. Note, The knots we cannot untie we must bring to him who alone can give an understanding. Christ <hi type="italic">knew they were desirous to ask him,</hi> but were bashful and ashamed to ask. Note, Christ takes cognizance of pious desires, though they be not as yet offered up, the <hi type="italic">groanings that cannot be uttered,</hi> and even <hi type="italic">anticipates them with the blessings of his goodness.</hi> Christ instructed those who he <hi type="italic">knew were desirous to ask him,</hi> though they did not ask. <hi type="italic">Before we call, he answers.</hi> Another reason why Christ explained it was because he observed them canvassing this matter among themselves: "<hi type="italic">Do you enquire this among yourselves?</hi> Well, I will make it easy to you." This intimates to us who they are that Christ will teach: (1.) The humble, that confess their ignorance, for so much their enquiry implied. (2.) The diligent, that use the means they have: "<hi type="italic">Do you enquire?</hi> You shall be taught. <hi type="italic">To him that hath shall be given.</hi>" <div eID="gen28244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28245" type="x-p"/> 2. See here <hi type="italic">how</hi> he explained it; not by a nice and critical descant upon the words, but by bringing the thing more closely to them; he had told them of <hi type="italic">not seeing him, and seeing him,</hi> and they did not apprehend the meaning, and therefore he explains it by their sorrowing and rejoicing, because we commonly measure things according as they affect us (<reference osisRef="John.16.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall weep and lament,</hi> for my departure, <hi type="italic">but the world shall rejoice</hi> in it; <hi type="italic">and you shall be sorrowful,</hi> while I am absent, <hi type="italic">but,</hi> upon my return to you, <hi type="italic">your sorrow will be turned into joy.</hi> But he says nothing of the <hi type="italic">little while,</hi> because he saw that this perplexed them more than any thing; and it is of no consequence to us to know <hi type="italic">the times and the seasons.</hi> Note, Believers have joy or sorrow according as they have or have not a sight of Christ, and the tokens of his presence with them. <div eID="gen28245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28246" type="x-p"/> (1.) What Christ says here, and in <reference osisRef="John.16.21-John.16.22">v. 21, 22</reference>, of their sorrow and joy, is primarily to be understood of the present state and circumstances of the disciples, and so we have, <div eID="gen28246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28247" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their grief foretold: <hi type="italic">You shall weep and lament, and you shall be sorrowful.</hi> The sufferings of Christ could not but be the sorrow of his disciples. They wept for him because they loved him; the pain of our friend is a pain to ourselves; when they slept, it was for sorrow, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.45">Luke xxii. 45</reference>. They wept for themselves, and their own loss, and the sad apprehensions they had of what would become of them when he was gone. It could not but be a grief to lose him for whom they had left their all, and from whom they had expected so much. Christ has given notice to his disciples beforehand to expect sorrow, that they may treasure up comforts accordingly. <div eID="gen28247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28248" type="x-p"/> [2.] The world's rejoicing at the same time: <hi type="italic">But the world shall rejoice.</hi> That which is the grief of saints is the joy of sinners. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those that are <hi type="italic">strangers to Christ</hi> will continue in their carnal mirth, and not at all interest themselves in their sorrows. <hi type="italic">It is nothing to them that pass by,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">Lam. i. 12</reference>. Nay, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that are <hi type="italic">enemies to Christ</hi> will rejoice because they hope they have conquered him, and ruined his interest. When the chief priests had Christ upon the cross, we may suppose they made merry over him, as those that dwell on earth over the slain witnesses, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. Let it be no surprise to us if we see others triumphing, when we are <hi type="italic">trembling for the ark.</hi> <div eID="gen28248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28249" type="x-p"/> [3.] The return of joy to them in due time: <hi type="italic">But your sorrow shall be turned into joy.</hi> As <hi type="italic">the joy of the hypocrite,</hi> so the sorrow of the true Christian, is <hi type="italic">but for a moment. The disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.</hi> His resurrection was <hi type="italic">life from the dead</hi> to them, and their sorrow for Christ's sufferings was turned into a joy of such a nature as could not be damped and embittered by any sufferings of their own. They were <hi type="italic">sorrowful, and yet always rejoicing</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>), had sorrowful lives and yet joyful hearts. <div eID="gen28249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28250" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is applicable to all the faithful followers of the Lamb, and describes the common case of Christians. <div eID="gen28250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28251" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their condition and disposition are both mournful; sorrows are their lot, and seriousness is their temper: those that are acquainted with Christ must, as he was, be <hi type="italic">acquainted with grief;</hi> they <hi type="italic">weep and lament</hi> for that which others make light of, their own sins, and the sins of those about them; they mourn with sufferers that mourn, and mourn for sinners that mourn not for themselves. <div eID="gen28251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28252" type="x-p"/> [2.] The world, at the same time, goes away with all the mirth; they laugh now, and spend their days so jovially that one would think they neither knew sorrow nor feared it. Carnal mirth and pleasures are surely none of the best things, for then the worst men would not have so large a share of them, and the favourites of heaven be such strangers to them. <div eID="gen28252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28253" type="x-p"/> [3.] Spiritual mourning will shortly be turned into eternal rejoicing. <hi type="italic">Gladness is sown for the upright in heart, that sow tears,</hi> and without doubt <hi type="italic">they will</hi> shortly <hi type="italic">reap in joy.</hi> Their sorrow will not only be followed with joy, but turned into it; for the most precious comforts take rise from pious griefs. Thus he illustrates by a similitude taken from a woman in travail, to whose sorrows he compares those of his disciples, for their encouragement; for it is the will of Christ that his people should be a comforted people. <div eID="gen28253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28254" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Here is the similitude or parable itself (<reference osisRef="John.16.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">A woman,</hi> we know, <hi type="italic">when she is in travail, hath sorrow,</hi> she is in exquisite pain, <hi type="italic">because her hour is come,</hi> the hour which nature and providence have fixed, which she has expected, and cannot escape; <hi type="italic">but as soon as she is delivered of the child,</hi> provided she be safely delivered, and the child be, though a <hi type="italic">Jabez</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.9">1 Chron. iv. 9</reference>), yet not a <hi type="italic">Benoni</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.18">Gen. xxxv. 18</reference>), then <hi type="italic">she remembers no more the anguish,</hi> her groans and complaints are over, and the after—pains are more easily borne, <hi type="italic">for joy that a man is born into the world,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anthropos</hi></hi>, one of the human race, a child, be it son or daughter, for the word signifies either. Observe, <div eID="gen28254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> The fruit of the curse, in the sorrow and pain of a woman in travail, according to the sentence (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">In sorrow shalt thou bring forth.</hi> These pains are extreme, the greatest griefs and pains are compared to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.6">Ps. xlviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Isa. xiii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.31">Jer. iv. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">vi. 24</reference>), and they are inevitable, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1 Thess. v. 3</reference>. See what this world is; all its roses are surrounded with thorns, all the children of men are upon this account foolish children, that they are <hi type="italic">the heaviness of her that bore them</hi> from the very first. This comes of sin. <div eID="gen28255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28256" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> The fruit of the blessing, in <hi type="italic">the joy there is for a child born into the world.</hi> If God had not preserved the blessing in force after the fall, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful and multiply,</hi> parents could never have looked upon their children with any comfort; but what is the fruit of a blessing is matter of joy; the birth of a living child is, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The parents' joy; it makes them very glad, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.15">Jer. xx. 15</reference>. Though children are certain cares, uncertain comforts, and often prove the greatest crosses, yet it is natural to us to rejoice at their birth. Could we be sure that our children, like John, would <hi type="italic">be filled with the Holy Ghost,</hi> we might, indeed, like his parents, have <hi type="italic">joy and gladness</hi> in their birth, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.14-Luke.1.15">Luke i. 14, 15</reference>. But when we consider, not only that they are born in sin, but, as it is expressed, that <hi type="italic">they are born into the world,</hi> a world of snares and a vale of tears, we shall see reason to rejoice with trembling, lest it should prove <hi type="italic">better for them that they had never been born.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It is such joy as makes the anguish not to be remembered, or <hi type="italic">remembered as waters that pass away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.16">Job xi. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Hæc olim meminisse juvabit.</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.41.51">Gen. xli. 51</reference>. Now this is very proper to set forth, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] The sorrows of Christ's disciples in this world; they are like travailing pains, sure and sharp, but not to last long, and in order to a joyful product; they are in <hi type="italic">pain to be delivered,</hi> as the church is described (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.2">Rev. xii. 2</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the whole creation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>. And, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Their joys after these sorrows, which will <hi type="italic">wipe away all tears,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the former things are passed away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Rev. xxi. 4</reference>. When they are born into that blessed world, and reap the fruit of all their services and sorrows, the toil and anguish of this world will be no more remembered, as Christ's were not, when <hi type="italic">he saw of the travail of his soul</hi> abundantly to his satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen28256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28257" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The application of the similitude (<reference osisRef="John.16.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You now have sorrow,</hi> and are likely to have more, <hi type="italic">but I will see you again,</hi> and you me, and then all will be well." <div eID="gen28257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28258" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Here again he tells them of their <hi type="italic">sorrow: "You now therefore have sorrow; therefore,</hi> because I am leaving you," as is intimated in the antithesis, <hi type="italic">I will see you again.</hi> Note, Christ's withdrawings are just cause of grief to his disciples. <hi type="italic">If he hide his face,</hi> they cannot be <hi type="italic">troubled.</hi> When the sun sets, the sun-flower will hang the head. And Christ takes notice of these griefs, has a bottle for the tears, and a book for the sighs, of all gracious mourners. <div eID="gen28258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28259" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> He, more largely than before, assures them of a return of joy, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Ps. xxx. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.11">11</reference>. He himself went through his own griefs, and bore ours, <hi type="italic">for the joy that was set before him;</hi> and he would have us encourage ourselves with the same prospect. Three things recommend the joy:—(<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The cause of it: "<hi type="italic">I will see you again.</hi> I will make you a kind and friendly visit, to enquire after you, and minister comfort to you." Note, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Christ will graciously return to those that wait for him, though <hi type="italic">for a small moment</hi> he has seemed <hi type="italic">to forsake them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.7">Isa. liv. 7</reference>. Men, when they are exalted, will scarcely look upon their inferiors; but the exalted Jesus will visit his disciples. They shall not only see him in his glory, but he will see them in their meanness. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Christ's returns are returns of joy to all his disciples. When clouded evidences are cleared up and interrupted communion is revived, <hi type="italic">then is the mouth filled with laughter.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The cordiality of it: <hi type="italic">Your heart shall rejoice.</hi> Divine consolation <hi type="italic">put gladness into the heart.</hi> Joy in the heart is solid, and not flashy; it is secret, and that which a <hi type="italic">stranger does not intermeddle with;</hi> it is sweet, and gives a good man satisfaction in himself; it is sure, and not easily broken in upon. Christ's disciples should heartily rejoice in his returns, sincerely and greatly. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) The continuance of it: <hi type="italic">Your joy no man taketh from you.</hi> Men will attempt to take their joy from them; they would if they could; but they shall not prevail. Some understand it of the eternal joy of those that are glorified; those that have <hi type="italic">entered into the joy of the Lord shall go no more out.</hi> Our joys on earth we are liable to be robbed of by a thousand accidents, but heavenly joys are everlasting. I rather understand it of the spiritual joys of those that are sanctified, particularly the apostles' joy in their apostleship. <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God,</hi> says Paul, in the name of the rest, <hi type="italic">who always causes us to triumph,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. A malicious world would have taken it from them, they would have lost it; but, when they took everything else from them, they could not take this; <hi type="italic">as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.</hi> They could not rob them of their joy, because they could not <hi type="italic">separate them from the love of Christ,</hi> could not rob them of their God, nor of their <hi type="italic">treasure in heaven.</hi>

<div eID="gen28259" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28260" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And in that day ye shall ask me nothing.
