Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give <hi type="italic">it</hi> you. <hi type="super">24</hi> Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full. <hi type="super">25</hi> These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall show you plainly of the Father. <hi type="super">26</hi> At that day ye shall ask in my name: and I say not unto you, that I will pray the Father for you: <hi type="super">27</hi> For the Father himself loveth you, because ye have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God. <div eID="gen28260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28261" type="x-p"/> An answer to their askings is here promised, for their further comfort. Now there are two ways of asking: asking by way of enquiry, which is the asking of the ignorant; and asking by way of request, which is the asking of the indigent. Christ here speaks of both. <div eID="gen28261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28262" type="x-p"/> I. By way of enquiry, they should not need to ask (<reference osisRef="John.16.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In that day you shall ask me nothing;</hi>" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk erotesete ouden</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">you shall ask no questions;</hi> "you shall have such a clear knowledge of gospel mysteries, by the opening of your understandings, that you shall not need to enquire" (as <reference osisRef="Heb.8.11">Heb. viii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">they shall not teach</hi>); "you shall have more knowledge on a sudden than hitherto you have had by diligent attendance." They had asked some ignorant questions (as <reference osisRef="John.9.2">ch. ix. 2</reference>), some ambitious questions (as <reference osisRef="Matt.18.1">Matt. xviii. 1</reference>), some distrustful ones (as <reference osisRef="Matt.19.27">Matt. xix. 27</reference>), some impertinent ones, (as <reference osisRef="John.21.21">ch. xxi. 21</reference>), some curious ones (as <reference osisRef="Acts.1.6">Acts i. 6</reference>); but after the Spirit was poured out, nothing of all this. In the story <hi type="italic">of the apostles' Acts</hi> we seldom find them asking questions, as David, <hi type="italic">Shall I do this?</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">Shall I go thither?</hi> For they were constantly under a divine guidance. In that weighty case of preaching <hi type="italic">the gospel to the Gentiles,</hi> Peter went, <hi type="italic">nothing doubting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.20">Acts x. 20</reference>. Asking questions supposes us at a loss, or at least at a stand, and the best of us have need to ask questions; but we should aim at such a full assurance of understanding that we may not hesitate, but be constantly led in a plain path both of truth and duty. <div eID="gen28262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28263" type="x-p"/> Now for this he gives a reason (<reference osisRef="John.16.25">v. 25</reference>), which plainly refers to this promise, that they should not need to ask questions: "<hi type="italic">These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs,</hi> in such a way as you have thought not so plain and intelligible as you could have wished, <hi type="italic">but the time cometh when I shall show you plainly,</hi> as plainly as you can desire, <hi type="italic">of the Father,</hi> so that you shall not need to ask questions." <div eID="gen28263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28264" type="x-p"/> 1. The great thing Christ would lead them into was the knowledge of God: "<hi type="italic">I will show you the Father,</hi> and bring you acquainted with him." This is that which Christ designs to give and which all true Christians desire to have. When Christ would express the greatest favour intended for his disciples, he tells them that it would, <hi type="italic">show them plainly of the Father;</hi> for what is the happiness of heaven, but immediately and everlastingly to see God? <hi type="italic">To know God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> is the greatest mystery for the understanding to please itself with the contemplation of; and to know him as our Father is the greatest happiness for the will and affections to please themselves with the choice and enjoyment of. <div eID="gen28264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28265" type="x-p"/> 2. Of this he had hitherto spoken to them in proverbs, which are wise and instructive sayings, but figurative, and resting in generals. Christ had spoken many things very plainly to them, and expounded his parables privately to the disciples, but, (1.) Considering their dulness, and unaptness to receive what he said to them, he might be said to speak in proverbs; what he said to them was as a book sealed, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.11">Isa. xxix. 11</reference>. (2.) Comparing the discoveries he had made to them, in what he had spoken to their ears, with what he would make to them when he would <hi type="italic">put his Spirit into their heart,</hi> all hitherto had been proverbs. It would be a pleasing surprise to themselves, and they would think themselves in a new world, when they would reflect upon all their former notions as confused and enigmatical, compared with their present clear and distinct knowledge of divine things. <hi type="italic">The ministration of the letter</hi> was nothing to <hi type="italic">that of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8-2Cor.3.11">2 Cor. iii. 8-11</reference>. (3.) Confining it to what he had said of <hi type="italic">the Father,</hi> and the counsels of <hi type="italic">the Father.</hi> what he had said was very dark, compared with what was shortly to be revealed, <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col. ii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen28265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28266" type="x-p"/> 3. He would speak to them <hi type="italic">plainly,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parresia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with freedom,</hi> of the Father. When the Spirit was poured out, the apostles attained to a much greater knowledge of divine things than they had before, as appears by the utterance the Spirit gave them, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.4">Acts ii. 4</reference>. They were led into the mystery of those things of which they had previously a very confused idea; and what the Spirit showed them Christ is here said to show them, for, as the Father speaks by the Son, so the Son by the Spirit. But this promise will have its full accomplishment in heaven, where we shall see the Father as he is, <hi type="italic">face to face,</hi> not as we do now, <hi type="italic">through a glass darkly</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1 Cor. xiii. 12</reference>), which is matter of comfort to us under the cloud of present darkness, by reason of which we cannot <hi type="italic">order our speech,</hi> but often disorder it. While we are here, we have many questions to ask concerning the invisible God and the invisible world; but in that day we shall see all things clearly, and <hi type="italic">ask no more questions.</hi> <div eID="gen28266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28267" type="x-p"/> II. He promises that by way of request they should ask nothing in vain. it is taken for granted that all Christ's disciples give themselves to prayer. He has taught them by his precept and pattern to be much in prayer; this must be their support and comfort when he had left them; their instruction, direction, strength, and success, must be fetched in by prayer. Now, <div eID="gen28267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28268" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is an express promise of a grant, <reference osisRef="John.16.23">v. 23</reference>. The preface to this promise is such as makes it inviolably sure, and leaves no room to question it: "<hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you,</hi> I pledge my veracity upon it." The promise itself is incomparably rich and sweet; the golden sceptre is here held out to us, with the word, <hi type="italic">What is thy petition, and it shall be granted?</hi> For he says, <hi type="italic">Whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it to you.</hi> We had it before, <reference osisRef="John.14.13">ch. xiv. 13</reference>. What would we more? The promise is as express as we can desire. (1.) We are here taught how to seek; we must <hi type="italic">ask the Father in Christ's name;</hi> we must have an eye to God as a Father, and come as children to him; and to Christ as Mediator, and come as clients. Asking of the Father includes a sense of spiritual blessings, with a conviction that they are to be had from God only. It included also humility of address to him, with a believing confidence in him, as a Father able and ready to help us. Asking in Christ's name includes an acknowledgment of our own unworthiness to receive any favour from God, a complacency in the method God has taken of keeping up a correspondence with us by his Son, and an entire dependence upon Christ as <hi type="italic">the Lord our Righteousness.</hi> (2.) We are here told how we shall speed: <hi type="italic">He will give it to you.</hi> What more can we wish for than to have what we want, nay, to have what we will, in conformity to God's will, for the asking? He <hi type="italic">will give it to you</hi> from whom <hi type="italic">proceedeth every good and perfect gift.</hi> What Christ purchased by the merit of his death, he needed not for himself, but intended it for, and consigned it to, his faithful followers; and having given a valuable consideration for it, which was accepted in full, by this promise he draws a bill as it were upon the treasury in heaven, which we are to present by prayer, and <hi type="italic">in his name</hi> to ask for that which is purchased and promised, according to the true intent of the new covenant. Christ had promised them great illumination by the Spirit, but they must pray for it, and did so, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.14">Acts i. 14</reference>. God will for this be enquired of. He had promised them perfection hereafter, but what shall they do in the mean time? They must continue praying. Perfect fruition is reserved for the land of our rest; asking and receiving are the comfort of the land of our pilgrimage. <div eID="gen28268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28269" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is an invitation for them to petition. It is thought sufficient if great men permit addresses, but Christ calls upon us to petition, <reference osisRef="John.16.24">v. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen28269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28270" type="x-p"/> (1.) He looks back upon their practice hitherto: <hi type="italic">Hitherto have you asked nothing in my name.</hi> This refers either [1.] To the matter of their prayers: "You have asked nothing comparatively, nothing to what you might have asked, and will ask when the Spirit is poured out." See what a generous benefactor our Lord Jesus is, above all benefactors; he gives liberally, and is so far from upbraiding us with the frequency and largeness of his gifts that he rather upbraids us with the seldomness and straitness of our requests: "<hi type="italic">You have asked nothing</hi> in comparison of what you want, and what I have to give, and have promised to give." We are told to <hi type="italic">open our mouth wide.</hi> Or, [2.] To the name in which they prayed. They prayed many a prayer, but never so expressly in the name of Christ as now he was directing them to do; for he had not as yet offered up that great sacrifice in the virtue of which our prayers were to be accepted, nor entered upon his intercession for us, the incense whereof was to perfume all our devotions, and so enable us to pray in his name. Hitherto they had cast out devils, and healed diseases, in the name of Christ, as a king and a prophet, but they could not as yet distinctly pray in his name as a priest. <div eID="gen28270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28271" type="x-p"/> (2.) He looks forward to their practice for the future: <hi type="italic">Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.</hi> Here, [1.] He directs them to ask for all that they needed and he had promised. [2.] He assures them that they shall <hi type="italic">receive.</hi> What we ask from a principle of grace God will graciously give: <hi type="italic">You shall receive it.</hi> There is something more in this than the promise that he will give it. He will not only give it, but give you to receive it, give you the comfort and benefit of it, <hi type="italic">a heart to eat of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Eccl. vi. 2</reference>. [3.] That hereby <hi type="italic">their joy shall be full.</hi> This denotes, <hi type="italic">First.</hi> The blessed effect of the <hi type="italic">prayer of faith;</hi> it helps to fill up the <hi type="italic">joy of faith.</hi> Would we have our joy full, as full as it is capable of being in this world, we must be <hi type="italic">much in prayer.</hi> When we are told to <hi type="italic">rejoice evermore,</hi> it follows immediately, <hi type="italic">Pray without ceasing.</hi> See how high we are to aim in prayer—not only at peace, but joy, a <hi type="italic">fulness of joy.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The blessed effects of the <hi type="italic">answer of peace:</hi> "Ask, and you shall receive that which will <hi type="italic">fill your joy.</hi>" God's gifts, through Christ, fill the treasures of the soul, they fill its joy, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>. "Ask for the gift of the Holy Ghost, and you shall receive it; and whereas other knowledge <hi type="italic">increaseth sorrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">Eccl. i. 18</reference>), the knowledge he gives will increase, will fill, <hi type="italic">your joy.</hi>" <div eID="gen28271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28272" type="x-p"/> 3. Here are the grounds upon which they might hope to speed (<reference osisRef="John.16.26-John.16.27">v. 26, 27</reference>), which are summed up in short by the apostle (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1 John ii. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have an advocate with the Father.</hi>" <div eID="gen28272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28273" type="x-p"/> (1.) We have an advocate; as to this, Christ saw cause at present not to insist upon it, only to make the following encouragement shine the brighter: "<hi type="italic">I say not unto you that I will pray the Father for you.</hi> Suppose I should not tell you that I will intercede for you, should not undertake to solicit every particular cause you have depending there, yet it may be a general ground of comfort that I have settled a correspondence between you and God, have erected a throne of grace, and consecrated for you a <hi type="italic">new and living way into the holiest.</hi>" He speaks as if they needed not any favours, when he had prevailed for the gift of the Holy Ghost to <hi type="italic">make intercession within them,</hi> as Spirit of adoption, crying <hi type="italic">Abba, Father;</hi> as if they had no further need of him to pray for them now, but we shall find that he does more for us than he says he will. Men's performances often come short of their promises, but Christ's go beyond them. <div eID="gen28273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28274" type="x-p"/> (2.) We have to do with a Father, which is so great an encouragement that it does in a manner supersede the other: "<hi type="italic">For the Father himself loveth you,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">philei hymas</hi></hi>, he is a friend to you, and you cannot be better befriended." Note, The disciples of Christ are the beloved of God himself. Christ not only turned away God's wrath from us, and brought us into a covenant of peace and reconciliation, but purchased his favour for us, and brought us into a covenant of friendship. Observe what an emphasis is laid upon this "<hi type="italic">The Father himself loveth you,</hi> who is perfectly happy in the enjoyment of himself, whose self-love is both his infinite rectitude and his infinite blessedness; yet he is pleased to love you." The Father himself, whose favour you have forfeited, and whose wrath you have incurred, and with whom you need an advocate, he himself now loves you. Observe, [1.] Why the Father loved the disciples of Christ: <hi type="italic">Because you have loved me, and have believed that I am come from God,</hi> that is, because you are my disciples indeed: not as if the love began on their side, but when by his grace he has wrought in us a love to him he is well pleased with the work of his own hands. See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What is the character of Christ's disciples; they love him, because they <hi type="italic">believe he came out from God,</hi> is the only-begotten of the Father, and his high-commissioner to the world. Note, Faith in Christ works by love to him, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Gal. v. 6</reference>. If we believe him to be the Son of God, we cannot but love him as infinitely lovely in himself; and if we believe him to be our Saviour, we cannot but love him as the most kind to us. Observe with what respect Christ is pleased to speak of his disciples' love to him, and how kindly he took it; he speaks of it as that which recommended them to his Father's favour: "You have loved me and believed in me when the world has hated and rejected me; and you shall be distinguished yourselves." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> See what advantage Christ's faithful disciples have, the Father loves them, and that because they love Christ; so well pleased is he in him that he is well pleased with all his friends. [2.] What encouragement this gave them in prayer. They need not fear speeding when they came to one that loved them, and wished them well. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> This cautions us against hard thoughts of God. When we are taught in prayer to plead Christ's merit and intercession, it is not as if all the kindness were in Christ only, and in God nothing but wrath and fury; no, the matter is not so, the Father's love and good-will appointed Christ to be the Mediator; so that we owe Christ's merit to God's mercy in giving him for us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Let it cherish and confirm in us good thoughts of God. Believers, that love Christ, ought to know that God loves them, and therefore to come boldly to him as children to a loving Father.

<div eID="gen28274" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discoveries of Himself.</title> <div sID="gen28275" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father. 29 His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb. <hi type="super">30</hi> Now are we sure that thou knowest all things, and needest not that any man should ask thee: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God. <hi type="super">31</hi> Jesus answered them, Do ye now believe? <hi type="super">32</hi> Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me. <hi type="super">33</hi> These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world. <div eID="gen28275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28276" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ here comforts his disciples with:— <div eID="gen28276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28277" type="x-p"/> I. With an assurance that, though he was leaving the world, he was returning to his Father, from whom he came forth <reference osisRef="John.16.28-John.16.32">v. 28-32</reference>, where we have, <div eID="gen28277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28278" type="x-p"/> 1. A plain declaration of Christ's mission from the Father, and his return to him (<reference osisRef="John.16.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">I came forth from the Father, and am come,</hi> as you see, <hi type="italic">into the world. Again, I leave the world,</hi> as you will see shortly, <hi type="italic">and go to the Father.</hi> This is the conclusion of the whole matter. There was nothing he had more inculcated upon them than these two things—whence he came, and whither he went, the <hi type="italic">Alpha</hi> and <hi type="italic">Omega</hi> of the <hi type="italic">mystery of godliness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>), that the Redeemer, in his entrance, was <hi type="italic">God manifest in the flesh,</hi> and in his exit was <hi type="italic">received up into glory.</hi> <div eID="gen28278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28279" type="x-p"/> (1.) These two great truths are here, [1.] Contracted, and put into a few words. Brief summaries of Christian doctrine are of great use to young beginners. The principles of the oracles of God brought into a little compass in creeds and catechisms have, like the beams of the sun contracted in a burning glass, conveyed divine light and heat with a wonderful power. Such we have, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28 Eccl.12.13 1Tim.1.15 Titus.2.11-Titus.2.12 1John.5.11">Job xxviii. 28; Eccl. xii. 13; 1 Tim. i. 15; Tit. ii. 11, 12; 1 John v. 11</reference>; much in a little. [2.] Compared, and set the one over against the other. There is an admirable harmony in divine truths; they both corroborate and illustrate one another; Christ's coming and his going do so. Christ had commended his disciples for believing that he came forth from God (<reference osisRef="John.16.27">v. 27</reference>), and thence infers the necessity and equity of his returning to God again, which therefore should not seem to them either strange or sad. Note, The due improvement of what we know and own would help us into the understanding of that which seems difficult and doubtful. <div eID="gen28279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28280" type="x-p"/> (2.) If we ask concerning the Redeemer <hi type="italic">whence he came,</hi> and <hi type="italic">whither he went,</hi> we are told, [1.] That he <hi type="italic">came from the Father,</hi> who sanctified and sealed him; and he came into this world, this lower world, this world of mankind, among whom by his incarnation he was pleased to incorporate himself. Here his business lay, and hither he came to attend it. He left his home for this strange country; his palace for this cottage; wonderful condescension! [2.] That, when he had done his work on earth, he left the world, and went back to his Father at his ascension. He was not forced away, but made it his own act and deed to leave the world, to return to it no more till he comes to put an end to it; yet still he is spiritually present with his church, and will be to the end. <div eID="gen28280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28281" type="x-p"/> 2. The disciples' satisfaction in this declaration (<reference osisRef="John.16.29-John.16.30">v. 29, 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lo, now speakest though plainly.</hi> It should seem, this one word of Christ did them more good than all the rest, though he had said many things likely enough to fasten upon them. The Spirit, as the wind, blows when and where, and by what word he pleases; perhaps a word that has been <hi type="italic">spoken once, yea twice,</hi> and not perceived, yet, being often repeated, takes hold at last. Two things they improved in by this saying:— <div eID="gen28281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28282" type="x-p"/> (1.) In knowledge: <hi type="italic">Lo, now speakest thou plainly.</hi> When they were in the dark concerning what he said, they did not say, <hi type="italic">Lo, now speakest thou obscurely,</hi> as blaming him; but now that they apprehend his meaning they give him glory for condescending to their capacity: <hi type="italic">Lo, now speakest thou plainly.</hi> Divine truths are most likely to do good when they are spoken plainly, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">1 Cor. ii. 4</reference>. Observe how they triumphed, as the mathematician did with his <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">heureka, heureka</hi></hi>, when he had hit upon a demonstration he had long been in quest of: <hi type="italic">I have found it, I have found it.</hi> Note, When Christ is pleased to speak plainly to our souls, and to bring us with open face to behold his glory, we have reason to rejoice in it. <div eID="gen28282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28283" type="x-p"/> (2.) In faith: <hi type="italic">Now are we sure.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28284" type="x-p"/> [1.] What was the matter of their faith: <hi type="italic">We believe that thou camest forth from God.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="John.16.27">v. 27</reference>) that they did believe this; "Lord" (say they) "we do believe it, and we have cause to believe it, and we know that we believe it, and have the comfort of it." <div eID="gen28284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28285" type="x-p"/> [2.] What was the motive of their faith—his omniscience. This proved him a teacher come from God, and more than a prophet, that he knew all things, which they were convinced of by this that he resolved those doubts which were hid in their hearts, and answered the scruples they had not confessed. Note, Those know Christ best that know him by experience, that can say of his power, It works in me; of his love, He loved me. And this proves Christ not only to have a divine mission, but to be a divine person, that he is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart, therefore the essential, eternal Word, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>. He has made all the churches to know that he searches the reins and the heart, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>. This confirmed the faith of the disciples here, as it made the first impression upon the woman of Samaria that Christ <hi type="italic">told her all the things that ever she did</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.29">ch. iv. 29</reference>), and upon Nathanael that Christ <hi type="italic">saw him under the fig-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.48-John.1.49">ch. i. 48, 49</reference>. <div eID="gen28285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28286" type="x-p"/> These words, <hi type="italic">and needest not that any man should ask thee,</hi> may bespeak either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ's aptness to teach. He prevents us with his instructions, and is communicative of the <hi type="italic">treasures of wisdom and knowledge</hi> that are hid in him, and needs not to be importuned. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His ability to teach: "Thou needest not, as other teachers, to have the learners' doubts told thee, for thou knowest, without being told, what they stumble at." The best of teachers can only answer what is spoken, but Christ can answer what is thought, what we are afraid to ask, as the disciples were, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.32">Mark ix. 32</reference>. Thus he <hi type="italic">can have compassion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">Heb. v. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen28286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28287" type="x-p"/> 3. The gentle rebuke Christ gave the disciples for their confidence that they now understood him, <reference osisRef="John.16.31-John.16.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. Observing how they triumphed in their attainments, he said, "<hi type="italic">Do you now believe?</hi> Do you now look upon yourselves as advanced and confirmed disciples? Do you now think you shall make no more blunders? Alas! you know not your own weakness; you will very shortly <hi type="italic">be scattered every man to his own,</hi>" &c. Here we have, <div eID="gen28287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28288" type="x-p"/> (1.) A question, designed to put them upon consideration: <hi type="italic">Do you now believe?</hi> [1.] "If now, why not sooner? Have you not heard the same things many a time before?" Those who after many instructions and invitations are at last persuaded to believe have reason to be ashamed that they stood it out so long. [2.] "If now, why not ever? When an hour of temptation comes, where will your faith be then?" As far as there is inconstancy in our faith there is cause to question the sincerity of it, and to ask, "Do we indeed believe?" <div eID="gen28288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28289" type="x-p"/> (2.) A prediction of their fall, that, how confident soever they were now of their own stability, in a little time they would all desert him, which was fulfilled that very night, when, upon his being seized by a party of the guards, <hi type="italic">all his disciples forsook him and fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">Matt. xxvi. 56</reference>. They were scattered, [1.] From one another; they shifted every one for his own safety, without any care or concern for each other. Troublous times are times of scattering to Christian societies; in the cloudy and dark day the flock of Christ is dispersed, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Ezek. xxxiv. 12</reference>. So Christ, as a society, is not visible. [2.] Scattered for him: <hi type="italic">You shall leave me alone.</hi> They should have been witnesses for him upon his trial, should have ministered to him in his sufferings; if they could have given him no comfort they might have done him some credit; but they were ashamed of his chain, and afraid of sharing with him in his sufferings, and left him alone. Note, Many a good cause, when it is distressed by its enemies, is deserted by its friends. The disciples had <hi type="italic">continued with Christ</hi> in his other temptations and yet turned their back upon him now; those that are tried, do not always prove trusty. If we at any time find our friends unkind to us, let us remember that Christ's were so to him. When they left him alone, they were scattered <hi type="italic">every man to his own;</hi> not to their own possessions or habitations, these were in Galilee; but to their own friends and acquaintance in Jerusalem; every one went his own way, where he fancied he should be most safe. Every man to secure his own; himself and his own life. Note, Those will not dare to suffer for their religion that <hi type="italic">seek their own things</hi> more than the <hi type="italic">things of Christ,</hi> and that look upon the things of this world as their <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta idia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">their own property,</hi> and in which their happiness is bound up. Now observe here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ knew before that his disciples would thus desert him in the critical moment, and yet he was still tender of them, and in nothing unkind. We are ready to say of some, "If we could have foreseen their ingratitude, we would not have been so prodigal of our favours to them;" Christ did foresee theirs, and yet was kind to them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He told them of it, to be a rebuke to their exultation in their present attainments: "<hi type="italic">Do you now believe?</hi> Be not high-minded, but fear; for you will find your faith so sorely shaken as to make it questionable whether it be sincere or no, in a little time." Note, even when we are taking the comfort of our graces, it is good to be reminded of our dangers from our corruptions. When our faith is strong, our love flaming, and our evidences are clear, yet we cannot infer thence that <hi type="italic">to-morrow shall be as this day.</hi> Even when we have most reason to think we stand, yet we have reason enough to take heed lest we fall. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He spoke of it as a thing very near. <hi type="italic">The hour was</hi> already <hi type="italic">come,</hi> in a manner, when they would be as shy of him as ever they had been fond of him. Note, A little time may produce great changes, both concerning us and in us. <div eID="gen28289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28290" type="x-p"/> (3.) An assurance of his own comfort notwithstanding: <hi type="italic">Yet I am not alone.</hi> He would not be thought to complain of their deserting him, as if it were any real damage to him; for in their absence he should be sure of his Father's presence, which was <hi type="italic">instar omnium—every thing: The Father is with me.</hi> We may consider this, [1.] As a privilege peculiar to the Lord Jesus; the Father was so with him in his sufferings as he never was with any, for still he was <hi type="italic">in the bosom of the Father.</hi> The divine nature did not desert the human nature, but supported it, and put an invincible comfort and an inestimable value into his sufferings. The Father had engaged to be with him in his whole undertaking (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">Ps. lxxxix. 21</reference>, &c.), and to preserve him (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa. xlix. 8</reference>); this emboldened him, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>. Even when he complained of his Father's forsaking him, yet he called him <hi type="italic">My God,</hi> and presently after was so well assured of his favourable presence with him as to commit his Spirit into his hand. This he had comforted himself with all along (<reference osisRef="John.8.29">ch. viii. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">He that sent me is with me, the Father hath not left me alone,</hi> and especially now at last. This assists our faith in the acceptableness of Christ's satisfaction; no doubt, the Father was well pleased in him, for he went along with him in his undertaking from first to last. [2.] As a privilege common to all believers, by virtue of their union with Christ; when they are alone, they are <hi type="italic">not alone,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the Father is with them. First,</hi> When solitude is their choice, when they are alone, as Isaac in the field, Nathanael under the fig-tree, Peter upon the house-top, meditating and praying, the Father is with them. Those that converse with God in solitude are never less alone than when alone. A good God and a good heart are good company at any time. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> When solitude is their affliction, their enemies lay them alone, and their friends leave them so, their company, like Job's, is made desolate; yet they are not so much alone as they are thought to be, <hi type="italic">the Father is with them,</hi> as he was with Joseph in his bonds and with John in his banishment. In their greatest troubles they are as one whom his father pities, as one whom his mother comforts. And, while we have God's favourable presence with us, we are happy, and ought to be easy, though all the world forsake us. <hi type="italic">Non deo tribuimus justum honorem nisi solus ipse nobis sufficiat—We do not render due honour to God, unless we deem him alone all-sufficient.</hi>—Calvin. <div eID="gen28290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28291" type="x-p"/> II. He comforts them with a promise of peace in him, by virtue of his victory over the world, whatever troubles they might meet with in it (<reference osisRef="John.16.33">v. 33</reference>): "<hi type="italic">These things have I spoken, that in me you might have peace;</hi> and if you have it not in me you will not have it at all, for <hi type="italic">in the world you shall have tribulation;</hi> you must expect no other, and yet may cheer up yourselves, for <hi type="italic">I have overcome the world.</hi>" Observe, <div eID="gen28291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28292" type="x-p"/> 1. The end Christ aimed at in preaching this farewell sermon to his disciples: <hi type="italic">That in him they might have peace.</hi> He did not hereby intend to give them a full view of that doctrine which they were shortly to be made masters of by the pouring out of the Spirit, but only to satisfy them for the present that his departure from them was really for the best. Or, we may take it more generally: Christ had said all this to them that by enjoying him they might have the best enjoyment of themselves. Note, (1.) It is the will of Christ that his disciples should have peace within, whatever their troubles may be without. (2.) Peace in Christ is the only true peace, and in him alone believers have it, for <hi type="italic">this man shall be the peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mic. v. 5</reference>. Through him we have peace with God, and so in him we have peace in our own minds. (3.) The word of Christ aims at this, <hi type="italic">that in him we may have peace.</hi> Peace is the <hi type="italic">fruit of the lips, and of his lips,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa. lvii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen28292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28293" type="x-p"/> 2. The entertainment they were likely to meet with in the world: "You shall not have outward peace, never expect it." Though they were sent to proclaim <hi type="italic">peace on earth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">good-will towards men,</hi> they must expect trouble on earth, and ill-will from men. Note, It has been the lot of Christ's disciples to have more or less tribulation in this world. Men persecute them because they are so good, and God corrects them because they are no better. Men design to cut them off from the earth, and God designs by affliction to make them meet for heaven; and so between both <hi type="italic">they shall have tribulation.</hi> <div eID="gen28293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28294" type="x-p"/> 3. The encouragement Christ gives them with reference hereto: <hi type="italic">But be of good cheer,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tharseite</hi></hi>. "Not only be of good comfort, but be of good courage; have a good heart on it, all shall be well." Note, In the midst of the tribulations of this world it is the duty and interest of Christ's disciples to be of good cheer, to keep up their delight in God whatever is pressing, and their hope in God whatever is threatening; as sorrowful indeed, in compliance with the temper of the climate, and yet always rejoicing, always cheerful (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>), even <hi type="italic">in tribulation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Rom. v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen28294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28295" type="x-p"/> 4. The ground of that encouragement: <hi type="italic">I have overcome the world.</hi> Christ's victory is a Christian triumph. Christ overcame the prince of this world, disarmed him, and cast him out; and still treads Satan under our feet. He overcame the children of this world, by the conversion of many to the faith and obedience of his gospel, making them the children of his kingdom. When he sends his disciples to preach the gospel to all the world, "<hi type="italic">Be of good cheer,</hi>" says he, "<hi type="italic">I have overcome the world</hi> as far as I have gone, and so shall you; though you have tribulation in the world, yet you shall gain your point, and captivate the world," <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. He overcame the wicked of the world, for many a time he put his enemies to silence, to shame; "And be you of good cheer, for the Spirit will enable you to do so too." He overcame the evil things of the world by submitting to them; he endured the cross, despising it and the shame of it; and he overcame the good things of it by being wholly dead to them; its honours had no beauty in his eye, its pleasures no charms. Never was there such a conqueror of the world as Christ was, and we ought to be encouraged by it, (1.) Because Christ has overcome the world before us; so that we may look upon it as a conquered enemy, that has many a time been baffled. Nay, (2.) He has conquered it for us, as the captain of our salvation. We are interested in his victory; by his cross the world is <hi type="italic">crucified to us,</hi> which bespeaks it completely conquered and put into our possession; all is yours, even <hi type="italic">the world.</hi> Christ having overcome the world, believers have nothing to do but to pursue their victory, and divide the spoil; and this we do by faith, <reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1 John v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">We are more than conquerors through him that loved us.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.16"/> <div eID="gen28295" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28298" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28297" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee: <hi type="super">2</hi> As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him. <hi type="super">3</hi> And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent. <hi type="super">4</hi> I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do. <hi type="super">5</hi> And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was. <div eID="gen28299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28300" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The circumstances of this prayer, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>. Many a solemn prayer Christ made in the days of his flesh (sometimes he continued all night in prayer), but none of his prayers are recorded so fully as this. Observe, <div eID="gen28300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28301" type="x-p"/> 1. The time when he prayed this prayer; when he had <hi type="italic">spoken these words,</hi> had given the foregoing farewell to his disciples, he prayed this prayer in their hearing; so that, (1.) It was a prayer after a sermon; when he had spoken from God to them, he turned to speak to God for them. Note, Those we preach to we must pray for. He that was to prophesy upon the dry bones was also to pray, <hi type="italic">Come, O breath, and breathe</hi> upon them. And the word preached should be prayed over, for God <hi type="italic">gives the increase.</hi> (2.) It was a prayer after sacrament; after Christ and his disciples had eaten the passover and the Lord's supper together, and he had given them a suitable exhortation, he closed the solemnity with this prayer, that God would preserve the good impressions of the ordinance upon them. (3.) It was a family-prayer. Christ's disciples were his family, and, to set a good example before the masters of families, he not only, as the son of Abraham, taught his household (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>), but, as a son of David, blessed his household (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">2 Sam. vi. 20</reference>), prayed for them and with them. (4.) It was a parting prayer. When we and our friends are parting, it is good to part with prayer, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.36">Acts xx. 36</reference>. Christ was parting by death, and that parting should be sanctified and sweetened by prayer. Dying Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs, dying Moses the twelve tribes, and so, here, dying Jesus the twelve apostles. (5.) It was a prayer that was a preface to his sacrifice, which he was now about to offer on earth, specifying the favours and blessings designed to be purchased by the merit of his death for those that were his; like a deed <hi type="italic">leading the uses of a fine,</hi> and directing to what intents and purposes it shall be levied. Christ prayed then as a priest now offering sacrifice, in the virtue of which all prayers were to be made. (6.) It was a prayer that was a specimen of his intercession, which he ever lives to make for us within the veil. Not that in his exalted state he addresses himself to his Father by way of humble petition, as when he was on earth. No, his intercession in heaven is a presenting of his merit to his Father, with a suing out of the benefit of it for all his chosen ones. <div eID="gen28301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> 2. The outward expression of fervent desire which he used in this prayer: He <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes to heaven,</hi> as before (<reference osisRef="John.11.41">ch. xi. 41</reference>); not that Christ needed thus to engage his own attention, but he was pleased thus to sanctify this gesture to those that use it, and justify it against those that ridicule it. It is significant of the lifting up of the soul to God in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Ps. xxv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Sursum corda</hi> was anciently used as a call to prayer, <hi type="italic">Up with your hearts,</hi> up to heaven; thither we must direct our desires in prayer, and thence we must expect to receive the good things we pray for. <div eID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> II. The first part of the prayer itself, in which Christ prays for himself. Observe here, <div eID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> 1. He prays to God as a Father: He <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes, and said, Father.</hi> Note, As prayer is to be made to God only, so it is our duty in prayer to eye him as a Father, and to call him <hi type="italic">our Father.</hi> All that have the Spirit of adoption are taught to cry <hi type="italic">Abba, Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.25">v. 25</reference>. For it will be of great use to us in prayer, both for direction and for encouragement, to call God as we hope to find him. <div eID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> 2. He prayed for himself first. Though Christ, as God, was prayed to, Christ, as man, prayed; thus <hi type="italic">it became him to fulfill all righteousness.</hi> It was said to him, as it is said to us, <hi type="italic">Ask, and I will give thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. What he had purchased he must ask for; and shall we expect to have what we never merited, but have a thousand times forfeited, unless we pray for it? This puts an honour upon prayer, that it was the messenger Christ sent on his errands, the way in which even he corresponded with Heaven. It likewise gives great encouragement to praying people, and cause to hope that even the <hi type="italic">prayer of the destitute</hi> shall not be despised; time was when he that is advocate for us had a cause of his own to solicit, a great cause, on the success of which depended all his honour as Mediator; and this he was to solicit in the same method that is prescribed to us, <hi type="italic">by prayers and supplications</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), so that he knows the heart of a petitioner (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exod. xxiii. 9</reference>), he knows the way. Now observe, Christ began with prayer for himself, and afterwards prayed for his disciples; this charity must begin at home, though it must not end there. We must love and pray for our neighbor as ourselves, and therefore must in a right manner love and pray for ourselves first. Christ was much shorter in his prayer for himself than in his prayer for his disciples. Our prayers for the church must not be crowded into a corner of our prayers; in making <hi type="italic">supplication for all saints,</hi> we have room enough to enlarge, and should not straiten ourselves. Now here are two petitions which Christ puts up for himself, and these two are one—that he might be glorified. But this one petition, <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me,</hi> is twice put up, because it has a double reference. To the prosecution of his undertaking further: <hi type="italic">Glorify me, that I may glorify thee,</hi> in doing what is agreed upon to be yet done, <reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.3">v. 1-3</reference>. And to the performance of his undertaking hitherto: "<hi type="italic">Glorify me, for I have glorified thee.</hi> I have done my part, and now, Lord, do thine," <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ here prays to be <hi type="italic">glorified,</hi> in order to his <hi type="italic">glorifying God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son</hi> according to thy promise, <hi type="italic">that thy Son may glorify thee</hi> according to his understanding. Here observe, <div eID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> [1.] What he prays for—that he might be glorified in this world: "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> when all the powers of darkness will combine to vilify thy Son; now, Father, glorify him." The Father glorified the <hi type="italic">Son</hi> upon earth, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Even in his sufferings, by the signs and wonders which attended them. When they that came to take him were thunder-struck with a word,—when Judas confessed him innocent, and sealed that confession with his own guilty blood,—when the judge's wife asleep, and the judge himself awake, pronounced him righteous,—when the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple rent, then the Father not only justified, but glorified the Son. Nay, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Even by his sufferings; when he was crucified, he was magnified, he was glorified, <reference osisRef="John.13.31">ch. xiii. 31</reference>. It was in his cross that he conquered Satan and death; his thorns were a crown, and Pilate in the inscription over his head wrote more than he thought. But, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Much more after his sufferings. The Father glorified the Son when he <hi type="italic">raised him from the dead,</hi> showed him openly to chosen witnesses, and poured out the Spirit to support and plead his cause, and to set up his kingdom among men, then he <hi type="italic">glorified him.</hi> This he here prays for, and insists upon. <div eID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> [2.] What he pleads to enforce this request. <div eID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He pleads relation: <hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son;</hi> thy Son as God, as Mediator. It is in consideration of this that the heathen are <hi type="italic">given him for his inheritance;</hi> for <hi type="italic">thou art my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7-Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 7, 8</reference>. The devil had tempted him to renounce his sonship with an offer of the kingdoms of this world; but he rejected the offer with disdain, and depended upon his Father for his preferment, and here applies himself to him for it. Note, Those that have received the adoption of sons may in faith pray for the inheritance of sons; if sanctified, then glorified: <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy Son.</hi> <div eID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He pleads the time: <hi type="italic">The hour is come;</hi> the season prefixed to an hour. The hour of Christ's passion was determined in the counsel of God. He had often said his hour was not yet come; but now it was come, and he knew it. <hi type="italic">Man knows not his time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>), but the Son of man did. He calls it <hi type="italic">this hour</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.27">ch. xii. 27</reference>), and here, <hi type="italic">the hour;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Mark.14.35">Mark xiv. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.21">ch. xvi. 21</reference>. For the hour of the Redeemer's death, which was also the hour of the Redeemer's birth, was the most signal and remarkable hour, and, without doubt, the most critical, that ever was since the clock of time was first set a going. Never was there such an hour as that, nor did ever any hour challenge such expectations of it before, nor such reflections upon it after. 1. "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> in the midst of which I need to be owned." Now is the hour when this grand affair is come to a crisis; after many a skirmish the decisive battle between heaven and hell is now to be fought, and that great cause in which God's honour and man's happiness are together embarked must now be either won or lost for ever. The two champions David and Goliath, Michael and the dragon, are now entering the lists; the trumpet sounds for an engagement that will be irretrievably fatal either to the one or to the other: "<hi type="italic">Now glorify thy Son,</hi> now give him victory over <hi type="italic">principalities and powers,</hi> now let <hi type="italic">the bruising of his heel</hi> be <hi type="italic">the breaking of the serpent's head,</hi> now let thy Son be so upheld as not to fail nor be discouraged." When Joshua went <hi type="italic">forth conquering and to conquer,</hi> it is said, <hi type="italic">The Lord magnified Joshua;</hi> so he <hi type="italic">glorified his Son</hi> when he made the cross his triumphant chariot. 2. "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> in the close of which I expect to be crowned; <hi type="italic">the hour is come</hi> when I am <hi type="italic">to be glorified,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">set at thy right hand.</hi>" Betwixt him and that glory there intervened a bloody scene of suffering; but, being short, he speaks as if he made little of it: <hi type="italic">The hour is come that I must be glorified;</hi> and he did not expect it till then. Good Christians in a trying hour, particularly a dying hour, may thus plead: "<hi type="italic">Now the hour is come,</hi> stand by me, appear for me, now or never: now <hi type="italic">the earthly tabernacle is to be dissolved, the hour is come that I should be glorified.</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He pleads the Father's own interest and concern herein: <hi type="italic">That thy Son may also glorify thee;</hi> for he had consecrated his whole undertaking to his Father's honour. He desired to be carried triumphantly through his sufferings to his glory, that he might glorify the Father two ways:—1. By <hi type="italic">the death of the cross,</hi> which he was now to suffer. <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> expressed the great intention of his sufferings, which was to retrieve his Father's injured honour among men, and, by his satisfaction, to come up to the glory of God, which man, by his sin, came short of: "Father, own me in my sufferings, that I may honour thee by them." 2. By the doctrine of the cross, which was now shortly to be published to the world, by which God's kingdom was to be re-established among men. He prays that his Father would so grace his sufferings, and crown them, as not only to take off <hi type="italic">the offence of the cross,</hi> but to make it, <hi type="italic">to those that are saved, the wisdom of God and the power of God.</hi> If God had not glorified Christ crucified, <hi type="italic">by raising him from the dead,</hi> his whole undertaking had been crushed; therefore <hi type="italic">glorify me, that I may glorify thee.</hi> Now thereby he hath taught us, (1.) What to eye and aim at in our prayers, in all our designs and desires—and that is, the honour of God. It being our chief end to glorify God, other things must be sought and attended to in subordination and subserviency to the Lord. "Do this and the other for thy servant, that thy servant may glorify thee. Give me health, that I may glorify thee with my body; success, that I may glorify thee with my estate," &c. <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name</hi> must be our first petition, which must fix our end in all our other petitions, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Peter iv. 11</reference>. (2.) He hath taught us what to expect and hope for. If we sincerely set ourselves to glorify our Father, he will not be wanting to do that for us which is requisite to put us into a capacity of glorifying him, to give us the grace he knows sufficient, and the opportunity he sees convenient. But, if we secretly honour ourselves more than him, it is just with him to leave us in the hand of our own counsels, and then, instead of honouring ourselves, we shall shame ourselves. <div eID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He pleads his commission (<reference osisRef="John.17.2-John.17.3">v. 2, 3</reference>); he desires to glorify his Father, in conformity to, and in pursuance of, the commission given him: "<hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son, as thou hast given him power, glorify him in the execution of the powers thou hast given him,</hi>" so it is connected with the petition; or, <hi type="italic">that thy Son may glorify thee</hi> according to <hi type="italic">the power given him,</hi> so it is connected with the plea. Now see here the power of the Mediator. <div eID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> The origin of his power: <hi type="italic">Thou hast given him power;</hi> he has it from God, <hi type="italic">to whom all power belongs.</hi> Man, in his fallen state, must, in order to his recovery, be taken under a new model of government, which could not be erected but by a special commission under the broad seal of heaven, directed to the undertaker of that glorious work, and constituting him sole arbitrator of the grand difference that was, and sole guarantee of the grand alliance that was to be, between God and man; so as to this office, he received his power, which was to be executed in a way distinct from his power and government as Creator. Note, The church's king is no usurper, as the prince of this world is; Christ's right to rule is incontestable. <div eID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> The extent of his power: He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Over all mankind. He has power in and over the world of spirits, the powers of the upper and unseen world are subject to him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Peter iii. 22</reference>); but, being now mediating between God and man, he here <hi type="italic">pleads his power over all flesh.</hi> They were men whom he was to subdue and save; out of that race he had a remnant given him, and therefore all that rank of beings was <hi type="italic">put under his feet.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Over mankind considered as corrupt and fallen, for so he is called <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. If he had not in this sense been flesh, he had not needed a Redeemer. Over this sinful race the Lord Jesus has all power; and <hi type="italic">all judgment,</hi> concerning them, <hi type="italic">is committed to him;</hi> power to bind or loose, acquit or condemn; <hi type="italic">power on earth to forgive sins</hi> or not. Christ, as Mediator, has the government of the whole world put into his hand; he is king of nations, has power even over those <hi type="italic">that know him not, nor obey his gospel;</hi> whom he does not rule, he over-rules, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">Ps. xxii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">lxxii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Matt. xxviii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.35">ch. iii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> The grand intention and design of this power: <hi type="italic">That he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.</hi> Here is the mystery of our salvation laid open. <div eID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Here is the Father making over the elect to the Redeemer, and giving them to him as his charge and trust; as the crown and recompence of his undertaking. He has a sovereign power over all the fallen race, but a peculiar interest in the chosen remnant; <hi type="italic">all things were put under his feet,</hi> but they were <hi type="italic">delivered into his hand.</hi> <div eID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Here is the Son undertaking to secure the happiness of those that were given him, that he would <hi type="italic">give eternal life to them.</hi> See how great the authority of the Redeemer is. He has lives and crowns to give, eternal lives that never die, immortal crowns that never fade. Now consider how great the Lord Jesus is, who has such preferments in his gift; and how gracious he is in giving eternal life to those whom he undertakes to save. [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] He sanctifies them in this world, gives them the spiritual life which is eternal life in the bud and embryo, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">ch. iv. 14</reference>. Grace in the soul is heaven in that soul. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] He will glorify them in the other world; their happiness shall be completed in the vision and fruition of God. This only is mentioned, because it supposes all the other parts of his undertaking, teaching them, satisfying for them, sanctifying them, and preparing them for that eternal life; and indeed all the other were in order to this; we are <hi type="italic">called to his kingdom and glory,</hi> and <hi type="italic">begotten to the inheritance.</hi> What is last in execution was first in intention, and <hi type="italic">that is eternal life.</hi> <div eID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Here is the subserviency of the Redeemer's universal dominion to this: He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh,</hi> on purpose that he might give eternal life to the select number. Note, Christ's dominion over the children of men is in order to the salvation of the children of God. <hi type="italic">All things are for their sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">2 Cor. iv. 15</reference>. All Christ's laws, ordinances, and promises, which are given to all, are designed effectually to convey spiritual life, and secure eternal life, to all that were given to Christ; he is <hi type="italic">head over all things to the church.</hi> The administration of the kingdoms of providence and grace are put into the same hand, that all things may be made to concur for good to the called. <div eID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> Here is a further explication of this grand design (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This is life eternal,</hi> which I am empowered and have undertaken to give, this is the nature of it, and this the way leading to it, <hi type="italic">to know thee the only true God,</hi> and all the discoveries and principles of natural religion, and Jesus Christ whom, thou has sent, as Mediator, and the doctrines and laws of that holy religion which he instituted for the recovery of man out of his lapsed state." Here is, <div eID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The great end which the Christian religion sets before us, and that is, eternal life, the happiness of an immortal soul in the vision and fruition of an eternal God. This he was to reveal to all, and secure to all that were given him. By the gospel <hi type="italic">life and immortality are brought to light,</hi> are brought to hand, a life which transcends this as much in excellency as it does in duration. <div eID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The sure way of attaining this blessed end, which is, by the right knowledge of God and Jesus Christ: "<hi type="italic">This is life eternal, to know thee,</hi>" which may be taken two ways—[<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] <hi type="italic">Life eternal</hi> lies in the knowledge of God and Jesus Christ; the present principle of this life is the believing knowledge of God and Christ; the future perfection of that life will be the intuitive knowledge of God and Christ. Those that are brought into union with Christ, and live a life of communion with God in Christ, know, in some measure, by experience, what eternal life is, and will say, "If this be heaven, heaven is sweet." See <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Ps. xvii. 15</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The knowledge of God and Christ leads to life eternal; this is the way in which Christ gives eternal life, by the knowledge of him that has called us (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2 Peter i. 3</reference>), and this is the way in which we come to receive it. The Christian religion shows us the way to heaven, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By directing us to God, as the author and felicity of our being; for Christ died to <hi type="italic">bring us to God.</hi> To know him as our Creator, and to love him, obey him, submit to him, and trust in him, as our owner ruler, and benefactor,—to devote ourselves to him as our sovereign Lord, depend upon him as our chief good, and direct all to his praise as our highest end,—<hi type="italic">this is life eternal.</hi> God is here called the <hi type="italic">only true God,</hi> to distinguish him from the false gods of the heathen, which were counterfeits and pretenders, not from the person of the Son, of whom it is expressly said that he is <hi type="italic">the true God and eternal life</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1 John v. 20</reference>), and who in this text is proposed as the object of the same religious regard with the Father. It is certain there is but one only living and true God and the God we adore is he. He is the true God, and not a mere name or notion; the only true God, and all that ever set up as rivals with him are vanity and a lie; the service of him is the only true religion. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By directing us to Jesus Christ, as the Mediator between God and man: <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.</hi> If man had continued innocent, the knowledge of the only true God would have been life eternal to him; but now that he is fallen there must be something more; now that we are under guilt, to know God is to know him as a righteous Judge, whose curse we are under; and nothing is more killing than to know this. We are therefore concerned to know Christ as our Redeemer, by whom alone we can now have access to God; it is life eternal to believe in Christ; and this he has undertaken to give to as many as were given him. See <reference osisRef="John.6.39-John.6.40">ch. vi. 39, 40</reference>. Those that are acquainted with God and Christ are already in the suburbs of life eternal. <div eID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ here prays to be glorified in consideration of his having glorified the Father hitherto, <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. The meaning of the former petition was, Glorify me in this world; the meaning of the latter is, Glorify me in the other world. <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee on the earth, and now glorify thou me.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> [1.] With what comfort Christ reflects on the life he had lived on earth: <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee, and finished my work;</hi> it is as good as finished. He does not complain of the poverty and disgrace he had lived in, what a weary life he had upon earth, as ever any man of sorrows had. He overlooks this, and pleases himself in reviewing the service he had done his Father, and the progress he had made in his understanding. This is here recorded, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For the honour of Christ, that his life upon earth did in all respects fully answer the end of his coming into the world. Note, 1. Our Lord Jesus had work given him to do by him that sent him; he came not into the world to live at ease, but to go <hi type="italic">about doing good,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">fulfill all righteousness.</hi> His Father gave him his work, his work in the vineyard, both appointed him to it and assisted him in it. 2. <hi type="italic">The work that was given him to do</hi> he finished. Though he had not, as yet, gone through the last part of his undertaking, yet he was so near being <hi type="italic">made perfect through sufferings</hi> that he might say, I have finished it; it was as good as done, he was giving it its finishing stroke <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eteleiosa</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I have finished.</hi> The word signifies his performing every part of his undertaking in the most complete and perfect manner. 3. Herein he glorified his Father; he pleased him, he praised him. It is the glory of God that <hi type="italic">his work is perfect,</hi> and the same is the glory of the Redeemer; what he is the author of he will be the finisher of. It was a strange way for the Son to glorify the Father by abasing himself (this looked more likely to disparage him), yet it was contrived that so he should glorify him: "<hi type="italic">I have glorified thee on the earth,</hi> in such a way as men on earth could bear the manifestation of thy glory." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is recorded for example to all, <hi type="italic">that we may follow his example.</hi> 1. We must make it our business to do the work God has appointed us to do, according to our capacity and the sphere of our activity; we must each of us do all the good we can in this world. 2. We must aim at the glory of God in all. We must glorify him on the earth, which he has given <hi type="italic">unto the children of men,</hi> demanding only this quit-rent; on the earth, where we are in a state of probation and preparation for eternity. 3. We must persevere herein to the end of our days; we must not sit down till we have finished our work, and <hi type="italic">accomplished as a hireling our day. Thirdly,</hi> It is recorded for encouragement to all those that rest upon him. If he has <hi type="italic">finished the work that was given him to do,</hi> then he is a complete Saviour, and did not do his work by the halves. And he that finished his work for us will finish it in us <hi type="italic">to the day of Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> [2.] See with what confidence he expects <hi type="italic">the joy set before him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now, O Father, glorify thou me.</hi> It is what he depends upon, and cannot be denied him. <div eID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> See here what he prayed for: <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>. All repetitions in prayer are not to be counted <hi type="italic">vain repetitions;</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">prayed, saying the same words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.44">Matt. xxvi. 44</reference>), and yet <hi type="italic">prayed more earnestly.</hi> What his Father had promised him, and he was assured of, yet he must pray for; promises are not designed to supersede prayers, but to be the guide of our desires and the ground of our hopes. Christ's being glorified includes all the honours, powers, and joys, of his exalted state. See how it is described. 1. It is a glory with God; not only, <hi type="italic">Glorify my name on earth,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Glorify me with thine own self.</hi> It was paradise, it was heaven, to be with his Father, as <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb. viii. 1</reference>. Note, The brightest glories of the exalted Redeemer were to be displayed within the veil, where the Father manifests his glory. The praises of the upper world are offered up <hi type="italic">to him that sits upon the throne and to the lamb</hi> in conjunction (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.13">Rev. v. 13</reference>), and the prayers of the lower world draw out grace and peace <hi type="italic">from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> in conjunction; and thus the Father has glorified him with himself. 2. It is <hi type="italic">the glory he had with God before the world was.</hi> By this it appears, (1.) That Jesus Christ, as God, had a being <hi type="italic">before the world was,</hi> co-eternal with the Father; our religion acquaints us with one that <hi type="italic">was before all things, and by whom all things consist.</hi> (2.) That his glory with the Father is from everlasting, as well as his existence with the Father; for he was from eternity <hi type="italic">the brightness of his Father's glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. As God's making the world only declared his glory, but made no real additions to it; so Christ undertook the work of redemption, not because he needed glory, for he had a glory <hi type="italic">with the Father before the world,</hi> but because we needed glory. (3.) That Jesus Christ in his state of humiliation divested himself of this glory, and drew a veil over it; though he was still God, yet he was <hi type="italic">God manifested in the flesh,</hi> not in his glory. He laid down this glory for a time, as a pledge that he would go through with his undertaking, according to the appointment of his Father. (4.) That in his exalted state he resumed this glory, and clad himself again with his former robes of light. Having performed his undertaking, he did, as it were, <hi type="italic">reposcere pignus—take up his pledge,</hi> by this demand, <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me.</hi> He prays that even his human nature might be advanced to the highest honour it was capable of, his body a glorious body; and that the glory of the Godhead might now be manifested in the person of the Mediator, Emmanuel, God-man. He does not pray to be glorified with the princes and great men of the earth: no; he that knew both worlds, and might choose which he would have his preferment in, chose it in the glory of the other world, as far exceeding all the glory of this. He had despised <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of this world and the glory of them,</hi> when Satan offered them to him, and therefore might the more boldly claim the glories of the other world. <hi type="italic">Let the same mind be in us.</hi> "Lord, give the glories of this world to whom thou wilt give them, but let me have my portion of glory in the world to come. It is no matter, though I be vilified with men; but, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thou me with thine own self.</hi>" <div eID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> See here what he pleaded: <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee;</hi> and now, in consideration thereof, <hi type="italic">glorify thou me.</hi> For, 1. There was an equity in it, and an admirable becomingness, <hi type="italic">that if God was glorified in him, he should glorify him in himself,</hi> as he had observed, <reference osisRef="John.13.32">ch. xiii. 32</reference>. Such an infinite value there was in what Christ did to glorify his Father that he properly merited all the glories of his exalted state. If the Father was a gainer in his glory by the Son's humiliation, it was fit the Son should be no loser by it at long run, in his glory. 2. It was according to the covenant between them, that if the Son would <hi type="italic">make his soul an offering for sin</hi> he should <hi type="italic">divide the spoil with the strong</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">12</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the kingdom should be his;</hi> and this he had an eye to, and depended upon, in his sufferings; it was <hi type="italic">for the joy set before him</hi> that <hi type="italic">he endured the cross:</hi> and now in his exalted state he still expects the completing of his exaltation, because he perfected his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">Heb. x. 13</reference>. 3. It was the most proper evidence of his Father's accepting and approving the work he had finished. By the glorifying of Christ we are satisfied that God was satisfied, and therein a real demonstration was given that the Father was well pleased in him as his beloved Son. 4. Thus we must be taught that those, and only those, who glorify God on earth, and persevere in the work God hath given them to do, shall be glorified with the Father, when they must be no more in this world. Not that we can merit the glory, as Christ did, but our glorifying God is required as an evidence of our interest in Christ, through whom eternal life is God's free gift.

<div eID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now they have known that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> For I have given unto them the words which thou gavest me; and they have received <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and have known surely that I came out from thee, and they have believed that thou didst send me. <hi type="super">9</hi> I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine. <hi type="super">10</hi> And all mine are thine, and thine are mine; and I am glorified in them. <div eID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> Christ, having prayed for himself, comes next to pray for those that are his, and he knew them by name, though he did not here name them. Now observe here, <div eID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> I. Whom he did not pray for (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I pray not for the world.</hi> Note, There is a world of people that Jesus Christ did not pray for. It is not meant of the world of mankind general (he prays for that here, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">That the world may believe that thou hast sent me</hi>); nor is it meant of the Gentiles, in distinction from the Jews; but the world is here opposed to the elect, who are given to Christ out of the world. Take the world for a heap of unwinnowed corn in the floor, and God loves it, Christ prays for it, and dies for it, <hi type="italic">for a blessing is in it;</hi> but, <hi type="italic">the Lord perfectly knowing those that are his,</hi> he eyes particularly those <hi type="italic">that were given him out of the world,</hi> extracts them; and then take the world for the remaining heap of rejected, worthless chaff, and Christ neither prays for it, nor dies for it, but abandons it, and <hi type="italic">the wind drives it away.</hi> These are called <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> because they are governed by the spirit of this world, and have their portion in it; for these Christ does not pray; not but that there are some things which he intercedes with God for on their behalf, as the dresser for the reprieve of the barren tree; but he does not pray for them in this prayer, that <hi type="italic">have not part nor lot</hi> in the blessings here prayed for. He does not say, I pray against the world, as Elias made intercession against Israel; but, <hi type="italic">I pray not for them,</hi> I pass them by, and leave them to themselves; they are <hi type="italic">not written in the Lamb's book of life,</hi> and therefore not in the breast-plate of the great high-priest.
