And miserable is the condition of such, as it was of those whom the prophet was forbidden to pray for, and more so, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jer. vii. 16</reference>. We that know not who are chosen, and who are passed by, must <hi type="italic">pray for all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1 Tim. ii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">4</reference>. While there is life, there is hope, and room for prayer. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">1 Sam. xii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> II. Whom he did pray for; not for angels, but for the children of men. 1. He prays <hi type="italic">for those that were given him,</hi> meaning primarily the disciples that had attended <hi type="italic">him in this regeneration;</hi> but it is doubtless to be extended further, to all who come under the same character, who receive and believe the words of Christ, <reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.8">8</reference>. 2. He prays <hi type="italic">for all that should believe on him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.20">v. 20</reference>), and it is not only the petitions that follow, but those also which went before, that must be construed to extend to all believers, in every place and every age; for he has a concern for them all, and calls <hi type="italic">things that are not as though they were.</hi> <div eID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> III. What encouragement he had to pray for them, and what are the general pleas with which he introduces his petitions for them, and recommends them to his Father's favour; they are five:— <div eID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> 1. The charge he had received concerning them: <hi type="italic">Thine they were, and thou gavest them me</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou whom thou hast given me.</hi> "Father, those I am now praying for are such as thou hast entrusted me with, and what I have to say for them is in pursuance of the charge I have received concerning them." Now, <div eID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is meant primarily of the disciples that then were, who were given to Christ as his pupils to be educated by him while he was on earth, and his agents to be employed for him when he went to heaven. They were given him to be the learners of his doctrine, the witnesses of his life and miracles, and the monuments of his grace and favour, in order to their being the publishers of his gospel and the planters of his church. When they left all to follow him, this was the secret spring of that strange resolution: they were given to him, else they had not given themselves to him. Note, The apostleship and ministry, which are Christ's gift to the church, were first the Father's gift to Jesus Christ. As under the law the Levites were given to Aaron (<reference osisRef="Num.3.9">Num. iii. 9</reference>), to him (the <hi type="italic">great high priest of our profession</hi>) the Father gave the apostles first, and ministers in every age, <hi type="italic">to keep his charge, and the charge of the whole congregation, and to do the service of the tabernacle.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8 Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 8, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. Christ received this gift for men, that he might give it to men. As this puts a great honour upon the ministry of the gospel, and magnifies that office, which is so much vilified; so it lays a mighty obligation upon the ministers of the gospel to devote themselves entirely to Christ's service, as being <hi type="italic">given to him,</hi> <div eID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> (2.) But it is designed to extend to all the elect, for they are elsewhere said to be given to Christ (<reference osisRef="John.6.37">ch. vi. 37</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.39">39</reference>), and he often laid a stress upon this, that those he was to save were given to him as his charge; to his care they were committed, from his hand they were expected, and concerning them he received commandments. He here shows, <div eID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Father had authority to give them: <hi type="italic">Thine they were.</hi> He did not give that which was none of his own, but covenanted that he had a good title. The elect, whom the Father gave to Christ, were his own in three ways:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> they were creatures, and their lives and beings were derived from him. When they were given to Christ to be <hi type="italic">vessels of honour,</hi> they were <hi type="italic">in his hand, as clay in the hand of the potter,</hi> to be disposed of as God's wisdom saw most for God's glory. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They were criminals, and their lives and beings were forfeited to him. It was a remnant of fallen mankind that was given to Christ to be redeemed, that might have been made sacrifices to justice when they were pitched upon to be the <hi type="italic">monuments of mercy;</hi> might justly have been <hi type="italic">delivered to the tormentors</hi> when they were delivered to the Saviour. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They were chosen, and their lives and beings were designed, for him; they were set apart for God, and were consigned to Christ as his agent. This he insists upon again (<reference osisRef="John.17.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">All things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee,</hi> which, though it may take in all that appertained to his office as Mediator, yet seems especially to be meant of those that were given him. "They <hi type="italic">are of thee,</hi> their being is of thee as the God of nature, their well-being is of thee as the God of grace; they <hi type="italic">are all of thee,</hi> and therefore, Father, I bring them all to thee, that they may be all for thee." <div eID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he did accordingly give them to the Son. <hi type="italic">Thou gavest them to me,</hi> as sheep to the shepherd, to be kept; as patients to the physician, to be cured; children to a tutor, to be educated; thus he will deliver up his charge (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">The children thou hast given me.</hi> They were delivered to Christ, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the election of grace might not be frustrated, <hi type="italic">that not one,</hi> no not <hi type="italic">of the little ones, might perish.</hi> That great concern must be lodged in some one good hand, able to give sufficient security, <hi type="italic">that the purpose of God according to election might stand. Secondly,</hi> That the undertaking of Christ might not be fruitless; they were <hi type="italic">given to him as his seed,</hi> in whom he should <hi type="italic">see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 10, 11</reference>), and might not <hi type="italic">spend his strength,</hi> and shed his blood, <hi type="italic">for nought, and in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa. xlix. 4</reference>. We may plead, as Christ does, "Lord, keep my graces, keep my comforts, for <hi type="italic">thine they were, and thou gavest them to me.</hi>" <div eID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> 2. The care he had taken of them to teach them (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have manifested thy name to them. I have given to them the words which thou gavest to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> (1.) The great design of Christ's doctrine, which was to manifest God's name, to declare him (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), to instruct the ignorant, and rectify the mistakes of a dark and foolish world concerning God, that he might be better loved and worshipped. <div eID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> (2.) His faithful discharge of this undertaking: <hi type="italic">I have</hi> done it. His fidelity appears, [1.] In the truth of the doctrine. It agreed exactly with the instructions he received from his Father. He gave not only the things, but the very <hi type="italic">words, that were given him.</hi> Ministers, in wording their message, must have an eye to <hi type="italic">the words which the Holy Ghost teaches.</hi> [2.] In the tendency of his doctrine, which was to manifest God's name. He did not seek himself, but, in all he did and said, aimed to magnify his Father. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is Christ's prerogative to manifest God's name to the souls of the children of men. <hi type="italic">No man knows the Father, but he to whom the Son will reveal him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. He only has acquaintance with the Father, and so is able to open the truth; and he only has access to the spirits of men, and so is able to open the understanding. Ministers may <hi type="italic">publish the name of the Lord</hi> (as Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">Deut. xxxii. 3</reference>), but Christ only can manifest that name. By the word of Christ God is revealed to us; by the Spirit of Christ God is revealed in us. Ministers may speak the words of God to us, but Christ can give us his words, can put them in us, as food, as treasure. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Sooner or later, Christ will manifest God's name to all that were given him, and will give them his word, to be the seed of their new birth, the support of their spiritual life, and the earnest of their everlasting bliss. <div eID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> 3. The good effect of the care he had taken of them, and the pains he had taken with them, (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have kept they word</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">they have known that all things are of thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">they have received thy words,</hi> and embraced them, have given their assent and consent to them, <hi type="italic">and have known surely that I came out from thee, and have believed that thou didst send me.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> (1.) What success the doctrine of Christ had among those <hi type="italic">that were given to him,</hi> in several particulars:— <div eID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> [1.] "They have received the words which I gave them, as the ground receives the seed, and the earth drinks in the rain." They attended to the words of Christ, apprehended in some measure the meaning of them, and were affected with them: they received the impression of them. The word was to them an <hi type="italic">ingrafted word.</hi> <div eID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> [2.] "<hi type="italic">They have kept thy word,</hi> have continued in it; they have conformed to it." Christ's commandment is then only kept when it is obeyed. Those that have to teach others the commands of Christ ought to be themselves observant of them. It was requisite that these should <hi type="italic">keep what was committed to them,</hi> for it was to be transmitted by them to every place for every age. <div eID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> [3.] "They have understood the word, and have been sensible on what ground they went in receiving and keeping it. They have been aware that thou art the original author of that holy religion which I am come to institute, <hi type="italic">that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee.</hi>" All Christ's offices and powers, all the gifts of the Spirit, all his graces and comforts, which God <hi type="italic">gave without measure to him,</hi> were all from God, contrived by his wisdom, appointed by his will, and designed by his grace, for his own glory in man's salvation. Note, It is a great satisfaction to us, in our reliance upon Christ, that he, and all he is and has, all he said and did, all he is doing and will do, are of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1 Cor. i. 30</reference>. We may therefore venture our souls upon Christ's mediation, for it has a good bottom. If the righteousness be of God's appointing, we shall be justified; if the grace be of his dispensing, we shall be sanctified. <div eID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> [4.] They have set their seal to it: <hi type="italic">They have known surely that I came out from God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>. See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What it is to believe; it is to <hi type="italic">know surely,</hi> to know <hi type="italic">that it is so of a truth.</hi> The disciples were very weak and defective in knowledge; yet Christ, who knew them better than they knew themselves, passes his word for them that they did believe. Note, We may know surely that which we neither do nor can know fully; <hi type="italic">may know the certainty of the things which are not seen,</hi> though we cannot particularly describe the nature of them. <hi type="italic">We walk by faith,</hi> which knows surely, <hi type="italic">not yet by sight,</hi> which knows clearly. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What it is we are to believe: <hi type="italic">that Jesus Christ came out from God,</hi> as he is the Son of God, in his person <hi type="italic">the image of the invisible God,</hi> and that God did not send him; that in his undertaking he is the ambassador of the eternal king: so that the Christian religion stands upon the same footing, and is of equal authority, with natural religion; and therefore all the doctrines of Christ are to be received as divine truths, all his commands obeyed as divine laws, and all his promises depended upon as divine securities. <div eID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> (2.) How Jesus Christ here speaks of this: he enlarges upon it, [1.] As pleased with it himself. Though the many instances of his disciples' dulness and weakness had grieved him, yet their constant adherence to him, their gradual improvements, and their great attainments at last, were his joy. Christ is a Master that delights in the proficiency of his scholars. He accepts the sincerity of their faith, and graciously passes by the infirmity of it. See how willing he is to make the best of us, and to say the best of us, thereby encouraging our faith in him, and teaching us charity to one another, [2.] As pleading it with the Father. He is praying for <hi type="italic">those that were given to him;</hi> and he pleads that they had given themselves to him. Note, The due improvement of grace received is a good plea, according to the tenour of the new covenant, for further grace; for so runs the promise. <hi type="italic">To him that hath shall be given.</hi> Those that keep Christ's word, and believe on him, let Christ alone to commend them, and, which is more, to recommend them to his Father. <div eID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads the Father's own interest in them (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I pray for them, for they are thine;</hi> and this by virtue of a joint and mutual interest, which he and the Father have in what pertained to each: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> Between the Father and Son there can be no dispute (as there is among the children of men) about <hi type="italic">meum</hi> and <hi type="italic">tuum—mine and thine,</hi> for the matter was settled from eternity; <hi type="italic">all mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> (1.) The plea particularly urged for his disciples: <hi type="italic">They are thine.</hi> The consigning of the elect to Christ was so far from making them less the Father's that it was in order to making them the more so. Note, [1.] All that receive Christ's word, and believe in him, are taken into covenant-relation to the Father, and are looked upon as his; Christ presents them to him, and they, through Christ, present themselves to him. Christ has <hi type="italic">redeemed us,</hi> not to himself only, but <hi type="italic">to God, by his blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9-Rev.5.10">Rev. v. 9, 10</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">first-fruits unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. [2.] This is a good plea in prayer, Christ here pleads it, <hi type="italic">They are thine;</hi> we may plead it for ourselves, <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me;</hi> and for others (as Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11">Exod. xxxii. 11</reference>), "<hi type="italic">They are thy people. They are thine;</hi> wilt thou not provide for thine own? Wilt thou not secure them, that they may not be run down by the devil and the world? Wilt thou not secure thy interest in them, that they may not depart from thee? <hi type="italic">They are thine,</hi> own them as thine." <div eID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> (2.) The foundation on which this plea is grounded: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> This bespeaks the Father and Son to be, [1.] One in essence. Every creature must say to God, <hi type="italic">All mine are thine;</hi> but none can say to him, <hi type="italic">All thine are mine,</hi> but he that is the same in substance with him and equal in power and glory. [2.] One in interest; no separate or divided interests between them. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What the Father has as Creator is delivered over to the Son, to be used and disposed of in subserviency to his great undertaking. <hi type="italic">All things are delivered to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>); the grant is so general that nothing is excepted but <hi type="italic">he that did put all things under him. Secondly,</hi> What the Son has as Redeemer is designed for the Father, and his kingdom shall shortly be delivered up to him. All the benefits of redemption, purchased by the Son, are intended for the Father's praise, and in his glory all the lines of his undertaking centre: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine.</hi> The Son owns none for his that are not devoted to the service of the Father; nor will any thing be accepted as a piece of service to the Christian religion which clashes with the dictates and laws of natural religion. In a limited sense, every true believer may say, <hi type="italic">All thine are mine;</hi> if God be ours in covenant, all he is and has is so far ours that it shall be engaged for our good; and in an unlimited sense every true believer does say, Lord, <hi type="italic">all mine are thine;</hi> all laid at his feet, to be serviceable to him. And what we have may be comfortably committed to God's care and blessing when it is cheerfully submitted to his government and disposal: "Lord, take care of what I have, for it is <hi type="italic">all thine.</hi>" <div eID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> 5. He pleads his own concern in them: <hi type="italic">I am glorified in them</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dedoxasmai</hi></hi>. (1.) <hi type="italic">I have been glorified in them.</hi> What little honour Christ had in this world was among his disciples; he had been glorified by their attendance on him and obedience to him, their preaching and working miracles in his name; and therefore <hi type="italic">I pray for them.</hi> Note, Those shall have an interest in Christ's intercession in and by whom he is glorified. (2.) "<hi type="italic">I am to be glorified in them</hi> when I am gone to heaven; they are to bear up my name." The apostles preached and wrought miracles <hi type="italic">in Christ's name; the Spirit in them glorified Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.14">ch. xvi. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am glorified in them,</hi> and therefore," [1.] "I concern myself for them." What little interest Christ has in this degenerate world lies in his church; and therefore it and all its affairs lie near his heart, within the veil. [2.] "Therefore I commit them to the Father, who has engaged to glorify the Son, and, upon this account, will have a gracious eye to those in whom he is glorified." That in which God and Christ are glorified may, with humble confidence, be committed to God's special care.

<div eID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And now I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee. Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we <hi type="italic">are.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled. <hi type="super">13</hi> And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves. <hi type="super">14</hi> I have given them thy word; and the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. <hi type="super">15</hi> I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. <hi type="super">16</hi> They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. <div eID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> After the general pleas with which Christ recommended his disciples to his Father's care follow the particular petitions he puts up for them; and, 1. They all relate to spiritual blessings in heavenly things. He does not pray that they might be rich and great in the world, that they might raise estates and get preferments, but that they might be kept from sin, and furnished for their duty, and brought safely to heaven. Note, The prosperity of the soul is the best prosperity; for what relates to this Christ came to purchase and bestow, and so teaches us to seek, in the first place, both for others and for ourselves. 2. They are such blessings as were suited to their present state and case, and their various exigencies and occasions. Note, Christ's intercession is always pertinent. Our <hi type="italic">advocate with the Father</hi> is acquainted with all the particulars of our wants and burdens, our dangers and difficulties, and knows how to accommodate his intercession to each, as to Peter's peril, which he himself was not aware of (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have prayed for thee.</hi> 3. He is large and full in the petitions, orders them before his Father, and <hi type="italic">fills his mouth with arguments,</hi> to teach us fervency and importunity in prayer, to be large in prayer, and dwell upon our errands at the throne of grace, wrestling as Jacob, <hi type="italic">I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.</hi> <div eID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> Now the first thing Christ prays for, for his disciples, is their preservation, in <reference osisRef="John.17.11-John.17.16">these verses</reference>, in order to which he commits them all to his Father's custody. Keeping supposes danger, and their danger arose <hi type="italic">from the world,</hi> the world wherein they were, <hi type="italic">the evil</hi> of this he begs they might be kept from. Now observe, <div eID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> I. The request itself: <hi type="italic">Keep them from the world.</hi> There were two ways of their being delivered from the world:— <div eID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> 1. By taking them out of it; and he does not pray that they might be so delivered: <hi type="italic">I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world;</hi> that is, <div eID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> (1.) "I pray not that they may be speedily removed by death." If the world will be vexatious to them, the readiest way to secure them would be to hasten them out of it to a better world, that will give them better treatment. Send chariots and horses of fire for them, to fetch them to heaven; Job, Elijah, Jonah, Moses, when that occurred which fretted them, prayed that they might be <hi type="italic">taken out of the world;</hi> but Christ would not pray so for his disciples, for two reasons:—[1.] Because he came to conquer, not to countenance, those intemperate heats and passions which make men impatient of life, and importunate for death. It is his will that we should take up our cross, and not outrun it. [2.] Because he had work for them to do in the world; the world, though sick of them (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.22">Acts xxii. 22</reference>), and therefore not worthy of them (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.38">Heb. xi. 38</reference>), yet could ill spare them. In pity therefore to this dark world, Christ would not have these lights removed out of it, but continued in it, especially for the sake of those in the world that were to <hi type="italic">believe in him through their word.</hi> Let not them be taken out of the world when their Master is; they must each in his own order die a martyr, but not till they have finished their testimony. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The taking of good people out of the world is a thing by no means to be desired, but rather dreaded and laid to heart, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa. lvii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Though Christ loves his disciples, he does not presently send for them to heaven, as soon as they are effectually called, but leaves them for some time in this world, that they may do good and glorify God upon earth, and be ripened for heaven. Many good people are spared to live, because they can ill be spared to die. <div eID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> (2.) "I pray not that they may be totally freed and exempted from the troubles of this world, and taken out of the toil and terror of it into some place of ease and safety, there to live undisturbed; this is not the preservation I desire for them." <hi type="italic">Non ut omni molestia liberati otium et delicias colant, sed ut inter media pericula salvi tamen maneant Dei auxilio—Not that, being freed from all trouble, they may bask in luxurious ease, but that by the help of God they may be preserved in a scene of danger;</hi> so Calvin. Not that they may be kept from all conflict with the world, but that they may not be overcome by it; not that, as Jeremiah wished, they might <hi type="italic">leave their people, and go from them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 2</reference>), but that, like Ezekiel, <hi type="italic">their faces may be strong against the faces of wicked men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.8">Ezek. iii. 8</reference>. It is more the honour of a Christian soldier by faith to <hi type="italic">overcome the world</hi> than by a monastical vow to retreat from it; and more for the honour of Christ to serve him in a city than to serve him in a cell. <div eID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> 2. Another way is by keeping them from the corruption that is in the world; and he prays they may be thus kept, <reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.15">15</reference>. Here are three branches of this petition:— <div eID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Holy Father, keep those whom thou hast given me.</hi> <div eID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ was now leaving them; but let them not think that their defence was departed from them; no, he does here, in their hearing, commit them to the custody of his Father and their Father. Note, It is the unspeakable comfort of all believers that Christ himself has committed them to the care of God. Those cannot but be safe whom the almighty God keeps, and he cannot but keep those whom the Son of his love commits to him, in the virtue of which we may by faith <hi type="italic">commit the keeping of our souls to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1 Pet. iv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He here puts them under the divine protection, that they may not be run down by the malice of their enemies; that they and all their concerns may be the particular care of the divine Providence: "<hi type="italic">Keep</hi> their lives, till they have done their work; keep their comforts, and let them not be broken in upon by the hardships they meet with; keep up their interest in the world, and let it not sink." To this prayer is owing the wonderful preservation of the gospel ministry and gospel church in the world unto this day; if God had not graciously kept both, and kept up both, they had been extinguished and lost long ago. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He puts them under the divine tuition, that they may not themselves run away from their duty, nor be led aside by the treachery of their own hearts: "<hi type="italic">Keep them</hi> in their integrity, keep them disciples, keep them close to their duty." We need God's power not only to put us into a state of grace, but to keep us in it. See, <reference osisRef="John.10.28-John.10.29">ch. x. 28, 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.15">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> [2.] The titles he gives to him he prays to, and them he prays for, enforce the petition. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He speaks to God as a <hi type="italic">holy Father.</hi> In committing ourselves and others to the divine care, we may take encouragement, 1. From the attribute of his holiness, for this is engaged for the preservation of his holy ones; he hath <hi type="italic">sworn by his holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>. If he be a holy God and hate sin, he will make those holy that are his, and keep them from sin, which they also hate and dread as the greatest evil. 2. From this relation of a Father, wherein he stands to us through Christ. If he be a Father, he will take care of his own children, will teach them and keep them; who else should? <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He speaks of them as those whom the Father had <hi type="italic">given him.</hi> What we receive as our Father's gifts, we may comfortably remit to our Father's care. "Father, keep the graces and comforts thou hast given me; the children thou hast given me; the ministry <hi type="italic">I have received.</hi>" <div eID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Keep</hi> them <hi type="italic">through thine own name.</hi> That is, [1.] Keep them for thy name's sake; so some. "Thy name and honour are concerned in their preservation as well as mine, for both will suffer by it if they either revolt or sink." The Old Testament saints often pleaded, for <hi type="italic">thy name's sake;</hi> and those may with comfort plead it that are indeed more concerned for the honour of God's name than for any interest of their own. [2.] Keep them in thy name; so others; the original is so, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en to onomati</hi></hi>. "Keep them in the knowledge and fear of thy name; keep them in the profession and service of thy name, whatever it cost them. Keep them in the interest of thy name, and let them ever be faithful to this; keep them in thy truths, in thine ordinances, in the way of thy commandments." [3.] Keep them by or through thy name; so others. "Keep them by thine own power, in thine own hand; keep them thyself, undertake for them, let them be thine own immediate care. Keep them by those means of preservation which thou hast thyself appointed, and by which thou hast made thyself known. Keep them by thy word and ordinances; let thy name be their strong tower, thy tabernacle their pavilion." <div eID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Keep them from the evil,</hi> or out of the evil. He had taught them to pray daily, <hi type="italic">Deliver us from evil,</hi> and this would encourage them to pray. [1.] "Keep them from the evil one, the devil and all his instruments; that wicked one and all his children. Keep them from Satan as a tempter, that either he may not have leave to sift them, or that their faith may not fail. Keep them from him as a destroyer, that he may not drive them to despair." [2.] "Keep them from the evil thing, that is sin; from every thing that looks like it, or leads to it. Keep them, that they do no evil," <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.7">2 Cor. xiii. 7</reference>. Sin is that evil which, above any other, we should dread and deprecate. [3.] "Keep them from the evil of the world, and of their tribulation in it, so that it may have no sting in it, no malignity;" not that they might be kept from affliction, but kept through it, that the property of their afflictions might be so altered as that there might be no evil in them, nothing to them any harm. <div eID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons with which he enforces these requests for their preservation, which are five:— <div eID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> 1. He pleads that hitherto he had kept them (<reference osisRef="John.17.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">While I was with them in the world, I have kept them in thy name,</hi> in the true faith of the gospel and the service of God; those that thou gavest me for my constant attendants I have kept, they are all safe, and none of them missing, none of them revolted nor ruined, <hi type="italic">but the son of perdition;</hi> he is lost, that the scripture might be fulfilled." Observe, <div eID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28366" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ's faithful discharge of his undertaking concerning his disciples: <hi type="italic">While he was with them, he kept them,</hi> and his care concerning them was not in vain. He kept them in God's name, preserved them from falling into any dangerous errors or sins, from striking in with the Pharisees, who would have <hi type="italic">compassed sea and land to make proselytes</hi> of them; he kept them from deserting him, and returning to the little all they had left for him; he had them still under his eye and care when he sent them to peach; <hi type="italic">went not his heart with them?</hi> Many that followed him awhile took offence at something or other, and went off; but he kept the twelve that they should not go away. He kept them from falling into the hands of persecuting enemies that sought their lives; kept them when he surrendered himself, <reference osisRef="John.18.9">ch. xviii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">While he was with them</hi> he kept them in a visible manner by instructions till sounding in their ears, miracles still done before their eyes; when he was gone from them, they must be kept in a more spiritual manner. Sensible comforts and supports are sometimes given and sometimes withheld; but, when they are withdrawn, yet they are not left comfortless. What Christ here says of his immediate followers is true of all the saints while they are here in this world; Christ keeps them <hi type="italic">in God's name.</hi> It is implied, [1.] That they are weak, and cannot keep themselves; their own hands are not sufficient for them. [2.] That they are, in God's account, valuable and worth the keeping; precious in his sight and honourable; his treasure, his jewels. [3.] That their salvation is designed, for to this it is that they are kept, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. As the wicked are reserved for the day of evil, so the righteous are preserved for the day of bliss. [4.] That they are the charge of the Lord Jesus; for as his charge he keeps them, and exposed himself like the good shepherd for the preservation of the sheep. <div eID="gen28366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28367" type="x-p"/> (2.) The comfortable account he gives of his undertaking: <hi type="italic">None of them is lost.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ will certainly keep all that were given to him, so that none of them shall be totally and finally lost; they may think themselves lost, and may be nearly lost (in imminent peril); but it is the Father's will that he should <hi type="italic">lose none,</hi> and none he will lose (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">ch. vi. 39</reference>); so it will appear when they come all together, and none of them shall be wanting. <div eID="gen28367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28368" type="x-p"/> (3.) A brand put upon Judas, as none of those whom he had undertaken to keep. He was among those that were given to Christ, but not of them. He speaks of Judas as already lost, for he had abandoned the society of his Master and his fellow-disciples, and abandoned himself to the devil's guidance, and in a little time would <hi type="italic">go to his own place;</hi> he is as good as lost. But the apostasy and ruin of Judas were no reproach at all to his Master, or his family; for, [1.] He was <hi type="italic">the son of perdition,</hi> and therefore not one of those that were given to Christ to be kept. He deserved perdition, and God left him to throw himself headlong into it. He was the <hi type="italic">son of the destroyer,</hi> as Cain, <hi type="italic">who was of that wicked one.</hi> That great enemy whom the Lord <hi type="italic">will consume</hi> is called a <hi type="italic">son of perdition,</hi> because he is a <hi type="italic">man of sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2 Thess. ii. 3</reference>. It is an awful consideration that one of the apostles proved a son of perdition. No man's place or name in the church, no man's privileges or opportunities of getting grace, no man's profession or external performances, will secure him from ruin, if his heart be not right with God; nor are any more likely to prove sons of perdition at last, after a plausible course of profession, than those that like Judas love the bag; but Christ's distinguishing Judas from those that were given him (for <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ei me</hi></hi> is adversative, not exceptive) intimates that the truth and true religion ought not to suffer for the treachery of those that are false to it, <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1 John ii. 19</reference>. [2.] The scripture was fulfilled; the sin of Judas was foreseen of God's counsel and foretold in his word, and the event would certainly follow after the prediction as a consequent, though it cannot be said necessarily to follow from it as an effect. See <reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Ps. xli. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.25">lxix. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.8">cix. 8</reference>. We should be amazed at the treachery of apostates, were we not <hi type="italic">told of it before.</hi> <div eID="gen28368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28369" type="x-p"/> 2. He pleads that he was now under a necessity of leaving them, and could no longer watch over them in the way that he had hitherto done (<reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference>): "Keep them now, that I may not lose the labour I bestowed upon them while I was with them. Keep them, <hi type="italic">that they may be one</hi> with us <hi type="italic">as we are</hi> with each other." We shall have occasion to speak of this, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>. But see here, <div eID="gen28369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28370" type="x-p"/> (1.) With what pleasure he speaks of his own departure. He expresses himself concerning it with an air of triumph and exultation, with reference both to the world he left and the world he removed to. [1.] "<hi type="italic">Now I am no more in the world.</hi> Now farewell to this provoking troublesome world. I have had enough of it, and now the welcome hour is at hand when I shall be <hi type="italic">no more in it.</hi> Now that I have finished the work I had to do in it, I have done with it; nothing remains now but to hasten out of it as fast as I can." Note, It should be a pleasure to those that have their home in the other world to think of being <hi type="italic">no more in this world;</hi> for when we have done what we have to do in this world, and are made meet for that, what is there here that should court our stay? When we receive a sentence of death within ourselves, with what a holy triumph should we say, "<hi type="italic">Now I am no more in this world,</hi> this dark deceitful world, this poor empty world, this tempting defiling world; no more vexed with its thorns and briars, no more endangered by its nets and snares; now I shall wander no more in this howling wilderness, be tossed no more on this stormy sea; <hi type="italic">now I am no more in this world,</hi> but can cheerfully quit it, and give it a final farewell." [2.] <hi type="italic">Now I come to thee.</hi> To get clear of the world is but the one half of the comfort of a dying Christ, of a dying Christian; the far better half is to think of going to the Father, to sit down in the immediate, uninterrupted, and everlasting enjoyment of him. Note, Those who love God cannot but be pleased to think of coming to him, though it be through the valley of the shadow of death. When we go, to be <hi type="italic">absent from the body,</hi> it is to be <hi type="italic">present with the Lord,</hi> like children fetched home from school to their father's house. "Now come I to thee whom I have chosen and served, and whom my soul thirsteth after; to thee the fountain of light and life, the crown and centre of bliss and joy; now my longings shall be satisfied, my hopes accomplished, my happiness completed, for <hi type="italic">now come I to thee.</hi>" <div eID="gen28370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28371" type="x-p"/> (2.) With what a tender concern he speaks of those whom he left behind: "<hi type="italic">But these are in the world.</hi> I have found what an evil world it is, what will become of these dear little ones that must stay in it? <hi type="italic">Holy Father, keep them;</hi> they will want my presence, let them have thine. They have now more need than ever to be kept, for I am sending them out further into the world than they have yet ventured; they must <hi type="italic">launch forth into the deep,</hi> and have business to do in these great waters, and will be lost if thou do not keep them." Observe here, [1.] That, when our Lord Jesus was going to the Father, he carried with him a tender concern for <hi type="italic">his own that are in the world;</hi> and continued to compassionate them. He bears their names upon his breast-plate, nay, upon his heart, and has <hi type="italic">graven them</hi> with the nails of his cross <hi type="italic">upon the palms of his hands;</hi> and when he is out of their sight they are not out of his, much less out of his mind. We should have such a pity for those that are launching out into the world when we are got almost through it, and for those that are left behind in it when we are leaving it. [2.] That, when Christ would express the utmost need his disciples had of divine preservation, he only says, <hi type="italic">They are in the world;</hi> this bespeaks danger enough to those who are bound for heaven, whom a flattering world would divert and seduce, and a malignant world would hate and persecute. <div eID="gen28371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28372" type="x-p"/> 3. He pleads what a satisfaction it would be to them to know themselves safe, and what a satisfaction it would be to him to see them easy: <hi type="italic">I speak this, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.13">v. 13</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28373" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ earnestly desired the fulness of the joy of his disciples, for it is his will that they should rejoice evermore. He was leaving them in tears and troubles, and yet took effectual care to <hi type="italic">fulfil their joy.</hi> When they thought their joy in him was brought to an end, then was it advanced nearer to perfection than ever it had been, and they were fuller of it. We are here taught, [1.] To found our joy in Christ: "It is <hi type="italic">my joy,</hi> joy of my giving, or rather joy that I am the matter of." Christ is a Christian's joy, his chief joy. Joy in the world is withering with it; joy in Christ is everlasting, like him. [2.] To build up our joy with diligence; for it is the duty as well as privilege of all true believers; no part of the Christian life is pressed upon us more earnestly, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">iv. 4</reference>. [3.] To aim at the perfection of this joy, that we may have it fulfilled in us, for this Christ would have. <div eID="gen28373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28374" type="x-p"/> (2.) In order hereunto, he did thus solemnly commit them to his Father's care and keeping and took them for witnesses that he did so: <hi type="italic">These things I speak in the world,</hi> while I am yet with them in the world. His intercession in heaven for their preservation would have been as effectual in itself; but saying this in the world would be a greater satisfaction and encouragement to them, and would enable them to <hi type="italic">rejoice in tribulation.</hi> Note, [1.] Christ has not only treasured up comforts for his people, in providing for their future welfare, but has given out comforts to them, and said that which will be for their present satisfaction. He here condescended in the presence of his disciples to publish his last will and testament, and (which many a testator is shy of) lets them know what legacies he had left them, and how well they were secured, that they might have strong consolation. [2.] Christ's intercession for us is enough to fulfil or joy in him; nothing more effectual to silence all our fears and mistrusts, and to furnish us with strong consolation, than this, that he always appears in the presence of God for us; therefore the apostle puts a <hi type="italic">yea rather</hi> upon this, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">Rom. viii. 34</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">Heb. vii. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen28374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28375" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads the ill usage they were likely to meet with in the world, for his sake (<reference osisRef="John.17.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have given them thy word</hi> to be published to the world, <hi type="italic">and they have received it,</hi> have believed it themselves, and accepted the trust of transmitting it to the world; and therefore <hi type="italic">the world hath hated them,</hi> as also because they are <hi type="italic">not of the world,</hi> any more than I." Here we have, <div eID="gen28375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28376" type="x-p"/> (1.) The world's enmity to Christ's followers. While Christ was with them, though as yet they had given but little opposition to the world, yet it hates them, much more would it do so when by their more extensive preaching of the gospel they would <hi type="italic">turn the world upside down.</hi> "Father, stand their friend," says Christ, "for they are likely to have many enemies; let them have thy love, for the world's hatred is entailed upon them. In the midst of those fiery darts, let them be <hi type="italic">compassed with thy favour as with a shield.</hi>" It is God's honour to take part with the weaker side, and to help the helpless. <hi type="italic">Lord, be merciful to them, for men would swallow</hi> them up. <div eID="gen28376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28377" type="x-p"/> (2.) The reasons of this enmity, which strengthen the plea. [1.] It is implied that one reason is because they had received the word of God as it was sent them by the hand of Christ, when the greatest part of the world rejected it, and set themselves against those who were the preachers and professors of it. Note, Those that receive Christ's good will and good word must expect the world's ill will and ill word. Gospel ministers have been in a particular manner hated by the world, because they call men out of the world, and separate them from it, and teach them not to conform to it, and so condemn the world. "<hi type="italic">Father, keep them</hi> for it is for thy sake that they are exposed; they are sufferers for thee." Thus the psalmist pleads, <hi type="italic">For thy sake I have borne reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.7">Ps. lxix. 7</reference>. Note, Those that keep the word of Christ's patience are entitled to special protection in the hour of temptation, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.10">Rev. iii. 10</reference>. That cause which makes a martyr may well make a joyful sufferer. [2.] Another reason is more express; the world hates them, because they <hi type="italic">are not of the world.</hi> Those to whom the word of Christ comes in power are not of the world, for it has this effect upon all that receive it in the love of it that it weans them from the wealth of the world, and turns them against the wickedness of the world, and therefore the world bears them a grudge. <div eID="gen28377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28378" type="x-p"/> 5. He pleads their conformity to himself in a holy non-conformity to the world (<reference osisRef="John.17.16">v. 16</reference>): "Father, keep them, for they are of my spirit and mind, <hi type="italic">they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.</hi>" Those may in faith commit themselves to God's custody, (1.) Who are <hi type="italic">as Christ was in this world,</hi> and tread in his steps. God will love those that are like Christ. (2.) Who do not engage themselves in the world's interest, nor devote themselves to its service. Observe, [1.] That Jesus Christ was not of this world; he never had been of it, and least of all now that he was upon the point of leaving it. This intimates, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His state; he was none of the world's favourites nor darlings, none of its princes nor grandees; worldly possessions he had none, not even <hi type="italic">where to lay his head;</hi> nor worldly power, he was no judge nor divider. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His Spirit; he was perfectly dead to the world, the prince of this world had nothing in him, the things of this world were nothing to him; not honour, for he <hi type="italic">made himself of no reputation;</hi> not riches, for <hi type="italic">for our sakes he became poor;</hi> not pleasures, for he <hi type="italic">acquainted himself with grief.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.8.23">ch. viii. 23</reference>. [2.] That therefore true Christians are not of this world. The Spirit of Christ in them is opposite to the spirit of the world. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is their lot to be despised by the world; they are not in favour with the world any more than their Master before them was. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is their privilege to be delivered from the world; as Abraham out of the land of his nativity. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is their duty and character to be dead to the world. Their most pleasing converse is, and should be, with another world, and their prevailing concern about the business of that world, not of this. Christ's disciples were weak, and had many infirmities; yet this he could say for them, They were not of the world, not of the earth, and therefore he recommends them to the care of Heaven.

<div eID="gen28378" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28379" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth. <hi type="super">18</hi> As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world. <hi type="super">19</hi> And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth. <div eID="gen28379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28380" type="x-p"/> The next thing he prayed for for them was that they might be sanctified; not only kept from evil, but made good. <div eID="gen28380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28381" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the petition (<reference osisRef="John.17.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sanctify them through thy truth,</hi> through thy word, for <hi type="italic">thy word is truth;</hi> it is true—it is truth itself. He desires they may be sanctified, <div eID="gen28381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28382" type="x-p"/> 1. As Christians. Father, make them holy, and this will be their preservation, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1 Thess. v. 23</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen28382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28383" type="x-p"/> (1.) The grace desired—sanctification. The disciples were sanctified, for they were not of the world; yet he prays, <hi type="italic">Father sanctify them,</hi> that is, [1.] "Confirm the work of sanctification in them, strengthen their faith, inflame their good affections, rivet their good resolutions." [2.] "Carry on that good work in them, and continue it; let the <hi type="italic">light shine more and more.</hi>" [3.] "Complete it, crown it with the perfection of holiness; sanctify them throughout and to the end." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the prayer of Christ for all that are his that they may be sanctified; because he cannot for shame own them as his, either here or hereafter, either employ them in his work or present them to his Father, if they be not sanctified. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that through grace are sanctified have need to be sanctified more and more. Even disciples must pray for sanctifying grace; for, if he that was the author of the good work be not the finisher of it, we are undone. Not to go forward is to go backward; <hi type="italic">he that is holy must be holy still,</hi> more holy still, pressing forward, soaring upward, as those that have not attained. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is God that sanctifies as well as God that justified, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">2 Cor. v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It is an encouragement to us, in our prayers for sanctifying grace, that it is what Christ intercedes for for us. <div eID="gen28383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28384" type="x-p"/> (2.) The means of conferring this grace—<hi type="italic">through thy truth, thy word is truth.</hi> Not that the Holy One of Israel is hereby limited to means, but in the <hi type="italic">counsel of peace</hi> among other things it was settled and agreed, [1.] That all needful truth should be comprised and summed up in the word of God. Divine revelation, as it now stands in the written word, is not only pure truth without mixture, but entire truth without deficiency. [2.] That this word of truth should be the outward and ordinary means of our sanctification; not of itself, for then it would always sanctify, but as the instrument which the Spirit commonly uses in beginning and carrying on that good work; it is the seed of the new birth (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>), and the food of the new life, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.1-1Pet.2.2">1 Pet. ii. 1-2</reference>. <div eID="gen28384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28385" type="x-p"/> 2. As ministers. "<hi type="italic">Sanctify them,</hi> set them apart for thyself and service; let their call to the apostleship be ratified in heaven." Prophets were said to be sanctified, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jer. i. 5</reference>. Priests and Levites were so. <hi type="italic">Sanctify them;</hi> that is, (1.) "Qualify them for the office, with Christian graces and ministerial gifts, to make them able ministers of the New Testament." (2.) "Separate them to the office, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.1">Rom. i. 1</reference>. I have called them, they have consented; Father, say <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to it." (3.) "Own them in the office; let thy hand go along with them; sanctify them by or in thy truth, as truth is opposed to figure and shadow; sanctify them really, not ritually and ceremonially, as the Levitical priests were, by anointing and sacrifice. Sanctify them to thy truth, the word of thy truth, to be the preachers of thy truth to the world; as the priests were sanctified to serve at the altar, so let them be to preach the gospel." <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13-1Cor.9.14">1 Cor. ix. 13, 14</reference>. Note, [1.] Jesus Christ intercedes for his ministers with a particular concern, and recommends to his Father's grace those stars he carries in his right hand. [2.] The great thing to be asked of God for gospel ministers is that they may be sanctified, effectually separated from the world, entirely devoted to God, and experimentally acquainted with the influence of that word upon their own hearts which they preach to others. Let them have the <hi type="italic">Urim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thummim, light</hi> and <hi type="italic">integrity.</hi> <div eID="gen28385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28386" type="x-p"/> II. We have here two pleas or arguments to enforce the petition for the disciples' sanctification:— <div eID="gen28386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28387" type="x-p"/> 1. The mission they had from him (<reference osisRef="John.17.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As thou hast sent me into the world,</hi> to be thine ambassador to the children of men, so now that I am recalled <hi type="italic">have I sent them into the world,</hi> as my delegates." Now here, <div eID="gen28387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28388" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ speaks with great assurance of his own mission: <hi type="italic">Thou hast sent me into the world.</hi> The great author of the Christian religion had his commission and instructions from him who is the origin and object of all religion. He was sent of God to say what he said, and do what he did, and be what he is to those that believe on him; which was his comfort in his undertaking, and may be ours abundantly in our dependence upon him; his record was on high, for thence his mission was. <div eID="gen28388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28389" type="x-p"/> (2.) He speaks with great satisfaction of the commission he had given his disciples "<hi type="italic">So have I sent them</hi> on the same errand, and to carry on the same design;" to preach the same doctrine that he preached, and to confirm it with the same proofs, with a charge likewise to commit to other faithful men that which was committed to them. He gave them their commission (<reference osisRef="John.20.21">ch. xx. 21</reference>) with a reference to his own, and it magnifies their office that it comes from Christ, and that there is some affinity between the commission given to the ministers of reconciliation and that given to the Mediator; he is called an <hi type="italic">apostle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">Heb. iii. 1</reference>), a <hi type="italic">minister</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.8">Rom. xv. 8</reference>), a <hi type="italic">messenger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal. iii. 1</reference>. Only they are sent as servants, he as a Son. Now this comes in here as a reason, [1.] Why Christ was concerned so much for them, and laid their case so near his heart; because he had himself put them into a difficult office, which required great abilities for the due discharge of it. Note, Whom Christ sends he will stand by, and interest himself in those that are employed for him; what he calls us out to he will fit us out for, and bear us up in. [2.] Why he committed them to his Father; because he was concerned in their cause, their mission being in prosecution of his, and as it were an assignment out of it. Christ <hi type="italic">received gifts for men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>), and then gave them to men (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>), and therefore <hi type="italic">prays aid</hi> of his Father to warrant and uphold those gifts, and confirm his grant of them. The Father <hi type="italic">sanctified him</hi> when <hi type="italic">he sent him into the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.36">ch. x. 36</reference>. Now, they being sent as he was, let them also be sanctified. <div eID="gen28389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28390" type="x-p"/> 2. The merit he had for them is another thing here pleaded (<reference osisRef="John.17.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">For their sakes I sanctify myself.</hi> Here is, (1.) Christ's designation of himself to the work and office of Mediator: <hi type="italic">I sanctified myself.</hi> He entirely devoted himself to the undertaking, and all the parts of it, especially that which he was now going about—the <hi type="italic">offering up of himself without spot unto God, by the eternal Spirit.</hi> He, as the priest and altar, sanctified himself as the sacrifice. When he said, Father, <hi type="italic">glorify thy name</hi>—Father, <hi type="italic">thy will be done</hi>—Father, I <hi type="italic">commit my spirit into thy hands,</hi> he paid down the satisfaction he had engaged to make, and so sanctified himself. This he pleads with his Father, for his intercession is made in the virtue of his satisfaction; <hi type="italic">by his own blood he entered into the holy place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb. ix. 12</reference>), as the high priest, on the day of atonement, sprinkled the blood of the sacrifice at the same time that he burnt incense within the veil, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.12">Lev. xvi. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.14">14</reference>. (2.) Christ's design of kindness to his disciples herein; it is <hi type="italic">for their sakes,</hi> that <hi type="italic">they may be sanctified,</hi> that is, that they may be martyrs; so some. "I sacrifice myself, that they may be sacrificed to the glory of God and the church's good." Paul speaks of his being offered, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6">2 Tim. iv. 6</reference>. Whatever there is in the <hi type="italic">death of the saints</hi> that is <hi type="italic">precious in the sight of the Lord,</hi> it is owing to the death of the Lord Jesus. But I rather take it more generally, that they may be saints and ministers, duly qualified and accepted of God. [1.] The office of the ministry is the purchase of Christ's blood, and one of the blessed fruits of his satisfaction, and owes its virtue and value to Christ's merit. The priests under the law were consecrated with the blood of bulls and goats, but gospel ministers with the blood of Jesus. [2.] The real holiness of all good Christians is the fruit of Christ's death, by which the gift of the Holy Ghost was purchased; he <hi type="italic">gave himself for his church,</hi> to <hi type="italic">sanctify it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25-Eph.5.26">Eph. v. 25, 26</reference>. And he that designed the end designed also the means, that they might be sanctified <hi type="italic">by the truth,</hi> the truth which Christ came into the world to bear witness to and died to confirm. The word of truth receives its sanctifying virtue and power from the death of Christ. Some read it, that they may be sanctified <hi type="italic">in truth,</hi> that is, truly; for as God must be served, so, in order to this, we must be sanctified, <hi type="italic">in the spirit, and in truth.</hi> And this Christ has prayed for, for all that are his; for <hi type="italic">this is his will, even their sanctification,</hi> which encourages them to pray for it,

<div eID="gen28390" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28391" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word; <hi type="super">21</hi> That they all may be one; as thou, Father, <hi type="italic">art</hi> in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one: 23 I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me. <div eID="gen28391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28392" type="x-p"/> Next to their purity he prays for their unity; for the wisdom from above is <hi type="italic">first pure, then peaceable;</hi> and amity is amiable indeed when it is like the ointment on Aaron's holy head, and the dew on Zion's holy hill. Observe, <div eID="gen28392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28393" type="x-p"/> I. Who are included in this prayer (<reference osisRef="John.17.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Not these only,</hi> not these only that are now my disciples" (the eleven, the seventy, with others, men and women that followed him when he was here on earth), "but <hi type="italic">for those also who shall believe on me through their word,</hi> either preached by them in their own day or written by them for the generations to come; I pray <hi type="italic">for them all,</hi> that they all may be one in their interest in this prayer, and may all receive benefit by it." Note, here, 1. Those, and those only, are interested in the mediation of Christ, that do, or shall, believe in him. This is that by which they are described, and it comprehends all the character and duty of a Christian. They that lived then, <hi type="italic">saw and believed,</hi> but they in after ages <hi type="italic">have not seen,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">have believed.</hi> 2. It is <hi type="italic">through the word</hi> that souls are brought to believe on Christ, and it is for this end that Christ appointed the scriptures to be written, and a standing ministry to continue in the church, while the church stands, that is, while the world stands, for the raising up of a seed. 3. It is certainly and infallibly known to Christ who shall believe on him. He does not here pray at a venture, upon a contingency depending on the treacherous will of man, which pretends to be free, but by reason of sin is <hi type="italic">in bondage with its children;</hi> no, Christ knew very well whom he prayed for, the matter was reduced to a certainty by the divine prescience and purpose; he knew who were given him, who being ordained to eternal life, were <hi type="italic">entered in the Lamb's book,</hi> and should undoubtedly believe, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.48">Acts xiii. 48</reference>. 4. Jesus Christ intercedes not only for great and eminent believers, but for the meanest and weakest; not for those only that are to be employed in the highest post of trust and honour in his kingdom, but for all, even those that in the eye of the world are inconsiderable. As the divine providence extends itself to the meanest creature, so does the divine grace to the meanest Christian. The good Shepherd has an eye even to <hi type="italic">the poor of the flock.</hi> 5. Jesus Christ in his mediation had an actual regard to those of the chosen remnant that were yet unborn, the people that <hi type="italic">should be created</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.31">Ps. xxii. 31</reference>), the <hi type="italic">other sheep</hi> which he <hi type="italic">must yet bring.</hi> Before they are <hi type="italic">formed in the womb he knows them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jer. i. 5</reference>), and prayers are filed in heaven for them beforehand, by him who <hi type="italic">declareth the end from the beginning, and calleth things that are not as though they were.</hi> <div eID="gen28393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28394" type="x-p"/> II. What is intended in this prayer (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">That they all may be one.</hi> The same was said before (<reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">that they may be one as we are,</hi> and again, <reference osisRef="John.17.22">v. 22</reference>. The heart of Christ was much upon this. Some think that the oneness prayed for in <reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference> has special reference to the disciples as ministers and apostles, that they might be one in their testimony to Christ; and that the harmony of the evangelists, and concurrence of the first preachers of the gospel, are owing to this prayer. Let them be not only of <hi type="italic">one heart,</hi> but of <hi type="italic">one mouth,</hi> speaking the same thing. The unity of the gospel ministers is both the beauty and strength of the gospel interest. But it is certain that the oneness prayed for in <reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference> respects all believers. It is the prayer of Christ for all that are his, and we may be sure it is an answered prayer—<hi type="italic">that they all may be one,</hi> one in us (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>), one <hi type="italic">as e are one</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.22">v. 22</reference>), made <hi type="italic">perfect in one,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.23">v. 23</reference>. It includes three things:— <div eID="gen28394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28395" type="x-p"/> 1. That they might all be <hi type="italic">incorporated in one body.</hi> "Father, look upon them all as one, and ratify that great charter by which they are embodied as one church. Though they live in distant places, from one end of heaven to the other, and in several ages, from the beginning to the close of time, and so cannot have any personal acquaintance or correspondence with each other, yet let them be united in me their common head." As Christ died, so he prayed, to <hi type="italic">gather them all in one,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.52">ch. xi. 52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen28395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28396" type="x-p"/> 2. That they might all be animated by one Spirit. This is plainly implied in this—<hi type="italic">that they may be one in us.</hi> Union with the Father and Son is obtained and kept up only by the Holy Ghost. <hi type="italic">He that is joined to the Lord in one spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.17">1 Cor. vi. 17</reference>. Let them all be stamped with the same image and superscription, and influenced by the same power. <div eID="gen28396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28397" type="x-p"/> 3. That they might all be <hi type="italic">knit together</hi> in the bond of love and charity, all of one heart. <hi type="italic">That they all may be one,</hi> (1.) In judgment and sentiment; not in every little thing—this is neither possible nor needful, but in the great things of God, and in them, by the virtue of this prayer, they are all agreed—that God's favour is better than life—that sin is the worst of evils, Christ the best of friends—that there is another life after this, and the like. (2.) In disposition and inclination. All that are sanctified have the same divine nature and image; they have all a new heart, and it is <hi type="italic">one heart.</hi> (3.) They are all one in their designs and aims. Every true Christian, <hi type="italic">as far as he is so,</hi> eyes the glory of God as his highest end, and the glory of heaven as his chief good. (4.) They are all one in their desires and prayers; though they differ in words and the manner of expressions, yet, having received the same <hi type="italic">spirit of adoption,</hi> and observing the same rule, they pray for the same things in effect. (5.) All one in love and affection. Every true Christian has that in him which inclines him to love all true Christians as such. That which Christ here prays for is that <hi type="italic">communion of saints</hi> which we profess to believe; the fellowship which all believers have with God, and their intimate union with all the saints in heaven and earth, <reference osisRef="1John.1.3">1 John i. 3</reference>. But this prayer of Christ will not have its complete answer till all the saints come to heaven, for then, and not till then, they shall be <hi type="italic">perfect in one,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.23">v. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">Eph. iv. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen28397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28398" type="x-p"/> III. What is intimated by way of plea or argument to enforce this petition; three things:— <div eID="gen28398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28399" type="x-p"/> 1. The oneness that is between the Father and the Son, which is mentioned again and again, <reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.21-John.17.23">21-23</reference>. (1.) It is taken for granted that the Father and Son are one, one in nature and essence, equal in power and glory, one in mutual endearments. The <hi type="italic">Father loveth the Son,</hi> and the Son always pleased the Father. They are one in design, and one in operation. The intimacy of this oneness is expressed in these words, <hi type="italic">thou in me, and I in thee.</hi> This he often mentions for his support under his present sufferings, when his enemies were ready to fall upon him, and his friends to fall off from him; yet he was in the Father, and the Father in him. (2.) This is insisted on in Christ's prayer for his disciples' oneness, [1.] As the pattern of that oneness, showing how he desired they might be one. Believers are one in some measure as God and Christ are one; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The union of believers is a strict and close union; they are united by a divine nature, by the power of divine grace, in pursuance of the divine counsels. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a holy union, in the Holy Spirit, for holy ends; not a body politic for any secular purpose. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is, and will be at last, a complete union. Father and Son have the same attributes, properties, and perfections; so have believers now, as far as they are sanctified, and when grace shall be perfected in glory they will be exactly consonant to each other, all changed into the same image. [2.] As the centre of that oneness; that they may be <hi type="italic">one in us,</hi> all meeting here. There is <hi type="italic">one God</hi> and <hi type="italic">one Mediator;</hi> and herein believers are one, that they all agree to depend upon the favour of this one God as their felicity and the merit of this one Mediator as their righteousness. That is a conspiracy, not a union, which doth not centre in God as the end, and Christ as the way. All who are truly united to God and Christ, who <hi type="italic">are one,</hi> will soon be <hi type="italic">united one to another.</hi> [3.] As a plea for that oneness. The Creator and Redeemer are one in interest and design; but to what purpose are they so, if all believers be not one body with Christ, and do not jointly receive grace for grace from him, as he has received it for them? Christ's design was to reduce revolted mankind to God: "Father," says he, "let all that believe be one, that <hi type="italic">in one body</hi> they may be reconciled" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15-Eph.2.16">Eph. ii. 15, 16</reference>), which speaks of the uniting of Jews and Gentiles in the church; that great mystery, that the Gentiles should be <hi type="italic">fellow-heirs, and of the same body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Eph. iii. 6</reference>), to which I think this prayer of Christ principally refers, it being one great thing he aimed at in his dying; and I wonder none of the expositors I have met with should so apply it. "Father, let the Gentiles that believe be incorporated with the believing Jews, and <hi type="italic">make of twain one new man.</hi>" Those words, <hi type="italic">I in them, and thou in me,</hi> show what that union is which is so necessary, not only to the beauty, but to the very being, of his church. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Union with Christ: <hi type="italic">I in them.</hi> Christ dwelling in the hearts of believers is the life and soul of the new man. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Union with God through him: <hi type="italic">Thou in me,</hi> so as by me to be in them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Union with each other, resulting from these: <hi type="italic">that they</hi> hereby <hi type="italic">may be made perfect in one.</hi> We are complete in him. <div eID="gen28399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28400" type="x-p"/> 2. The design of Christ in all his communications of light and grace to them (<reference osisRef="John.17.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The glory which thou gavest me,</hi> as the trustee or channel of conveyance, <hi type="italic">I have</hi> accordingly <hi type="italic">given them,</hi> to this intent, <hi type="italic">that they may be one, as we are one;</hi> so that those gifts will be in vain, if they be not one." Now these gifts are either, (1.) Those that were conferred upon the apostles, and first planters of the church. The glory of being God's ambassadors to the world—the glory of working miracles—the glory of gathering a church out of the world, and erecting the throne of God's kingdom among men—this glory was given to Christ, and some of the honour he put upon them when he sent them to <hi type="italic">disciple all nations.</hi> Or, (2.) Those that are given in common to all believers. The glory of being in covenant with the Father, and accepted of him, of being laid in his bosom, and designed for a place at his right hand, was the glory which the Father gave to the Redeemer, and he has confirmed it to the redeemed. [1.] This honour he says he <hi type="italic">hath given them,</hi> because he hath intended it for them, settled it upon them, and secured it to them upon their believing Christ's promises to be real gifts. [2.] This was given to him to give to them; it was conveyed to him in trust for them, and he was faithful to him that appointed him. [3.] He gave it to them, that they <hi type="italic">might be one.</hi> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> to entitle them to the privilege of unity, that by virtue of their common relation to <hi type="italic">one God the Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">one Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> they might be truly denominated one. The gift of the Spirit, that great glory which the Father gave to the Son, by him to be given to all believers, makes them one, for he works <hi type="italic">all in all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1 Cor. xii. 4</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To engage them to the duty of unity. That in consideration of their agreement and communion in one creed and one covenant, one Spirit and one Bible—in consideration of what they have in one God and one Christ, and of what they hope for in one heaven, they may be of one mind and one mouth.
