Worldly glory sets men at variance; for if some be advanced others are eclipsed, and therefore, while the disciples dreamed of a temporal kingdom, they were ever and anon quarrelling; but spiritual honours being conferred alike upon all Christ's subjects, they being all <hi type="italic">made to our God kings and priests,</hi> there is no occasion for contest nor emulation. The more Christians are taken up with the glory Christ has given them, the less desirous they will be of vain-glory, and, consequently, the less disposed to quarrel. <div eID="gen28400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28401" type="x-p"/> 3. He pleads the happy influence their oneness would have upon others, and the furtherance it would give to the public good. This is twice urged (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the world may believe that thou hast sent me.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="John.17.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the world may know it,</hi> for without knowledge there can be no true faith. Believers must know what they believe, and why and wherefore they believe it. Those who believe <hi type="italic">at a venture,</hi> venture too far. Now Christ here shows, <div eID="gen28401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28402" type="x-p"/> (1.) His good-will to the world of mankind in general. Herein he is of his Father's mind, as we are sure he is in every thing, that he would have all men to be saved, and to <hi type="italic">come to the knowledge of the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1 Tim. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2 Pet. iii. 9</reference>. Therefore it is his will that all means possible should be used, and no stone left unturned, for the conviction and conversion of the world. We know not who are chosen, but we must in our places do our utmost to further men's salvation, and take heed of doing any thing to hinder it. <div eID="gen28402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28403" type="x-p"/> (2.) The good fruit of the church's oneness; it will be an evidence of the truth of Christianity, and a means of bringing many to embrace it. <div eID="gen28403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28404" type="x-p"/> [1.] In general, it will recommend Christianity to the world, and to the good opinion of those that are without. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The embodying of Christians in one society by the gospel charter will greatly promote Christianity. When the world shall see so many of those that were its children called out of its family, distinguished from others, and changed from what they themselves sometimes were,—when they shall see this society raised by the foolishness of preaching, and kept up by miracles of divine providence and grace, and how admirably well it is modelled and constituted, they will be ready to say, <hi type="italic">We will go with you, for we see that God is with you. Secondly,</hi> The uniting of Christians in love and charity is the beauty of their profession, and invites others to join with them, as the love that was among those primo-primitive Christians, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.42-Acts.2.43">Acts ii. 42, 43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.32-Acts.4.33">iv. 32, 33</reference>. When Christianity, instead of causing quarrels about itself, makes all other strifes to cease,—when it cools the fiery, smooths the rugged, and disposes men to be kind and loving, courteous and beneficent, to all men, studious to preserve and promote peace in all relations and societies, this will recommend it to all that have any thing either of natural religion or natural affection in them. <div eID="gen28404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28405" type="x-p"/> [2.] In particular, it will beget in men good thoughts, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of Christ: They will know and believe that <hi type="italic">thou hast sent me,</hi> By this it will appear that Christ was sent of God, and that his doctrine was divine, in that his religion prevails to join so many of different capacities, tempers, and interests in other things, in one body by faith, with one heart by love. Certainly he was sent by the God of power, who fashions men's hearts alike, and the God of love and peace; when the worshippers of God are one, he is one, and his name one. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of Christians: They will <hi type="italic">know that thou hast loved them as thou hast loved me.</hi> Here is, 1. The privilege of believers: <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> himself loveth them with a love resembling his love to his Son, for they are loved in him with an everlasting love. 2. The evidence of their interest in this privilege, and that is their being one. By this it will appear that God loves us, if we <hi type="italic">love one another with a pure heart;</hi> for wherever <hi type="italic">the love of God is shed abroad in the heart</hi> it will change it into the same image. See how much good it would do to the world to know better how dear to God all good Christians are. The Jews had a saying, <hi type="italic">If the world did but know the worth of good men, they would hedge them about with pearls.</hi> Those that have so much of God's love should have more of ours.

<div eID="gen28405" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28406" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world. <hi type="super">25</hi> O righteous Father, the world hath not known thee: but I have known thee, and these have known that thou hast sent me. <hi type="super">26</hi> And I have declared unto them thy name, and will declare <hi type="italic">it:</hi> that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them. <div eID="gen28406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28407" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A petition for the glorifying of all those that were given to Christ (<reference osisRef="John.17.24">v. 24</reference>), not only these apostles, but all believers: <hi type="italic">Father, I will that they may be with me.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28408" type="x-p"/> 1. The connection of this request with those foregoing. He had prayed that God would preserve, sanctify, and unite them; and now he prays that he would crown all his gifts with their glorification. In this method we must pray, first for grace, and then for glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>); for in this method God gives. Far be it from the only wise God to come under the imputation either of that <hi type="italic">foolish builder who without a foundation built upon the sand,</hi> as he would if he should glorify any whom he has not first sanctified; or of that <hi type="italic">foolish builder who began to build and was not able to finish,</hi> as he would if he should sanctify any, and not glorify them. <div eID="gen28408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28409" type="x-p"/> 2. The manner of the request: <hi type="italic">Father, I will.</hi> Here, as before, he addresses himself to God as a Father, and therein we must do likewise; but when he says, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">thelo</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I will,</hi> he speaks a language peculiar to himself, and such as does not become ordinary petitioners, but very well became him who paid for what he prayed for. (1.) This intimates the authority of his intercession in general; his word was with power in heaven, as well as on earth. He entering <hi type="italic">with his own blood into the holy place,</hi> his intercession there has an uncontrollable efficacy. He intercedes as a king, for he is a priest upon his throne (like Melchizedek), a king-priest. (2.) It intimates his particular authority in this matter; he had a power to <hi type="italic">give eternal life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.2">v. 2</reference>), and, pursuant to that power, he says, <hi type="italic">Father, I will.</hi> Though now he <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant,</hi> yet that power being to be most illustriously exerted when he shall come the second time in the glory of a judge, to say, <hi type="italic">Come ye blessed,</hi> having that in his eye, he might well say, <hi type="italic">Father, I will.</hi> <div eID="gen28409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28410" type="x-p"/> 3. The request itself—that all the elect might come to be with him in heaven at last, to see his glory, and to share in it. Now observe here, <div eID="gen28410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28411" type="x-p"/> (1.) Under what notion we are to hope for heaven? wherein does that happiness consist? three things make heaven:—[1.] It is to be where Christ is: <hi type="italic">Where I am;</hi> in the paradise whither Christ's soul went at death; in the third heavens whither his soul and body went at his ascension:—<hi type="italic">Where I am,</hi> am to be shortly, am to be eternally. In this world we are but <hi type="italic">in transitu—on our passage;</hi> there we truly are where we are to be for ever; so Christ reckoned, and so must we. [2.] It is to be with him where he is; this is not tautology, but intimates that we shall not only be in the same happy place where Christ is, but that the happiness of the place will consist in his presence; this is <hi type="italic">the fulness of its joy.</hi> The very heaven of heaven is to be with Christ, there in company with him, and communion with him, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Phil. i. 23</reference>. [3.] It is to <hi type="italic">behold his glory, which the Father</hi> has given him. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The glory of the Redeemer is the brightness of heaven. That glory before which angels cover their faces was his glory, <reference osisRef="John.12.41">ch. xii. 41</reference>. The Lamb is the light of the new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Rev. xxi. 23</reference>. Christ will <hi type="italic">come in the glory of his Father,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he is the brightness of his glory.</hi> God shows his glory there, as he does his grace here, through Christ. "<hi type="italic">The Father has given me this glory,</hi>" though he was as yet in his low estate; but it was very true, and very near. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The felicity of the redeemed consists very much in the beholding of this glory; they will have the immediate view of his glorious person. <hi type="italic">I shall see God in my flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.26-Job.19.27">Job xix. 26, 27</reference>. They will have a clear insight into his glorious undertaking, as it will be then accomplished; they will see into those springs of love from which flow all the streams of grace; they shall have an appropriating sight of Christ's glory (<hi type="italic">Uxor fulget radiis mariti—The wife shines with the radiance of her husband</hi>), and an assimilating sight: they shall <hi type="italic">be changed into the same image, from glory to glory.</hi> <div eID="gen28411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28412" type="x-p"/> (2.) Upon what ground we are to hope for heaven; no other than purely the mediation and intercession of Christ, because he hath said, <hi type="italic">Father, I will.</hi> Our sanctification is our evidence, for <hi type="italic">he that has this hope in him purifies himself;</hi> but it is the will of Christ that is our title, <hi type="italic">by which will we are sanctified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">Heb. x. 10</reference>. Christ speaks here as if he did not count his own happiness complete unless he had his elect to share with him in it, for it is <hi type="italic">the bringing of many sons to glory that makes the captain of our salvation perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen28412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28413" type="x-p"/> 4. The argument to back this request: <hi type="italic">for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.</hi> This is a reason, (1.) Why he expected this glory himself. Thou wilt <hi type="italic">give it to me, for thou lovedst me.</hi> The honour and power given to the Son as Mediator were founded in the Father's love to him (<reference osisRef="John.5.20">ch. v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">the Father loves the Son,</hi> is infinitely well pleased in his undertaking, and <hi type="italic">therefore has given all things into his hands;</hi> and, the matter being concerted in the divine counsels from eternity, he is said to love him as Mediator <hi type="italic">before the foundation of the world.</hi> Or, (2.) Why he expected that those who <hi type="italic">were given to him</hi> should be with him to share in his glory: "<hi type="italic">Thou lovedst me,</hi> and them in me, and canst deny me nothing I ask for them." <div eID="gen28413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28414" type="x-p"/> II. The conclusion of the prayer, which is designed to enforce all the petitions for the disciples, especially the last, that they may be glorified. Two things he insists upon, and pleads:— <div eID="gen28414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28415" type="x-p"/> 1. The respect he had to his Father, <reference osisRef="John.17.25">v. 25</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28416" type="x-p"/> (1.) The title he gives to God: <hi type="italic">O righteous Father.</hi> When he prayed that they might be sanctified, he called him <hi type="italic">holy Father;</hi> when he prays that they may be glorified, he calls him <hi type="italic">righteous Father;</hi> for it is a <hi type="italic">crown of righteousness which the righteous Judge shall give.</hi> God's righteousness was engaged for the giving out of all that good which the Father had promised and the Son had purchased. <div eID="gen28416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28417" type="x-p"/> (2.) The character he gives of the world that lay in wickedness: <hi type="italic">The world has not known thee.</hi> Note, Ignorance of God overspreads the world of mankind; this is the darkness they sit in. Now this is urged here, [1.] To show that these disciples need the aids of special grace, both because of the necessity of their work—they were to bring a world that knew not God to the knowledge of him; and also, because of the difficulty of their work—they must bring light to those that rebelled against the light; therefore keep them. [2.] To show that they were qualified for further peculiar favours, for they had that knowledge of God which the world had not. <div eID="gen28417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28418" type="x-p"/> (3.) The plea he insists upon for himself: <hi type="italic">But I have known thee.</hi> Christ knew the Father as no one else ever did; knew upon what grounds he went in his undertaking, knew his Father's mind in every thing, and therefore, in this prayer, came to him with confidence, as we do to one we know. Christ is here suing out blessings for those that were his; pursuing this petition, when he had said, <hi type="italic">The world has not known thee,</hi> one would expect it should follow, <hi type="italic">but they have known thee;</hi> no, their knowledge was not to be boasted of, <hi type="italic">but I have known thee,</hi> which intimates that there is nothing in us to recommend us to God's favour, but all our interest in him, and intercourse with him, result from, and depend upon, Christ's interest and intercourse. We are unworthy, but he is worthy. <div eID="gen28418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28419" type="x-p"/> (4.) The plea he insists upon for his disciples: <hi type="italic">And they have known that thou hast sent me;</hi> and, [1.] Hereby they are distinguished from the unbelieving world. When multitudes to whom Christ was sent, and his grace offered, would not <hi type="italic">believe that God had sent him,</hi> these knew it, and believed it, and were not ashamed to own it. Note, To know and believe in Jesus Christ, in the midst of a world that persists in ignorance and infidelity, is highly pleasing to God, and shall certainly be crowned with distinguishing glory. Singular faith qualifies for singular favours. [2.] Hereby they are interested in the mediation of Christ, and partake of the benefit of his acquaintance with the Father: "<hi type="italic">I have known thee,</hi> immediately and perfectly; and these, though they have not so known thee, nor were capable of knowing thee so, yet <hi type="italic">have known that thou hast sent me,</hi> have known that which was required of them to know, have known the Creator in the Redeemer." Knowing Christ as sent of God, they have, in him, known the Father, and are introduced to an acquaintance with him; therefore, "Father, look after them for my sake." <div eID="gen28419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28420" type="x-p"/> 2. The respect he had to his disciples (<reference osisRef="John.17.26">v. 26</reference>): "I have led them into the knowledge of thee, and will do it yet more and more; with this great and kind intention, <hi type="italic">that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them.</hi>" Observe here, <div eID="gen28420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28421" type="x-p"/> (1.) What Christ had done for them: <hi type="italic">I have declared unto them thy name.</hi> [1.] This he had done for those that were his immediate followers. <hi type="italic">All the time that he went in and out among them,</hi> he made it his business to declare his Father's name to them, and to beget in them a veneration for it. The tendency of all his sermons and miracles was to advance his Father's honours, and to spread the knowledge of him, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>. [2.] This he had done for all that believe on him; for they had not been brought to believe if Christ had not made known to them his Father's name. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We are indebted to Christ for all the knowledge we have of the Father's name; he declares it, and he opens the understanding to receive that revelation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those whom Christ recommends to the favour of God he first leads into an acquaintance with God. <div eID="gen28421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28422" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he intended to do yet further for them: <hi type="italic">I will declare it.</hi> To the disciples he designed to give further instructions after his resurrection (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.3">Acts i. 3</reference>), and to bring them into a much more intimate acquaintance with divine things by the pouring out of the Spirit after his ascension; and to all believers, into whose hearts he hath shined, he shines more and more. Where Christ has <hi type="italic">declared his Father's name, he will declare it;</hi> for <hi type="italic">to him that hath shall be given;</hi> and those that know God both need and desire to know more of him. This is fitly pleaded for them: "Father, own and favour them, for they will own and honour thee." <div eID="gen28422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28423" type="x-p"/> (3.) What he aimed at in all this; not to fill their heads with curious speculations, and furnish them with something to talk of among the learned, but to secure and advance their real happiness in two things:— <div eID="gen28423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28424" type="x-p"/> [1.] Communion with God: "Therefore I have given them the knowledge of thy name, of all that whereby thou hast made thyself known, <hi type="italic">that thy love,</hi> even that <hi type="italic">wherewith thou hast loved me, may be,</hi> not only towards them, but <hi type="italic">in them;</hi>" that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "Let them have the fruits of that love for their sanctification; let <hi type="italic">the Spirit of love,</hi> with which thou hast filled me, <hi type="italic">be in them.</hi>" Christ declares his Father's name to believers, that with that divine light darted into their minds a divine love may be shed abroad in their hearts, to be in them a commanding constraining principle of holiness, that they may partake of a divine nature. When God's love to us comes to be in us, it is like the virtue which the loadstone gives the needle, inclining it to move towards the pole; it draws out the soul towards God in pious and devout affections, which are as the spirits of the divine life in the soul. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "Let them have the taste and relish of that love for their consolation; let them not only be interested in the love of God, by having God's name declared to them, but, by a further declaration of it, let them have the comfort of that interest; that they may not only know God, but <hi type="italic">know that they know him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1John.2.3">1 John ii. 3</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the love of God</hi> thus <hi type="italic">shed abroad in the heart</hi> that fills it with joy, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Rom. v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">5</reference>. This God has provided for, that we may not only be satisfied with his loving kindness, but be satisfied of it; and so may live a life of complacency in God and communion with him; this we must pray for, this we must press after; if we have it, we must thank Christ for it; if we want it, we may thank ourselves. <div eID="gen28424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28425" type="x-p"/> [2.] Union with Christ in order hereunto: <hi type="italic">And I in them.</hi> There is no getting into the love of God but through Christ, nor can we keep ourselves in that love but by abiding in Christ, that is, having him to abide in us; nor can we have the sense and apprehension of that love but by our experience of the indwelling of Christ, that is, the Spirit of Christ in our hearts. It is <hi type="italic">Christ in us that</hi> is <hi type="italic">the</hi> only <hi type="italic">hope of glory</hi> that will <hi type="italic">not make us ashamed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col. i. 27</reference>. All our communion with God, the reception of his love to us with our return of love to him again, passes through the hands of the Lord Jesus, and the comfort of it is owing purely to him. Christ had said but a little before, <hi type="italic">I in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.23">v. 23</reference>), and here it is repeated (though the sense was complete without it), and the prayer closed with it, to show how much the heart of Christ was sent upon it; all his petitions centre in this, and with this <hi type="italic">the prayers of Jesus, the Son of David, are ended: "I in them;</hi> let me have this, and I desire no more." It is the glory of the Redeemer to dwell in the redeemed: it is his <hi type="italic">rest for ever,</hi> and he has desired it. Let us therefore make sure our union with Christ, and then take the comfort of his intercession. <hi type="italic">This</hi> prayer had an end, but <hi type="italic">that</hi> he ever lives to make.  <chapter eID="John.17"/> <div eID="gen28425" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28428" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28427" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ in the Garden; The Treachery of Judas; The Ear of Malachus Cut Off; Christ Yields Himself a Prisoner.</title> <div sID="gen28429" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples. <hi type="super">3</hi> Judas then, having received a band <hi type="italic">of men</hi> and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons. <hi type="super">4</hi> Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye? <hi type="super">5</hi> They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am <hi type="italic">he.</hi> And Judas also, which betrayed him, stood with them. 6 As soon then as he had said unto them, I am <hi type="italic">he,</hi> they went backward, and fell to the ground. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then asked he them again, Whom seek ye? And they said, Jesus of Nazareth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Jesus answered, I have told you that I am <hi type="italic">he:</hi> if therefore ye seek me, let these go their way: <hi type="super">9</hi> That the saying might be fulfilled, which he spake, Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Simon Peter having a sword drew it, and smote the high priest's servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant's name was Malchus. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said Jesus unto Peter, Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it? <hi type="super">12</hi> Then the band and the captain and officers of the Jews took Jesus, and bound him, <div eID="gen28429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28430" type="x-p"/> The hour was now come that <hi type="italic">the captain of our salvation,</hi> who was to be <hi type="italic">made perfect by sufferings,</hi> should engage the enemy. We have here his entrance upon the encounter. The day of recompence is in his heart, and <hi type="italic">the year of his redeemed is come, and his own arm works the salvation,</hi> for he has no second. <hi type="italic">Let us turn aside now, and see this great sight.</hi> <div eID="gen28430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28431" type="x-p"/> I. Our Lord Jesus, like a bold champion, takes the field first (<reference osisRef="John.18.1-John.18.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had spoken these words,</hi> preached the sermon, prayed his prayer, and so finished his testimony, he would lose no time, but <hi type="italic">went forth</hi> immediately out of the house, out of the city, by moon-light, for the passover was observed at the full moon, <hi type="italic">with his disciples</hi> (the eleven, for Judas was otherwise employed), and <hi type="italic">he went over the brook Cedron,</hi> which runs between Jerusalem and the mount of Olives, <hi type="italic">where was a garden,</hi> not his own, but some friend's, who allowed him the liberty of it. Observe, <div eID="gen28431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28432" type="x-p"/> 1. That our Lord Jesus entered upon his sufferings <hi type="italic">when he had spoken these words,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Matt.26.1">Matt. xxvi. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">When he had finished all these sayings.</hi> Here it is intimated, (1.) That our Lord Jesus took his work before him. The office of the priest was to teach, and pray, and offer sacrifice. Christ, after teaching and praying, applies himself to make atonement. Christ had said all he had to say as a prophet, and now he addresses himself to the discharge of his office as a priest, to <hi type="italic">make his soul an offering for sin;</hi> and, when he had gone through this, he entered upon his kingly office. (2.) That having by his sermon prepared his disciples for this hour of trial, and by his prayer prepared himself for it, he then courageously went out to meet it. When he had put on his armour, he entered the lists, and not till then. Let those that suffer according to the will of God, in a good cause, with a good conscience, and having a clear call to it, comfort themselves with this, that Christ will not engage those that are his in any conflict, but he will first do that for them which is necessary to prepare them for it; and if we receive Christ's instructions and comforts, and be interested in his intercession, we may, with an unshaken resolution, venture through the greatest hardships in the way of duty. <div eID="gen28432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28433" type="x-p"/> 2. That <hi type="italic">he went forth with his disciples.</hi> Judas knew what house he was in in the city, and he could have staid and met his sufferings there; but, (1.) He would do as he was wont to do, and not alter his method, either to meet the cross or to miss it, when his hour was come. It was his custom when he was at Jerusalem, after he had spent the day in public work, to retire at night <hi type="italic">to the mount of Olives;</hi> there his quarters were, in the skirts of the city, for they would not make room for him in the palaces, in the heart of the town. This being his custom, he could not be put out of his method by the foresight of his sufferings, but, as Daniel, did then just <hi type="italic">as he did aforetime,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Dan. vi. 10</reference>. (2.) He was as unwilling that there should be <hi type="italic">an uproar among the people</hi> as his enemies were, for it was not his way <hi type="italic">to strive or cry.</hi> If he had been seized in the city, and a tumult raised thereby, mischief might have been done, and a great deal of blood shed, and therefore he withdrew. Note, When we find ourselves involved in trouble, we should be afraid of involving others with us. It is no disgrace to the followers of Christ to fall tamely. Those who aim at honour from men value themselves upon a resolution to sell their lives as dearly as they can; but those who know that their blood is precious to Christ, and that not a drop of it shall be shed but upon a valuable consideration, need not stand upon such terms. (3.) He would set us an example in the beginning of his passion, as he did at the end of it, of retirement from the world. <hi type="italic">Let us go forth to him, without the camp, bearing his reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">Heb. xiii. 13</reference>. We must lay aside, and leave behind, the crowds, and cares, and comforts, of cities, even holy cities, if we would cheerfully take up our cross, and keep up our communion with God therein. <div eID="gen28433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28434" type="x-p"/> 3. That he went <hi type="italic">over the brook Cedron.</hi> He must go over this to go to <hi type="italic">the mount of Olives,</hi> but the notice taken of it intimates that there was something in it significant; and it points, (1.) At David's prophecy concerning the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.7">Ps. cx. 7</reference>), that <hi type="italic">he shall drink of the brook in the way;</hi> the brook of suffering in the way to his glory and our salvation, signified by <hi type="italic">the brook Cedron, the black brook,</hi> so called either from the darkness of the valley it ran through or the colour of the water, tainted with the dirt of the city; such a brook Christ drank of, when it lay in the way of our redemption, and <hi type="italic">therefore shall he lift up the head,</hi> his own and ours. (2.) At David's pattern, as a type of the Messiah. In his flight from Absalom, particular notice is taken of his <hi type="italic">passing over the brook Cedron, and going up by the ascent of mount Olivet, weeping,</hi> and all that were with him in tears too, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.23">2 Sam. xv. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">30</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Son of David,</hi> being driven out by the rebellious Jews, who would <hi type="italic">not have him to reign over them</hi> (and Judas, like Ahithophel, being in the plot against him), passed over the brook in meanness and humiliation, attended by a company of true mourners. The godly kings of Judah had burnt and destroyed the idols they found at <hi type="italic">the brook Cedron;</hi> Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2 Chron. xv. 16</reference>; Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.14">2 Chron. xxx. 14</reference>; Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">2 Kings xxiii. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">6</reference>. Into that brook the abominable things were cast. Christ, <hi type="italic">being now made sin for us,</hi> that he might abolish it and take it away, began his passion by the same brook. Mount Olivet, where Christ began his sufferings, lay on the east side of Jerusalem; mount Calvary, where he finished them, on the west; for in them he had an eye to such as should <hi type="italic">come from the east and the west.</hi> <div eID="gen28434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28435" type="x-p"/> 4. That he entered into a garden. This circumstance is taken notice of only by this evangelist, that Christ's sufferings began in a garden. In the garden of Eden sin began; there the curse was pronounced, there the Redeemer was promised, and therefore in a garden that promised seed entered the lists with the old serpent. Christ was buried also in a garden. (1.) Let us, when we walk in our gardens, take occasion thence to meditate on Christ's sufferings in a garden, to which we owe all the pleasure we have in our gardens, for by them the curse upon the ground for man's sake was removed. (2.) When we are in the midst of our possessions and enjoyments, we must keep up an expectation of troubles, for our gardens of delight are in a vale of tears. <div eID="gen28435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28436" type="x-p"/> 5. That he had his disciples with him, (1.) Because he used to take them with him when he retired for prayer. (2.) They must be witnesses of his sufferings, and his patience under them, that they might with the more assurance and affection preach them to the world (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.48">Luke xxiv. 48</reference>), and be themselves prepared to suffer. (3.) He would take them into the danger to show them their weakness, notwithstanding the promises they had made of fidelity. Christ sometimes brings his people into difficulties, that he may magnify himself in their deliverance. <div eID="gen28436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28437" type="x-p"/> 6. That Judas the traitor <hi type="italic">knew the place,</hi> knew it to be the place of his usual retirement, and probably, by some word Christ had dropped, knew that he intended to be there that night, for want of a better closet. A solitary garden is a proper place for meditation and prayer, and after a passover is a proper time to retire for private devotion, that we may pray over the impressions made and the vows renewed, and clench the nail. Mention is made of Judas's knowing the place, (1.) To aggravate the sin of Judas, that he would betray his Master, notwithstanding the intimate acquaintance he had with him; nay, and that he would make use of his familiarity with Christ, as giving him an opportunity of betraying him; a generous mind would have scorned to do so base a thing. Thus has Christ's holy religion been <hi type="italic">wounded in the house of its friends,</hi> as it could not have been wounded any where else. Many an apostate could not have been so profane, if he had not been a professor; could not have ridiculed scriptures and ordinances, if he had not known them. (2.) To magnify the love of Christ, that, though he knew where the traitor would seek him, thither he went to be found of him, now that he knew his <hi type="italic">hour was come.</hi> Thus he showed himself willing to suffer and die for us. What he did was not by constraint, but by consent; though as man he said, <hi type="italic">Let this cup pass away,</hi> as Mediator he said, "<hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> I come with a good will." It was late in the night (we may suppose eight or nine o'clock) when Christ went out to the garden; for it was not only his <hi type="italic">meat and drink,</hi> but his rest and sleep, <hi type="italic">to do the will of him that sent him.</hi> When others were going to bed, he was going to prayer, going to suffer. <div eID="gen28437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28438" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">The captain of our salvation</hi> having taken the field, the enemy presently comes upon the spot, and attacks him (<reference osisRef="John.18.3">v. 3</reference>): Judas with his men comes thither, commissioned by the chief priests, especially those among them that were Pharisees, who were the most bitter enemies to Christ. This evangelist passes over Christ's agony, because the other three had fully related it, and presently introduces Judas and his company that came to seize him. Observe, <div eID="gen28438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28439" type="x-p"/> 1. The persons employed in this action—<hi type="italic">a band of men and officers from the chief priests, with Judas.</hi> (1.) Here is a multitude engaged against Christ—<hi type="italic">a band of men,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">speira</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">cohors, a regiment,</hi> a Roman band, which some think was five hundred men, others a thousand. Christ's friends were few, his enemies many. Let us therefore <hi type="italic">not follow a multitude to do evil,</hi> nor fear a multitude designing evil to us, <hi type="italic">if God be for us.</hi> (2.) Here is a mixed multitude; the band of men were Gentiles, Roman soldiers, a detachment out of the guards that were posted in the tower of Antonia, to be a curb upon the city; the <hi type="italic">officers of the chief priests,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyperetas</hi></hi>. Either their domestic servants, or the officers of their courts, were Jews; these had an enmity to each other, but were united against Christ, who came to <hi type="italic">reconcile both to God in one body.</hi> (3.) It is a commissioned multitude, not a popular tumult; no, they have received orders <hi type="italic">from the chief priests,</hi> upon whose suggestion to the governor that this Jesus was a dangerous man, it is likely they had a warrant from him too to take him up, <hi type="italic">for they feared the people.</hi> See what enemies Christ and his gospel have had, and are likely to have, numerous and potent, and therefore formidable: ecclesiastical and civil powers combined against them, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 1, 2</reference>. Christ said it would be so (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.18">Matt. x. 18</reference>), and found it so. (4.) All under the direction of Judas. He <hi type="italic">received</hi> this <hi type="italic">band of men;</hi> it is probable that he requested it, alleging that it was necessary to send a good force, being as ambitious of the honour of commanding in chief in this expedition as he was covetous of <hi type="italic">the wages of</hi> this <hi type="italic">unrighteousness.</hi> He thought himself wonderfully preferred from coming in the rear of the contemptible twelve to be placed at the head of these formidable hundreds; he never made such a figure before, and promised himself, perhaps, that this should not be the last time, but he should be rewarded with a captain's commission, or better, if he succeeded well in this enterprise. <div eID="gen28439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28440" type="x-p"/> 2. The preparation they had made for an attack: They came <hi type="italic">with lanterns, and torches, and weapons.</hi> (1.) If Christ should abscond, though they had moonlight, they would have occasion for their lights; but they might have spared these; the second Adam was not driven, as the first was, to hide himself, either for fear or shame, <hi type="italic">among the trees of the garden.</hi> It was folly to light a candle to seek the Sun by. (2.) If he should resist, they would have occasion for their arms. <hi type="italic">The weapons of his warfare were spiritual,</hi> and at these <hi type="italic">weapons</hi> he had often beaten them, and <hi type="italic">put them to silence,</hi> and therefore they have now recourse to other <hi type="italic">weapons, swords and staves.</hi> <div eID="gen28440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28441" type="x-p"/> III. Our Lord Jesus gloriously repulsed the first onset of the enemy, <reference osisRef="John.18.4-John.18.6">v. 4-6</reference>, where observe, <div eID="gen28441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28442" type="x-p"/> 1. How he received them, with all the mildness imaginable towards them, and all the calmness imaginable in himself. <div eID="gen28442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28443" type="x-p"/> (1.) He met them with a very soft and mild question (<reference osisRef="John.18.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Knowing all things that should come upon him,</hi> and therefore not at all surprised with this alarm, with a wonderful intrepidity and presence of mind, undisturbed and undaunted, he <hi type="italic">went forth</hi> to meet them, and, as if he had been unconcerned, softly asked, "<hi type="italic">Whom seek you?</hi> What is the matter? What means this bustle at this time of night?" See here, [1.] Christ's foresight of his sufferings; He <hi type="italic">knew all those things that should come upon him,</hi> for he had bound himself to suffer them. Unless we had strength, as Christ had, to bear the discovery, we should not covet to know what shall come upon us; it would but anticipate our pain; <hi type="italic">sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof:</hi> yet it will do us good to expect sufferings in general, so that when they come we may say, "It is but what we looked for, the cost we sat down and counted upon." [2.] Christ's forwardness to his sufferings; he did not run away from them, but went out to meet them, and reached forth his hand to take the bitter cup. When the people would have forced him to a crown, and offered to make him a king in Galilee, but he withdrew, and hid himself (<reference osisRef="John.6.15">ch. vi. 15</reference>); but, when they came to force him to a cross, he offered himself; for he came to this world to suffer and went to the other world to reign. This will not warrant us needlessly to expose ourselves to trouble, for we know not when our hour is come; but we are called to suffering when we have no way to avoid it but by sin; and, when it comes to this, let <hi type="italic">none of these things move</hi> us, for they cannot hurt us. <div eID="gen28443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28444" type="x-p"/> (2.) He met them with a very calm and mild answer when they told him whom they were in quest of, <reference osisRef="John.18.5">v. 5</reference>. They said, <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth;</hi> and he said, <hi type="italic">I am he.</hi> [1.] It should seem, <hi type="italic">their eyes were held, that they could not know him.</hi> It is highly probable that many of the Roman band, at least the officers of the temple, had often seen him, if only to satisfy their curiosity; Judas, however, to be sure, knew him well enough, and yet none of them could pretend to say, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man</hi> we seek. Thus he showed them the folly of bringing lights to see for him, for he could make them not to know him when they saw him; and he has herein shown us how easily he can infatuate the counsels of his enemies, and make them lose themselves, when they are seeking mischief. [2.] In their enquiries for him they called him <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> which was the only title they knew him by, and probably he was so called in their warrant. It was a name of reproach given him, to darken the evidence of his being the Messiah. By this it appears that they knew him not, whence he was; for, if they had known him, surely they would not have persecuted him. [3.] He fairly answers them: <hi type="italic">I am he.</hi> He did not improve the advantage he had against them by their blindness, as Elisha did against the Syrians, telling them, <hi type="italic">This is not the way, neither is this the city;</hi> but improves it as an opportunity of showing his willingness to suffer. Though they called him Jesus of Nazareth, he answered to the name, for he despised the reproach; he might have said, <hi type="italic">I am not he,</hi> for he was <hi type="italic">Jesus of Bethlehem;</hi> but he would by no means allow equivocations. He has hereby taught us to own him, whatever it cost us; not to be <hi type="italic">ashamed of him or his words;</hi> but even in difficult times <hi type="italic">to confess Christ crucified, and manfully to fight under his banner. I am he,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Ego eimi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I am he,</hi> is the glorious name of the blessed God (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>), and the honour of that name is justly challenged by the blessed Jesus. [4.] Particular notice is taken, in a parenthesis, <hi type="italic">that Judas stood with them.</hi> He that used to stand with those that followed Christ now stood with those that fought against him. This describes an apostate; he is one that changes sides. He herds himself with those with whom his heart always was, and with whom he shall have his lot in the judgment-day. This is mentioned, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To show the impudence of Judas. One would wonder where he got the confidence with which he now faced his Master, and <hi type="italic">was not ashamed, neither could he blush;</hi> Satan in his heart gave him a whore's forehead. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To show that Judas was particularly aimed at in the power which went along with that word, <hi type="italic">I am he,</hi> to foil the aggressors. It was an arrow levelled at the traitor's conscience, and pierced him to the quick; for Christ's coming and his voice will be more terrible to apostates and betrayers than to sinners of any other class. <div eID="gen28444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28445" type="x-p"/> 2. See how he terrified them, and obliged them to retire (<reference osisRef="John.18.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They went backward, and,</hi> like men thunder-struck, <hi type="italic">fell to the ground.</hi> It should seem, they did not fall forward, as humbling themselves before him, and yielding to him, but backward, as standing it out to the utmost. Thus Christ was declared to be more than a man, even when he was trampled upon as <hi type="italic">a worm, and no man.</hi> This word, <hi type="italic">I am he,</hi> had revived his disciples, and raised them up (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.27">Matt. xiv. 27</reference>); but the same word strikes his enemies down. Hereby he showed plainly, <div eID="gen28445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28446" type="x-p"/> (1.) What he could have done with them. When he struck them down, he could have struck them dead; when he spoke them <hi type="italic">to the ground,</hi> he could have spoken them to hell, and have sent them, like Korah's company, the next way thither; but he would not do so, [1.] Because the hour of his suffering was come, and he would not put it by; he would only show that his life was not forced from him, but <hi type="italic">he laid it down of himself,</hi> as he had said. [2.] Because he would give an instance of his patience and forbearance with the worst of men, and his compassionate love to his very enemies. In striking them down, and no more, he gave them both a call to repent and space to repent; but <hi type="italic">their hearts were hardened,</hi> and all was in vain. <div eID="gen28446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28447" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he will do at last with all his implacable enemies, <hi type="italic">that will not repent to give him glory; they shall flee, they shall fall, before him.</hi> Now the scripture was accomplished (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.12">Ps. xxi. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou shalt make them turn their back,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Ps. xx. 8</reference>. And it will be accomplished more and more; <hi type="italic">with the breath of his mouth he will slay the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.21">Rev. xix. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Quid judicaturus faciet, qui judicandus hoc facit?</hi>—<hi type="italic">What will he do when he shall come to judge, seeing he did this when he came to be judged?</hi>—Augustine. <div eID="gen28447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28448" type="x-p"/> IV. Having given his enemies a repulse, he gives his friends a protection, and that by his word too, <reference osisRef="John.18.7-John.18.9">v. 7-9</reference>, where we may observe, <div eID="gen28448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28449" type="x-p"/> 1. How he continued to expose himself to their rage, <reference osisRef="John.18.7">v. 7</reference>. They did not lie long where they fell, but, by divine permission, got up again; it is only in the other world that God's judgments are everlasting. When they were down, one would have thought Christ should have made his escape; when they were up again, one would have thought they should have let fall their pursuit; but still we find, (1.) They are as eager as ever to seize him. It is in some confusion and disorder that they recover themselves; they cannot imagine what ailed them, that they could not keep their ground, but will impute it to any thing rather than Christ's power. Note, There are hearts so very hard in sin that nothing will work upon them to reduce and reclaim them. (2.) He is as willing as ever to be seized. When they were fallen before him, he did not insult over them, but seeing them at a loss, asked them the same question, <hi type="italic">Whom seek you?</hi> And they gave him the same answer, <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth.</hi> In his repeating the question, he seems to come yet closer to their consciences: "Do you not know <hi type="italic">whom you seek?</hi> Are you not aware that you are in error, and will you meddle with your match? Have you not had enough of it, but will you try the other struggle? <hi type="italic">Did ever any harden his heart against God and prosper?</hi>" In their repeating the same answer, they showed an obstinacy in their wicked way; they still call him <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> with as much disdain as ever, and Judas is as unrelenting as any of them. <hi type="italic">Let us therefore fear lest,</hi> by a few bold steps at first in a sinful way, <hi type="italic">our hearts be hardened.</hi> <div eID="gen28449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28450" type="x-p"/> 2. How he contrived to secure his disciples from their rage. He improved this advantage against them for the protection of his followers. When he shows his courage with reference to himself, <hi type="italic">I have told you that I am he,</hi> he shows his care for his disciples, <hi type="italic">Let these go their way.</hi> He speaks this as a command to them, rather than a contract with them; for they lay at his mercy, not he at theirs. He charges them therefore as <hi type="italic">one having authority: "Let these go their way;</hi> it is at your peril if you meddle with them" This aggravated the sin of the disciples in forsaking him, and particularly Peter's in denying him, that Christ had given them this pass, or warrant of protection, and yet they had not faith and courage enough to rely upon it, but betook themselves to such base and sorry shifts for their security. When Christ said, <hi type="italic">Let these go their way,</hi> he intended, <div eID="gen28450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28451" type="x-p"/> (1.) To manifest his affectionate concern for his disciples. When he exposed himself, he excused them, because they were not as yet fit to suffer; their faith was weak, and their spirits were low, and it would have been as much as their souls, and the lives of their souls, were worth, to bring them into sufferings now. <hi type="italic">New wine</hi> must not be <hi type="italic">put into old bottles.</hi> And, besides, they had other work to do; they must go their way, for they are to go into all the world, to preach the gospel. <hi type="italic">Destroy them not, for a blessing is in them.</hi> Now herein, [1.] Christ gives us a great encouragement to follow him; for, though he has allotted us sufferings, yet he considers our frame, will wisely time the cross, and proportion it to our strength, and will <hi type="italic">deliver the godly out of temptation,</hi> either from it, or through it. [2.] He gives us a good example of love to our brethren and concern for their welfare. We must not consult our own ease and safety only, but others, as well as our own, and in some cases more than our own. There is a generous and heroic love, which will enable us to <hi type="italic">lay down our lives for the brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1 John iii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen28451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28452" type="x-p"/> (2.) He intended to give a specimen of his undertaking as Mediator. When he offered himself to suffer and die, it was that we might escape. He was our <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antipsychos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a sufferer in our stead;</hi> when he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> he said also, <hi type="italic">Let these go their way;</hi> like the ram offered instead of Isaac. <div eID="gen28452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28453" type="x-p"/> 3. Now herein he confirmed the word which he had spoken a little before (<reference osisRef="John.17.12">ch. xvii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Of those whom thou gavest me, I have lost none.</hi> Christ, by fulfilling that word in this particular, gave an assurance that it should be accomplished in the full extent of it, not only for those that were now with him, but for all that should believe on him through their word. Though Christ's keeping them was meant especially of the preservation of their souls from sin and apostasy, yet it is here applied to the preservation of their natural lives, and very fitly, for even the body was a part of Christ's charge and care; he is to <hi type="italic">raise it up at the last day,</hi> and therefore to preserve it as well as <hi type="italic">the spirit and soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1 Thess. v. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17-2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 17, 18</reference>. Christ will preserve the natural life for the service to which it is designed; it is given to him to be used for him, and he will not lose the service of it, but will be magnified in it, <hi type="italic">whether by life or death;</hi> it shall be held in life as long as any use is to be made of it. Christ's witnesses shall not die till they have given in their evidence. But this is not all; this preservation of the disciples was, in the tendency of it, a spiritual preservation. They were now so weak in faith and resolution that in all probability, if they had been called out to suffer at this time, they would have shamed themselves and their Master, and some of them, at least the weaker of them, would have been lost; and therefore, that he might <hi type="italic">lose none,</hi> he would not expose them. The safety and preservation of the saints are owing, not only to the divine grace in proportioning the strength to the trial, but to the divine providence in proportioning the trial to the strength. <div eID="gen28453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28454" type="x-p"/> V. Having provided for the safety of his disciples, he rebukes the rashness of one of them, and represses the violence of his followers, as he had repulsed the violence of his persecutors, <reference osisRef="John.18.10-John.18.11">v. 10, 11</reference>, where we have, <div eID="gen28454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28455" type="x-p"/> 1. Peter's rashness. He had a sword; it is not likely that he wore one constantly as a gentleman, but they had two swords among them all (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.38">Luke xxii. 38</reference>), and Peter, being entrusted with one, drew it; for now, if ever, he thought it was his time to use it; and <hi type="italic">he smote one of the high priest's servants,</hi> who was probably one of the forwardest, and aiming, it is likely, to cleave him down the head, missed his blow, and only <hi type="italic">cut off his right ear. The servant's name,</hi> for the greater certainty of the narrative, is recorded; it <hi type="italic">was Malchus,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Malluch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.10.4">Neh. x. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen28455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28456" type="x-p"/> (1.) We must here acknowledge Peter's good-will; he had an honest zeal for his Master, though now misguided. He had lately promised to venture his life for him, and would now make his words good. Probably it exasperated Peter to see Judas at the head of this gang; his baseness excited Peter's boldness, and I wonder that when he did draw his sword he did not aim at the traitor's head. <div eID="gen28456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28457" type="x-p"/> (2.) Yet we must acknowledge Peter's ill conduct; and, though his good intention did excuse, yet it would not justify him. [1.] He had no warrant from his Master for what he did. Christ's soldiers must wait the word of command, and not outrun it; before they expose themselves to sufferings, they must see to it, not only that their cause be good, but their call clear. [2.] He transgressed the duty of his place, and resisted the powers that were, which Christ had never countenanced, but forbidden (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Matt. v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">that you resist not evil</hi> [3.] He opposed his Master's sufferings, and, notwithstanding the rebuke he had for it once, is ready to repeat, <hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself;</hi> suffering be <hi type="italic">far from thee;</hi> though Christ had told him that he must and would suffer, and that his hour was now come. Thus, while he seemed to fight for Christ, he fought against him. [4.] He broke the capitulation his Master had lately made with the enemy. When he said, <hi type="italic">Let these go their way,</hi> he not only indented for their safety, but in effect passed his word for their good behaviour, that they should go away peaceably; this Peter heard, and yet would not be bound by it. As we may be guilty of a sinful cowardice when we are called to appear, so we may be of a sinful forwardness when we are called to retire. [5.] He foolishly exposed himself and his fellow disciples to the fury of this enraged multitude. If he had cut off Malchus's head when he cut off his ear, we may suppose the soldiers would have fallen upon all the disciples, and have hewn them to pieces, and would have represented Christ as not better than Barabbas. Thus many have been guilty of self-destruction, in their zeal for self-preservation. [6.] Peter played the coward so soon after this (denying his Master) that we have reason to think he would not have done this but that he saw his Master cause them to fall on the ground, and then he could deal with them; but, when he saw him surrender himself notwithstanding, his courage failed him; whereas the true Christian hero will appear in the cause of Christ, not only when it is prevailing, but when it seems to be declining; will be on the right side, though it be not the rising side. <div eID="gen28457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28458" type="x-p"/> (3.) We must acknowledge God's over-ruling providence in directing the stroke (so that it should do no more execution, but only cut off his ear, which was rather marking him than maiming him), as also in giving Christ an opportunity to manifest his power and goodness in healing the hurt, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.51">Luke xxii. 51</reference>. Thus what was in danger of turning to Christ's reproach proved an occasion of that which redounded much to his honour, even among his adversaries. <div eID="gen28458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28459" type="x-p"/> 2. The rebuke his Master gave him (<reference osisRef="John.18.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Put up thy sword into the sheath,</hi> or scabbard; it is a gentle reproof, because it was his zeal that carried him beyond the bounds of discretion. Christ did not aggravate the matter, only bade him <hi type="italic">do so no more.</hi> Many think their being in grief and distress will excuse them if they be hot and hasty with those about them; but Christ has here set us an example of meekness in sufferings. Peter must put up his sword, for it was the <hi type="italic">sword of the Spirit</hi> that was to be committed to him—<hi type="italic">weapons of warfare not carnal,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">mighty.</hi> When Christ with a word felled the aggressors, he showed Peter how he should be armed with a <hi type="italic">word, quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword,</hi> and with that, not long after this, he laid Ananias and Sapphira dead at his feet. <div eID="gen28459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28460" type="x-p"/> 3. The reason for this rebuke: <hi type="italic">The cup which my Father has given me, shall I not drink it?</hi> Matthew relates another reason which Christ gave for this rebuke, but John preserves this, which he had omitted; in which Christ gives us, (1.) A full proof of his own submission to his Father's will. Of all that was amiss in what Peter did, he seems to resent nothing so much as that he would have hindered his sufferings now that his <hi type="italic">hour was come:</hi> "What, <hi type="italic">Peter,</hi> wilt thou step in between the cup and the lip? <hi type="italic">Get thee hence, Satan.</hi>" If Christ be determined to suffer and die, it is presumption for Peter in word or deed to oppose it: <hi type="italic">Shall I not drink it?</hi> The manner of expression bespeaks a settled resolution, and that he would not entertain a thought to the contrary. He was willing to drink of this cup, though it was a bitter cup, an infusion of the wormwood and the gall, the cup of trembling, a bloody cup, the <hi type="italic">dregs of the cup of the Lord's wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22">Isa. li. 22</reference>. He drank it, that he might put into our hands the cup of salvation, the cup of consolation, the cup of blessing; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he is willing to drink it, because <hi type="italic">his Father put it into his hand.</hi> If his Father will have it so, it is for the best, and be it so. (2.) A fair pattern to us of submission to God's will in every thing that concerns us. We must <hi type="italic">pledge</hi> Christ in the cup that he drank of (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.23">Matt. xx. 23</reference>), and must argue ourselves into a compliance. [1.] It is but a <hi type="italic">cup;</hi> a small matter comparatively, be it what it will. It is not a sea, a red sea, a dead sea, for it is not hell; it is light, and but for a moment. [2.] It is a cup that is given us; sufferings are gifts. [3.] It is given us by a Father, who has a Father's authority, and does us no wrong; a Father's affection, and means us no hurt. <div eID="gen28460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28461" type="x-p"/> VI. Having entirely reconciled himself to the dispensation, he calmly surrendered, and yielded himself a prisoner, not because he could not have made his escape, but because he would not. One would have thought the cure of Malchus's ear should have made them relent, but nothing would win upon them. <hi type="italic">Maledictus furor, quem nec majestast miraculi nec pietas beneficii confringere potuit</hi>—<hi type="italic">Accursed rage, which the grandeur of the miracle could not appease, nor the tenderness of the favour conciliate.</hi>—Anselm. Observe here, <div eID="gen28461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28462" type="x-p"/> 1. How they seized him: <hi type="italic">They took Jesus.</hi> Only some few of them could lay hands on him, but it is charged upon them all, for they were all aiding and abetting. In treason there are not accessaries; all are principals. Now the scripture was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">Bulls have compassed me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">Ps. xxii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">compassed me like bees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Ps. cxviii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">The breath of our nostrils is taken in their pit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">Lam. iv. 20</reference>. They had so often been frustrated in their attempts to seize him that now, having got him into their hands, we may suppose they flew upon him with so much the more violence. <div eID="gen28462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28463" type="x-p"/> 2. How they secured him: <hi type="italic">They bound him.</hi> This particular of his sufferings is taken notice of only by this evangelist, that, as soon as ever he was taken, he was bound, pinioned, handcuffed; tradition says, "They bound him with such cruelty that the blood started out at his fingers' ends; and, having bound his hands behind him, they clapped an iron chain about his neck, and with that dragged him along." See <hi type="italic">Gerhard. Harm.</hi> cap. 5. <div eID="gen28463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28464" type="x-p"/> (1.) This shows the spite of his persecutors. They bound him, [1.] That they might torment him, and put him in pain, as they bound Samson to afflict him. [2.] That they might disgrace him, and put him to shame; slaves were bound, so was Christ, though free-born. [3.] That they might prevent his escape, Judas having told them to hold him fast. See their folly, that they should think to fetter that power which had but just now proved itself omnipotent. [4.] They bound him as one already condemned, for they were resolved to prosecute him to the death, and that he should die as a fool dieth, that is, as a malefactor, with his hands bound, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.33-2Sam.3.34">2 Sam. iii. 33, 34</reference>. Christ had bound the consciences of his persecutors with the power of his word, which galled them; and, to be revenged on him, they laid these bonds on him.

<div eID="gen28464" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ before Annas and Caiaphas; The Fall of Peter; Christ Arraigned; Peter Again Denies Christ.</title> <div sID="gen28465" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And led him away to Annas first; for he was father in law to Caiaphas, which was the high priest that same year. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now Caiaphas was he, which gave counsel to the Jews, that it was expedient that one man should die for the people. 15 And Simon Peter followed Jesus, and <hi type="italic">so did</hi> another disciple: that disciple was known unto the high priest, and went in with Jesus into the palace of the high priest. <hi type="super">16</hi> But Peter stood at the door without. Then went out that other disciple, which was known unto the high priest, and spake unto her that kept the door, and brought in Peter. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then saith the damsel that kept the door unto Peter, Art not thou also <hi type="italic">one</hi> of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself. <hi type="super">19</hi> The high priest then asked Jesus of his disciples, and of his doctrine. <hi type="super">20</hi> Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing. <hi type="super">21</hi> Why askest thou me? ask them which heard me, what I have said unto them: behold, they know what I said. 22 And when he had thus spoken, one of the officers which stood by struck Jesus with the palm of his hand, saying, Answerest thou the high priest so? <hi type="super">23</hi> Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me? <hi type="super">24</hi> Now Annas had sent him bound unto Caiaphas the high priest. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Simon Peter stood and warmed himself. They said therefore unto him, Art not thou also <hi type="italic">one</hi> of his disciples? He denied <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and said, I am not. <hi type="super">26</hi> One of the servants of the high priest, being <hi type="italic">his</hi> kinsman whose ear Peter cut off, saith, Did not I see thee in the garden with him? <hi type="super">27</hi> Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew. <div eID="gen28465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28466" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's arraignment before the high priest, and some circumstances that occurred therein which were omitted by the other evangelists; and Peter's denying him, which the other evangelists had given the story of entire by itself, is interwoven with the other passages. The crime laid to his charge having relation to religion, the judges of the spiritual court took it to fall directly under their cognizance. Both Jews and Gentiles seized him, and so both Jews and Gentiles tried and condemned him, for he died for the sins of both. Let us go over the story in order. <div eID="gen28466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28467" type="x-p"/> I. Having seized him, they <hi type="italic">led him away to Annas first,</hi> before they brought him to the court that was sat, expecting him, in the house of Caiaphas, <reference osisRef="John.18.13">v. 13</reference>. 1. They <hi type="italic">led him away,</hi> led him in triumph, as a trophy of their victory; led him <hi type="italic">as a lamb to the slaughter,</hi> and they led him through the sheep-gate spoken of <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh. iii. 1</reference>. For through that they went from the mount of Olives into Jerusalem. They hurried him away with violence, as if he had been the worst and vilest of malefactors. We had been led away of our own impetuous lusts, and led captive by Satan at his will, and, that we might be rescued, Christ was led away, led captive by Satan's agents and instruments. 2. They led him away to their masters that sent them. It was now about midnight, and one would think they should have put him in ward (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.12">Lev. xxiv. 12</reference>), should have led him to some prison, till it was a proper time to call a court; but he is hurried away immediately, not to the justices of peace, to be committed, but to the judges to be condemned; so extremely violent was the prosecution, partly because they feared a rescue, which they would thus not only leave no time for, but give a terror to; partly because they greedily thirsted after Christ's blood, as <hi type="italic">the eagle that hasteth to the prey.</hi> 3. They led him to Annas first. Probably his house lay in the way, and was convenient for them to call at to refresh themselves, and, as some think, to be paid for their service. I suppose Annas was old and infirm, and could not be present in council with the rest at that time of night, and yet earnestly desired to see the prey. To gratify him therefore with the assurance of their success, that the old man might sleep the better, and to receive his blessing for it, they produce their prisoner before him. It is sad to see those that are old and sickly, when they cannot commit sin as formerly, taking pleasure in those that do. Dr. Lightfoot thinks Annas was not present, because he had to attend early that morning in the temple, to examine the sacrifices which were that day to be offered, whether they were without blemish; if so, there was a significancy in it, that Christ, the great sacrifice, was presented to him, and sent away bound, as approved and ready for the altar. 4. This Annas was father-in-law to Caiaphas the high priest; this kindred by marriage between them comes in as a reason either why Caiaphas ordered that this piece of respect should be done to Annas, to favour him with the first sight of the prisoner, or why Annas was willing to countenance Caiaphas in a matter his heart was so much upon. Note, Acquaintance and alliance with wicked people are a great confirmation to many in their wicked ways. <div eID="gen28467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28468" type="x-p"/> II. Annas did not long detain them, being as willing as any of them to have the prosecution pushed on, and therefore sent him bound to Caiaphas, to his house, which was appointed for the rendezvous of the sanhedrim upon this occasion, or to the usual place in the temple where the high priest kept his court; this is mentioned, <reference osisRef="John.18.24">v. 24</reference>. But our translators intimate in the margin that it should come in here, and, accordingly, read it there, <hi type="italic">Annas had sent him.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen28468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28469" type="x-p"/> 1. The power of Caiaphas intimated (<reference osisRef="John.18.13">v. 13</reference>). He was <hi type="italic">high priest that same year.</hi> The high priest's commission was during life; but there were now such frequent changes, by the Simoniacal artifices of aspiring men with the government, that it was become almost an annual office, a presage of its final period approaching; while they were undermining one another. God was overturning them all, that he might come whose right it was. Caiaphas was high priest that same year when Messiah was to be cut off, which intimates, (1.) That when a bad thing was to be done by a high priest, according to the foreknowledge of God, Providence so ordered it that a bad man should be in the chair to do it. (2.) That, when God would make it to appear what corruption there was in the heart of a bad man, he put him into a place of power, where he had temptation and opportunity to exert it. It was the ruin of Caiaphas that he was high priest that year, and so became a ringleader in the putting of Christ to death. Many a man's advancement has lost him his reputation, and he had not been dishonoured if he had not been preferred. <div eID="gen28469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28470" type="x-p"/> 2. The malice of Caiaphas, which is intimated (<reference osisRef="John.18.14">v. 14</reference>) by the repeating of what he had said some time before, that, right or wrong, guilty or innocent, <hi type="italic">it was expedient that one man should die for the people,</hi> which refers to the story <reference osisRef="John.11.50">ch. xi. 50</reference>. This comes in here to show, (1.) What a bad man he was; this was that Caiaphas that governed himself and the church by rules of policy, in defiance of the rules of equity. (2.) What ill usage Christ was likely to meet with in his court, when his case was adjudged before it was heard, and they were already resolved what to do with him; <hi type="italic">he must die;</hi> so that his trial was a jest. Thus the enemies of Christ's gospel are resolved, true or false, to run it down. (3.) It is a testimony to the innocency of our Lord Jesus, from the mouth of one of his worst enemies, who owned that he fell a sacrifice to the public good, and that it was not just he should die, but <hi type="italic">expedient</hi> only. <div eID="gen28470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28471" type="x-p"/> 3. The concurrence of Annas in the prosecution of Christ. He made himself a partaker in guilt, (1.) With the captain and officers, that without law or mercy had bound him; for he approved it by continuing him bound when he should have loosed him, he not being convicted of any crime, nor having attempted an escape. If we do not what we can to undo what others have ill done, we are accessaries <hi type="italic">ex post facto—after the fact.</hi> It was more excusable in the rude soldiers to bind him than in Annas, who should have known better, to continue him bound. (2.) With the chief priest and council that condemned him, and prosecuted him to death. This Annas was not present with them, yet thus he wished them <hi type="italic">good speed,</hi> and became a <hi type="italic">partaker of their evil deeds.</hi> <div eID="gen28471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28472" type="x-p"/> III. In the house of Caiaphas, Simon Peter began to deny his Master, <reference osisRef="John.18.15-John.18.18">v. 15-18</reference>. <div eID="gen28472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28473" type="x-p"/> 1. It was with much ado that Peter got into the hall where the court was sitting, an account of which we have <reference osisRef="John.18.15-John.18.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. Here we may observe, <div eID="gen28473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28474" type="x-p"/> (1.) Peter's kindness to Christ, which (though it proved no kindness) appeared in two things:—[1.] That he <hi type="italic">followed Jesus</hi> when he was <hi type="italic">led away;</hi> though at first he fled with the rest, yet afterwards he took heart a little, and followed at some distance, calling to mind the promises he had made to adhere to him, whatever it should cost him. Those that had followed Christ in the midst of his honours, and shared with him in those honours, when the people cried Hosanna to him, ought to have followed him now in the midst of his reproaches, and to have shared with him in these. Those that truly love and value Christ will follow him all weathers and all ways. [2.] When he could not get in where Jesus was in the midst of his enemies, he <hi type="italic">stood at the door without,</hi> willing to be as near him as he could, and waiting for an opportunity to get nearer. Thus when we meet with opposition in following Christ we must show our good-will. But yet this kindness of Peter's was no kindness, because he had not strength and courage enough to persevere in it, and so, as it proved, he did but run himself into a snare: and even his following Christ, considering all things, was to be blamed, because Christ, who knew him better than he knew himself, had expressly told him (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">ch. xiii. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whither I go thou canst not follow me now,</hi> and had told him again and again that he would deny him; and he had lately had experience of his own weakness in forsaking him. Note, We must take heed of tempting God by running upon difficulties beyond our strength, and venturing too far in a way of suffering. If our call be clear to expose ourselves, we may hope that God will enable us to honour him; but, if it be not, we may fear that God will leave us to shame ourselves. <div eID="gen28474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28475" type="x-p"/> (2.) The other disciple's kindness to Peter, which yet, as it proved, was no kindness neither. St. John several times in this gospel speaking of himself as another disciple, many interpreters have been led by this to fancy that this other disciple here was John; and many conjectures they have how he should come to be known to the high-priest; <hi type="italic">propter generis nobilitatem—being of superior birth,</hi> saith <hi type="italic">Jerome, Epitaph. Marcel.,</hi> as if he were a better gentleman born than his brother James, when they were both the sons of Zebedee the fisherman; some will tell you that he had sold his estate to the high priest, others that he supplied his family with fish, both which are very improbable. But I see no reason to think that this other disciple was John, or one of the twelve; other sheep Christ had, which were not of the fold; and this might be, as the Syriac read it, <hi type="italic">unus ex discipulis aliis—one of those other disciples</hi> that believe in Christ, but resided at Jerusalem, and kept their places there; perhaps Joseph of Arimathea, or Nicodemus, known to the high priest, but not known to him to be disciples of Christ. Note, As there are many who seem disciples and are not so, so there are many who are disciples and seem not so. There are good people hid in courts, even in Nero's, as well as hid in crowds. We must not conclude a man to be no friend to Christ merely because he has acquaintance and conversation with those that were his known enemies.
