Now, [1.] This other disciple, whoever he was, showed a respect to Peter, in introducing him, not only to gratify his curiosity and affection, but to give him an opportunity of being serviceable to his Master upon his trial, if there were occasion. Those that have a real kindness for Christ and his ways, though their temper may be reserved and their circumstances may lead them to be cautious and retired, yet, if their faith be sincere, they will discover, when they are called to it, which way their inclination lies, by being ready to do a professed disciple a good turn. Peter perhaps had formerly introduced this disciple into conversation with Christ, and now he requites his kindness, and is not ashamed to own him, though, it should seem, he had at this time but a poor downcast appearance. [2.] But this kindness proved no kindness, nay a great diskindness; by letting him into the high priest's hall, he let him into temptation, and the consequence was bad. Note, The courtesies of our friends often prove a snare to us, through a misguided affection. <div eID="gen28475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28476" type="x-p"/> 2. Peter, having got in, was immediately assaulted with the temptation, and foiled by it, <reference osisRef="John.18.17">v. 17</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen28476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28477" type="x-p"/> (1.) How slight the attack was. It was but a silly maid, of so small account that she was set to keep the door, that challenged him, and she only asked him carelessly, <hi type="italic">Art not thou one of this man's disciples?</hi> probably suspecting it by his sheepish look, and coming in timorously. We should many a time better maintain a good cause if we had a <hi type="italic">good heart on it,</hi> and could put a <hi type="italic">good face on it.</hi> Peter would have had some reason to take the alarm if Malchus had set upon him, and had said, "This is he that cut off my ear, and I will have his head for it;" but when a maid only asked him, <hi type="italic">Art not thou one of them?</hi> he might without danger have answered, <hi type="italic">And what if I am?</hi> Suppose the servants had ridiculed him, and insulted over him, upon it, those can bear but little for Christ that cannot <hi type="italic">bear this;</hi> this is but <hi type="italic">running with the footmen.</hi> <div eID="gen28477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28478" type="x-p"/> (2.) How speedy the surrender was. Without taking time to recollect himself, he suddenly answered, <hi type="italic">I am not.</hi> If he had had the boldness of the lion, he would have said, "It is my honour that I am so;" or, if he had had the wisdom of the serpent, he would have kept silence at this time, for it was an evil time. But, all his care being for his own safety, he thought he could not secure this but by a peremptory denial: <hi type="italic">I am not;</hi> he not only denies it, but even disdains it, and scorns her words. <div eID="gen28478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28479" type="x-p"/> (3.) Yet he goes further into the temptation: <hi type="italic">And the servants and officers stood there, and Peter with them</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.18">v. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen28479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28480" type="x-p"/> [1.] See how the servants made much of themselves; the night being cold, they made a fire in the hall, not for their masters (they were so eager in persecuting Christ that they forgot cold), but for themselves to refresh themselves. They cared not what became of Christ; all their care was to sit and warm themselves, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amos vi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28481" type="x-p"/> [2.] See how Peter herded himself with them, and made one among them. <hi type="italic">He sat and warmed himself. First,</hi> It was a fault bad enough that he did not attend his Master, and appear for him at the upper end of the hall, where he was now under examination. He might have been a witness for him, and have confronted the false witnesses that swore against him, if his Master had called him; at least, he might have been a witness to him, might have taken an exact notice of what passed, that he might relate it to the other disciples, who could none of them get in to hear the trial; he might have learned by his Master's example how to carry himself when it should come to his turn to suffer thus; yet neither his conscience nor his curiosity could bring him into the court, but he sits by, as if, like Gallio, he cared for none of these things. And yet at the same time we have reason to think his heart was as full of grief and concern as it could hold, but he had not the courage to own it. <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation. Secondly,</hi> It was much worse that he joined himself with those that were his Master's enemies: <hi type="italic">He stood with them, and warmed himself;</hi> this was a poor excuse for joining with them. A little thing will draw those into bad company that will be drawn to it by the love of a good fire. If Peter's zeal for his Master had not frozen, but had continued in the heat it seemed to be of but a few hours before, he had not had occasion to warm himself now. Peter was much to be blamed, 1. Because he associated with these wicked men, and kept company with them. Doubtless they were diverting themselves with this night's expedition, scoffing at Christ, at what he had said, at what he had done, and triumphing in their victory over him; and what sort of entertainment would this give to Peter? If he said as they said, or by silence gave consent, he involved himself in sin; if not, he exposed himself to danger. If Peter had not so much courage as to appear publicly for his Master, yet he might have had so much devotion as to retire into a corner, and weep in secret for his Master's sufferings, and his own sin in forsaking him; if he could not have done good, he might have kept out of the way of doing hurt. It is better to abscond than appear to no purpose, or bad purpose. 2. Because he desired to be thought <hi type="italic">one of them,</hi> that he might not be suspected to be a disciple of Christ. Is this Peter? What a contradiction is this to the prayer of every good man, <hi type="italic">Gather not my soul with sinners! Saul among the prophets</hi> is not so absurd as David among the Philistines. Those that deprecate the lot of the scornful hereafter should dread the <hi type="italic">seat of the scornful</hi> now. It is ill warming ourselves with those with whom we are in danger of burning ourselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen28481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28482" type="x-p"/> IV. Peter, Christ's friend, having begun to deny him, the high priest, his enemy, begins to accuse him, or rather urges him to accuse himself, <reference osisRef="John.18.19-John.18.21">v. 19-21</reference>. It should seem, the first attempt was to prove him a seducer, and a teacher of false doctrine, which this evangelist relates; and, when they failed in the proof of this, then they charged him with blasphemy, which is related by the other evangelists, and therefore omitted here. Observe, <div eID="gen28482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28483" type="x-p"/> 1. The articles or heads upon which Christ was examined (<reference osisRef="John.18.19">v. 19</reference>): concerning <hi type="italic">his disciples and his doctrine.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28484" type="x-p"/> (1.) The irregularity of the process; it was against all law and equity. They seize him as a criminal, and now that he is their prisoner they have nothing to <hi type="italic">lay to his charge;</hi> no libel, no prosecutor; but the judge himself must be the prosecutor, and the prisoner himself the witness, and, against all reason and justice, he is put on to be his own accuser. <div eID="gen28484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28485" type="x-p"/> (2.) The intention. The <hi type="italic">high priest then</hi> (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oun</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> which seems to refer to <reference osisRef="John.18.14">v. 14</reference>), because he had resolved that Christ must be sacrificed to their private malice under colour of the public good, examined him upon those interrogatories which would touch his life. He examined him, [1.] Concerning his disciples, that he might charge him with sedition, and represent him as dangerous to the Roman government, as well as to the Jewish church. He asked him who were his disciples—what number they were—of what country—what were their names and characters, insinuating that his scholars were designed for soldiers, and would in time become a formidable body. Some think his question concerning his disciples was, "What is now become of them all? Where are they? Why do they not appear?" upbraiding him with their cowardice in deserting him, and thus adding to the affliction of it. There was something significant in this, that Christ's calling and owning his disciples was the first thing laid to his charge, for it was <hi type="italic">for their sakes</hi> that he <hi type="italic">sanctified himself</hi> and suffered. [2.] Concerning his doctrine, that they might charge him with heresy, and bring him under the penalty of the law against false prophets, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.9-Deut.13.10">Deut. xiii. 9, 10</reference>. This was a matter properly cognizable in that court (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.12">Deut. xvii. 12</reference>), therefore a prophet could not perish but at Jerusalem, where that court sat. They could not prove any false doctrine upon him; but they hoped to extort something from him which they might distort to his prejudice, and to make him an offender for some word or other, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa. xxix. 21</reference>. They said nothing to him concerning his miracles, by which he had done so much good, and proved his doctrine beyond contradiction, because of these they were sure they could take no hold. Thus the adversaries of Christ while they are industriously quarrelling with his truth, willfully shut their eyes against the evidences of it, and take no notice of them. <div eID="gen28485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28486" type="x-p"/> 2. The appeal Christ made, in answer to these interrogatories. (1.) As to his disciples, he said nothing, because it was an impertinent question; if his doctrine was sound and good, his having disciples to whom to communicate it was no more than what was practised and allowed by their own doctors. If Caiaphas, in asking him concerning his disciples, designed to ensnare them, and bring them into trouble, it was in kindness to them that Christ said nothing of them, for he had said, <hi type="italic">Let these go their way.</hi> If he meant to upbraid him with their cowardice, no wonder that he said nothing, for <div eID="gen28486" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen28487"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28488"/>Rudet hæc opprobria nobis,<l eID="gen28488" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28489"/>Et dici potuisse, et non potuisse refelli—<l eID="gen28489" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28490"/>Shame attaches when charges are exhibited<l eID="gen28490" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen28491"/>that cannot be refuted:<l eID="gen28491" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen28487"/> <div sID="gen28492" type="x-p"/> he would say nothing to condemn them, and could say nothing to justify them. (2.) As to his doctrine, he said nothing in particular, but in general referred himself to those that heard him, being not only made manifest to God, but made manifest also in their consciences, <reference osisRef="John.18.20-John.18.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. <div eID="gen28492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28493" type="x-p"/> [1.] He tacitly charges his judges with illegal proceedings. He does not indeed speak evil of the rulers of the people, nor say now to these princes, <hi type="italic">You are wicked;</hi> but he appeals to the settled rules of their own court, whether they dealt fairly by him. <hi type="italic">Do you indeed judge righteously?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.58.1">Ps. lviii. 1</reference>. So here, <hi type="italic">Why ask you me?</hi> Which implies two absurdities in judgment: <hi type="italic">First, "Why ask you me now</hi> concerning my doctrine, when you have already condemned it?" They had made an order of court for excommunicating all that owned him (<reference osisRef="John.9.22">ch. ix. 22</reference>), had issued out a proclamation for apprehending him; and now they come to ask what his doctrine is! Thus was he condemned, as his doctrine and cause commonly are, unheard. <hi type="italic">Secondly, "Why ask you me?</hi> Must I accuse myself, when you have no evidence against me?" <div eID="gen28493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28494" type="x-p"/> [2.] He insists upon his fair and open dealing with them in the publication of his doctrine, and justifies himself with this. The crime which the sanhedrim by the law was to enquire after was the clandestine spreading of dangerous doctrines, enticing secretly, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deut. xiii. 6</reference>. As to this, therefore, Christ clears himself very fully. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As to the manner of his preaching. He spoke openly, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parresia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with freedom and plainness of speech;</hi> he did not deliver things ambiguously, as Apollo did his oracles. Those that would undermine the truth, and spread corrupt notions, seek to accomplish their purpose by sly insinuation, putting queries, starting difficulties, and asserting nothing; but Christ explained himself fully, with, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> his reproofs were free and bold, and his testimonies express against the corruptions of the age. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As to the persons he preached to: <hi type="italic">He spoke to the world,</hi> to all that had <hi type="italic">ears to hear,</hi> and were willing to hear him, high or low, learned or unlearned, Jew or Gentile, friend or foe. His doctrine feared not the censure of a mixed multitude; nor did he grudge the knowledge of it to any (as the masters of some rare invention commonly do), but freely communicated it, as the sun does his beams. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> As to the places he preached in. When he was in the country, he preached ordinarily in the synagogues—the places of meeting for worship, and on the sabbath-day-the time of meeting; when he came up to Jerusalem, he preached the same doctrine in the temple at the time of the solemn feasts, when the Jews from all parts assembled there; and though he often preached in private houses, and on mountains, and by the sea-side, to show that his word and worship were not to be confined to temples and synagogues, yet what he preached in private was the very same with what he delivered publicly. Note, The doctrine of Christ, purely and plainly preached, needs not be ashamed to appear in the most numerous assembly, for it carries its own strength and beauty along with it. What Christ's faithful ministers say they would be willing all the world should hear. Wisdom cries in the places of concourse, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">viii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">ix. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> As to the doctrine itself. He <hi type="italic">said nothing in secret</hi> contrary to what he said in public, but only by way of repetition and explication: <hi type="italic">In secret have I said nothing;</hi> as if he had been either suspicious of the truth of it, or conscious of any ill design in it. He sought no corners, for he feared no colours, nor said any thing that he needed to be ashamed of; what he did speak in private to his disciples he ordered them to proclaim on the house-tops, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">Matt. x. 27</reference>. God saith of himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa. xlv. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have not spoken in secret;</hi> his commandment is not hidden, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.11">Deut. xxx. 11</reference>. And the righteousness of faith speaks in like manner, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6">Rom. x. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Veritas nihil metuit nisi abscondi—truth fears nothing but concealment.</hi>—Tertullian. <div eID="gen28494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28495" type="x-p"/> [3.] He appeals to those that had heard him, and desires that they might be examined what doctrine he had preached, and whether it had that dangerous tendency that was surmised: "<hi type="italic">Ask those that heard me what I said unto them;</hi> some of them may be in court, or may be sent for out of their beds." He means not his friends and followers, who might be presumed to speak in his favour, but, Ask any impartial hearer; ask your own officers. Some think he pointed to them, when he said, <hi type="italic">Behold, they know what I said,</hi> referring to the report which they had made of his preaching (<reference osisRef="John.7.46">ch. vii. 46</reference>), <hi type="italic">Never man spoke like this man.</hi> Nay, you may ask some upon the bench; for it is probable that some of them had heard him, and had been put to silence by him. Note, The doctrine of Christ may safely appeal to all that know it, and has so much right and reason on its side that those who will judge impartially cannot but witness to it. <div eID="gen28495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28496" type="x-p"/> V. While the judges were examining him, the servants that stood by were abusing him, <reference osisRef="John.18.22-John.18.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. <div eID="gen28496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28497" type="x-p"/> 1. It was a base affront which one of the officers gave him; though he spoke with so much calmness and convincing evidence, this insolent fellow <hi type="italic">struck him with the palm of his hand,</hi> probably on the side of his head or face, saying, <hi type="italic">Answerest thou the high priest so?</hi> as if he had behaved himself rudely to the court. <div eID="gen28497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28498" type="x-p"/> (1.) He <hi type="italic">struck him,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">edoke rhapisma</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he gave him a blow.</hi> Some think it signifies a blow with a rod or wand, from <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">rhabdos</hi></hi>, or with the staff which was the badge of his office. Now the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">I gave my cheeks,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis rhapismata</hi></hi> (so the LXX.) <hi type="italic">to blows,</hi> the word here used. And <reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic. v. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek;</hi> and the type answered (<reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job xvi. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">They have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully.</hi> It was unjust to strike one that neither said nor did amiss; it was insolent for a mean servant to strike one that was confessedly a person of account; it was cowardly to strike one that had his hands tied; and barbarous to strike a prisoner at the bar. Here was a breach of the peace in the face of the court, and yet the judges countenanced it. Confusion of face was our due; but Christ here took it to himself: "Upon me be the curse, the shame." <div eID="gen28498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28499" type="x-p"/> (2.) He checked him in a haughty imperious manner: <hi type="italic">Answerest thou the high priest so?</hi> As if the blessed Jesus were not good enough to speak to his master, or not wise enough to know how to speak to him, but, like a rude and ignorant prisoner, must be controlled by the jailor, and taught how to behave. Some of the ancients suggest that this officer was Malchus, who owed to Christ the healing of his ear, and the saving of his head, and yet made him this ill return. But, whoever it was, it was done to please the high priest, and to curry favour with him; for what he said implied a jealousy for the dignity of the high priest. Wicked rulers will not want wicked servants, who will <hi type="italic">help forward the affliction</hi> of those whom their masters persecute. There was a successor of this high priest that commanded the bystanders to smite Paul thus <hi type="italic">on the mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.23.2">Acts xxiii. 2</reference>. Some think this officer took himself to be affronted by Christ's appeal to those about him concerning his doctrine, as if he would have vouched him to be a witness; and perhaps he was one of those officers that had spoken honourably of him (<reference osisRef="John.7.46">ch. vii. 46</reference>), and, lest he should now be thought a secret friend to him, he thus appears a bitter enemy. <div eID="gen28499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28500" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ bore this affront with wonderful meekness and patience (<reference osisRef="John.18.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I have spoken evil,</hi> in what I have now said, <hi type="italic">bear witness of the evil.</hi> Observe it to the court, and let them judge of it, who are the proper judges; but if well, and as it did become me, <hi type="italic">why smitest thou me?</hi>" Christ could have answered him with a miracle of wrath, could have struck him dumb or dead, or have withered the hand that was lifted up against him. But this was the day of his patience and suffering, and he answered him with the <hi type="italic">meekness of wisdom,</hi> to teach us not to avenge ourselves, not to render <hi type="italic">railing for railing,</hi> but with the <hi type="italic">innocency of the dove</hi> to bear injuries, even when with the <hi type="italic">wisdom of the serpent,</hi> as our Saviour, we show the injustice of them, and appeal to the magistrate concerning them. Christ did not here <hi type="italic">turn the other cheek,</hi> by which it appears that that rule, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Matt. v. 39</reference>, is not to be understood literally; a man may possibly <hi type="italic">turn the other cheek,</hi> and yet have his heart full of malice; but, comparing Christ's precept with his pattern, we learn, (1.) That in such cases we must not be our own avengers, nor judges in our own cause. We must rather receive than give the second blow, which makes the quarrel; we are allowed to defend ourselves, but not to avenge ourselves: the magistrate (if it be necessary for the preserving of the public peace, and the restraining and terrifying of evil-doers) is to be the avenger, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>. (2.) Our resentment of injuries done us must always be rational, and never passionate; such Christ's here was; <hi type="italic">when he suffered,</hi> he reasoned, but <hi type="italic">threatened not.</hi> He fairly expostulated with him that did him the injury, and so may we. (3.) When we are called out to suffering, we must <hi type="italic">accommodate ourselves</hi> to the inconveniences of a suffering state, with patience, and by one indignity done us be prepared to receive another, and to make the best of it. <div eID="gen28500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28501" type="x-p"/> VI. While the servants were thus abusing him, Peter was proceeding to deny him, <reference osisRef="John.18.25-John.18.27">v. 25-27</reference>. It is a sad story, and none of the least of Christ's sufferings. <div eID="gen28501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28502" type="x-p"/> 1. He repeated the sin the second time, <reference osisRef="John.18.25">v. 25</reference>. While he was warming himself with the servants, as one of them, they asked him, <hi type="italic">Art not thou one of his disciples?</hi> What dost thou here among us? He, perhaps, hearing that Christ was examined about his disciples, and fearing he should be seized, or at least smitten, as his Master was, if he should own it, flatly denied it, and said, <hi type="italic">I am not.</hi> <div eID="gen28502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28503" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was his great folly to thrust himself into the temptation, by continuing in the company of those that were unsuitable for him, and that he had nothing to do with. He staid to warm himself; but those that warm themselves with evil doers grow cold towards good people and good things, and those that are fond of the devil's fire-side are in danger of the devil's fire. Peter might have stood by his Master at the bar, and have warmed himself better than here, at the fire of his Master's love, which <hi type="italic">many waters could not quench,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.8.6-Song.8.7">Cant. viii. 6, 7</reference>. He might there have warmed himself with zeal for his Master, and indignation at his persecutors; but he chose rather to warm with them than to warm against them. But how could one (one disciple) be warm alone? <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.11">Eccl. iv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen28503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28504" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was his great unhappiness that he was again assaulted by the temptation; and no other could be expected, for this was a place, this an hour, of temptation. When the judge asked Christ about his disciples, probably the servants took the hint, and challenged Peter for one of them, "Answer to thy name." See here, [1.] The subtlety of the tempter in running down one whom he saw falling, and mustering a greater force against him; not a maid now, but all the servants. Note, Yielding to one temptation invites another, and perhaps a stronger. Satan redoubles his attacks when we give ground. [2.] The danger of bad company. We commonly study to approve ourselves to those with whom we choose to associate; we value ourselves upon their good word and covet to stand right in their opinion. As we choose our people we choose our praise, and govern ourselves accordingly; we are therefore concerned to make the first choice well, and not to mingle with those whom we cannot please without displeasing God. <div eID="gen28504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28505" type="x-p"/> (3.) It was his great weakness, nay, it was his great wickedness, to yield to the temptation, and to say, <hi type="italic">I am not one</hi> of his disciples, as one ashamed of that which was his honour, and afraid of suffering for it, which would have been yet more his honour. See how the <hi type="italic">fear of man brings a snare.</hi> When Christ was admired, and caressed, and treated with respect, Peter pleased himself, and perhaps prided himself, in this, that he was a disciple of Christ, and so put in for a share in the honours done to his Master. Thus many who seem fond of the reputation of religion when it is in fashion are ashamed of the reproach of it; but we must take it <hi type="italic">for better and worse.</hi> <div eID="gen28505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28506" type="x-p"/> 2. He repeated the sin the third time, <reference osisRef="John.18.26-John.18.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Here he was attacked by one of the servants, who was kinsman to Malchus, who, when he heard Peter deny himself to be a disciple of Christ, gave him the lie with great assurance: "<hi type="italic">Did not I see thee in the garden with him?</hi> Witness my kinsman's ear." Peter then denied again, as if he knew nothing of Christ, nothing of the garden, nothing of all this matter. <div eID="gen28506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28507" type="x-p"/> (1.) This third assault of the temptation was more close than the former: before his relation to Christ was only suspected, here it is proved upon him by one that saw him with Jesus, and saw him draw his sword in his defence. Note, Those who by sin think to help themselves out of trouble do but entangle and embarrass themselves the more. Dare to be brave, for truth will out. <hi type="italic">A bird of the air</hi> may perhaps <hi type="italic">tell the matter</hi> which we seek to conceal with a lie. Notice is taken of this servant's being akin to Malchus, because this circumstance would make it the more a terror to Peter. "Now," thinks he, "I am gone, my business is done, there needs no other witness nor prosecutor." We should not make any man in particular our enemy if we can help it, because the time may come when either he or some of his relations may have us at their mercy. He that may need a friend should not make a foe. But observe, though here was sufficient evidence against Peter, and sufficient provocation given by his denial to have prosecuted him, yet he escapes, has no harm done him nor attempted to be done. Note, We are often drawn into sin by groundless causeless fears, which there is no occasion for, and which a small degree of wisdom and resolution would make nothing of. <div eID="gen28507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28508" type="x-p"/> (2.) His yielding to it was no less base than the former: <hi type="italic">He denied again.</hi> See here, [1.] The nature of sin in general: <hi type="italic">the heart is hardened by the deceitfulness of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.13">Heb. iii. 13</reference>. It was a strange degree of effrontery that Peter had arrived to on a sudden, that he could with such assurance stand in a lie against so clear a disproof; but <hi type="italic">the beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water,</hi> when once the fence is broken men easily go from bad to worse. [2.] Of the sin of lying in particular; it is a fruitful sin, and upon this account <hi type="italic">exceedingly sinful:</hi> one lie needs another to support it, and that another. It is a rule in the devil's politics <hi type="italic">Male facta male factis tegere, ne perpluant</hi>—<hi type="italic">To cover sin with sin, in order to escape detection.</hi>

<div eID="gen28508" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ in the Judgment-Hall; Christ Arraigned before Pilate.</title> <div sID="gen28509" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Then led they Jesus from Caiaphas unto the hall of judgment: and it was early; and they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover. <hi type="super">29</hi> Pilate then went out unto them, and said, What accusation bring ye against this man? <hi type="super">30</hi> They answered and said unto him, If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee. <hi type="super">31</hi> Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death: <hi type="super">32</hi> That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spake, signifying what death he should die. 33 Then Pilate entered into the judgment hall again, and called Jesus, and said unto him, Art thou the King of the Jews? 34 Jesus answered him, Sayest thou this thing of thyself, or did others tell it thee of me? <hi type="super">35</hi> Pilate answered, Am I a Jew? Thine own nation and the chief priests have delivered thee unto me: what hast thou done? <hi type="super">36</hi> Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence. <hi type="super">37</hi> Pilate therefore said unto him, Art thou a king then? Jesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a king. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice. <hi type="super">38</hi> Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault <hi type="italic">at all.</hi> <hi type="super">39</hi> But ye have a custom, that I should release unto you one at the passover: will ye therefore that I release unto you the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">40</hi> Then cried they all again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Now Barabbas was a robber. <div eID="gen28509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28510" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Christ's arraignment before Pilate, the Roman governor, in the <hi type="italic">prætorium</hi> (a Latin word made Greek), the prætor's house, or <hi type="italic">hall of judgment;</hi> thither they hurried him, to get him condemned in the Roman court, and executed by the Roman power. Being resolved on his death, they took this course, 1. That he might be put to death the more legally and regularly, according to the present constitution of their government, since they became a province of the empire; not stoned in a popular tumult, as Stephen, but put to death with the present formalities of justice. Thus he was treated as a malefactor, <hi type="italic">being made sin for us.</hi> 2. That he might be put to death the more safely. If they could engage the Roman government in the matter, which the people stood in awe of, there would be little danger of an uproar. 3. That he might be put to death with more reproach to himself. <hi type="italic">The death of the cross,</hi> which the Romans commonly used, being of all deaths the most ignominious, they were desirous by it to put an indelible mark of infamy upon him, and so to sink his reputation for ever. This therefore they harped upon, <hi type="italic">Crucify him.</hi> 4. That he might be put to death with less reproach to them. It was an invidious thing to put one to death that had done so much good in the world, and therefore they were willing to throw the odium upon the Roman government, to make that the less acceptable to the people, and save themselves from the reproach. Thus many are more afraid of the scandal of a bad action than of the sin of it. See <reference osisRef="Acts.5.28">Acts v. 28</reference>. Two things are here observed concerning the prosecution:—(1.) Their policy and industry in the prosecution: <hi type="italic">It was early;</hi> some think about two or three in the morning, others about five or six, when most people were in their beds; and so there would be the less danger of opposition from the people that were for Christ; while, at the same time, they had their agents about, to call those together whom they could influence to cry out against him. See how much their heart was upon it, and how violent they were in the prosecution. Now that they had him in their hands, they would lose no time till they had him upon the cross, but denied themselves their natural rest, to push on this matter. See <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic. ii. 1</reference>. (2.) Their superstition and vile hypocrisy: <hi type="italic">The chief priests and elders,</hi> though they came along with the prisoner, that the thing might be done effectually, <hi type="italic">went not into the judgment-hall,</hi> because it was the house of an uncircumcised Gentile, <hi type="italic">lest they should be defiled,</hi> but kept out of doors, <hi type="italic">that they might eat the passover,</hi> not the paschal lamb (that was eaten the night before) but the passover-feast, upon the sacrifices which were offered on the fifteenth day, <hi type="italic">the Chagigah,</hi> as they called it, the passover-bullocks spoken of <reference osisRef="Deut.16.2">Deut. xvi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.24">2 Chron. xxx. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.8-2Chr.35.9">xxxv. 8, 9</reference>. These they were to eat of, and therefore would not go into the court, for fear of touching a Gentile, and thereby contracting, not a legal, but only a traditional pollution. This they scrupled, but made no scruple of breaking through all the laws of equity to persecute Christ to the death. <hi type="italic">They strained at a gnat, and swallowed a camel.</hi> Let us now see what passed at <hi type="italic">the judgment-hall.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen28510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28511" type="x-p"/> I. Pilate's conference with the prosecutors. They were called first, and stated what they had to say against the prisoner, as was very fit, <reference osisRef="John.18.29-John.18.32">v. 29-32</reference>. <div eID="gen28511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28512" type="x-p"/> 1. The judge calls for the indictment. Because they would not come into the hall, <hi type="italic">he went out to them</hi> into the court before the house, to talk with them. Looking upon Pilate as a magistrate, that we may give every one his due, here are three things commendable in him:—(1.) His diligent and close application to business. If it had been upon a good occasion, it had been very well that he was willing to be called up early to the judgment-seat. Men in public trusts must not love their ease. (2.) His condescending to the humour of the people, and receding from the honour of his place to gratify their scruples. He might have said, "If they be so nice as not to come in to me, let them go home as they came;" by the same rule as we might say, "If the complainant scruple to take off his hat to the magistrate, let not his complaint be heard;" but Pilate insists not upon it, bears with them, and goes out to them; for, when it is for good, we should <hi type="italic">become all things to all men.</hi> (3.) His adherence to the rule of justice, in demanding the accusation, suspecting the prosecution to be malicious: "<hi type="italic">What accusation bring you against this man?</hi>" What is the crime you charge him with, and what proof have you of it? It was a law of nature, before Valerius Publicola made it a Roman law, <hi type="italic">Ne quis indicta causa condemnetur—No man should be condemned unheard.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Acts.25.16-Acts.25.17">Acts xxv. 16, 17</reference>. It is unreasonable to commit a man, without alleging some cause in the warrant, and much more to arraign a man when there is no bill of indictment found against him. <div eID="gen28512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28513" type="x-p"/> 2. The prosecutors demand judgment against him upon a general surmise that he was a criminal, not alleging, much less proving, any thing in particular <hi type="italic">worthy of death or of bonds</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.18.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">If he were not a malefactor,</hi> or evildoer, <hi type="italic">we would not have delivered him to thee</hi> to be condemned. This bespeaks them, (1.) Very rude and uncivil to Pilate, a company of ill-natured men, that affected to despise dominion. When Pilate was so complaisant to them as to come out to treat with them, yet they were to the highest degree out of humour with him. He put the most reasonable question to them that could be; but, if it had been the most absurd, they could not have answered him with more disdain. (2.) Very spiteful and malicious towards our Lord Jesus: right or wrong, they will have him to be a malefactor, and treated as one. We are to presume a man innocent till he is proved guilty, but they will presume him guilty who could prove himself innocent. They cannot say, "He is a traitor, a murderer, a felon, a breaker of the peace," but they say, "He is an evil-doer." He an evil-doer who <hi type="italic">went about doing good!</hi> Let those be called whom he had cured, and fed, and taught; whom he has rescued from devils, and raised from death; and let them be asked whether he be an evil-doer or no. Note, It is no new thing for the best of benefactors to be branded and run down as the worst of malefactors. (3.) Very proud and conceited of themselves, and their own judgment and justice, as if their delivering a man up, under the general character of a malefactor, were sufficient for the civil magistrate to ground a judicial sentence upon, than which what could be more haughty? <div eID="gen28513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28514" type="x-p"/> 3. The judge remands him to their own court (<reference osisRef="John.18.31">v. 31</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Take you him, and judge him according to your</hi> own <hi type="italic">law,</hi> and do not trouble me with him." Now, (1.) Some think Pilate herein complimented them, acknowledging the remains of their power, and allowing them to exert it. Corporal punishment they might inflict, as <hi type="italic">scourging in their synagogues;</hi> whether capital or no is uncertain. "But," saith Pilate, "go as far as your law will allow you, and, if you go further, it shall be connived at." This he said, willing to do the Jews a pleasure, but unwilling to do them the service they required. (2.) Others think he bantered them, and upbraided them with their present state of weakness and subjection. They would be the sole judges of the guilt. "Pray," saith Pilate, "if you will be so, go on as you have begun; you have found him guilty by your own law, condemn him, if you dare, by your own law, to carry on the humour." Nothing is more absurd, nor more deserves to be exposed, than for those to pretend to dictate, and boast of their wisdom, who are weak and in subordinate stations, and whose lot it is to be dictated to. Some think Pilate here reflects upon the law of Moses, as if it allowed them what the Roman law would by no means allow—the judging of a man unheard. "It may be your law will suffer such a thing, but ours will not." Thus, through their corruptions, the law of God was blasphemed; and so is his gospel too. <div eID="gen28514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28515" type="x-p"/> 4. They disown any authority as judges, and (since it must be so) are content to be prosecutors. They now grow less insolent and more submissive, and own, "<hi type="italic">It is not lawful for us to put any man to death,</hi> whatever less punishment we may inflict, and this is a malefactor whom we would have the blood of." <div eID="gen28515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28516" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some think they had lost their power to give judgment in matters of life and death only by their own carelessness, and cowardly yielding to the darling iniquities of the age; so Dr. Lightfoot <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk exesti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">It is not</hi> in our power to pass sentence of death upon <hi type="italic">any,</hi> if we do, we shall have the mob about us immediately. <div eID="gen28516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28517" type="x-p"/> (2.) Others think their power was taken from them by the Romans, because they had not used it well, or because it was thought too great a trust to be lodged in the hands of a conquered and yet an unsubdued people. Their acknowledgement of this they designed for a compliment to Pilate, and to atone for their rudeness (<reference osisRef="John.18.30">v. 30</reference>), but it amounts to a full evidence that <hi type="italic">the sceptre was departed from Judah,</hi> and therefore that now the Messiah was come, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. If the Jews have no power <hi type="italic">to put any man to death,</hi> where is the sceptre? Yet they ask not, <hi type="italic">Where is the Shiloh?</hi> <div eID="gen28517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28518" type="x-p"/> (3.) However, there was a providence in it, that either they should have not power to put any man to death, or should decline the exercise of it upon this occasion, <hi type="italic">That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying what death he should die,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.32">v. 32</reference>. Observe, [1.] In general, that even those who designed the defeating of Christ's sayings were, beyond their intention, made serviceable to the fulfilling of them by an overruling hand of God. <hi type="italic">No word of Christ shall fall to the ground;</hi> he can never either deceive or be deceived. Even <hi type="italic">the chief priests,</hi> while they persecuted him as <hi type="italic">a deceiver,</hi> had their spirit so directed as to help to prove him true, when we should think that by taking other measures they might have defeated his predictions. <hi type="italic">Howbeit, they meant not so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. [2.] Those sayings of Christ in particular were fulfilled which he had spoken concerning his own death. Two sayings of Christ concerning his death were fulfilled, by the Jews declining to <hi type="italic">judge him according to their law. First,</hi> He had said that he should be <hi type="italic">delivered to the Gentiles,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">they should put him to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.19">Matt. xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.33">Mark x. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.32-Luke.18.33">Luke xviii. 32, 33</reference>), and hereby that saying was fulfilled. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He had said that he should be crucified (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.19">Matt. xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.2">xxvi. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">lifted up,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">xii. 32</reference>. Now, if they had <hi type="italic">judged him by their law,</hi> he had been stoned; burning, strangling, and beheading, were in some cases used among the Jews, but never crucifying. It was therefore necessary that Christ should be put to death by the Romans, that, being <hi type="italic">hanged upon a tree,</hi> he might be <hi type="italic">made a curse for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Gal. iii. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">his hands and feet</hi> might be <hi type="italic">pierced.</hi> As the Roman power had brought him to be born at Bethlehem, so now to die upon a cross, and both according to the scriptures. It is likewise determined concerning us, though not discovered to us, <hi type="italic">what death we shall die,</hi> which should free us from all disquieting cares about that matter. "Lord, what, and when, and how thou hast appointed." <div eID="gen28518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28519" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Pilate's conference with the prisoner, <reference osisRef="John.18.33">v. 33</reference>, &c., where we have, <div eID="gen28519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28520" type="x-p"/> 1. The prisoner set to the bar. Pilate, after he had conferred with the chief priests at his door, entered into the hall, and called for Jesus to be brought in. He would not examine him in the crowd, where he might be disturbed by the noise, but ordered him to be brought <hi type="italic">into the hall;</hi> for he made no difficulty of going in among the Gentiles. We by sin were become liable to the judgment of God, and were to be brought before his bar; therefore <hi type="italic">Christ, being made sin and a curse for us,</hi> was arraigned as a criminal. Pilate entered into judgment with him, that God might not enter into judgment with us. <div eID="gen28520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28521" type="x-p"/> 2. His examination. The other evangelists tell us that his accusers had laid it to his charge that <hi type="italic">he perverted the nation, forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar,</hi> and upon this he is examined. <div eID="gen28521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28522" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a question put to him, with a design to ensnare him and to find out something upon which to ground an accusation: "<hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho basileus</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that king of the Jews</hi> who has been so much talked of and so long expected—Messiah the prince, art thou he? Dost thou pretend to be he? Dost thou call thyself, and wouldest thou be thought so?" For he was far from imagining that really he was so, or making a question of that. Some think Pilate asked this with an air of scorn and contempt: "What! <hi type="italic">art thou a king,</hi> who makest so mean a figure? <hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews,</hi> by whom thou art thus hated and persecuted? <hi type="italic">Art thou king de jure—of right,</hi> while the emperor is only king <hi type="italic">de facto—in fact?</hi>" Since it could not be proved he ever said it, he would constrain him to say it now, that he might proceed upon his own confession. <div eID="gen28522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28523" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ answers this question with another; not for evasion, but as an intimation to Pilate to consider what he did, and upon what grounds he went (<reference osisRef="John.18.34">v. 34</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Sayest thou this thing of thyself,</hi> from a suspicion arising in thy own breast, <hi type="italic">or did others tell it thee of me,</hi> and dost thou ask it only to oblige them?" [1.] "It is plain that thou hast no reason to <hi type="italic">say this of thyself.</hi>" Pilate was bound by his office to take care of the interests of the Roman government, but he could not say that this was in any danger, or suffered any damage, from any thing our Lord Jesus had ever said or done. He never appeared in worldly pomp, never assumed any secular power, never acted as a judge or divider; never were any traitorous principles or practices objected to him, nor any thing that might give the least shadow of suspicion. [2.] "If others <hi type="italic">tell it thee of me,</hi> to incense thee against me, thou oughtest to consider who they are, and upon what principles they go, and whether those who represent me as an <hi type="italic">enemy to Cæsar</hi> are not really such themselves, and therefore use this only as a pretence to cover their malice, for, if so, the matter ought to be well weighed by a judge that would do justice." Nay, if Pilate had been as inquisitive as he ought to have been in this matter, he would have found that the true reason why the chief priests were outrageous against Jesus was because he did not set up a temporal kingdom in opposition to the Roman power; if he would have done this, and would have wrought miracles to bring the Jews out of the Roman bondage, as Moses did to bring them out of the Egyptian, they would have been so far from siding with the Romans against him that they would have made him their king, and have fought under him against the Romans; but, not answering this expectation of theirs, they charged that upon him of which they were themselves most notoriously guilty-disaffection to and design against the present government; and was such an information as this fit to be countenanced? <div eID="gen28523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28524" type="x-p"/> (3.) Pilate resents Christ's answer, and takes it very ill, <reference osisRef="John.18.35">v. 35</reference>. This is a direct answer to Christ's question, <reference osisRef="John.18.34">v. 34</reference>. [1.] Christ had asked him whether he spoke of himself. "No," says he; "<hi type="italic">am I a Jew,</hi> that thou suspectest me to be in the plot against thee? I know nothing of the Messiah, nor desire to know, and therefore interest not myself in the dispute who is the Messiah and who not; the dispute who is the Messiah and who not; it is all alike to me." Observe with what disdain Pilate asks, <hi type="italic">Am I a Jew?</hi> The Jews were, upon many accounts, an honourable people; but, having corrupted the covenant of their God, <hi type="italic">he made them contemptible and base before all the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.8-Mal.2.9">Mal. ii. 8, 9</reference>), so that a man of sense and honour reckoned it a scandal to be counted a Jew. Thus good names often suffer for the sake of the bad men that wear them. It is sad that when a Turk is suspected of dishonesty he should ask, "What! do you take me for a Christian?" [2.] Christ had asked him whether others told him. "Yes," says he, "and those <hi type="italic">thine own people,</hi> who, one would think would be biased in favour of thee, and <hi type="italic">the priests,</hi> whose testimony, <hi type="italic">in verbum sacerdotis—on the word of a priest,</hi> ought to be regarded; and therefore I have nothing to do but to proceed upon their information." Thus Christ, in his religion, still suffers by those that are of his own nation, even the priests, that profess relation to him, but do not live up to their profession. [3.] Christ had declined answering that question, <hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> And therefore Pilate puts another question to him more general, "<hi type="italic">What hast thou done?</hi> What provocation hast thou given to thy own nation, and particularly the priests, to be so violent against thee? Surely there cannot be all this smoke without some fire, what is it?" <div eID="gen28524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28525" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ, in his next reply, gives a more full and direct answer to Pilate's former question, <hi type="italic">Art thou a king?</hi> explaining in what sense he was a king, but not such a king as was any ways dangerous to the Roman government, not a secular king, for his interest was not supported by secular methods, <reference osisRef="John.18.36">v. 36</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28526" type="x-p"/> [1.] An account of the nature and constitution of Christ's kingdom: It <hi type="italic">is not of this world.</hi> It is expressed negatively to rectify the present mistakes concerning it; but the positive is implied, it is <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven,</hi> and belongs to another world. Christ is a king, and has a kingdom, but <hi type="italic">not of this world. First</hi> Its rise is not from this world; the kingdoms of men arise <hi type="italic">out of the sea and the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.3">Dan. vii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1 Rev.13.11">Rev. xiii. 1, 11</reference>); but <hi type="italic">the holy city comes from God out of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>. His kingdom is not by succession, election, or conquest, but by the immediate and special designation of the divine will and counsel. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Its nature is not worldly; it is a kingdom within men (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.21">Luke xvi. 21</reference>), set up in their hearts and consciences (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Rom. xiv. 17</reference>), its riches spiritual, its powers spiritual, and <hi type="italic">all its glory within.</hi> The ministers of state in Christ's kingdom have not <hi type="italic">the spirit of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1 Cor. ii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Its guards and supports are not worldly; its weapons are spiritual. It neither needed nor used secular force to maintain and advance it, nor was it carried on in a way <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings or provinces;</hi> it did not in the least interfere with the prerogatives of princes nor the property of their subjects; it tended not to alter any national establishment in secular things, nor opposed any kingdom but that of sin and Satan. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Its tendency and design are not worldly. Christ neither aimed nor would allow his disciples to aim at the pomp and power of <hi type="italic">the great men of the earth. Fifthly,</hi> Its subjects, though they are in the world, yet <hi type="italic">are not of the world;</hi> they <hi type="italic">are called and chosen out of the world,</hi> are born from, and bound for, another world; they are neither the world's pupils nor its darlings, neither governed by its wisdom nor enriched with its wealth. <div eID="gen28526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28527" type="x-p"/> [2.] An evidence of the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom produced. If he had designed an opposition to the government, he would have fought them at their own weapons, and would have repelled force with force of the same nature; but he did not take this course: <hi type="italic">If my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews,</hi> and my kingdom be ruined by them. But, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His followers did not offer to fight; there was no uproar, no attempt to rescue him, though the town was now full of Galileans, his friends and countrymen, and they were generally armed; but the peaceable behaviour of his disciples on this occasion was enough <hi type="italic">to put to silence the ignorance of foolish men. Secondly,</hi> He did not order them to fight; nay, he forbade them, which was an evidence both that he did not depend upon worldly aids (for he could have summoned <hi type="italic">legions of angels</hi> into his service, which showed that his <hi type="italic">kingdom was from above</hi>), and also that he did not dread worldly opposition, for he was very willing to be <hi type="italic">delivered to the Jews,</hi> as knowing that what would have been the destruction of any worldly kingdom would be the advancement and establishment of his; justly therefore does he conclude, <hi type="italic">Now</hi> you may see <hi type="italic">my kingdom is not from hence;</hi> in the world but not of it. <div eID="gen28527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> (5.) In answer to Pilate's further query, he replies yet more directly, <reference osisRef="John.18.37">v. 37</reference>, where we have, [1.] Pilate's plain question: "<hi type="italic">Art thou a king then?</hi> Thou speakest of a kingdom thou hast; art thou then, in any sense, a king? And what colour hast thou for such a claim? Explain thyself." [2.] The good confession which our Lord Jesus witnessed before Pontius Pilate, in answer to this (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1 Tim. vi. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou sayest that I am a king,</hi> that is, It is as thou sayest, I am a king; for <hi type="italic">I came to bear witness of the truth. First,</hi> He grants himself to be a king, though not in the sense that Pilate meant. The Messiah was expected under the character of a king, <hi type="italic">Messiah the prince;</hi> and therefore, having owned to Caiaphas that he was the Christ, he would not disown to Pilate that he was king, lest he should seem inconsistent with himself. Note, Though Christ <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant,</hi> yet even then he justly claimed the honour and authority of a king. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He explains himself, and shows how he is a king, as <hi type="italic">he came to bear witness of the truth;</hi> he rules in the minds of men by the power of truth. If he had meant to declare himself a temporal prince, he would have said, <hi type="italic">For this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world,</hi> to rule the nations, to conquer kings, and to take possession of kingdoms; no, <hi type="italic">he came to be a witness,</hi> a witness for the God that made the world, and against sin that ruins the world, and by this <hi type="italic">word of his testimony</hi> he sets up, and keeps up, his kingdom. It was foretold that he should be <hi type="italic">a witness to the people,</hi> and, as such, <hi type="italic">a leader and commander to the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa. lv. 4</reference>. Christ's kingdom was not of this world, in which <hi type="italic">truth faileth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.15">Isa. lix. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare—He that cannot dissemble knows not how to reign</hi>), but of that world in which truth reigns eternally. Christ's errand into the world, and his business in the world, were <hi type="italic">to bear witness to the truth.</hi> 1. To reveal it, to discover to the world that which otherwise could not have been known concerning God and his will and <hi type="italic">good-will to men,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.26">xvii. 26</reference>. 2. To confirm it, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.8">Rom. xv. 8</reference>. By his miracles <hi type="italic">he bore witness to the truth</hi> of religion, the truth of divine revelation, and of God's perfections and providence, and the truth of his promise and covenant, <hi type="italic">that all men through him might believe.</hi> Now by doing this he is a king, and sets up a kingdom. (1.) The foundation and power, the spirit and genius, of Christ's kingdom, is truth, divine truth. When he said, <hi type="italic">I am the truth,</hi> he said, in effect, I am a king. He conquers by the convincing evidence of truth; he rules by the commanding power of truth, and <hi type="italic">in his majesty rides prosperously, because of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">Ps. xlv. 4</reference>. It is with his truth that he shall judge the people, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.13">Ps. xcvi. 13</reference>. It is the sceptre of his kingdom; he <hi type="italic">draws with the cords of a man,</hi> with truth revealed to us, and received by us in <hi type="italic">the love of it;</hi> and thus he <hi type="italic">brings thoughts into obedience.</hi> He came <hi type="italic">a light into the world,</hi> and rules as the sun by day. (2.) The subjects of this kingdom are those that are <hi type="italic">of the truth.</hi> All that by the grace of God are rescued from under the power of <hi type="italic">the father of lies,</hi> and are disposed to receive the truth and submit to the power and influence of it, will hear Christ's voice, will become his subjects, and will bear faith and true allegiance to him. Every one that has any real sense of true religion will entertain the Christian religion, and they belong to his kingdom; by the power of truth he makes them willing, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.3">Ps. xc. 3</reference>. All that are in love with truth will hear the voice of Christ, for greater, better, surer, sweeter truths can nowhere be found than are found in Christ, by whom <hi type="italic">grace and truth came;</hi> so that, by <hi type="italic">hearing Christ's voice,</hi> we know that we are <hi type="italic">of the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.19">1 John iii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen28528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> (6.) Pilate, hereupon, puts a good question to him, but does not stay for an answer, <reference osisRef="John.18.38">v. 38</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">What is truth?</hi> and <hi type="italic">immediately went out again.</hi> <div eID="gen28529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is certain that this was a good question, and could not be put to one that was better able to answer it. Truth is that <hi type="italic">pearl of great price</hi> which the human understanding has a desire for and is in quest of; for it cannot rest but in that which is, or at least is apprehended to be, truth. When we <hi type="italic">search the scriptures,</hi> and attend the ministry of the word, it must be with this enquiry, <hi type="italic">What is truth?</hi> and with this prayer, <hi type="italic">Lead me in thy truth, into all truth.</hi> But many put this question that have not patience and constancy enough to persevere in their search after truth, or not humility and sincerity enough to receive it when they have found it, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.7">2 Tim. iii. 7</reference>. Thus many deal with their own consciences; they ask them those needful questions, "What am I?" "What have I done?" but will not take time for an answer. <div eID="gen28530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is uncertain with what design Pilate asked this question. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Perhaps he spoke it as a learner, as one that began to think well of Christ, and to look upon him with some respect, and desired to be informed what new notions he advanced and what improvements he pretended to in religion and learning. But while he desired to hear some new truth from him, as Herod to see some miracle, the clamour and outrage of the priests' mob at his gate obliged him abruptly to let fall the discourse. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Some think he spoke it as a judge, enquiring further into the cause now brought before him: "Let me into this mystery, and tell me what the truth of it is, the true state of this matter." <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Others think he spoke it as a scoffer, in a jeering way: "Thou talkest of truth; canst thou tell what truth is, or give me a definition of it?" Thus he makes a jest of the everlasting gospel, that great truth which the chief priests hated and persecuted, and which Christ was now witnessing to and suffering for; and like men of no religion, who take a pleasure in bantering all religions, he ridicules both sides; and therefore Christ made him no reply. <hi type="italic">Answer not a fool according to his folly; cast not pearls before swine.</hi> But, though Christ would not tell Pilate what is truth, he has told his disciples, and by them has told us, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">ch. xiv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> III. The result of both these conferences with the prosecutors and the prisoner (<reference osisRef="John.18.38-John.18.40">v. 38-40</reference>), in two things:— <div eID="gen28532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> 1. The judge appeared his friend, and favourable to him, for, <div eID="gen28533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> (1.) He publicly declared him innocent, <reference osisRef="John.18.38">v. 38</reference>. Upon the whole matter, <hi type="italic">I find in him no fault at all.</hi> He supposes there might be some controversy in religion between him and them, wherein he was as likely to be in the right as they; but nothing criminal appears against him. This solemn declaration of Christ's innocency was, [1.] For the justification and honour of the Lord Jesus. By this it appears that though he was treated as the worst of malefactors he had never merited such treatment. [2.] For explaining the design and intention of his death, that he did not die for any sin of his own, even in the judgement of the judge himself, and therefore he died as a sacrifice for our sins, and that, even in the judgment of the prosecutors themselves, <hi type="italic">one man should die for the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.11.50">ch. xi. 50</reference>. This is he that <hi type="italic">did no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa. liii. 9</reference>), who was to <hi type="italic">be cut off, but not for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>. [3.] For aggravating the sin of the Jews that prosecuted him with so much violence. If a prisoner has had a fair trial, and has been acquitted by those that are proper judges of the crime, especially if there be no cause to suspect them partial in his favour, he must be believed innocent, and his accusers are bound to acquiesce. But our Lord Jesus, though brought in not guilty, is still run down as a malefactor, and his blood thirsted for. <div eID="gen28534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> (2.) He proposed an expedient for his discharge (<reference osisRef="John.18.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have a custom, that I should release to you a prisoner at the passover;</hi> shall it be this king of the Jews? He proposed this, not to the chief priests (he knew they would never agree to it), but to the multitude; it was an appeal to the people, as appears, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.15">Matt. xxvii. 15</reference>. Probably he had heard how this Jesus had been attended but the other day with the hosannas of the common people; he therefore looked upon him to be the darling of the multitude, and the envy only of the rulers, and therefore he made no doubt but they would demand the release of Jesus, and this would stop the mouth of the prosecutors, and all would be well. [1.] He allows their custom, for which, perhaps, they had had a long prescription, in honour of the passover, which was a memorial of their release. But it was adding to God's words, as if he had not instituted enough for the due commemoration of that deliverance, and, though an act of mercy, might be injustice to the public, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">Prov. xvii. 15</reference>. [2.] He offers to release Jesus to them, according to the custom. If Pilate had had the honesty and courage that became a judge, he would not have named an innocent person to be competitor with a notorious criminal for this favour; if he <hi type="italic">found no fault in him,</hi> he was bound in conscience to discharge him. But he was willing to trim the matter, and please all sides, being governed more by worldly wisdom than by the rules of equity. <div eID="gen28535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28536" type="x-p"/> 2. The people appeared his enemies, and implacable against him (<reference osisRef="John.18.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">They cried all again</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Not this man,</hi> let not him be released, <hi type="italic">but Barabbas.</hi> Observe, (1.) How fierce and outrageous they were. Pilate proposed the thing to them calmly, as worthy their mature consideration, but they resolved it in a heat, and gave in their resolution with clamour and noise, and in the utmost confusion. Note, The enemies of Christ's holy religion cry it down, and so hope to run it down; witness the outcry at Ephesus, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">Acts xix. 34</reference>. But those who think the worse of things or persons merely for their being thus exclaimed against have a very small share of constancy and consideration. Nay, there is cause to suspect a deficiency of reason and justice on that side which calls in the assistance of popular tumult. (2.) How foolish and absurd they were, as is intimated in the short account here given of the other candidate: <hi type="italic">Now Barabbas was a robber,</hi> and therefore, [1.] A breaker of the law of God; and yet he shall be spared, rather than one who reproved the pride, avarice, and tyranny of the priests and elders. Though Barabbas be a robber, he will not rob them of Moses's seat, nor of their traditions, and then no matter. [2.] He was an enemy to the public safety and personal property. The clamour of the town is wont to be against robbers (<reference osisRef="Job.30.5">Job xxx. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Men cried after them as after a thief</hi>), yet here it is for one. Thus those do who prefer their sins before Christ. Sin is a robber, every base lust is a robber, and yet foolishly chosen rather than Christ, who would truly enrich us.  <chapter eID="John.18"/> <div eID="gen28536" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen28539" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28538" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Arraigned before Pilate.</title> <div sID="gen28540" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Pilate therefore took Jesus, and scourged <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> And the soldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on his head, and they put on him a purple robe, 3 And said, Hail, King of the Jews! and they smote him with their hands. <hi type="super">4</hi> Pilate therefore went forth again, and saith unto them, Behold, I bring him forth to you, that ye may know that I find no fault in him. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And <hi type="italic">Pilate</hi> saith unto them, Behold the man! <hi type="super">6</hi> When the chief priests therefore and officers saw him, they cried out, saying, Crucify <hi type="italic">him,</hi> crucify <hi type="italic">him.</hi> Pilate saith unto them, Take ye him, and crucify <hi type="italic">him:</hi> for I find no fault in him. <hi type="super">7</hi> The Jews answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God. <hi type="super">8</hi> When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he was the more afraid; <hi type="super">9</hi> And went again into the judgment hall, and saith unto Jesus, Whence art thou? But Jesus gave him no answer. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee? <hi type="super">11</hi> Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power <hi type="italic">at all</hi> against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin. <hi type="super">12</hi> And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Cæsar's friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Cæsar. <hi type="super">13</hi> When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha. <hi type="super">14</hi> And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King! <hi type="super">15</hi> But they cried out, Away with <hi type="italic">him,</hi> away with <hi type="italic">him,</hi> crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Cæsar. <div eID="gen28540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28541" type="x-p"/> Here is a further account of the unfair trial which they gave to our Lord Jesus. The prosecutors carrying it on with great confusion among the people, and the judge with great confusion in his own breast, between both the narrative is such as is not easily reduced to method; we must therefore take the parts of it as they lie. <div eID="gen28541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28542" type="x-p"/> I. The judge abuses the prisoner, though he declares him innocent, and hopes therewith to pacify the prosecutors; wherein his intention, if indeed it was good, will by no means justify his proceedings, which were palpably unjust. <div eID="gen28542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28543" type="x-p"/> 1. He ordered him to be whipped as a criminal, <reference osisRef="John.19.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Pilate,</hi> seeing the people so outrageous, and being disappointed in his project of releasing him upon the people's choice, <hi type="italic">took Jesus, and scourged him,</hi> that is, appointed the lictors that attended him to do it. Bede is of opinion that Pilate scourged Jesus himself with his own hands, because it is said, <hi type="italic">He took him and scourged him,</hi> that it might be done favourably. Matthew and Mark mention his scourging after his condemnation, but here it appears to have been before. Luke speaks of Pilate's offering to <hi type="italic">chastise him, and let him go,</hi> which must be before sentence. This scourging of him was designed only to pacify the Jews, and in it Pilate put a compliment upon them, that he would take their word against his own sentiments so far. The Roman scourgings were ordinarily very severe, not limited, as among the Jews, to <hi type="italic">forty stripes;</hi> yet this pain and shame Christ submitted to for our sakes. (1.) <hi type="italic">That the scripture might be fulfilled,</hi> which spoke of his being <hi type="italic">stricken, smitten, and afflicted,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the chastisement of our peace</hi> being <hi type="italic">upon him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">Isa. liii. 5</reference>), of his giving his back to the smiters (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>), of the ploughers ploughing upon his back, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Ps. cxxix. 3</reference>. He himself likewise had foretold it, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.19">Matt. xx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.34">Mark x. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.33">Luke xviii. 33</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">That by his stripes we might be healed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4">1 Pet. ii. 4</reference>. We deserved to have been chastised <hi type="italic">with whips and scorpions,</hi> and <hi type="italic">beaten with many stripes,</hi> having known our Lord's will and not done it; but Christ underwent the stripes for us, bearing the rod of his Father's wrath, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">Lam. iii. 1</reference>. Pilate's design in scourging him was that he might not be condemned, which did not take effect, but intimated what was God's design, that his being scourged might prevent our being condemned, we having fellowship in his sufferings, and this did take effect: the physician scourged, and so the patient healed. (3.) That stripes, for his sake, might be sanctified and made easy to his followers; and they might, as they did, rejoice in that shame (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Acts v. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.22-Acts.16.25">xvi. 22, 25</reference>), as Paul did, who was <hi type="italic">in stripes above measure,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2 Cor. xi. 23</reference>. Christ's stripes take out the sting of theirs, and alter the property of them. <hi type="italic">We are chastened of the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1 Cor. xi. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen28543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28544" type="x-p"/> 2. He turned him over to his soldiers, to be ridiculed and made sport with as a fool (<reference osisRef="John.19.2-John.19.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The soldiers,</hi> who were the governor's life-guard, <hi type="italic">put a crown of thorns upon his head;</hi> such a crown they thought fittest for such a king; <hi type="italic">they put on him a purple robe,</hi> some old threadbare coat of that colour, which they thought good enough to be the badge of his royalty; and they complimented him with, <hi type="italic">Hail, king of the Jews</hi> (like people like king), and then <hi type="italic">smote him with their hands.</hi> <div eID="gen28544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28545" type="x-p"/> (1.) See here the baseness and injustice of Pilate, that he would suffer one whom he believed an innocent person, and if so an excellent person, to be thus abused and trampled on by his own servants. Those who are under the arrest of the law ought to be under the protection of it; and their being secured is to be their security. But Pilate did this, [1.] To oblige his soldiers' merry humour, and perhaps his own too, notwithstanding the gravity one might have expected in a judge. <hi type="italic">Herod,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">his men of war,</hi> had just before done the same, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.11">Luke xxiii. 11</reference>. It was as good as a stage-play to them, now that it was a festival time; as the Philistines made sport with Samson. [2.] To oblige the Jews' malicious humour, and to gratify them, who desired that all possible disgrace might be done to Christ, and the utmost indignities put upon him. <div eID="gen28545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28546" type="x-p"/> (2.) See here the rudeness and insolence of the soldiers, how perfectly lost they were to all justice and humanity, who could thus triumph over a man in misery, and one that had been in reputation for wisdom and honour, and never did any thing to forfeit it. But thus hath Christ's holy religion been basely misrepresented, dressed up by bad men at their pleasure, and so exposed to contempt and ridicule, as Christ was here. [1.] They clothe him with a mock-robe, as if it were a sham and a jest, and nothing but the product of a heated fancy and a crazed imagination.
