And as Christ is here represented as a king in conceit only, so is his religion as a concern in conceit only, and God and the soul, sin and duty, heaven and hell, are with many all chimeras. [2.] They crown him with thorns; as if the religion of Christ were a perfect penance, and the greatest pain and hardship in the world; as if to submit to the control of God and conscience were to thrust one's head into a thicket of thorns; but this is an unjust imputation; <hi type="italic">thorns and snares are in the way of the froward,</hi> but roses and laurels in religion's ways. <div eID="gen28546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28547" type="x-p"/> (3.) See here the wonderful condescension of our Lord Jesus in his sufferings for us. Great and generous minds can bear any thing better than ignominy, any toil, any pain, any loss, rather than reproach; yet this the great and holy Jesus submitted to for us. See and admire, [1.] The invincible patience of a sufferer, leaving us an example of contentment and courage, evenness, and easiness of spirit, under the greatest hardships we may meet with in the way of duty. [2.] The invincible love and kindness of a Saviour, who not only cheerfully and resolutely went through all this, but voluntarily undertook it for us and for our salvation. Herein he commended his love, that he would not only die for us, but die as a fool dies. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He <hi type="italic">endured the pain;</hi> not the pangs of death only, though in the death of the cross these were most exquisite; but, as if these were too little, he submitted to those previous pains. Shall we complain of a thorn in the flesh, and of being buffeted by affliction, because we need it to hide pride from us, when Christ humbled himself to bear those thorns in the head, and those buffetings, to save and teach us? <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2 Cor. xii. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He <hi type="italic">despised the shame,</hi> the shame of a fool's coat, and the mock-respect paid him, with, <hi type="italic">Hail, king of the Jews.</hi> If we be at any time ridiculed for well-doing, let us not be ashamed, but glorify God, for thus we are partakers of Christ's sufferings. He that bore these sham honours was recompensed with real honours, and so shall we, if we patiently suffer shame for him. <div eID="gen28547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28548" type="x-p"/> II. Pilate, having thus abused the prisoner, presents him to the prosecutors, in hope that they would now be satisfied, and drop the prosecution, <reference osisRef="John.19.4-John.19.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Here he proposes two things to their consideration:— <div eID="gen28548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28549" type="x-p"/> 1. That he had not found any thing in him which made him obnoxious to the Roman government (<reference osisRef="John.19.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I find no fault in him;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oudemian aitian heurisko</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I do not find in him the least fault,</hi> or <hi type="italic">cause of accusation.</hi> Upon further enquiry, he repeats the declaration he had made, <reference osisRef="John.18.38">ch. xviii. 38</reference>. Hereby he condemns himself; if he found no fault in him, why did he scourge him, why did he suffer him to be abused? None ought to suffer ill but those that do ill; yet thus many banter and abuse religion, who yet, if they be serious, cannot but own they find no fault in it. If he found no fault in him, why did he bring him out to his prosecutors, and not immediately release him, as he ought to have done? If Pilate had consulted his own conscience only, he would neither have scourged Christ nor crucified him; but, thinking to trim the matter, to please the people by scourging Christ, and save his conscience by not crucifying him, behold he does both; whereas, if he had at first resolved to crucify him, he need not have scourged him. It is common for those who think to keep themselves from greater sins by venturing upon less sins to run into both. <div eID="gen28549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28550" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had done that to him which would make him the less dangerous to them and to their government, <reference osisRef="John.19.5">v. 5</reference>. He brought him out to them, wearing the crown of thorns, his head and face all bloody, and said, "<hi type="italic">Behold the man</hi> whom you are so jealous of," intimating that though his having been so popular might have given them some cause to fear that his interest in the country would lessen theirs, yet he had taken an effectual course to prevent it, by treating him as a slave, and exposing him to contempt, after which he supposed the people would never look upon him with any respect, nor could he ever retrieve his reputation again. Little did Pilate think with what veneration even these sufferings of Christ would in after ages be commemorated by the best and greatest of men, who would glory in that cross and those stripes which he thought would have been to him and his followers a perpetual and indelible reproach. (1.) Observe here our Lord Jesus shows himself dressed up in all the marks of ignominy. He came forth, willing to be made a spectacle, and to be hooted at, as no doubt he was when he came forth in this garb, knowing that he was set for a <hi type="italic">sign that should be spoken against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Luke ii. 34</reference>. Did he go forth thus bearing our reproach? Let us go forth to him <hi type="italic">bearing his reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">Heb. xiii. 13</reference>. (2.) How Pilate shows him: <hi type="italic">Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man. He saith unto them:</hi> so the original is; and, the immediate antecedent being <hi type="italic">Jesus,</hi> I see no inconvenience in supposing these to be Christ's own words; he said, "<hi type="italic">Behold the man</hi> against whom you are so exasperated." But some of the Greek copies, and the generality of the translators, supply it as we do, Pilate saith unto them, with a design to appease them, <hi type="italic">Behold the man;</hi> not so much to move their pity, Behold a man worthy your compassion, as to silence their jealousies, Behold a man not worthy your suspicion, a man from whom you can henceforth fear no danger; his crown is <hi type="italic">profaned, and cast to the ground,</hi> and now all mankind will make a jest of him. The word however is very affecting: <hi type="italic">Behold the man.</hi> It is good for every one of us, with an eye of faith, to behold the man Christ Jesus in his sufferings. <hi type="italic">Behold this king with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him,</hi> the crown of thorns, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">Cant. iii. 11</reference>. "Behold him, and be suitably affected with the sight. Behold him, and mourn because of him. Behold him, and love him; be still <hi type="italic">looking unto Jesus.</hi>" <div eID="gen28550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28551" type="x-p"/> III. The prosecutors, instead of being pacified, were but the more exasperated, <reference osisRef="John.19.6-John.19.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen28551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28552" type="x-p"/> 1. Observe here their clamour and outrage. <hi type="italic">The chief priests,</hi> who headed the mob, <hi type="italic">cried out</hi> with fury and indignation, and their officers, or servants, who must say as they said, joined with them in crying, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi> The common people perhaps would have acquiesced in Pilate's declaration of his innocency, but their leaders, the priests, <hi type="italic">caused them to err.</hi> Now by this it appears that their malice against Christ was, (1.) Unreasonable and most absurd, in that they offer not to make good their charges against him, nor to object against the judgment of Pilate concerning him; but, though he be innocent, he must be crucified. (2.) It was insatiable and very cruel. Neither the extremity of his scourging, nor his patience under it, nor the tender expostulations of the judge, could mollify them in the least; no, nor could the jest into which Pilate had turned the cause, put them into a pleasant humour. (3.) It was violent and exceedingly resolute; they will have it their own way, and hazard the governor's favour, the peace of the city, and their own safety, rather than abate of the utmost of their demands. Were they so violent in running down our Lord Jesus, and in crying, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him?</hi> and shall not we be vigorous and zealous in advancing his name, and in crying, <hi type="italic">Crown him, Crown him?</hi> Did their hatred of him sharpen their endeavours against him? and shall not our love to him quicken our endeavours for him and his kingdom? <div eID="gen28552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28553" type="x-p"/> 2. The check Pilate gave to their fury, still insisting upon the prisoner's innocency: "<hi type="italic">Take you him and crucify him,</hi> if he must be crucified." This is spoken ironically; he knew they could not, they durst not, crucify him; but it is as if he should say, "You shall not make me a drudge to your malice; I cannot with a safe conscience crucify him." A good resolve, if he would but have stuck to it. He found no fault in him, and therefore should not have continued to parley with the prosecutors. Those that would be safe from sin should be deaf to temptation. Nay, he should have secured the prisoner from their insults. What was he armed with power for, but to protect the injured? The guards of governors ought to be the guards of justice. But Pilate had not courage enough to act according to his conscience; and his cowardice betrayed him into a snare. <div eID="gen28553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28554" type="x-p"/> 3. The further colour which the prosecutors gave to their demand (<reference osisRef="John.19.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have a law, and by our law,</hi> if it were but in our power to execute it, <hi type="italic">he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.</hi> Now here observe, (1.) They <hi type="italic">made their boast of the law,</hi> even when <hi type="italic">through breaking the law they dishonoured God,</hi> as is charged upon the Jews, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.23">Rom. ii. 23</reference>. They had indeed an excellent law, far exceeding the statutes and judgments of other nations; but in vain did they boast of their law, when they abused it to such bad purposes. (2.) They discover a restless and inveterate malice against our Lord Jesus. When they could not incense Pilate against him by alleging that he pretended himself a king, they urged this, that he pretended himself a God. Thus they turn every stone to take him off. (3.) They pervert the law, and make that the instrument of their malice. Some think they refer to a law made particularly against Christ, as if, being a law, it must be executed, right or wrong; whereas there is a woe to them that <hi type="italic">decree unrighteous decrees,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">write the grievousness which they have prescribed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1">Isa. x. 1</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mic.6.16">Mic. vi. 16</reference>. But it should seem they rather refer to the law of Moses; and if so, [1.] It was true that blasphemers, idolaters, and false prophets, were to be put to death by that law. Whoever falsely pretended to be the Son of God was guilty of blasphemy, <reference osisRef="Lev.24.16">Lev. xxiv. 16</reference>. But then, [2.] It was false that Christ pretended to be the Son of God, for he really was so; and they ought to have enquired into the proofs he produced of his being so. If he said that he was the Son of God, and the scope and tendency of his doctrine were not to draw people from God, but to bring them to him, and if he confirmed his mission and doctrine by miracles, as undoubtedly he did, beyond contradiction, by their law they ought to <hi type="italic">hearken to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.18-Deut.18.19">Deut. xviii. 18, 19</reference>), and, if they did not, they were to be <hi type="italic">cut off.</hi> That which was his honour, and might have been their happiness, if they had not stood in their own light, they impute to him as a crime, for which he ought not to be crucified, for this was no death inflicted by their law. <div eID="gen28554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28555" type="x-p"/> IV. The judge brings the prisoner again to his trial, upon this new suggestion. Observe, <div eID="gen28555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28556" type="x-p"/> 1. The concern Pilate was in, when he heard this alleged (<reference osisRef="John.19.8">v. 8</reference>): When he heard that his prisoner pretended not to royalty only, but to deity, he was <hi type="italic">the more afraid.</hi> This embarrassed him more than ever, and made the case more difficult both ways; for, (1.) There was the more danger of offending the people if he should acquit him, for he knew how jealous that people were for the unity of the Godhead, and what aversion they now had to other gods; and therefore, though he might hope to pacify their rage against a pretended king, he could never reconcile them to a pretended God. "If this be at the bottom of the tumult," thinks Pilate, "it will not be turned off with a jest." (2.) There was the more danger of offending his own conscience if he should condemn him. "Is he one" (thinks Pilate) "that makes himself <hi type="italic">the Son of God?</hi> and what if it should prove that he is so? What will become of me then?" Even natural conscience makes men afraid of being found <hi type="italic">fighting against God.</hi> The heathen had some fabulous traditions of incarnate deities appearing sometimes in mean circumstances, and treated ill by some that paid dearly for their so doing. Pilate fears lest he should thus run himself into a premunire. <div eID="gen28556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28557" type="x-p"/> 2. His further examination of our Lord Jesus thereupon, <reference osisRef="John.19.9">v. 9</reference>. That he might give the prosecutors all the fair play they could desire, he resumed the debate, went into the judgment-hall, and asked Christ, <hi type="italic">Whence art thou?</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28558" type="x-p"/> (1.) The place he chose for this examination: He <hi type="italic">went into the judgment-hall</hi> for privacy, that he might be out of the noise and clamour of the crowd, and might examine the thing the more closely. Those that would find out the truth as it is in Jesus must get out of the noise of prejudice, and retire as it were into the judgment-hall, to converse with Christ alone. <div eID="gen28558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28559" type="x-p"/> (2.) The question he put to him: <hi type="italic">Whence art thou?</hi> Art thou from men or from heaven? From beneath or from above? He had before asked directly, <hi type="italic">Art thou a King?</hi> But here he does not directly ask, <hi type="italic">Art thou the Son of God?</hi> lest he should seem to meddle with divine things too boldly. But in general, "<hi type="italic">Whence art thou?</hi> Where wast thou, and in what world hadst thou a being, before thy coming into this world?" <div eID="gen28559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28560" type="x-p"/> (3.) The silence of our Lord Jesus when he was examined upon this head; but <hi type="italic">Jesus gave him no answer.</hi> This was not a sullen silence, in contempt of the court, nor was it because he knew not what to say; but, [1.] It was a patient silence, that the scripture might be fulfilled, <hi type="italic">as a sheep before the shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa. liii. 7</reference>. This silence loudly bespoke his submission to his Father's will in his present sufferings, which he thus accommodated himself to, and composed himself to bear. He was silent, because he would say nothing to hinder his sufferings. If Christ had avowed himself a God as plainly as he avowed himself a king, it is probable that Pilate would not have condemned him (for he was afraid at the mention of it by the prosecutors); and the Romans, though they triumphed over the <hi type="italic">kings of the nations</hi> they conquered, yet stood in awe of their gods. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">If they had known</hi> him to be the <hi type="italic">Lord of glory,</hi> they would <hi type="italic">not have crucified him;</hi> and how then could we have been saved? [2.] It was a prudent silence. When the chief priests asked him, <hi type="italic">Art thou the Son of the Blessed?</hi> he answered, <hi type="italic">I am,</hi> for he knew they went upon the scriptures of the Old Testament which spoke of the Messiah; but when Pilate asked him he knew he did not understand his own question, having no notion of the Messiah, and of his being the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> and therefore to what purpose should he reply to him whose head was filled with the pagan theology, to which he would have turned his answer? <div eID="gen28560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28561" type="x-p"/> (4.) The haughty check which Pilate gave him for his silence (<reference osisRef="John.19.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Speakest thou not unto me?</hi> Dost thou put such an affront upon me as to stand mute? What <hi type="italic">knowest thou not</hi> that, as president of the province, <hi type="italic">I have power,</hi> if I think fit, <hi type="italic">to crucify thee, and have power,</hi> if I think fit, to <hi type="italic">release thee?</hi>" Observe here, [1.] How Pilate magnified himself, and boasts of his own authority, as not inferior to that of Nebuchadnezzar, of whom it is said that <hi type="italic">whom he would he slew, and whom he would he kept alive.</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">Dan. v. 19</reference>. Men in power are apt to be puffed up with their power, and the more absolute and arbitrary it is the more it gratifies and humours their pride. But he magnifies his power to an exorbitant degree when he boasts that he has power to crucify one whom he had declared innocent, for no prince or potentate has authority to do wrong. <hi type="italic">Id possumus, quod jure possumus—We can do that only which we can do justly.</hi> [2.] How he tramples upon our blessed Saviour: <hi type="italic">Speakest thou not unto me?</hi> He reflects upon him, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As if he were undutiful and disrespectful to those in authority, not speaking when he was spoken to. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As if he were ungrateful to one that had been tender of him: "Speakest thou not to me who have laboured to secure thy release?" <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> As if he were unwise for himself: "Wilt thou not speak to clear thyself to one that is willing to clear thee?" If Christ had indeed sought to save his life, now had been his time to have spoken; but that which he had to do was to lay down his life. <div eID="gen28561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28562" type="x-p"/> (5.) Christ's pertinent answer to this check, <reference osisRef="John.19.11">v. 11</reference>, where, <div eID="gen28562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28563" type="x-p"/> [1.] He boldly rebukes his arrogance, and rectifies his mistake: "Big as thou lookest and talkest, <hi type="italic">thou couldest have no power at all against me,</hi> no power to scourge, no power to crucify, <hi type="italic">except it were given thee from above.</hi>" Though Christ did not think fit to answer him when he was impertinent (then <hi type="italic">answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like him</hi>), yet he did think fit to answer him when he was imperious; then <hi type="italic">answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.4-Prov.26.5">Prov. xxvi. 4, 5</reference>. When Pilate used his power, Christ silently submitted to it; but, when he grew proud of it, he made him know himself: "All the power thou hast is given thee from above," which may be taken two ways:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> As reminding him that his power in general, as a magistrate, was a limited power, and he could do no more than God would suffer him to do. God is the fountain of power; and the <hi type="italic">powers that are,</hi> as they are ordained by him and derived from him, so they are subject to him. They ought to go no further than his law directs them; they can go no further than his providence permits them. They are God's hand and his sword, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 13, 14</reference>. Though the axe may <hi type="italic">boast itself against him that heweth therewith,</hi> yet still it is but a tool, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa. x. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">15</reference>. Let the proud oppressors know that there is <hi type="italic">a higher than they,</hi> to whom they are accountable, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>. And let this silence the murmurings of the oppressed, <hi type="italic">It is the Lord.</hi> God has bidden Shimei curse David; and let it comfort them that their persecutors can do no more than God will let them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As informing him that his power against him in particular, and all the efforts of that power, were <hi type="italic">by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. Pilate never fancied himself to look so great as now, when he sat in judgment upon such a prisoner as this, who was looked upon by many as the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> and king of Israel, and had the fate of so great a man at his disposal; but Christ lets him know that he was herein but an instrument in God's hand, and could no nothing against him, but by the appointment of Heaven, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.27-Acts.4.28">Acts iv. 27, 28</reference>. <div eID="gen28563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28564" type="x-p"/> [2.] He mildly excuses and extenuates his sin, in comparison with the sin of the ringleaders: "<hi type="italic">Therefore he that delivered me unto thee</hi> lies under greater guilt; for thou as a magistrate hast <hi type="italic">power from above,</hi> and art in thy place, thy sin is less than theirs who, from envy and malice, urge thee to abuse thy power." <div eID="gen28564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28565" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is plainly intimated that what Pilate did was sin, a great sin, and that the force which the Jews put upon him, and which he put upon himself in it, would not justify him. Christ hereby intended a hint for the awakening of his conscience and the increase of the fear he was now under. The guilt of others will not acquit us, nor will it avail in the great day to say that others were worse than we, for we are not to be judged by comparison, but must <hi type="italic">bear our own burden.</hi> <div eID="gen28565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28566" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Yet theirs that delivered him to Pilate was the greater sin. By this it appears that all sins are not equal, but some more heinous than others; some comparatively as gnats, others as camels; some as motes in the eyes, others as beams; some as pence, others as pounds. <hi type="italic">He that delivered Christ to Pilate</hi> was either, 1. The people of the Jews, who cried out, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi> They had seen Christ's miracles, which Pilate had not; to them the Messiah was first sent; they were his own; and to them, who were now enslaved, a Redeemer should have been most welcome, and therefore it was much worse in them to appear against him than in Pilate. 2. Or rather he means Caiaphas in particular, who was at the head of the conspiracy against Christ, and first advised his death, <reference osisRef="John.11.49-John.11.50">ch. xi. 49, 50</reference>. The sin of Caiaphas was abundantly greater than the sin of Pilate. Caiaphas prosecuted Christ from pure enmity to him and his doctrine, deliberately and of malice prepense. Pilate condemned him purely for fear of the people, and it was a hasty resolution which he had not time to cool upon. 3. Some think Christ means Judas; for, though he did not immediately deliver him into the hands of Pilate, yet he betrayed him to those that did. The sin of Judas was, upon many accounts, greater than the sin of Pilate. Pilate was a stranger to Christ; Judas was his friend and follower. Pilate found no fault in him, but Judas knew a great deal of good of him. Pilate, though biassed, was not bribed, but Judas took a <hi type="italic">reward against the innocent;</hi> the sin of Judas was a leading sin, and let in all that followed. He was a <hi type="italic">guide to them that took Jesus.</hi> So great was the sin of Judas that <hi type="italic">vengeance suffered him not to live;</hi> but when Christ said this, or soon after, he was gone <hi type="italic">to his own place.</hi> <div eID="gen28566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28567" type="x-p"/> V. Pilate struggles with the Jews to deliver Jesus out of their hands, but in vain. We hear no more after this of any thing that passed between Pilate and the prisoner; what remains lay between him and the prosecutors. <div eID="gen28567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28568" type="x-p"/> 1. Pilate seems more zealous than before to get Jesus discharged (<reference osisRef="John.19.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thenceforth,</hi> from this time, and for this reason, because Christ had given him that answer (<reference osisRef="John.19.11">v. 11</reference>), which, though it had a rebuke in it, yet he took kindly; and, though Christ found fault with him, he still continued to find no fault in Christ, but <hi type="italic">sought to release him,</hi> desired it, endeavoured it. <hi type="italic">He sought to release him;</hi> he contrived how to do it handsomely and safely, and so as not to disoblige the priests. It never does well when our resolutions to do our duty are swallowed up in projects how to do it plausibly and conveniently. If Pilate's policy had not prevailed above his justice, he would not have been long seeking to release him, but would have done it. <hi type="italic">Fiat justitia, ruat c&#339;lum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let justice be done, though heaven itself should fall.</hi> <div eID="gen28568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28569" type="x-p"/> 2. The Jews were more furious than ever, and more violent to get Jesus crucified. Still they carry on their design with noise and clamour as before; so now they cried out. They would have it thought that the commonalty was against him, and therefore laboured to get him cried down by a multitude, and it is no hard matter to pack a mob; whereas, if a fair poll had been granted, I doubt not but it would have been carried by a great majority for the releasing of him. A few madmen may out-shout many wise men, and then fancy themselves to speak the sense (when it is but the nonsense) of a nation, or of all mankind; but it is not so easy a thing to change the sense of the people as it is to misrepresent it, and to change their cry. Now that Christ was in the hands of his enemies his friends were shy and silent, and disappeared, and those that were against him were forward to show themselves so; and this gave the chief priests an opportunity to represent it as the concurring vote of all the Jews that he should be crucified. In this outcry they sought two things:—(1.) To blacken the prisoner as an enemy to Cæsar. He had refused the kingdoms of this world and the glory of them, had declared his kingdom not to be of this world, and yet they will have it that he <hi type="italic">speaks against Cæsar;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antilegei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he opposes Cæsar,</hi> invades his dignity and sovereignty. It has always been the artifice of the enemies of religion to represent it as hurtful to kings and provinces, when it would be highly beneficial to both. (2.) To frighten the judge, as no friend to Cæsar: "If thou <hi type="italic">let this man go</hi> unpunished, and let him go on, <hi type="italic">thou art not Cæsar's friend,</hi> and therefore false to thy trust and the duty of thy place, obnoxious to the emperor's displeasure, and liable to be turned out." They intimate a threatening that they would inform against him, and get him displaced; and here they touched him in a sensible and very tender part. But, of all people, these Jews should not have pretended a concern for Cæsar, who were themselves so ill affected to him and his government. They should not talk of being friends to Cæsar, who were themselves such back friends to him; yet thus a pretended zeal for that which is good often serves to cover a real malice against that which is better. <div eID="gen28569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28570" type="x-p"/> 3. When other expedients had been tried in vain, Pilate slightly endeavoured to banter them out of their fury, and yet, in doing this, betrayed himself to them, and yielded to the rapid stream, <reference osisRef="John.19.13-John.19.15">v. 13-15</reference>. After he had stood it out a great while, and seemed now as if he would have made a vigorous resistance upon this attack (<reference osisRef="John.19.12">v. 12</reference>), he basely surrendered. Observe here, <div eID="gen28570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28571" type="x-p"/> (1.) What it was that shocked Pilate (<reference osisRef="John.19.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he heard that saying,</hi> that he could not be true to Cæsar's honour, nor sure of Cæsar's favour, if he did not put Jesus to death, then he thought it was time to look about him. All they had said to prove Christ a malefactor, and that therefore it was Pilate's duty to condemn him, did not move him, but he still kept to his conviction of Christ's innocency; but, when they urged that it was his interest to condemn him, then he began to yield. Note, Those that bind up their happiness in the favour of men make themselves an easy prey to the temptations of Satan. <div eID="gen28571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28572" type="x-p"/> (2.) What preparation was made for a definitive sentence upon this matter: <hi type="italic">Pilate brought Jesus forth,</hi> and he himself in great state took the chair. We may suppose that he called for his robes, that he might look big, and then <hi type="italic">sat down in the judgment-seat.</hi> <div eID="gen28572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28573" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ was condemned with all the ceremony that could be. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To bring us off at God's bar, and that all believers through Christ, being judged here, might be acquitted in the court of heaven. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To take off the terror of pompous trials, which his followers would be brought to for his sake. Paul might the better stand at Cæsar's judgment-seat when his Master had stood there before him. <div eID="gen28573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28574" type="x-p"/> [2.] Notice is here taken of the place and time. <div eID="gen28574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The place where Christ was condemned: in a <hi type="italic">place called the Pavement, but in Hebrew, Gabbatha,</hi> probably the place where he used to sit to try causes or criminals. Some make <hi type="italic">Gabbatha</hi> to signify an <hi type="italic">enclosed place,</hi> fenced against the insults of the people, whom therefore he did the less need to fear; others an <hi type="italic">elevated place,</hi> raised that all might see him. <div eID="gen28575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The time, <reference osisRef="John.19.14">v. 14</reference>. It was the preparation of the passover, and <hi type="italic">about the sixth hour.</hi> Observe, 1. The day: It was the preparation of the passover, that is, for the passover-sabbath, and the solemnities of that and the rest of the days of the feast of unleavened bread. This is plain from <reference osisRef="Luke.23.54">Luke xxiii. 54</reference>, <hi type="italic">It was the preparation, and the sabbath drew on.</hi> So that this preparation was for the sabbath. Note, Before the passover there ought to be preparation. This is mentioned as an aggravation of their sin, in persecuting Christ with so much malice and fury, that it was when they should have been purging out the old leaven, to get ready for the passover; but the better the day the worse the deed. 2. The hour: <hi type="italic">It was about the sixth hour.</hi> Some ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts read it about the third hour, which agrees with <reference osisRef="Mark.15.25">Mark xv. 25</reference>. And it appears by <reference osisRef="Matt.27.45">Matt. xxvii. 45</reference> that he was upon the cross before the sixth hour. But it should seem to come in here, not as a precise determination of the time, but as an additional aggravation of the sin of his prosecutors, that they were pushing on the prosecution, not only on a solemn day, the <hi type="italic">day of the preparation,</hi> but, from the third to the sixth hour (which was, as we call it, church-time) on that day, they were employed in this wickedness; so that for this day, though they were priests, they dropped the temple-service, for they did not leave Christ till the sixth hour, when the darkness began, which frightened them away. Some think that the sixth hour, with this evangelist, is, according to the Roman reckoning and ours, six of the clock in the morning, answering to the Jews' first hour of the day; this is very probable, that Christ's trial before Pilate was at the height about six in the morning, which was then a little after sun-rising. <div eID="gen28576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28577" type="x-p"/> (3.) The rencounter Pilate had with the Jews, both priests and people, before he proceeded to give judgment, endeavouring in vain to stem the tide of their rage. <div eID="gen28577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28578" type="x-p"/> [1.] He saith unto the Jews, <hi type="italic">Behold your king.</hi> This is a reproof to them for the absurdity and malice of their insinuating that this Jesus made himself a king: "<hi type="italic">Behold your king,</hi> that is, him whom you accuse as a pretender to the crown. Is this a man likely to be dangerous to the government? I am satisfied he is not, and you may be so too, and let him alone." Some think he hereby upbraids them with their secret disaffection to Cæsar: "You would have this man to be your king, if he would but have headed a rebellion against Cæsar." But Pilate, though he was far from meaning so, seems as if he were the voice of God to them. Christ, now crowned with thorns, is, as a king at his coronation, offered to the people: "<hi type="italic">Behold your king,</hi> the king whom God hath set upon his holy hill of Zion;" but they, instead of entering into it with acclamations of joyful consent, protest against him; they will not have a king of God's choosing. <div eID="gen28578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28579" type="x-p"/> [2.] They cried out with the greatest indignation, <hi type="italic">Away with him, away with him,</hi> which speaks disdain as well as malice, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aron, aron</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">Take him,</hi> he is none of ours; we disown him for our kinsman, much more for our king; we have not only no veneration for him, but no compassion; <hi type="italic">away with him</hi> out of our sight:" for so it was written of him, he is one <hi type="italic">whom the nation abhors</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Isa. xlix. 7</reference>), and they <hi type="italic">hid as it were their faces from him</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2-Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 2, 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Away with him from the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.22.22">Acts xxii. 22</reference>. This shows, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How we deserved to have been treated at God's tribunal. We were by sin become odious to God's holiness, which cried, <hi type="italic">Away with them, away with them,</hi> for God is <hi type="italic">of purer eyes than to behold iniquity.</hi> We were also become obnoxious to God's justice, which cried against us, "<hi type="italic">Crucify them, crucify them,</hi> let the sentence of the law be executed." Had not Christ interposed, and been thus rejected of men, we had been for ever rejected of God. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It shows how we ought to treat our sins. We are often in scripture said to crucify sin, in conformity to Christ's death. Now they that crucified Christ did it with detestation. With a pious indignation we should run down sin in us, as they with an impious indignation ran him down who was made sin for us. The true penitent casts away from him his transgressions, <hi type="italic">Away with them, away with them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa. ii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">xxx. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">crucify them, crucify them;</hi> it is not fit that they should live in my soul, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">Hos. xiv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen28579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28580" type="x-p"/> [3.] Pilate, willing to have Jesus released, and yet that it should be their doing, asks them, <hi type="italic">Shall I crucify your king?</hi> In saying this, he designed either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To stop their mouths, by showing them how absurd it was for them to reject one who offered himself to them to be their king at a time when they needed one more than ever. Have they no sense of slavery? No desire of liberty? No value for a deliverer? Though he saw no cause to fear him, they might see cause to hope for something from him; since crushed and sinking interests are ready to catch at any thing. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To stop the mouth of his own conscience. "If this Jesus be a king" (thinks Pilate), "he is only kin of the Jews, and therefore I have nothing to do but to make a fair tender of him to them; if they refuse him, and will have their king crucified, what is that to me?" He banters them for their folly in expecting a Messiah, and yet running down one that bade so fair to be he.

<div eID="gen28580" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Condemned; The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen28581" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Then delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus, and led <hi type="italic">him</hi> away. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he bearing his cross went forth into a place called <hi type="italic">the place</hi> of a skull, which is called in the Hebrew Golgotha: 18 Where they crucified him, and two other with him, on either side one, and Jesus in the midst. <div eID="gen28581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28582" type="x-p"/> We have here sentence of death passed upon our Lord Jesus, and execution done soon after. A mighty struggle Pilate had had within him between his convictions and his corruptions; but at length his convictions yielded, and his corruptions prevailed, the fear of man having a greater power over him than the fear of God. <div eID="gen28582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28583" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">Pilate gave judgment</hi> against Christ, and signed the warrant for his execution, <reference osisRef="John.19.16">v. 16</reference>. We may see here, 1. How Pilate sinned against his conscience: he had again and again pronounced him innocent, and yet at last condemned him as guilty. Pilate, since he came to be governor, had in many instances disobliged and exasperated the Jewish nation; for he was a man of a haughty and implacable spirit, and extremely wedded to his humour. He had seized upon the Corban, and spent it upon a water-work; he had brought into Jerusalem shields stamped with Cæsar's image, which was very provoking to the Jews; he had sacrificed the lives of many to his resolutions herein. Fearing therefore that he should be complained of for these and other insolences, he was willing to gratify the Jews. Now this makes the matter much worse. If he had been of an easy, soft, and pliable disposition, his yielding to so strong a stream had been the more excusable; but for a man that was so wilful in other things, and of so fierce a resolution, to be overcome in a thing of this nature, shows him to be a bad man indeed, that could better bear the wronging of his conscience than the crossing of his humour. 2. How he endeavoured to transfer the guilt upon the Jews. He <hi type="italic">delivered him</hi> not to his own officers (as usual), but to the prosecutors, the chief priests and elders; so excusing the wrong to his own conscience with this, that it was but a permissive condemnation, and that he did not put Christ to death, but only connived at those that did it. 3. How Christ was <hi type="italic">made sin for us.</hi> We deserved to have been condemned, but Christ was condemned for us, that to us there might be <hi type="italic">no condemnation.</hi> God was now entering into judgment with his Son, that he might not enter into judgment with his servants. <div eID="gen28583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28584" type="x-p"/> II. Judgment was no sooner given than with all possible expedition the prosecutors, having gained their point, resolved to lose not time lest Pilate should change his mind, and order a reprieve (those are enemies to our souls, the worst of enemies, that hurry us to sin, and then leave us no room to undo what we have done amiss), and also lest there should be <hi type="italic">an uproar among the people,</hi> and they should find a greater number against them than they had with so much artifice got to be for them. It were well if we would be thus expeditious in that which is good, and not stay for more difficulties. <div eID="gen28584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28585" type="x-p"/> 1. They immediately hurried away the prisoner. The chief priests greedily flew upon the prey which they had been long waiting for; now it is drawn into their net. Or <hi type="italic">they,</hi> that is, the soldiers who were to attend the execution, they took him and led him away, not to the place whence he came, and thence to the place of execution, as is usual with us, but directly to the place of execution. Both the priests and the soldiers joined in leading him away. Now was the <hi type="italic">Son of man delivered into the hands of men,</hi> wicked and unreasonable men. By the law of Moses (and in appeals by our law) the prosecutors were to be the executioners, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.7">Deut. xvii. 7</reference>. And the priests here were proud of the office. His being <hi type="italic">led away</hi> does not suppose him to have made any opposition, but <hi type="italic">the scripture must be fulfilled,</hi> he was <hi type="italic">led as a sheep to the slaughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.32">Acts viii. 32</reference>. We deserved to have been <hi type="italic">led forth with the workers of iniquity</hi> as criminals to execution, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">Ps. cxxv. 5</reference>. But he was led forth for us, that we might escape. <div eID="gen28585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28586" type="x-p"/> 2. To add to his misery, they obliged him as long as he was able, to carry his cross (<reference osisRef="John.19.17">v. 17</reference>), according to the custom among the Romans; hence <hi type="italic">Furcifer</hi> was among them a name of reproach. Their crosses did not stand up constantly, as our gibbets do in the places of execution, because the malefactor was nailed to the cross as it lay along upon the ground, and then it was lifted up, and fastened in the earth, and removed when the execution was over, and commonly buried with the body; so that every one that was crucified had a cross of his own. Now Christ's carrying his cross may be considered, (1.) As a part of his sufferings; he endured the cross literally. It was a long and thick piece of timber that was necessary for such a use, and some think it was neither seasoned nor hewn. The blessed body of the Lord Jesus was tender, and unaccustomed to such burdens; it had now lately been harassed and tired out; his shoulders were sore with the stripes they had given him; every jog of the cross would renew his smart, and be apt to strike the thorns he was crowned with into his head; yet all this he patiently underwent, and it was but the <hi type="italic">beginning of sorrows.</hi> (2.) As answering the type which went before him; Isaac, when he was to be offered, carried the wood on which he was to be bound and with which he was to be burned. (3.) As very significant of his undertaking, the Father having <hi type="italic">laid upon him the iniquity of us all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">Isa. liii. 6</reference>), and he having to <hi type="italic">take away sin</hi> by <hi type="italic">bearing it in his own body upon the tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1 Pet. ii. 24</reference>. He had said in effect, <hi type="italic">On me be the curse;</hi> for he was made a curse for us, and therefore on him was the cross. (4.) As very instructive to us. Our Master hereby taught all his disciples to take up their cross, and follow him. Whatever cross he calls us out to bear at any time, we must remember that he bore the cross first, and, by bearing it for us, bears it off from us in great measure, for thus he hath made <hi type="italic">his yoke easy, and his burden light.</hi> He bore that end of the cross that had the curse upon it; this was the heavy end; and hence all that are his are enabled to call their afflictions for him <hi type="italic">light,</hi> and <hi type="italic">but for a moment.</hi> <div eID="gen28586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28587" type="x-p"/> 3. They brought him to the place of execution: He <hi type="italic">went forth,</hi> not dragged against his will, but voluntary in his sufferings. He went forth out of the city, for he was <hi type="italic">crucified without the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">Heb. xiii. 12</reference>. And, to put the greater infamy upon his sufferings, he was brought to the common place of execution, as one in all points <hi type="italic">numbered among the transgressors,</hi> a place called <hi type="italic">Golgotha, the place of a skull,</hi> where they threw dead men's skulls and bones, or where the heads of beheaded malefactors were left,—a place <hi type="italic">ceremonially unclean;</hi> there Christ suffered, because he was <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">purge our consciences from dead works,</hi> and the pollution of them. If one would take notice of the traditions of the elders, there are two which are mentioned by many of the ancient writers concerning this place:—(1.) That Adam was buried here, and that this was the place of his skull, and they observe that where death triumphed over the first Adam there the second Adam triumphed over him. Gerhard quotes for this tradition Origen, Cyprian, Epiphanius, Austin, Jerome, and others. (2.) That this was that mountain in the land of Moriah on which Abraham offered up Isaac, and the ram was a ransom for Isaac. <div eID="gen28587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28588" type="x-p"/> 4. There they crucified him, and the other malefactors with him (<reference osisRef="John.19.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">There they crucified him.</hi> Observe (1.) What death Christ died; the death of the cross, a bloody, painful, shameful death, a cursed death. He was nailed to the cross, as a sacrifice bound to the altar, as a Saviour fixed for his undertaking; his ear nailed to God's door-post, to serve him for ever. He was lifted up as the brazen serpent, hung between heaven and earth because we were unworthy of either, and abandoned by both. His hands were stretched out to invite and embrace us; he hung upon the tree some hours, dying gradually in the full use of reason and speech, that he might actually resign himself a sacrifice. (2.) In what company he died: <hi type="italic">Two others with him.</hi> Probably these would not have been executed at that time, but at the request of the chief priests, to add to the disgrace of our Lord Jesus, which might be the reason why one of them reviled him, because their death was hastened for his sake. Had they taken two of his disciples, and crucified them with him, it had been an honour to him; but, if such as they had been partakers with him in suffering, it would have looked as if they had been undertakers with him in satisfaction. Therefore it was ordered that his fellow-sufferers should be the worst of sinners, that he might <hi type="italic">bear our reproach,</hi> and that the merit might appear to be his only. This exposed him much to the people's contempt and hatred, who are apt to judge of persons by the lump, and are not curious in distinguishing, and would conclude him not only malefactor because he was yoked with malefactors, but the worst of the three because put in the midst. But thus the scripture was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">He was numbered among the transgressors.</hi> He did not die at the altar among the sacrifices, nor mingle his blood with that of bulls and goats; but he died among the criminals, and mingled his blood with theirs who were sacrificed to public justice. <div eID="gen28588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28589" type="x-p"/> And now let us pause awhile, and with an eye of faith look upon Jesus. Was ever sorrow like unto his sorrow? See him who was clothed with glory stripped of it all, and clothed with shame-him who was the <hi type="italic">praise of angels</hi> made a <hi type="italic">reproach of men</hi>—him who had been with eternal delight and joy in the bosom of his Father now in the extremities of pain and agony. See him bleeding, see him struggling, see him dying, see him and love him, love him and live to him, and study what we shall render.

<div eID="gen28589" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Inscription on the Cross; The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen28590" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And Pilate wrote a title, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS. <hi type="super">20</hi> This title then read many of the Jews: for the place where Jesus was crucified was nigh to the city: and it was written in Hebrew, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Greek, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Latin. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then said the chief priests of the Jews to Pilate, Write not, The King of the Jews; but that he said, I am King of the Jews. <hi type="super">22</hi> Pilate answered, What I have written I have written. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also <hi type="italic">his</hi> coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. <hi type="super">24</hi> They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be: that the scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did. <hi type="super">25</hi> Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the <hi type="italic">wife</hi> of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. <hi type="super">26</hi> When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son! <hi type="super">27</hi> Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own <hi type="italic">home.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst. <hi type="super">29</hi> Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a sponge with vinegar, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon hyssop, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> to his mouth. <hi type="super">30</hi> When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost. <div eID="gen28590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28591" type="x-p"/> Here are some remarkable circumstances of Christ's dying more fully related than before, which those will take special notice of who covet to know Christ and him crucified. <div eID="gen28591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28592" type="x-p"/> I. The title set up over his head. Observe, <div eID="gen28592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28593" type="x-p"/> 1. The inscription itself which Pilate wrote, and ordered to be fixed to the top of the cross, declaring the cause for which he was crucified, <reference osisRef="John.19.19">v. 19</reference>. Matthew called it, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aitia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the accusation;</hi> Mark and Luke called it <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epigraphe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the inscription;</hi> John calls it by the proper Latin name, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">titlos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the title:</hi> and it was this, <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,</hi> Pilate intended this for his reproach, that he, being <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> should pretend to be king of the Jews, and set up in competition with Cæsar, to whom Pilate would thus recommend himself, as very jealous for his honour and interest, when he would treat but a titular king, a king in metaphor, as the worst of malefactors; but God overruled this matter, (1.) That it might be a further testimony to the innocency of our Lord Jesus; for here was an accusation which, as it was worded, contained no crime. If this be all they have to lay to his charge, surely he has done nothing worthy of death or of bonds. (2.) That it might show forth his dignity and honour. This is Jesus a Saviour, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Nazoraios</hi></hi>, the blessed Nazarite, sanctified to God; this is the <hi type="italic">king of the Jews, Messiah the prince,</hi> the <hi type="italic">sceptre</hi> that <hi type="italic">should rise out of Israel,</hi> as Balaam had foretold; dying for the good of his people, as Caiaphas had foretold. Thus all these three bad men witnessed to Christ, though they meant not so. <div eID="gen28593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28594" type="x-p"/> 2. The notice taken of this inscription (<reference osisRef="John.19.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many of the Jews read it,</hi> not only those of Jerusalem, but those out of the country, and from other countries, strangers and proselytes, that came up to worship at the feast. Multitudes read it, and it occasioned a great variety of reflections and speculations, as men stood affected. Christ himself was set for a sign, a title. Here are two reasons why the title was so much read:—(1.) Because the place where Jesus was crucified, though without the gate, was yet <hi type="italic">nigh the city,</hi> which intimates that if it had been any great distance off they would not have been led, no not by their curiosity, to go and see it, and read it. It is an advantage to have the means of knowing Christ brought to our doors. (2.) Because it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin, which made it legible by all; they all understood one or other of these languages, and none were more careful to bring up their children to read than the Jews generally were. It likewise made it the more considerable; everyone would be curious to enquire what it was which was so industriously published in the three most known languages. In the Hebrew the oracles of God were recorded; in Greek the learning of the philosophers; and in Latin the laws of the empire. In each of these Christ is proclaimed king, in whom are hid all the treasures of revelation, wisdom, and power. God so ordering it that this should be written in the three then most known tongues, it was intimated thereby that Jesus Christ should be a Saviour to all nations, and not to the Jews only; and also that every nation should hear <hi type="italic">in their own tongue the wonderful works</hi> of the Redeemer. Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, were the vulgar languages at that time in this part of the world; so that this is so far from intimating (as the Papists would have it) that the scripture is still to be retained in these three languages, that on the contrary it teaches us that the knowledge of Christ ought to be diffused throughout every nation in their own tongue, as the proper vehicle of it, that people may converse as freely with the scriptures as they do with their neighbours. <div eID="gen28594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28595" type="x-p"/> 3. The offence which the prosecutors took at it, <reference osisRef="John.19.21">v. 21</reference>. They would not have it written, <hi type="italic">the king of the Jews;</hi> but that he said of himself, <hi type="italic">I am the king of the Jews.</hi> Here they show themselves, (1.) Very spiteful and malicious against Christ. It was not enough to have him crucified, but they must have his name crucified too. To justify themselves in giving him such bad treatment, they thought themselves concerned to give him a bad character, and to represent him as a usurper of honours and powers that he was not entitled to. (2.) Foolishly jealous of the honour of their nation. Though they were a conquered and enslaved people, yet they stood so much upon the punctilio of their reputation that they scorned to have it said that this was their king. (3.) Very impertinent and troublesome to Pilate. They could not but be sensible that they had forced him, against his mind, to condemn Christ, and yet, in such a trivial thing as this, they continue to tease him; and it was so much the worse in that, though they had charged him with pretending to be the king of the Jews, yet they had not proved it, nor had he ever said so. <div eID="gen28595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28596" type="x-p"/> 4. The judge's resolution to adhere to it: "<hi type="italic">What I have written I have written,</hi> and will not alter it to humour them." <div eID="gen28596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28597" type="x-p"/> (1.) Hereby an affront was put upon the chief priests, who would still be dictating. It seems, by Pilate's manner of speaking, that he was uneasy in himself for yielding to them, and vexed at them for forcing him to it, and therefore he was resolved to be cross with them; and by this inscription he insinuates, [1.] That, notwithstanding their pretences, they were not sincere in their affections to Cæsar and his government; they were willing enough to have a king of the Jews, if they could have one to their mind. [2.] That such a king as this, so mean and despicable, was good enough to be the king of the Jews; and this would be the fate of all that should dare to oppose the Roman power. [3.] That they had been very unjust and unreasonable in prosecuting this Jesus, when there was no fault to be found in him. <div eID="gen28597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28598" type="x-p"/> (2.) Hereby honour was done to the Lord Jesus. Pilate stuck to it with resolution, that he was the king of the Jews. What he had written was what God had first written, and therefore he could not alter it; for thus it was written, that Messiah the prince should be <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>. This therefore is the true cause of his death; he dies because the king of Israel must die, must thus die. When the Jews reject Christ, and will not have him for their king, Pilate, a Gentile, sticks to it that he is a king, which was an earnest of what came to pass soon after, when the Gentiles submitted to the kingdom of the Messiah, which the unbelieving Jews had rebelled against. <div eID="gen28598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28599" type="x-p"/> II. The dividing of his garments among the executioners, <reference osisRef="John.19.23-John.19.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. Four soldiers were employed, who, <hi type="italic">when they had crucified Jesus,</hi> had nailed him to the cross, and lifted it up, and him upon it, and nothing more was to be done than to wait his expiring through the extremity of pain, as, with us, when the prisoner is turned off, then they went to make a dividend of his clothes, each claiming an equal share, and so they <hi type="italic">made four parts,</hi> as nearly of the same value as they could, <hi type="italic">to every soldier a part;</hi> but <hi type="italic">his coat,</hi> or upper garment whether cloak or gown, being a pretty piece of curiosity, <hi type="italic">without seam, woven from the top throughout,</hi> they agreed to <hi type="italic">cast lots for it.</hi> Here observe, 1. The shame they put upon our Lord Jesus, in stripping him of his garments before they crucified him. The shame of nakedness came in with sin. He therefore who was made sin for us bore that shame, to roll away our reproach. He was stripped, that we might be clothed with <hi type="italic">white raiment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>), and that when we are unclothed <hi type="italic">we may not be found naked.</hi> 2. The wages with which these soldiers paid themselves for crucifying Christ. They were willing to do it for his old clothes. Nothing is to be done so bad, but there will be found men bad enough to do it for a trifle. Probably they hoped to make more than ordinary advantage of his clothes, having heard of cures wrought by the touch of the hem of his garment, or expecting that his admirers would give any money for them. 3. The sport they made about his seamless coat. We read not of any thing about him valuable or remarkable but this, and this not for the richness, but only the variety of it, for it was <hi type="italic">woven from the top throughout;</hi> there was no curiosity therefore in the shape, but a designed plainness. Tradition says, his mother wove it for him, and adds this further, that it was made for him when he was a child, and, like the Israelites' clothes in the wilderness, <hi type="italic">waxed not old;</hi> but this is a groundless fancy. The soldiers thought it a pity to rend it, for then it would unravel, and a piece of it would be good for nothing; they would <hi type="italic">therefore cast lots for it.</hi> While Christ was in his dying agonies, they were merrily dividing his spoils. The preserving of Christ's seamless coat is commonly alluded to to show the care all Christians ought to take that they rend not the church of Christ with strifes and divisions; yet some have observed that the reason why the soldiers would not rend Christ's coat was not out of any respect to Christ, but because each of them hoped to have it entire for himself. And so many cry out against schism, only that they may engross all the wealth and power to themselves. Those who opposed Luther's separation from the church of Rome urged much the <hi type="italic">tunica inconsutilis—the seamless coat;</hi> and some of them laid so much stress upon it that they were called the <hi type="italic">Inconsutilistæ—The seamless.</hi> 4. The fulfilling of the scripture in this. David, in spirit, foretold this very circumstance of Christ's sufferings, in that passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">Ps. xxii. 18</reference>. The event so exactly answering the prediction proves, (1.) That <hi type="italic">the scripture</hi> is the word of God, which foretold contingent events concerning Christ so long before, and they came to pass according to the prediction. (2.) That Jesus is the true Messiah; for in him all the Old-Testament prophecies concerning the Messiah had, and have, their full accomplishment. <hi type="italic">These things therefore the soldiers did.</hi> <div eID="gen28599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28600" type="x-p"/> III. The care that he took of his poor mother. <div eID="gen28600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28601" type="x-p"/> 1. His mother attends him to his death (<reference osisRef="John.19.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">There stood by the cross,</hi> as near as they could get, <hi type="italic">his mother,</hi> and some of his relations and friends with her. At first, they stood near, as it is said here; but afterwards, it is probable, the soldiers forced them to stand afar off, as it is said in Matthew and Mark: or they themselves removed out of the ground. (1.) See here the tender affection of these pious women to our Lord Jesus in his sufferings. When all his disciples, except John, has forsaken him, they continued their attendance on him. Thus <hi type="italic">the feeble were as David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.8">Zech. xii. 8</reference>): they were not deterred by the fury of the enemy nor the horror of the sight; they could not rescue him nor relieve him, yet they attended him, to show their good-will. It is an impious and blasphemous construction which some of the popish writers put upon the virgin Mary standing by the cross, that thereby she contributed to the satisfaction he made for sin no less than he did, and so became a joint-mediatrix and co-adjutrix in our salvation. (2.) We may easily suppose what an affliction it was to these poor women to see him thus abused, especially to the blessed virgin. Now was fulfilled Simeon's word, <hi type="italic">A sword shall pierce through thy own soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Luke ii. 35</reference>. His torments were her tortures; she was upon the rack, while he was upon the cross; and her heart bled with his wounds; and <hi type="italic">the reproaches wherewith they reproached</hi> him fell on those that attended him. (3.) We may justly admire the power of divine grace in supporting these women, especially the virgin Mary, under this heavy trial. We do not find his mother wringing her hands, or tearing her hair, or rending her clothes, or making an outcry; but, with a wonderful composure, <hi type="italic">standing by the cross,</hi> and her friends with her. Surely she and they were strengthened by a divine power to this degree of patience; and surely the virgin Mary had a fuller expectation of his resurrection than the rest had, which supported her thus. We know not what we can bear till we are tried, and then we know who has said, <hi type="italic">My grace is sufficient for thee.</hi> <div eID="gen28601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28602" type="x-p"/> 2. He tenderly provides for his mother at his death. It is probable that Joseph, her husband, was long since dead, and that her son Jesus had supported her, and her relation to him had been her maintenance; and now that he was dying what would become of her? He saw her standing by, and knew her cares and griefs; and he saw John standing not far off, and so he settled a new relation between his beloved mother and his beloved disciple; for he said to her, "<hi type="italic">Woman, behold thy son,</hi> for whom henceforward thou must have a motherly affection;" and to him, "<hi type="italic">Behold thy mother,</hi> to whom thou must pay a filial duty." And so <hi type="italic">from that hour,</hi> that hour never to be forgotten, <hi type="italic">that disciple took her to his own home.</hi> See here, <div eID="gen28602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28603" type="x-p"/> (1.) The care Christ took of his dear mother. He was not so much taken up with a sense of his sufferings as to forget his friends, all whose concerns he bore upon his heart. His mother, perhaps, was so taken up with his sufferings that she thought not of what would become of her; but he admitted that thought. <hi type="italic">Silver and gold he had none</hi> to leave, no estate, real or personal; his clothes the soldiers had seized, and we hear no more of the bag since Judas, who had carried it, hanged himself. He had therefore no other way to provide for his mother than by his interest in a friend, which he does here. [1.] He calls her <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> not mother, not out of any disrespect to her, but because mother would have been a cutting word to her that was already wounded to the heart with grief; like Isaac saying to Abraham, <hi type="italic">My father.</hi> He speaks as one that was <hi type="italic">now no more in this world,</hi> but was already dead to those in it that were dearest to him. His speaking in this seemingly slight manner to his mother, as he had done formerly, was designed to obviate and give a check to the undue honours which he foresaw would be given to her in the Romish church, as if she were a joint purchaser with him in the honours of the Redeemer. [2.] He directs her to look upon John as her son: "Behold him as thy son, who stands there by thee, and be as a mother to him." See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> An instance of divine goodness, to be observed for our encouragement. Sometimes, when God removes one comfort from us, he raises up another for us, perhaps where we looked not for it. We read of children which the church shall have after she has lost the other, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa. xlix. 21</reference>. Let none therefore reckon all gone with one cistern dried up, for from the same fountain another may be filled. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> An instance of filial duty, to be observed for our imitation. Christ has here taught children to provide, to the utmost of their power, for the comfort of their aged parents. When David was in distress, he took care of his parents, and found out a shelter for them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3">1 Sam. xxii. 3</reference>); so the Son of David here. Children at their death, according to their ability, should provide for their parents, if they survive them, and need their kindness. <div eID="gen28603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28604" type="x-p"/> (2.) The confidence he reposed in the beloved disciple. It is to him he says, <hi type="italic">Behold thy mother,</hi> that is, I recommend her to thy care, be thou as a son to her to guide her (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.18">Isa. li. 18</reference>); and <hi type="italic">forsake her not when she is old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.22">Prov. xxiii. 22</reference>. Now, [1.] This was an honour put upon John, and a testimony both to his prudence and to his fidelity. If he who knows all things had not known that John loved him, he would not have made him his mother's guardian. It is a great honour to be employed for Christ, and to be entrusted with any of his interest in the world. But, [2.] It would be a care and some charge to John; but he cheerfully accepted it, <hi type="italic">and took her to his own home,</hi> not objecting the trouble nor expense, nor his obligations to his own family, nor the ill-will he might contract by it. Note, Those that truly love Christ, and are beloved of him, will be glad of an opportunity to do any service to him or his. <hi type="italic">Nicephoras's Eccl. Hist. lib. 2 cap. 3,</hi> saith that the virgin Mary lived with John at Jerusalem eleven years, and then died. Others, that she lived to remove with him to Ephesus. <div eID="gen28604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28605" type="x-p"/> IV. The fulfilling of the scripture, in the giving of him vinegar to drink, <reference osisRef="John.19.28-John.19.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen28605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28606" type="x-p"/> 1. How much respect Christ showed to the scripture (<reference osisRef="John.19.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Knowing that all things</hi> hitherto <hi type="italic">were accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled,</hi> which spoke of his drinking in his sufferings, <hi type="italic">he saith, I thirst,</hi> that is, he called for drink. <div eID="gen28606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28607" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was not at all strange that he was thirsty; we find him <hi type="italic">thirsty</hi> in a journey (<reference osisRef="John.4.6-John.4.7">ch. iv. 6, 7</reference>), and now thirsty when he was just at his journey's end. Well might he thirst after all the toil and hurry which he had undergone, and being now in the agonies of death, ready to expire purely by the loss of blood and extremity of pain. The torments of hell are represented by a violent thirst in the complaint of the rich man that begged for a <hi type="italic">drop of water to cool his tongue.</hi> To that everlasting thirst we had been condemned, had not Christ suffered for us. <div eID="gen28607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28608" type="x-p"/> (2.) But the reason of his complaining of it is somewhat surprising; it is the only word he spoke that looked like complaint of his outward sufferings. When they scourged him, and crowned him with thorns, he did not cry, O my head! or, My back! But now he cried, <hi type="italic">I thirst.</hi> For, [1.] He would thus express <hi type="italic">the travail of his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. He thirsted after the glorifying of God, and the accomplishment of the work of our redemption, and the happy issue of his undertaking. [2.] He would thus take care to see the scripture fulfilled. Hitherto, all had been accomplished, and he knew it, for this was the thing he had carefully observed all along; and now he called to mind one thing more, which this was the proper season for the performance of. By this it appears that he was the Messiah, in that not only the scripture was punctually fulfilled in him, but it was strictly eyed by him. By this it appears <hi type="italic">that God was with him of a truth</hi>—that in all he did he went exactly according to the word of God, taking care <hi type="italic">not to destroy, but to fulfil, the law and the prophets.</hi> Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The scripture had foretold his thirst, and therefore he himself related it, because it could not otherwise be known, saying, <hi type="italic">I thirst;</hi> it was foretold that his tongue should cleave to his jaws, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Ps. xxii. 15</reference>. Samson, an eminent type of Christ, when he was laying <hi type="italic">the Philistines heaps upon heaps,</hi> was himself <hi type="italic">sore athirst</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.15.18">Judg. xv. 18</reference>); so was Christ, when he was upon the cross, <hi type="italic">spoiling principalities and powers. Secondly,</hi> The scripture had foretold that in his thirst he should have vinegar given him to drink, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">Ps. lxix. 21</reference>. They had given him vinegar to drink before they crucified him (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.34">Matt. xxvii. 34</reference>), but the prophecy was not exactly fulfilled in that, because that was not in his thirst; therefore now he said, <hi type="italic">I thirst,</hi> and called for it again: then he would not drink, but now he received it Christ would rather court an affront than see any prophecy unfulfilled. This should satisfy us under all our trials, that the will of God is done, and the word of God accomplished. <div eID="gen28608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28609" type="x-p"/> 2. See how little respect his persecutors showed to him (<reference osisRef="John.19.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was set a vessel full of vinegar,</hi> probably according to the custom at all executions of this nature; or, as others think, it was now set designedly for an abuse to Christ, instead of the cup of wine which they used to give <hi type="italic">to those that were ready to perish;</hi> with this <hi type="italic">they filled a sponge,</hi> for they would not allow him a cup, <hi type="italic">and they put it upon hyssop,</hi> a hyssop-stalk, and with this heaved it to his mouth; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyssopo perithentes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they stuck it round with hyssop;</hi> so it may be taken; or, as others, they mingled it with hyssop-water, and this they gave him to drink when he was thirsty; a drop of water would have cooled his tongue better than a draught of vinegar: yet this he submitted to for us. <hi type="italic">We had taken the sour grapes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">thus his teeth were set on edge;</hi> we had forfeited all comforts and refreshments, and therefore they were withheld from him. When heaven denied him a beam of light earth denied him a drop of water, and put vinegar in the room of it. <div eID="gen28609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28610" type="x-p"/> V. The dying word wherewith he breathed out his soul (<reference osisRef="John.19.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had received the vinegar,</hi> as much of it as he thought fit, <hi type="italic">he said, It is finished;</hi> and, with that, <hi type="italic">bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28611" type="x-p"/> 1. What he said, and we may suppose him to say it with triumph and exultation, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Tetelestai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> a comprehensive word, and a comfortable one. (1.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the malice and enmity of his persecutors had now done their worst; <hi type="italic">when he had received</hi> that last indignity in <hi type="italic">the vinegar they gave him, he said,</hi> "This is the last; I am now going out of their reach, <hi type="italic">where the wicked cease from troubling.</hi>" (2.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the counsel and commandment of his Father concerning his sufferings were now fulfilled; it was a <hi type="italic">determinate counsel,</hi> and he took care to see every iota and tittle of it exactly answered, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. He had said, when he entered upon his sufferings, <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done;</hi> and now he saith with pleasure, <hi type="italic">It is done.</hi> It was <hi type="italic">his meat and drink to finish his work</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.34">ch. iv. 34</reference>), and the meat and drink refreshed him, when they gave him gall and vinegar. (3.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, all the types and prophecies of the Old Testament, which pointed at the sufferings of the Messiah, were accomplished and answered. He speaks as if, now that <hi type="italic">they had given him the vinegar,</hi> he could not bethink himself of any word in the Old Testament that was to be fulfilled between him and his death but it had its accomplishment; such as, his being <hi type="italic">sold for thirty pieces of silver, his hands and feet being pierced, his garments divided, &c.;</hi> and now that this is done. <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> (4.) <hi type="italic">It is finished,</hi> that is, the ceremonial law is abolished, and a period put to the obligation of it. The substance is now come, and all the shadows are done away. Just now <hi type="italic">the veil is rent, the wall of partition is taken down,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the law of commandments contained in ordinances,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 14, 15</reference>.
